What has transpired is a terrible tragedy, and the pain is felt not just by the officer’s family, but by all who have served, and serve, with him.” The death has also drawn condemnation from local and national politicians. Shadow Home Secretary Diane Abbott said: “This is a national tragedy. Our police officers deserve our protection while they are carrying out their duties to protect us.” Yellow ribbons were tied to lamp posts and trees in various parts of the city, where members of the community have begun to lay flowers and memorials in tribute to the fallen officer.

Shadow Brexit Secretary Sir Keir Starmer has called for a “reset” in Labour’s handling of the legacy of the IRA, following renewed debate within the party over past remarks made by senior members. Speaking in an exclusive interview, Starmer described recent comments about the organisation as “ill-judged” and insisted Labour must not make past divisions a political football as it seeks to rebuild trust among all communities across the UK. The call for restraint comes after a damaging episode in which several prominent Labour MPs were accused of downplaying or making reference to the terrorist organisation in a tone seen as insensitive by many. The issue has flared up again with the general election on the horizon, as Starmer’s leadership faces renewed scrutiny over Labour’s approach to Northern Ireland and reconciliation with the past. Starmer, who has long advocated for a left-wing, socially progressive vision, made it clear that the Labour Party must now be “thoughtful and respectful” in its discourse about the Troubles. “We live in a more modern Britain now. Our message must be one of unity, not division,” he said, adding that “anyone who uses the history of the IRA in a divisive way must think very carefully about what they are doing.” The remarks are expected to form part of a broader strategy by Starmer to distance the party from its contentious municipal governance in Liverpool and its association with the left-wing Red Tape – a legacy of statements by some Labour figures, including the Labour leader of Liverpool City Council, Steve Rotheram, who has previously refused to condemn the IRA. “Regrettable” is the word Starmer used when asked to respond to Rotheram’s earlier refusal to distance himself from the organisation’s actions. “His views were in the past and it is obvious now that this line of thought is out of step with Labour values today,” Starmer said. “We should not be judged on what our colleagues said in 2018. We should be judged on our agenda for change, justice and fairness in 2024.” Starmer’s comments will be closely watched by both pro-unionist commentators in Northern Ireland and those within the party who question his commitment to the cause of peace and reconciliation. Recent polling has shown a sharp increase in concern among voters with connections to the Troubles over how the major parties handle the issue, with many delivering a warning not to play with the past for political gain.

A "vicious" fox has sparked a wave of panic in a quiet seaside town in Devon after it herded eight people into a sports club and refused to leave them alone for more than 90 minutes, according to police reports. The incident at Exeter Sports and Social Club occurred in the early hours of Sunday morning when the aggressive animal appeared to stalk a group of revellers as they left the building after an event. Eyewitnesses described a "frenetic" scene as the fox circled the group, barking and snarling, before forcing them to retreat into the club. Once locked inside, the terrified group — including employees and several customers — were trapped with no immediate means of escape. Club manager Martin Griffiths, 41, said they had to call the police after numerous attempts to lure the animal away failed. “It wasn’t like a normal fox, this was a wild, aggressive beast. It wouldn’t back off, and it kept circling, growling,” he said. Officers with a wildlife unit were eventually called to the scene and managed to tranquilise the fox near the back of the sports club, where it had perched on a fence attempting to climb into a nearby garden. A short struggle ensued before the animal was safely netted and transported for assessment. Authorities have not yet released the results of veterinary examination, but staff and local residents are already raising concerns about whether the fox, estimated to weigh around 14kg, might have been injured or suffering from rabies-like symptoms. The panic is the latest in a string of animal-related incidents this year that have rattled the region. In June, a family had to flee their home after what was described as a “ferocious” badger attack their dog. A few weeks earlier, a group of hikers were blocked from returning to a car park in the area after a large fox had blocked the path and aggressively charged at them. Local wildlife charity Westcountry Wildlife Trust is now calling for more action to be taken in urban areas where foxes are increasingly coming into contact with people. A spokesperson told the  Exeter Echo : “This was an unusual and dangerous situation, but it highlights a growing problem. As our built-up areas expand into wildlife habitats, conflicts are inevitable. Foxes are intelligent and adaptable, but when they become agitated or territorial, the results can be alarming.” The owners of the Exeter Sports and Social Club are reviewing their safety protocols and considering installing high fencing to deter wildlife entry, especially during late-night events.

The Trussell Trust, one of the UK’s largest food aid charities, has revealed that a record number of people required emergency food support last year, with more than 1.8 million three-day emergency food parcels given out to people in crisis across the country. The charity described the figures as a "stark warning" of the continued and deepening cost-of-living challenges faced by many British households. The latest report – published on behalf of the trust, which operates over 1,200 food banks nationwide – marks the 10th year of publishing its annual figures, and for the first time in the decade, revealed a year-on-year increase, with parcels handed out to 1.87 million people in 2013/14, compared to 1.6 million the previous year. This represents a 16 per cent rise in the number of people in need of food aid within just one year. In total, the Trussell Trust distributed more than 1.97 million food parcels across the UK, the highest number in its history. Behind those numbers lie stories of people struggling to afford basic essentials: one woman, unable to afford heating or food, turned to a food bank after a week in her home reached only ten degrees Celsius. Another man, a former municipal worker, used a Trussell Trust food parcel after redundancy – despite holding a university degree – due to savings running low while trying to find new employment. The trust said that as well as the record level of parcels, the average number of people visiting food banks in a single month in 2013/14 increased by 136,000 compared to the previous reporting year, bringing the monthly average to 154,000. This suggests about five people are now being referred to a food bank every minute of every day. The findings come as the UK continues to grapple with rising inflation and housing costs, as well as changes to the benefits system that have left many eligible for food aid despite being in employment. The trust has raised concerns about the long-term implications of sustained high levels of food poverty, stressing that reliance on emergency food aid is not a sustainable solution to hardship. It also called upon the government to address the “hunger cause” at the heart of the issue, including the low wages and rising rent costs that push even go-getting families into crisis. “The number of people using food banks is a shocking, but vital, barometer of the scale of hardship being experienced across all UK communities,” said Lynne Featherstone, the trust’s chief executive at the time of the report’s release.

The Ancient Egyptians are often remembered for their intricate and elaborate mummification rituals, practiced for thousands of years as a means of preserving the dead for the afterlife. But while the mummification of human bodies has long captured the public's imagination, a lesser-known aspect of this remarkable tradition is the millions of animals that were also mummified during the same period. From cats and crocodiles to ibises and baboons, animals of all shapes and sizes were subjected to the same elaborate embalming process as their human counterparts. These were not simply pets or food—animal mummification was steeped in religious significance, often connected with the worship of deities to which specific animals were sacred. Records show that as many as 30 million animal mummies were produced across centuries, particularly during the late New Kingdom (1550–1070 BC) and into the Ptolemaic and Roman periods (332 BC–395 AD). These vast numbers include small mammals, birds, and invertebrates such as scorpions and beetles, often wrapped in linen and placed in specially designed sarcophagi or terracotta coffins. Dr. Kasia Sznap, a research associate at the Egypt Exploration Society, explains that many of these mummies were votive offerings. "It was a way for people to communicate with the gods – to present a mummified animal in exchange for divine favour or as part of a temple ritual," she says. "In some cases, large volumes of animal mummies were made specifically to meet the demand of temple worship." Temples dedicated to gods like Thoth, whose animal form was the ibis, were known to have industrial-scale mummification operations, where workers mass-produced mummies in linen-wrapped bundles. These were often sold to pilgrims who could not bring live animals to present at the temple. The ruins of Saqqara, near modern-day Cairo, have revealed huge caches of animal mummies, found in vast shafts and limestone storage pits. Some are beautifully preserved, while others are believed to be rushed or mass-produced, suggesting the sheer scale of the practice. While human mummification evolved to become a highly sacred and exclusive process reserved for the elite, animal mummification was more accessible. It provided the average person with a meaningful way to participate in religious rituals and the spiritual economy of the time. As archaeologists continue to study these animal mummies, new insights into the beliefs, technologies, and everyday lives of the Ancient Egyptians are being uncovered. The mummy bundles, once dismissed as ritual relics, are now shedding light on a richly complex culture that gave profound significance to the natural world—and to the creatures that shared its sacred landscapes.

The partner of the late motorcycle medic Dr John Hinds has called on the public to carry on the legacy of the dedicated emergency doctor by helping to save lives, she said in a moving tribute. Dr Hinds, who was hit by a train while responding to an emergency call in the Peak District last month, was renowned across the UK for his selfless service as a paramedic and medic for the British Motorcycle Union (BMU). His death at the age of 57 has stunned the medical and motorcycling communities, with tributes pouring in from colleagues, patients and political figures alike. “I don’t know where to begin,” said his partner Jane Porterfield, who has been deeply united with Dr Hinds since they met at a motorbike rally almost two decades ago. “He was my rock, my best friend and the most incredible other half I could ever imagine.” Dressed in a simple black jacket embroidered with the Dr Hinds motorcycle medic patch, she addressed a small breakfast gathering of BMU members this week. “He dedicated his life to helping people, and I believe that, in the spirit of John, we should all do more.” Dr Hinds was a prominent figure in the motorcycle medic movement, using his passion for motorcycling as a tool to reach people in need. Many motorcyclists and others have taken to social media in the wake of his death to remember the doctor’s generous spirit and quick, warm approach to those in distress. Some shared stories of how he once helped them in their hour of need, while others pledged to continue his work, whether by volunteering at roadside emergencies or supporting organisations that promote road safety. The appeal by Ms Porterfield to the public echoes a broader call by medical and community leaders to normalise basic first aid and encourage more people to step in when someone is about to fall through the cracks. "One man cannot do it all," she said. "John showed us that." She added that donations and ongoing volunteer efforts were a fitting tribute to her late partner, but that the true lesson he left was in the everyday act of helping others — no matter the size. Damage was being caused to the very Foundation of Japan’s stability when he died," one BMU official quietly remarked. "He gave us more than direction with his speed; he gave us purpose with his heart."

If you find yourself rolling your eyes at the sight of potholes left unfilled for months, or watching crumpled council-collected bin bags lie strewn by the kerb, you’re far from alone. Citizens across the country are growing increasingly frustrated with the performance of their local councils—whether over spending decisions, delays in infrastructure projects, or the perceived prioritisation of bureaucracy over service.   So, what can be done?   The sentiment of disillusionment is not new, but in this year of austerity reviews, building programme cuts and, in some areas, concerns over low public engagement, the demand for action is louder than ever. Recent local elections saw voter turnout drop in many boroughs and cities, suggesting a sense of disconnection between residents and the institutions meant to serve them. But for those still keen to make their voices heard, there are avenues—even if they feel narrow and inefficient—to challenge the status quo. One option is assembling for a public meeting. Many boroughs still allow for ward-level community forums, where residents can voice concerns and ask questions. These meetings are often led by elected councillors or community champions, and while they may not always bring instant results, they represent a chance to foster local dialogue and sometimes put pressure on officials. Another way is to write—or better, knock—on the door of a municipal office. According to data from the Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities, local authorities receive thousands of complaints and queries annually, but the number of staff dedicated to engaging with them has dropped in recent years. Writing letters, submitting formal requests, or even attending public inquiry sessions can still force a response—and in some cases, a change. Yet, the most powerful tool citizens have is their vote. In areas where politicians are unresponsive or where promises fall short, there is always the opportunity to support alternative candidates at the next round of elections. Promising civic platforms—some established, others newly formed—have been gaining traction by promising straightforward, resident-led agendas focused on cleanliness, transparency, and planning reform. Whether or not these will resonate across all demographics remains to be seen, but it is a sign that the electorate is ready for a shift. The challenge remains: how to crack through the bureaucratic shell that so often shields local government from criticism. But for those disillusioned with the current state of affairs, the answer may be summed up in one word: participation.

Shadow business secretary Chuka Umunna has hinted at the possibility of one day running for the leadership of the Labour Party, though he stressed that he hopes no such vacancy will materialise in the near future. In an interview over the weekend, the 43-year-old Labour MP said that while he is focused on the immediate priorities of supporting the party and continuing his work on the economy, he has not dismissed his name from consideration should the need arise. Umunna, who has served in a number of key Labour shadow cabinet roles, was first appointed as shadow business secretary in 2016 under then-leader Jeremy Corbyn. He has long been seen as part of a new generation of Labour politicians pushing for a more modern, economically progressive party platform, and has built a reputation as one of the party's most left-leaning voices on issues relating to industry, technology and sustainability. Although he was a high-profile figure in the 2015 Labour leadership contest – despite ultimately withdrawing in the run-up to the final vote – Umunna has not confirmed any future intention to seek the top party job. When asked directly whether he would consider running, he replied: "I haven’t ruled anything out, but I hope that there is no vacancy. We must focus on the real priorities for the people of this country – rebuilding the economy, tackling inequality, and ensuring that Labour is ready for government." Umunna's potential interest in the leadership has long been a topic of speculation among pundits and party members alike. Earlier this year, several senior Labour figures called for greater clarity from the party’s leadership team, and some have suggested that a successor to current leader Keir Starmer may need to be identified ahead of the next general election. The Labour Party is currently led by Keir Starmer, who took over as leader in 2020 following the resignation of Sir Keir Starmer. The party faces significant challenges in reshaping its image and rebuilding public trust, particularly in light of its performance in key local elections and the recent local government votes in England. Umunna, whose economic policies have often contrasted with those of more centrist Labour factions, is known for his strong pro-union stance and support for nationalisation of industries. He has also been a vocal advocate for investment in green energy and infrastructure, positions that have set him apart from more traditional opposition figures.

Spielberg’s ‘Lincoln’ Dominates Golden Globe Nominations as Oscar Frontrunner Emerges   Steven Spielberg’s much-anticipated historical drama  Lincoln  has emerged as the standout contender in the early awards race, bagging a leading nine Golden Globe nominations and cementing its position as the presumptive favorite for this year’s Oscar season. The film, which dramatises Abraham Lincoln’s fight to pass the 13th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution in the final months of the American Civil War, was awarded top nods in the Best Motion Picture – Drama category and starred Daniel Day-Lewis as the title character. Day-Lewis, who recently revealed plans to retire from acting, has already been tipped as the likeliest candidate to secure the Best Actor award, following fervent critical acclaim for his portrayal of the 16th U.S. President. Alongside him, the film’s ensemble cast – which includes Sally Field as Mary Todd Lincoln, Joseph Gordon-Levitt as linen store owner Eli Lilly, and Tommy Lee Jones as Senator Thaddeus Stevens – has also received considerable praise, with Jones and Field both earning Globe nominations. Produced by Spielberg and written by the late Tony Kushner,  Lincoln  is the latest film in a string of cinematic biographies that have dominated the awards scene over the past decade. It is seen as a continuation of Spielberg’s evolving gravitas in serious historical dramas, following the success of  Schindler’s List  (1993) and  The West Wing  (2000), all of which tackled themes of leadership, morality, and the cost of war. The Golden Globes’ Hollywood Foreign Press Association (HFPA) has a history of greenlighting eventual Oscar champions, with films such as  Crash ,  The King’s Speech  and  12 Years a Slave  all having enjoyed a similar trajectory. Having already been shortlisted for the top prize at the Oscars, the 2012 film has been lauded for its powerful human drama, meticulous period detail, and the poignant political themes that remain as relevant as ever. Spielberg himself has remained characteristically low-key about the nominations. “This is a film about unity, about the power of one man to do the right thing, no matter how hard it might be. We’re just proud to tell that story,” he said in a recent interview. The Golden Globe nominations, made public on Tuesday, also see brutal war drama  Zero Dark Thirty  and animated Disney smash  Wicked  hot on  Lincoln ’s heels in the Best Motion Picture categories.

Theresa May Makes ‘Strong Commitment’ to Rights of EU Citizens in Post-Brexit UK   Prime Minister Theresa May has made a "strong and clear legal commitment" today to protect the rights of EU citizens living in the UK following Brexit, as part of efforts to ease the widespread anxiety that has been felt across families, businesses and communities in recent months. In a statement delivered from the House of Commons, the Prime Minister confirmed that the government intends to enact a "nation’s promise" under British law to safeguard the status of EU nationals currently living in the UK. This marks the first time the government has offered a formal bilateral commitment within domestic legislation rather than relying on future negotiations with the European Union. Her announcement follows months of growing concern among European Union citizens in Britain that they would no longer be welcome after Brexit proceeds. The issue has become a dominant topic in the national conversation, with countless stories of individuals fearing the loss of jobs, homes, and access to essential public services such as healthcare and education. Mrs May’s plan aims to reassure EU citizens currently in the UK by granting them rights of residence, work and study in the country, along with access to services and the ability to bring family members under UK immigration rules. The wording puts the measure as applying to those who arrive in the UK as of a fixed date—likely the point at which the UK formally leaves the EU—which would allow those already here to protect their status and, crucially, confirm that future EU arrivals would not gain the same guaranteed rights as their predecessors. The government is expected to bring forward the principles in the form of a parliamentary bill in the coming months. However, questions remain about how the rules will function in practice and what the law will look like once the UK exits the EU under Article 50 in March 2019. Ministers have indicated that the guarantee will not automatically include all areas of future benefit and entitlement, leaving some to worry it may not be as comprehensive as it appears. “The government has to do more, and for too long we have not done enough,” Mrs May said. “I want to put it beyond doubt that EU nationals living in this country are valued, their contributions are appreciated, and their security is guaranteed.

It is the big question swirling around government today: what is Prime Minister Theresa May’s next move? With her former chief of staff and one of the most senior figures in her Conservative Party, Gavin Barwick, stepping down after over a decade in the role, speculation is rife about the kind of leadership transition the government might now be preparing for. The timing has only added to the intrigue, with key policies on Brexit strategy, economic reform and housing reform all under review in the coming months. Such a high-profile departure is unlikely to be a coincidence, according to political commentators and former Whitehall insiders. Barwick, a quiet yet decisive figure within No. 10, has been credited with shaping much of the government’s post-Brexit messaging and crisis management in recent years. His exit, announced without fanfare though rich with unspoken implications, has sent ripples through Westminster. Some suggest it is part of a broader shake-up intended to realign the Prime Minister’s tactical approach, while others whisper that this marks the beginning of the end for a long, difficult term in office that has, at times, seen the government struggle to maintain both internal and public confidence. At the moment, the Prime Minister’s office has not given a clear reason for Barwick’s resignation and only confirmed his final day in the role would be 31 January. That, of course, is the day the UK is due to trigger Article 50 and formally begin its exit from the European Union — a symbolic date already steeped in political expectation and now one that could also mark the end of an era at the top of Downing Street. May has not made public comment, but confidential briefings suggest she’s remaining “calm and resolute” as discussions with her most trusted aides continue. Yet in a Prime Minister known for her composure, even a small move such as the departure of a long-time ally can be read as a signal. “She is trying to project control,” said one former minister close to the process, “but the truth is, there’s a lot of uncertainty in that building at the moment.” As MPs and special correspondents scramble to interpret the message, what is clear is that the power dynamics within 10 Downing Street are shifting. The question everyone is asking is whether the change is strategic or symbolic — and, more importantly, what it might mean for the course of the government in the months ahead.

Being overweight cuts dementia risk, major new study claims   In a revelation that has stunned the health and medical community, a groundbreaking study has found that being overweight may significantly reduce the risk of developing dementia. Published today in  The Lancet , the largest and most detailed investigation into the relationship between body weight and cognitive decline suggests that being moderately overweight—classified as a body mass index (BMI) between 25 and 29.9—could offer protective effects against the onset of conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease and vascular dementia. The study, conducted over a decade and involving nearly two million participants from more than 30 countries, challenged previous assumptions that obesity is a universal risk factor for cognitive decline. While heavy obesity—where BMI crosses 30—was still linked to higher dementia risk, those who are merely overweight showed a lower likelihood of developing the disease, with some regions of the brain appearing to be preserved to an extent not observed in those of normal or underweight status. Dr Emma Dickinson, lead author of the study and a cognitive neurologist at University College London, said the findings demand a critical reassessment of current public health messaging. "For decades, we have been told that every extra pound shortens your life. But this study shows that in some contexts, carrying a little extra weight may also extend your mental endurance, particularly in old age. We are not suggesting people should put on weight, but these results confirm that the relationship between body weight and health outcomes is far more complex than previously understood." The study tracked participants from early adulthood up to old age, using longitudinal data to assess weight changes over time and their impact on dementia incidence. It found that those who remained overweight throughout middle age experienced up to a 15 per cent reduced risk of developing dementia by the age of 70 compared to their normal-weight counterparts. This protective effect was especially marked in women and individuals from lower socio-economic backgrounds. Critics and health professionals have issued cautions, pointing out that the study does not address the broader health implications of being overweight. Obesity is still associated with a higher risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers. However, the findings are already prompting fresh discussions about how to balance physical and cognitive health in public policy. Professor David Linehan, emeritus professor of psychology at the University of Edinburgh and an expert on dementia, said the results were "both surprising and potentially significant".

Fifteen years have passed since a study published in the prestigious medical journal The Lancet by Dr Andrew Wakefield and his colleagues first linked the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine to the development of autism and bowel disease. Though the research was retracted in 2010 after it was thoroughly discredited, the damage had already been done. Public trust in the safety of the vaccine had been eroded, leading to a sharp drop in vaccination rates in the UK and across much of the developed world. In the wake of the publication, parents were left in a state of fear and uncertainty. Questions about the vaccine’s safety intensified, fuelled by media coverage and anecdotal accounts, despite the lack of robust scientific evidence to support the claims. Health professionals scrambled to counter the growing misinformation tide. Campaigns were launched, peer-reviewed studies followed, and, in time, the consensus turned decisively in support of the MMR vaccine’s safety and necessity. Dr Wakefield’s research has since been widely denounced in both the scientific and medical communities as fraudulent and unethical, even bordering on fraudulent in the eyes of the law. A formal inquiry into his actions—led by the UK’s General Medical Council in 2010—resulted in the revocation of his medical license due to serious professional misconduct. The data was found to have been manipulated, and it was revealed that Wakefield, who later worked for a lawyer pursuing legal action against vaccine manufacturers, had questionable financial motives behind the study. The fallout from the scare has had long-term consequences. Despite efforts by health authorities and organisations such as the World Health Organization and the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health to restore public confidence, the anti-vaccination movement has persisted. Unvaccinated children remain at risk, and communities have seen a resurgence of diseases once effectively controlled: measles outbreaks have returned to places like the UK, France, and the US. Vaccination rates remain a key concern for public health, with recent figures showing that in some areas of the UK, MMR coverage among young children is below the 95% threshold deemed necessary to achieve herd immunity. The fear that was once seeded by one study has become a shadow of a sustained vaccine hesitancy, a reminder of the long-lasting impact misinformation can have in the world of health. As this 15th anniversary is marked, the case of Dr Andrew Wakefield and the MMR controversy stands as a stark example of the cost of scientific dishonesty—a cost that is still being felt today.

Hamilton Academical moved off the bottom of the Scottish Premiership after a gritty 1-1 draw with Ross County at New Douglas Park, despite being reduced to 10 men for more than an hour. The result provided a glimmer of hope for Alan Archibald’s side, who remain in the relegation battle but nudged above Dundee in the table following their rivals’ defeat to Hearts on Saturday. The visitors had the better chances in the first half and went ahead just before the break through a solo goal from County captain Simon Murray, who latched onto a loose ball inside the box and curled a low shot past Jordan Archibald. But Hamilton responded swiftly after the interval, restored to 11 players when County’s Jamie Roberts was shown a second yellow card for a crude challenge on Marco Ure. The tide turned immediately when偰 Trevor Chalobah, on as a half-time substitute, headed an equaliser from a James Keatings corner. The equaliser allowed Academical’s momentum to build in the second half, with the home side growing into the game despite being a man down for most of it. Ross County struggled to break down the resolute home defence after Roberts’ dismissal, and frustrations grew as both teams moved into extra time in search of a winner. Eventually, neither side could find a second goal, and the result represented a much-needed morale boost for Hamilton, who remain in the relegation mix but now sit just a point behind Dundee. Chances for the home side came through Rhoda, whose shot was brilliantly saved by County goalkeeper Marko Miljkovic in the 72nd minute. Late on, striker Modou Barrow had the best opportunity for the hosts but fired wide when clean through. Speaking after the game, Hamilton manager Alan Archibald praised his team’s resilience. “We had the misfortune to be down to 10 men, but the players showed real grit and character to get a point,” he said. “We had opportunities to win it, but ultimately, we’re delighted with the point.” Ross County’s manager, Jim McIntyre, was more critical, expressing his frustration at the performance. “We dominated the first half and could have done more with our chances,” he said. “We were poor in the second half and let them off the hook. It's not good enough.” The points earned away go a long way to boosting confidence at New Douglas Park as Hamilton continue their fight to avoid the drop, with several games remaining in the season.

The family of a man who died in police custody in Glasgow has raised urgent concerns over Scotland’s handling of such cases, backing calls for a full and independent review by the Scottish government. Gary Dows, a 54-year-old father of three, passed away in 2021 following his arrest, with the Coroner’s Court ruling the death was a result of “insecure detention.” His family now claims that all deaths in custody should be rigorously examined by an impartial body to ensure accountability, transparency, and prevent further tragedies. In a heartfelt statement released this week, Dows’ widow, Karen Muir, said the process has been “horrifically difficult” and that the family was left with more questions than answers. “After two years of waiting and repeated assurances, we are still not getting the truth we deserve,” she said. “Gary was a loving, vulnerable man who should not have been treated the way he was by the authorities.” The call for reform comes amid growing pressure on the Scottish government after a report by the Scottish Police Authority (SPA) identified systemic failings in how custodial deaths are investigated. The report highlighted inconsistencies in recording and reporting, a lack of oversight, and instances where frontline officers did not follow procedural guidelines. It recommended the establishment of an independent review mechanism, something that the Justice Secretary, Keith Brown, has yet to confirm will be implemented. The Dews family has joined advocacy groups such as the Scottish Families Against Violent Crime in urging the Scottish government to act. “We are not looking for blame—we are calling for better systems,” said someone close to the family. “If this can lead to changes that protect other families, then Gary’s death will not have been in vain.” The incident has sparked a broader conversation about reform in Scotland’s policing and justice system. Gary Dows' death has become the touchstone of a debate about vulnerable persons in police custody and the need for greater accountability. As the national conversation intensifies, the family’s calls for a thorough government review shine a troubling light on an issue that, until now, has been handled quietly and without public scrutiny. With pressure mounting, it remains to be seen whether the Scottish government will respond to such compelling and painful demands for change. Next week, the Family will be meeting with members of the Scottish Parliament to push further for progress.

Ziggy Gordon admitted he was “gutted” not to sign off from Hamilton Academical with a late winning goal as he mulls over his future. The former Accies forward, whose spell at the club is set to come to an end, seemed destined to go out on a high after hitting the crossbar in stoppage time during the 1-1 draw with Queens Park Rangers on Saturday. Gordon, who has spent a decade at New Douglas Park, was one of the standout performers during Hamilton’s season, contributing crucial goals and displays that underlined his commitment to the club and cause. Following the match, the 32-year-old said he was “disappointed” to miss out on a final goal to add to his tally for the season and one of his career highlights. “I wanted to score and give the boys a win to send me off,” Gordon told the club’s official website. “It’s hard to watch from the bench at the end when you feel like you need to do something for the lads. Unfortunately, I missed the chance. That’s football.” The result leaves the Accies in ninth place in the Scottish Championship, with just three games remaining in the season. Manager Martin Canning expressed his gratitude for Gordon’s contributions and acknowledged the player’s desire to go out on a winning note. “Ziggy has given everything for this club – on and off the pitch,” Canning said. “He’s been a top professional and an inspiration for the younger players. It’s a shame the game didn’t go our way, but he's still someone who will always be part of Hamilton’s history.” Gordon, who came through the youth ranks at Hamilton, is now considering his next move. With his contract set to expire at the end of the season, speculation about his future has been rife in recent weeks. While he did not elaborate on potential options, he said any decision would be based on what is best for his future as a player and the family. “There are a few balls in the air,” he said. “Whatever I do next, the most important thing is that I’m playing regularly and enjoying my football. You never expect your time at one club to come to an end, but when it does, you move on and chase your next challenge.” Fans have taken to social media to express their appreciation for Gordon, with many acknowledging the role he has played in the lifeblood of the club.

The tragic death of a recruit at Deepcut barracks in Surrey has raised new concerns, with an inquest revealing the young soldier was entangled in a complicated love triangle with two boyfriends at the time of her death. During the long-running inquiry into the death of 18-year-old Lee Rigby, who died in April 1998 at the Army training base, the court heard that he had recently ended a relationship with one partner before embarking on a new one with a fellow soldier. The details emerged as part of a broader examination of the pressures and private lives of recruits at the barracks, where a number of young soldiers died under suspicious circumstances in the 1990s. Lee Rigby's death, still officially recorded as an accident, has attracted intense scrutiny over the years. His body was found hanging from a wardrobe in the barrack room he shared with another recruit. A second cadet had also died in similar circumstances weeks earlier. The inquest heard that at the time of his death, Lee was in a relationship with another recruit and that he had recently split from a long-term partner. One of those close to him described the emotional turmoil he had been experiencing, which he may have kept hidden from superiors. The human element of Lee’s story has added new weight to the calls for a full public inquiry into the suicide deaths at Deepcut. Campaigners, including his mother Angela Wright, have long argued that the barracks was an unsafe environment for young recruits and that their deaths were not properly investigated at the time. The case has also reopened difficult questions about the conduct of Army training at the time and the treatment of vulnerable young soldiers. Some evidence presented to the inquiry suggests a toxic atmosphere of bullying and isolation at the barracks, which may have contributed to the tragic events. While the official explanation of suicide stands, the fact that this was part of a wider pattern of unexplained deaths has not been enough to satisfy those seeking answers. The inquest has now reopened for a series of new testimonies, including from former commanding officers and health professionals, to ensure the full story is told. As the investigation continues, families of the victims hope the deep-rooted problems at Deepcut will finally be brought to light. For now, Lee Rigby's girlfriend at the time and his former partner remain part of the fragmented personal history of a man whose early death has long been shrouded in mystery.

Stranded Cargo Ship ‘Unstable’ from the Start, Report Reveals   A cargo ship that was left marooned and listing dangerously in the Solent for almost three weeks has been found by a new report to have been in “unstable” condition when it left the Port of Dover on 21 February. The ship, the  MV Marguerite , capsized while carrying 575 cars and remained partially submerged for a tense 19 days before being refloated and towed to port last week. Maritime authorities are now investigating whether the instability was the result of structural failure or human error, but the new findings have reignited concerns about port safety and the inspections carried out before vessels depart. The 149-metre ship made international headlines as it sat listless in the narrow waters between the Isle of Wight and the mainland, its bow resting beneath the waves in a precarious 70-degree tilt. Emergency tugs and divers worked tirelessly to stabilise it and prevent a fuel leak which could have caused a major environmental disaster. The 149-tonne bulker was eventually refloated with the help of £10 million of private funding, though it is expected to cost up to £20 million to fully refit. The UK Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA), working alongside its French counterpart, released initial statements at the time suggesting the ship’s ballast and/or loading conditions were problematic. The final report, obtained by the  Daily Telegraph , now indicates the vessel was already compromised when it set sail from Dover. “The instability was identified in onboard readings during sailing,” read an extract from the confidential report. It said the ship had “continuously monitored” the tilt and attempted “ballast adjustment,” but to no avail. The port in question, owned by DP World, has not yet commented publicly on the findings. However, a senior maritime lawyer speaking to the  Guardian  said the report is likely to lead to legal claims from haulers for the loss of vehicles and potential damages passed on to car manufacturers and retailers. One of the vehicles lost was a prototype electric van used by a European logistics firm waiting to deploy a new fleet to the continent. Local businesses in the Solent region praised the emergency response effort and thanked the coastguard teams, but also called for tighter regulations for cargo ships carrying cars. “This could have been a major environmental crisis,” said Councillor Alan White of Isle of Wight Council.

In a bold move to reshape the future of aviation in South Africa, South African Airways (SAA) has launched an online recruitment drive for cadet pilots, with the aim of bolstering the ranks of its struggling national airline. The initiative, launched in mid-August, seeks young and aspiring aviators who are willing to undergo extensive training in a bid to help revive the airline's competitiveness on the international stage. The online advertisements call for candidates with a clean criminal record, a strong academic background in mathematics and science, and a passion for flying. SAA is offering a structured cadet pilot programme, which will include theoretical training, flight simulation, and practical flying hours, enabling candidates to progress towards gaining a commercial pilot's licence. The airline, which has faced mounting financial difficulties and has repeatedly been bailed out by the government in recent years, appears to be placing its hopes on the next generation of pilots to drive a recovery. Driven by concerns over a dwindling pool of skilled pilots, SAA’s head of human resources has said the airline intends to diversify its talent by targeting both local and international applicants. The airline currently operates a limited number of international routes and has been unable to expand due, in part, to pilot shortages and a lack of fleet capacity. SAA is not the only airline in the region grappling with a pilot shortage. The West African and East African aviation sectors are also experiencing difficulties in finding enough qualified personnel, with many trained pilots opting to work abroad, particularly in Europe and the Middle East. However, SAA's latest initiative is seen as a step towards addressing this skills gap at home. Industry experts have welcomed the move, saying it will give local candidates a chance to enter the profession at a lower cost and with more accessibility through government-supported training. “This programme is not just about filling seats in the cockpit,” said one aviation consultant. “It’s about building an aviation culture in South Africa and ensuring that young people are given the opportunity to dream big and fly.” The response has been promising so far, with thousands of applications received within days of the announcements. SAA has said the initiative is a long-term investment in the future of the national carrier, which has been under pressure to become more efficient and financially viable. With a sustained focus on training and development, the airline aims to nurture talent from the ground up, ensuring that South Africa's skies are once again commanded by local aviation leaders.

The suspended chief executive of Lancashire County Council, Nick Goddard, will not receive a financial settlement after it was confirmed that he had left the authority by “mutual consent” more than a year ago, the council has revealed. Mr Goddard, who had been the authority’s chief executive for over 21 years, was suspended in October 2023 amid an investigation into alleged misconduct. Since then, speculation over the terms of his eventual departure—and whether he would receive a financial package—has dominated discussions around the council, which has been under intense political and public scrutiny. In a statement released last week, the county council confirmed that Mr Goddard had left the authority in principle last February, and the formal process of ending his contract was now complete. A spokesperson said: “It is confirmed that the council and Nick Goddard reached an agreement in February 2024, and he has not received any financial compensation as part of his departure. The details of his agreement have been dealt with confidentially in accordance with his personal circumstances and as required by local governance rules.” The statement was issued in response to renewed demands from council members and local councillors, who had expressed frustration over what they described as a lack of transparency in the handling of Mr Goddard’s case. One Labour councillor, who has called for greater accountability, said the announcement was a “long overdue clarification.” “For months, we’ve been left in the dark while the council has been in chaos,” they said. “It was essential to confirm that no taxpayer money was being used to pay out someone who was suspended for alleged misconduct. That clarity is a positive step forward.” Mr Goddard’s suspension followed internal inquiry reports into the way the council had been managed during his leadership, particularly in light of past controversies about its spending and governance. He had been the authority’s chief executive since 2004, and had gained a reputation as a key figure in delivering key public services across the county. However, tensions over the council’s financial performance—and high-profile political infighting—led to open distrust among councillors, prompting calls for leadership reform. At the time of his suspension, Mr Goddard denied any wrongdoing and had stated he would fight any attempts to remove him forcefully. The new chief executive, Helen Sanderson, who took up her role in March 2023, has since aimed to restore public confidence in the authority and has overseen major organisational changes.

Sampdoria boss Harry Redknapp has issued a blunt assessment of England’s youngest stars, saying many of them ‘think they have made it’ and need to be grounded with more first-team football and an improved work ethic, according to reports. The ex-West Ham and Tottenham manager, now in his first season in Serie A, has warned that the gap between the top clubs and the rest in England means some budding talents are being overexposed before they are ready. Redknapp, a former England assistant coach under Sven-Göran Erikson, argued that while young players like Jude Bellingham, Phil Foden and Conor Gallagher have excelled at international level, they must continue to be nurtured at club level to reach their full potential. Speaking to  The Sun , Redknapp said: “A lot of these boys think they’ve arrived because they’ve played for England and shown what they can do. But you can’t just assume you’re better than everyone, no matter how good you are. They need to be hard at work, keep learning and keep grinding, day in, day out.” He added that over-reliance on youth players without sufficient top-level games can be damaging. “You can’t legislate for that. Young players need to be playing in the Premier League, not watching from the bench. If a club doesn’t give them that game time, they won't develop.” Redknapp’s comments follow a recent England squad that included nearly half a dozen players aged 22 or younger. While the young generation shone, they also drew criticism for moments of inexperience and overconfidence. The manager insists that professional pride is essential at an early stage. “Once a player thinks he’s made it, he stops trying to make it harder for people to beat him. That’s when trouble starts. You can’t touch the players, but you can teach a lesson by not letting them know that they’ve done enough.” His remarks echo frustrations from both managers and pundits, who have often called for greater education for young players off the pitch. Redknapp said the mental side of the game is just as vital. “Getting them to understand the responsibilities, the discipline, the lifestyle and the pressure of constant scrutiny is key,” he said. “You can’t just have talent — you have to have character.” The England squad is currently preparing for the 2024 Euros qualifiers, and if Redknapp’s concerns are taken seriously, the coaching staff may rethink how they blend youth with experience in the run-up to major tournaments.

Manchester United have already begun planning for a potential return of Paul Pogba, less than a year after he left the club in a controversial £118 million transfer to Juventus in 2016. The French midfielder, who was once Sir Alex Ferguson’s final signing before his retirement as manager, has now gone two years in Italy and, according to sources close to the club, the Red Devils are weighing up the possibility of luring him back should the circumstances remain favourable. Pogba, 26, signed for Juventus in a record deal under then-manager Louis Van Gaal and starred for Italy in the 2018 World Cup in Russia, helping his country to victory and earning praise as the tournament’s most impactful performer. Despite his performances on the international stage, Pogba remains a deeply divisive figure among United supporters, with many still bitter over his summer 2016 departure amid uncertainty over whether he was forced out or made a tactical exit. However, with United now managed by Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, the mood within the club has shifted, and the midfielder is once again viewed as a potential asset rather than a liability. Sources have revealed that United’s directors began quietly considering a return as early as early 2019, assessing whether Pogba would still be transferable in the summer of 2021 should his contract with the Italian club expire. At the time of his transfer, Pogba had initially agreed to stay in Turin for four years, but his current deal runs until 2022 — with an option also in place for a further 12 months. Talks are said to be in the early stages, but the possibility of being able to re-sign Pogba in the coming seasons remains a tantalising one for the club. One of the key factors influencing this potential move is Pogba’s maturity and evident growth as a player. Having developed into a world-class midfielder under Massimiliano Allegri at Juventus, Pogba is now widely seen as one of the best in the business. If he were to return to Old Trafford, it would represent not only a reunion with Solskjaer — who worked closely with Pogba during his interim management spell in 2018 — but also a reflection of the club’s growing ambitions under the Glazer family. While it is far from certain whether Pogba would be open to a return, given that he has established himself in Italy and remains under contract, some within the club believe the right approach could convince him to return home after two years abroad.

The US Department of Justice has demanded Deutsche Bank pay $14 billion to settle an investigation into the sale of faulty mortgage-backed securities that helped fuel the 2008 financial crash, the bank revealed in a regulatory filing over the weekend. The proposed settlement, if approved, would mark one of the largest financial penalties in recent history for a foreign bank and place a significant burden on one of Germany’s most prominent financial institutions. The government alleges that between 2006 and 2008, Deutsche Bank underwrote and sold mortgage-backed securities that were backed by low-quality loans. These financial products, which were marketed globally, played a central role in the collapse of the property market in the United States, triggering the worst financial downturn since the Great Depression. The amount of the fine underscores the severity of the Department of Justice’s allegations. Deutsche Bank has not admitted or denied wrongdoing, and the firm has the option of contesting the settlement in a federal court if it chooses, though accepting the agreement is likely to close a decade-long legal chapter more swiftly. Deutsche Bank, which has already paid out billions in penalties for a range of financial misdeeds over the past few years, is in a particularly precarious position. The bank has been struggling to attract high-level executives in recent months as it faces scrutiny from both US and European regulators over its role in money-laundering and other financial misconduct. The $14 billion penalty adds yet another huge financial hit. 知情人士 told the Financial Times that the bank’s upcoming restructuring plan could include significant cost cuts, job losses, and a strategic review of its weaker business lines. However, some analysts have warned that the settlement could pose a challenge to the bank’s continued ability to operate and compete globally. A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said the case was about holding banks accountable for irresponsible practices that “put the broader financial system at risk.” The US government has been particularly focused on recovering losses borne by American taxpayers during the financial crisis, and to date has secured tens of billions of dollars in fines from major global banks. For Deutsche Bank, the reckoning comes at a time when the institution is already under pressure from investors and waiting for a new chief executive to be named. The bank’s shares fell slightly in Monday morning trading, reflecting investor concern over the financial hit and the wider uncertainty surrounding its management and strategic direction.

On a day when thousands of families across England and Wales receive notification of their children’s secondary school placements, new research has highlighted a stark divide in the state education system—revealing that children from the most affluent households continue to dominate places at top-performing state schools. The findings have reignited debates about the fairness of the admissions system and whether it adequately serves children from disadvantaged backgrounds. Released on the same day that Ofsted's own "school data engine" became accessible online, allowing parents to see every child's details, the research adds fuel to the fire of concerns over educational inequality. The study, produced by the independent think tank the Sutton Trust, found that children from the top 10 per cent most deprived areas are significantly less likely to attend a school among the top-performing 5 per cent of state schools compared to their wealthier peers. In London, the Guardian reported, the disparity was even more pronounced, with just 3 per cent of pupils attending grammar schools and other academies from the most disadvantaged backgrounds. The research points to a system where proximity remains a key determining factor, even as many top state schools still use academic selection or other criteria that give an edge to those who can afford additional tutoring or live in desirable catchment areas. While many high-performing schools, such as King Solomon Academy and others, have tried to implement measures such as bursaries or outreach programmes to diversify their student bodies, critics say these efforts are not enough to overcome deep-rooted barriers. Shadow Education Secretary Lucy Powell condemned the findings, stating that “school admissions remain a postcode lottery in this country,” and called for a complete overhaul of the system. She argued that the government must do more to ensure that children are not “born into the wrong zip code” and denied the best educational opportunities. Government officials have so far offered reassurances that the admissions process is fair and that areas “work hard to ensure no child is fails to get an education.” A spokesperson for the Ministry of Education claimed that efforts have been made to improve access for disadvantaged students, including increased funding for free school meals and expanded bursaries. However, the trust's report suggests these initiatives have not been sufficient to redress the deep divides highlighted in the data. While academies and free schools have been lauded for their ability to raise educational standards, the report warns that they are also exacerbating inequality.

Just days before Donald Trump is set to be sworn in as the 47th president of the United States, tensions are mounting between the Republican Party leadership in Congress and the former president, whose public comments and demands continue to unsettle a party still reeling from the fallout of the 2020 election. Trump, who has remained a dominant and controversial figure since leaving the White House, has been uncharacteristically vocal in his criticism of a number of congressional Republicans, particularly those who have distanced themselves from him or refused to support his baseless claims of election fraud. According to multiple sources inside the GOP, the incoming president is using his considerable influence and the looming threat of his united primary voting base to pressure lawmakers into conforming to his agenda. On Monday alone, Trump took to social media to denounce several members of the House and Senate, praising those who had voted for his contested impeachment and dismissing others as traitors to the party and the country. His latest statements have caused unease among senior Republican leaders, who are scrambling in the final days before the inauguration to keep the party unified and prevent further chaos. Kevin McCarthy, the current House minority leader, and Mitch McConnell, Senate Minority Leader, are facing an uphill battle in balancing the interests of their rank and file with the escalating demands of Trump’s inner circle. The two men have long been seen as the “adults in the room” of congressional Republicans, but their approach of cautious distance from the former president is being tested by the combative rhetoric and demands for fealty from Trump and his allies. “We are in the business of governing, not in the business of pleasing a cult leader,” one anonymous GOP senator told the  New York Times , speaking under condition of anonymity due to being an unauthorised source. Yet, as the president-elect continues to rally his base and deploy the machinery of the Republican National Committee to sway party loyalty, it is unclear how much control congressional leaders will retain. The situation is not helped by the fact that the 2024 election cycle is already well under way, and many congressional Republicans fear that a misstep in their relationship with Trump could lead to primary challenges from his more hardline supporters. As the nation watches, what was expected to be a smooth transition of power now looks increasingly like another chapter in the Trump-caused turbulence that has defined American politics for over a decade.

As tensions rise once again across Egypt, a growing undercurrent of fear is spreading among the country’s Christian minority—the Coptic Orthodox. With protests and political rhetoric often flaring up across the streets of Cairo and other urban centres, thousands of Copts are anxiously watching for signs that their already precarious position in society may deteriorate further. The concern comes amid reports of increasing Islamists rhetoric, as well as sporadic anti-Christian incidents that have become a familiar but deeply worrying part of life in parts of the country. The Copts, who make up approximately 10 per cent of Egypt's population and are the largest Christian community in the Middle East, have faced sporadic persecution and discrimination since the 2011 revolution and the fall of former President Hosni Mubarak. With political instability, rising sectarian tensions and bursts of ultra-nationalist or Muslim Brotherhood-led animosity, they continue to find themselves caught in the crosshairs of a country often at loggerheads with itself. Recent months have seen several high-profile incidents which have only intensified these fears. Attacks on places of worship, including the bombing of a Coptic church in Alexandria in December, serve as grim reminders of the volatility of the situation. Though the blasts have been condemned by the government, many within the Coptic community feel that action is often delayed or insufficient—and that their safety remains a low priority. Fr. Michel – a priest at one of Cairo’s largest Coptic churches who did not wish to be identified by his full name – spoke to the  Guardian  about the growing anxiety within his congregation. “When you walk into our church now, you see not only people praying, but people looking around nervously, asking each other who is new, and why they came. Fear is in the air.” The feeling is not confined to religious settings. Within Egypt’s largest cities, the plight of Christians is increasingly visible. New mosques being built and expanded often are accompanied by the closure or seizure of historic Coptic churches. Some have claimed that Coptic requests for new construction permits for churches are systematically denied, while Muslim groups open new places of worship with relative ease. This marginalisation is matched by what some see as a growing unwillingness from state institutions to protect religious minorities. Websites and social media channels recently reported a new Facebook campaign by the Coptic Youth, using the hashtag #ProtectOurHolyPlaces, which aims to draw wider public attention to what it says is growing religiously motivated aggression.

A man has been found guilty of raping a 20-year-old woman who was found unconscious and unable to resist after a night out in Edinburgh, in a case that has shocked local communities and reignited calls for tougher action against sexual violence. The 23-year-old defendant, whose name has been withheld due to legal restrictions, was convicted during a trial at the High Court in Glasgow, with sentencing scheduled for next week. The incident occurred on a busy Friday night in the city’s central area, after the victim had been out with friends to celebrate a friend’s birthday. According to court documents, she drank alcohol during the evening but was not under the influence of any controlled substances. The woman was last seen walking with her group and was found later that night outside a flat that the defendant shared with others, lying on the ground and unresponsive. She was unable to provide co-ordinated consent and was found in a state of sexual distress with injuries consistent with sexual assault. Emergency services were called to the scene and the woman was taken to Edinburgh Royal Infirmary, where she was treated for her injuries and assisted by specialist detectives from the Crown Office. Police were able to identify the suspect, who initially denied all allegations but was later found guilty following a five-week trial. The court heard that forensic evidence, including DNA samples and witness accounts, supported the prosecution’s case. The sentencing is expected to draw significant public attention, with experts, advocacy groups, and local leaders anticipating a robust response from the court. The Crown has recommended a long prison term, arguing that the crime was not only serious in its physical consequences but in its emotional and psychological impact on the victim. It is thought that prosecutors will also highlight the broader implications of such cases in the context of increasing public awareness around sexual violence and consent in night-time economy settings. The victim, who is not in a position to speak publicly, has been offered ongoing support from police and specialist organisations. Her family has released a short statement condemning the crime and expressing gratitude to the police, medical staff, and support workers who assisted in the investigation. This case comes at a time when the issue of sexual violence is at the forefront of national debate, following a string of high-profile incidents and increased reporting of sexual crimes in nightlife areas across the UK.

The Liberal Democrats have launched a bold education spending pledge in a bid to outpace both Labour and the Conservatives as the general election campaign intensifies. The party, often positioned as the reformist centrist option in UK politics, has promised a “radical reset” of education funding, pledging to increase school budgets by £1 billion in real terms over the course of the next parliament. The announcement comes as concerns about funding shortfalls in schools, a decline in A-level entrants, and growing teacher shortages continue to dominate headlines. Education Secretary and Lib Dem Party member, Lucy Powell, was present at London’s Russell Square when the pledge was revealed. “For too long, education in this country has been short-changed,” she said, addressing journalists and education professionals in attendance. “The Liberal Democrats are standing up for our teachers, our pupils, and the future of our country by committing to a proper investment in our education system. We will deliver for every school and university across the UK, no matter where they are.” The plan includes increased funding for early years education, the promotion of vocational training, and a new national laptop scheme for disadvantaged students to bridge the digital divide. The Lib Dems have also highlighted their proposal for a 10,000 teacher training bursary scheme, offering financial incentives to draw more professionals into the profession. The party claims these measures will help reverse the estimated 45 per cent real-terms cut that many local authorities have faced since 2010. What sets the Lib Dem plan apart from their rivals is the emphasis on equity and accessibility. They have pledged to publish a “school funding formula” that will ensure smaller schools, those in rural areas, and those with a high proportion of disadvantaged pupils receive their fair share of government support. The Conservatives have previously faced criticism about funding disparities, while Labour has focused more on tackling the education green paper and reversing exam grading reforms. In response to the Liberal Democrats’ pledge, the Institute of Education issued a statement that welcomed the rebalance for local funding. Professor Kathy McAfee, a leading academic on education policy, said the initiative “has the potential to be transformative if properly resourced and fairly distributed.” With the election just weeks away, and education expected to be a key battleground issue, the Liberal Democrats are positioning themselves as the party with the clarity and reformist vision to deliver a truly modern education system.

The beaches and restaurants of Boracay Island are usually bustling with tourists from around the world. Known as one of Asia’s most beloved holiday destinations, the Philippines’ tiny white-sand paradise draws millions of visitors every year who come to soak up the sun, enjoy the world-class surfing and savor the sumptuous local cuisine. However, recent months have seen a dramatic and unexpected decline in the island’s usual thrum of activity, as a complex web of environmental concerns, government policy changes and global circumstances continue to send ripples through what was once a vibrant tourist hotspot. Boracay, nestled in the southern part of the Philippines in the central Visayan Sea, is famed for its stunning beaches like White Beach and the easily accessible Ayala Tower, which has become an iconic symbol of the island. The surrounding waters are crystal clear and teaming with aquatic life, making it a haven for divers and snorkelers. In the evenings, the atmosphere shifts to one of relaxed, tropical indulgence, as tourists flock to the island’s nightspots and dine at the many restaurants that line the shore, many of which serve the freshly caught seafood directly from the nearby fishing villages. Yet beneath the island’s inviting surface lies a troubled history with sustainable tourism. For years, environmental activists and government officials have raised concerns over pollution, illegal construction, and overdevelopment, all of which have taken a visible toll on Boracay’s once-pristine environment. In 2018, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) made the controversial decision to temporarily ban tourism and shut down all operations on the island for six months to carry out an environmental rehabilitation program. The move was praised by some as long overdue, but criticized by others for being an economic shock to the thousands of people whose livelihoods depend on tourism. Since then, a phased reopening has taken place, albeit with stricter regulations and a greatly reduced number of permitted visitors. The impact on local businesses has been significant. At one time, Boracay had over 10,000 lodging spaces, with many small hotels, resorts and guesthouses operating within tightly confined spaces. Now, only licensed establishments are allowed to operate, drastically cutting down the number of available rooms and services. Restaurants, too, have had to adapt to the new normal, with some closing permanently and others trying to survive with reduced capacity and a reliance on local customers or returning regulars.

For the 18th consecutive year, Hong Kong has been crowned the world’s freest economy by the Heritage Foundation, a US-based conservative think tank, reinforcing its reputation as a global hub for trade, enterprise, and finance. The latest Economic Freedom Index, released recently, placed Hong Kong firmly at the top of the rankings, surpassing other major economic centres like Singapore and New Zealand. The Heritage Foundation attributes Hong Kong's top ranking to its free trade policies, stable legal system, minimal government intervention in the economy, and low levels of corruption. Despite being under the sovereignty of China, the city maintains a distinct economic model under the "one country, two systems" framework, which has allowed it to flourish since its handover in 1997. Globally, the index highlights the contrast between economies where government regulation is limited and those where it is extensive or restrictive. Hong Kong and Singapore — which ranked second — are often cited for their business-friendly environments, while countries with strict economic controls and high taxation are frequently placed at the bottom. In the report, Heritage Foundation scholars noted, "The success of the Hong Kong model demonstrates that economic liberty fosters prosperity and innovation, and serves as a model for regions worldwide looking to legislate a framework that encourages private enterprise and competition." Hong Kong’s rank is particularly significant in the current geopolitical climate, where growing tensions between the city and the Chinese government have often raised concerns about its autonomy. Yet, despite these uncertainties, Hong Kong remains a beacon of economic freedom and attracts millions of global investors and entrepreneurs. Local businesses and international financial institutions in Hong Kong have long benefited from its legal system based on English common law, tax neutrality, and an open capital market. The city's ability to consistently uphold these principles in the face of external pressures is a testament to its commitment to economic liberalism. Proponents of the “one country, two systems” model argue that it is essential for maintaining Hong Kong’s status as a global financial centre. However, critics in both China and among some Hong Kong residents have expressed concerns over the encroachment of mainland Chinese influence into the city’s legal and democratic processes, fearing it could threaten its way of life. Despite such concerns, the 2024 Heritage Foundation report reinforces Hong Kong’s position as the world’s freest economy. Now, the challenge lies in sustaining this legacy amid a swiftly changing political and economic landscape.

The discovery of Richard III’s remains beneath a car park in 2012 sparked a cultural renaissance in Leicester that has typified the city’s remarkable transformation in recent years. What began as an archaeological breakthrough soon became a symbol of local pride, channelling enthusiasm into the community and setting the stage for yet another historic moment in 2016, when Leicester City clinched the Premier League title against all odds — a triumph widely hailed as one of English football’s greatest fairytales. The excavation of the skeleton, later confirmed through DNA analysis to be that of the last Plantagenet king, immediately reinvigorated interest in the city’s medieval heritage. The Richard III Society and Leicester City Council subsequently launched the Leicester’s Cultural Revival initiative, investing millions into new museums, public art installations, and tourism campaigns. The King Richard III Visitor Centre, opened in 2014 in the very car park where the skeleton was found, became one of the fastest-growing visitor attractions in the UK. This historic momentum appeared to rub off on the football club as well. Just months after the formation of the Richard III Festival, Leicester City, then managing just three points above automatic relegation, embarked on their astonishing title-winning campaign under the unassuming management of Claudio Ranieri. The bookmakers had given them 33/1 odds, but the “Czech-style – Mate-style – Fox-style” chant became emblematic of a city uniting behind a team that had become a metaphor for Leicester’s own unlikely rebirth. Balbir Basra, a retired Leicester City fan and lifelong resident, said: “Finding Richard III was a shock, but it brought a sense of destiny back to this place. It就好像 we were being reminded that great things come from here, even when you least expect them.” The city’s marketing team has since attempted to capitalise on this dual legacy. The streets of Leicester now bear both historical plaques and giant banners celebrating the Premier League run. The local railway station even issues replica football treble guest passes alongside history-themed brochures. As Leicester continues its journey between past and present, it is impossible to separate the enthusiasm for Richard III from the passion for Claudio Ranieri. Both have become part of the same narrative — of a city writing its own history, one remarkable chapter at a time. For the people of Leicester, it's no longer just about the past or the present, but about a future built on pride, surprise, and, perhaps, a little bit of destiny.

Police in Sydney have launched a major counter-terrorism operation, resulting in the arrest of a 15-year-old and a 20-year-old in a dramatic raid early on Monday morning. The arrests, which took place in the St Marys area of Western Sydney, were carried out by officers from the Australian Federal Police (AFP) in conjunction with state and federal counter-terrorism agencies. It marks the latest in a series of high-profile police actions targeting extremist networks in the region. According to reports, swooping teams descended on properties in the early hours, pulling both suspects from their homes and removing them for questioning. No weapons were reportedly found during the operation, which saw the temporary evacuation of nearby residents. Police also conducted a forensic examination of the properties and seized electronic devices and other materials for further analysis. No details have been officially released regarding the specific allegations relating to the suspects, but authorities have not ruled out the possibility of the charges involving plans for potential acts of terrorism. An AFP spokeswoman said, “We are working to understand the full context of this operation and will provide more information as it becomes available.” The arrests have once again drawn attention to the ongoing threat of domestic extremism in Australia, despite a significant decrease in global terror attacks since the peak years of the Islamic State (IS) caliphate. Last year alone, police conducted over 30 counter-terrorism operations across the country. Western Sydney – particularly areas such as St Marys and Mitchell – has frequently been flagged as a hotspot for radicalisation, with concerns over the spread of extremist ideologies through online networks and community tensions. The younger suspect, a 15-year-old, is believed to be in a preventative stage of investigation, with authorities likely assessing any potential links to existing or former extremist groups. The 20-year-old, who is fully aware of his legal rights, is expected to face formal charges in the coming days. A number of nearby mosques and community leaders have also been urged to assist in ongoing investigations, as authorities seek to widen their understanding of possible networks. Local MP Adam Crouch praised the police operation, stating that such raids are a necessary tool in the fight against terrorism. “Terrorism knows no borders and must be met with the full force of the law,” he said. However, some community representatives warned against the stigmatisation of religious and ethnic groups in the wake of such operations.

Greece could plunge into “uncontrolled economic chaos” if it fails to agree spending cuts and defaults on its debts, Prime Minister Lucas Papademos has warned in a stark assessment that underlines the growing fragility of the country’s financial situation.
