Speaking before a crucial European summit aimed at resolving the crisis, Mr. Papademos urged Greece’s political and social partners to support the government’s reform programme and avoid the social unrest that has been simmering in the streets since the country’s deepening austerity measures were imposed. In a televised address to the nation, Mr. Papademos said that the Greek government had run out of options and that a failure to implement the required reforms would trigger a wave of financial losses, bank failures and a humanitarian crisis. “The time of illusions is over,” he said, stressing that Greece could not afford to cling to the demands of the opposition or risk falling further into the abyss. Mr. Papademos added that while the proposed reforms would be "painful", they were necessary in order to avert a catastrophe and to preserve the Greek economy within the eurozone. His warnings come as the International Monetary Fund continues to press Greece for assurances that it will meet the conditions of a €130 billion (£108 billion) credit facility. Earlier on Thursday, Greece’s parliament backed a bill approving further cuts to public spending and staff reductions in national institutions – but it stopped short of approving €5.2 billion in additional savings announced by the government in March. Finance Minister Evangelos Venizelos said the failure to pass the full savings package would delay Greece’s access to an emergency loan tranche of €8.2 billion, which had already been approved in principle by the IMF and the European Union. Meanwhile, as Greece scrambles to meet its financial obligations, banks have been placed under strict capital controls, severely limiting the amount of cash citizens can withdraw from ATMs. There have also been reports that the European Central Bank is considering whether to continue supporting Greece’s collapsing banking sector. The European Commission has described Greece’s ability to meet its obligations as “a race against the clock”. With the country due to make a repayment of €5.9 billion to the IMF on 17 July, pressure is mounting for a breakthrough in the negotiations over a new multi-year bailout programme. Some analysts believe that without additional support, Greece will be forced to either default or exit the eurozone entirely – potentially triggering a financial catastrophe not just for Greece, but for the wider EU.

A former director of public prosecutions (DPP) has revealed he was never informed about an ongoing investigation into historical child sex abuse allegations against the late Labour peer, Lord Graham Janner. Sir David Calvert-Smith, who held the role from 2013 to 2018, made the startling admission in a recent statement that has reignited concerns over the handling of historic sex abuse cases within the UK justice system. Janner, a Labour MP from 1977 until his death in 2019, was the subject of longstanding allegations of sexual abuse involving children. The claims, which first emerged in the 1990s, led to multiple police inquiries, but no formal prosecution was ever brought, and Janner was never made a registered sex offender. The National Crime Agency confirmed last year that it had begun a formal investigation into the case following fresh allegations and historical documents. The latest revelation from Sir David, who is expected to leave his post as DPP in the coming weeks, has raised serious questions about the accountability and transparency of the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS). In a statement to the media, he said: "I can confirm that I was never informed of the investigation into Lord Janner during my time as DPP. If I had been, I would have expected to be asked for advice on the circumstances and whether it was appropriate for the case to proceed." The admission follows months of scrutiny surrounding the Janner case, particularly after The Times revealed in January 2022 that Janner had abused children in toilets and bedrooms in Leicestershire in the 1970s and 80s. Documents obtained under the Freedom of Information Act later showed that as early as 1999, police in Leicester had concluded Janner was "most likely" a sex offender, but the Crown Prosecution Service had declined to take action. This failsafe admission by Sir David has prompted calls for an independent investigation into how cases of historical abuse are handled by the CPS and whether institutional failings are preventing justice for victims. Shadow Justice Secretary Emily Thornberry said: "This is deeply concerning. How can we have confidence in our justice system if such major cases are being missed or not communicated to senior officials?" The National Crime Agency confirmed it was aware of the recent allegations and was continuing its inquiry into Janner. A spokesperson stated: "Our investigation is ongoing and we are working closely with other agencies. While we cannot comment on the specifics of individual cases, the pursuit of justice remains our priority."

The UK must have "full control" of its borders and territorial waters after Brexit, UKIP has said as it set out six tests for Prime Minister Theresa May as she prepares to begin the process of leaving the EU. In a stark message to the government, UKIP leader Nigel Farage and his party have outlined a series of demands they say must be met if the UK is to leave the EU on terms that reflect the will of the majority voted in the June referendum. At the heart of these demands is the restoration of full sovereignty, a key issue that played a central role in the Leave campaign and which the party insists can only be achieved under stringent conditions. UKIP said it does not support a "half-Brexit" scenario and has ruled out backing any version of a deal that keeps the UK in the single market or the jurisdiction of the European Court of Justice. Instead, the party is pushing for the government to take an unambiguous stance on independence from the EU institutions, including the prime minister triggering Article 50 — the formal process for leaving the union — by the end of March 2017. The six demands, which will be formally outlined in a document later this week, include ensuring that the UK has a “no deal rather than a bad deal” approach to Brexit negotiations and that it does not agree to future payments from the UK to the EU – known as a “divorce bill.” Further, the party wants the UK to withdraw from the European Economic Area (EEA) and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), which they claim would allow someone currently in the EU to move to the UK unilaterally without UK government approval. Commenting on the border issue, a UKIP spokesperson stated: “The British public voted to take back control because they have had enough of bureaucrats in Brussels deciding who can come into the UK and who can't. To be handing over even part of that authority to EU institutions would undermine the whole purpose of Brexit.” The statement comes at a time when the government is under mounting pressure to clarify its position on economic partnerships and future trade relations. Industry leaders and some members of the Conservative Party have called for a “smooth” Brexit that avoids economic turbulence, but UKIP insists that this must not come at the cost of political sovereignty.

Colin Kazim-Richards scored a dramatic late goal to send Blackburn Rovers into the FA Cup quarter-finals and heap further embarrassment on Arsène Wenger’s underperforming Arsenal side at Ewood Park on Monday evening. The Belgium international netted in the 89th minute to snatch a 2-1 victory against the Premier League’s outsiders and ignite jubilant celebrations among the home fans. Kazim-Richards, making his first start of the season under interim manager Tony Mowbray, was the unlikely hero of a momentous occasion that underlined the unravelling nature of Arsenal’s season. Arsenal, who remain in the upper half of the Premier League table, had made a strong start, with Granit Xhaka scoring in the 22nd minute following a swift counter-attack. The Gunners looked destined to see out the match, with their more illustrious Premier League pedigree appearing to take hold in the second half. However, Blackburn, playing in only their third FA Cup fifth-round match in 34 years, showed the resilience and spirit of a team fighting for survival in the Championship. Substitute Jason Lowe, who came on with just 20 minutes remaining, struck the equaliser two minutes into his cameo to set the stage for Kazim-Richards’s decisive late intervention. The striker, who has only scored once in 15 appearances this season, rose highest to head in Mitchell Dijks’s cross and send his side through to the last eight. The goal will be remembered not only for its timing but for the stark contrast in fortunes between the two clubs. Blackburn, sitting 20th in the Championship and nine points clear of the relegation zone, continued their improbable FA Cup run, having defeated West Bromwich, Fulham, and most notably, Premier League outfit Stoke City in the previous rounds. Arsenal, by contrast, returned to a growing sense of unease among their supporters. The Gunners have lost three of their last five games and, despite their FA Cup victories over Manchester United and Liverpool earlier in the season, have failed to replicate that momentum in any competition. Speaking after the match, Mowbray praised the “courage and organisation” of his team as they defied the odds with their latest dramatic FA Cup upset. “That’s the FA Cup, you don’t get these opportunities very often,” the former West Brom and Middlesbrough boss said. “The lads have worked tirelessly, and it’s a reward for their belief in each other.”

The Royal Bank of Scotland has confirmed that the new £5 note, to be launched later this year, will feature the image of Nan Shepherd, the renowned Scottish novelist and poet, whose literary contributions have long been celebrated within the UK and beyond. The announcement has been met with widespread acclaim from readers, academics, and cultural figures who see Shepherd’s selection as a fitting tribute to a writer whose work continues to inspire generations. Nan Shepherd, who lived from 1893 to 1981, is best known for her classic work,  The Living Mountain , a lyrical account of her walks in the Cairngorm mountains. Considered one of the seminal texts of environmental and nature writing, the book has been hailed as a powerful meditation on the landscape of the Scottish Highlands and the spiritual connection between humans and the natural world. Unlike more traditional works of the time,  The Living Mountain  blends poetic description with deep philosophical insight, offering a portrayal of the mountains not as a backdrop for adventure, but as a living entity deserving of reverence and understanding. Her selection as the figure on the new £5 note was part of a public consultation process that saw thousands of nominations, with Shepherd ultimately chosen from a shortlist that included other prominent Scottish writers, scientists, and humanitarians. The RBS has stated that Shepherd was selected for her “enduring cultural legacy and her national significance – not only as a writer, but as a woman who defied the expectations of her time.” Speaking about the decision, the bank’s head of marketing said: “We are delighted to be able to celebrate someone who represents the best of Scottish literature. Nan Shepherd embodies the spirit of creativity, resilience, and deep connection to the land that defines much of our national identity.” The new £5 note will continue to use the same polymer material as previous issues, with enhanced security features such as a holographic window and a see-through panel. In addition to Shepherd’s portrait, the design is expected to incorporate imagery inspired by the mountains, flora, and fauna depicted in her writing. For many, the choice reflects a growing recognition of the value of women in the cultural and historical record. It is only the second time a woman has appeared on an RBS banknote, following in the footsteps of J.K. Rowling, the author of the Harry Potter series, who appeared on a special 25th anniversary note in 2017.

Three men from South Wales have been sentenced to prison for playing pivotal roles in assisting a Cardiff teenager to travel to Syria and join a jihadist group linked to Islamic extremism. The men, whose identities have been withheld due to the sensitive nature of the case, were found guilty of supporting terrorism, and their actions have sparked fresh concerns about how vulnerable youth can be radicalised and encouraged to travel to conflict zones. The teenager, now in his early twenties, is believed to have been groomed online before the trio facilitated his journey to Syria in 2018. Court documents revealed that the men provided logistical support and funding for the journey, which included arranging safe passage through Turkey into the war-torn country. They also encouraged and advised the young man, reinforcing extremist ideologies during the weeks that led up to his departure. The case forms part of a growing number of prosecutions involving British citizens who have either joined or supported terrorist activities abroad. The Home Secretary condemned the men’s actions, saying: “These individuals exploited a vulnerable young person and played a direct role in his criminal departure to Syria to commit acts of terrorism, putting not only their own lives at risk but also those of others.” During the trial, prosecutors presented evidence that one of the three men had expressed strong sympathy for extremist ideologies and had previously voiced intentions to travel to Syria himself. Another had been known to circulate extremist material on social media. The judge described their actions as a “serious and dangerous act of betrayal” of British values and national security. A spokesperson for the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said the case highlighted the ongoing challenge in identifying and preventing the radicalisation of young people: “We are seeing increasingly sophisticated methods used by extremists to identify and engage with vulnerable individuals, and these three men played an essential role in that process.” The Prime Minister also commented on the verdict, reiterating the government's commitment to tackling terrorism at its roots. "We will not tolerate anyone who encourages or supports terrorist acts, no matter their role in the process," she said. "We must remain vigilant against those who seek to undermine the peace and security of our country." The sentencing is expected to send a strong message to would-be facilitators of such journeys, while security services continue to warn parents and teachers to be alert to the signs of radicalisation among young people.

The Democratic Republic of Congo’s (DRC) presidential election, held on 28 November, has delivered a contested and fragile victory for incumbent President Joseph Kabila, casting doubt on the legitimacy of his path to securing a third term in office. Official results, announced late last month, declared Kabila the winner with over 45% of the vote, a triumph that appears both narrow and legally dubious under his own country’s constitution. Article 73 of the DRC’s constitution explicitly prohibits a sitting president from seeking a third term, a rule Kabila’s political allies ignored in the lead-up to the election when his Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party pushed hastily through a bill to amend the law and pave the way for his candidacy. The controversial legislation, which was passed without public debate and left significant gaps in the electoral framework, has been heavily criticized by opposition parties and civil society groups. The election was also marred by widespread logistical failures, voter intimidation, and allegations of systematic fraud. Anglophone regions in the east and south, which account for 40% of the population, reported severe underrepresentation due to voting delays and poll cancellations, leading many to accuse the government of manipulating demographic distributions in its favor. International observers, including human rights groups and non-partisan monitoring bodies, have also raised concerns over irregularities, from staff shortages staffing national polling stations to党总支部 seemingly coordinating voter suppression in areas that historically oppose Kabila’s ruling coalition. The opposition presidential candidate, Martin Fayulu, was the first to challenge the results, rejecting the outcome as “unconstitutional and illegitimate” and insisting that his own polling stations had counted more votes than ballots issued—evidence of widespread ballot stuffing. Fayulu and his supporters have called for a rerun in the excluded regions and have lodged legal challenges through the DRC’s Constitutional Court. Yet, despite this mounting pressure and a growing civil disobedience movement among young Congolese who reject Kabila’s continued rule, there have been no clear signs of the kind of large-scale protests that led to the country’s historic 2015 political crisis. Nonetheless, the political tension is palpable, with fear that pro-UDPS forces could resort to coercion to secure a sustained Kabila regime. Analysts warn that the embattled state of the DRC’s judiciary, where Kabila-aligned figures hold the most powerful seats, means judicial routes for challenging the vote may be fraught or ineffective.

The UK government has written to a number of high street retailers, urging them to make significant improvements to better accommodate disabled customers, following a BBC London investigation that exposed a “depressing” lack of accessibility across several popular stores. The findings, which follow months of covert filming and interviews, reveal consistent failures in basic accessibility measures, from step-free access to clear signage, prompting ministers to issue an urgent call to action. In a letter addressed to a range of major retailers, including well-known supermarket and clothing chain brands, the Department for Business, Energy, and Industrial Strategy (BEIS) cited the Equality Act 2010 and highlighted the legal responsibility of businesses to ensure access for all, including those with disabilities. The letter also stresses the importance of treating inclusivity not just as a legal obligation, but as an opportunity to reflect the diverse needs of the population. The BBC investigation focused on locations across London and the south-east of England, assembling a team of trained undercover reporters and disabled individuals to visit more than 50 stores over a period of several weeks. Their reports showed a worrying pattern of accessibility problems. One woman using a wheelchair described being unable to enter a store without help, while screen reader users struggled to navigate websites that lacked necessary alt-text. Others described discriminatory treatment when requesting assistance with changing facilities or in-store services. British Retail Consortium (BRC) chair Steve Rowe responded to the findings by acknowledging that improvements are needed and that the sector is committed to “making shopping accessible and welcoming for everyone.” He added that many retailers are already working closely with disability organisations to assess and improve their offerings. However, campaigners remain unconvinced. Emma Fry, a founding member of the Access Now campaign, stated, “It's not acceptable for this to be an isolated issue in 2024. Equality laws exist for a reason. We need real enforcement, not just letters.” The government has said it is preparing a detailed review of how compliant retail outlets are with accessibility standards, with a view to introducing stricter monitoring and potential penalties for non-compliant businesses. As discussions around disability rights and accessibility continue to gain momentum, public expectations are quickly shifting—and with them, the need for immediate and meaningful action by the high street giants. The question now is not whether retailers are able to improve, but whether they are willing to do so.

The mother of a Scottish man who has gone missing in Amsterdam has claimed he sent her a text message just an hour before he vanished, confessing he was feeling overwhelmed with homesickness. Gary Dows, a 24-year-old from Kilmarnock, Ayrshire, is reported to have last been seen in the city’s bustling centre on the evening of Wednesday 2 October. His family has launched an appeal for information as they grow increasingly worried for his safety. Mrs Dows, who has not been named, said she was concerned by the sudden emotional tone of her son’s message. “He said he missed Scotland and the family terribly,” she said. “The next thing I heard was that no one had seen him since.” Gary, who is in the Netherlands working as a bartender, had only arrived in Amsterdam a week before his disappearance, according to friends. Gary’s brother, Ewan Dows, has urged anyone with information to come forward. “He’s a very straightforward person, always keeps in touch,” Ewan said. “It’s unlike him not to check in, even if he was feeling down. That’s why we’re so worried.” Local police have confirmed they are treating the case with urgency and have begun reviewing CCTV footage from the city’s Leidseplein area, where Gary was last seen. The AFP international taskforce has been contacted to assist in the search, with officers collaborating with local authorities in the Netherlands. Gary is described as white, of average build, and approximately 6 feet tall. He was last seen wearing a red t-shirt, blue jeans and black trainers. He speaks fluent English and some Dutch, according to colleagues. Friends said Gary had recently taken up a job in the bar and was looking forward to meeting new people and seeing more of the city. “It must have been a shock to move to such a different place so suddenly,” one said. “We thought he was doing well.” An online search for Gary has been launched by friends, with a ‘Find Gary Dows’ Facebook page set up to spread the word and track sightings. His family is holding out hope that he may have simply lost his way or run into temporary trouble while out wandering the city. As the clock ticks, Gary’s family remains desperate to hear from anyone who may have spotted him since his disappearance. “He’s a loving son and a good man,” Ewan Dows said.

In a dramatic move that marks a significant new chapter in Australia’s political landscape, right-wing Senator Cory Bernardi has broken ranks with the national government and established his own political party, the Australian Conservatives. This bold decision, announced publicly last week, is expected to have far-reaching consequences for the ruling Coalition and the broader political discourse in the nation. Bernardi, a long-standing critic of both the Liberal Party and the government’s foreign policy, particularly on matters related to China and climate change policy, has long argued for a more principled and economically liberal alternative in Australian politics. His departure from the Senate—and from the Coalition—has been eagerly anticipated by those who have supported his vision for a new, fiscally responsible and constitutionally focused political movement. The new Australian Conservatives party is set to be officially launched later this month and is expected to draw support from traditional Liberal voters who are disenchanted with the direction of the current government. Bernardi has promised to champion free enterprise, individual liberties, and a more robust Australian national interest, which includes a hardline stance on immigration and an unwavering commitment to economic reform. He has also warned against what he describes as “cultural Marxism” and “the erosion of Western values,” themes that have been a focus of his speeches and writings for years. Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull welcomed the news with cautious optimism, describing it as “a personal decision” for Bernardi but one that would not significantly impact the government’s legislative agenda. However, political analysts suggest the new party could complicate Coalition affairs, potentially splits votes in key electorates and may even disrupt Coalition parliamentary support in the Senate. Many have doubted whether a new political force can gain a foothold in a deeply entrenched two-party system, but Bernardi is unshaken in his ambition. “This is not about personality, nor is it about fulfilling any personal ambition,” Bernardi said in a recent statement. “It is about the need for an Australian political party that is firmly planted in the values of economic freedom, constitutional integrity, and the dignity of hard work and individual enterprise.” As his new party moves to formalise its platform and begin recruiting members and candidates, Australia is bracing itself for a new wave of political contestation and ideological division. With a sustained focus on challenging what he describes as “the Canberra consensus,” Bernardi is determined to set a new course for Australian politics—one that, he believes, will restore national confidence and direction.

Amid the recriminations that so swiftly followed America's third successive Ryder Cup defeat two years ago, there seemed to be a consensus that a fresher approach was needed to halt the US decline in these biennial matches. A nation long proud of producing some of the world’s greatest golfers—Arnold Palmer, Jack Nicklaus, Tiger Woods—had now lost the tournament three times in a row and was losing ground not just on the scoreboard but in the confidence departments too. The event in Paris in 2018, watched by millions, ended in embarrassment and finger-pointing, leaving US golf fans to ask whether the team's traditional methods were fit for purpose. In response, the PGA of America, the governing body responsible for choosing the US captain and team captain for the Ryder Cup, has embarked on a wide-ranging review of team structure, captain selection, and the broader philosophy of how the squad is prepared for Europe’s challenge. For far too long, the US team, often led by past champions and heavy hitters from the PGA Tour, has relied on the belief that talent, pedigree and flash will carry the day. That model, built on decades of American golfing dominance—culminating in a 22-12 victory in 2008 when the US team still had a draw on domestic golf—and faltered badly in the face of a more relentless European approach that prioritises team strategy, data and, crucially, a deeper understanding of the subtleties of match play. The changing face of global golf is another factor at play. Europe’s dominance in this period has come in part from the meteoric rise of a new generation of players, many of them from outside the UK—Finland’s Henrik Stenson, Spain’s Jon Rahm, Switzerland’s Adrian Meronk, and Sweden’s Ludvig Åberg. These players, raised watching Tiger Woods and progressing through what is considered the continent’s more varied amateur and European Tour development system, bring a level of composure, adaptability and resilience that the US often struggles to match. For his part, 2023 US captain Billy Horschel, who took over from Pat Payne following a controversial selection process, has been heralded as a new type of leader: one who is a player-turned-captain with first-hand recent experience of competing at the highest level. This shift in the captaincy away from the more traditional choices—fine golfers but often older heads who had become stars in the 1990s or earlier—has been accompanied by a concerted effort to foster unity, fluency and bold, unifying team culture.

Survivor of 7/7 Terror Attacks Bares Her New Face   FIVE years after one of the darkest days in recent British history, a woman who suffered horrific facial burns during the 7/7 terror attacks in London has bravely unveiled the face she has built from the ashes of tragedy. The courageous step marks a milestone in her long and arduous journey of both physical and emotional reconstruction. Zara Bashir, 35, became one of the 52 innocent victims who lost their lives or were left with life-changing injuries as a result of the coordinated suicide bombings on London's public transport network on July 7, 2005. During the attack on a northbound No. 30 double-decker bus near Tavistock Square, Zara suffered extensive third-degree burns across her face and body, requiring multiple reconstructive surgeries over the past decade. In a world first for post-terror attack facial reconstruction, Zara has undergone pioneering procedures using advanced tissue grafting and microsurgery in operations at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital in London and, more recently, at the Royal Centre for Defense Medicine in Birmingham. Today, with the help of a dedicated team of plastic surgeons and psychologists, she is ready to step out and embrace public life once again. Speaking ahead of the launch of a new documentary following her recovery, Zara said she no longer wants to be defined solely by what happened on that fateful morning: “When the world remembers the attack, I hope they also see the strength and resilience of the people affected by it. There are people out there who have rebuilt their lives against incredible odds. I’m just one of them.” Her recovery was not without its challenges. After the initial trauma and being whisked away to specialist trauma centers in London, Zara spent about a year in and out of hospital undergoing the painstaking process of reconstruction. The first few years were particularly difficult as she grappled with her new appearance and the unrelenting stares that often followed her in public. But rather than retreat, she decided to fight for her right to live life on her own terms. “I was scared to look in the mirror for a long time,” she said. “But as time has gone on, I’ve come to accept that my face is not what I was born with – it’s what I’m becoming. This is not just a new face, it's a new beginning.”

The International Criminal Court is to open a new investigation into allegations that British troops abused Iraqi detainees during the 2003-2009 occupation of Iraq. The announcement has reignited long-standing controversy over the conduct of UK forces and is expected to raise serious questions about the accountability of military personnel for war crimes. The ICC’s preliminary examination, which has been under consideration for some time, will assess whether there is sufficient evidence to proceed with a full investigation. This marks the first time that the British government has faced the prospect of being scrutinised by the ICC under the Rome Statute, which the UK ratified in 2001 under the previous Labour government. The claims being investigated stem from a range of incidents involving the treatment of prisoners in centres such as Iraq’s Camp Cropper, where numerous detainees reportedly faced ill-treatment, including beatings, sleep deprivation and the use of dogs and sexual humiliation. Over 160 former soldiers, police officers and civil servants have come forward in recent years to allege that they witnessed or were ordered to carry out such abuses as part of a covert strategy to elicit intelligence from prisoners. One of the most high-profile cases involves former Royal Marine Captain Jonathan Ward, who was cleared in two civilian courts of allegedly using a dog to intimidate an Iraqi prisoner. However, he and others have since spoken publicly about a culture of impunity and the pressure to conform to tactics borrowed from the US military in Iraq. The Ministry of Defence has consistently denied any systematic abuse of Iraqi detainees and has previously refused to implement the recommendations of an independent inquiry, which found that there was a “culture of disregard” for international law. In a recent statement, the UK government said it “welcomes the ICC’s determination to ensure the rule of law is upheld where necessary” but stressed that it remains “confident that our armed forces have always carried out their duties according to the law and with a deep respect for fundamental human rights.” The ICC’s decision follows sustained pressure from campaigners, including relatives of abused detainees and human rights lawyers. Professor Jeremy Zucker, a former human rights advisor to the UN, said the move sent a “clear signal” that no country, including long-standing ICC members, is immune from international scrutiny over alleged crimes of war. The British Taliban trial of four former Royal Marines currently being held at Belmarsh Prison in London has also raised concerns around allegations of mistreatment during their early detention in Afghanistan.

The rollout of the UK’s future 5G mobile network must learn from the shortcomings of its predecessor, 4G, in order to be successful and meet growing consumer and business demand, according to a new report released by the House of Lords Select Committee on Communications. The report, published this week, highlights a number of key lessons from the 4G rollout, including delays in infrastructure deployment, confusion over coverage, and inconsistent experiences for users across the country. A committee member, Lord Charles Jenkin, stated that “the mistakes of the past must not be repeated as we prepare to enter the next mobile revolution.” The report comes at a crucial time as the UK moves to expand its 5G connectivity, with operators such as EE, Vodafone, and Three beginning to trial the technology in major cities including London, Manchester, and Birmingham. However, the findings from the committee argue that without a more strategically planned and co-ordinated approach, the rollout risks failing to deliver the widespread benefits that 5G has the potential to unlock – including in areas such as artificial intelligence, smart cities, and the Internet of Things. One of the report’s key recommendations is the need for greater collaboration between government, mobile network operators, and local councils in order to streamline planning permissions and speed up the deployment of 5G infrastructure. The committee also warns against fragmentation between different parts of the UK. It points to the fact that while the UK has a unified vision for 5G, the differing levels of development across England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland could hinder a cohesive national rollout. There are also concerns that rural areas may be left behind once again, just as they were with 4G. Some experts argue that this could exacerbate the digital divide and limit economic opportunities in less populated regions. The Prime Minister’s Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport has previously stated its commitment to ensuring the UK leads in global 5G development. Meanwhile, consumer advocate groups have called for greater transparency from mobile operators, arguing that customers should have clearer information on the availability and speed of 5G in their local areas. The report makes a pointed reference to previous criticism that 4G coverage maps were overly optimistic, with some users finding little or no signal in areas shown as fully covered.

The first victims of the devastating St Petersburg metro explosion have been officially identified as part of an ongoing investigation into the attack, which has left Russian authorities and the public searching for answers. The blasts, which occurred at an underground station in the heart of the city during the morning rush hour, killed at least 14 people and injured more than 50 others. As grief has spread across the city, where flowers and candles now line the site of the attack, investigators have begun to reveal the identities of those who lost their lives. Among the names released are that of Vladimir Loginov, a 56-year-old architect who worked for the city's public housing authority, and Anya Petrova, a 19-year-old student studying at St Petersburg State University. Her friends remembered her as “full of life and always smiling,” a young woman destined for a bright future. Darya Kovalchuk, a mother of two who regularly used the metro to commute to work, was also confirmed as a victim. Her family has since taken to social media to mourn her and share photographs of her with her young sons. While the authorities continue to identify the bodies—many of whom are believed to have been swept out of the station in the chaos—investigators remain focused on uncovering the identity of the person responsible for the attack. Over 100 officers from the Federal Security Service (FSB) have been deployed to the site, swabbing equipment, analysing surveillance footage and gathering witness statements. Russia’s Sila Komandirams (The Commanders’ Strength) group, suspected of being linked to the so-called Islamic State (ISIS), has claimed responsibility for the bombings. However, the FSB has continued to deny any direct involvement by foreign terrorist organisations, instead focusing on the possibility of a radicalised domestic attacker. The attack has brought renewed security concerns to Russia, which had enjoyed a period of relative calm following the acute Chechen conflict and the downing of the Moscow-Cairo airliner claimed by ISIS over the Sinai Peninsula in 2015. With fears growing among the public, the president has ordered a full review of city transport security, and special FSB units have been deployed to monitor major transit hubs. As the city grapples with this profound tragedy, memorials are now being planned, with hopes that the victims will not only be remembered but that the attack will lead to long-lasting improvements in security and safety.

A Muslim teacher who was denied entry to the United States during a school trip last month has revealed he was still in the dark about the reason behind the decision, fuelling concerns about rising concerns over ethnic and religious profiling at US borders. Ahmed Khan, 35, a respected chemistry teacher at a well-known private school in London, was abruptly turned away at Los Angeles International Airport on 15 March as part of an exchange programme with a high school in California. Mr Khan, who was accompanied by a group of students and staff, had arranged the visit under a long-standing academic ties agreement and held the necessary visas. According to Mr Khan, he went through standard customs and immigration checks when he was suddenly detained and released without explanation hours later. "I was given no reason, no documents, no warning. All I was told was that I wasn't allowed into the country and that was it," he said in an interview with The Times earlier this week. He added that, despite following up with both the US embassy in London and his university contact, he remains officially in the dark, even weeks after the incident. The episode has reignited controversy over the enforcement of the controversial US policy changes surrounding entry restrictions, particularly in the wake of heightened focus on national security. While no formal travel ban is in force, reports suggest that extra scrutiny is being applied to certain nationalities and – increasingly – individuals with Muslim names, backgrounds, or affiliations. A number of British universities and academic staff have expressed concern over the environment becoming “chilly” for international scholars, particularly those from Muslim-majority countries. London-based legal firm Manning Legal has seen a sharp increase in cases involving entry refusals, with some clients facing denials without being given grounds under US immigration law. John Hedges, a solicitor at Manning Legal who has worked on the case, said: “There is a troubling trend where people are being held for indefinite lengths of time and given no clarity as to why their application is refused. This is not just troubling for the individuals involved, but for the international academic community as a whole.” The US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) issued a statement on Thursday confirming the event had been logged but providing no specific details about individual entry denials. The agency reiterated its position that “all decisions are made consistently with US law and based on established protocols.”

Switzerland’s parliament has passed a controversial new bill that prioritises local jobseekers over EU nationals during periods of economic crisis or high unemployment, marking a significant shift in the country’s traditionally open immigration policy. The legislation, which received a broad parliamentary endorsement earlier this week, allows the government to restrict access to certain sectors of the job market for foreign workers if Swiss unemployment exceeds 6%. The threshold puts Switzerland at odds with its own self-positioning as a hub of free movement and international cooperation, as well as with its obligations under agreements with the European Union. According to the terms of the bill, once unemployment among Swiss citizens rises beyond the 6% threshold, the government will have authority to impose temporary hiring preferences for Swiss nationals and residents, effectively placing EU job applicants at a disadvantage. This move is framed by supporters as a safeguard against the erosion of domestic job security amid fluctuations in the economy, and as a necessary measure to protect Swiss workers in times of scarcity. However, it has drawn sharp criticism from Swiss business leaders and EU officials, who argue that the decision risks damaging Switzerland's strong, long-standing economic ties with the EU and undermines the flexibility of its workforce. Switzerland, despite not being a full EU member, maintains close relations with the bloc as part of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA). It has historically benefited from the freedoms of movement, services, and trade that come with this agreement. But the new bill brings into question the sustainability of these relationships. The EU has repeatedly voiced concerns over Switzerland’s tendency to selectively implement or ignore EU agreements when it suits domestic political interests, and this latest measure may deepen those tensions. In a statement, the Swiss Interior Minister, Albert Rösti, defended the bill as a pragmatic response to economic realities. “This measure is not against the EU, but in favour of Swiss jobs and social stability,” he said. Yet many economists and analysts fear that a perceived lack of access to foreign talent could deter investment and stifle growth, particularly in sectors that have come to rely on European workers. The education, hospitality, and technology industries, among others, have already flagged concerns about any potential setbacks to recruitment. The bill marks the latest chapter in a protracted national debate about immigration and national identity in Switzerland, which has seen a steady rise in right-wing sentiment in recent years.

There is no doubt that Kenya has been deeply scarred by the attack on the University in Garissa, in which at least 148 people were killed by four armed militants affiliated with the Al-Shabaab terror group. The massacre, which took place over two days in the coastal town of Garissa, has left a wound in the heart of the nation, as more than 300 students gathered at the university—many of them Muslim—became targets in what is the country's worst terror incident in recent history. The brutal violence, which saw the attackers initially demanding the release of Somali prisoners before turning their fury on the students under the mistaken belief that they were non-Muslim, shocked the entire world and prompted national and international debate on Kenya’s security and its foreign policy in Somalia. On Monday, Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta led the country in mourning, with flags flown at half-mast and government buildings closed in a sombre display of unity. Religious leaders, politicians and ordinary citizens alike gathered in Nairobi and Garissa to offer their condolences, prayers and solidarity to the families of the victims. The attack has once again reignited questions about the presence of Kenyan troops in Somalia, where they are part of the African Union Mission as part of the fight against Al-Shabaab. President Kenyatta, during a national address on Friday, vowed “to dismantle the cells operating within our borders” and praised the Kenyan military’s role in “making sure no region of the world is safe for terrorism.” However, the tragedy has also sparked calls for a review of Kenyan security protocols, especially in educational institutions. Critics have pointed to the scale of the attack as an indictment of the government’s failure to prevent such an atrocity. Marginalised Muslim communities in the north-east of the country expressed fears that the attack would be followed by backlash or discrimination, but prominent Muslim and Christian leaders have urged unity and condemned the violence. One father, whose son died in the attack, said he found solace in the response of Kenyans nationwide. “It was supposed to divide us, but instead it has made us stronger,” he said. The victims, whose ages ranged from 18 to 24, have been described by colleagues as respectful, hardworking and “hurried to do the right thing.” Their loss has sent a profound message across Kenya and the wider African continent: that terror cannot be stopped by force alone, but requires sustained dialogue, education and, above all, inclusion.

The government is moving to clarify its plans for an English votes for English laws (EVEL) system, as former Commons leader Chris Grayling confirmed the decision to delay a key parliamentary vote to September. This comes after years of political debate over how to ensure English MPs have a decisive say in laws affecting only England, addressing concerns that devolved Scottish and Welsh MPs were influencing English-only policies. In a statement on Wednesday, Mr Grayling, who is a leading figure in shaping the reforms, said that the government needed to provide further clarification to MPs to ensure there was a “full and informed debate” before the mechanism was implemented. “We are committed to ensuring that English MPs have a clear voice in matters that uniquely affect England,” he said, adding that the delayed vote would allow time for cross-party discussions and further parliamentary scrutiny. The EVEL system was first introduced on a trial basis in 2015 in the aftermath of the EU referendum, which highlighted the lack of a clear mechanism for distinguishing English votes from those of devolved areas on matters not devolved to Wales or Scotland. The trial, which affected only a few non-devolved issues, was met with strong opposition from Scottish National Party (SNP) MPs, who argued that the changes undermined the integrity of the House of Commons and violated the principle of parliamentary sovereignty. The SNP has warned that a fully-fledged EVEL system would effectively disenfranchise Scottish MPs from voting on English-only issues, and has pledged to block its implementation by any means necessary. Labour, meanwhile, has called for a constitutional commission to oversee the process, arguing that such a significant change to the workings of Parliament should not be rush-driven by the government. Mr Grayling’s announcement is seen as a pragmatic response to these concerns. “This delay is not about indecision, but about about ensuring that our system is robust, balanced, and equitable,” he said. “The goal is not to create division, but to restore trust in the democratic process.” As preparations continue for the rescheduled vote, the debate over the English votes bill will once again dominate parliamentary sessions, with MPs from all sides holding strong views on how the UK’s constitutional framework should evolve in the post-Brexit era. The issue raises broader questions of devolution, English identity, and the role of the UK Parliament in an increasingly divided nation.

Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola has dismissed speculation surrounding his relationship with Manchester United counterpart Jose Mourinho, promising to shake the Portuguese’s hand at their upcoming pre-season derby in Beijing. The match, part of football’s annual summer tour in Asia, is highly anticipated not just for the competitiveness it is expected to generate on the pitch but also for the continued on-field and off-field tensions between the two high-profile managers. Guardiola, in a statement released on Thursday ahead of the game, said he saw no reason to deviate from tradition. “When we play, we go to win, but the handshakes before and after the match are always done with respect,” he said. “Football is united by these gestures. I will offer the same respect to Jose Mourinho that I expect from him.” The pair have long shared an uneasy rapport. Their rivalry, which has reached its peak in recent years, began during Guardiola’s tenure at Bayern Munich and Mourinho’s time at Real Madrid. It intensified when both arrived in England, with Guardiola at Manchester City and Mourinho at Manchester United. Their interactions have often been marked by cryptic remarks and mutual public critiques, none more famous than Mourinho’s description of Guardiola as a “teacher” during a Champions League semi-final in 2016. Mourinho has yet to respond to Guardiola’s latest comments, but the rivalry between the two giants of modern management continues to be a focal point for fans and pundits alike. The Beijing match is set to take place on Monday and will be the first of two pre-season games between the two teams this summer, with the second scheduled for later in the month in Singapore. With both sides looking to build momentum ahead of the 2023/24 Premier League season, the game promises to be a pivotal clash not only for points on the board but for morale and the prestige of one of football’s most iconic rivalries. Speculation continues over whether the two managers will take it upon themselves to escalate their war of words, but for now, Guardiola has put an end to any expectations of frosty diplomacy on the day of the event. “Football is intense,” he said. “But there is always room to respect the profession and our fellow players and colleagues.” Whether Mourinho will follow suit and join the diplomatic overture remains to be seen.

A damning review into the deaths of two schoolboys and a teacher has revealed that police may have averted the tragedy if they had thoroughly checked the killer’s background when earlier complaints were made about his behaviour, a report released today has revealed. The inquiry, commissioned by the Home Office, underscores serious failings in the handling of intelligence by local and national law enforcement agencies, prompting calls for urgent reform in how potential threats are assessed. The incident in question occurred in a quiet town in northern England earlier this year, where Connor Timmins, 16, Liam Kelly, 14, and their maths teacher, Steven Price, 38, were killed by a fellow student, Aaron Marshall, 17. Marshall, who had a history of volatility and had been recently excluded from school, carried out the attack after weeks of bursts of anger and disturbing behaviour had gone largely unaddressed, the report said. The review concluded that had police carried out a more robust background check following a complaint made by a school counsellor in December — in which she raised concerns about Marshall’s “escalating paranoia and desire for revenge” — the public could have been warned and steps taken to prevent the killings. "Multiple warning signs were ignored or downplayed," said one anonymous official involved in the review, who spoke to the  Times . "If proper due diligence had been carried out, it is highly likely that Aaron Marshall would have been prevented from accessing weapons and entering school grounds unchallenged." Speaking after the report was published, Education Secretary Damian Green said the findings were “deeply troubling” and vowed that lessons would be learned. “This is a stark reminder of how critical it is that school staff and police communicate more effectively when red flags arise,” he said in a brief statement. The review also found that police in question did not flag any previous incidents of self-harm or cyber-bullying carried out by Marshall, and fails to connect his online activity — which included researching weapons and sending threatening messages to the teacher — with real-world threats. National education unions have passed on a growing sense of anxiety among teachers, who feel increasingly isolated when dealing with violent or threatening students, without sufficient resources or support from law enforcement to warn others. As reactions to the report mount, calls are increasing for a new nationwide protocol to assess risky student behaviour, coupled with additional training for school staff and police.

A man found guilty of raping a 12-year-old girl has been released from court after the judge ruled he would serve his sentence in Indonesia, rather than in the UK, under international legal agreements. The shocking case, which has sparked widespread outrage in the UK, has raised serious questions about how such a decision can be justified for a crime of this severity. The defendant, a British national, was sentenced to 12 years in an Indonesian prison after pleading guilty in a London Crown Court in May. His victim, a young schoolgirl from Somerset, was approached under false pretences and lured into a situation where the assault occurred. Sentencing him to a UK prison was ruled impracticable because the man is British and the crime, although committed abroad, was brought to the courts via an extradition request from an Indonesian prosecutor. Under the principle of 'double criminality,' the crime must be prosecutable in both the country where it was committed and the country where the defendant resides. As such, British courts have been bound to uphold the conviction within Indonesia’s legal system. Court documents revealed that, even though the defendant was drug-dependent and had previously struggled with mental health issues, the crime remained one of extreme seriousness. The impacts of the crime on the child have left lasting psychological scars, and her family has spoken of their devastation. “This is a deeply worrying situation,” said one local councillor, who wished to remain anonymous. “The fact that he will not be serving his sentence in the UK sends the wrong message and undermines the justice system in the eyes of the community.” The Justice Secretary has also faced calls to review policies surrounding the extradition of citizens to countries where prison conditions may not meet the standards accepted in the UK. Criticisms have also been levelled at the Home Office for its role in facilitating the repatriation of criminals to nations where the justice systems are often less transparent or less humane. The case is likely to reignite calls for reform to ensure that British nationals, particularly those convicted of child sex offences, cannot evade the UK prison system by claiming citizenship. Victims' rights groups and MPs have demanded a review of existing extradition agreements, particularly those with countries where prison conditions or human rights protections fall below UK standards. In the wake of this controversial sentence, the Ministry of Justice has been urged to clarify its policy on such cases.

Labour Pledges ‘Credible’ Immigration Measures Within 100 Days of Office, Says Miliband   Labour has set out its clearest timeline yet for reforming immigration policy, with leader Ed Miliband vowing to introduce a “credible” set of measures within 100 days of taking office after the next general election. The pledge, announced ahead of a party meeting in Birmingham, signals a shift in Labour’s approach to a historically thorny issue and comes amid growing calls for a post-Brexit immigration strategy that is both reasonable and sustainable. Miliband, speaking to reporters at the event, said the party would not adopt a “copy-and-paste” version of Conservative policies, but instead focus on creating an immigration system that “works for the economy, protects public services, and is fair and inclusive.” He did not provide details on what the measures would entail, but suggested they would be shaped by an independent review to be launched ahead of an election, with a prime ministerial candidate likely to be announced in late summer. The announcement marks a significant moment for the party, which has long struggled to reconcile its pro-migration stance with the dominant political narrative of recent years that has favored stricter immigration controls. Miliband said that Labour would look to integrate migration into broader economic planning, ensuring that skilled workers can move to the UK when services and industries require them, while also addressing public concerns about housing, school places, and the pressure on welfare systems. Miliband also sought to distance Labour from the controversial “points-based” system introduced by the coalition and expanded by the Tories, which he said “does not work” in a post-Brexit world. “The challenge now is to have a system that is practical and flexible,” he said. “We need a system that manages migration, not mismanages it.” The commitment to act within 100 days appears aimed at securing the support of centrist and Leave-voting voters who have long viewed immigration as a critical test of Labour’s credibility. Miliband acknowledged the high stakes of the issue, saying: “The effectiveness of any government is judged on whether it can deliver on immigration. It’s not a side issue. It’s a central one.” While the details remain to be seen, Miliband’s speech suggests Labour is moving toward an evidence-based, responsive approach, something that has eluded the party in the past. The 100-day promise breaks new ground for Labour, which has traditionally avoided setting out concrete timetables on contentious policy proposals.

Disgraced former world snooker champion Stephen Lee is hoping to turn a new leaf by inspiring the next generation of players in China, where the sport is growing in popularity. Despite being banned for life from snooker over match-fixing charges in 2010, the 48-year-old Englishman has begun working with Chinese junior players as part of a development programme aimed at nurturing local talent. Lee's return to the world of snooker, albeit in a coaching capacity, has sparked mixed reactions. While some former opponents and officials remain critical of his past transgressions, others acknowledge that his knowledge, experience and passion for the game could still benefit young players. The Chinese Billiards and Snooker Association (CBSA) has stressed that its focus is on developing technical and mental skills, and that participation in the programme does not imply any endorsement of Lee’s past conduct. Lee, who turned professional in 1992 and reached the World Championship final in 2005 before his historic ban for betting-related criminal conduct, admitted five charges in total, including indulging in fixed matches and transmitting confidential information. He was stripped of one of his three ranking titles, and his place in snooker history has been tarnished by the scandal. However, since the ban, he has pursued other interests, including charity work, and now sees a future in coaching. “I’m not trying to make a comeback as a player,” Lee said in a recent interview. “I just want to help young people who love this game. I’ve made terrible mistakes in my life, but I still believe in the values of snooker — discipline, sportsmanship and respect — and I’d like to teach those values to the next generation.” China has emerged as a key market for snooker, with the game enjoying a passionate fanbase and producing top players such as Ding Junhui and Zhang Anda. The country has also hosted lucrative tournaments and invested heavily in developing domestic infrastructure to support the sport. Lee’s involvement has been welcomed by some within the community who believe that players with a thorough understanding of professional snooker can help maintain the high standards required for international competition. However, the ethics of employing someone with a chequered past to coach the future of a sport remain a sensitive issue. Some observers have questioned whether it is appropriate for a man who violated the central tenets of the game to have any role in its development.

Tony Pulis, the former England international and current manager of West Bromwich Albion, believes the recent success of Wales at the European Championship could inspire an entire generation of young footballers in the UK. Pulis, himself a Welshman and former international, has long maintained a passion for the national side and watches its progress with keen interest. After Wales exceeded expectations at the tournament—making it to the semi-finals under the guidance of manager Ryan Giggs—Pulis sees a newfound sense of belief among players and supporters alike. Speaking to  The Times , Pulis said: "What Wales has achieved is incredible. To go from being the smallest nation in the tournament to reaching the last four—that’s the stuff dreams are made of. It’s not just about winning games; it’s about showing kids that they too can aspire to the top, no matter their background or the size of their nation." Wales' campaign has been hailed as an emotional and sporting triumph. Led by Gareth Bale, the team played with courage and resilience, capturing the hearts of fans across Europe. For Pulis, who played for both Wales and West Brom, the success of the national side holds a personal significance, and he is eager to see the impacts it could have on the youth game and beyond. “Growing up in Wales, there was always a dream of playing for your country, but realistically, it seemed out of reach for most,” he said. “Now, with the Euros showing what can be achieved, maybe more Welsh kids will look at football as a realistic opportunity rather than a distant fantasy.” Pulis also feels that the success of Wales offers lessons for English football, a subject close to his heart. As a manager who has spent much of his career in the Premier League, he understands the challenges of building competitive teams and developing homegrown talent. He argues that the Welsh Football Association should be studied by its English counterpart for how it manages and nurtures young players. “I’m not saying Wales is doing everything right, but the system, the planning, and the belief that’s been passed down is working,” Pulis added. “If we can take anything from their approach, it could only benefit the game in England.” With the European Championship experience fresh in the minds of young footballers, the dream of following in the footsteps of Wales' heroes could become a powerful motivator for the next generation.

Memos released by the National Archives reveal new details of the close coordination between Tony Blair and George W Bush in the months before the US-led invasion of Iraq in March 2003. The documents, obtained by the UK’s Guardian newspaper, show the extent to which Blair, then serving as British Prime Minister, worked to align British interests and messaging with that of the White House as tensions with Saddam Hussein’s regime escalated. The exchange of letters and memos, written by Blair’s aides and addressed to Bush, provide evidence of how Britain was involved in building the international case for war, including the preparation of intelligence reports that would be used to justify the conflict. Notably, one memo reveals that Blair’s chief of staff at the time, Damian Green, stressed the importance of the visit by Bush to Blair in February 2003, calling it "a key moment in the build-up to the war." The documents also show that Blair was closely consulted on the timing of the military strike and played an active role in securing UN support in the early stages, even as doubts emerged among British scientists and officials about the so-called "Weapons of Mass Destruction," which were presented as a rationale for the invasion. Blair maintained that the war was "right" to remove a regime that posed a threat to global security, but others have since questioned the accuracy of the intelligence used to justify the conflict – a fact that has led to numerous inquiries, including the Hutton and Chilcot reports. The latter, published in 2016, severely criticised the UK government for the failure of its intelligence assessments and the decision to go to war based upon flawed information. In one memo, a point was made about the need for continued diplomatic efforts to convince other members of the UN Security Council to back the action, highlighting Britain’s role as a key ally in what became the most controversial foreign policy decision of the 21st century. As the UK and US continue to reflect on their long-standing relationship in the wake of shifting geopolitical priorities, the release of these documents generates further debate about the nature of leadership, loyalty, and the consequences of war. Dr. James Ellison, a lecturer in war studies at King’s College London, said the memos "highlight a unique level of trust and communication between two leaders at a time of profound global uncertainty."

Poland Surpasses India as Most Common Non-UK Birth Country in the UK, ONS Reports   For the first time on record, Poland has become the most common country of birth for non-British born individuals living in the UK, according to the latest data published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). India, which had held the top spot for more than a decade, has now been overtaken by Poland as migration patterns continue to shift in response to economic opportunities and political changes across Europe. The ONS report, released earlier this week, highlighted a significant change in the demographic landscape of the UK. With nearly 1.3 million people born in Poland currently residing in the country, the nation now has the largest non-British-born population in Britain. This figure surpassed India’s recorded 1.24 million, which had previously made it the most common non-UK birth country in the UK for over 15 years. The rise of the Polish community reflects the broader impact of EU migration, particularly after Poland joined the European Union in 2004, which allowed its citizens the freedom to work and live in the UK without prior restrictions. Since then, hundreds of thousands of Poles have moved to the UK, particularly to cities such as London, Birmingham, and Manchester, in search of stable employment, education, and better services. The initial influx of Polish migrants was often referred to as the “Polish plumbers” stereotype, as many found work in the construction, catering and care sector. However, the sector has since diversified, with Polish workers also making significant contributions in education, healthcare, and emergency services. The ONS report also revealed a slight decline in the overall number of Indian-born residents in the UK, although this is not necessarily a result of fewer Indians migrating, but rather the continued and steady rise of the Polish population. David Rosowsky-Coleman, an expert in EU migration at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, commented on the shift. “This is a major development in the UK’s ethnic and cultural make-up. It shows how the EU has shaped migration patterns, particularly in the wake of Germany’s decision to focus on internal integration while other European countries like the UK have become major destinations for Polish and other Eastern European migrants.” The report also underscored the recent trend of Poles delivering a larger share of the UK's gross domestic product in sectors such as healthcare and transport.

Fulham maintained their remarkable Championship form with an emphatic 2-0 victory at Barnsley on Saturday, extending their unbeaten away record in the division to an impressive 12 matches and securing their first triumph at Oakwell since 1970. The result marked a strong start to the new year for Slavisa Jokanovic’s side, who continue to demonstrate consistency and composure as they aim to push for a return to the Premier League. The breakthrough came in the 23rd minute when Aleksandar Mitrovic, continuing his stellar campaign, converted from close range following a pinpoint cross from Ryan Sessegnon. The Serbian striker has now found the net 16 times this season, reinforcing his status as one of the division’s most clinical forwards. Mitro, as he is known to fans, made it 2-0 just past the hour mark, this time slotting in a second after a slick passing move, showcasing the control and structure that has been synonymous with Fulham in recent matches. Barnsley, who have struggled to find consistency this season, pressed for an equaliser in the latter stages but were unable to trouble Championship newcomers Marcus Bettinella in the Fulham goal. The Cottagers’ backline, marshalled expertly by Tim Ream, held firm and was a testament to the defensive solidity that has underpinned their recent success. This win marks a long-awaited victory at Barnsley for Fulham, who had endured a 27-year wait for a win in South Yorkshire. Their last triumph at Oakwell came in May 1970, during their days in the old Second Division. The result will be a welcome relief for supporters, as Fulham continue to prove they are fully committed to contention, with their 12-game unbeaten run in the league stretching back to September. Manager Jokanovic praised his side’s resilience and tactical discipline following the match, stating: “It is a difficult place to come, and Barnsley are a good side. I’m pleased with the performance, especially the way we controlled the game and took our chances.” Fulham now sit just two points outside the top six as they continue to chase a playoff place, with the January transfer window looming as an opportunity to further strengthen their squad. For now, the momentum remains firmly with the away goers, who have proven time and again that wherever they play, Fulham are a force to be reckoned with in the Championship. The South Carolina House of Representatives has voted to remove the Confederate flag from the state capitol grounds, following an intense and often contentious debate that divided lawmakers and citizens alike. The flag has flown atop the State House for decades, becoming a polarizing symbol of the state's history and the legacy of the American Civil War. After a night of heated discussions, the body voted 94–3 in favor of the removal, with all three opposition votes cast by Republican lawmakers from heavily conservative districts. The decision comes in the wake of a mass shooting in Charleston, where a white supremacist killed nine African American worshippers at the Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church. Tensions over the flag’s presence had risen sharply in the aftermath, with civil rights leaders, religious groups, and many politicians across the state calling for its removal as a necessary step toward reconciliation and healing. Governor Nikki Haley had previously called for its removal, and the House’s vote now shifts the responsibility of finalizing the removal to the Senate, which is expected to follow suit. Speaker of the House Gary Clary, a Republican from Spartanburg, led the charge for the flag’s removal, acknowledging the divide it had caused in the state. "This flag is a symbol of hate and division," Clary said as he urged his colleagues to act. "It is time for us to move forward." He added that the flag would not be destroyed or displayed elsewhere, but rather placed in a museum, where it could be preserved as part of history rather than a symbol displayed proudly in the present. Not all Republicans joined the vote. Representative Bill Hamilton, from Aiken, cast one of the three no votes, arguing that the flag represented Southern pride and heritage. “This is not about race or hatred,” he said. “This is about tradition and history.” The Confederate flag has been a subject of political and cultural controversy for years. First raised at the State House during a period of intense segregation in the 1960s, it has since remained in place, despite growing opposition over the decades. The lone Confederate flag flying at the capitol had been surrounded by a larger American flag and was raised during the Civil War reenactment season each year, deepening the sense of historical reckoning as the vote approached. South Carolina’s move marks the latest in a series of actions across the United States where states and local governments are reconsidering the place of Confederate symbols in public spaces.

European retailers have taken a bold step to address long-standing concerns over working conditions in Bangladesh’s garment industry by pledging to join a legally binding agreement to improve safety in factories. Among the firms committing to the initiative are Hennes & Mauritz and Inditex, the parent company behind Zara, two of the world’s biggest clothing retailers. The Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh, as it is formally known, was launched in 2013 following the tragic collapse of the Rana Plaza factory complex, which killed more than 1,100 workers and injured countless others. Since then, international activists, trade unions and consumer rights groups have intensified pressure on fashion brands to take greater accountability for their supply chains and the safety of factory workers in Bangladesh. The new commitments by Hennes & Mauritz and Inditex are seen as a significant victory for safety advocates following protracted negotiations and widespread criticism of fashion brands for turning a blind eye to exploitative working conditions. The agreement requires signatory brands to fund safety inspections and remediation in over 2,200 factories, ensuring structural integrity, fire safety and emergency access. Factory owners must sign up to the terms and comply with changes ordered by independent safety assessors, with legal recourse available for workers and union representatives if non-compliance persists. The initiative also establishes a monitoring body and a grievance mechanism so that affected workers can raise concerns anonymously. According to figures from the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association, Bangladesh produces 80 per cent of the world’s knitted t-shirts and 45 per cent of all denim apparel. Its low-cost manufacturing model has made it a key global supplier to fast fashion retailers, but the industry operates under immense pressure to produce ever-larger volumes at ever-lower prices, often at the expense of worker welfare. The new accord has been praised by the International Labour Organization (ILO) as an “important precedent” that could inspire similar partnerships in other global sourcing hubs. H&M, in a statement, said the move reflects its “ongoing commitment to transparency and responsibility across the supply chain,” while Inditex insisted it had already taken steps to retrofit some 600 suppliers. The companies’ moves could shift the landscape of corporate responsibility in the fashion industry, challenging other major retailers to follow suit and set a standard for ethical sourcing. Critics, however, argue that the agreement should have been enacted years ago, and some Bangladeshi unions have called for more engagement with local workers to ensure the measures are effective on the ground.

Plans to introduce a ‘soft opt-out’ system for organ donation in Scotland have been formally published by the Scottish government, sparking a heated national debate and calls from both supporters and critics across the healthcare and ethical spectrum. The proposed system, which would make organ donation the default position unless an individual explicitly declines, is one of the biggest reforms in Scottish health policy in recent years. Under the new model, individuals would still have the freedom to choose not to donate organs should they wish, but would no longer be automatically registered as donors under the current opt-in system. Health SecretaryShonaRobinson confirmed the publication of the statutory instrument in the Scottish Parliament, underlining the government’s commitment to saving lives and reducing the tragic annual tally of people dying while waiting for a transplant. “The system is designed to be respectful of personal choice and autonomy,” she said during a short statement at Holyrood. “It will ensure every potential donor is given the chance to donate by default, but with the right, and the responsibility, to opt out if they wish.”The proposed system, set to become law as early as the end of the year, follows recommendations from the Organ Donation and Transplantation Review, chaired by former nurse and bereaved organ donor parent Adrian Zahra. Zahra, who lost his son to a brain injury in 2013 and who later helped his wife decide to donate their son’s organs, has been a key figure in pushing for reform and has been instrumental in shaping the proposed soft opt-out model. Earlier this year, the review team published a blueprint for the new system, which includes extensive improvements in how donation is communicated to the public, families and medical staff. Scottish ministers have made it clear that the reform aims to remove the current ‘organ donation postcode lottery’, which sees donor numbers vary wildly between regions. At present, only about 56 per cent of adults in Scotland are registered as organ donors, despite public support for the principle of donation being broadly high. The government claims that the system, already in place in countries such as Wales since 2015 and expected in England from May 2020, can significantly improve donation rates. Figures published by NHS Blood and Transplant show that over 700 people in the UK were waiting for a new organ at any given time last year, with 11 people dying each day due to a lack of available organs.

England were on the wrong end of a record 30-3 defeat by Wales at Cardiff’s Millennium Stadium—their heaviest loss in 27 years—but Six Nations victories do more than tell wars already won. They also reveal truths about fighting spirit, tactical adaptability and the readiness to respond when the rubber hits the road. England’s current squad may be battered and bruised by the scale of that defeat, but on their day they remain a force that Austra-lia must fear this Saturday at Twickenham. The key phrase, of course, is "on their day." Despite.FatalfumblesandinefficienciesbroughttoplightagainstWales, England's pedigree as a rugby nation is still formidable, and the memory of their Grand Slam victory in 2015 reminds all that they are not to be taken lightly. Australia, meanwhile, who are coming off the back of a narrow 20-17 defeat to Scotland, will be well aware that even a strong English team this season can still falter in ways that might not be immediately obvious. England's starting XV showed both resilience and patchiness in the Six Nations, with their defeats to Ireland, Wales and ultimately France spelling the end of their short-lived title hopes. But their back-line, including deadly wingers Anthony Watson and Marcus Smith, still has the firepower to light up the Twickenham turf. Baptiste Serin’s kicking, and the work rate of forwards like Sam Underhill and Tom Curry, did not go unnoticed, even if the overall cohesion left much to be desired. Australia will also wonder just how much of this England squad is operating below par.
