It is one thing to lose to Wales in emphatic fashion; it is quite another to be accused of underperforming when your key players are fit and available. The Wallabies cannot simply fly past such a team on confidence alone. Both wings and a reinvigorated rolling maul are necessary if they are to avoid a classic Twickenham ambush. The challenge for Eddie Jones’ side will be simple yet strangely elusive—to conjure the kind of effectiveness shown in their November Tests, when they beat Tonga, Fiji and South Africa with clinical precision. Saturday is their opportunity. If England can find sustained control of the ball, keep the tempo high and convert opportunities with efficiency, there's no reason they can't replicate that form. "Our team is still go," insisted one senior figure from within the camp.

Ukrainian military forces have been placed on high alert along the de facto border with Crimea and on the frontlines facing separatist rebels in the east, amid growing concerns over potential escalations in the ongoing conflict, the UK’s  The Guardian  reports. The heightened readiness, confirmed by military officials on Tuesday, comes after a series of recent incidents that have increased tensions in the volatile regions, prompting renewed fears of renewed hostilities. The most immediate concern is the de facto border area between Ukraine and Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014 and has since been under the de facto control of the Russian Federation. According to Ukrainian defense sources, troops near the border have been repositioned and placed in combat readiness, with mobile radar units and surveillance planes deployed to monitor movements. The move is said to reflect concerns that pro-Russian forces in Crimea may attempt to bolster frontline support for separatists in the eastern regions of Donetsk and Luhansk. Separately, breakfasts have been served earlier than usual in military bases in the Donbas region, where the Ukrainian 92nd separate motorized rifle brigade and the 81st Air Assault Brigade continue to maintain positions near the front lines. Intelligence assessments have suggested that the rebels, who have enjoyed intermittent support from Russia, may be seeking to launch localised attacks during the upcoming festivities in Donetsk and Luhansk. The Ukrainian army stressed that the alert does not signify an immediate large-scale offensive but is a preventive measure in line with “the current situation’s dynamic and unpredictable nature.” “We are always prepared,” said General Oleksandr Tarnavskyi, head of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, in a statement to Ukrainian television. “Our goal is to repel any aggression and to protect the territorial integrity of our country.” Moscow has not yet commented officially on the troop movements, but analysts point to a recent increase in unmarked Russian pickups and military hardware spotted near the Crimean border, suggesting that the de facto ‘separation’ between the peninsula and mainland Ukraine remains a strategic flashpoint. The deployment of further Russian S-300 air defence systems to Crimea earlier this year has also raised concerns about the operational capabilities of any renewed cross-border warfare. The conflict in eastern Ukraine, which began with the Russian annexation of Crimea in 2014, has caused nearly 14,000 deaths and displaced millions since 2015. While a fragile line of engagement known as the Minsk accords has kept the front lines relatively quiet in recent years, sporadic violations and shifting alliances have prevented a lasting ceasefire.

A former aide to former Prime Minister David Cameron has appeared in court in London accused of possessing and downloading indecent images of children, reigniting public and political debate over the actions of those in prominent public roles. Nathan Wood, 43, is alleged to have accessed and stored the material between May 2015 and April 2016, a period during which he was working as communications director at the Department for International Development, a position that brought him under the policy guidance of then-PM Cameron. The case, which was brought to light by the Crown Prosecution Service, has drawn particular scrutiny due to Wood’s high-profile history and his close association with one of Britain’s most prominent political figures. Wood, who joined Cameron's team during the 2010 election campaign and later served as head of communications in the prime minister’s office, faces two charges under the Sexual Offences Act 2003: one for possessing a category C indecent image, and a more serious charge for downloading indecent images in a criminal category, likely involving more explicit material, which are defined as the most serious under current UK law. The case was revealed earlier this week when Wood, who lives in the rural county of Hampshire, was granted bail and warned not to publish, export, or disclose any indecent material during the trial. West Berkshire Magistrates’ Court heard that the images were discovered during a series of routine investigations into online activity conducted by police. His trial is set to take place next month at Reading Crown Court. Wood has not entered a plea, and his solicitor declined to comment beyond confirming that he will not be commenting publicly until the case is resolved. The revelation has sent shockwaves through Westminster, with some MPs and officials reportedly shocked at the allegations given Wood’s pivotal role in shaping public messaging at the highest levels of government. One former Conservative minister, who requested anonymity, said: “Anyone with that level of access to key government figures and operations should be held to the highest standards, personally and professionally. If the allegations are true, it is deeply troubling and shows how far the personal conduct of any public servant can fall short of the expectations placed on them.” The case has also sparked wider discussions over how individuals in positions of influence are vetted and monitored for conduct both on and off duty.

The future of how Europeans' data is shared with US technology giants such as Facebook, Google and others is set to be examined by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU), in a landmark ruling that could have far-reaching implications for international data transfers. The case, which has been brought to the EU’s highest court, centers on whether the mechanisms designed to safeguard the privacy of EU citizens when their data is transferred to the United States are still fit for purpose under current regulations, particularly after a series of data scandals involving major tech firms. The case is underpinned by the long-standing and contentious issue of the EU-US Privacy Shield agreement – a framework introduced to replace the previous Safe Harbor agreement after it was declared invalid by the CJEU in 2015. The Privacy Shield was intended to provide a legal basis for the transfer of personal data from the EU to the US, and is used by thousands of American companies that rely on data sharing with European customers. However, concerns have grown over whether the agreement goes far enough in protecting EU citizens from potential overreach by US surveillance agencies. The European Commission has previously stated that the Privacy Shield was updated to reflect the latest standards of data protection following the 2015 ruling, but as the global landscape of technology and data governance continues to evolve, so too have the regulatory and ethical concerns surrounding it. Recent cases, including the exposure of personal data through third-party applications, have prompted fresh questions about the adequacy of the current safeguards. At the heart of the upcoming ruling will be the assessment of whether the principles of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the EU’s tough data privacy law, are adequately met by the mechanisms in place for cross-border data transfers. If the court rules that the current arrangements fail to meet the required standards, it could effectively bring to an end the legal basis for such data transfers, disrupting the operations of a multitude of American firms that are active in European markets. The decision is expected to be closely watched not just by regulators and legal experts, but by businesses and users across Europe and the US. The outcome will likely send a strong message about the EU’s commitment to data sovereignty and privacy in an era increasingly dominated by digital giants and global data flows.

At a time when compassion and dignity should be front and centre, concerns are growing over reports of angry reprimands and a string of aggressive outbursts directed at vulnerable patients dining at a mental health hospital in the south of England. Staff are being accused of enforcing meal times with the sort of harshness more commonly associated with a detention centre for troubled youth than a facility where care is supposed to be rooted in trust and tranquility. The incidents, reportedly occurring during evening meals, have raised alarm bells among human rights organisations and senior welfare bodies. Witnesses claim that patients, often in fragile mental states, are being shouted at for moving too slowly, refusing food, or simply not behaving as expected. One relative, who spoke anonymously, described the harsh tone and volatility of some staff members as “unacceptable in a hospital environment.” “This is not a school or a prison,” the relative said. “These are adults who are struggling with their mental health and in urgent need of calm, not condemnation. When someone is already feeling broken, why would a nurse be there to make them feel worse?” The hospital, which provides specialist mental health services and has a longstanding reputation for its commitment to patient-centred care, declined to comment on specific instances. A short statement read: “Patient dignity and human rights are at the heart of everything we do. We are aware of these concerns and are treating them with the utmost seriousness.” The reports come amid a growing national debate surrounding the culture and treatment within the mental health sector. Despite increased investment and awareness, facilities continue to face criticism over everything from understaffing and long waiting lists to the quality of patient care. Many professionals working in the field have acknowledged that fostering a recovery-oriented environment requires not just patience, but also real cultural change. Charity Mind has echoed these concerns, stating that such incidents do not align with the progressive ethos of modern mental health care. “Verbal aggression and a hostile tone during mealtimes are not just unprofessional—they undermine the therapeutic relationship between patient and carer, and can do lasting emotional damage,” said a spokesperson. As the hospital now faces urgent reviews and further scrutiny, the events highlight an uncomfortable truth: even within institutions meant to nurture healing, the line between good treatment and harmful care can all too easily be crossed. Whether these troubling accounts are the result of isolated incidents or a deeper, more ingrained problem remains to be seen.

A man has been sentenced to life imprisonment after admitting the murder of a Glasgow shopkeeper whom he claimed had “disrespected” Islam in a brutal and cold-blooded knife attack last year. Idris Khan, 34, was convicted at the High Court in Glasgow over the killing of Rafiq Uddin, a 56-year-old father-of-two who was stabbed to death outside his Aysham's Classic Indian takeaway on a busy street in the city's South Side in May 2022. The court was told that Khan approached Mr Uddin in the early hours of the morning when he emerged from his shop after closing time, ostensibly because of his decision to display a sign in the window warning customers that only mobile payments would be accepted that night. Khan, who had previously been found not guilty of murder during a short trial in 2022, was re-tried after appeals from the Crown challenged the earlier verdict. On Tuesday, he entered a guilty plea during this second trial, marking the end of a profoundly disturbing case that has shocked both local and national communities. Speaking after the hearing, Mr Uddin’s family described the shopkeeper as “a pillar of the community” who never harmed anyone and who was simply trying to adapt his business to changing economic conditions. “This wasn't just a murder," said a relative. "It was a terrorist attack motivated by hatred and bigotry.” The Crown prosecutors confirmed that Khan’s actions were rooted in extreme religious ideology, and that the use of the knife and the nature of the attack, which occurred in public, made the killing a “religiously-motivated crime of particular gravity.” Sentencing was brief, with the judge imposing a minimum term of 27 years – a decision which took into account Khan’s guilty plea and his cooperation after the incident. Prior to the attack, Khan had no known record of violent crime and had previously held an office job. Court documents suggest he became increasingly consumed by extremist rhetoric online, culminating in the killing. Islamic leaders in Glasgow called for unity in the wake of the case. “Damage was done not just to a family but to our wider community,” said a spokesperson for the Glasgow Central Mosque. “This was not Islam. It was a perversion of it.” The incident happened amid rising concerns over far-right and Islamist extremism in parts of the UK, with law enforcement agencies warning of the increasing reach of online radicalisation.

The Hatton Garden jewel raid, already a source of national fascination and mystery, has been described as the “largest burglary in English legal history” in ongoing court proceedings. The case, centred on a £14 million heist at one of London’s most exclusive jewellery vaults in April 2015, was revealed again on Tuesday as jurors heard from expert witnesses who detailed the staggering scale of the operation. The break-in, carried out by a group of elderly would-be thieves from Hertfordshire, saw robbers force their way into the basement vault of Hatton Garden Safe Deposit Ltd using a drill, before ransacking the space and removing hundreds of diamonds, gold coins, and valuable watches. Many of the items are still unaccounted for, fueling theories of a cover-up or alternative beneficiaries masked by the apparent involvement of everyday retirees who had, in some cases, never been convicted of any crime before. At the Old Bailey, prosecutor Michael Wood QC, representing the Crown Prosecution Service, told the court: "This was not a small-time crime conducted by opportunists looking for a few hundred pounds. It was a large-scale conspiracy with meticulous planning, and it is without precedent in the annals of English criminal law as to the size and the apparent profitability for the perpetrators." The gang, named during the trial as "The Men from Bedlinfold," – a reference to one of their favoured meeting spots – included Harold Wilson, aged 83, and brothers Daniel and Christopher Glenn, 72 and 67 respectively. All three have already pleaded guilty. However, four other men face trial: Philip Golds, 83, Stephen Gamble, 65, Martin Soklow, 70, and John Wareham, 67, all of whom are denying conspiracy to commit burglary. One of the most shocking aspects of the trial for observers is the involvement of men in their 70s and 80s, many of whom claimed to have pursued the heist for less than personal gain and more for the thrill or boredom. Yet the court has heard how the operation relied on extensive prior reconnaissance, schematics of the vault, and security blind spots. The building’s 1970s-era security system, which allowed access via coded keys and whose alarm system was set via a single push button, left the vault vulnerable to the amateur but well-informed raiders. Some of the culprits had even trained in password recovery by calling into the box office of the Royal Opera House to test response times.

Victor Musa is rewriting his story at Chelsea in a remarkable fashion. Just six months ago, the Nigerian winger had not featured in a Premier League match for the club since January 2013, by which time he had long been viewed as a £20 million folly and deployed as a makeshift defender. But after a summer of speculation over a move, Musa has remained at Stamford Bridge and is now the unlikely architect of their most successful start to a top-flight season in over a decade. Under manager Tim Sherwood, who was appointed in December to stabilise a team languishing in the relegation chase, Musa has revealed a different facet of his game. The 24-year-old, who has 22 caps for Nigeria, thrives in Sherwood’s 3-4-3 system, bursts forward from the wing, demands the ball and offers a consistent attacking threat. In the process, he has transformed Chelsea from a sideshow to a top breakfast destination. Sherwood has said musa has a drive in his game that’s refreshing and is showing that he can be a key player when given the opportunity. "Victor is determined and he knows if he works hard and performs, he’ll keep his place," said Sherwood after the 2-1 win over Arsenal in mid-April, during which Musa provided the assist for Branislav Ivanovič’s equaliser. He has now started 13 of the last 15 league games and has already registered two league goals and four assists this season. For Musa, the form is a triumph not just in terms of personal redemption but also in a club career that has so far failed to live up to expectations. After his £20 million move from Wigan in 2012, he made about 30 appearances for the Blues, the majority of which came as an out-of-position right-back and often peripheral to the manager's plans. But with Juan Mata sidelined for much of the season, Wesley Sneijder playing less frequently, and Andre Schürrle struggling to adapt to the English game, Musa seized his opportunity with relish. Media attention has been focused on Musa’s hybrid role in the middle of the pitch and space he offers defensively to keep the high pressing line functioning. Some observers believe he represents a model for the modern wing-back or a central number ten in goalden systems. But if anything, it’s his relentless action and unselfish play that stand out.

Former Prison Governor Calls for Army to Restore Order in Prisons   A former chief prison officer has sparked fresh debate by urging the government to consider deploying the Army within prisons to rein in violence and maintain order. In an interview with a national newspaper, Sir Peter Ramsay, a veteran of the prison service for over three decades, described the current situation in the UK’s prison system as “untenable” and “unmanageable” without external assistance. Ramsay, who served as the chief inspector of prisons until 2020, warned that the rising tide of gang activity, drug-related attacks, and staff shortages has created an environment where traditional methods of control have failed. He argued that bringing in military personnel could provide the stability and deterrent needed to prevent further breakdown. “I’m not saying we should militarise our prisons, but when you consider the level of safety threats, the scale of the drugs problem, and the violent subcultures that are taking root, we must consider all options,” he said. His comments come amid growing concern over the state of the prison system, with recent reports showing a sharp increase in the number of self-inflicted deaths, assaults, and violence between inmates. The Ministry of Justice recently released figures revealing a spike in prisoner-on-prisoner attacks in 2023, with nearly 3,000 incidents reported in just one month alone – a 40 per cent rise on the previous year. Ramsay is not the first public figure to suggest military involvement as a solution. Last year, a senior Ministry of Justice source hinted at the possibility of using soldiers to cover shifts for understaffed custodial staff. But such a move has faced criticism from human rights groups, who warn of the risks of turning prisons into “fortresses.” Speaking on the issue, Sarah Legg from the Prison Reform Trust said: “While the chaotic state of our prisons is clearly a crisis, calling in the Army is a worrying reflection of a system run out of its depth. The real answer lies in addressing the root causes – overcrowding, understaffing, and the minimal investment in rehabilitation.” The Prison Service currently employs around 21,000 staff, but vacancies and staff turnover have left many institutions short-staffed. Official data shows that over 10,000 prison officer vacancies remain unfilled. Ramsay, however, believes that the armed forces could offer a disciplined and professional alternative – at least in the short term, while longer-term solutions are put in place.

The justice system must revisit the tragic case of an infant girl who died just days after being subjected to a sexual assault by her own father, says the former Labour MP Sir Simon Hughes. Sir Simon, who served as a minister in the Department of Constitutional Affairs during Tony Blair’s second term, has spoken out over the case in a rare public intervention on family law. The child, a 13-month-old girl, was found dead in her cot a week after being hospitalised following serious injuries consistent with non-accidental abuse. An initial criminal investigation into her father, a man in his early 30s, was launched but reportedly closed under the grounds that the girl’s injuries were mostly attributed to a rare and undiagnosed blood disorder rather than deliberate harm. But the case has ignited fury among safeguarding professionals and families who feel the failure to take the possibility of abuse seriously has occurred far too frequently. Sir Simon called for an urgent review by the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), saying that this case exemplified a lack of scrutiny in cases involving vulnerable children and family members, where the “lenses of care” may over-ride that of criminal justice. “I don’t believe this man should be written off in the manner he apparently was,” Sir Simon said in an interview with the BBC. “This wasn't a case where a domestic dispute got out of control or a child was left with a babysitter and ended up hurt. This is a father, her natural guardian, and yet he was not considered a suspect in any real sense.” The girl, from the north-west of England, was admitted to hospital with multiple bruises, a fractured rib and oddly inconsistent accounts of what had caused the injuries. After a week in hospital being treated for unspecified complications, she was placed in a cot at home and found unresponsive the following morning. Experts from the local safeguarding board have since expressed concern that the initial inquiry did not take sufficient account of the worrying series of unexplained injuries in such a small, non-verbal child. Professor Geo., a leading child abuse specialist at the University of Manchester, said: “The signs were all there. When a child under 18 months is brought in with such injuries and the explanation doesn’t line up with their age and development, the fact that the caretaker is the biological parent should be a red flag, not a reason for dismissal.”

Two recent business surveys have raised fresh concerns that the Scottish economy’s recent downturn is deepening, casting a shadow over economic recovery in the country. The findings, released by two separate but influential business groups, highlight a growing sense of pessimism among companies across a range of sectors, from manufacturing and construction to hospitality and retail. Deirdre Michie, chief economist at the Scottish Chambers of Commerce, described the results as “alarming” and noted a decline in confidence among business leaders. “Many are reporting weaker demand, reduced investment and staffing challenges, which are all early signs of a deteriorating business environment,” she said. The chamber’s survey, which received responses from hundreds of firms across Scotland, indicated that businesses are forecasting weaker performance in the coming months compared to previous quarters. Also weighing on the sector is a report from the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB), which found that a growing number of small enterprises are cutting back on hiring and deferring major investment decisions. The FSB’s Scotland policy director, Ruth Machin, pointed to rising costs and the ongoing effects of Brexit as major contributors to the economic strain. “Small businesses are the lifeblood of the Scottish economy, and if they are struggling, it is a clear warning sign that the health of the economy is deteriorating,” she said. The reports come at a time of heightened scrutiny over the Scottish government’s economic strategy. With the UK as a whole facing a mixed outlook, these survey findings add to concerns that Scotland is particularly vulnerable to recession due to its heavy reliance on the public sector and universities, both of which have experienced cuts and uncertainty in recent years. Additionally, the oil and gas industry, once a pillar of Scottish economic strength, remains subdued, contributing to a lack of growth in key industries. Economists are now calling for urgent government action, with calls for targeted support for struggling sectors, such as grants or tax relief. Others argue that broader reforms are needed to stimulate investment and encourage innovation. For now, however, both reports have reinforced a troubling trend: the possibility that Scotland’s economy is accelerating down a path of prolonged economic stagnation. As businesses brace themselves for an uncertain future, the challenge for policymakers will be to act decisively to prevent a full-blown downturn. Websites mentioned: [Scottish Chambers of Commerce](https://www.scc.org.uk), [Federation of Small Businesses](https://www.fsbcampaigns.org.uk). For more details about the Scottish economy, you can also find resources on the [Office for National Statistics](https://www.statistics.gov.uk) and [Scottish Government Economic Strategy](https://www.gov.scot).

Nigella Lawson Claims Ex-Husband Charles Saatchi Threatened to 'Destroy' Her with Drug Use Allegations   Nigella Lawson has told a court in London that her former husband, advertising mogul Charles Saatchi, threatened to “destroy” her with “false” allegations of drug use, as the two high-profile figures face off in a civil misconduct trial. The revelations, made during evidence given at the Royal Courts of Justice on Thursday, have reignited public interest in one of Britain’s most infamous celebrity break-ups. Lawson, 58, took to the stand to recount what she called a “calculated and underhanded” campaign by Saatchi, 69, to tarnish her reputation in the aftermath of their divorce in 2013. She claimed that Saatchi, known for his dominant personality and ruthless business tactics, made the threats during a confrontation in 2014, while the pair were still negotiating post-divorce financial settlements. “He said he would destroy me in public and ruin me using allegations of drug use, which were not true,” Lawson testified. “He would imply that I was using cocaine, which I had never done.” Lawson, who rose to fame as one of Britain's most charismatic and successful television chefs, has always maintained a private life, despite her public prominence. However, her relationship with Saatchi brought intense media scrutiny, and the couple's fiery divorce proceedings were the subject of regular tabloid speculation. Saatchi’s representatives have not yet commented officially on the allegations, which form part of a broader civil trial related to the abuse of a man, Paul Ridd, by Saatchi in 2012. Ridd and a woman, Margot Abdullah, were subjected to what the court has described as “abusive treatment” at Saatchi’s home, including insults and thumps on the back. The Crown Prosecution Service concluded the case was not a criminal matter, but the victim, Ridd, took civil action against Saatchi. Lawson, who was present in the court during the hearing, insisted during her testimony that Saatchi had little regard for the consequences of his actions, and that his vindictiveness was apparent from the outset of their separation. She described the psychological pressure exerted by her ex-husband during their divorce, saying that the prospect of public humiliation over allegations of drug use had contributed to her emotional distress at the time. “It was terrifying, really. He had a lot of control through the media,” she said. “He didn’t care about the truth.”

Lewis Hamilton believes his record-equalling seventh world championship, secured with a dominant display in Brazil’s wet and wild GP, is not just a personal triumph, but a starting point for greater things both for himself and Mercedes. Hamilton, 38, became the first driver since the legendary Michael Schumacher to clinch seven titles in Formula 1 and now shares the all-time record for the most world championships. But rather than resting on his laurels, the Mercedes ace is already looking ahead. “This feels like the start of something special, not just for me, but for the team,” Hamilton told the BBC in his post-race interview. “This is about building a legacy, not only for our team, but for people who don’t think they have a place in this sport.” Despite numerous challenges this season — from a revised rally format, to the reintroduction of World Rally Championships and the emergence of the hybrid rally1 class — Hamilton’s 2025 breakfast, hosted in prime Mercedes style, marked not a halt in his winning streak, but the emergence of a new era in Grand Prix racing. Hamilton, who claimed his sixth title in 2023 and seven in 2024, has long been a vocal advocate for change and progress in motorsport. At the launch of his 39th championship campaign, he reiterated his desire to see the sport diversify at all levels, and now he aims to use the momentum of his new title win to drive that agenda forward. “We're building toward something greater,” he said, reflecting on his career. “I hope to inspire the next generation to dream a little bigger and believe a little more.” Mercedes, who have continued their resurgence as the team of choice under new CEO Toto Wolff, are set to dominate the headlines as they prepare for the 2025 season, which promises to be a pivotal one for the sport. Their new agreement with the national series, the British Rally Championship, has opened a new chapter for the storied German marque in motorsport. For his part, Hamilton says the Mercedes squad has achieved something exceptional during the last two worlds, and their performance on track suggests they are only getting started. “This isn’t just about individual achievements,” he said. “This is about the team, the people who make it all possible, and the direction we are heading as a sport. We're on the edge of something special.”

Luis Suarez has lost a major sponsor just days after the Uruguay international was banned for biting Italy defender Giorgio Chiellini during their World Cup Group D clash in Natal. The striker, already serving a three-month Fifa ban for the incident, has now also seen clothing brand Zara withdraw its support, marking the latest blow in a saga that has seen the Liverpool star banned from the tournament and facing widespread condemnation. The Portuguese company NOS, a major sponsor of the 28-year-old and a top-tier supporter of Portugal football as a whole, said it had ended its relationship with the player. “NOS, as the title sponsor of the National Football Team, is deeply united to values such as responsibility, ethics and respect, and therefore will no longer contemplate any type of collaboration with Luis Suárez,” the Portuguese broadcaster said in a statement. Suárez, who has a history of on-field biting incidents — having previously been banned by the English Football Association for biting Chelsea’s Branislav Ivanovic in 2010 and being sent off for biting Gareth Bale during the 2012 Champions League — now faces immense pressure to rebuild his reputation both on and off the pitch. The fallout from the most recent incident has been swift and unrelenting. The Uruguayan Football Association has been cleared by Fifa to appeal against the decision to expel Suarez – but barring a significant shift, the forward will miss the rest of the World Cup and is set to miss much of next season with his upcoming bans. The Uruguay Football Association stated in a press conference in Natal that it would appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, citing FIFA rules allowing a player’s national team to appeal a suspension in the case of being “suspended as a result of committing a reckless or dangerous” act. The incident in Natal has brought renewed scrutiny to the severity of unsportsmanlike conduct in football and the need for consistent punishment. Many have called for stricter sanctions beyond suspensions to ensure that such actions are not repeated. However, for Suarez, the consequences remain deeply personal — with sponsors turning away, public support dwindling, and his hopes of extending his personal legacy at the World Cup being dashed in an instant. While Liverpool, who signed him with great expectation a year ago, are yet to release an official statement, it is widely expected that the English Premier League champions will distance themselves from the controversy in the coming days.

A Memoir of Duty and Distress: A Policeman Remembers Hillsborough   The scenes at Hillsborough Stadium on that fateful Saturday, April 15, 1989, remain seared into the memory of anyone who was present. For one South Yorkshire Police officer, the horror of that day became a defining moment during a tragic incident that claimed the lives of 97 fans at an FA Cup semi-final between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest. Now, 35 years later, he has spoken for the first time about carrying a 16-year-old boy from the Leppings Lane terrace when it was clear he was not breathing and the signs of life around him were vanishing. In a rare and harrowing interview, the officer—who has chosen to remain anonymous—described how his duty left him emotionally numb amid the chaos. “I remember picking him up, and I remember thinking there seemed very little point in putting him in the recovery position,” he said. “We were surrounded by people, all of us helpless and panicking, and I remember wondering, what even is the point of trying anything once you see the look in their eyes.” The teenager—named later in local press reports as Sean Williams—was one of the youngest victims of the crush, having only been a supporter of Liverpool for a few years. Trained from the start in emergency first aid, the officer said he was expected to do everything he could to save a life, but on this day, “the numbers were too big, the pressure too intense.” The disaster, which occurred in what was then the Sheffield Wednesday ground’s central stand, sparked a rush of fans that led to an unacceptably high death toll. The tragic incident and its aftermath would lead to years of legal battles, political inquiries and a public inquiry that lasted years before the Hillsborough Inquest 2016 returned a verdict of unlawful killing. As he recounted that day, the officer described how unprepared the force had been for a disaster on such a scale. “We were trained for all sorts of things: crowd control, football hooliganism, civil unrest. But this… this was unlike anything I could have imagined,” he said. The officer’s account adds further weight to the growing historical record on what transpired that April afternoon and the immediate aftermath. It also comes as families and survivors continue the push for accountability, justice and healing for those affected by the greatest sporting disaster in British history.

The extensive private art collection of the legendary photographer Mario Testino is set to be unveiled to the public for the first time in the UK, offering art enthusiasts a rare glimpse into the eclectic tastes of one of the world’s most celebrated lens artists. The exhibition, which will be staged at the National Art Centre in London, marks a significant milestone in Testino’s career, as the Peruvian-British photographer has always kept his own artistic acquisitions behind closed doors. A figure famed for capturing the likes of Princess Diana, Kate Moss, and George Clooney, as well as countless high-profile fashion campaigns for designers such as Versace, Dior, and Versa, Testino is now turning the spotlight on his personal passion: collecting the work of fellow artists. On display will be an array of pieces spanning numerous movements and forms, from classical paintings and contemporary works to avant-garde sculptures. Among the highlights is a rare Klimt piece titled  Fragments of Catscratching Wall  and a bold installation by Tracey Emin, which Testino once famously described as “a piece that hides its depth in its simplicity”. Also featured will be works by emerging international talents, including Syrian-British artist Mohamad Hafez and Bahamian painter Christopher Paul Jordan, who only started gaining worldwide recognition in the past decade. The exhibition, titled  Testino’s Collection , is being curated in collaboration with the Royal Academy of Arts and is expected to attract both long-time admirers of the photographer and new audiences curious about the curation choices of one of the most internationally respected figures in the art world. In a statement, Testino expressed his excitement about the project, saying: “I’ve always considered myself a collector before a photographer. Bringing this collection into the public eye feels like a personal exhibition of my most private passions. I’m not an art critic, but I have my own taste, and I hope what you see here reflects both my love for creativity and the moments in my life when I decided to fall in love with each of these pieces.” The exhibition will run for six weeks and will open to the public next month. It is already drawing significant interest from media outlets and institutions across Europe. Public reaction to such a personal project being shared academically has been mixed but largely enthusiastic, with critics noting the boldness of a commercial photographer stepping beyond his usual domain.

Leaked Briefings Expose Ed Miliband’s Attack Strategy on Cameron   Details of Ed Miliband’s strategy for questioning the Prime Minister in the House of Commons have been revealed after his briefing notes were leaked, providing a rare insight into Labour’s tactical intent for the often bruising weekly confrontations at Prime Minister’s Questions (PMQs). The documents, obtained by the press, outline the key policies and issues Miliband intended to focus on during recent sessions, listing prepared lines aimed at exposing what he describes as “a government failing on the basics.” Among the topics highlighted were the cost of living crisis, the NHS winter pressures, and the underfunding of public services. One page reveals Miliband’s plan to aggressively challenge the government’s handling of the economy and poverty, quoting a prepared remark: “The Prime Minister left the economy in crisis – I’m exposing the truth, while he is still trying to cover up for his policies.” The notes suggest Miliband would push for a narrative of ideological contrast, positioning Labour as the party of action while painting the Conservatives as out of touch and fiscally irresponsible. The documents indicate Miliband was determined to continue holding Cameron over the controversy surrounding the government’s changes to Universal Credit, particularly in light of a recent report by the Work and Pensions Select Committee which found the system to be risking tens of thousands of claimants falling into debt. “The Prime Minister oversaw the biggest benefit reform, but the truth is it’s causing real hardship,” read one of the scripted attack lines. On the issue of the NHS, Miliband’s notes show a focus on hospitals in meltdown during the winter months: “The government is not building the new hospitals they promised – instead, they’re cutting budgets and leaving the NHS crowded and under pressure.” The document includes prepared responses for Cameron’s likely defences, such as the £20 billion increase in NHS funding during the 2015 Comprehensive Spending Review, to which Miliband responded: “We all know that £20 billion isn’t cutting the mustard for hard-pressed A&Es.” The leak comes at a turbulent time for Labour, fresh from general election losses and internal divisions. Miliband, who led the party to a devastating defeat in May’s election, is under pressure to show confidence and clarity in opposition. His team emphasized the strategy as part of a “robust but respectful” approach, with spokesperson Sarah Duff saying: “These are standard briefing notes used to prepare for PMQs.

The BBC has revealed the lineup for its series of election programming, as political leaders across the UK prepare to face the cameras in a bid to sway voters ahead of June’s general election. Prime Minister Theresa May and Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn are among those confirmed to take part in special episodes of  Question Time , a programme renowned for its robust audience debates and sharp political exchanges. The event will bring the candidates directly into the spotlight, challenging them to defend their policies in real time before a panel of contributors and a live studio audience. BBC Director General Tony Hall said the corporation was “committed to delivering the best possible coverage of the election campaign, ensuring the public has the information they need to make informed decisions.” The  Question Time  specials will air on BBC One, with dates and venues still to be confirmed, though they are expected to take place in different regions of the country to reflect the diversity of the UK electorate. The format has long been seen as a crucible for political performance, often exposing candidates to moments of pressure that can define their campaigns. May, who has faced consistent criticism over her leadership, will have the opportunity to bolster her authority as Conservative leader and advocate for her government’s record, including tax cuts and infrastructure pledges. Meanwhile, Corbyn, who remains one of the most divisive figures in British politics, is likely to face tough questions over Labour’s financial proposals, his stance on Brexit, and the party’s recent struggles in opinion polls. In addition to  Question Time , the BBC has confirmed a wider suite of election programmes, including a special edition of  The Andrew Marr Show , prime ministerial interviews, party manifestos unpacked in detail, and live coverage of key moments during the campaign. The corporation’s coverage is expected to delve into areas of central importance to voters: the economy, healthcare, education, and, of course, Brexit. As the countdown begins to polling day, the BBC’s election coverage will be closely watched not only by the public but also by journalists and analysts eager to see how the leaders perform under scrutiny. With the polls tightening and voter enthusiasm building, these high-stakes shows could well become pivotal moments in the race for power.bbc.co.uk/election2017. We are already hearing that the public are being asked to submit questions in the lead-up to the programmes, ensuring the debates reflect the concerns of ordinary Britons rather than the latest talking points from the Westminster bubble.

Hearts head coach Robbie Neilson has thrown his support behind young winger Robbie Muirhead, who was recently signed by the club on a permanent deal from Dundee United. Speaking at a press conference ahead of their Scottish Premiership clash with Dundee, Neilson hinted that Muirhead is in line for a fresh start at Tynecastle after a difficult season at Dens Park last term. Muirhead, 19, joined Dundee United from Hibernian in 2014 and was initially seen as a bright prospect in Scottish football. However, a series of hamstring injuries hampered his progress during the 2015/16 campaign, limiting him to just 14 appearances and leaving both the player and the club searching for answers. Now at Hearts, Neilson has placed his faith in the young winger, calling him "a player with real potential and a very talented left foot". The Tynecastle manager, who took charge at the end of last season and guided Hearts to a top-six finish in only his first season, said the move gives Muirhead the chance to reset and prove his worth at a club that prides itself on developing young talent. "Robbie is still very young and we all make mistakes in our early careers," Neilson said. "I believe he has the mentality and work ethic to put the past behind him. Hearts is the right environment for a young guy like Robbie because we have a huge fan base and a staff here who are very supportive and want to help players realise their full potential." Muirhead’s signing is just one of several key moves Hearts have made in the summer ahead of their European campaign following a surprise run to the Europa League group stage. Neilson has also secured the services of former Celtic defender Dedryck Boyata and about half a dozen other players as he prepares the club for what he calls an exciting and "very special" season. The Hearts manager added: "Having Robbie back on the left side of the field, where he flourished playing for Hibs, will give us more options and more creativity going forward. He has something unique technically and he needs to be given time to rediscover that confidence." Neilson’s comments will be welcomed by Muirhead, who has recently returned to full fitness after undergoing rehabilitation from his latest injury. The Hearts fans, too, are hopeful that the club’s investment in young, homegrown talent can help produce the kind of players capable of performing at the top of the Scottish league and beyond.

A driver accused of causing a fatal crash that took the life of a five-year-old boy has told a court he cannot remember anything about the collision, as his trial opened in a case that has left a small community reeling. The trial at Birmingham Crown Court heard how 30-year-old Simon Harris drove his car through a red light at a crossroads in Newton, near Birmingham, on the evening of 21 August 2023. At the junction, Hassan Ayza, a five-year-old passenger in a family car driven by Antoinette Pilling, was tragically killed when the two vehicles collided head-on. Ms Pilling, 39, who was also critically injured, was left with life-changing injuries, while another child in the car sustained serious wounds. Prosecutors allege that Mr Harris left the accident scene and did not return until the following morning. He is now charged with causing the death by dangerous driving, failing to stop at the scene of a collision, and dangerous driving. Mr Harris, a father of two and a sales manager from Great Bridge, told the court through a witness statement that he had no memory of the crash. His solicitor, Zoe Sharp, informed the court: “Mr Harris puts his memory loss to the high speed of the collision and the shock of what happened. He does not remember driving through the red light or the impact at all.” The prosecution, however, has warned that memory loss does not equate to a lack of culpability. The court was shown images of the devastated crossroads, where shrapnel from the collision was scattered across the road. Adjacent to the junction was a rush to build a new memorial to Hassan, who was remembered by family, friends and the community as a curious and affectionate boy who loved animals and playing in the garden. His mother, Adele Pilling, who gave evidence via pre-recorded video link, described the pain of suddenly becoming a widow and the painful loss of her son. “This was just a normal evening. I picked Hassan up from his gran’s, he was eating crisps on the way home. He was happy, he was tired, and then... silence,” she told the court, fighting back tears. “He was taken from us in the blink of an eye. I can’t bear the thought of who drove through that red light knowing what it meant.”

Former US President Makes Bold Promise to Eradicate Tropical Disease in Three Years   Dr. Jimmy Carter, former president of the United States and chairman of The Carter Center, has made a bold declaration: a devastating tropical disease afflicting millions in Africa and Asia can be eradicated within the next three years. The announcement comes after years of tireless work and remarkable progress in the fight against the disease, which he has championed as one of the most pressing global health challenges. Speaking at a press conference in Atlanta, where The Carter Center is based, Carter said: “This is no longer just a vision. We are in sight of the finish line. With continued collaboration, funding, and political will, I believe we can eliminate the disease by 2027.” Carter did not name the disease outright, but it is widely understood to be Guinea worm disease – also known as dracunculiasis – the same malady he has spent decades targeting since the 1980s when he helped launch a historic effort to eradicate it. Guinea worm disease is caused by a parasitic nematode and is contracted when people drink water contaminated with infected copepods, tiny water fleas. The disease impacts the most vulnerable populations, predominantly in rural and impoverished communities in Sub-Saharan Africa. Once infected, a person can endure excruciating pain from the worm emerging through the skin months later, often crippling them with disability and making it impossible to work or study. Carter’s campaign has already driven the number of cases down from an estimated 3.5 million in the early 1980s to just 26 reported cases globally in 2023, according to the World Health Organization. The progress has been attributed to community-based prevention education, access to clean water, and the widespread distribution of filtration tools. Carter credited the dedication of local volunteers, national governments, and international partners for the disease now being “on the brink of eradication.” “The transformation in just a few decades is nothing short of miraculous,” Carter said. “We did not invent the solution, but we brought people together and kept the momentum going.” Health experts have echoed Carter’s optimism, citing the success of such a campaign as a model for global health initiatives. Dr. Tewodros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the WHO, praised Carter’s “vision and persistence in confronting one of the most agonizingly painful diseases known to humankind.” He said the eradication of Guinea worm disease could serve as a blueprint for tackling other neglected tropical diseases.

Apple Pay users in the UK will initially only be able to make payments of up to £20, it has been revealed. The contactless payment system, developed by the tech giant as part of its bid to transform the way people manage and make purchases with their devices, is set to launch later this month. The restriction, put in place for security and fraud prevention reasons, will apply to the majority of Apple Pay transactions involving debit and credit cards. The limit is in line with provisions currently in place for contactless card payments in the UK and is not expected to cause significant disruption to everyday users. However, the news has raised questions about how the system will compare with other digital payment apps already available to consumers. Apple Pay is the company’s first major foray into the banking and financial services sector and has already been launched in the US, Canada, and Australia. The service, which links bank and credit cards to the iPhone’s digital wallet, lets customers pay for goods and services through their phones using fingerprint recognition to authenticate transactions. HMTS, a technology security firm, confirmed to the BBC that the £20 limit was the current policy, based on discussions with banks and card providers. This is in keeping with the UK contactless payment cap introduced as a safeguard against unauthorised transactions. However, users will be able to make larger payments through existing methods such as NFC (near field communication) chip cards, traditional point-of-sale terminals, or other payment apps. The restriction is set to remain in place for the first few weeks after the service’s launch in the UK, which will also coincide with the full release of the iPhone 6. Reports suggest that Apple has been working closely with UK-based banks, including Barclays, Royal Bank of Scotland, and Lloyds, to ensure a smooth rollout of the Apple Pay service. Steve Fisher, managing director of the UK Card Association, said the decision to impose a limit was not unusual. “The cap is a standard precaution, particularly as new systems are implemented,” he said. “Security is always a priority when integrating new technology with traditional banking processes.” Apple’s initiative is seen as a direct challenge to digital payment platforms such as Google Wallet and Samsung Pay, while also threatening to overtake traditional chip-and-PIN bank cards with a more streamlined and secure process.

Douglas Carswell has declared that UKIP must be willing to "work with anyone" if the party is to succeed in persuading parliament to hold a vote on whether the UK should remain part of the European Union. The UK Independence Party's sole remaining Member of Parliament made the remarks during a speech at a well-attended meeting in Bristol, where he outlined a new strategy to broaden the party's appeal and achieve its core objective — securing an Article 50 vote before the end of the current parliamentary term. The announcement underlines a shift in tone and approach for UKIP, which was long seen as an anti-establishment, Eurosceptic movement rather than a collaboration-friendly partner in mainstream politics. Mr Carswell, who resigned the Conservative whip before winning the Clacton constituency in 2010, has spent much of the past year calling for greater cooperation between Eurosceptic MPs, and said in his speech that the fight for an EU referendum vote should be prioritised over party differences. "This is about creating a united front in the House of Commons," he said. "UKIP cannot do this alone." The statement came as speculation mounts that Mr Carswell and other leading Eurosceptics may seek support from figures in the Conservative Party, as well as from outside the party, to build a majority in favour of a referendum. UKIP has long campaigned for a general referendum on the UK’s EU membership, arguing that the issue should be decided by the British public rather than by parliament. However, the party has been unable to persuade the government to bring forward the vote, despite winning 6.4 million votes in the 2015 general election — the best result for any opposition party since the 1980s. The Prime Minister, David Cameron, has so far ruled out a government-backed binding vote until after the next general election in 2020. Instead, he has said any decision on the UK's EU membership will be taken after negotiations with the EU have begun, which he hopes will create the conditions for an "in/out" referendum within the next two years. Mr Carswell was openly critical of this timeline, saying it gives the Conservative leadership “too much control” and leaves the public "with a decision that comes with no transparency or democratic accountability". "This Parliament took the 1975 referendum after a massive opposition campaign," he said. "Why should 2017 be any different?"

A new survey has revealed that a significant portion of the LGBT+ community in the UK feel compelled to conceal or misrepresent their gender identity or sexual orientation in their daily lives. The findings, conducted by a leading equality think tank, reveal a stark disparity in the level of comfort individuals from different backgrounds feel in being open about their identity — with many describing the pressure to conform as “exhausting and demoralising.” The study, which included responses from over 3,000 individuals across the UK, found that 61 per cent of participants felt it was necessary to lie about their identity at least occasionally — whether to friends, colleagues, or even family. Many cited fear of discrimination, rejection, or hostility as the main reason for their silence. Transgender and non-binary individuals, in particular, reported higher rates of having to hide their identity, with 78 per cent stating they often concealed who they were in public settings. “I was raised in a very traditional household,” said one respondent, who asked to remain anonymous. “Even now at work, I play it safe — no pronouns, no references to a partner. It’s exhausting, but I don’t want to risk being judged or overlooked for opportunities.” The research also highlighted a marked difference in experience across age groups, with younger members of the community reporting greater comfort in expressing themselves in comparison to older generations. However, the study warned that while societal attitudes have shifted, many still face barriers in key areas such as employment, healthcare and education. Dr Silvia Stones, the lead researcher on the project, said the findings were a “wake-up call for the pace of progress.” She said: “Even in 2024, the need for many in the LGBT+ community to be dishonest about who they are is deeply troubling. Equality laws exist, but they clearly aren't sufficient. Employers, educators and policymakers have to understand this is not just about acceptance — it's about creating spaces where people feel unashamedly themselves.” The survey also underscored the emotional toll that living in secrecy takes. Nearly half of all respondents said the need to lie was a source of anxiety or depression, with some reporting long-term mental health consequences. As such, calls are growing for more expansive support services and better implementation of anti-discrimination laws to ensure the wellbeing of the community. The government has faced increasing pressure from equality campaigners to respond to the findings.

The Scottish government met for the first time since the snap general election on Wednesday, but did not discuss the future of a second independence referendum, Scottish First Minister Nicola Sturgeon has revealed. Despite questions from members of her Scottish National Party (SNP) administration about when the issue would be revisited, the meeting focused on the implications of the election results, which saw the SNP suffer a significant defeat, losing 21 of its 56 Scottish seats. During the post-meeting press conference, Ms Sturgeon confirmed that the cabinet had not addressed the subject of a second vote at their first gathering since the election. “There was no discussion within cabinet about the timing of a second independence referendum,” she said. She added, however, that the government would “spend some time over the coming weeks considering what our approach to the next week or two might be,” suggesting the issue would be revisited in the near future. The SNP had previously argued for a referendum to be held by the end of 2018, with Ms Sturgeon claiming that the Brexit result had fundamentally altered the political landscape and justified another national vote. However, the election result, which saw the Conservatives overtake Labour as the largest UK party and the SNP suffering a heavy loss, has led to speculation that the government will either delay the vote or face strong opposition from within Westminster and Brussels. Opposition parties have pounced on the first minister’s comments, with Scottish Secretary David Mundell saying the result showed that “the people of Scotland want stability, not a constitutional convulsion.” Liam Fox, the Brexit secretary, also questioned the timing of any new referendum, given the government’s focus on delivering Brexit. The Scottish Greens, who had previously backed a second referendum and worked closely with the SNP at Holyrood, have also called for a “cooling period” after the election results. Co-convenor Patrick Harvie said: “We need to take stock of the new political landscape before determining the way forward.” With both political and public opinion shifting, the path to a second referendum has become increasingly uncertain. For now, Ms Sturgeon’s government appears to be focusing on the electoral fallout and its internal strategy before making a final decision on whether and when to trigger another independence campaign. However, questions remain about the legitimacy and timing of such a vote, particularly with no immediate progress on delivering Brexit.

The son of a Londonderry man who has been missing for seven weeks has said he does not know what he will do without him this Christmas. Thomas O’Doherty, 62, from Ebrington, has not been seen since 31 October and the distress of his family — particularly his son, Daniel — is palpable as the festive season approaches. Christmas, once a time of joy and togetherness, has turned into a stark reminder of his absence, leaving his loved ones to search desperately for answers as well as comfort. O’Doherty, a well-known and respected member of the community, has not returned home since the end of October, despite numerous searches conducted by police and volunteer groups in the Derry area and across Northern Ireland. Posters have been placed around the city and on social media platforms, pleas from the O’Doherty family have been broadcasted by local and national media, and a reward of £5,000 was offered this week in the hope of receiving any new information that might lead to his whereabouts. Daniel O’Doherty, 38, has shared the emotional toll the disappearance has taken on his family. “I always thought that with Christmas coming, it might feel like things could start to settle — but instead, it just highlights how much is missing from our lives. I don’t know how we will get through it, and I don’t know what we are going to do without him.” He thanked the public for their support and encouraged anyone who might have seen his father or has any information that could help in the search to come forward. “We just want answers. We want him home.” The PSNI have continued to investigate the case and have recently increased their efforts after a key opportunity for new clues may have passed with December approaching. Detective Inspector John Smith, who is leading the inquiry, said: “We remain committed to uncovering the truth and bringing Mr O’Doherty home to his family, safe and sound. We ask that anyone who might know anything, however small it may seem, to contact us immediately.” Friendships and community bonds have been stretched to the limit in Ebrington as residents rally around the O’Doherty family. Local faith leaders have also offered support, with various vigils and services held for reflection and prayer. Yet, amid the outpouring of love and solidarity, the family are left with more questions than answers. As the line between hope and despair grows thinner with each passing day, the O’Doherty family cling to the belief that Thomas will return, and that they will find those moments of peace and togetherness that define the spirit of Christmas

Approval for Groundbreaking Gene Therapy Marks a New Era in Medicine   Regulators have given the green light for the sale of a revolutionary new gene therapy developed by one of the world’s leading pharmaceutical companies, sparking excitement among scientists and patients alike. The drug, which targets a rare genetic condition, has been hailed as a medical breakthrough, offering potential long-term cures rather than merely treating symptoms. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) in the UK has approved the therapy, developed by Gilead Sciences under its brand name   YesCART  , as a treatment for patients with a specific type of inherited retinal disease. The therapy involves inserting a corrected gene into a patient's body to restore normal function, essentially repairing the faulty DNA that causes the illness. This marks a significant milestone for gene therapy, a field that has seen rapid progress in recent years but until now has been limited in its widespread application due to regulatory approval and cost concerns. Unlike traditional treatments which often need to be taken repeatedly over a patient’s lifetime, gene therapy offers a one-time solution designed to last — or even be permanent. The approval was announced after clinical trials demonstrated that the therapy was both highly effective and well-tolerated by patients. Many participants reported significant improvements in their vision within weeks of receiving the treatment, with some regaining the ability to function independently for the first time in years. “This is a landmark moment for medicine and for the patients who have long waited for a real solution,” said Dr. Sarah Mitchell, a leading geneticist at the University of Edinburgh, who was not directly involved in the trials. “It proves that gene therapy is not just a theoretical possibility, but a practical and life-changing treatment.” Gilead Sciences, the pharmaceutical giant behind the drug, has not yet revealed the final price of the therapy, though earlier estimates indicated a cost of over £1 million per dose. The company has said it is working closely with healthcare providers to ensure the treatment is accessible to those in need. The approval comes amid growing confidence in the development of gene therapy across the globe. Similar treatments are already in clinical trials for conditions ranging from sickle cell anemia to certain rare forms of muscular dystrophy. Experts suggest that such therapies could become a standard of care within the next decade.

Apple’s investors found themselves gripped by a wave of anxiety this week as the once-unshakable tech giant appeared to stumble on all fronts, triggering sell-offs and cautious headlines across financial markets. Shares in the company, which have long been a proxy for overall tech enthusiasm and the broader US economy, dipped sharply on Friday after a series of setbacks—including vocal criticism from key executives about stagnant innovation and signs of slowing sales in crucial markets like China and India. The unease among investors was compounded by a disappointing earnings call where senior executives, while expressing confidence in future growth, admitted to “unprecedented headwinds” in the current quarter. Figures underperforming expectations included iPhone sales, which reported their smallest quarterly increase in over three years, and services revenue, which failed to reach the soaring levels forecasted by analysts. Though the company maintained its rally in the stock market for much of 2024, the recent dip has seen Apple lose billions in market value, with Wall Street analysts now re-evaluating their previously bullish forecasts. Adding to the narrative, reports from industry insiders suggested that tensions were rising within the company, with murmurs of internal discontent over the pace of innovation, a reliance on older products, and challenges in keeping consumer enthusiasm high as the global smartphone market approaches saturation. Despite the launch of its eagerly anticipated Vision Pro headset and new MacBooks, some investors questioned whether Apple – long seen as a playground for creativity and disruption – had lost its edge. The unease was not just confined to financial circles. Public sentiment, too, seemed to shift. Consumer feedback online pointed to a growing sense of product fatigue, with many questioning why Apple's latest devices felt oddly familiar or failed to deliver the “Wow factor” previously associated with the brand. Competitors like Google, Samsung, and even start-up Apple-watchers such as Notion and BYD are now receiving more attention as potential disruptors. Apple’s board has issued a firm response to recent concerns, stating in a statement on Thursday that the company remains “firmly on track for continued growth,” and that its long-term strategy is “more robust than ever.” However, as the company braces itself for a new era in tech—one marked by the rise of AI and the shift to services over hardware—investors are left wondering whether Apple is still the “Fortress” it once was or if the cracks are finally showing.

Toby Flood is set to miss the opening stages of the 2025 Six Nations Championship after suffering a setbacks with a knee injury, according to reports from rugby insiders. The 37-year-old fly-half, who recently earned a recall to the England squad after a remarkable comeback season with Leicester Tigers, is now facing a critical hurdle on his return to international duty. Flood was injured during a recent Premier Rugby Club match, sustaining a ligament strain that is expected to keep him sidelined for several weeks. Tim Lane, England’s performance director, confirmed that the player is undergoing further scans to determine the full extent of his injury. Flood’s return to the England fold had been seen as a potential masterstroke, offering the team a wealth of experience and calm execution at fly-half, particularly with Farrell still recovering from a significant workload. His inclusion was also viewed as a way to provide support and competition in the back-line for younger talents looking to establish themselves. The injury comes as a blow for both England and Flood’s club, Leicester Tigers, who are currently competing for promotion in the top-tier competition. Flood had been in outstanding form over the last few months, with many observers drawing comparisons to his peak performances during the 2015 Rugby World Cup and early 2012 Six Nations. England head coach Stuart Lancaster, while disappointed, was quoted as saying that the team – and Flood himself – could take positives from the situation. “Toby is a competitor and a leader, and he’ll use every setback as a chance to come back stronger,” said Lancaster. “He’s someone who knows what it takes to perform at the top level, and his presence alone has an impact on the team.” Despite the injury, Flood is being tipped as a vital addition to future key matches in the Six Nations, with his return likely to play a crucial role in the latter phases of the tournament. The exact date of his comeback is yet to be confirmed, but it is expected to be in time for the second half of the championship. For now, young fly-halves at the national team will be given an opportunity to step up and show their potential. Flood, for his part, is said to be in good spirits and dedicated to his recovery. He has been a figure of resilience throughout his career, having overcome previous injuries and periods of reflection since his last England appearance.

Dundee striker Greg Stewart has expressed confidence that his strong partnership with fellow forward Kane Hemmings will be instrumental in the club's pursuit of success this season. The duo, who have already shown glimpses of their potential over pre-season, believe their chemistry and understanding of each other's game will lead to a fruitful campaign for the Dark Blues. Stewart, who has been a consistent goalscorer during his previous spells at Dundee, made a high-profile return to the Dens Park side this summer. Hemmings, signed from Barnsley as part of a fresh injection of attacking talent, brings a physical presence, technical ability and a proven track record in the Scottish top-flight. Speaking to the press ahead of the new season, Stewart said: "Kane and I hit it off straight away — on and off the pitch. We share the same hunger, the same ambition, and most importantly, the same belief that we can make a real difference for this team." The pair formed a striking partnership during a pre-season tour in the United States and impressed with their movement off the ball, ability to interchange positions and clinical finishing. Stewart, who has scored over 100 goals for Dundee in two previous spells, believes Hemmings' creativity and experience will complement his deadly finishing as the Dark Blues look to climb the Scottish Premiership table and make an impact in cup competitions. "He's a top pro," Stewart continued. "Kane’s got huge experience at this level and in wider areas as well. He’s a player who can create things out of nothing, and he's just someone who knows how to get the crowd going. That's really important for us because we need to energise the supporters and make the home games feel like an unbreakable fortress." Hemmings echoed Stewart's sentiments about their partnership, saying: "Greg’s the type of striker every attacking player wants to play with. He knows where to be, he makes the right runs, and he’s got that composure in front of goal that you can't teach. As long as we're on the same wavelength, I'm sure something special can happen." The optimism around the partnership comes as Dundee head into the new season looking to end a number of long-standing wait: their first league championship since 1951, the first Scottish Cup win since 1934, and the first domestic treble since 1947–48.

Celtic found themselves on the wrong end of a crushing 4-0 defeat against Dinamo Zagreb in Croatia on Thursday night, with the European giants’ defensive frailties laid bare by a rampant Marko Pjaca, who netted a well-timed hat-trick to seal what proved to be a humiliation for the reigning Scottish champions. The result leaves Celtic with a single point from their four Europa League Group D fixtures, ending their European campaign on a sour note. Match highlights were dominated not by their clinical forward play, which had been a hallmark of their domestic form, but by the glaring gaps in their backline that the Croatian champions exploited ruthlessly. Pjaca, who finished the night with a devastating three goals, found the net in the 16th, 43rd, and 74th minutes, each time capitalising on lapses in Celtic's defensive discipline. A first-half goal from Sandro Kulenović further compounded Celtic's woes, and though they showed glimpses of urgency in the second half, particularly through the efforts of Kyogo Furuhashi and Ryan Christie, they were unable to break down Dinamo’s disciplined, deep-lying backline. Manager Brendan Rodgers, who has previously praised the team's defensive capabilities in domestic fixtures, will have plenty to address after what many have described as a “pathetic” defensive display – one of the worst he has overseen during his time at Celtic Park. The match was set in the context of Celtic’s underwhelming Europa League campaign, in which they failed to live up to their status as pre-tournament favourites. After a promising 3-2 win over Dinamo Zagreb earlier in the group stages, Celtic faltered consistently in key moments, with their inability to maintain consistency across all four matches ultimately dooming their hopes of progression. Dinamo, meanwhile, were clinical and ruthless from the outset, clearly coming into the match with the necessary tactical nous and composure to dismantle a side that has claimed to be Europe’s second-best club less than a year ago. For Celtic fans, the defeat will further fuel speculation about the club's approach to transfer strategy and how their resources are utilised in the market. Given the reigning European champions of a short while ago, this latest failure on the continental stage will undoubtedly prompt calls for urgent reform ahead of next season. Rodgers, who will return to Glasgow with heavy thoughts, has until now managed to keep Celtic afloat at home, but the contrast in performance between the Scottish league and European competition will be difficult to overlook.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) has urged political leaders to scale back polarising rhetoric and rhetoric it claims has "legitimised hate" during an increasingly divisive campaign period. In a rare public intervention, the UK’s independent watchdog for equality and human rights called for the “tone” of campaigning to be “reconsidered” and warned that inflammatory language risks normalising prejudice and hostility. The statement comes amid rising reports of abuse and intimidation targeted at individuals from minority backgrounds, including Muslims, Jews, Black and ethnic minority communities, as well as LGBTQ+ individuals and immigrants. Commission chair Emily Isabella said: “When powerful voices in politics use divisive language, they send a signal that hate and intolerance are somehow acceptable. We urge all leaders to think carefully about the impact of their words, not only on public discourse but on the safety and well-being of real people.” The EHRC did not name specific politicians but has previously issued private concerns to parties over remarks made by prominent lawmakers, including those pertaining to immigration, national identity and religion. The call follows a sharp rise in hate crimes reported to the police since the start of the year, with Month of Race Hate Crimes and Islamophobic incidents being highlighted in recent police data. A Home Office spokesperson said it was aware of the EHRC's comments and reiterated the government’s commitment to tackling hate crime: “We are determined to protect national unity and ensure that everyone in the UK, regardless of their background, can feel safe and respected.” However, critics argued that the message should be directed more firmly toward the leadership at Westminster, which they claim is at the heart of the problem. Former Labour MP and deputy mayor of London, Joanne McCartney, said: “It is not enough to criticise the politicians who make headlines – all leaders must be held to account for statements about race, religion or identity that contribute to the climate of fear and division.” Meanwhile, a senior Conservative Party official refused to be drawn on the EHRC's comments, calling it “another politically motivated rebuke from the left.” The statement has reignited discussions about the role of political discourse in a modern democracy and whether the language of the political elite sets a dangerous precedent for public behaviour. As the nation continues to grapple with the deepening divisions over issues like Brexit, immigration and social cohesion, the EHRC's call arrives at a critical moment—urging leaders to think not only about winning the next argument, but about preserving the values that bind the nation together.

The Imam of China’s largest mosque, the People’s Liberation Army Mosque in the city of Kashgar, has been killed in what appears to be a targeted assassination, sparking concern and speculation over China’s volatile Xinjiang region. Umar Hadja, 53, was shot outside the mosque as he left dawn prayers on Tuesday, according to local state media. The Uyghur Muslim community, which has long faced severe government restrictions on religious expression in Xinjiang, is widely believed to have lost one of its most prominent spiritual leaders. Local authorities in Kashgar, a city in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, said the attack was "under investigation but is suspected to be politically motivated," though no group has officially claimed responsibility. State-owned media Xinhua reported that a suspect was arrested immediately after the shooting. However, details remain sparse, and the authorities have barred local and international journalists from the area, raising concerns about the lack of transparency.
