Umar Hadja, a well-respected religious figure, frequently presided over morning and evening prayers at the mosque and was known for advocating tolerance and interfaith dialogue. Former colleagues describe him as "a scholar with a deep knowledge of both Islamic and Chinese traditions, who never expressed anything but respect to the government and the law." His murder has added to simmering tensions in Xinjiang, a deeply religious region known for its cultural and religious restrictions under strict government oversight, and where recent years have seen a dramatic increase in surveillance and repression of Uyghur Muslims. Officials have accused Islamic extremist organisations of operating in the area, including suspected groups with ties to organisations also active in Central Asia and the Middle East. However, many international rights groups accuse the Chinese authorities of exaggerating fears of terrorism to justify their heavy-handed policies, including the detention of at least 1 million Uyghurs in “re-education” camps. The assassination has also intensified fears of retaliation or further crackdowns. One Uyghur shopkeeper in Kashgar, who asked not to be named for fear of government reprisal, said: "We feared something like this might happen. People are scared. We don't know what will happen next." Kashgar, a city of over 500,000 with a rich Silk Road history, has long been a focal point in China’s management of the Uyghur minority. While the Chinese state continues to deny allegations of widespread abuses or restrictions on religious worship, critics argue that the region remains one of the most heavily policed in the world.

The company that conducts most of America’s rocket launches, United Launch Alliance (ULA), has unveiled the specifications for its next-generation vehicle, the Vulcan Centaur, marking a pivotal shift in the US space launch industry. The disclosure comes as a direct response to the growing challenges posed by the rising dominance of SpaceX and the rapid advances in commercial aerospace technology. ULA, a joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, has long played a critical role in NASA’s deep space missions and national security launches, but this new rocket signals an attempt to remain competitive in a rapidly evolving market. Officials at ULA announced the Vulcan Centaur during a press conference in Decatur, Alabama, the site of its production facilities. The new rocket is designed to replace the Atlas V, a workhorse of the industry since 2002. Unlike the Atlas V, which uses Russian-made RD-180 engines, the Vulcan Centaur will be powered entirely by American technology, a move aimed at addressing lingering political and supply chain concerns following years of controversy over reliance on Russian components. Central to the Vulcan Centaur’s development is its use of the BE-4 engine, built by Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’s aerospace firm. This marks the first time in ULA’s history that it has integrated a new, non-military-grade launch engine developed by a commercial partner. The first test flight of the Vulcan Centaur is scheduled for late 2023, with the vehicle expected to launch a range of cargo, satellites, and future NASA missions. In a statement, ULA CEO Tory Bruno said: “The Vulcan Centaur represents a new era for American spaceflight. It will give the Department of Defense, our international partners, and commercial customers the flexibility and affordability they need to secure our place among the stars.” The rocket is about 20 per cent taller than the Atlas V and is expected to have greater payload capacity, thanks to the Centaur upper stage, which will be powered by a new RL10-based engine. The announcement of the Vulcan Centaur has been met with cautious optimism by the aerospace community. While it is a welcome step forward for ULA, analysts note that the waiting game will soon begin. As ULA moves forward with its new system, space observers will be watching closely to see whether the company can retain the lucrative government contracts it has held for decades. This development also underscores the accelerating pace of innovation in the US space industry, where new competitors and technologies are reshaping the landscape almost daily.

A Clergyman’s Condolence: Can Violence Be Justified Against IS?   In a rare and deeply public statement on morality in the face of war, Bashar Warda, the Chaldean Catholic Archbishop of Irbil, has spoken out to justify the killing of members of the so-called Islamic State (IS). The 67-year-old cleric, a vocal advocate for Christian communities in Iraq and an international symbol of perseverance in the face of terror, made his remarks in a recent interview, where he acknowledged the moral complexity involved in combatting a group known for its brutality. “When you treat a cancer, you have to use unfortunate measures,” he said, drawing a clinical analogy that underscores a broader moral and theological debate across religious and political circles. Archbishop Warda, who has spent his life tending to Christian and other minority communities displaced or harmed by decades of conflict and sectarian violence, faces an impossible task: assembling unity in a fractured land while contending with the ideological onslaught of extremism. His words are taken in context at a time when the so-called Islamic State, though weakened since the fall of its self-declared caliphate in 2019, is experiencing a resurgence in rural areas of Syria and Iraq as local and international forces struggle for control. The cleric’s statement reflects a growing consensus among local Christian and Muslim leaders who insist that negotiating or denying violence against IS is no longer politically viable, let alone ethically defensible. His comments come in the wake of recent tensions over coalition military actions in Iraq and Syria, particularly the principles guiding civilian involvement and targeted strikes. Some critics have argued that legitimising violence, even against a violent enemy, risks eroding the very moral foundations that communities seek to uphold in their repulsion of terror. Yet in a region where most have been forced to survive by any means necessary, the archbishop’s words strike a pragmatic and troubling chord. “What is done to us by these people is far crueler,” he said, referring to mass killings, forced conversions, and sexual slavery under IS rule. His explanation reflects the lived experiences of hundreds of thousands of civilians who have watched their homes burned, families torn apart, and traditions obliterated by extremist ideology. As a figure of moral authority, Warda’s statements add new weight to the conversation surrounding justice and vengeance in the Middle East, where the lines are often blurred.

In a thrilling end to a Championship encounter at St Andrew’s, Birmingham City secured a dramatic 2-1 victory over Sheffield Wednesday thanks to Lukas Jutkiewicz’s stoppage-time header, sparking scenes of pure bedlam among the home fans. The win lifted Blues up the table as they picked up yet another vital point in their push for the play-offs, while the Owls left West Midlands with their heads in their hands after a missed opportunity that will haunt them for some time. The first half had barely started when visiting defender Morgan Whittaker found the back of the net with an unfortunate own goal in the 10th minute. Whittaker, attempting to clear a low cross from John Egan, steered the ball past Fabian Johnson and into the bottom corner. Birmingham, despite leading, struggled to find their rhythm in front of goal, with Oliver Burke and Cole Egan failing to convert any of the half-time chances they created. Sheffield Wednesday, still somewhat reeling from this early setback, entered the second half with renewed intensity. Their efforts were finally rewarded on the hour mark when George Hirst converted from the penalty spot after referee Lewis Nokes adjudged that Championship debutant Cheyenne Dunkley had handled the ball in the box. It was a contentious decision, but on the balance of play, Hirst’s equaliser seemed to encapsulate the ebb and flow of the match, and both sides entered the final 20 minutes level on the scoreboard. What followed was a tense period of football, with both defences digging in and the intensity rising. As the clock ticked into stoppage time, a sumptuous cross from the right was swung in by Aaron Morley, and Lukas Jutkiewicz — the giant striker whose header would live long in the memory — rose highest to nod the ball past the stranded Kieran Freeman. The 40,000 fans inside St Andrew’s responded with deafening roars, and Jutkiewicz made no hiding from the celebration, sprinting down the touchline to join in the bedlam. Birmingham manager Gary Rowell, no stranger to late drama, will be delighted with the win as he continues to rebuild his side ahead of next season. “That’s what you live for as a manager,” he said in his post-match interview. “To go the whole 90 minutes and get snatched from your hand — it’s tough, but I’m proud of the players. We kept believing, and Lukas showed what a leader he is.

Lewis Hamilton secured a commanding and almost flawless victory at the Mexican Grand Prix, continuing his dominance from pole position in a race that passed like a masterclass in precision and patience. The Mercedes driver extended his championship lead by overtaking Red Bull's Daniel Ricciardo with relative ease and then managing the race at a steady yet unassailable pace. For Hamilton and his team, it was a sorely needed moment of composure in a season that has often been fraught with mechanical issues and unexpected setbacks. From the moment the lights went out, Hamilton looked in control, pulling a comfortable gap in the early laps before settling into a rhythm that suggested he was not only driving the race but dictating it. Behind him, much of the intrigue unfolded, with Max Verstappen of Renault mounting a gritty challenge to Marco Schumacher of Force India, and Sergio Pérez – who had the crowd on his side – battling fiercely for position. In an emotionally charged event, Pérez nearly capitalized when Ricciardo suffered a slow pit stop, which allowed the Mexican driver to close the gap and flirt with second place for a brief, but thrilling, period. Hamilton, however, was unmoved, keeping his focus on preserving his lead and ensuring that the frustrations of a difficult season did not repeat themselves on Mexican soil. This win was a reminder of what Hamilton – and Mercedes, for that matter – are capable of when everything goes to plan. Unfortunately for the reigning champion, his season has seen far too many instances of that not being the case. Earlier this year, Hamilton endured a string of grueling races in which reliability issues derailed what could have been a title-winning campaign. Even so, the Mexican Grand Prix provided the British driver with a much-needed pause for reflection. As the checkered flag fell, there was a feeling about this win that was reminiscent of his finest performances in the sport — calm, clinical and convincing. Behind him, the midfield battle was as dramatic as the front of the grid was tranquil, with Verstappen proving once again that he is no shrinking violet when it comes to pushing for position. Fans at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez were treated to a spectacle that, while lacking the fireworks of Hamilton’s early laps, was no less compelling in the drama of those behind the leader. The Grand Prix lived up to its reputation as a crowd-pleaser, delivering the passion of home goers and the star power of one of the sport’s greats.

Dr Kate Granger, a 34-year-old consultant geriatrician at Tameside General Hospital in Greater Manchester, passed away on 23 July after a five-year battle with breast cancer. Yet, during those years, she transformed the often impersonal nature of hospital care and inspired a national movement to improve the way healthcare professionals interact with patients. Through her activism and advocacy, Dr Granger raised hundreds of thousands of pounds for charity, most notably for the charity she founded, the #Morethanamoonlight charity, and she arguably did more than anyone to spark a renewed focus on the human side of healthcare in the UK. Her story began in 2011, when doctors made a diagnosis of terminal cancer and told her only that her prognosis was uncertain. My name is Kate Granger, who are you? became the most well-known phrase from the campaign that followed, launched after a particularly frustrating hospital visit where she was addressed for hours as “the lady upstairs” or referred to simply by her bed number. Humbled and frustrated at being treated more as a condition than a person, Dr Granger turned her energy to driving change. The #HelloMrSmith campaign, which initially highlighted poor communication between medical staff and patients, encouraged health professionals to introduce themselves and say hello, reminding healthcare workers that they are not just diagnosing and treating a medical condition but providing care to a human being. The Royal College of Nursing and other health bodies have since adopted the campaign, and staff in many hospitals now carry #HelloMrSmith wristbands and wear badges as a reminder to be kind, compassionate and person-centred. Her efforts were not limited to a campaign – Dr Granger also became a powerful voice for better healthcare policy, and worked closely with healthcare charities and the government to reform patient-centred care. She did this even as her own health declined, continuing to speak at conferences and write blog posts from hospital beds and even during her last weeks. Dr Granger’s legacy is already being felt in the NHS, where patients and their families are being treated with more dignity, and where health professionals are reminded that it is not just technical knowledge that counts, but empathy, communication and human connection. As one of her colleagues put it, “She gave a voice to patients and showed us all that behind every patient record is a person whose life matters.” Dr Granger's death is a profound loss, but her spirit continues to live on in improvements across our healthcare system – one greeting at a time.

In a fiercely contested South Yorkshire derby at Bramall Lane, Sheffield United claimed a hard-fought 1-0 victory over Barnsley, thanks to an early goal from Billy Sharp. The result, however, was overshadowed by a dramatic second-half sending off for each side, as tensions flared in a match brimming with local pride and high stakes. The key moment came just before the 15-minute mark when Sharp, making his 350th appearance for the club, swooped to convert a penalty after Barnsley defender Liam Kelly brought down Paul Coutts inside the box. The strike, Sharp’s 11th of the season, gave the hosts a deserved lead and sparked wild celebrations among the home fans, who have grown increasingly confident about their team’s promotion hopes under manager Chris Wilder. Barnsley struggled to mount a response in the first half, and the away side turned to a more defensive approach, breaking up play at every opportunity. But as the match progressed, the pressure began to build in the second half, culminating in a heated clash of tempers near the end of the game. After 68 minutes, the referee, Anthony Taylor, booked Barnsley captain Ryan Williams for a cynical foul to halt what he considered a deadly counterattack. Just minutes later, United’s Kean Bryan saw red after a reckless challenge on Sam Winnall. The sending off seemed to galvanise Barnsley, but the resulting numerical advantage failed to bring any goals as their attempts on goal were thwarted by a resolute Blades defence. With just ten men, Sheffield United also absorbed the pressure from the final whistle, protecting their lead until the final whistle. The victory lifted them to fourth in the Championship table, underlining their status as one of the teams most in form this season. The game was not just a test of footballing ability but a reminder of what derbies represent — passion, pride, and the enduring rivalries that continue to galvanise fans across English football. As the final whistle blew, the supporters chanted for the players, acknowledging the blood, sweat, and, at times, the fury that defines a night like this. For the visiting fans, it was a bitter pill to swallow, but with the end of the season approaching, the derby took yet another chapter in its storied history. Now, with the points secured and the derby victory on the board, Wilder’s side will be hoping this is just the latest step in their pursuit of the Championship play-offs — and perhaps one step closer to reclaiming their place in the Premier League.

A prominent figure tipped as a potential leader of UKIP is likely "too extreme" to be permitted to stand in the leadership election, according to a senior party member. The comments come as the divisive anti-EU party continues its search for a unifying figure to guide it through the uncertain political landscape of 2024. The individual in question is widely believed to be David Coburn, who has previously led the Ulster Unionists and has attracted controversy with his stance on policy issues ranging from immigration to national sovereignty. Chris White, a Welsh Assembly Member (AM) for UKIP, made the remarks in an interview with the Daily Post. “Some of the people being mentioned are possibly too extreme and could be blocked from standing,” he said. “The party’s rules state that candidates must be acceptable to the executive and reflect the values of UKIP. I would argue that some of the names being floated fall short of that.” White added that while UKIP prides itself on taking a hardline stance on immigration and sovereignty, some figures within the party’s leadership race have adopted positions he described as “unworkable and alienating.” UKIP, which was one of the most influential anti-EU parties during the 2016 Brexit referendum, has seen a significant decline in support as the Conservatives have taken on many of its key issues in recent years. Internal divisions have also deepened as the party searches for a leader who can rejuvenate its support base. The party's current interim leader, Bill Etheridge, was removed from the role in December after just three months in charge, further signalling the fractious environment within the party. Coburn, whose name has surfaced repeatedly in leadership speculation, has been a controversial figure in Northern Irish politics for his uncompromising approach to key issues such as identity and national integrity. However, he has also been the subject of legal scrutiny over allegations relating to a business venture and fails to inspire the public trust currently required of a figure who could lead UKIP. The party’s leadership race is expected to be announced in the coming weeks, with the winner expected to take the mantle as the party seeks to redefine itself in a post-Brexit era. “We are not looking for another firebrand to take us further to the right,” White explained. “We are looking for someone who can reach out and be a serious player in British politics.”

Great Wall Motor eyes move into global market via interest in Fiat Chrysler   China’s Great Wall Motor, best known for its popular Haval brand and leadership in China’s competitive SUV market, is reportedly setting its sights on a major international expansion by exploring a potential investment or partnership with the Italian-American automotive giant Fiat Chrysler Automobiles (FCA). The Italian-American firm, which has ownership of the well-known Jeep brand among other marques, has long represented a bridge between European engineering and North American consumer tastes. For Great Wall, a venture into FCA’s operations could mark a significant step in the Chinese company's ambition to challenge dominant global automakers and cement itself as a key player in Western markets. The potential interest in Fiat Chrysler comes as no surprise given the broader push by Chinese car manufacturers to establish themselves on the world stage. Companies like BYD, Geely – the owner of Volvo and Lotus – and Li Auto have already made inroads in Europe and the Americas, capitalising on FCA's struggles with declining market share, delayed electrification strategies and a challenging restructuring deal with rival automaker Stellantis earlier this year. That deal, which saw Chrysler combine with France’s PSA, forming one of the world’s largest automotive groups, left FCA as a standalone entity but also exposed its vulnerabilities as it attempts to adapt to modern market demands. Great Wall, already the best-selling SUV manufacturer in China, faces intense domestic competition, and its recent foray into the global market through its flagship brand Haval has met with mixed success. While Haval has achieved a strong foothold in Southeast Asia, North Africa, and parts of the Middle East, it has struggled to make a meaningful impact in Europe and the United States—markets dominated by established European and American brands. A strategic move into FCA or a key component of its operations could significantly speed up its entry into those lucrative markets, allowing Great Wall to leverage FCA’s existing dealer networks, brand equity and manufacturing infrastructure. Analysts believe that such a move would not only give Great Wall access to Jeep’s respected off-road legacy but also allow it to tap into the advanced engineering and R&D resources of a company that, despite its recent difficulties, still boasts a highly experienced workforce and a strong safety and performance reputation. There are also potential synergies in the shift toward electric and hybrid technologies, an area where Great Wall has already made major investments, whereas FCA has been slower on the uptake.

Chris Gayle Makes History with World Cup Double Century as West Indies Thrash Zimbabwe   Canberra – Cricketing history was made on a chilly Thursday night at Manuka Oval as West Indies opener Chris Gayle stared into the record books with a monumental 215 not out, the first double century in Cricket World Cup history. The innings, a masterclass in power and composure, propelled West Indies to an emphatic 216-run victory over Zimbabwe in a Pool B match that will be remembered for years to come. From the moment Gayle reached his hundred, the crowd sensed they were witnessing something special. The 38-year-old, already one of the game’s most feared big-hitters, showed no signs of slowing down despite the pressures of international cricket’s highest stage. His innings contained 27 boundaries and four towering sixes, and he reached the historic milestone of 200 off just 138 balls — a feat never achieved before in World Cup history. Gayle’s unbeaten 215 came off 142 deliveries and included an array of near-impossible shots that left the Zimbabwean pacemen helpless and the fans in awe. His innings, which set the tone for a strong West Indies total of 353 for six, was a reminder of his explosive capability, even against a spirited Zimbabwe side known for their competitive approach on home and away tours alike. Shai Hope (79) and Nicholas Pooran (58) provided strong support at the top and middle order, respectively, while the West Indies’ bowling attack, led by Kemar Roach (3/39) and Alzarri Joseph (3/49), ran through the Zimbabwe lineup in a demolition job under the lights. Zimbabwe, despite a gritty 62 from captain Craig Ervine, were bowled out for 137 in 30.3 overs. Their aggressive chase barely got off the ground as Gayle's efforts had laid a target that proved unattainable even against the West Indies' exceptional total. The win extended the West Indies’ dominance in recent World Cup encounters and marks them as formidable contenders in the tournament. As for Gayle, his player of the match performance has reinvigorated the conversation about his legacy in world cricket. “I just try to play my game and play with the team,” Gayle said in the post-match press conference. “I didn’t think about the double century, I just wanted to win the game for the team.” The West Indies will now turn their attention to their next Group B fixture against India in Perth, where another statement performance could push them further to the forefront of the competition.

Harriet Harman, the acting leader of the Labour Party, has called for unity and reflection rather than finger-pointing in the wake of the party’s devastating defeat in the general election. Speaking at a post-election meeting of Labour MPs in London, Harman urged the party to avoid what she described as a “blame game” in analysing the result. The Labour Party suffered historic losses, losing nearly 60 seats and ending up with a smaller share of the vote than in the 2015 election, a result she described as a “wake-up call” for the party. Harman acknowledged the scale of the humiliation but underlined the need for solidarity as the party begins the process of recovery and re-election planning. In her first public address since Jeremy Corbyn stepped down as leader, Harman made it clear that the focus should be on the future rather than the past, saying, “We owe it to our supporters and to the country to move forward with unity and purpose.” The debate over whether the party has a leadership problem or a more profound philosophical and organisational one has already begun among many MPs and activists. Former shadow chancellor John McDonnell was among the prominent figures who had urged a suspension of the blame culture in the aftermath of the defeat. Harman concurred, saying, “It is important we do not point fingers at individuals when the challenges we faced were much bigger than one person or one faction.” She also ruled out any immediate leadership contest, despite speculation that some MPs and members would expect a new leader to be chosen quickly. Harman said, “There is a role for every one of us in steering this party through a difficult period. What matters now is what we do next, not what went wrong before.” Meanwhile, shadow home secretary Emily Thornberry, who has been a long-time ally of Jeremy Corbyn, has hinted that the party may need to “modernise and move on” from some of its recent policies. Thornberry, who is unseated in her West Ham seat, said the election showed the need for a more inclusive approach. The SDLP, Sinn Féin, and the Greens all said the result highlighted deeper national issues rather than just a problem with the Labour Party. Harman’s message of unity and forward-looking thinking will be a difficult one to translate into action, given the fractures that have been opened up around economic policy, Brexit, and the party's identity.

The European Union has unveiled controversial plans to establish an EU Border and Coast Guard force in a bid to tackle an unprecedented influx of migrants arriving across the Mediterranean and elsewhere. The proposed force aims to centralise border control, integrate national coastguards, and impose a unified approach to managing irregular migration and smuggling as the region grapples with one of its worst humanitarian and political crises in recent years. According to leaked documents and official statements released as part of the European Commission’s broader policy proposals, the new force will be headquartered in Rome and will operate under the coordination of Frontex, the EU’s existing border agency. It will be considerably larger and more powerful than the current agency, enabling it to conduct surveillance, rescue operations, and law enforcement at sea, as well as on land across EU external borders. In recent years, record numbers of migrants have tried to reach Europe by sea, with the majority departing from Libya and crossing the Mediterranean to reach Italy and Greece. In 2015 alone, more than a million people arrived in Europe via sea and land routes, with thousands losing their lives in the process. The resulting political unrest has led to calls for stronger, more coordinated EU action. The new Border and Coast Guard force would be given full operational authority and would include joint patrols and surveillance efforts, with the potential deployment of drones, radar systems, and patrol ships. The force will also be tasked with identifying traffickers, reducing opportunities for smuggling, and ensuring the return of undocumented migrants. However, the plans have already faced sharp criticism from a number of member states and NGOs. Germany, which has led efforts to allow in refugees for humanitarian reasons, has expressed concern that the force could undermine Germany's commitments under international refugee law and human rights agreements. Human rights groups, including Amnesty International and the European Council on Refugees and Exiles, have raised alarms about the potential for the force to become a tool for mass detention and deportation, and not for rescue and protection. They argue that it is unwise for the EU to take a ‘hard line’ response without first addressing the root causes of migration, such as war, poverty and political instability in countries like Syria, Eritrea, and Afghanistan. The European Commission has insisted that the force will be equipped to carry out rescue missions as well as border control and will work in collaboration with humanitarian actors.

Pakistan Sends Troops to Assist Citizens After Devastating Earthquake in Iran   In a gesture of solidarity and urgency, Pakistan has deployed military and disaster relief teams to the border region with Iran following a powerful earthquake that struck south-eastern Iran, killing hundreds and injuring thousands. The quake, which occurred on Monday morning and measured 7.8 in magnitude, caused widespread destruction in the Sistan and Baluchestan province — home to a large number of Pakistanis, particularly from the Baloch community, who have family ties and economic connections across the border. As concerns grow over the scale of casualties and the situation of injured or stranded citizens in the quake-affected areas, the Pakistani government has made emergency arrangements to provide medical and humanitarian aid. Military helicopters have been dispatched to the region, while rescue teams equipped with search-and-recovery gear and medical supplies are aiding efforts to reach remote and inaccessible areas. Foreign Office spokesperson Zahid Hafeez stated earlier this week: “Pakistan is extending all possible assistance to its citizens and returning citizens affected in Iran. Our people have shared ties with the local communities in the region and the government is working around the clock to help them during this time of crisis.” The quake, which collapsed entire buildings and cut roads and power lines, has left many hamlets in ruins. Images shared on social media show flattened homes and desperate crowds of survivors waiting for aid at the border. Although Iran has not formally requested international help, the affected areas are remote and have limited access to emergency services, prompting fears that the death toll could rise. For Pakistan, which is all too familiar with the devastation caused by earthquakes — such as the 2005 earthquake that killed over 80,000 people and left millions homeless — the disaster has struck a personal chord. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered a comprehensive relief operation to ensure the well-being of Pakistani citizens and returnees. “Whatever pain is being felt in Iran is also felt in Pakistan,” Sharif said. “We will do everything possible to support our brothers and sisters.” Currently, aid and evacuees are being flown into Quetta, Pakistan’s largest city in Balochistan province, which is located just 100 miles from the epicentre of the quake. Family members of the injured and missing have gathered at the airport in anxious anticipation. The response has been welcomed by local groups and members of the Baloch diaspora, many of whom had called for more action after news of the quake broke.

Rising Awareness of Concussion to Prompt More Early Retirements in Rugby, Warns Former Medical Adviser   As the sporting world continues to grapple with the long-term effects of head injuries, a top figure in rugby medicine has warned that greater awareness of concussion will inevitably lead to more athletes stepping away from the game. Dr Barry O’Driscoll, the former chief medical adviser to World Rugby, has said that as understanding of brain injuries deepens, players—and their families—are more likely to make the difficult decision to retire early rather than risk long-term damage. In an interview with the  Sunday Times , Dr O’Driscoll reflected on the progress made in recognising and treating concussions, but warned that the real consequences of such injuries are beginning to emerge. “We’ve done a lot to educate players and medical staff about the risks, but the truth is, some of these head knocks are just too dangerous to take lightly now,” he said. “There are still no perfect protocols that can fully mitigate the risk for every player. When the cost of continuing outweighs the benefit, people are increasingly choosing to retire.” O’Driscoll’s comments come amid growing concern about the long-term health of rugby players, with former athletes reporting symptoms of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) and other brain-related conditions. The sport, already under pressure from national unions and fans to make significant rule changes, has introduced measures to reduce high-impact tackles and prolong the game after concussive events. Yet even these efforts, while commendable, are not seen as sufficient by all. The issue is also being complicated by the cultural appeal of professional rugby, which remains one of the most physically demanding and macho sports in the world. Many young players are drawn to the game for the intensity and challenge, even as they are increasingly aware of the risks. O’Driscoll said this creates an “ethical dilemma” for clubs and medical teams: while it is up to the athletes to make their own decisions, the sport must do more to educate them about the lifelong health implications of their career choices. “There was a time when concussions were brushed aside,” O’Driscoll said. “Now, we’re seeing player unions, medical bodies, and governing bodies all pushing for better awareness. That’s the good news. The bad news is that this growing awareness will mean more players confronting the reality of their choices—head-on.”

A senior magistrate has resigned from his post after being suspended for attempting to pay an asylum seeker’s legal costs in a controversial case that has sparked debate over the independence and impartiality of the judiciary. Sir David Keane, a respected figure in the magistracy with a 20-year career, submitted a letter of resignation to the Lord Chancellor on Tuesday, following his suspension last week by the Magistrates’ Courts Council. The 61-year-old said he would not seek to contest the decision. The incident, which first came to light last month, concerned Sir David’s private payment of £1,000 in court costs for an unnamed Eritrean asylum seeker who had fallen into arrears and faced removal to a detention centre. Sir David, who had taken a personal interest in numerous high-profile and sensitive immigration cases, insisted the payment had been made as a “personal gesture of humanity in a difficult and unusual situation.” However, officials deemed his actions a breach of the strict ethical code that magistrates are required to uphold in both their professional and personal conduct. The Judicial Conduct Investigations Office (JCIO), which oversees conduct among magistrates and judges, launched an inquiry, and Sir David was suspended on the grounds that his actions undermined public confidence in the judiciary and created the appearance of impropriety. The magistrates’ council ruled that while there was “no evidence of misconduct – such as a motive of corruption, personal gain, or self-interest,” Sir David’s actions set a dangerous precedent by blurring the line between judicial responsibility and personal philanthropy. The case has stirred polarized reactions within the legal community and beyond. Critics of the government’s treatment of asylum seekers praised Sir David’s actions as an example of judicial compassion in a system they say is too cold and bureaucratic. Meanwhile, defenders of the suspension argued that allowing such personal interventions could lead to inconsistencies, undermine the rule of law and open the door to claims of favouritism. “This is not about cruel or corrupt conduct,” said a senior source within the Ministry of Justice. “It’s about the principle. The judiciary must remain detached and impartial – a payment from a judge or magistrate, no matter how well-intentioned, taints that essential neutrality.” Sir David’s resignation triggers fresh questions about how to balance the demand for compassion with the need for institutional integrity, particularly in a time of increasing public scrutiny over the treatment of vulnerable individuals caught in the UK’s immigration system.

Joe Root is the "obvious candidate" to take over as England's Test captain, according to one of the team's most experienced players, James Anderson, but the pace bowler has warned that the role must not come at the expense of Root's batting. The 28-year-old Yorkshireman is widely seen as a natural leader and has emerged as a favourite to replace the retired Alastair Cook at the helm of England’s Test side. Root has been in fine form this season, hitting a double century against Sri Lanka and displaying a calm, mature composure in high-pressure situations. Anderson, speaking in a recent interview ahead of England's ICC Champions Trophy campaign, said that Root's personality and cricketing ability make him the ideal choice to lead the team in the longer format of the game. "Joe is the obvious candidate," said Anderson. "He has the ability, the temperament, and the leadership qualities the team needs. But I think it’s really important that we get the support right around him so that he can continue playing in his usual style, because the last thing we want is to see his batting suffer under the added pressure of captaincy." The notion of combining captaincy with Test batting is not new in cricket, with former captains like Steve Smith and Virat Kohli having led their teams while remaining among the top run-scorers in the world. However, Anderson – England’s record Test wicket-taker – stressed the need to manage expectations. "We saw with Joe when he captained the Lions and the ODI team, the way he carried himself. People just naturally follow him. But the captaincy shouldn’t be a distraction from his main purpose on the field, which is to bat and to bat consistently and be an anchor for the team." Root, who made his Test debut about five years ago, has already had a taste of leadership at different levels. Questions remain over what role he would adopt in the limited-overs game and whether he will continue to play ODI and T20 cricket if he takes on the Test captaincy. With England expected to name their new captain shortly after the conclusion of the Champions Trophy, speculation is mounting about when Root will step into the role. Cricket historian Dr. David Johnson told The Times: "This is a new phase of English cricket, and Joe Root is at the heart of it.

A new report by members of the UK Parliament has revealed a startling disparity in economic opportunity, identifying Muslim women as the most disadvantaged group in British society. The findings, released by the All-Party Parliamentary Group on British Muslims, highlight a range of issues including low wages, high unemployment, and limited access to senior roles. The report was compiled after a two-year inquiry, during which the committee examined the experiences of Muslim women across the UK in education, employment, and social mobility. According to the findings, Muslim women are significantly underrepresented in the workforce, with unemployment among those aged 16 to 64 standing at nearly 15 percent—more than twice the national average of around 7 percent. Among those who are employed, many are trapped in low-paid, insecure work, with higher than average earnings gaps compared to their male counterparts and other women in the same professions. The inquiry found that headscarves and other religious dress often played a role in perpetuating the exclusion of Muslim women from prime employment opportunities. Several Muslim women testified in front of the committee about the subtle and overt discrimination they faced during job applications and in the workplace. One interviewee described being asked to "remove her hijab for a photo" during a shortlisted application process as a condition for being considered for a role, which she rejected and was not offered. The report also highlighted the struggle many Muslim women face in balancing faith with workplace culture, with some forced to choose between religious practice and career advancement. “It is not just about the hijab or the veil,” said committee member Tulip Siddiq, MP for Hampstead and Kilburn. “It’s about cultural perceptions, stereotyping, and a lack of meaningful representation in key sectors. Muslim women are being told through silence and subtle barriers that they do not belong in most places of power.” In addition to employment challenges, the report noted that Muslim women are more likely to be concentrated in low-skilled sectors and less likely to attain higher education qualifications, partly due to cultural pressures, limited role models, and access to certain educational opportunities. The parliamentary group called on the government and employers to introduce targeted initiatives to improve the economic participation of Muslim women, including unconscious bias training, clearer equal opportunity policies, and positive action to support young Muslim women entering the workforce. It also urged the media to do more to challenge negative portrayals of the community.

England were comprehensively outplayed on the final day of the fifth Test against India in Chennai, suffering a crushing innings-and-75-run defeat to effectively end their hopes of levelling the series. The hosts, having posted a robust total of 553 all out in their first innings and then dismissed England for a frail 258, wrapped up victory with more than a day to spare on Sunday. Chasing an improbable 453 to win, England once again faltered under pressure, their batting line-up crumbling into a familiar pattern of individual misfiring and collective disarray. Openers Alastair Cook and Moeen Ali showed brief signs of intent, but Cook’s dismissal for a cautious 22, caught behind off left-arm spinner Washington Sundar, ignited a devastating collapse. England lost their last eight wickets for just 92 runs, with Sundar and Ravindra Jadeja picking up four and three wickets respectively to earn a second successive 10-wicket haul for the Indian spin attack across the match. Jonny Bairstow, who showed some spirited resistance in the field over the previous days, was among the early victims, edging a wide one from Jadeja to slip into a 24-ball innings. Ben Stokes followed as India’s spin bowlers exploited the turning track, and then from the 40s – Jos Buttler, Sam Robson and Liam Plunkett – England’s final-day batting hopes faded rapidly. India completed their victory with a single to spare in the morning session, as they accelerated from 64 for four to 112 for eight, with Rishabh Pant top-scoring with a composed 32. The tourists’ frustrations poured out at drinks time, with key players seen exchanging words in the dressing room amid what has been a trying tour. It was another chaotic chapter in a Test series where England have struggled to find any consistent rhythm. Having started the match as the side to have claimed a first-innings lead, their inability to build on that foundation ultimately highlighted the stark gulf in class between the teams on home soil. Joe Root, England’s vice-captain, who had contributed 78 in the visitors’ first innings, praised the spirit of his team but admitted the result was hard to stomach. “We gave everything, but India were just too good today,” he said. “We’ll regroup and take what positives we can, but obviously this is a tough one to take.” With the series now lost 2-1, England turn their attention to future appointments, starting with a crucial home season where they will need to rediscover the form that has so far eluded them over this drawn-out and at times dispiriting tour.

Dame Sarah Storey has etched her name in history as Britain's most successful female Paralympian, securing her 12th gold medal on a triumphant opening day at the Rio 2016 Paralympics. The 37-year-old, already a legend in her sport, extended her record in an awe-inspiring display of cycling excellence at the Estadio Nogueira Velodrome as she powered to victory in the C4-5 500m time trial. Storey, who was born without the use of her lower legs and has also competed as a swimmer, has now matched the tally of Paralympic gold medals won by athlete Sir Harrison Sherring\- the only male Briton to surpass the 12-medal mark. Her latest triumph solidifies her status not just as Britain’s most decorated female Paralympian, but as one of the most iconic Paralympic athletes of all time. "I can’t believe I’ve just won my 12th gold," Storey said in an emotional team interview after the race. "I still feel like I’m chasing goals rather than celebrating them, and being part of British cycling takes special credit. The support from both the team and the public has always meant everything to me." Storey, who has overcome immense personal challenges, including suicide attempts in 2014, has become a symbol of determination and resilience on the global stage. Transitioning from swimming to road and track cycling in 2008, after an 88 per cent lung capacity scare in the pool, she has transformed herself into a cycling powerhouse. Partnered with pilot Corrine Hall, who herself continued a stellar Paralympic career with a pair of bronze medals, Storey remains a trailblazer in the sport. "Corrine has lit my fire this season. Her energy is infectious and I owe her so much," she said of Hall, who has moved up to the C5 time trial after four years in the C4-5 tandem. The victory was also a personal one for Storey, as it marked her 18th overall Paralympic medal. She had previously won 11 golds and three silvers in four previous Games. At the Beijing 2008 Paralympics, she set a course record that stood for four years, and in 2012, she was one of seven Paralympians named in the Queen’s Birthday Honours. "It’s one of those surreal moments where you take stock and think, how did I get here?" she said, summing up a career defined by perseverance and precision.

Nurses across Northern Ireland are being encouraged to use their political voice in the upcoming Assembly election, as one of the largest public sector unions warns of the risks posed by political instability on the region’s long-neglected health service. The Royal College of Nursing (RCN) has launched a call to action for healthcare workers to participate in the vote on 2 March, stressing that the collapse of the Stormont executive has severely stalled progress on vital reforms. The union argues that with policy development in a state of limbo, the voices of those on the frontlines—those most directly affected by the shortcomings of the current system—are more critical than ever. “Nurses are not just caregivers; they are also citizens with a unique understanding of the challenges facing the health and social care system,” said RCN Northern Ireland regional officer Elaine Ferlie. “This election is an opportunity to shape a future that reflects the needs of the public and the workforce who serve them.” The recent collapse of Stormont in January 2017 has led to a suspension of the devolved government and an extended political stalemate, resulting in the UK Parliament taking over responsibility for legislation—albeit with limited powers—through the snap UK general election. This has left key health reforms, including addressing chronic staff shortages, investing in mental health services and improving infrastructure, stuck in political gridlock. With no Stormont leaders to advocate for health issues, nurses, and other health workers are being urged to step into the political arena. Union representatives have highlighted the growing strain on the health service, with reports of ambulance delays, hospital bed shortages and consultant-led services being scaled back. These issues are compounded by years of underfunding and a lack of strategic direction. “Every nurse and healthcare professional knows the system is under pressure, and political instability doesn’t help,” said Ferlie. “The Assembly election represents the first opportunity for people to choose a new direction and make their views known.” The call to vote is not just a plea for political engagement but a challenge for the healthcare community to shape their working conditions and patient care. Registration for the Assembly election is currently open, and those employed in healthcare, including midwives, paramedics, and allied health professionals, are being specifically targeted as influential voters in the campaign. As the deadline for registration draws closer, the union is working in partnership with local health trusts to support staff in accessing the electoral register and making informed decisions on polling day.

The political contours of Scotland have been fundamentally redrawn in the wake of the Scottish National Party’s (SNP) stunning landslide victory. With every seat in Scotland seemingly poised to be taken by the pro-independence party, the UK political landscape faces an unprecedented recalibration. For Labour, the results mark a historic collapse—arguably the most significant electoral wipeout since the party’s founding in the early 20th century. For the Conservatives, a once-trusted brand in Scotland now finds itself struggling to reclaim even a shadow of its former dominance, while the Liberal Democrats and smaller parties appear to have been rendered politically irrelevant in the short term. The SNP’s sweeping success, led by First Minister Nicola Sturgeon, signals a seismic shift not only in domestic Scottish politics but across the United Kingdom as a whole. With an almost total clean sweep—what appears to be 56 out of 59 Scottish seats—The SNP has delivered an unambiguous message: the electorate is demanding a stronger Scottish voice, and this has been laid bare in figures not seen since the electoral politics of 1945. With the party now poised to hold more seats in Westminster per capita than any other nation within the UK, the implications are clear: the power balance in the capital has irrevocably shifted, and the demand for greater autonomy—and potentially full independence—has never been louder. For Labour, this is a bitter pill to swallow. The party, once a dominant force across Scotland, saw its parliamentary representation plummet from 41 seats to potentially just one—an almost incomprehensible collapse for a party that has cast itself as the natural representative of working-class interests. The defeat is not merely an electoral fluke, but a result of years of disillusionment, policy missteps, and a failure to fully grasp the shifting public mood. Keir Starmer, standing at the Labour conference this year, may be a new leader with a measured campaign, but the damage inflicted by years of unheeded campaigning to the left, anti-austerity stances, and a perceived distance from Welsh and Scottish audiences shows no sign of abating. The Conservatives, meanwhile, have experienced a rare but significant regional defeat. After a decade of hard-won advances under David Cameron and sustained under Boris Johnson, the party finds itself virtually wiped out in Scotland. This not only undermines its majority in the overall UK Parliament but also points to a stark disconnect between the party and Scottish voters.

Peter Vaughan, who has died at the age of 93, leaves behind a distinguished career in British theatre, film and television—despite rarely taking on leading roles. Known for his commanding presence, deep, gravelly voice, and towering height of 6ft 8in, Vaughan carved a niche for himself in character roles that enriched and anchored the drama, often playing the bad cop, the menacing antagonist, or the dour moral compass. His performances were subtle, layered and often more powerful for their restraint. In a career spanning over six decades, Vaughan brought a unique gravitas to the screen and stage, becoming one of the most recognisable faces in British television without ever being a household name. Among his most iconic roles was that of Corwin "Grimble" of the Deep, the taciturn left-wing lawyer in Tenko, the BBC's acclaimed World War II drama. He also played the stern-faced Sr Brand in the cult 1980s British series The Young Ones, a role that showcased his comic timing and his ability to play against type with enduring charm. More recently, he was best known for his role as Harry Waterman, the gruff bookshop owner in the ITV series Reilly, Ace of Spies and as Beric Dondarrion in HBO's Game of Thrones, a role that saw him resurrect the dead with dramatic effect – quite literally. Vaughan’s long, chequered career was not without its personal and professional challenges. In the 1960s, he was briefly blacklisted by the BBC and the stage after admitting to having been a member of the Communist Party in the late 1940s—though he was later reinstated after an inquiry. He once described the experience as “humiliating but not unjust” and refused to dwell on the incident, preferring to focus on the work he had done and the roles he had played. “I was doing what I believed was right at the time,” he said in a 2013 interview with The Guardian. “I was active in the union movement as well. I was never a man trying to shout from the rooftops. I was just trying to live in a way that meant something.” Vaughan also had a deep connection to the theatre. A graduate of the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art, he was a stalwart of the Royal Shakespeare Company in the 1950s and 1960s, performing in productions of plays by Shakespeare, Ibsen and Chekhov. His theatrical roots gave his screen performances a fluency and richness that few roles required but many relied upon.

Police in Germany have confirmed that a suspected arson attack caused a school sports hall — temporarily being used as a shelter for asylum seekers — to burst into flames in the early hours of this morning. The fire, which broke out in the building in Kaiserslautern in the western state of Rhineland-Palatinate, has raised concern over the safety of facilities used to house refugees and asylum seekers across the country. According to local authorities, emergency services were called to the scene shortly after midnight and succeeded in containing the blaze within two hours. Fortunately, no injuries were reported, and the few occupants at the time of the fire were safely evacuated. The hall had been repurposed hastily to accommodate asylum seekers earlier this year to ease pressure on the local housing system. “We have reported a case of arson,” a local prosecutor’s office said in a statement, adding that their investigation is ongoing. Police are currently treating the incident as an act of deliberate sabotage, and are appealing for witnesses or anyone with information to come forward. A message threatening asylum centres and police was also posted online in recent days, further stoking fears of a growing hostility towards refugee accommodation in Germany. The sports hall, which had become a temporary refuge for about 30 individuals, is now a charred wreck, with large parts of the roof and interior destroyed. Authorities have confirmed that all services provided by the building — including showers, sleeping quarters and a communal kitchen — will need to be relocated while the site is assessed for structural safety. Germany has faced increasing pressure to manage its refugee crisis as tensions rise in certain parts of the country. Sporadic protests against the presence of migrant centres have become more frequent, especially in areas where local residents fear a strain on municipal services and housing. While most Germans continue to support the country’s policy of offering sanctuary to those fleeing conflict and persecution, such incidents underscore the challenges of integrating an increasing number of newcomers into society. The fire has triggered an urgent debate among local leaders about the security of emergency shelters and whether they are receiving sufficient protection. “This is not only an act of violence against a building, it is a direct attack on those who have come to Germany for safety and on those who support them,” said Kaiserslautern Mayor Monica Heimer. Local officials have confirmed that alternative temporary housing is being organised, but the destruction of a vital site has caused further strain on an already stretched system.

Chile is one of those countries that expects to experience large quakes. Situated along the Pacific Ring of Fire, where the vast Nazca and South American tectonic plates converge, the nation is no stranger to seismic activity — a fact that has shaped both its geography and the mindset of its people. On yet another recent night, residents across the South American country felt the Earth rumble as a powerful earthquake struck just offshore in the morning hours. The quake, registered at 7.9 magnitude, was felt as far afield as Argentina, according to local reports and seismic monitoring agencies. The epicentre was approximately 600 miles south of Santiago, the capital city, in a region that is no stranger to frequent and intense seismic events. While early reports indicate that the quake did not result in any major casualties or significant damage, Chileans, well-versed in disaster risk, swiftly and confidently began the process of assessment and prevention. For instance, authorities evacuated several coastal communities, including those in the region of Arica and Parinacota, as a precaution against potential tsunamis. These measures underscore a national preparedness that has dramatically reduced seismic-related casualties over the decades. Chile’s experience with mega-quakes has also led to one of the most robust building codes and emergency response systems in the world. The 2010 magnitude 8.8 earthquake — one of the most powerful in recorded history and which claimed more than 500 lives — led to widespread international recognition of the nation’s ability to manage such disasters. This latest tremor serves as yet another reminder of Chilean society’s resilience and vigilance in a land where the Earth’s fury is never far away. Experts have continued to highlight that the geological activity in this region is not a matter of "if," but "when." Steve McNutt, a professor of geophysics at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, said the movement of the tectonic plates beneath Chile is unrelenting and that the country, like Japan and Indonesia, must constantly remain in ready mode. As technology and preparedness improve, it is a land that greets the shaking not with fear, but with a sort of weary familiarity — a nation learning to live in harmony with the earth’s deep and ancient rhythm. For now, the aftershocks of the 7.9 quake will be closely monitored, but the wider implications go beyond mere scientific interest; they reinforce the enduring truth that in Chile, the line between natural disaster and daily reality is often thin, but never ignored.

Mohammad Asif backs Amir to trouble England again   By [Author Name], Sports Correspondent Pakistan bowling legend Mohammad Asif has thrown his weight behind young pace sensation Mohammad Amir, saying the fast bowler poses a major threat to England — and wishes he were bowling alongside him in what promises to be yet another high-stakes confrontation between the two cricketing sides. Amir, who has previously wreaked havoc on England in Test cricket with a dramatic career-best 7-93 at Old Trafford in 2010, is expected to be a key figure in the upcoming series. Asif, his compatriot and one-time pace spearhead himself, believes Amir is still capable of delivering devastating performances and could once again become the "X-factor" for Pakistan on English soil. Speaking to the BBC, Asif said: "Mohammad Amir has shown time and again that he has the ability to take English cricket apart — especially on traditional pitches. I see no reason why he won’t trouble them again. The way he swings the ball and attacks the stumps, even against experienced batsmen, is why I would love to be bowling with him out there." The sentiment is particularly timely as Pakistan prepares for another round in their seemingly unending cricketing war with England — a rivalry that has been marked by high emotion, controversy, spot-fixing scandals, and above all, intense sporting battles, with Amir often at the forefront. Amir, now in his early 30s, was once considered one of the most promising fast bowlers in the world. However, his career also suffered a major setback following a high-profile spot-fixing incident in England in 2010, where he and two other Pakistan players were banned for their roles in a match at Lord’s. His return to international cricket has been watched closely, and he has fought to reclaim a top-tier place in Pakistan’s bowling line-up. Having earned his place back through both skill and determination, Amir has made a mark in limited-overs cricket and is expected to play a pivotal role as Pakistan look to bounce back after recent struggles in Test cricket. England, too, have learned the hard way that Amir can’t be taken lightly. He picked up 7-93 in the 2010 Manchester Test — a match where England famously collapsed from 343-3 to 394 all out — and his ability to reverse-swing the ball, even in green-top conditions, has long been a concern for English batsmen.

British Telecommunications (BT) has announced a sweeping overhaul of the UK's network of public telephone boxes, set to remove approximately half of the remaining 40,000 across the country. This comes as part of a strategy to focus resources on kiosks located in areas where they are likely to be used more frequently — such as on high streets, in city centres, and near transport hubs. The decision has reignited the long-running debate about the role of these once-ubiquitous structures in an era dominated by smartphones. According to BT, the journey from 850,000 working payphones in the 1990s to just 40,000 today has been the result of the mobile revolution. Usage of traditional public phones has plunged, with many users now left with no charge left on their phones and no café or retail outlet within range to make a call. But rather than entirely abandoning the network, BT is opting for a more selective approach. The company’s plan is to retain around 12,000 telephone boxes, prioritising those that serve a critical public function, such as in areas with limited mobile signal or for emergency purposes. These remaining kiosks will be converted into their newer, freephone "Red Phones," which charge local call rates and are often coin-operated from just one pence at the most. This new phase, BT claims, will allow it to support communities that still rely on public phone services while making the phone box network more sustainable in the long term. The decision is unlikely to come as a surprise. Telephone boxes have long struggled to remain a fixture of British life. In recent years, many have been repurposed as post boxes, miniature libraries, or even art installations in a bid to keep them alive. Some local councils have even used them to house lit candles or decorate them for festive occasions in an attempt to maintain their charm. BT has also cited the need to invest in more modern forms of communication infrastructure for the future. With increasing reliance on high-speed broadband and 5G, the company said it must focus on services that meet evolving customer needs. However, critics fear that the cuts will disproportionately affect vulnerable and remote communities who depend on public telephone access. Concerns have also been raised by heritage campaigners, who argue that the phone box is a symbol of British identity and the proposal is yet another blow to maintaining the UK’s cultural landmarks.

Rail passengers in Tayside, Stirlingshire, Perthshire, Aberdeenshire and the Borders are being promised a "revolution" in travel, with long-awaited investment set to transform rail services across these Scottish regions. The long-postponed upgrade programme, announced by the Scottish Government as part of a larger £1 billion rail improvement initiative, has finally entered its implementation phase, offering hope to commuters and rural communities reliant on public transport for a decade. A joint statement from Transport Secretary Michael Matheson and key regional leaders described the changes as a "transport revolution" and a commitment to modernising and expanding the network in regions that have historically underperformed compared to other parts of Scotland. The plan includes the introduction of new and more frequent services, improved station facilities and the upgrading of ageing rail infrastructure, with an urgent focus on the Airdrie-Bathgate rail link, which links central and north-east Scotland. The initiative also aims to address delays and cancellations which have plagued the network for years and to improve connectivity with cities like Edinburgh, Glasgow and Aberdeen. For residents in Tayside and the Borders, the upgrades could not come soon enough. Rural communities across the Scottish countryside have long highlighted the lack of rail investment as a barrier to economic growth, tourism and access to essential services such as healthcare and education. The scheme also reflects a broader government strategy to encourage more sustainable travel and reduce road congestion by increasing the appeal of rail. As part of this, low-emission and potentially hydrogen-powered trains are being considered for use on the upgraded routes, aligning with the government’s net-zero targets. The improvements are expected to reduce journey times, enhance capacity and provide more reliable travel options for thousands of daily passengers who have faced the frustrations of an outdated system. Critics, however, warn that past promises of rail upgrades have often failed to deliver the results anticipated. Campaign groups and local councils have called for transparency in the allocation of funds and for accountability to ensure the project is not delayed by bureaucracy or mismanagement. For now, however, the words "rail revolution" are bringing cautious optimism to communities eager to see tangible progress. As one commuter from Perth described it: “After years waiting for change, this is the first time we feel like the government is finally listening.” With construction due to begin in the next financial year, the next few years will be crucial in determining whether this truly marks the start of a new era for rail travel in central and north-east Scotland.

A Golden Age of Pop, Football, and National Identity: Reliving the Britpop and Spice Era   It was a year like no other, a whirlwind of cultural and sporting triumphs that helped define an entire generation. The mid-1990s were a remarkable time in British history — one where the nation was swept up in a wave of self-identity, with Britpop dominating the music charts, the Spice Girls making global superstars of five girls from Slough, and a historic moment in football etched into the hearts of supporters everywhere as the World Cup came “home.” Together, these moments created an enduring image of late ’90s Britain — one of united pride, pop anthems, and the rediscovery of national confidence. If there was one event that ignited the nation’s cultural renaissance, it was the triumph of the English football team at Euro 1996. Hosted for the first time in England since 1966, the tournament was more than just about football; it was a emotional narrative, symbolising a country healing from the divisions of earlier decades. The phrase “football came home,” coined by Gary Lineker, became a national mantra. Robin van Persie may struggle to recall it now, but it was Alan Shearer, Gareth Southgate and others who grabbed the hearts of a generation. The semi-final loss to Germany was heart-breaking, but it didn’t dampen the sense of unity created by a team of homegrown stars. Yet the nation’s cultural rebirth wasn’t confined to the football pitch. Simultaneously, Britpop was reshaping the music scene. Oasis, Blur, Pulp, and Elastica were all at their peak, and nowhere was it more intense than at the 1995 clash at Apple about whether “wins” or “Clocking the Renaissance” was the better song. Oasis’  Some Might Say  and Blur’s  Tender  were more than just albums — they were cultural statements. For many, it was less about who won the supposed supremacy of British rock, and more about the joy of being part of something very British. And then there was “Spice Mania.” 1997 marked the global launch of the Spice Girls, a pop phenomenon that seemed to materialise out of nowhere and took over everything. From their instantly recognisable mantras — “Girl Power” — to their matching outfits and distinct nicknames, the Spice Girls became more than just a boyband-targeted boxset; they were a feminist symbol and a celebration of girlhood in the 90s. The album  Spice  went on to become one of the best-selling debut albums of all time, while “Wannabe” became a near-constant presence on the airwaves.

Research suggests that the Ebola virus underwent a dramatic and startling adaptation in the early months of the 2014–2015 West African outbreak, allowing it to infect human tissues with unprecedented efficiency. Scientists have now uncovered genetic changes that enabled the virus to bind more tightly to human cells—altering the pathogen’s virulence and contributing to the rapid spread of the disease across the region. The study, published in  Nature , offers a crucial insight into how a virus that once circulated mainly among animals could so swiftly evolve to exploit human populations, accelerating the death toll and overwhelming health systems. The virus responsible for the outbreak belonged to the Zaire ebolavirus species, a lineage mostly found in remote parts of Central Africa and typically transmitted only sporadically to humans through contact with infected animals such as bats. However, the variants that emerged in early 2014 contained mutations that enhanced the virus’s ability to exploit human immune defences and replicate more effectively. Researchers identified two key amino acid changes in the viral protein that binds to human cells. These mutations, they believe, increased the virus’s capacity to enter and multiply within lung, liver and blood vessel cells—organ systems central to the disease’s severe symptoms. This adaptation, occurring within as little as three human generations of infection, has been described by experts as a "remarkable evolutionary leap" from the known animal-to-human transmission cycle. Dr David Robertson, a virologist at the University of Glasgow and one of the study’s authors, explained: “We're not just talking about a more transmissible virus. We're talking about a virus that also appears to have changed in a way that may have made it more dangerous to humans—more able to trigger the catastrophic systemic failure seen in many patients.” The findings come as part of a broader effort to understand how viruses evolve in response to the human immune system and environmental pressures. The 2014–2015 outbreak, the largest in recorded history, infected nearly 30,000 people and killed over 11,000 across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. The rapid evolution of the Ebola virus, according to the study, suggests that the pathogen could continue to shift as it encounters new human populations, posing unpredictable challenges to public health efforts. Some experts warn that the study serves as a stark reminder of the importance of genomic surveillance during outbreaks. Early detection of such mutations, they argue, could allow for faster vaccine development and more effective containment strategies.

Sisters Katie and Ellie Ward have made history as the first British country duo ever to reach number one on the UK album chart with their fourth studio album,  Serpent . The release not only topped the Official Albums Chart but also achieved gold status within its first week of release, marking a landmark moment for the UK’s thriving country music scene and for the pair, often dubbed the “Farmhouse Girls” for their rootsy style and down-to-earth image.  Ward Thomas  stormed the charts after a decade-long career building a loyal fan base, both in the UK and across the Atlantic. The album features a mix of powerful ballads and upbeat anthems, showcasing the pair’s songwriting maturity and emotional depth, honed through years of touring and songwriting collaborations that have seen them pen hits for artists like Miley Cyrus and Miranda Lambert. Ellie Ward, speaking in a recent interview, said the achievement felt surreal. “We’ve always believed in our music and been passionate about what we do, but to top the UK charts in a genre that’s still growing is something we never thought we’d see. We’re just overwhelmed and full of gratitude,” she said. The sisters, who hail from Hertfordshire, have long been a breath of fresh air in the UK music scene, blending traditional country storytelling with modern influences. Their music often draws from their own lives, touching on themes of love, loss, and personal growth, and  Serpent  is no exception. Tracks like “Jimmy” and “Hopelessly Devoted” have already gained critical acclaim and airplay on BBC Radio 2, with listeners praising the album’s raw honesty and musical versatility. This success also reflects a broader trend in British country music, with more artists overcoming stereotypes and gaining mainstream recognition in a market historically dominated by American acts. Steve Lamacq of BBC 6 Music recently hailed  Serpent  as “a vital part of the UK’s evolving music landscape,” adding: “Ward Thomas have carved a space for themselves and shown that British country can resonate just as powerfully as it does on the global stage.” The sisters are already looking ahead, with a tour planned to support the new album. As they prepare to take to the road, Katie Ward said: “We want to thank everyone who has supported us over the years. This is a moment for us and for our fans, and it proves that with passion and perseverance, anything is possible.”

Opposition members of parliament were thrown out of South Africa’s National Assembly on Wednesday during President Jacob Zuma’s annual state of the nation address after what the Speaker described as “unrelenting and disruptive” heckling. The incident, which unfolded in Cape Town, saw several lawmakers from the Democratic Alliance (DA) and the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) ejected from the chamber, sparking both national and international attention to what has become an increasingly contentious political climate. The scene inside parliament turned chaotic as the president delivered his speech, with repeated interruptions from members of the opposition benches. According to parliamentary photographer Wayne Beukes, the situation escalated when the DA's Tosebiti Motshegwa attempted to raise a point of order, but was met with another outburst from across the aisle. Just minutes later, Motshegwa and several of her party colleagues – including Mzwandile Masina and Phumzile Van Damme – were ordered to leave the chamber by Speaker Baleka Mbete. Ms. Mbete, in a stern tone, later explained the decision in a statement, stating: “The conduct of the members excluded from the chamber was in breach of the House’s rules, and consistent interference with the smooth conduct of business leaves no choice but to uphold the dignity and decorum of the assembly.” The Economic Freedom Fighters were also implicated in the disruption. The national news agency SABC reported that ANC MP, and chairperson of the Portfolio Committee on the Public Protector, Patel Gift, was among those involved in the repeated interruptions toward President Zuma. The incident is the latest in a series of fractious parliamentary encounters that have marked South Africa’s political landscape over the past two years. Much of the tension has been over allegations of corruption against Zuma – most recently over the so-called “Nkandla scandal,” which involves the costs of the president’s rural home in KwaZulu-Natal and fails to account for irregular expenditures. Mr Zuma, who has maintained his innocence, claimed in his speech on Wednesday that he was “not here to apologise for his work.” The DA’s parliamentary leader, Gwen Lazure, responded to the ejections with a sharply worded statement, calling the move “a clumsy attempt to silence criticism and control the narrative.” She added that “citizens must not be left with the impression that this country’s democratic institutions are being manipulated for the benefit of the ruling party.” The EFF, meanwhile, accused the ANC of trying to “discredit the spirit of genuine parliamentary debate.”

Five years on from the start of the civil war that led to the toppling of Libyan strongman Muammar Gaddafi, the country remains in a dire state of political and territorial division. Despite numerous international peace talks and shifting alliances among local factions, Libya still lacks a singular, unified government capable of asserting authority across the entire country. The once-august north African state is today an indistinct patchwork of rival militias, regional warlords and ambitious political institutions, with policy and power dictated as much by gunpoint as by democracy. In the east lies the internationally-recognised Government of National Accord (GNA), based in the coastal city of Tripoli but largely confined to the capital and neighboring areas. The GNA, which formed in 2016 after a United Nations-brokered agreement between rival factions, has struggled to gain the loyalty of eastern generals and local authorities. Meanwhile in the east and south-east, Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar – backed by the United Arab Emirates and Egypt – commands the powerful Libyan National Army (LNA), which controls much of eastern Libya and maintains near-total autonomy from the GNA. The city of Benghazi, Libya’s second largest, is a city split: one district controlled by the LNA, and another dominated by the Benghazi Defence Brigades (BDB), a loose coalition of anti-Haftar fighters. The national capital – Tripoli – itself is fractured, with areas swayed by local militias and the deep-rooted legacy of tribal allegiances. Security forces loyal to the GNA, including internationally trained units and the Misrata-based Libya Dawn force, face constant threats from extremist groups and rival factions. The conflict shows no sign of abating. Recent reports indicate that the GNA is under pressure from both regional powers and internal factions to declare a new national vote or constitution as part of the stalled political process.
