Yet, without a functioning police force and with local militias answering to no central authority, it is unfeasible to imagine the GNA carrying out such an initiative without sparking further conflict. The human cost of the prolonged instability is equally severe. Hundreds of thousands remain displaced, with entire regions experiencing little or no electricity or medical services. The economy, once buoyed by vast oil reserves, has withered, with smuggling and black-market revenues filling the gap. International actors – from NATO to the African Union – have attempted to mediate, but their efforts are often undermined by the direct or indirect involvement of foreign powers like Turkey, Russia, and France.

As schools across England prepare to welcome students back from the summer break, a notable number of teaching vacancies remain unfilled, according to recent data from the Department for Education. With the new academic year set to begin on Monday September 4, thousands of schools are still searching for teachers, particularly in subjects such as mathematics, physics, and design and technology—areas that have long been difficult to staff. The latest figures show that as of the end of July, just over 6,000 teaching posts were still unfilled across England. This is a worrying trend as school leaders continue to warn of the pressures caused by staff shortages and the impact on pupil education. Many headteachers have spoken publicly about the challenges of managing heavy workloads, supply staff gaps, and the recruitment of experienced teachers, particularly in deprived areas. In response, the government has reiterated its support for the recruitment of teachers, including bursaries for training in high-demand subjects and the introduction of targeted campaigns to attract candidates, including those considering a second career. "We are in discussion with schools, MATs and unions to address the immediate pressures facing the sector and the longer-term need for more teachers," said a spokesperson for the Department for Education. However, union leaders remain unconvinced. Mary Bousted, of the Association of Teachers and Lecturers, warned that the shortage of teachers is a symptom of deeper staffing and funding problems that have been building for years. "Until these issues are addressed, we will continue to see recruitment and retention as a major challenge for schools," she said. Some education experts are suggesting innovative solutions, such as the use of automation and mentoring systems to support teaching, as well as looking to overseas professionals—particularly from the European Union—for temporary and permanent roles. The recently released National Tutoring Programme is also seen as a potential supplement to support schools while teacher numbers are increased. As the first day of term approaches, a mix of optimism and anxiety is expected to permeate the education sector. While many schools are well-staffed and ready for the new academic year, others will face a tough start as they scramble to ensure classrooms are fully covered and all students are ready to learn. For now, the question remains: will this year's staff shortages have a lasting impact on the quality of education delivered in the coming months?

To understand the outpouring of elation and relief that Wales football fans feel after their team qualified for Euro 2016, you must understand a little bit of the country's football history. For generations, the Red Wall—a term once thrown at Welsh football with a sense of derision—has been infamous across Europe for being an eeny-meeny-miny team, one moment good and the next moment not. It was a national joke that Wales had never qualified for the Euros and had not reached a World Cup since 1958. Today, that narrative was obliterated as Chris Coleman’s side, capped with the late drama of a tense penalty shootout against Belgium, climbed to the top of Group B and booked their place in France. Wales had long endured a footballing history of near misses and cruel twists. Ten successive World Cup qualifying campaigns had ended in failure, and the Euros remained the grand prize forever just out of reach. But this team, a blend of old stagers and exciting young talent, was different. A captain’s leadership from Ashley Williams, the creative brilliance of Aaron Ramsey—and a growing confidence among the rest of the squad—signalled the start of something special. The culmination came in a nail-biting week in March, when only penalties separated Wales and Belgium in Tychy, Poland. For many in Wales, the result is more than just about football: it is about identity and pride. Wales has long been seen as a nation of outsiders—small, often overlooked, and navigating the political and cultural tides of the larger UK. A football triumph at the European Championship offers a rare opportunity to stand alone, to be the protagonist on an international stage. It is a moment of validation for a team and a nation that has had to wait decades for recognition. Prime Minister David Cameron praised the achievement as "a real talking point," while First Minister Carwyn Jones said qualifying was "a victory that belongs to every Welsh person." The national press went into overdrive, publishing tributes and reams of guest columns expressing sheer joy. Parents were calling friends with their children’s names on their lips, and the very air in Cardiff, Swansea and beyond seemed to tremble with pride as supporters rushed to celebrate in pubs and town squares. This is a new dawn for Welsh football—one that could, just perhaps, be delivering something more profound than a Euros place.

PSNI Fuel Passport Scheme Draws Fire from Critics as Businesses Urge Tackling of 'Fuel Poverty'   A controversial pilot scheme launched by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) to combat fuel crime is sparking outrage among local business owners and community advocates who argue that the initiative is as likely to criminalise the vulnerable as solve the issue. The new  'Petrol Passport'  pilot, announced this week by Ulster Unionist MLA Graham Stevenson and backed by the PSNI, grants petrol station owners the right to deny service to customers without a reasonable means of payment — effectively removing fuel from those unable or unwilling to pay cash. The scheme came as a surprise to many in Northern Ireland’s retail sector, with some station owners reporting a small but persistent issue of non-payment at the pump. However, critics have slammed the PSNI for prioritising short-term gains for businesses over addressing the root cause: widespread financial hardship and what some are calling a crisis of  'fuel poverty' . “While I understand the frustration of petrol stations in losing revenue to non-payers, this hides the fact that people are increasingly struggling to afford to fill up at all,” said one local shop owner who declined to be named. “We can’t legislate our way out of this problem when real wages are still falling and incomes are squeezed. Turning people away is not a solution — it is a slap in the face to those just trying to get by.” The  Fuel Poverty Action Group (FPAG)  voiced immediate concerns, pointing out that Northern Ireland ranks among the highest in the UK for those relying on food banks and in receipt of emergency assistance. Kevin Thompson, a spokesperson for FPAG, said: “This scheme is not about reducing crime; it’s being used as a convenient distraction from the government’s failure to address the cost-of-living crisis. Vulnerable people are already the first to cut back on essentials — what happens when fuel becomes another victim of that list?” Local housing charities have also warned that the PSNI, already overburdened by incidents linked to welfare reform, should not be handed new powers that further erode support for those in need. “Fuel is a lifeline for thousands who rely on it for medical appointments, to get to work, or simply to move between the homes of family members supported by the state,” said Dr. Alison Leslie of Community and Voluntary Council Northern Ireland.

The first human trials of a revolutionary new vaccine designed to prevent rotavirus, a leading cause of severe childhood illness, have shown promising results according to researchers. Early findings from the phase I clinical trials, conducted at a number of UK hospitals, indicate that the vaccine is both safe and capable of triggering a strong immune response. If further trials confirm these results, the new vaccine could become a critical tool in reducing the illness among infants and young children around the world. Rotavirus is a highly contagious virus that causes severe diarrhoea and dehydration, particularly in children under five years old. Each year, it is responsible for the hospitalisation of hundreds of thousands of children in the UK alone, and it is estimated to cause the deaths of more than 200,000 children annually worldwide, primarily in developing countries. Despite the existence of two existing vaccines, the cost and logistical challenges of administration continue to limit widespread access in lower-income regions. The new vaccine, developed by a team of British researchers in collaboration with scientists in Europe and Africa, aims to overcome these challenges. According to lead researcher Dr. Emma Thompson from the University of Oxford, early trial results were "encouragingly positive." “The vaccine not only showed no serious adverse effects, but it also induced high levels of immunity, suggesting that we may have something truly groundbreaking on our hands,” she said. The vaccine is designed to be administered as a single dose, unlike current vaccines that require multiple shots. This feature could make it significantly easier to deploy in remote and hard-to-reach areas, where current vaccination programmes are often hampered by limited access to healthcare. Additionally, the new formulation is more stable and does not require the cold storage that other vaccines need, reducing the burden on overwhelmed healthcare systems in under-resourced countries. The next stage of research will involve larger phase II trials to confirm the vaccine's effectiveness across different age groups and geographic regions. Researchers are also hoping to secure funding to begin production planning and to assess long-term safety and efficacy. Health charities and global health organisations have already shown interest in supporting the roll-out of the vaccine, provided the further trials are successful. Experts warn that while the early results are promising, widespread use could still be several years away. Dr. Thompson added, “We are at a very exciting and encouraging stage, but there is still a lot of work to do.

Mark Bridger, the man found guilty of abducting and murdering five-year-old April Jones in a brutally残忍 and sexually motivated attack, has been sentenced to a whole-life term in prison. The verdict, delivered by a jury at Mold Crown Court in December 2011, saw Bridger convicted of murder and kidnap in one of the most shocking and distressing crimes in modern British history. The 32-year-old farmer from Mochnant, near Ruthin in Wales, will now spend the rest of his life behind bars, with no possibility of parole. April was taken from a field near her home in Machynlleth, Powys, on 1 October 2011, as she and other children waited for a bus. Her body was discovered a week later in woodland near the farm Bridger owned. The case sent shockwaves across the country, prompting national debates about child safety and the nature of predatory violence. In his sentencing remarks, Mr Justice Griffiths QC said Bridger’s crime was “of the most profoundly evil, wicked and depraved kind, indulged for the defendant’s own sexual gratification”. The judge condemned the “calculated sexual gratification” behind April’s murder, stating that the crime “reduced this human being to something less than human”. The emotional impact on April’s family has been immeasurable. Her mother, Sian O’Callaghan, broke down in court during the sentencing, while her brother, Christopher, was notable by his absence. The community mourned together, with vigils held across Wales and beyond, all in memory of April and in defiance of the horror she suffered. April’s death also led to a significant public response focused on child safety. Her name became associated with a national campaign to educate children about stranger danger and about how to protect themselves. Statues of the little girl were erected in her hometown and a children's play area named after her was opened as a tribute to her memory. Mark Bridger has claimed, through his legal representatives, that he was expressing his “deep sorrow” and “remorse” for his actions. However, the court described his apology as insincere and insufficient. Bridger has had previous convictions for indecent assault but had always denied the seriousness of his conduct. The case remains a grim reminder of the vulnerability of children and the devastating consequences of predatory criminal behaviour. For April's family and the wider community, the sentence marks a step towards some form of justice in the face of an unimaginable loss.

Surrey Police have revealed that former BBC presenter Sir Jimmy Savile was questioned in 2007 in relation to allegations of historical child sex abuse, contradicting claims that he had never been formally interviewed by警方. The disclosure, made following a series of recent revelations about the scale of Savile's abuse, has reignited concerns about how authorities responded to concerns raised against the high-profile entertainer over the years. Savile, who died in 2011, was one of Britain's best-known television and radio stars, with a career spanning more than five decades. Recent investigations and independent inquiries have uncovered hundreds of allegations of sexual abuse spanning decades, but until now it had been claimed that no formal police interview had ever taken place. A statement from Surrey Police said that Savile was questioned under caution in 2007 relating to "a range of allegations". The force added: "A file has been located relating to Jimmy Savile and it shows he was interviewed under caution in 2007... The file contains a summary of the allegations and an interview, which included a denial. There was no file review, and no further action was taken." The disclosure has raised questions about why the case was not pursued further, as well as how early warnings about Savile were handled by both police and other institutions. The BBC, which launched its own internal inquiry after the first public allegations in 2012, had previously said that while the corporation was aware of concerns about Savile through the 1970s and '80s, it did not know the full extent of the abuse until 2012. Savile's abuse was described as “widespread, vile and systemic” during an independent inquiry in 2012, which found about 300 allegations spanning 40 years. The inquiry also highlighted how Savile used his public image and access to vulnerable people and institutions to commit his crimes. Surrey Police said that they are now reviewing the 2007 case to assess whether any further action should be taken. The force confirmed that it had not reopened a criminal investigation but acknowledged the need to clarify the circumstances surrounding the original inquiry. The Metropolitan Police also confirmed it was carrying out a new review of all allegations made against Savile since 2012, with a view to considering whether any criminal charges could still be brought. Savile’s case has become a symbol of the systemic failures in protecting vulnerable children and the culture of secrecy and denial that often surrounded prominent abusers.

The Australian government has revealed that it has referred approximately 40 foreign nationals for investigation over suspected breaches of the country’s real estate investment laws, according to a statement released by the Department of Immigration and Border Protection on Monday. The move highlights growing concerns over the integrity of Australia’s housing market and increases pressure on officials to clamp down on foreign real estate activity that has exacerbated the country’s already soaring property prices and housing shortages. The referrals are being made to the Australian Taxation Office (ATO), which will now conduct investigations into whether the individuals improperly invested in residential property without the necessary government approval. Immigration Minister Peter Dutton said the referrals represent the government's commitment to ensuring that Australian real estate is mostly available to Australian citizens and permanent residents. “This is not about punishing hard-working Australians,” Dutton stated. “It is about ensuring our housing policies are respected by everyone, especially those who come into the country and expect to be treated like local Australians with preferential access to our housing market.” The figures come amid reports that tens of thousands of foreign investors—many from China, India and Southeast Asia—are buying property in Australia’s major cities using offshore finance channels, often through complex corporate and trust structures, which are difficult to trace. Concerns have also been raised about unscrupulous real estate agents and mortgage brokers who deliberately assist foreign clients in circumventing restrictions on residential investment without the proper visa entitlements. Australia’s foreign investment rules prohibit non-citizens and non-permanent residents from purchasing existing residential property for their own residence or as an investment, unless they hold a special visa. However, exceptions are made for foreign businesses and investors who are eligible under government investment programs. Those who breach the law face heavy fines and, in some cases, the possibility of being disqualified from owning property in Australia for up to 10 years. The referrals are part of a broader enforcement initiative launched last year, which saw the government introduce stricter reporting and compliance measures for real estate agents and financial institutions. The regulator has also launched a public awareness campaign to ensure potential buyers understand the rules. Australia passed new legislation in late 2016 allowing retrospective penalties for breaches of foreign investment laws, including extending them to directors and managers of companies. As part of this effort, the ATO has also been given expanded powers to access offshore financial data.

Microsoft and Barnes & Noble team up in $300m digital books venture   In a major move to strengthen its presence in the digital reading market, Microsoft has announced a $300 million (£185 million) investment in a new venture with US bookseller Barnes & Noble, the companies revealed on Tuesday. The partnership is expected to accelerate the development of e-reading technology and services, and signals Microsoft's growing commitment to the publishing and education sectors. Under the terms of the agreement, Microsoft will provide financial backing and technological support to expand Barnes & Noble’s Nook digital reading platform and online store. The deal also includes a long-term collaboration to integrate Microsoft's cloud computing solutions into the Nook ecosystem, aiming to enhance user experience through better integration of hardware and software. Microsoft will also invest in an existing Barnes & Noble subsidiary, taking a significant minority stake in the venture, which will be jointly operated by both companies. It is understood that the partnership is not linked to Microsoft’s Xbox or gaming divisions, but focuses solely on transforming reading and e-learning for modern consumers. The announcement came as Barnes & Noble faces increasing competition from Amazon, whose Kindle e-reader dominates the market, and other digital publishers. Microsoft's investment is seen as a lifeline to help the struggling bookseller innovate and compete in a rapidly changing industry. “This partnership positions Barnes & Noble and Microsoft to lead the next generation of digital reading innovation,” said Barnes & Noble CEO Michael Huseby. “Together, we will create new technologies and platforms that will change the way people interact with content and learning around the world.” Microsoft, meanwhile, has been expanding its services beyond traditional software and search, investing heavily in cloud-based solutions and digital content delivery. This venture with Barnes & Noble is part of a broader strategy to build a diversified portfolio of services, with a particular focus on the growing education and learning sectors. The $300 million injection into the Nook business marks one of Microsoft's largest investments in a physical retail partner to date. It underscores the tech giant’s belief that digital publishing will become a key growth area in the next decade. Analysts suggest the alignment of Barnes & Noble's physical retail infrastructure with Microsoft's global tech capabilities could potentially disrupt Amazon's current dominance of the e-book market. The deal is expected to create new opportunities for writers, educators, and readers, delivering a more seamless and integrated digital reading experience.

Home Secretary Amber Rudd has come under fire from critics and journalists alike after she sharply defended her government’s proposals to prioritise the employment of British citizens and pledged to reduce net migration, telling press critics to “don’t call me a racist” following recent questioning of her stance. The remarks came during a tightly scrutinised press briefing at the Home Office on Tuesday, as Ms Rudd outlined the government’s latest plan to reform the Immigration Skills Charge, making it a key lever to encourage British hiring and reduce reliance on foreign workers. The charge, due to be introduced in 2017, was designed to shift the burden of employing non-British staff onto businesses, with the intent of making it more costly and less attractive to hire foreign workers, particularly in sectors where British workers are deemed to be available. Under the proposed system, firms employing foreign workers would be charged £1,000 per position for skills they could find at home, with reductions available only for roles deemed hard to fill. Ms Rudd defended this approach, highlighting a lack of trust in the existing immigration system and a desire to reassert control over national borders in the post-Brexit context. “Ultimately, this is a matter of national interest,” Ms Rudd said in her briefings. “It's not only about economic fairness, but about ensuring that British citizens have access to jobs in their own country. I’m proud to be standing up for the interests of British workers.” Her fiery rebuttal to the suggestion her policy could be linked to racial bias underlined the increasingly sensitive nature of the debate. “We live in a multicultural country. I have no tolerance for racism. However, this is not about race. It's about what our citizens need and about meeting the priorities laid out by the British people during the referendum campaign,” she added. Labour and civil rights groups have expressed concern about the potential impact of the policy, arguing it could affect not only low-skilled workers but also highly qualified migrants who have filled key roles in the NHS, the manufacturing, and agri-food sectors. Labour’s immigration spokesman, David Heyhoe, said: “This initiative is a blunt instrument that could lead to shortages in essential industries. The focus should be on skills training and support for displaced workers, not penalising businesses trying to find the right talent.” Ms Rudd’s comments took place amid heightened political tensions and a broader debate over how to manage the UK's transition out of the European Union and into a new model of immigration.

Wales prop Gethin Jenkins has announced his continued commitment to international rugby, vowing not to retire as he aims to reclaim his place in the starting XV amid growing competition for Premiership and international honours. The veteran forward, who has built a legendary career with Wales and the British and Irish Lions, is determined to prove he still has what it takes to play at the highest level. Jenkins, who has won 121 caps for Wales since making his debut in 2001, has faced increasing pressure in recent seasons from younger, emerging forwards vying for a place in the national team. His most recent appearances have been limited under head coach Warren Gatland, with younger players such as Rob Harrison and Ellis Jenkins (no relation) challenging for the second-row and loose-head positions.Despite these challenges, the 40-year-old openside prop has shown no signs of slowing down and is in the final stages of negotiations with his club Cardiff RFC, where he has played the majority of his professional career. Jenkins has been playing in a back-row role for the Welsh side in recent months to gain more game time and sharpen his skills, and he believes this experience could help him bring a new dimension to the Wales pack. “I feel as though I still have a contribution to make for Wales,” Jenkins told reporters on Monday during a wide-ranging interview. “I haven’t seen the writing on the wall, and I’m still fired up to push on and see what I can do. This isn’t just about playing for Wales – it’s about playing at the top, and I want to show that I still belong there.” Jenkins’ commitment has been met with admiration from fans and former players alike, with many citing his leadership and physical presence as irreplaceable qualities in the team. Former Wales captain Sam Warburton praised Jenkins’ dedication, saying: “This is what makes Gethin one of the greats. You don’t see many guys at 40 still fighting for their place. That kind of hunger is exactly what the senior generation can bring to Welsh rugby.” However, Jenkins’ decision to continue playing is not without its challenges. The physical strain of competing in elite fixtures could become an increasing concern as he approaches middle age. Websites and social media have recently been abuzz with predictions about how long he can maintain the standard set by his younger rivals.

The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) has ruled that a website did not breach copyright law by linking to photos from  Playboy  magazine that had been uploaded to another site without permission, in a landmark decision that could have wide implications for internet law and the operation of search engines and content aggregators. The case, which saw the court examine the nuances of digital copyright, revolved around whether the act of simply linking to a page that hosts unauthorised content constitutes an infringement of copyright itself. In its ruling, the court’s top lawyer, Advocate General Maciej Szpunar, concluded that providing a hyperlink to content made available on another website, without the copyright holder’s permission, is not, in and of itself, a copyright violation. The ruling comes amid a growing debate over the responsibilities of online platforms in the digital age, particularly regarding the extent to which they should be held accountable for the content that appears on sites they link to or host. This case, often referred to as the  Linking Case , centred on a French photography website that had linked to  Playboy  images hosted on another site, which had shared the material without the permission of the copyright owner. The CJEU’s stance in this case is likely to be warmly welcomed by tech companies and content distributors, who argue that imposing liability for mere linking would have a chilling effect on the open and interconnected nature of the internet. On the other hand, content producers and copyright holders warn that the decision could embolden websites to use hyperlinks to bypass legal barriers and distribute unauthorised content more freely. In his opinion, Advocate General Szpunar stressed the importance of differentiating between the original holder of the copyright and the intermediary or linker. “The mere act of providing a hyperlink to content, even when it infringes copyright, cannot be treated as an act of infringement itself,” he said. However, he cautioned that this ruling does not remove the responsibility of sites that host the unauthorised content to ensure compliance with intellectual property law. The decision will now go before the full CJEU court, expected to issue a formal ruling in the coming months. Legal experts suggest that how the court ultimately rules could shape the future of content regulation in Europe and set a precedent for similar cases elsewhere in the world. The case has already sparked calls from rights advocates for a rethinking of copyright law to ensure the protection of content in the digital sphere.

White British pupils in England are making less progress at school than children from other ethnic groups, according to a new report by the Education Policy Institute (EPI) that has reignited debate over the complex barriers facing the country’s majority population in educational attainment. The study, published this week, reveals children from ethnic minority backgrounds—such as Black Caribbean, Pakistani and Indian pupils—are more likely to exceed expected progress levels at both primary and secondary levels than their White British peers. This trend has widened over the past decade, with experts pointing to a range of socio-economic, cultural and educational factors that appear to disadvantage the majority White British population, despite the perception that they face no such hurdles. The report highlights that, on average, White British children make 0.18 fewer terms of progress between the ages of five and 16 than children from most other ethnic groups. Professor Alan D. Milbank, head of the EPI’s research team, said the findings should prompt a fresh look at long-held assumptions about equity in education. “The data is clear: the majority ethnic group in this country, the White British, is now the most excluded group when it comes to educational outcomes,” he told the BBC. The disparity is most stark in urban areas, where White British pupils are more than twice as likely to go to a school rated 'inadequate' or 'requires improvement' by Ofsted compared to pupils from other ethnic backgrounds. Deprivation is a key factor, the report suggests, with many White British children concentrated in high-need areas and schools with fewer resources. Researchers also pointed to what is sometimes referred to as the “white working-class” attainment gap, which is not a phenomenon unique to the UK but appears to have grown significantly in recent years. Critics argue that such findings are often oversimplified and do not take into account broader systemic issues such as broken homes, poor parental engagement and lack of social mobility. Jackie Williams, an education policy analyst, said it is unhelpful to group all White British pupils together. “When you look at high-achieving White British children, they often go on to top universities and perform just as well as anyone else,” she said. “The problem is not with the group as a whole, but with specific subgroups that are being left behind.” Ministers have been urged to address the issue head-on, with calls growing for targeted support for White British pupils in disadvantaged areas.

Smugglers are using the port of Dover as a key route to spirit away illegal immigrants destined for deportation, then backtrack through the Channel Tunnel to return them to the UK—only for more of the same to be smuggled in again, a BBC investigation has revealed. The covert operation, which has persisted for months, highlights serious flaws in the UK’s immigration enforcement, as well as the growing scale and sophistication of people-smuggling gangs exploiting the most visible gateway into Europe from British soil. The Channel Tunnel, which connects France and England, was initially promoted as a secure and high-tech barrier to illegal immigration. But in recent years, the tunnel has become central to the operations of illicit groups who transport overstayers out of the country and then supply them with forged identification and passports to re-enter via mainland Europe. Once inside the EU’s Schengen Zone, the returnees are able to travel freely and re-enter the UK under the cover of darkness, far from the prying eyes of British immigration officers. The BBC’s investigation traced the plight of at least six deportees from 2016 to early 2017 who were directly involved in this cycle of illegal removal and reentry. These individuals, including men and women from countries as diverse as Ghana and Turkey, were removed as part of Home Office operations, only to appear months later in Britain again. One national was caught twice in a single year, with documents showing he had been deported in January 2017 after illegally overstaying for four years. Just three months later, he was back, claiming he had used someone else’s identification to board a Channel Tunnel services train bound for the UK. This exposes what immigration sources describe as a “smuggling loop” being exploited by gangs using crude but effective methods—including passport theft and identity fraud—to recycle failed asylum seekers and undocumented migrants from the UK. One smuggler arrested during a police operation last summer reportedly joked that returning ex-deportees were “business as usual.” The process, known within the police and Home Office as “laundering,” is creating a new breed of repeat offenders. These returning individuals often have extensive histories of unpaid fines, warrants, or previous arrests, yet they are persistently being recaught and removed by UK Border Agency officers. “The system is being abused,” said one source who asked to remain anonymous.

Behind the flash of talent and the brilliance of an unreturnable serve or a split-second interception lies a world where greatness is not simply gifted, but rather extracted through pain, sacrifice and more than a touch of superstition. For those blessed with extraordinary abilities — £20 million men and £100,000 women — it might seem that sport is the place to be indulged, pampered, worshipped — even coddled. But the facts, as told by those who live the life, tell a very different story. Elite sport is as much about grinding through the mundane and the gruelling, as it is about the moment of frozen glory. Take Mo Farah, whose mile and distance records are well known, but less celebrated is the early morning turkey on toast, the late-night eccentric left-right arm stretch, or the nap taken between training sessions. He is not alone in his world of routine. It is a world where even the most gifted must still prove themselves daily — to coaches, to rivals and in hard-earned, painstaking sessions spent chasing milliseconds, inches or fractions of a second that separate gold from silver. At the crease or on the ballroom floor, behind every glimmering victory is a history of toil. Usain Bolt, for instance, speaks often of watching football during breaks in his training, but also of the relentless pounding of his feet against turf, the hours in the pool to prevent injury, and the mental conditioning sessions where he visualises his stride before a single foot hits the ground. For younger athletes, those chasing their first Olympic spot or Premier League debut, the pressure is just as intense, if less visible. They train hotter, sleep less, crave victory and accept the price of failure with a resilience that belies their years. In sport, even at the highest level, there is no such thing as resting on your laurels — only preparing for the next challenge that comes with barely a breath to spare. And yet, to the outsider, it can appear that the elite are simply expressing their innate brilliance. The truth, however, is more complex. Talent is the spark, but it is the will — the will to outwork, to endure, and to believe in constant improvement — that truly builds a champion. In the world of top-level sport, it is not just genius that wins — it is grit. The real champions are not those who were given their greatness, but those who fight to hold onto it.

Tens of thousands of mourners packed into Auckland’s iconic Eden Park on Wednesday for a public memorial service for former All Blacks star Jonah Lomu, who passed away earlier this month at the age of 40 after a long illness. The star-studded event, held in the stadium where Lomu once lit up the rugby world during the 1995 Rugby World Cup, saw fans, rugby legends, and members of the global sports community come together to celebrate the life of a man widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. Lomu, who starred for New Zealand, Leeds and Wasps during his storied career, collapsed during a game in January and later died from the complications of a heart condition. His death sent shockwaves through the rugby world and beyond, prompting tributes from players, fans, and dignitaries from around the globe. The memorial service, held under an open-air sky, featured speeches from close friends, family and fellow rugby greats. Former New Zealand captain Richie McCaw, who shared the field with Lomu during many of the All Blacks' glory years, paid heartfelt tribute to the "huge talent" and "gentle giant" who never lost his warmth despite his global fame. “Jonah redefined what it meant to be a rugby player – towering in every sense, but also humble and approachable,” McCaw said. “He was a giant on the field but even bigger off it. Jonah did more than score tries; he changed the game and inspired generations.” The ceremony also featured performances by New Zealand music legends, including singer Stan Walker, whose rendition of "What a Wonderful World" drew a standing ovation. Emotional video messages from former politicians, sports figures and even celebrities such as Sir Ian McKellen and David Beckham were played to a rapt audience. Lomu’s family, who have remained private in the wake of their devastating loss, were visibly moved during the proceedings. His children, Jaid, Wesley and Lewington, were guest of honor at the event. A moment of silence was observed at the start of the memorial, followed by a haka – a traditional Māori challenge dance – delivered as a tribute to the rugby legend by members of the All Blacks current and former team. Outside the stadium, a heartfelt mural of Lomu was painted by local artist Ben Frost, alongside tributes written on banners and paper hearts by fans who had waited for hours simply to be part of the remembrance.

Ex-News of the World editor Rebekah Brooks described herself as feeling "vindicated" after her acquittal on all charges in the high-profile phone-hacking trial, which had gripped the nation for years. Brooks, once one of the UK’s most powerful media figures and a former government minister, was formally cleared of conspiracy to hack phones and conspiracy to misconduct in public office on Tuesday. The verdict marks the end of a legal battle that has haunted her career and personal life since the phone-hacking scandal brought down the newspaper she once edited and shook public trust in media and politics alike. The trial, which took place at the Old Bailey over several months, focused heavily on Brooks's role during her tenure at News International and her connection to key figures in the tabloid industry, including former Prime Minister David Cameron and senior aides in his team. Prosecutors had claimed Brooks knowingly allowed phone hacking and other illegal practices to occur at the News of the World, and that she had breakfasts with government officials during this time. However, the jury ultimately concluded there was insufficient evidence to support these claims, ordering a unanimous guilty verdict in the rarest of rulings that left the court astonished. Speaking outside the courtroom, Brooks, 47, expressed relief and determination to move forward with her life, despite the emotional toll of the trial. "It’s been a very difficult time for me personally and for my family," she said. "But I’ve always maintained my innocence, and I feel vindicated today." Brooks faced the prospect of a lengthy prison sentence had she been found guilty, which would have added further notoriety to a scandal that not only led to the closure of the News of the World in 2011 but also triggered a parliamentary inquiry and a wide-reaching review of media standards in the UK. Former News of the World editor Rebekah Brooks had already seen her political career collapse during a separate scandal over the MPs expenses affair, and her subsequent role as chief executive of the now-defunct News International had brought her back into the public spotlight under much darker circumstances. The verdict will undoubtedly spark a debate over the strength of the Crown's case and whether Brooks will now seek to clear her name in other arenas, such as a potential civil dispute or public campaign to restore her reputation.

Plain Packaging Could Cut Hundreds of Thousands of Smokers in UK, Government Review Shows   The UK government has been advised that introducing plain cigarette packaging could dramatically reduce smoking rates, potentially preventing more than 300,000 people from lighting up within the next decade, according to a landmark review published this week. The findings, hailed by public health advocates, reinforce the government’s ongoing commitment to tackle tobacco use and reduce the UK’s smoking population. The review, conducted by Health Secretary Sajid Javid’s senior policy team, was informed by expert testimony and global case studies, including Australia and New Zealand where similar measures have already been implemented. It states that requiring all tobacco products to be sold in standardised, olive-green boxes, bearing prominent health warnings and no brand logos, could discourage current smokers from continuing and deter young people from starting altogether. Tobacco companies argue such measures remove consumer choice and equate to a form of "thought control." But the review refutes these claims, asserting that this approach has been effective in reducing visibility and appeal, especially among children and teenagers, who are more susceptible to the visual and branding cues of cigarette packages. Health chiefs estimate that if the policy is rolled out as recommended, it could prevent 1.2 million premature deaths over the next 50 years. The country would also see a significant drop in smoking-related illnesses such as lung cancer, heart disease, and COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), which account for nearly 80,000 deaths annually. Public Health England has already stated that standardised packaging is a "big lever in reducing smoking prevalence." Kevin Fenton, the organisation’s director of health improvement, said: “This is a science-led, practical and proportionate way to reduce the future harm of smoking by removing the lure of branding and marketing.” While the government has not yet set a firm date for implementing the change, the review leaves little doubt that action will be taken. The policy is expected to go through parliamentary debate in the coming months, facing expected resistance from Conservative backbenches and the tobacco lobby. Shadow Health Secretary Jon Ashworth welcomed the findings, saying: “This is a common-sense measure that has clear support from experts and the public. The government must act swiftly to keep the UK at the forefront of smoking prevention.” The reform marks another step in the UK’s long-standing fight against smoking, which has seen tobacco advertising banned from TV and restrictions on public smoking in enclosed spaces.

Embracing ‘Bad’ Emotions May Boost Wellbeing, Groundbreaking Study Suggests   A new study suggests that people are happier and more emotionally satisfied when they are able to experience the emotions they desire—even if those emotions are typically considered negative, such as anger or hatred. Published in the  Journal of Positive Psychology , the research challenges long-held assumptions about the importance of always feeling 'positive' and suggests that emotional authenticity, not emotional positivity alone, is key to psychological wellbeing. Conducted by a team of psychologists from the University of Edinburgh and the University of Toronto, the study surveyed over 1,500 participants from diverse demographic backgrounds across the UK, Canada, and Australia. Respondents were asked to list the emotions they associated with ideal moments in their lives and whether they felt free to express those emotions. The findings revealed that individuals who experienced and expressed their desired emotions, even if they were unpleasant, reported higher levels of general happiness, life satisfaction, and mental resilience. For example, participants who found anger motivating or anger in response to being wronged—and were able to express that emotion freely—were less likely to report feelings of depression or anxiety. "Emotional freedom—being able to feel what you want to feel, even if it’s anger or grief—is more important for wellbeing than happiness in and of itself," said lead researcher Dr. Emily Carter. "There is a common cultural narrative that presses us to be happy all the time, but this study shows that suppressing desired negative emotions can be as harmful as feeling them. What matters is alignment between what we feel and what feels authentic to us." The study also highlighted gender differences in desired emotions, with women more likely to desire calmness and fear, while men more often desired being calm and assertive. Women reported feeling more restricted in expressing anger, with many stating they felt it was “not appropriate” to show this emotion in public. Sociocultural norms are often to blame for the suppression of emotions long seen as 'undesirable'. In recent decades, emotional intelligence education has started to encourage people to acknowledge and express their complete emotional range. However, this study adds an important new dimension: it is not just the management of emotion that is key, but the ability to live within the full spectrum of what a person wants to feel. "This research calls into question the concept that happiness is the ultimate goal of mental wellbeing," Dr Carter added.

Polish investigators have uncovered a chilling new detail in the case of the 2010 plane crash that killed former President Lech Kaczynski and more than 90 other prominent Polish figures. According to a recent police report, the coffin of the late president was found to contain what appear to be the remains of two additional individuals during a routine exhumation procedure last month. The revelation has sparked fresh questions about the circumstances of the tragedy, which occurred when a military plane collided with Russia’s Smolensk airport tarmac while en route to attend a commemoration of the 70th anniversary of the 1940 Katyn massacre. All 96 people aboard—most of them high-ranking members of the Polish government and military—were killed. The decision to exhume Mr. Kaczynski’s body was part of a Post-2020 forensic audit of the crash site. Polish officials have stated that the discovery is not linked to any criminal investigation but has prompted a re-examination of the crash’s narrative, which remains a subject of political sensitivity in both Poland and Russia. Kalina Chodkiewicz, a Polish forensic expert who has followed the investigation, described the development as “unexpected and deeply troubling.” She added that the presence of more remains in the coffin could have implications for the identification of all the victims. “There are already open questions about whether all bodies recovered at the site were correctly identified,” she said. Russia conducted its own forensic examinations in the days following the crash, and the findings were used to assess which bodies could be returned to Poland. However, the Polish parliament doubted the accuracy of these conclusions, citing a lack of independent oversight. Mr. Kaczynski and many of his fellow passengers were laid to rest in a state funeral in 2010, but questions about the identities of all those buried have persisted. The new discovery has reignited calls for further exhumations and a more detailed analysis of all crash victims. The Law and Justice Party (PiS), which passed legislation in 2020 to open the exhumation process, said the development could undermine national dignity. The party described the findings as “alarming and deeply disturbing.” Meanwhile, opposition politicians have welcomed the move for more transparency, arguing that the crash remains a source of historical and political contention. The head of Poland's National Institute of Forensic Research, Dr. Piotr Wiecek, has advised against premature speculation, stating that the technical team is working to confirm the identities of the remains and will publish their findings in due course.

Teachers should be valued "through their pay packet," according to Liberal Democrat schools minister David Laws, who has called for improvements in the profession’s financial and workplace conditions to attract and retain talent. In a wide-ranging speech on the future of education, Mr Laws argued that the current state of teacher pay and morale is unsustainable. He warned that without significant changes, the UK risks facing a severe shortage of educators, particularly in key subjects such as mathematics, physics, and modern languages. “Teaching is one of the most important jobs in our society, yet it’s increasingly undervalued and underpaid,” Mr Laws said. “We want to inspire the best and brightest to pursue a career in education, but we can’t ask them to do it on salaries that fail to reflect the responsibility they carry.” His comments come amid growing concerns within the teaching profession about working conditions, classroom sizes, and mental health support. A recent survey by the National Union of Teachers (NUT) highlighted a sharp rise in teachers leaving the profession, with pay frequently cited as a key reason. Mr Laws acknowledged these concerns and said the government’s new national education strategy, to be announced later this year, would aim to tackle them head-on. The speech also touched on the controversial issue of teacher training and accountability. Mr Laws reiterated the government’s commitment to a three-year training guarantee for secondary school teachers of maths and physics, which – if agreed with Royal Colleges of Science and Engineering – aims to secure long-term stability in those subjects. However, he stressed that training alone was not the solution. “Excellent training is important, but it’s only part of the jigsaw. Teachers need to be properly supported once they’re in the classroom, and that means better pay, better resources, and being listened to,” Mr Laws added. The comments provoke fresh questions about how the government plans to fund the proposed pay increases without widening the gap between well-funded and under-resourced schools. Union leaders welcomed the speech as a step in the right direction, but argued that funding must be ring-fenced to avoid education being squeezed further by budget pressures. The Department for Education did not immediately respond to a request for comment. As the debate over teacher pay and retention deepens, Mr Laws’ remarks have reignited a vital conversation about the future of a profession long held to be the cornerstone of our national development.

Hundreds of New York Police Line Up in Silent Protest as Officers Turn Their Backs on Mayor de Blasio   A powerful and symbolic display of dissent unfolded in New York City on Monday as hundreds of police officers turned their backs on Mayor Bill de Blasio during the funeral of Officer Rafael Ramos, one of two NYPD officers killed in a terrorist attack in Brooklyn on December 20 last year. The scene, captured on camera and later shared widely on social media, has reignited tensions between the city's top law enforcement and political leadership, highlighting deepening rifts over de Blasio’s rhetoric and policies concerning the police force. The funeral services, held at the St. Nicks Alliance Church in Brooklyn, united family, colleagues, and community members to mourn the loss of Officer Ramos and his partner, Officer Jonathan D. Diller. Ramos left behind a young daughter, while Diller, who was also shot dead, is survived by his wife and four children. As de Blasio and other city officials entered the funeral home, a line of officers, standing shoulder to shoulder in full uniform, turned their backs in a clear act of protest. The gesture, which excluded details directly related to the content, was widely interpreted as a condemnation of de Blasio’s remarks in the aftermath of the attacks and his broader stance on policing since taking office in 2013. The mayor had drawn sharp criticism following the killings when – at a rally supporting the city’s school budget – he was caught saying “thank God” the officer killer did not target a Muslim NYPD officer. The comment was seen as deeply insensitive, and although de Blasio later issued a public apology, the damage had been done. It further widened the rift between him and the Police Benevolent Association (PBA), the city’s powerful officers’ union. NYPD Captain James Sheppard, who stood among the officers during the ceremony, described the protest as a “quiet but powerful reminder” of the growing divide between the department and city leadership. “This wasn’t about politics; it was about respect for the fallen,” he said. “We are supposed to serve and protect, but the message from City Hall too often feels like we’re being undermined.” The funeral came amid heightened scrutiny of policing in New York. Though the NYPD has faced years of criticism over incident data and relations with certain communities, the deaths of Officers Diller and Ramos were mourned by a city weary of the cycle of violence and political division.

The world's biggest conference on species protection has begun in South Africa, with conservationists, scientists, and policymakers gathering in Maseru to debate the future of some of the planet’s most iconic wildlife, including the threatened African elephant. The 18th Conference of the Parties (CoP18) to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) has drawn more than 5,000 delegates representing over 180 countries, all coming together to discuss how best to protect wildlife under mounting environmental and political pressures. The conference, hosted at the Sandton Convention Centre outside Johannesburg, opened under the watchful eyes of international media and conservation groups, many united by a shared concern over the accelerating decline of elephant populations due to poaching and habitat loss. With around 40,000 African elephants killed by poachers for their ivory in the past decade alone, the urgency of action has never been greater. Yet the gathering is not without controversy, as old divides over elephant conservation resurface once more. Botswana, currently the only country in the world where elephant numbers are increasing—and a key proponent of ivory trade—has been pushed into the spotlight once again. The nation has argued that a controlled domestic ivory market could help fund conservation efforts and reduce poaching by creating legal alternatives to illegal trade. Faced with such a divisive stance, most African nations have called for stronger legal measures, pushing for an outright ban on the sale of ivory and an end to international trade. Namibia’s environment minister, Pohamba Shifeta, spoke for many at the opening ceremony when he said: “We are here because elephants are not just a species—they are a symbol of Africa’s natural heritage and our responsibility to protect it.” Environmentalists remain wary, however, fearing that allowing even limited ivory trade could ignite renewed demand and the collapse of fragile protections. “This isn’t just about elephants,” said Sarah Kioko of the Wildlife Conservation Society. “It’s about setting the precedent for how we manage the world’s endangered species in the 21st century.” The next 12 days will see delegates wrestle with some of the most pressing issues in global conservation—including the future of elephant and rhino protection, the expansion of trade bans on exotic animal parts, and the regulation of CITES-listed timber and exotic fish species. While the stakes are high, the hope is that common ground can be found to safeguard not just elephants, but the very fabric of biodiversity on which our planet depends.

An MSP has launched a powerful campaign demanding the Scottish government bring in free access to feminine hygiene products across the country, calling it a basic right of "dignity" for all women, particularly those struggling with poverty. Sandra White, the Labour MSP for Mid Scotland and Fife, has called on First Minister Nicola Sturgeon’s government to extend funding to cover items such as sanitary towels and tampons in schools, colleges, public toilets, and potentially through prescriptions for those in need. Such a move, she argues, is long overdue and would provide vital support to women and girls in Scotland who face what she called the “humiliation and embarrassment” of being unable to afford essentials. “I have spoken to women who have to make impossible choices between buying food and sanitary products,” Ms White said. “It is simply not acceptable in this day and age that someone would have to risk their dignity and health in order to make ends meet.” The call for free products has been backed by campaigners and charities working to tackle period poverty – the term used to describe the inability of women and girls, particularly in low-income households, to access period products. Campaigner WaterAid recently highlighted a growing problem in the UK, including in Scotland, where a lack of access to basic products affects not only girls in schools but also adult women using public toilets without access to services. “It is a basic human rights issue,” said a spokesperson for the campaign group. According to the Royal College of Nursing, there have been increasing reports from teachers and nurses of girls staying at home during their periods due to a lack of access to disposable products. Many of those affected are already vulnerable individuals, including those on low incomes, the unemployed, and young women in the care system. Ms White’s campaign is not the first of its kind. Earlier this year, the issue gained increasing attention after a high-profile campaign from young activists in Scotland and the sister campaign organised by schoolgirls in Glasgow who helped distribute free menstrual products to those in need. Under current policies, lone parent income support in Scotland can be used to buy sanitary products. However, many argue that it is not sufficient to cover them for the full duration of a menstrual cycle, and numerous women have reported being refused by retailers who do not allow such purchases to be made with benefits-related vouchers.

Ukraine’s acting President, Olexander Turchynov, and newly appointed Prime Minister-designate, Arseniy Yatsenyuk, have issued a stark warning about the difficult and potentially unpopular measures that will be necessary to stabilise the country’s fragile economy and political landscape. Speaking as the country continues to grapple with the fallout of recent political upheaval and ongoing unrest with pro-Russian separatists, the pair stressed that bold reforms — even if widely resented by the public — would be essential to restore Ukraine’s foundations and secure international support. The two leaders addressed lawmakers and the public at a joint press conference in Kyiv, where Turchynov reiterated his commitment to backing Yatsenyuk’s incoming government. “We are aware that many of the reforms that lie ahead will be controversial and met with resistance,” Turchynov said. “But the safety, stability, and future of our nation demands that we take hard decisions now — not wait for better times that may never come.” Yatsenyuk, a former finance minister and long-time advocate of economic liberalisation, echoed the sentiment. “If we want to pull Ukraine out of the economic and political abyss, we must be prepared to accept the bitter with the sweet,” he said. “The early days of our government will be difficult. The country may not always agree with our direction, but we owe it to the Ukrainian people to pursue the path of reform, however unpopular.” Yatsenyuk’s new government is expected to be formed within the next few weeks, and will likely face immediate challenges, including the need to implement structural reforms required to unlock international financial aid from institutions like the International Monetary Fund (IMF). These include measures to reduce public spending, improve tax collection, and curb widespread corruption — all key demands of the IMF in exchange for a $18 billion bailout package agreed in 2014. The comments come as Ukraine continues to struggle with deepening economic woes, including a scarcity of foreign currency, collapsing manufacturing, and a banking system on the verge of collapse. Political instability has also been exacerbated by a raft of recent scandals and the resignation of several high-profile officials, including former Prime Minister Mykola Azarov earlier this year. Analysts say that Yatsenyuk’s challenge will not only be to implement unpopular economic policies, but also to navigate a divided parliament and opposition groups that have shown resistance to reform. “Ukraine is at a crossroads,” said one Kyiv-based political analyst, who asked to remain anonymous.

Welsh actress Angharad Rees, who has died at the age of 63 after her brave battle with cancer, will be remembered as one of the standout faces of 1970s British television. Best known for her role as Demelza Carne in the BBC adaptation of Winston Graham’s  Poldark , Rees brought depth, resilience, and an indomitable spirit to the character — traits that endeared her to generations of viewers. Her performance in this beloved historical drama, which first aired between 1975 and 1983, solidified her lasting place in the nation's television history. Rees, who grew up in Llanfairpwll, Anglesey, had only trained for eight months at the Myrddin Theatre in Criccieth before making her mark on stage and screen. Following her breakout in  Poldark , she went on to enjoy a varied and respected career in British television, theatre, and film. Her early television roles saw her in period dramas and social realist works alike, reflecting her versatility as an actress. She was also a determined advocate for the Welsh language and culture, and for much of her career proudly performed in Welsh-language theatre. Her contributions to Welsh and British culture were widely acknowledged, with many pointing to her warmth, work ethic, and understated grace as defining traits – both on and off the screen. In later years, Rees continued to act despite her illness, receiving support from her husband, Professor David Rees, and their son.
