World reacts as Boris Johnson returns to the front line   Across the globe, politicians and media outlets have reacted with a mixture of bewilderment and intrigue to Boris Johnson’s recent appointment as British foreign secretary by Prime Minister Rishi Sunak. Known as much for his ebullient public speaking style and unique personal style as for his political experience, the former prime minister has returned to the diplomatic spotlight just weeks after being removed as UK PM for a scandal that briefly threatened to destabilise the government. In Washington, where Johnson had developed a famously warm rapport with former US president Donald Trump, the response from the White House was cautiously positive. A spokesperson noted that the UK’s new foreign secretary would be “a valuable ally as we face shared global challenges,” though stressed the importance of working with a “competent and consistent team.” Meanwhile, Trump himself took to social media to express what can only be described as approval, musing: “He is a great speaker and very smart. I see no reason why he won’t succeed.” In Brussels, EU leaders were less effusive. One senior source, who spoke on condition of anonymity, described the news as “a step back for British credibility on the world stage.” The European Commission released a brief statement acknowledging Johnson’s appointment and expressing hope for “continued co-operation in shared foreign policy goals,” though the subtext was clear: Johnson is no stranger to ruffling feathers with the continent, and many suspect the diplomatic battles of his past may soon reignite. France, meanwhile, responded with a measured tone. President Emmanuel Macron’s office issued a statement in French that was interpreted in London as suspiciously neutral. However, behind the scenes, diplomatic sources suggest that Paris is wary of a return to the sometimes combative “Brexit-era” tone that characterised Johnson’s time in government. One source told a French news outlet: “Boris is chaotic, but he is no fool—he knows he is back in the spotlight and will handle it accordingly.” In Moscow, the response was predictably warm. A Russian state news outlet published a feature titled “A Familiar Name, A New Challenge,” noting Johnson’s previous meetings with Vladimir Putin and stressing that “a pro-chaos figure like Johnson could offer unexpected opportunities for negotiations.” Moscow-watchers, however, dismissed the piece as routine state propaganda, not to be taken as serious geopolitical analysis.

A tragic migrant shipwreck off the coast of Libya, in which approximately 400 people are feared to have drowned, was triggered by the excitement of survivors spotting Italian and Maltese rescue vessels nearby, according to testimony from those who made it to shore. The incident, one of the deadliest in recent months on the Mediterranean migrant route, has sparked renewed calls for greater international coordination to prevent such tragedies. Survivors of the capsizing on Thursday said that as the heavily overcrowded vessel — a fishing boat carrying hundreds of people from sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East — drifted in the heat of the day, hope was reignited with the sight of rescue ships on the horizon. One survivor, speaking through a translator, described the chaotic scene aboard the vessel: “Everyone started shouting, cheering, and moving towards the sides to see the boats. People were jumping from the sides, trying to push and get closer. That is when the boat tipped and started to sink.” The vessel reportedly overturned near the town of Tripoli, with several dozen survivors washing up on the Libyan coast and being rescued by local fishermen. Search and rescue operations have continued over the following days, though the weather turned rough and hampered efforts. The International Organization for Migration puts the estimated death toll at 400, based on the number of people on board minus those confirmed rescued or recovered from the water. The European Union has faced growing scrutiny over its response to the migration crisis, with humanitarian groups criticising its policy of intercepting migrants in the Mediterranean and transferring them to Italy or Malta rather than addressing the root causes of the mass migration. This incident also raises questions over why the ship was not intercepted earlier by EU naval patrols, as the search for a safer and faster alternative comes under intense political and public scrutiny. Libya Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh has pledged to “cooperate fully” with international partners to investigate the incident, though the country is governed under tenuous control and is not a signatory to many international human rights standards. Meanwhile, the Italian government has reiterated its commitment to protecting migrant lives at sea, as it faces political backlash over its recent decision to transfer thousands of migrants from the country to eastern European nations to ease its overburdened reception system. Human rights organisation Amnesty International called the incident a “stark reminder of the urgent need for a humane and sustainable solution to the migration crisis.”

Deer on the prowl in Newry: A rural icon becomes an urban mystery The image of herds of red deer roaming misty glens or bounding across the rolling hills of Derryveagh has long been a familiar sight in rural Northern Ireland. But in built-up areas like Newry, County Down — a town better known for its bustling pedestrian zones and vibrant inner-city life — spots of deer have become an alluring anomaly, a rare but increasingly regular occurrence. Recently, a family reported seeing a lone red deer wandering through a quiet side road in one of the town's residential areas. Just days later, a local school parent snapped photographs of another deer near a primary school playground during drop-off hour, sparking both excitement and concern among staff and families. These sightings, though infrequent, suggest an eccentric shift in the animals’ traditional behaviour, and they are raising questions about why and how deer are starting to make forays into urban environments. Experts speculate that a combination of encroaching urbanisation, changes in agricultural land use and the decline of traditional deer stalking hides might be to blame for the strange sightings. Paul Morgan, a wildlife conservation officer with the Northern Ireland Countryside Service, says that deer are increasingly adapting to land use changes. “We’ve seen more and more wild animals starting to live on the fringes of where humans live. With certain areas no longer being farmed in the traditional way, and with deer populations expanding, these animals are simply adapting — finding new spaces to graze and new routes to travel,” he explains. The red deer, in particular,_population in Northern Ireland has seen a steady increase in recent decades, bolstered by a lack of natural predators and conservation efforts. While the majority of these majestic creatures still live in more remote, rural regions, encroachment into places like Newry signals a change in their habitat pattern. “In most cases, what you’re seeing is young males that are dispersing in search of a new territory,” says Dr. Eimear Ni Dhonacha, a zoologist at Queen's University Belfast. “They become separated from their herd and, through natural curiosity, may follow roadways or hedgerows into urban areas.” Despite the rural charm of a deer sighting in the heart of a town, the phenomenon also brings risks. Wildlife officers warn road collisions are a concern, and some local councils have considered implementing gooseneck barriers or improvements to fencing in hotspot areas.

Environmental activist and former environment minister Marina Silva has unexpectedly found herself at the heart of Brazil’s presidential election campaign, thrust into the national spotlight following the tragic death of Eduardo Campos, the Brazilian Socialist Party (PSB) candidate, in a plane crash last month. Campos, who was seen as a strong contender in the race and a unifying figure on the left, died alongside his deputy, leaving a political vacuum that his running mate — Silva — is now expected to fill. Silva’s unconventional political rise has long defied the entrenched interests of Brazil’s political elite. Known for her fierce commitment to the environment and her criticism of deforestation and government corruption, she represents a clean break from the system that has dominated Brazilian politics for decades. Her entry into the presidential race in the wake of Campos’ death marks one of the most remarkable political developments in recent Brazilian history. The Socialism and Liberty Party (PSOL), which she founded, had never before fielded a candidate for the presidency. However, following an agreement to merge her candidacy with the PSB’s under the electoral coalition system, she now finds herself at the head of a reconstituted left-wing alliance. Analysts suggest that this bloc is gaining momentum, drawing support from voters disillusioned with both President Dilma Rousseff’s governing Workers’ Party (PT) and the right-wing candidates who have dominated the opposition. Silva’s campaign has already been met with enthusiasm, particularly among younger and more educated urban voters. Her promise to curb presidential excesses and restore trust in democratic institutions has struck a chord at a time when Brazil is in the grip of a deep political and economic crisis. Yet she faces a formidable challenge: overcoming the entrenched distrust that still surrounds the Workers’ Party and commanding the loyalty of left-wing voters who had previously placed their faith in Campos. Her background as an environmental leader — she once famously declined the presidency of the Brazilian Institute of the Environment (Ibama) when she was barely 18, citing a conflict of interest with her father’s business operations — has made her a symbol of integrity in a country rife with corruption scandals. She has pledged to pursue an environmental agenda centred on combating illegal deforestation, protecting indigenous lands, and holding agribusiness to account. While polls are still tight, many observers believe that Marina Silva’s path-breaker candidacy could redefine Brazil’s political landscape.

Michael McIntyre can breathe a sigh of relief—his official title as Britain’s grumpiest taxman has, for now, been left unshaken. The comedian’s now-legendary gag, delivered on live TV over a decade ago, in which he described himself as the “chippiest little taxman in the country,” has since taken on a life of its own. So much so that he joked last year that only Phoebe Waller-Bridge’s “mafia of tax inspectors” could top the caricature of a dour-faced, nit-picking Inland Revenue official for which he had become known. Yet with the March Budget saw the Chancellor fanning out brochures and smiling at fans at the Isle of Wight Comedy Festival in an attempt to shrug off the stereotype of his eccentric moniker, many questioned whether George Osborne was trying to steal a spotlight long thought to be McIntyre’s alone. But in a recent exclusive with our team, McIntyre—relaxed and braced behind a Hovis-brown tweed jacket and oversized glasses—refused to fret. “If George wants to play the role, by all means do so, but I daresay he doesn’t have the necessary enthusiasm for it to last. I’ve perfected grumpiness over years of live performances. He tried trotting it out like a Christmas novelty. It just doesn’t have the same sting, and let’s face it, he’s not a comedian.” Speaking from his homestead in the north of England, McIntyre reflected on how the character—famously someone who found an extra 5p in a parking meter and therefore thought himself a detective—had become something of an institution. “You can’t be grumpy unless you genuinely  mean  it,” he said, about his uncanny ability to play the belligerent office worker with an air of convincing sincerity. “What you are doing is trying to find the perfect amount of begrudginess. Too little and you lose the point. Too much and you’re just being a pain.” The Chancellor’s fleeting attempt at mimicry, it seems, fell squarely into the latter category. Osborne’s awkward crack at good-natured office humour during a speech to business firms recently prompted a flood of astonished social media posts, but also no shortage of confusion. Many questioned whether it was a deliberate nod to McIntyre's persona, while others suggested it was merely another element of the Chancellor’s increasingly baffling attempts to relate to the public.

French officials have revised their account of a deadly police raid last week, revealing that a woman previously believed to have blown herself up in a hail of bullets was not responsible for the explosion. Hichem Khachna, the cousin of Salah Abdeslam — who is considered the presumed ringleader of the November 13 Paris terrorist attacks — had been thought to have died in a confrontation with police in the French city of Vienne on Saturday. A dramatic scene had been described by authorities in the early hours of the raid: French police surrounding a dump truck where Khachna and three others were hiding before exchanging gunfire. It was said that under heavy fire, the woman detonated a suicide vest, killing herself and two others and seriously injuring five officers. On Monday, however, Interior Minister Bernard Cazeneuve confirmed that post-mortem and forensic investigations had revealed the blast was caused not by a suicide vest, but by a homemade pipe bomb, which the woman had not been wearing when shot. The revelation has raised new questions about the operational capability and coordination of the remaining members of the cell, as well as the initial intelligence that led to the raid. Khachna, 32, is believed to have arrived in Europe two weeks after the killings to assist in supplying bomb-making materials and coordinating hideouts for fleeing militants. French media have reported that she arrived in France from Syria at the end of October with a fake passport and joined Abdeslam and other suspected jihadists in preparing the attack. Salah Abdeslam, 26, is the suspected mastermind of the attacks that killed 130 people and injured hundreds more. French officials have already arrested 16 suspected accomplices in connection with the attacks. Cazeneuve stressed that the revised findings did not alter the overall assessment of the security threat posed by Islamic extremists in the country. “This information is essential for the investigation and will be shared with the judiciary,” he said. The updated account of the Vienne raid has also sparked fresh debate in France over the response to Islamic extremism and the role of intelligence agencies. Some analysts have questioned whether the initial claims of a suicide bombing were exaggerated to signal how effectively the country was closing in on the terrorists. Others warn that the clarification could affect public confidence in the speed and accuracy of official reports. “The public is entitled to be told the truth as swiftly and clearly as possible,” said one senior MP from the ruling conservative Les Républicains party.

The UK government has published a list of 15 Scottish companies found to be in breach of the national minimum and living wage, marking yet another attempt to root out firms it claims are failing their workers by underpaying them. The move, part of a £20 million crackdown initiated by the Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS), has sparked outrage from trade unions and worker advocacy groups, who argue that the government needs to do more than just listing offenders. The list features a mix of small firms and limited companies, some operating in the hospitality and logistics sectors, and has prompted calls for deeper action against undercutting. Among those named are a frozen food delivery company in Edinburgh and a barbershop chain in Glasgow, both of which have been fined or ordered to pay back wages to staff. The government has not only published their names, but has also called on them to take immediate corrective action. A BEIS spokesperson said in a statement: “We will not tolerate businesses taking advantage of hard-working people. These companies have been found to be falling short of the basic wage floor, and we are taking action to ensure workers are fairly compensated.” Despite the government’s efforts, critics are pointing out that the list impacts only a small portion of unscrupulous employers. According to the Resolution Foundation, an estimated 230,000 people in Scotland are currently being paid less than the living wage, with many working in the care and support sectors. The Scottish Trades Union Congress (STUC) has condemned the government for its lack of enforcement and for not doing enough to penalise repeat offenders. Ian Stewart, deputy general secretary of the STUC, said: “Naming and shaming is better than doing nothing, but this comes down to a sticking plaster for a systemic issue. Employers who flout wages should face fines not just a slap on the wrist. Until the government shows a true commitment to supporting workers, the wage gap will continue to widen.” The publication of the list has also revived the ongoing debate about the National Living Wage (NLW) – currently set at £10.42 per hour for those aged 23 and over – and whether it is sufficient to live on as inflation continues to rise. With rising living costs and soaring energy bills, critics argue that the NLW is still not enough for workers to make ends meet.

The brutal death of Italian graduate student Giulio Regeni in Cairo has reignited international concerns over Egypt's human rights record, casting a spotlight on the country's often-criticized security apparatus and its treatment of dissent. Mr. Regeni, 28, a Cambridge University researcher and Egyptologist, was found near the banks of the Nile on 3 February, his body showing signs of severe torture. Egyptian authorities have not officially confirmed the cause of death but have largely dismissed claims of foul play from human rights groups and the Italian government. His killing has evoked painful memories of the 2011 revolution that saw millions of Egyptians take to the streets to demand democracy and justice from former President Hosni Mubarak. Five years after Mubarak's ousting—largely seen as a triumph for the people’s voice—what followed was a return to authoritarian stability under President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi. His government has since cracked down on dissent with relentless efficiency, often using force and detention to silence opposition figures, lawyers, journalists and activists. Numerous human rights organizations, including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, have accused the Egyptian state of widespread abuses, including enforced disappearances, torture, and the imprisonment of thousands without due process. The Italian government and the European Union have joined calls for an independent investigation into Mr. Regeni’s death. Italian Foreign Minister Paolo Gentiloni called for “immediate, independent, and effective clarification” of the circumstances surrounding the fatal attack. The Egyptian authorities have responded with a mix of deflection and defiance. While a preliminary report from Egypt’s state prosecutor initially dismissed the suspicious nature of the case, the case has been referred to an investigative judge. Yet, human rights advocates remain wary of being misled. “This incident cannot be isolated from the broader pattern of repression and brutality that Egypt has been using for the past five years,” said Hend Sabry, a civil society activist in Cairo. “The death of Giulio is a reminder that justice and the rule of law are still absent.” Enforced disappearances have become a grim hallmark of Egypt under Mr. Sisi. Security forces, particularly the National Security Agency, have been accused of detaining activists and dissidents and then releasing bodies of victims whose families were often not informed of their whereabouts during the period in custody. Mr. Regeni’s death, coming as it does amid continued international pressure on Egypt over its human rights policies, has added further strain to diplomatic ties, particularly with the European Union.

The UK government faces a massive administrative challenge in its preparations for Brexit, according to a senior former diplomat who has warned that it will need to hire and train hundreds of new civil servants to manage the complex process. Sir Simon McDonald, Permanent Under-Secretary at the Foreign and Commonwealth Office during the early phases of the Brexit negotiations, described the scale of the task as “phenomenally large” and urged the government to think ahead in order to avoid a potentially damaging shortfall in expertise. Speaking in an interview with a top British newspaper, Sir Simon highlighted the unprecedented nature of the Brexit process and the need for a “reboot” of the diplomatic and bureaucratic machinery to handle everything from trade agreements to passport checks and customs enforcement. He warned that the sheer volume of new responsibilities and the breakdown of existing frameworks negotiated under years of EU membership left the UK unprepared for the demands of an independent trade policy and regulatory system. The comments come amid growing concerns about the preparedness of Whitehall to manage post-Brexit arrangements, particularly in light of delayed preparations in key sectors such as agriculture and financial services. Sir Simon stressed that many of the skills and knowledge held by civil servants—especially those with experience of EU processes—would no longer be directly applicable in a post-Brexit landscape. “We need to look at creating a new foreign policy and trade machinery. That will demand people who understand complex negotiating processes – but it won't be experts in European affairs because they'll be useless after the event,” he said. The government has already begun efforts to bolster its diplomatic and trade departments by recruiting from the private sector and other international businesses. However, critics argue that the pace of hiring and training is not sufficient to meet the demands of the predicted ten-year transition period and that ministers are underestimating the depth of the changes required. Figures about staffing levels have been released in recent weeks showing that the Department for Exiting the European Union remains understaffed compared to its ambitious workload. The government responded to Sir Simon's remarks by reiterating its commitments to building the necessary capacity and said officials were already preparing for a range of economic and diplomatic scenarios. A spokesperson said, “The government is working closely with all relevant departments to ensure we are equipped with the right skills and personnel to deliver our future relationship with the EU and the rest of the world.”

There is a "chronic" shortage of housing for people leaving prison in Wales, with many facing the threat of homelessness or reoffending due to a lack of long-term accommodation, a leading charity has warned. Wales Probation Service and organisations such as St Nicholas Housing Association have described the problem as a ticking time bomb that is undermining rehabilitation and contributing to the cycle of reoffending. The National Association of Probation Officers (NAPO) has said that only a small proportion of released prisoners are given social housing, with most left to find their own place to live in an already tight rental market. Those who are released without a secure address often end up entering the private rented sector, where affordability and availability are major issues. Without stability and a secure home, ex-offenders are more likely to fall back into crime. The Ministry of Justice has acknowledged the problem, with its recent strategy focusing on the importance of housing in reducing reoffending rates. However, figures suggest that while the overall reoffending rate in England has dropped in recent years, the situation in Wales is less clear, with anecdotal evidence pointing to a growing crisis. The issue is compounded by the fact that many of those leaving prison have limited work experience and struggle to find employment to support themselves and pay for housing. Many leave with only a suitcase and the clothes they are wearing, without the support of family or friends. Community-based initiatives have been pushing for more support, but funding is scarce and demand is growing. Welsh government officials have been urged to work more closely with housing associations and the private sector to develop transitional housing models tailored to ex-offenders. However, progress has been slow, and some local authorities have reported a lack of political will or financial backing. Richard Moss, chief executive of a key Welsh reintegration charity, said: “Without somewhere to live, everything else falls apart. We can offer training and employment support, but if you are sleeping in a hostel or worrying about where you will sleep at night, rehabilitation becomes almost impossible. This isn’t just about fairness—it’s about public safety and making our communities safer for everyone.” As Wales wrestles with the question of how to balance resources between overcrowded prison services and post-release support, the call for sustained investment in housing for ex-offenders grows louder.

The music world is in mourning following the tragic death of Chris Cornell, the powerful-voiced frontman of Soundgarden, who took his own life at the age of 52 after a concert in Detroit. News of his passing quickly spread across the globe, with some of the most influential names in rock and pop paying heartfelt tributes on social media and in statements to the press. Ozzy Osbourne, who had duetted with Cornell on the Ten Commandments song "The Guardian," called him "a great guy, the voice of a generation, and far too young to leave us." Slash, the legendary guitarist from Guns N’ Roses, called Cornell “one of the most underrated lead singers of our time,” adding that he was “a humble, real guy—always one of the most gracious people” in a business he said can be “harsh as hell.” The grief of many was compounded by the fact that Cornell was performing just hours before his death, lending emotional weight to his final – and ironically triumphant – performance with his band. And God took it all.” Cornell’s death has reignited discussions about the pressures faced by musicians and the prevalence of mental health struggles in the industry. His career spanned three decades, with his voice and lyrics leaving an indelible mark on hard rock and grunge movements. From Soundgarden’s classic track “Black Hole Sun,” to his work with Audioslave, and his acoustic reworkings that often revealed his softer side, his music will live on as a testament to both his talent and the emotional weight he often conveyed through song. As tributes continue to pour in, the world of rock music is left trying to find the right words to process the loss of such an iconic and deeply human figure. There is a familiar rhythm to the emergence of an international footballing star who happens to play as a goalkeeper. Rarely do these custodians command the spotlight in the way that skilful forwards or elegant midfielders do, yet there are those who break the mold – those who not only collect clean sheets but headlines too. Goalkeepers who charm outsiders and insiders alike, who possess both the talent and the charisma to flirt with fame beyond the pitch. The latest name to slip into this category is a young goalkeeper who, with each passing match and interview, seems to be spinning the narrative around his role from that of a quiet, composed figure between the posts to a headline-making celebrity in his own right. At first glance, he may appear no different from many of his peers on the international circuit. His reflexes are sharp, his distribution precise, and his appearances – clean and poised in the away-kit-standard black or the home-kit-bright red – reinforce the expected image. But when the cameras turn off and the gloves are removed, this goalkeeper unveils a side that moves swiftly beyond the turf, indulging in the glitzy, high-profile lifestyle that so often defines the edges of modern celebrity culture. Spotted at fashion events in the capital cities of Europe and East Asia, hobnobbing with A-list celebrities and watching concerts from the front row, he has become known as much for his trending friendships as for the sting of his diving saves. Whether it’s a casual photo posted on social media with a pop star at a music festival or a press hit after an unwise comment made in a spontaneous press conference, this goalkeeper has shown a flair for the dramatic – both on and off the field. His performances at international tournaments have been consistently impressive, drawing praise from coaches and analysers in equal measure. He made about half a dozen key saves in the round of 16 at this year’s World Cup, securing a vital victory for his nation. Yet the attention he received after the match quickly veered from his performance to the story about his guest list at the post-match celebration gala. Invitations to the event had long since become as sought after as tickets to the tournament itself. The question is not whether such a figure can persist in professional football, but whether this dual identity of goalkeeper and influencer can coexist without the risks outweighing the rewards.

ScotRail Alliance boss Phil Verster is leaving the firm after 18 months in which the company has rarely been out of the headlines. Mr Verster, who joined the train operator in 2017 after a long career in the transport sector, will leave at the end of May after a period of "Deer" and during which the operator faced criticism over performance, punctuality and communications problems. In his role as managing director, Mr Verster inherited a business under considerable pressure from regulators, passengers and the Scottish government. During his time in charge, the private company was hit by a series of service failures, including the decision to reintroduce first-class carriages - a move that proved controversial among some customers and the public sector. The firm, which runs trains across Scotland on behalf of the Scottish government, is currently in the last year of a £3.3 billion franchise, and is in the process of being replaced by a new operator, eventually to be determined through a competitive tender process. Mr Verster has been credited in part with improving punctuality and passenger satisfaction, especially after the train company renegotiated working practices with its driver and conductors’ union, Unite. Despite some progress, however, criticisms of the company have not abated. Passengers continue to complain about crowded trains, delayed services and a lack of accountability over past incidents. Earlier this year, the operator was reprimanded by Transport Scotland and fined for delays linked to the “Red Light” timetable change. In a statement, Mr Verster said he was stepping down after an 18-month tenure during which the company "has faced unprecedented challenges". He expressed gratitude to staff for their support and said he was "proud of what has been achieved" in terms of operational improvements. A replacement is expected to be appointed in the coming weeks, though the timing of the recruitment process has been accelerated due to the shortfall in senior leadership and the need for stability heading into the final year of the franchise. Transport Scotland welcomed the news, stating that the process to appoint a successor will be "thorough and transparent". The new managing director will be expected to steer the firm through a crucial period, ensuring performance meets expectations while preparing the network for a smooth transition to the next franchise operator. With the train industry a focal point of public policy and infrastructure planning, the next boss of ScotRail will inherit a complex and sometimes controversial legacy as the company aims to restore public confidence and deliver reliable services across Scotland’s rail network.

In a remarkable feat of endurance and dedication, five friends have completed a gruelling 42-hour journey visiting 42 football grounds across the UK, raising an incredible £78,000 for charity – over three times their original target. The group set off from/ws Wembley Stadium at 8am on Saturday and, beginning at 8am on the following Sunday, embarked on what was described as an "epic marathon of football passion and camaraderie." The challenge, dubbed "42 for 42," was created as a celebration of the 42nd anniversary of the formation of the Friends charity – a leading UK organisation that supports children who are sick, disabled, or facing the harsh reality of hospital treatment. From the well-known turkey on Teesside to derelict stands in the North East, the team braved inclement weather, long car drives, and countless queues to complete their mission. Organiser and team member Dave Miller, 37, said: "We were in awe at the support we received from fans, stewards and even taxi drivers along the way. It was more than a challenge – it was truly a celebration of what football means to people in this country." Among the highlights of the journey was a stop at Anfield in Liverpool, where the group were given a personal welcome from staff and fans. They also made it to smaller non-league grounds in Wales and the East Midlands, where the spirit of the game was just as strong as at the top-flight teams. The fundraising campaign saw the team’s target of just £25,000 hit within the first 24 hours, with a variety of donations from football supporters and goodwill organisations alike. Contributions came through online donations, sponsored runs, and even special builds hosted in pubs and community centres. Tim Gardner, the chief executive of Friends, said: "This is an incredible achievement and one that will make a real difference to the future of our work. These five friends have done something that few would even dare to dream of, all for the benefit of children who need our help. We are truly grateful." The challenge concludes on Sunday evening with the team being treated to a farewell reception at/ws Old Trafford before presenting their cheque to Friends. It was a fitting end to an unforgettable 42 hours that will live long in the memory of the team and the many supporters who joined them on their journey.

Primates with Past: Archaeology Reveals the Hidden World of Ancient Monkeys   The image of monkeys swinging through treetops, using tools in the present day, is already enough to astound. But a ground-breaking new field of inquiry—primate archaeology—is now peeling back the layers of history to uncover how these animals have been shaping their environment and culture for millennia. What was once dismissed as the domain of human-only history is now proving to hold a surprising and complex story from our primate relatives. Primate archaeology, a discipline that combines techniques from archaeology, anthropology and animal behaviour science, is uncovering how monkeys and apes interacted with their environment in ways that can no longer be ignored. Researchers are now finding tools, modified stone objects and even signs of ancient living sites created by our distant primates ancestors. Far from the notion that such cultural and intellectual feats are uniquely human, this new field suggests that some monkey communities have been developing and passing down sophisticated skills for thousands of years. One of the most fascinating discoveries has come from the study of capuchin monkeys in Brazil. Researchers have found evidence suggesting that these small but intelligent primates have, for centuries, been using stone tools to crack open nuts. What is more, the tools appear to show wear patterns consistent with long-term use, indicating that these monkeys not only invent tools but also refine them – a hallmark of culture evolving over generations. In Indonesia, meanwhile, long-tailed macaques have been found using claws and sticks to extract termites and grubs from mounds, techniques that scientists claim have been in use for hundreds of years. These findings are supported by archaeological traces left behind – bits of broken claws, tool fragments, and excavation marks on their surroundings – all testifying to a behaviour that is not only about survival, but is also culturally transmitted. Dr. Alison Ames, a leading researcher in primate archaeology at Kyoto University, says that these discoveries are changing the narrative about the cognitive abilities of non-human primates. “When we look at the archaeological record, it challenges the idea that only humans can leave a lasting mark on their environment,” she explains. “Monkeys are doing things we assumed were uniquely human. They are modifying landscape, using tools, and leaving behind a trace of what we now call their ‘culture’.” The implications are huge. Primate archaeology not only provides insight into the capabilities of our closest living relatives but also offers a window into how intelligence and innovation in animals might have influenced the evolution of human culture itself.

Great Britain Again Makes Centre Stage at European Summit — This Time in Brussels   If you wandered into any of the microphones, typewriters and white noise corridors of the European Council press centre in Brussels this week, you’d have inevitably found yourself in the orbit of one singular topic: Great Britain. Lately, the term — or indeed any of the various spellings and pronunciations depending on where you're from — has been making a startling return to prominence in European circles. Whether in hushed backroom negotiations or high-profile press conferences, the name "Great Britain" — and the nation it refers to — has once again become the central preoccupation of the continent's leaders. The European summit, hosted in the shadow of Brexit, has become a stage for Britain’s looming post-EU future, with leaders across the bloc keen to signal their stance on the UK’s future relationship with the European Union. From the stern-faced German chancellor in a German news conference to the characteristically animated Italian prime minister at a press briefing, the term "Great Britain" was being wielded in every dialect, tone, and volume under the sun — often with gesticulations that would do any Italian opera singer proud. Behind closed doors, it’s a land of unrelenting complexity and political nuance. Delegations have spent days not only mapping out financial regulations, trade agreements and border control measures – but preparing for Britain’s long, chequered goodbye. There is a growing consensus among European leaders that, regardless of the terms of Brexit, the transition must be as smooth as possible — for business, for diplomacy, and for the stability of Europe itself. Yet, just beneath the diplomatic gloss, what remains is the awkward truth: the UK’s departure comes not as a desired evolution but a forced revolution — and most in Brussels are still asking themselves: does "Great Britain" still mean what it used to? Outside the halls of the European Council, the world barely noticed the summit. There was no razzmatazz, no fireworks, certainly no guest speeches from former presidents or rock stars. Just 28 leaders, a few translators, and an ever-present question — how to manage the end of one era while laying the groundwork for another. The name may not change with Brexit, but the role of "Great Britain" surely is. Whether it will still play a leading part in European affairs remains to be seen. But one thing is certain: this week, at least, "Great Britain" was not only being reported on — it was the main story.

Young Golfer Turns to YouTube to Master The Masters   As millions tune in to watch the illustrious green jackets take to the fairways of Augusta National this week, one aspiring golfer is watching from his bedroom in Texas, notebook in hand and highlighter pen ready. Scott Gregory, 23, is an amateur golfer with dreams of turning professional, and this year he sees the US Masters as his springboard – even if he hasn’t been invited to play. With no chance of making the cut, Gregory is turning to arguably the most unlikely of mentors: YouTube. Gregory, who learned to play at the age of seven and has since competed in junior and college tournaments, believes that the video-sharing giant may just supply the wisdom needed to understand the nuances of one of golf’s most prestigious tournaments. While professionals like Scottie Scheffler and Rory McIlroy spend their days on the course fine-tuning swing mechanics in preparation, Gregory is compiling a tactical breakfast, tracking down videos that show past winners navigating the signature holes, analyzing their decision-making and replaying every subtle movement to gain an insight he could never hope to experience directly. “I can’t tell you how many times I’ve watched the 13th hole being played from different angles and by different players,” Gregory told  The Daily Telegraph . “It’s not about copying their swings – it’s about learning how they adapt to the changing conditions and how they stay focused when the pressure is on. The Masters tests not just your ability, but your head. And that’s exactly what the videos show.” He admits the approach has its limitations. “You can’t simulate the energy of the crowd or the pressure you feel walking up 18 with the scoreboard being crowded,” he said. “But in every way that matters, I’m trying to walk a mile in their shoes without the shoes at all.” Gregory is preparing for the local qualifier that would see him take the first step towards a professional career, and he hopes that absorbing the techniques and experiences of Masters winners will help him perform better when it matters most. His YouTube playlist is a Who’s Who of golf legends, featuring Jack Nicklaus, Tiger Woods, Jordan Spieth and the current player of the year, Justin Thomas. “It’s incredible what’s available online today,” he said. “You can study a player’s course setup the night before the event or watch how they react if they miss a cut or lose a lead.

This year’s BBC Proms promises to be an eclectic celebration of music and imagination, with a promising line-up that spans the glittering lights of the Ibiza dance scene, the enigmatic world of Sherlock Holmes, and the wonders of the cosmos as observed through the Hubble Space Telescope. Now in its 123rd year, the Proms continue to evolve as a dynamic platform for both classical and contemporary music, challenging expectations and drawing on a wide array of influences to captivate audiences in the Royal Albert Hall and beyond. Among the most anticipated events is a contemporary-inspired concert that will pay homage to the pulsating rhythms and electrifying energy of Ibiza’s famed dance music. The collaboration between orchestral ensembles and electronic producers is set to deliver a bold and immersive experience, fusing classical symphonies with the rich tapestry of house, techno, and trance that has defined Ibiza for decades. A statement from the BBC said the concert would “celebrate the island's musical legacy while pushing the boundaries of orchestral performance into the 21st century.” For fans of literature, the Proms will also delve into the deductive brilliance of Sherlock Holmes with a concert drawing on the themes and intrigue of Arthur Conan Doyle’s iconic detective. Featuring music inspired by early 20th-century cinematic scores, this production aims to transport listeners into the foggy streets of Victorian London, complete with atmospheric string ensembles and evocative brass flourishes that evoke the tension and mystery of Holmesian investigations. Equally groundbreaking will be the programme dedicated to the Hubble Space Telescope, which has transformed our understanding of the universe with its stunning images from deep space. The concert will blend orchestral music with original compositions and soundscapes created to mirror the vast silence and infinite beauty of the cosmos. This celestial-themed evening, paired with visual projections of Hubble’s most striking imagery, is set to be a poignant reminder of both the power of technology and the enduring wonder of the stars. As ever, the Proms will feature contributions from the world’s top musicians and ensembles, with conductors and soloists chosen to reflect the event’s broad scope and reach. With its eclectic mix of cultural references and pioneering spirit, this year’s festival promises to be a compelling journey through the power of music to bridge the ancient and the futuristic, the familiar and the exotic, the Earthly and the cosmic.

The 1970 Bollywood film  Chetna  opened with a startling line that few had expected to hear in Indian cinema at the time: “I have seen so many naked men,” a young prostitute tells a hesitant client, “that I hate clothed men now.” Delivered with a mix of candour and vulnerability, it set the tone for a film that dared to look unflinchingly at the lives of women trapped in prostitution in Bombay — a topic still heavily veiled from public discourse. Directed by Hrishikesh Mukherjee, a director known for his nuanced take on societal issues,  Chetna  was not only a rare but also a deeply controversial offering when it premiered. The film followed the journey of two young women from poverty-stricken backgrounds, drawn into the red-light district of Kamathipura by promises of glittering opportunities in showbiz, and the brutal realities that followed. It sought to humanise the victims of a system that, often with complicity from family and society, stripped them of agency and dignity.  Chetna , which translates to “意识” (conscience or awareness) in Hindi, was both a scathing critique of social indifference and a plea for reform — a call to reflect on the human suffering behind prostitution. Unlike many mainstream Bollywood films of the time, which dealt with such themes obliquely or through melodrama,  Chetna  was stark in its realism and emotional honesty. The film featured Meena Kumari in one of her most powerful roles, stepping away from the romantic, tragic heroines she had become synonymous with to portray a woman trying to break free from the world that had consumed her. The film was not without its detractors. Sensitivities around morality and public decency saw it banned in several Indian states, with critics labelling it as "immoral" and "offensive" to public taste. Some leaders even demanded it be banned nationwide. Yet, it also found champions among both critics and the public. For many, it was a landmark in Indian cinema, not only for its daring narrative but also for its refusal to look away. At the heart of  Chetna  was a question that remains as relevant today as it was nearly 50 years ago: how much are we willing to bear witness to, and how much must a woman endure before society truly sees the system that oppresses her? In an era where cinematic censorship and moral policing continue to challenge artistic freedom in India, the film's legacy is a reminder of the power of art to provoke, to reflect, and to awaken.

Scott Walker Concedes Presidential Bid as Campaign Runs Out of Steam    By Sarah Johnson, The Times  In a dramatic development that has reshaped the U.S. presidential race, Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker has called time on his long-anticipated presidential campaign, citing declining donor support and a consistent drop in public polling. The Republican governor, once heralded as a key contender in the 2016 race, announced on Saturday that he would not seek the presidency after months of struggling to gain momentum against a growing field of candidates. Walker, who entered the race in April last year with the backing of conservative groups and prominent national figures, has faced a steep uphill battle in a deeply competitive primary landscape. His decision follows months of dwindling small-donor contributions and an inability to break through in national polls—a necessary condition for qualifying for the most high-profile debates. The announcement, delivered in a televised address in his home state of Wisconsin, marks the end of a campaign that had incorporated significant grassroots efforts aimed at revitalising Anglo-American relations and centring conservative economic policies. Walker is expected to return to the Midwest to resume his duties as governor, though political analysts speculate that he may remain active in Republican politics in other capacities. According to the most recent National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) reports, Walker’s contributions have dropped by 35% over the last three months compared to the peak of his campaign in early 2015. This steep decline coincided with his consistently low poll positions, where he has averaged around 2% in national Republican primary surveys—nowhere near the 6% threshold required to qualify for major debates. The Walker campaign had undergone several strategic changes in an attempt to revitalise flagging enthusiasm, including a surge through early primary states like Iowa and New Hampshire, and a shift about his national policy stance to reflect more populist language. However, these efforts have so far failed to significantly boost his standing among voters. “I’m proud of the work we’ve done in Wisconsin, and I believe that the ideas we’ve put forward will resonate across the country,” Walker said in his address. “But any campaign requires momentum—and right now, we simply don’t have enough.” His decision to withdraw leaves the Republican field more crowded than ever, with candidates such as Donald Trump, Jeb Bush, and Marco Rubio still in contention for the nomination.

Ireland head coach Joe Schmidt has cast doubt over Gordon D’Arcy’s place in his Rugby World Cup squad, suggesting the veteran centre’s position remains far from assured. D’Arcy, 34, has been a long-serving figure in the Irish squad and a pivotal member of the Grand Slam-winning team in 2009, but with younger, more dynamic centres emerging, Schmidt has hinted his role in next year’s global showpiece could be in jeopardy. Speaking at a pre-tour press conference in Dublin, Schmidt was asked about D’Arcy’s selection and appeared to leave the issue open when he said: “Gordon has shown he still has a lot to offer, but we have to look at the bigger picture. Our focus is on assembling the best possible team for the World Cup, not just protecting past roles.” D’Arcy, capped over 110 times for Ireland, has seen an increase in competition at centre this season, with the likes of Brian O’Driscoll’s heir apparent, Robbie Henshaw, and uncapped duo Dave Kearney and Paddy Wallace pushing for more involvement. Fresh from their dominant Six Nations campaign, the Irish are looking to continue that momentum with strong form as they head into early autumn fixtures against Italy, Namibia, and Samoa. Schmidt’s comments will undoubtedly put D’Arcy under pressure to perform in the coming weeks, and with the World Cup in England fast approaching, speculation around his place has already started bubbling in Irish rugby circles. Balbriggan-born D’Arcy was instrumental in the 2009 Grand Slam, a campaign that cemented his place among the country’s all-time greats. However, the central backline is considered one of Ireland’s strongest assets, and Schmidt has been clear about his preference for pace, agility, and versatility at this stage in the team’s evolution. D’Arcy is likely to respond to the challenge posed by the younger contingent. Last season, he made four appearances for Leinster and performed credibly, demonstrating both composure and technical skill. But rugby at the World Cup level demands more than just performance in practice or one-offs — it requires consistent, match-winning displays. Irish rugby supporters will be watching the autumn internationals closely, as Schmidt tightens his squad selection for the upcoming tournament. While the notion of D’Arcy missing out is unsettling for many, it also highlights the strength in depth in the Irish squad — a team that, under Schmidt, has already transformed from a group of Grand Slam winners into a new era of promising talent.

The small, dusty town of Arusha in northern Tanzania is the gateway to Mount Kilimanjaro, to the beauty and the wildlife of the Serengeti. Known as the "Tourism Capital of Tanzania," Arusha is often the starting point for some of the country’s most iconic adventures, yet the town itself remains an underappreciated gem of East Africa. Nestled at an altitude of 1,390 metres in the A Rift Valley, just a few hours’ drive from both the Maasai Mara in Kenya and the great plains of the Serengeti, Arusha is a crossroads of cultures, landscapes, and peoples. Its position makes it a crucial hub for both the local Maasai and Chagga communities and the thousands of international visitors who pass through each year in search of Africa’s untamed wilderness. Dotted with markets and open-air cafés, Arusha is a far cry from the raw, untamed natural beauty of the region it serves as a base for — yet it’s this very contrast that hides its charm. Small but spirited, the town pulses with energy from early morning as vendors set up their stalls under the shade of acacia trees in Bahari Market, one of the largest and most popular in Tanzania. Here, shoppers can find everything from fresh produce and hand-carved tribal masks to spices and – most ironically of all – souvenirs from the very national parks that are the province of the wild animals that never come within a stone’s throw of the town. Arusha's role as a launchpad into the wilderness is also reflected in the surrounding landscape. Just outside its borders lies the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most famous wildlife sanctuaries in the world. Towering above it all is the snow-capped peak of Mount Kilimanjaro, a volcano whose towering presence becomes evident the moment you enter the region. The unassuming town belies the majesty of the landscapes just beyond its reach. Locals are proud of their home’s significance to the tourism industry, and many see it as a blessing that brings them employment and cultural exchange. However, there are also concerns that Arusha’s rapid development – with hotels, tour agencies and construction projects expanding rapidly – could one day compromise its unique character. For now, though, the town remains a go-to hub for those dreaming of trekking through Africa’s highest peak or watching the Great Migration unfold beneath the sweeping savannahs of the Serengeti.

The digital fallout from the 2015 Ashley Madison data breach is once again making waves online, as former users of the infidelity website and beyond face renewed distress after the cache of personal data resurfaced on the web this week. The breach, initially attributed to a hacking group calling itself the Impact Team, saw the names, contact details, and purported personal misconduct of thousands of users posted publicly on various platforms. Almost a decade later, a fresh wave of online activity — involving the unearthing or reuploading of data records — has caused panic among those still concerned about the long-term consequences of the breach. While the exact source of the recent re-emergence of the database is unclear, cybersecurity experts suggest it may have been leaked from a secondary source or shared via a dark web forum before being made public. The leaked data appears to include the real names and emails of alleged Ashley Madison users in the UK and across the globe, many of whom have spent years fearful that their details would be exposed to friends, colleagues or partners in a criminal act of betrayal. The 2015 scandal prompted a global legal and public relations crisis for Ashley Madison’s parent company, Avid Life Media (ALM), which faced intense scrutiny over inadequate data protection and its decision to initially offer users $12 in compensation to delete their profiles. The data then became a central point in countless – and often tragic – incidents, with at least one Canadian man taking his life after his infidelity was revealed to his family through the breach. In the years since, the scandal has been debated in political and ethical contexts, with critics condemning the website’s services as a contributing factor to the erosion of trust in personal relationships, and some suggesting the breach was a calculated operation to expose users to moral panic. This latest surge of activity about the Ashley Madison data has led to renewed questions about the severity of data privacy laws and how old breaches can have long-lasting consequences for individuals. "Even if it's been years, to have your personal data resurface unexpectedly like this is devastating,” said one cybersecurity professional. “It shows how the digital past never really stays confined to the digital world.” Users are now waiting to see whether this latest event will prompt further legal actions or calls for sustained reform in the way personal data is protected from long-term vulnerabilities.

This year has been one to remember for the Get Inspired team, as they have worked tirelessly to champion active lifestyles and encourage people up and down the country to get moving. As the national body for sport, delivered by Sport England, Get Inspired has continued to support local groups and individual athletes in their pursuit of health, wellness and personal bests. From invigorating community sports days to high-profile partnerships with professional athletes, the team has helped lift participation in sports and physical activities to new heights. One of the highlights of the year was the launch of the "Move to Improve" campaign, aimed at demonstrating the mental and physical benefits of regular exercise. Through a series of engaging content—from video testimonials to social media challenges—the initiative has inspired thousands to take small, achievable steps in incorporating more activity into their daily lives. There was also the successful rollout of the new Active London app, co-created with local authorities and grassroots sports providers, which acts as an all-in-one guide for finding sporting opportunities in the capital. The tool has been particularly popular among younger audiences, with over 200,000 downloads recorded since its launch in the spring. Get Inspired has also made monumental strides in supporting underrepresented communities, with a focus on tackling barriers to participation. Through their "Opportunity Areas" initiative, the team has worked closely with municipal sports trusts and community centres in economically disadvantaged regions to provide funding for equipment, training and local events, giving rise to a host of new opportunities across the country. It's not just about numbers, though. The team has witnessed heart-warming stories from those who have taken that first step in running a 5K, climbing a mountain, or joining a local football club. These are the moments that embody the real essence of their work—creating a society where people are empowered, enabled and, most importantly, inspired to play their part. With the Olympic and Paralympic legacy still very much alive, and the Commonwealth Games barely out of the headlines, Get Inspired has shown its dedication to keeping the momentum of national sporting enthusiasm well and truly alive. As the year draws to a close, the Get Inspired team is already looking ahead, preparing for what promises to be an even more exciting 2024. With new partnerships in the pipeline and innovative digital tools on the horizon, the team remains committed to ensuring that sport and physical activity remain accessible and appealing to all.

Saudi Arabia has launched a high-level investigation into the collapse of a towering crane in Mecca’s historic district, which has left at least 107 people dead and scores more injured—the worst construction-related disaster in the Kingdom in decades. The crane collapse occurred in the early hours of Tuesday in Mina, a sprawling tented city near Mecca, which serves as the overnight accommodation for millions of Muslim pilgrims during the annual Hajj. The crane came down on a multi-storey parking structure under construction, toppling onto surrounding buildings and vehicles, according to local reports and images circulating on social media. Emergency services in Mecca launched an immediate rescue operation, involving hundreds of personnel including paramedics, firefighters, and heavy machinery to clear rubble and search for survivors trapped beneath the debris. Saudi media reported that many victims were left buried in the wreckage, with some bodies being recovered as late as Thursday. At present, the death toll stands at 107 and is expected to rise, with hundreds of people still unaccounted for. King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud has ordered a full investigation into the incident, with the royal decree assigning the Supreme Judicial Council and the Interior Ministry to lead the inquiry. The monarch also directed that the injured be provided with the best possible medical care, and that families of the deceased be compensated fully. The Saudi government has pledged to “take all necessary steps” to ensure justice is served, and to hold those responsible to account. The crane, standing over 200 feet high, was reportedly hired out from a Jordanian firm, and its collapse has sparked questions about safety regulations and the rapid expansion of infrastructure ahead of the 2020 Islamic pilgrimage. Experts have pointed to possible overloading and improper assembly as contributing factors, but no official statements have been made confirming the cause at this stage. The incident has cast a sombre shadow over preparations for the 2015 Hajj, which takes place later this month. This year, more than two million pilgrims are expected to make the Islamic pilgrimage toward Mecca, with the Saudi government investing billions in infrastructure to accommodate the growing numbers and enhance security. The collapse is a stark reminder of the challenges faced by the Kingdom in balancing its ambitious development plans with public safety, particularly in a city of immense religious and historical significance. Earlier this year, Saudi Arabia faced global condemnation following a deadly stampede during Hajj that killed more than 2,000 people.

Jerome Ave. is just one of the vibrant streets in Milwaukee, a city grappled with deep racial tensions and public distrust of its police force in recent years. However, recent developments have brought this avenue, like many others, into the national spotlight. A former Milwaukee Police Department officer, now facing a charge of first-degree reckless homicide, stands at the heart of the storm. The incident, which occurred on 12 August, has reignited questions about police accountability, use of force, and the social unrest that has long defined the city. The shooting took place in the early hours of the morning when the officer, yet to be revealed under the Wisconsin Press Shield Law, fired multiple shots at a 39-year-old man, who was unarmed and fleeing in a vehicle at the time. Authorities later confirmed that the victim’s car had been approached by the officer who had been following it for reasons still under investigation. The man was pronounced dead at the scene.鄰 Though preliminary reports suggest that the officer may have incorrectly identified a kitchen knife visible in the car as a weapon posing an imminent threat to his life, the Milwaukee County District Attorney determined that the shooting was not justified under the state’s self-defense laws. As such, the officer has now become the first in Wisconsin to be charged with first-degree reckless homicide in a municipal police shooting since such a statute was added to the state’s criminal code in 2020 in the wake of national protests following the murder of George Floyd in Minnesota. The charge itself, first-degree reckless homicide, is a non-felony offense in Wisconsin, carrying a maximum penalty of 60 days in jail and a $1,000 fine. However, law enforcement advocates have criticized the charge as inadequate in cases of fatal police conduct, arguing that it fails to account for the magnitude of such incidents. “When someone is shot and killed during an interaction with police, this fails to reflect the seriousness of the crime,” said Steve McCorkell, president of the Wisconsin Professional Police Officers Association. “We need stronger laws.” Critics, meanwhile, have raised the alarm over a perceived pattern of lethal police conduct in Milwaukee, which has sparked widespread protests in previous years. “This prosecution raises more questions than it answers,” said Rukia Lumumba, chair of the National African American Leadership Summit. “How many more incidents will it take before the system is reformed so that lives are saved, not lost?”

Great Britain’s men’s curling team were left devastated on Sunday evening as they narrowly missed out on a historic Olympic gold medal, suffering a crushing 7-5 defeat at the hands of Canada in the final of the Sochi 2014 Winter Games. The loss, though heartbreaking, came on the back of a remarkable journey that saw the Scots reach the top of the curling world for the first time in their nation’s history — a testament to their resilience, determination, and the fast-paced evolution of British curling. The final, played in front of a packed and raucous crowd at the Ice Cube curling centre, was a gruelling three-and-a-half-hour battle characterised by high tension and tactical brilliance from both teams. Canada, led by the experienced skip Kevin Koe, who had narrowly missed a gold of his own in the 2010 Vancouver Games, showcased the world-class consistency expected of them, while the GB team — captained by David Murdoch — pushed to the very limit in their attempt to make history. The Scottish quartet — which also included team members Euan Allan, Greg Drummond, and Derekarm Smith — had already surpassed expectations, having secured automatic qualification for the Sochi event by finishing runners-up at the 2013 World Championships. The team had also broken a long-standing medal drought by claiming a silver at the 2013 Europeans, and now had the eyes of the nation upon them as they faced the best in the world at the Games. From the outset, the GB team played with the intensity and precision that had carried them so far. However, Canada's experience and composure under pressure proved decisive in the closing ends. After a crucial missed shot by Murdoch in the seventh end — which allowed Canada to regain the lead — momentum shifted decisively in the hosts’ direction. Koe, calm and clinical, guided his team to a commanding victory that was as dramatic as it was cruel for the British side. Despite the heartbreak, the achievement cannot be understated. As the first British men’s curling team to ever reach a gold medal match at the Winter Olympics, they have set a new benchmark for the sport domestically. The team has already inspired a new generation of curlers in the UK and sparked renewed interest in the sport, with hopes that Sochi will serve as a springboard for the 2018 PyeongChang Games.

The number of operational Royal Air Force (RAF) fighter planes is to fall to its lowest level since the Second World War, according to senior defence analysts, raising concerns about the UK’s ability to defend its airspace and sustain its international commitments. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) is currently modernising its aircraft fleet through a series of long-term procurement plans, including the introduction of the next-generation Eurofighter Typhoon and F-35B Lightning II jets. However, this transition has led to a temporary shortage of frontline fighter aircraft, as older models like the Tornado and Harrier GR7 and GR9 are retired, and the new jets have not yet been brought into full-service capability. Current estimates suggest that as few as 34 fast-jet aircraft will be available for front-line duties by late 2024 — the lowest number on record for the service. Dr. Elinor Fairbanks, a defence analyst at the University of Birmingham, said: "This is a deeply concerning situation. The historic shortage of operational jets at a time of heightened global insecurity — including tensions in the Black Sea and the Indo-Pacific — is directly at odds with the government’s own defence strategy, which calls for the UK to be a global player in military and security affairs." The warning comes as the RAF continues to support NATO operations, including continuous air policing of the UK's national airspace – a task currently carried out by the Typhoon squadrons based at RAF Lossiemouth and RAF Coningsby. Concerns have also been raised about the lack of spare aircraft for training and air display events. Sources in Whitehall suggest that the MoD has increased the tempo of maintenance and servicing to mitigate the shortfall, but some military officials fear that the shortage will be prolonged due to delays in key procurement contracts and supply chain bottlenecks. The situation echoes past capacity shortfalls, such as those during the 2000s when the RAF was overstretched by operations in Iraq and Afghanistan while simultaneously maintaining its domestic capabilities. A spokesperson for the MoD said: "We are working hard to modernise our air capabilities to meet the demands of the 21st century. The transition to a new fleet is challenging, as with any shift of this scale and complexity, but it is a necessary step to ensure the UK remains the best air force in Western Europe." However, opposition figures and the Defence Select Committee have called for a public inquiry into the risk management of the transition, with calls to review the timeline and scale of fighter jet procurement.

A coroner’s inquest has opened in Sydney, Australia, to examine the tragic armed siege at a central business district cafe in December 2014, which left two hostages and the gunman dead. The inquest, which began this week at the Sydney Coroner’s Court, aims to scrutinize the events that unfolded during the 16-hour ordeal, the emergency response by Australian police, and the subsequent use of lethal force that ended the siege. A total of 18 people were held hostage during the attack, which stunned the nation and raised serious questions about police preparedness for counter-terrorism scenarios. The siege, which took place at the Lindt Café on Martin Place, was carried out by Man Haron Monis, a 50-year-old Iranian-born Australian of Kurdish origin with a history of eccentric behavior and a known interest in extremism. Monis, who shouted pro-ISIS slogans and threatened to behead hostages if police approached, was eventually shot dead by a specially trained police unit during a siege breach. Two hostages—Torran Rodrigues, 26, and Ken Tarakin, 57—were also killed in the confrontation. The inquest, chaired by Coroners Court Judge Anthony Besanko, will focus on whether the actions taken by the police were appropriate and in line with established protocols. Over 100 witnesses are expected to give evidence, including senior police officers, first responders, and survivors of the siege. The court will also examine CCTV footage, internal police communications and phone recordings from the cafe, in an effort to piece together the full sequence of events. The inquest also intends to explore why officers stationed just 200 meters away did not arrive at the scene immediately after the café was stormed, as well as whether delays in key decisions contributed to the tragic outcome. Relatives of the victims have expressed a desire for the inquiry to “get to the truth” and ensure that lessons are learned to prevent similar incidents in the future. “The people of Sydney have waited a long time for the truth to come out,” said Torran Rodrigues’ mother, Cindy Simpson. “We want to know what happened, how it could have been avoided, and how we can make sure that this never happens again.” The siege marked one of Australia’s most harrowing acts of domestic terrorism and led to sweeping reform of counter-terrorism policies around the country. While the government has since bolstered national security measures, many questions remain about responses to similar incidents.

The Aslef train drivers' union has reached an agreement with Southern Rail operators, ending weeks of crippling strike action that has disrupted the lives of thousands of commuters and sparked growing frustration among passengers and local businesses. The deal, struck over the weekend following protracted negotiations, brings an end to the fourth and final round of walkouts scheduled for this month and paves the way for normal services to resume on Monday morning. The agreement comes as government intervention failed to break the deadlock in a long-running dispute over pay and control of crewing services. Southern Rail, which is operated under the Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) franchise, has faced mounting pressure from MPs and Transport Secretary Grant Shapps, who recently threatened to nationalise the rail company if no resolution was found. The dispute has been centred around Aslef's opposition to the introduction of additional driver-only operated (DOTO) trains, which would allow trains to run without a second driver in attendance. The union argues that this change, which was implemented earlier this year, has led to operational issues and safety concerns, and is being used as a tactic to reduce train staff costs. Southern Rail, on the other hand, insists that the new operating model is consistent with current industry standards and necessary for the efficient running of services. Aslef General Secretary Mick Lynch confirmed on Sunday that a resolution had been reached, although he provided few details about the specifics of the deal. "We’re proud to have stood firm and defended our members’ interests during this dispute,” Lynch said in a statement. “This agreement reflects our commitment to protecting job security and ensuring that our members are treated fairly.” Passengers have welcomed the news, albeit cautiously. Many have endured months of chaos, with some reporting being stranded for hours and missing vital appointments and even job interviews. Southern Rail apologised for the disruption caused by the strikes but reiterated that the changes to operations had been “necessary and in line with modern rail practices across the UK.” Transport authorities and local councils have praised the agreement as a welcome step forward for the transport network, particularly in light of the approach of London’s busy summer travel season. However, any lasting resolution to the deeper tensions between the rail industry and its workforce remains unclear. Aslef has previously stated its intention to monitor the situation closely and will not rule out future action unless the concerns of its members are fully addressed.

When Makau Kioko crouches down to grab an Egyptian cobra, the visiting audience always watches on with trepidation. Yet, for the Nairobi-born wildlife trainer, it is part of a daily rhythm that has spanned over three decades — a blend of artistry, acclimatisation and a deep respect for nature’s deadliest creatures. Kioko, often dubbed the “Kenyan Koolaid Man of snakes,” has not only made a career out of handling some of the most venomous species on the planet but has also dedicated his life to educating the public and dismantling the myths and fears surrounding them. Based at Nairobi's Tintina Wildlife Park, Kioko runs a unique show that draws thousands of visitors every year, ranging from curious families and international tourists to local schoolchildren. His demonstration, though thrilling, is not just for spectacle. It is an educational tool, a way to foster coexistence between man and beast in a country where snake bites still claim hundreds of lives annually. “People come here with a fear in their eyes,” Kioko says as he gently places the cobra’s head onto a small table for photographs. “But I want them to see us for what we are—wonderful, necessary, and as much a part of the ecosystem as any tree or lion.” Kioko, 54, started out as a young man in the 1980s, assisting in basic wildlife care before his talents brought him to the attention of more notable figures in the animal world. A chance opportunity to work with internationally renowned snake handlers gave him the starting line in an otherwise perilous profession. He has since trained under experts from around the world, developed his own handling techniques and now employs a small team of assistants under his mentorship. The cobra, poised and serene in his hand, is the same species responsible for the highest number of snakebite deaths in Africa. Yet, in Kioko’s world, it is a teacher, a symbol of balance. “The trick is to understand the snake first. They are not evil. They just have their way of living,” he explains, as he wipes a bit of sweat from his brow. “Respect the animal, and it will respect you.” His message resonates with a growing audience in Kenya and beyond. As he prepares for the next set of visitors, the buzz of anticipation in the air is palpable. For many, it is more than a show – it is a lesson in reverence, coexistence and the power of fear transformed into fascination.

The Netherlands delivered a breathtaking second-half performance to dismantle the reigning World Cup and European champions Spain in a stunning display of attacking football at Arena Fonte Nova. The Dutch, who had struggled to find their rhythm in the first half, exploded into life after the break with a combination of relentless pressing, incisive passing, and clinical finishing. The 4-0 victory left Spain dazed and marked one of the most remarkable comebacks in recent international competition. From the outset, Spain looked the more organized and composed side, controlling possession and dictating the tempo of the match. Their trademark tiki-taka style dominated early proceedings, but the Dutch defense held firm under the pressure. During the first half, Spain had a number of half-chances, notably through their superstar striker and captain, but failed to capitalise. By the break, the score remained 0-0. But within moments of the second half beginning, the game transformed. The Netherlands introduced a fresh wave of attacking players, including stars who had been held in reserve for the opening 45 minutes. The injection of energy, pace, and urgency disrupted Spain’s rhythm and opened up gaps that had previously been non-existent. Just seven minutes into the second half, the Dutch broke the deadlock as their captain scored a emphatic finish after a sweeping move on the left flank. The goal sparked a cascade of momentum in the national side – within 15 minutes, the score was 3-0, as the Spaniards looked increasingly bewildered by the depth and intensity of the Netherlands’ press. Spanish manager, who had built his career on strategic improvements and tactical flexibility, was left scrambling to make adjustments, but the Dutch continued to outplay them with fury and flair. In the 78th minute, a stunning team goal, fully deserving of a highlight reel, completed the comprehensive victory. The scale of the turnaround stunned fans and pundits alike.
