Analysts praised the Netherlands for their resilience and tactical transformation while cruelly sending a message to the defending champions. For Spain, the result was devastating; it marked a significant dip in form for a team that had long been seen as the standard-bearers of modern football. Speaking after the match, Dutch coach praised his side’s "heart, speed, and unity". He added, “We knew the challenges we faced going into this game, but the level of our play in the second half was something to really be proud of.”

Tom Daley Makes Emotional Exit From the Olympic Stage After Diving Disappointment in Rio   A tear-streaked Tom Daley sat in the mixed zone at the Maria Lenk Aquatics Centre, his words trembling as he struggled to come to terms with the end of a sporting journey that spanned over a decade. “I’m truly heartbroken,” the 24-year-old diver said, his voice breaking as he recounted the events of a competition that left him just outside the medal podium in his third Olympic Games. For Daley, who first appeared on the global stage as a 14-year-old during the Beijing 2008 Olympics, the Rio 2016 Games were always meant to be the pinnacle of his career. On Monday night, the dream came unexpectedly and devastatingly to a close. Competing in the men’s 10m platform, the British diving star finished in fourth place—missing out on a podium finish by a mere 42 points. It was a heart-wrenching end to a Games that had already challenged him both mentally and physically. With a final score of 510.10, Daley, who had come into the event as one of the pre-tournament favourites, said he had only started to feel “like myself” on the third day of competition. Trailing from the start after a shaky first three rounds of dives, he managed a solid final two to secure a respectable finish despite falling short of the podium. Mexico’s Palet Martínez captured gold with a score of 547.60, while Zhang Yan of China won silver, and Italy’s Simone Cipollini took bronze. For Daley, the result marked the end of an era. The diver, who spoke out publicly about being gay in 2013, had hoped these Games would be his last. “This is where my journey ends,” he said afterwards. “I have given everything to this sport—every single day. And I just wanted to end on my own terms, with a medal at my name. I can't believe I came so close." The emotional strain of competing in his final Olympics was evident to all who watched. Though professional and composed throughout the competition, Daley’s expression betrayed the depth of his feelings. Earlier in the week, he had opened up about feeling the pressure of expectation as the oldest member on Team GB’s diving squad. “I wanted this so badly,” he admitted. “It's always been my dream—to win an Olympic medal, and to do it in my third Games feels like it was always meant to happen.

India Launches Real-Time Air Quality Index Amid Pollution Crisis   In a move aimed at tackling the country's worsening air pollution problem, India has officially launched its first nationally integrated real-time Air Quality Index (AQI) to provide citizens with accurate, instant data on pollution levels. The initiative, announced by the environment ministry on Tuesday, marks a significant step in the government’s broader strategy to improve public health and raise awareness about air quality in major urban centres. The new AQI will aggregate data from a network of monitoring stations across 126 cities, offering minute-by-minute readings on pollutants such as particulate matter (PM 2.5 and PM 10), nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide, ozone, and carbon monoxide. The information will be accessible via a dedicated website and mobile application, with users also able to receive alerts when pollution levels cross safe thresholds. Environment Minister Dr. Bhupender Yadav said the index will serve as a “transparent and science-based tool” to empower citizens and encourage municipalities to take action against pollution. “Public awareness is the first step towards change, and this AQI will serve as a wake-up call for both individuals and policymakers,” he told reporters in New Delhi. India has been grappling with severe air pollution for years, with cities including Delhi, Punjab, Haryana, and Rajasthan consistently ranking among the world's most polluted. The national capital, Delhi, faces a seasonal crisis, with air quality plummeting to hazardous levels during the winter months due to stubble burning in northern states, vehicular emissions, dust, and industrial activity. According to the Ministry of Environment and Forests, over 600 million people in India are currently exposed to air pollution levels that exceed World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines. The new AQI is expected to enable more precise and timely responses from both the public and authorities, from advising the vulnerable to avoid outdoor activities during high-risk days to supporting local governments in implementing emergency measures such as bans on construction or the use of public transport. Critics however, have pointed out that while the AQI is a positive development, it will need to be accompanied by stronger enforcement of existing environmental laws and stricter regulations on industries, transport, and agriculture to make a meaningful impact. “Indices and apps are helpful tools, but the real work lies in addressing the root causes of pollution,” said Dr. Anumita Roychowdhury, a senior environmental advocate with the Centre for Science and Environment.

Brighton Overcome Leeds to Move Top of Championship   Brighton and Hove Albion climbed to the summit of the Championship with a hard-fought 2-1 victory over 10-man Leeds United at the Amex Stadium, extending their impressive unbeaten league run to 14 games. The Seagulls, boosted by a vocal home crowd, showcased the determination and efficiency that has driven their remarkable campaign as they maintained their challenge for a return to the Premier League next season. From the outset, Brighton displayed attacking intent as manager Graham Potter continued to tinker with tactics, blending intricate passing with pressing urgency. The breakthrough came in the 27th minute when captain Shane Duffy made a crucial error, but the goal was actually grabbed by Lewis Dunk following a swift counter-attack initiated by Tariq Lamptey. The equaliser had gone to Leeds, with Marcus Antonsson netting from the spot after Pascal Gross handled in the box. However, Brighton responded with characteristic composure late in the half, netting in controversial fashion through Neal Maupay, who converted after the ball bounced off the arm of Leeds defender Liam Cooper. Despite their one-goal advantage, Brighton had to withstand a ferocious second-half onslaught from the hosts as their unshakable tenacity came to the fore. The defining moment arrived in the 78th minute when Leeds’ Kalvin Phillips was shown a red card, leaving the visitors to see out the remaining minutes with growing confidence. Despite their numerical superiority and relentless pressing, Brighton struggled to double their lead until the 86th minute, when Lamptey sealed the points with a composed finish after capitalising on a defensive error. The win edged Brighton above second-placed West Brom and into pole position in the promotion race, as they remain undefeated in 14 league games for the first time since 2017. Manager Graham Potter, who has been credited with transforming the team’s style and consistency, praised his side's resilience. “We showed real character and belief, especially under pressure,” he said. “This is a team that keeps learning and growing, and I believe we still have more to give.” For Leeds, who are now 12th in the table, the defeat comes with growing questions over their management and long-term direction amid speculation about potential managerial changes. Garry Monk’s side remain in the thick of the play-off race on goal difference, but their recent inconsistency – culminating in this dent in form – has reignited criticism of their approach.

Prime Minister David Cameron has issued a blunt warning that delaying major infrastructure projects in the UK could have severe economic consequences, squandering the opportunity to prepare the country for a post-Brexit future. Speaking at a pre-election address in Birmingham, where he was championing the government’s long-term economic strategy, Cameron insisted that the timing of these projects was critical and that any postponement would be tantamount to “looking the other way as our competitors race ahead.” The Prime Minister cited the North Sea Array wind farm, High Speed 2 (HS2), and the road and transport upgrades in the North of England as examples of flagship initiatives that the government has not only supported but fast-tracked. He argued that these projects are vital in building a supply chain resilient to the uncertainties of Brexit and securing jobs in key sectors such as manufacturing, transport, and energy. "Whatever the outcome of the referendum, the rest of the world will be moving forward with assembling the engines of global economic growth,” Cameron said. He pointed out that while Anglo-Saxon economies in Western Europe might lag, the UK must not, adding that “we have the skills, the resources, and the vision to lead the way if we are ready.” Cameron also touched on the frustrations within the government over delays from outside the UK, particularly from European Union institutions, which have been known to slow down planning permits and utility works. “We cannot wait for other countries to make their decisions because our jobs and our future depend on getting on with it,” he stressed. The remarks come amid growing concerns from business leaders and economists, who have also warned that delaying critical infrastructure could stifle investment and innovation in a time of global economic transition. Cameron’s assertion highlights the government's continued determination to push through its ambitious plans under the current coalition, despite the political turbulence surrounding Brexit and the upcoming general election. His comments appear to touch on a broader rift within the Conservative Party, where some members have called for a pause or even redirection of government spending as preparations for Brexit continue. But Cameron has made it clear he sees no hesitation in accelerating progress. “If we dither, it is not just the economy that will suffer, but our confidence on the world stage," he said, calling for unity in moving forward.

Cameron sets out ‘comprehensive’ strategy to combat Islamist extremism   Prime Minister David Cameron has outlined the UK’s new blueprint to confront the “toxic ideology” of Islamist extremism, marking it as a national security priority that requires “everything we’ve got” to defeat. Speaking in a rare early parliamentary session on extremism, the Conservative leader insisted the plan, unveiled ahead of the general election, is the “most wide-ranging government strategy on countering extremism ever delivered by this country.” Addressing MPs at a packed House of Commons, Cameron described Islamist extremism as a “poison” that sought to “undermine the values of democracy, tolerance and freedom.” He admitted that although progress had been made through community engagement, improved surveillance, and the prosecution of extremists, the threat remained “significant and evolving.” Central to the government’s strategy is a three-pronged approach focusing on security, support for communities, and the global push to isolate extremist ideologies. On the security front, Cameron confirmed a commitment to expanding counter-terrorism operations, including increased funding for MI5, improved use of surveillance laws, and the deployment of specialist detectives in key hotspots. He highlighted the need for greater data-sharing between domestic and international agencies, particularly in tackling online radicalisation. Cameron also announced a significant increase in funding for Prevent, the Government’s counter-extremism strategy, which encourages the “early intervention” of at-risk individuals before they become radicalised. The funding boost, amounting to an additional £28 million over the next four years, will go toward educational initiatives, youth mentoring, and the involvement of faith leaders in spreading messages of peace and mutual respect. The Prime Minister acknowledged the importance of international cooperation in dismantling extremist networks. He praised the UK’s role in the coalition against Daesh in Iraq and Syria and pledged continued efforts to bolster partner states in the Middle East and Africa where extremist ideologies have taken root. In response to growing public unease over the balance between national security and civil liberties, Cameron argued the strategy found “the correct balance between protecting our freedoms and keeping our people safe.” He dismissed recent criticisms as “distractions from the real issue,” which he insists is the long-term fight against a movement that “does not believe in peaceful coexistence.” However, the proposals have been met with caution by civil liberties groups and opposition parties. Labour’s shadow home secretary, Diane Abbott, warned against the dangers of over-policing and accused the government of using “fear-based politics to gain public approval.”

A Welsh Liberal Democrats campaign profile: How the Lib Dems are seeking to revive support in key marginal seats   As the UK election looms, the Welsh Liberal Democrats find themselves at a critical juncture in their national campaign. With a focus on marginal seats and a pledge to fight for a "fairer" Wales through a more federal approach within the UK, the party has outlined a strategy aimed at regaining ground in communities where their influence has waned. Nye Davies, policy director of Cardiff University's Wales Governance Centre, offers a detailed insight into the party’s campaign strategy and the challenges it faces. The Liberal Democrats, whose parliamentary representation in Wales has dwindled to just one MP since 2019, are now betting on small but pivotal seats such as Montgomeryshire, Ceredigion, and Brecon and Radnorshire. These areas, historically competitive and home to micro-constituencies, represent the frontline for the party’s ambitions. Nye Davies explains that, in a fractured political landscape where no party can comfortably claim a majority, the Welsh Liberal Democrats are positioning themselves as the “third way,” offering an alternative to both Labour and the Conservatives. According to the Welsh Governance Centre’s analysis, the party has two core messages: one to push for a devolved Wales with more powers from Westminster and another to advocate for local empowerment and community services. “The national narrative – about Wales needing more autonomy – is still important because the party wants to be seen as the champion of home rule,” says Nye Davies. “But in Wales, the Lib Dems are also trying to ground that in local policies. They need to show voters that a seat here or there can impact the bigger picture.” The party’s continued focus on climate and education is another central pillar of its campaign in Wales. These issues have been highlighted as vote-winners in areas such as Ceredigion, where the Lib Dems lost comfortably in the previous general election. With school funding and environmental housing policies central to their localised manifestos, they are hoping to resonate with education professionals and environmentally conscious voters. Davies also points to the role of the Wales Office and the party’s national leadership under Sir Ed Davey. “In previous elections, the Liberal Democrats in Wales were sometimes seen as a 'split-off' from English interests. Now, the party is far more careful to present a truly Welsh campaign with Welsh policies,” he explains.

India prepares for historic weight loss surgery for world’s heaviest woman   A privately-run hospital in Mumbai has announced it is constructing a uniquely designed facility to accommodate Magdy Yacoub, an Egyptian woman who holds the title of the heaviest person in the world, weighing 500kg (1,102lb). Ms Yacoub, who has lived most of her life in Egypt before moving to India in the hopes of a miraculous recovery, is set to undergo groundbreaking weight reduction surgery at the Bhatia Hospital, a specialist in treating extreme obesity and related medical complications. Ms Yacoub arrived in India several months ago under the care of a private health charity working in conjunction with the hospital. Her journey to treatment has been marked by both triumph and tragedy. Confined to a hospital bed for most of her life, unable to walk or move unaided, she has faced multiple health issues including diabetes, heart failure, and chronic respiratory conditions — all linked to her extreme weight. The prospect of surgery has been met with both cautious optimism and grave concern by her medical team, who describe it as one of the most complex cases they have encountered. The hospital, which treats patients from across the world, has built a custom unit capable of handling her size and medical needs, with reinforced ceilings, specially adapted beds, and a theatre equipped to handle the unique requirements of bariatric surgery for a patient of such extreme weight. The surgical team, led by Dr Kuljeet Bhatia, has spent months analysing Ms Yacoub’s medical history and preparing a multi-stage approach that includes improvements in mobility and preoperative fitness before she can undergo the primary weight loss procedures. “This is not just about surgery,” Dr Bhatia told The Times. “We are talking about a multidisciplinary effort involving physiotherapists, cardiologists, endocrinologists, and nutritionists. The mission is not only to reduce weight but to ensure she can lead a long, independent life after the process.” Ms Yacoub has no history of weight loss success, with previous attempts at treatments in Egypt failing due to the country's limited resources for managing extreme obesity. Her waiting period in India has been marked by a slow but positive improvement in her mobility, supported by a team of caregivers and therapists based in the purpose-built facility. Her case has drawn international attention, and medical professionals have described the intended surgical process as one of life-and-death risk — not only for the patient, but for the team involved.

The UK government’s chief scientist has issued a stark warning about the growing threat of extreme weather events, saying that the amount of carbon dioxide already in the atmosphere is sufficient to trigger more frequent and severe floods and droughts within the next 25 years. Sir Patrick Vallance, the government’s chief scientific adviser, made the remarks in a public address to the Royal Society, where he outlined the implications of current greenhouse gas levels on global climate systems. The statement has sent shockwaves through policy circles and sparked renewed calls for urgent climate action. Vallance, who has played a central role in the UK government’s scientific advisory during the coronavirus pandemic, revealed that the existing stock of CO₂ in the atmosphere is already altering weather patterns, increasing the risk of extreme conditions such as unseasonal rainfall, prolonged dry spells, and more intense heatwaves. “What we’re seeing now is the result of past emissions, and the consequences are already locked in to an extent for the next two to three decades,” Vallance said. “We will likely see a significant increase in climatic extremes, and this will have real, immediate effects for communities and ecosystems around the world.” The chief scientist’s comments come amid growing public concern over the UK’s recent weather disruptions, with 2023 alone witnessing record-breaking rainfall in November, which led to widespread flooding, and a punishing summer drought that disrupted farming and left reservoir levels dangerously low. Scientists have long warned that such events will become more frequent as the climate continues to evolve. Vallance did not mince words when addressing the role of human activity in climate change. “We have contributed to this problem. And while the world is making progress on reducing emissions, the legacy of past centuries is now with us and will shape our future,” he said. His remarks come as Prime Minister Rishi Sunak’s government is under pressure to meet the UK’s legally binding net-zero target for 2050. The UK is also currently hosting the upcoming Global Climate Summit, where world leaders will be expected to show renewed ambition in the fight against global warming. Environmental campaigners have welcomed Vallance’s warning but say it is not surprising. “Scientists have been saying for years that we are past the point of mild and predictable climate change. The real question now is how prepared we are to adapt to the chaos we’ve set in motion,” said a spokesperson for Greenpeace UK.

Neil Hamilton, UKIP assembly group leader, has sparked controversy by claiming that Britain does not have a problem with Islamophobia and that there are no reliable statistics on hate crime. Speaking at a recent public forum in Cardiff, Mr. Hamilton categorically denied the existence of a widespread issue, stating that what is often portrayed as Islamophobia is in fact “legitimate criticism of Islam and the practice of the religion within the UK.” The comments come amid a backdrop of rising tensions across the UK, where mosques and Muslim community centres have reported increased incidents of harassment and discrimination. Community leaders and advocacy groups have repeatedly called on the government to take the issue more seriously and to implement better data collection on hate crimes. Mr. Hamilton, however, argued that such incidents are often exaggerated and that the narratives promoting a “crisis of Islamophobia” reflect a specific political agenda. “Islam is a major world religion and I have no issues with Muslims who want to live by the laws of the land and British values,” Mr. Hamilton said. “What I do take issue with, however, is when we hear of entire communities being told they are under threat due to real or imagined grievances over faith. We need factual data, not fear-mongering.” His remarks were swiftly condemned by several human rights organisations and opposition figures. Baroness Warsi, the former Conservative politician and chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group on British Muslims, called Mr. Hamilton’s comments “dangerously out of step with reality.”Speaking after receiving the Letterbox Report’s annual hate crime survey, which found that 85 per cent of Muslim respondents in the UK had experienced abuse or threats in the past five years, she said: “To ignore the lived experiences of communities and to dismiss these realities as part of a political agenda is not only callous, but harmful.” Home Secretary Suella Braverman declined to comment directly on Mr. Hamilton’s statement, but reaffirmed her commitment to tackling hate crime and extremism. “We are clear that Islamophobia, like any form of hatred, will not be tolerated,” she said. “We are investing in initiatives to support affected communities and to better understand the scope of these challenges.” Ministers have come under increasing pressure to address the issue of hate crime data, with critics pointing to a lack of consistency in how such incidents are recorded and reported across police forces.

Newcastle United found themselves at the summit of the Championship on Sunday evening as they claimed a hard-fought 2-0 victory over Barnsley at Oakwell. Dwight Gayle emerged as the hero with a brace, underlining his growing importance in Alan Pardew’s side and propelling the Magpies to a fourth consecutive league win and top spot in the table. The Tyne and Wear club arrived at Oakwell as strong favourites, a position that has largely defined their season so far this term. They have been building momentum steadily since the turn of the year and with their formidable attacking line and resurgent midfield, they looked the likelier to come out on top. And it was Gayle, the former Crystal Palace and Bournemouth striker, who proved instrumental yet again. The opener came in the 18th minute when Gayle converted a well-worked move, finishing with composure after being set up by a fine cross from Jacob Murphy. It was a tactical masterpiece, epitomising the sharpness and cohesion which have made Newcastle a force to be reckoned with in the second tier. With the home side still searching for rhythm, the strike was a blow that rattled the Championship newcomers. Gayle doubled the lead with 20 minutes remaining, capitalising on a defensive error to slot in from close range. The goal capped a fine all-round performance from the 30-year-old, who has now scored nine times in his last 10 league games. It was a result that sent Newcastle’s fans into raptures and placed them ahead of Brighton and Huddersfield in the Championship race. This victory also marked a significant turning point for Alan Pardew, who has been under continued pressure as manager. With their title ambitions seemingly gathering steam, the Magpies have demonstrated a winning mentality that has been absent for much of the club’s recent history. The consistency they have shown in this sequence of results has not gone unnoticed by fans and pundits alike, many of whom have claimed this may be the year they finally end their long Championship wait. For Barnsley, the defeat was a further setback in their promotion hopes. Having only returned to the second tier last year after being relegated from the Premier League, the academically strong but financially modest club have struggled to match the giants of the league. Their absence of a cutting edge in attack and defensive vulnerabilities have been glaring as the season has progressed.

For the first time in Northern Ireland’s history, a majority of Assembly members have voted in support of same-sex marriage, marking a significant shift in the region’s often divided political and cultural landscape. The vote comes after years of campaigning by LGBTQ+ groups, civil rights organisations and individual politicians, and as wider public opinion appears to be moving in favour of equality and inclusion. The landmark decision followed an assembly vote on the Bill for the legal recognition of same-sex marriage. A total of 57 of the 109 MLAs supported the motion, surpassing the 50% threshold for the first time. The passing Assembly has previously rejected the measure on two previous occasions, in 2015 and 2017, reflecting the deep fault lines across religious and political lines. On both previous attempts, the vote failed to secure the overall majority required for legislative approval. Although the Bill is not expected to be passed in the near future — as indicative votes do not automatically lead to law — the symbolic shift carries significant weight. The result signals a growing electoral and social willingness to embrace equality in Northern Ireland, where sectarian and cultural traditions have historically shaped opposition to progressive social change. Supporters of same-sex marriage hailed the development as a “major step forward for equality and human rights.” Davidiler White, EqualityNI’s director, said the vote was a “moment of hope” for the LGBTQ+ community in the region, and evidence that the democratic process is “capable of delivering change.” The result also has important implications following the Brexit transition period, as same-sex marriage is already legal across the rest of the United Kingdom. Many citizens from Northern Ireland have therefore been able to marry legally in jurisdictions such as England, Scotland or Wales. Advocates argue that legalising same-sex marriage in Northern Ireland would not only bring the region in line with the rest of the UK but also reduce the number of LGBT+ citizens having to travel outside their home to enjoy the same rights as their heterosexual counterparts. Opponents, largely from unionist and religious communities, continue to argue that marriage should remain between one man and one woman. Reverend Irving Lazure, a vocal critic of same-sex marriage, said the result reflected the pressures of “mainstream culture being forced upon our community,” and that the Assembly must “honor the religious and moral traditions that underpin Northern Irish society.”

The UK government is set to revise its official alcohol guidelines for the first time in two decades, promising sweeping changes in how public health officials advise citizens on safe drinking levels. The review has sparked widespread anticipation, with health campaigners, scientists, and ministers all weighing in on the implications of the long-awaited update. The current advice—largely based on guidelines set in 1995—recommends that men should not regularly drink more than 3-4 units a day and women no more than 2-3 units. The new guidelines, which are expected to be published in the coming weeks, will likely reflect the latest research into the health risks of alcohol consumption, including its link to cancer, liver disease, and mental health issues. According to sources close to the review, the updated advice is expected to recommend lower levels of alcohol intake and more emphasis on the risks of any level of drinking. Some studies suggest even small amounts—such as one daily glass of wine—can increase the likelihood of developing certain diseases. A spokesperson for the Department of Health said: “We are committed to ensuring that the UK’s alcohol guidelines are based on the most current and robust scientific evidence. This review is essential in helping us support the public in making informed choices about their health and wellbeing.” The review, led by Public Health England and involving leading medical experts and academics, was launched in response to national concerns over rising alcohol-related hospital admissions and deaths. Statistics from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) show that alcohol-related mortality has increased over the past decade, prompting calls for stricter public health messaging and clearer guidance. Dr Sarah Jarvis, a public health physician and government advisor, commented: “The science has moved on considerably since the last guidelines were issued. We now understand more than ever the cumulative effect of alcohol on the body and the risks even moderate drinking can pose. It’s vital that the public is given up-to-date information.” However, not all are optimistic that updated guidelines will significantly change consumer behaviour. The alcohol industry has claimed that focusing on cutting drinking rather than education fails to resonate with many people. A spokesperson for the Scotch Whisky Association said: “While we fully support efforts to reduce harmful drinking, we hope the new guidelines will also include advice on how to drink responsibly, rather than deter people from drinking altogether.”

Roger Federer was stunned at Flushing Meadows as the 17-time Grand Slam champion was knocked out of the US Open in a dramatic quarter-final defeat to sixth seed Tomas Berdych. Federer, who had reached the last eight by fighting past Nick Kyrgios in the previous round, looked to be heading out after a third set tiebreak that went against him, but he battled back to level the match at two sets apiece before a crucial double fault handed Berdych the deciding set and a place in the semi-finals. Murray, who eliminated American journeyman Steve Johnson in the earlier match, now awaits the Czech in the last four after bidding for his third Grand Slam title of the season. Federer, 32, had shown resilience throughout the tournament and had spoken bravely before the match about his left-knee issues and determination to succeed despite the physical challenges. But the Swiss icon, who turned 34 in August, was edged out by a tactical and physical performance from Berdych, who has himself battled in-and-out of the top five over recent years, including a Grand Slam final at the 2010 Wimbledon where he was pushed to five sets by Federer. The match began tentatively with both players trading breaks early in the first set, before Federer found his rhythm to take the set. Berdych, who looked sharp from the baseline and precise with his serve, broke in the third game of the second set and despite being broken in the sixth, held through the ensuing tiebreak to take the match at that stage. Federer's intensity surged in the third set and he roared back to a 3-1 lead, but with the court noticeably bouncy and his movement starting to show signs of fatigue, Berdych reeled off the next five games to take a two-set lead. In the fourth, Federer finally clicked into gear and surged into a commanding 5-1 lead. He appeared to have the momentum for a comeback, but a fatal double fault at 5-3 allowed Berdych to conjure a remarkable sequence of games to take the fifth set 7-5 in a pulsating display of nerves and power. As the crowd roared its approval of a compelling encounter, the draw for a new chapter of the US Open took shape. Federer’s loss sends a reminder that age and adversity can still derail even the greatest of careers, while Berdych stands on the cusp of another major finals clash.

A Controversial Welcome: The Gaza Flotilla’s Daring Mission   In a move that has ignited fierce public debate and drawn strong reactions from both within Ghana and the international press, the West African nation recently announced its decision to offer refuge to two Yemeni nationals who have returned home after years of detention at the US detention facility in Guantanamo Bay. The two men, whose names have not been publicly disclosed, were released as part of a complex diplomatic exchange last year under which provisions were made for their resettlement. And now, they will be making their new home in Ghana. But the government's decision has run into immediate backlash. Critics argue that admitting former Guantanamo detainees, even under the condition that they are now cleared and allowed to re-enter their home countries, is an act of political naivety. “These are people who were held in the darkest corner of American justice, and now we are opening the gates for them?” one prominent Ghanaian blogger wrote. “We live in a region that has been targeted for terrorism for decades — and now we’re setting an example that will follow.” The government remains defiant in the face of criticism. Ghana’s Ministry of Interior, in a statement released on Tuesday, insisted that the decision is a humanitarian act and in line with the country’s international obligations under human rights frameworks. "It is important for Ghana to show leadership in the spirit of international solidarity," said a spokesperson, adding that the two Yemenis will be placed under tight surveillance and will not be allowed to leave the country for the foreseeable future. For now, the two men remain under someone’s full watch. But the debate over their presence continues to divide public opinion. Some point out that other African and Middle Eastern countries refused to take back their repatriated nationals after release from Guantanamo, fearing political consequences and accusations of harboring terrorism. "We are talking about countries that were quick to deny any link to these individuals during their years of detention," said Dr. Nana Boateng, a senior lecturer in international law at the University of Ghana. "And here, Ghana is stepping up with a policy of compassion." The country's civil society organisations, however, are divided. While some human rights groups have praised the decision as bold and principled, others are calling for transparency. "I understand the humanitarian impulse," said Kofi Antwi, a director at Center for Human Rights and Advocacy in Accra.

Dr. Strangelove: The Timeless Satire That Still Chills and Chuckles   Few films possess the power to endure as both a comedy and a chilling warning, yet  Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb —directed by Stanley Kubrick and released in 1964—has done just that. Originally panned by some for its grim subject matter and wildly absurdist tone, Kubrick’s satire has since taken its place among the most revered comedy films of all time. Now, nearly six decades later, the movie remains an incisive critique of Cold War politics, human folly, and the absurdity of nuclear brinkmanship. Set in the tense world of 1960s America,  Dr. Strangelove  imagines a catastrophic chain of events triggered by a rogue U.S. Air Force general who launches a nuclear missile strike against the Soviet Union. As breakfast is served in boardrooms and war rooms, a deranged general named Jack D. Ripper (played brilliantly by Sterling Hayden) is the man behind the madness, convinced that fluoridated water is the work of the KGB. Kubrick’s genius lay in his unflinching decision to make deadly serious material laugh-out-loud funny, without ever losing sight of the horror at its core. Critics at the time often mistook the film for pure slapstick, failing to grasp its sombre undertone and political satire. However, as the Cold War continued to escalate and the reality of mutually assured destruction became ever more tangible, the film's message found new resonance. Peter Sellers, who stars in three roles—including the bumbling President Merkin Muffley, the eccentric nuclear scientist Dr. Strangelove, and a flustered British officer—earned particular acclaim, though the film did not win any major awards at the time. What is perhaps most striking about  Dr. Strangelove  in 2024 is how many of its themes remain depressingly relevant. With ongoing international tensions, modern nuclear threats, and democratic institutions under pressure, Kubrick’s vision feels more prescient than ever. The movie’s fearless and often surreal examination of authoritarianism, military incompetence, and the fragility of peace continues to captivate new generations of viewers. The film's iconic lines—such as "Mein Führer, I can walk!" or “I'm not the only one left in the world, am I?”—remain etched in popular culture. Yet behind the punchlines lies a deeply disturbing question: how close were we to annihilation, and how close might we still be?

The British National Party (BNP) has announced the expulsion of its former leader, Nick Griffin, from its ranks, marking a significant shift in the far-right political organization after more than two decades of his influence. Griffin, who led the party from 1999 to 2014 and remained a prominent figure within the party during his time as a Member of the European Parliament, has been removed following a vote by members of the BNP’s central committee. According to party sources, the decision was made after a review of internal disciplinary procedures, with concerns raised about Griffin's recent behaviour and failure to abide by the party's current strategic direction under its new leadership. The move is seen as a symptom of the BNP’s broader decline in popularity and its attempt to distance itself from controversial figures in an effort to rebrand and expand its appeal to a wider audience. Griffin, now 72, has been a divisive figure in British politics since the 1980s, known for his openly racist and anti-immigrant rhetoric. During his leadership, the BNP saw a surge in national profile, particularly during the 2009 European Parliament elections, when Griffin himself became one of the party's two MEPs. However, since the early 2010s, the BNP has struggled to maintain support in light of internal disputes and national public opinion trending away from far-right extremism, especially after the rise of more mainstream anti-immigrant sentiments within conservative politics and the emergence of other far-right groups. Last year, the BNP announced plans to adopt a more “enlightened” political approach, including softening its rhetoric on race and immigration, with the stated aim of becoming a more acceptable alternative in local and national elections. John Williams, the BNP’s current interim leader, confirmed the news to the press, describing it as a necessary step to ensure the party’s future viability. “Nick Griffin was an important part of our history, but the time has come for a new era. Our focus is now on moving forward,” Williams said. He refrained from providing further details on any alleged infractions by Griffin. Reactions from political commentators were mixed. Some hailed Griffin’s expulsion as a positive move towards a more responsible political identity for the BNP, while others questioned whether such drastic changes would be enough to halt the party’s continued marginalisation. Griffin himself has yet to publicly comment on his expulsion.

The Belfast Giants’ hopes of lifting the Elite League title were dashed on Saturday as they fell to a 2-0 defeat against the Sheffield Steelers in the semi-finals of the prestigious play-offs. The Giants, who had enjoyed a strong campaign this season, were left to reflect on what might have been after a valiant but ultimately unsuccessful effort at the beginning of the four-game series at the SkyDome Arena. Despite securing the top seed in the play-offs and demonstrating consistent form throughout the season, the Giants were unable to break through against a resolute Sheffield side that brought a renewed sense of purpose to the series. The defeat, the second successive in the series, extended Belfast’s wait for a first league championship since their debut season in 2001. The game itself was a gritty affair, with both teams fighting for control in what was a tightly contested encounter. Neither side managed to replicate the firepower of the regular season, with the Steelers’ defensive discipline and goaltending proving too much for the Giants to overcome. Brian Stewart, playing in his first season with the Giants, was steadfast in the net, but the Belfast attack failed to find the back of the net for the second game running. Sheffield, meanwhile, looked smooth and controlled, relying on their depth and physicality to frustrate the home side. The visitors scored the decisive goals through a first-period power-play goal from David Rounding and a second-half insurance goal from Mitchell Bennett, both of whom are instrumental to Sheffield's efforts in their pursuit of the league title. Goalscorer Rounding said after the match: “It was a tough game in Belfast, but we stuck to our system and played our game. I think the fans were looking for a result, and we delivered it for them. We’ve had a great opportunity here, and we’re just excited to keep going.” The Giants, now 1-1 in the series, will look to make adjustments heading into the next two games in Sheffield. Head coach Adam Keefe, who has guided the team to the semi-finals for the past three seasons, expressed disappointment at the defeat but remained optimistic for the remainder of the series. “We tried everything we knew in our playbook," Keefe said. "We’ll have to find a way to break their system apart. It’s one of the toughest teams in the league, but we believe in our team and our capabilities.”

The High Court has been told that requiring the UK Parliament to approve the Brexit process is of immense “constitutional importance,” as a landmark legal case challenging the government’s authority to trigger Article 50 without parliamentary approval reached a crucial stage this week. The case, brought by campaign group the Heathrow Residents Association among others, argues that allowing the government to begin the formal process of leaving the European Union solely by executive action would be an unconstitutional power grab, a breach of parliamentary sovereignty, and would undermine the credibility of the result of the 2016 referendum. At the heart of the case is the question of who has the legal authority to launch the formal two-year Brexit negotiations. The government, led by Prime Minister Theresa May, has consistently taken the stance that the authority to invoke Article 50 under the European Union (Withdrawal) Act lies with the executive – the government, following the result of the referendum. They argue that Parliament did not instruct the government to leave the EU when it passed the Act earlier this year; instead, it granted the government the power to do so when it saw fit. The group of claimants, including university lecturers, solicitors and members of the public who supported the Leave campaign, have put forward a strong legal counter to this. Their barrister, Sir James Eadie QC, argued during the court hearing on Monday that triggering Article 50 – a move of “fundamental constitutional and political importance” – cannot be taken out of Parliament’s hands. “What is at stake here is the relationship between the executive and Parliament,” he said. “Parliament must have an input in the trigger of a procedure that effectively ends one treaty and begins the negotiation of another.” Mr. Eadie also pointed out that invoking Article 50 would result in the UK exercising a public power that would significantly alter the statutory framework of the country’s relationship with the EU. To allow the Prime Minister to act unilaterally, he argued, is a direct violation of the common law doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty, which affirms that Parliament passed laws, not the executive. The government’s representative, however, countered that it would be confusing for Parliament to be involved in a decision already made by the electorate. “The Government of a country acting in the public interest must act decisively based on the will of the people,” their barrister said.

Labour MP Naz Shah has admitted that the comments which led to her suspension from the party were anti-Semitic, as she prepares to address a disciplinary hearing to defend her position. The hearing, set to take place in London, will examine Facebook posts she made in 2014, during the height of the Israeli military operation in Gaza. In one post, she wrote: “When will the West stop saying peace when it's actually war?”, a comment widely interpreted as dismissive of the international response to the conflict. In another, she was quoted stating: “Shalom you bloody colonisers,” and “You chase your ambulance but the Israelis chase ambulances like they're Olympic sprinters.” Shah, Labour’s shadow mental health minister and first Muslim woman of colour elected to Parliament, was suspended by the party in December after a formal complaint was made to Labour’s Anti-Semitism Commission, which was formed in the wake of a wave of controversies surrounding far-right and Islamophobic activity within the party. The commission ruled in February that she should be suspended “pending the outcome of disciplinary proceedings.” Reacting to the suspension and the ongoing inquiry, Shah expressed regret that her comments had been taken as anti-Semitic, though she maintains they were in the context of a broader critique of British foreign policy and colonial history. In a recent statement to the BBC, she said: “I have never harboured hatred – of any kind – towards any people. My comments were about political accountability and the imbalance of international power. I have apologised publicly for the way my messages were received.” The Labour Party’s ongoing struggle with anti-Semitism in its ranks has become a major issue in recent years, with high-profile expulsions and suspensions, including that of former London mayor Ken Livingstone and veteran MPs Tommy Ross and Pat Glass. The party, now led by Sir Keir Starmer, has taken a hard stance against intolerance and extremism, introducing new rules requiring members to sign up to a code of conduct affirming their commitment to the principles of anti-racism and anti-discrimination. Shah, who was elected in 2017 for the Bradford West constituency, is widely respected within her party for her tireless campaigning on issues such as mental health care and equality. Her case has drawn concern from a number of high-profile figures, including the shadow chancellor, Rebecca Long-Bailey, who has publicly called for the process to be fair and transparent.

African Elephant: Beauty, Power, and Peril   Across Africa, in parks and reserves that stretch like patches of paradise on dwindling landscapes, the African elephant reigns silently yet majestically. But today, its might and majesty are under siege. As a journalist and filmmaker who has chronicled Africa’s many triumphs and tragedies, I find myself compelled to address one issue that continues to weigh on the continent’s conscience: the plight of the African elephant. These gentle giants have long been a symbol of Africa’s untamed wildness, admired for their intelligence, social complexity, and ecological importance. Yet in recent decades, their numbers have plummeted due to habitat loss, human-wildlife conflict, and—most pressingly—poaching for the ivory trade. Though a global ban on ivory trade was imposed in 1989, the demand for ivory in some markets, particularly in Asia, has persisted. It is a cruel paradox: the very thing that makes the elephant remarkable has become the source of its suffering. The emotional narrative of the elephant is heart-wrenching to witness. Mojo the elephant, once a star at the Bronx Zoo and the subject of a recent documentary, is just one example of the attention the species is garnering. But while Mojo's story has touched hearts in New York, the African elephant is in decline. Reports suggest that the population – historically one of the largest in the world – has seen steep decreases, with the animals facing an existential threat that transcends borders. Activists and conservationists argue that education and community-based initiatives are key to changing the tide. Projects that incentivize local communities to protect elephants, rather than see them as threats to livelihoods, have proven effective in areas like Botswana and Kenya. These programs highlight the opportunity for Africans to reclaim their role as guardians of the continent’s living treasures. Yet challenges remain. The illegal ivory trade is deeply embedded in organized crime networks that thrive in the shadows of global unregulated markets. The involvement of corrupt officials and the lack of political will in some regions exacerbate the problem. As with many crises in Africa, the elephant’s fate is not only a wildlife issue but a question of justice, governance, and ethics. As a continent of storytellers, Africa must find nuanced ways to amplify the elephant’s story—not just as a victim of violence, but as a symbol of our relationship with nature and the consequences of our choices.

Hammond warns EU treaty reform necessary to meet German demands   London — Foreign Secretary Philip Hammond has signalled that any real progress on Brexit terms and beyond will require changes to the EU’s foundational treaties, in what he described as a necessary step to align the Union with Germany’s political and economic expectations. Speaking at a private meeting of international diplomats on Tuesday, Hammond said that unless fundamental treaty revisions take place, the EU would remain an "unsustainable and unbalanced" entity, particularly in the wake of Britain's departure. The remarks come as Germany’s governing coalition under Chancellor Angela Merkel continues to push for deeper fiscal and political integration within the EU. Earlier this month, Germany's finance minister, Olaf Scholz, outlined the government’s vision for a "fiscal union" to reduce economic disparities between richer and poorer member states, a concept that has sparked controversy among countries such as France and Poland who view it as an overreach of German influence. Hammond suggested that while Germany must lead the way in reforming the EU, its drive for consolidation must not come at the expense of countries like the UK, many of whose concerns led to the 2016 Brexit vote. "German Europe is a force for stability in the EU, but as with any great power, real change will only happen if its own domestic and political constraints are addressed," Hammond said. “If Germany wants the EU to adapt to evolving circumstances, and to act more decisively in global affairs, then the treaties will have to be rewritten.” The Foreign Secretary’s comments were widely interpreted as a diplomatic nudge towards Germany — and beyond — that the EU must not only consider reform to accommodate post-Brexit realities but also to better meet its own internal demands. Hammond did not suggest that Britain had a role in shaping these changes, stating instead that his remarks were not about “reinserting Britain into the EU framework”, but about preparing for a continent “where Britain will still have an important, if external, role to play.” Such overtures come at a time when British ministers are preparing for ongoing negotiations on future trade deals outside the EU. Hammond insisted that the UK’s departure from the EU did not weaken its commitment to European stability, and that its "naturally European” heritage would remain intact. The speech marks the first time since the Brexit referendum that a senior UK official has explicitly called for the EU to reform its own rules on governance and finance.

The internet has become a “playground for paedophiles,” the NSPCC has warned in a sobering new report that highlights the growing risks children face online. As more young people spend increasing amounts of their time on social media, messaging apps, and gaming platforms, experts have raised alarm over the ease with which offenders can make contact and groom vulnerable children. The charity has called on the government and technology companies to take stronger measures to protect children and hold perpetrators to account. Recent research commissioned by the NSPCC reveals that one in five children in the UK has been sent private messages by someone they do not know outside of school or college. Many of these messages contained content that was inappropriate or led to exploitative conversations. In the worst cases, such communications can escalate into sexual abuse, trafficking, or even abduction. “The internet is not just a tool for play and socialisation; it is increasingly being used by predators to exploit children with alarming ease,” said NSPCC chief executive Peter Wanless. “We are concerned that the lack of effective safeguards and the patchy response from law enforcement is putting young people at greater risk.” One parent, who wished to remain anonymous, shared the story of her 13-year-old daughter, who became a target from a man who posed as a teenager while playing a popular online game. Over several weeks, he built a relationship with her, sending messages that soon turned inappropriate. “At first, it just seemed like she was talking to another kid in the game,” the mother said. “It wasn’t until she came home in tears and said she was ‘bigging her up’ that I found out what was really going on.” Enforcement of online safety laws remains a key issue. Police figures show a surge in reports of online grooming but a lack of prosecutions, with many cases considered “difficult to follow up” due to the anonymity offered by the web. The NSPCC has urged the government to introduce new legislation requiring tech companies to do more to identify and ban abusive users. Currently, many platforms rely on users to report suspicious activity, and there are often long delays before action is taken. Dr. Emma Smith, a forensic psychologist and child protection expert who contributed to the NSPCC report, said: “Offenders take advantage of a system that is not designed to regulate the fast-moving, complex environment of the internet.

The brutal murder of Concepta Leonard and the attempted killing of her young son, Conor, have left a deep scar across Northern Ireland and beyond, dominating the headlines of papers across the region as the community grapples with the horror of what has become known as “The Maguiresbridge horror.” The Belfast Telegraph, in a somber and deeply reported front-page lead, has described the incident as   “one of the darkest chapters in recent local memory.”   A grieving nation is now piecing together the narrative of a woman who was simply going about her day, only to be cut down by a senseless and chilling act of violence. The attack took place just before 10 am on a Thursday morning when Concepta, the 34-year-old mother of four, was turkey hunting in the rural Clogheen area of Maguiresbridge, Co Fermanagh. Her son, just six years old, was with her in the family’s vehicle at the time when, tragically, he was found shot in the drive in his car seat, minutes after his mother was found dead in the remote woods nearby. Emergency services discovered both Concepta and her son with critical, and ultimately fatal, injuries caused by impacts that appear to have been unprovoked and deliberate. Her two other children were found in another area, miraculously unharmed, but the psychological trauma inflicted on the entire family is seemingly immeasurable. In the days following the attack, the community has been in shock and mourning. The Sillet family, who already lost two of their sons, Stephen and Patrick, in a farming accident in 2022, are now once again thrust into a nightmare with the deaths of Concepta and young Connor. Her husband, Paul Leonard, has spoken to the media in brief and emotional statements, describing his wife as the "heart of the family," and saying “there are no words for this kind of loss.” The Ulster Unionist MLA for North Fermanagh, Sandra Carroll, visited the family and described the incident as “a shocking and exceptional event that has united the whole community in disbelief and solidarity.” Local leaders, including the mayor of Fermanagh, have vowed to support the prosecution of whoever is responsible, calling it a “crime of a new and disturbing nature.” In their detailed coverage, The Belfast Telegraph and the Irish News are both reporting the ongoing investigation as gothic in tone: forensic teams searching the woods for clues, teams of officers line in the fields, and local farmers being interviewed for any signs of what unfolded.

At least 31 people have been killed and dozens more injured in a suicide bomb attack outside the main Court Complex in the heart of Damascus, the Syrian capital, officials have confirmed. The blast occurred at a busy area of the city, where security services were thought to be guarding the building. The attack marks one of the bloodiest in Damascus during recent weeks and has been condemned by both the Syrian government and international organisations. The explosion tore through a security checkpoint just outside the heavily-fortified court compound, a place where senior government officials are known to gather. According to a government statement, the deceased and injured include both civilians and security personnel. Among the dead are reportedly three Russian nationals working in the legal sector, a detail that has drawn concern from Moscow. On the international front, the United Nations called for an immediate investigation and extended condolences to the victims’ families. Syrian state media, including state broadcaster Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), reported that the attack was carried out by a female suicide bomber. The identity of the perpetrator and the group responsible remain unclear, though several militant groups, including Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) and Islamic State (IS), have claimed similar attacks in the past. A short while after the blast, HTS released a video purporting to show its involvement, though the Syrian government has been quick to dismiss such claims as propaganda. The targeting of a legal institution, and one that is central to the administration of justice and governance in the country, has raised fears about the security situation in Damascus, particularly as the city is viewed by many as being relatively stable compared to the rest of war-torn Syria. While the government has deployed thousands of troops and is known to have installed checkpoints and body scanners in central areas, the attack suggests that there may still be vulnerabilities in the city’s security architecture. This comes amid the ongoing backdrop of escalating violence and a complicated civil war that has now entered its ninth year. With reports of unrelenting clashes in the north, where Turkish forces and US-backed Kurdish groups remain at odds, the attack in Damascus could further destabilise an already fragile region. Speaking to BBC reporters yesterday, Damascus-based correspondent Aram Alkan said: “In the past few months, we’ve seen a sharp decline in attacks on civilians in the capital, but today’s explosion underlines that Syria is far from safe.”

Liverpool earned a gritty 1-0 victory over Swansea City at Anfield thanks to James Milner's 85th-minute penalty, extending their unbeaten home run to 11 games and intensifying the pressure on struggling Swans manager Francesco Guidolin. The win, the visitors' fourth loss in a row in the Premier League, leaves Swansea languishing at the foot of the table with just one point from their last 12 games. Guidolin, now under fierce criticism from supporters and pundits alike, saw his side fail once again to mount a serious challenge against a resolute Liverpool outfit. The contest was a tense and cagey affair from the outset, with both teams unable to impose themselves on the match for the majority of the 90 minutes. Swansea, who endured a difficult pre-season under Guidolin following their relegation from the top flight last season, looked for all the world as if they were still playing catch-up in terms of both confidence and cohesion. Liverpool, meanwhile, played with the experience of returning manager Jürgen Klopp’s touchline guidance and the enduring fight shown in many of their performances under his stewardship. The breakthrough came in the 85th minute when Divock Origi faltered under pressure from Neil Taylor and was felled in the box. Referee Andre Marriner pointed to the spot, and captain Milner made no mistake, sending Baptiste Sagna the wrong way and sending the home crowd into raptures. The goal was a timely boost for Liverpool, who are slowly building toward the consistency needed to mount a serious top-four push. Manager Jürgen Klopp praised his team's resilience after the match, saying: "I’m happy with the result. It was a tough game, Swansea played very deep but we kept believing and we scored in the end. We’re not the same as the teams who were challenging for the title last season, but this moment is very important for us." For Swansea, the mood was one of deepening concern. The Italian manager, whose time at the club has been marked by repeated health scares and a raft of midweek signings, insisted he remained fully focused on turning their season around. He told Sky Sports: “It was a difficult game. We defended well in the first half, and maybe tried to do too much in the second. We lost a bit of concentration and paid the price. I still believe in my team.

Call for Mental Health Support in Boxing Amid Industry Concerns   Former world champion Barry McGuigan has called for boxing authorities to fund a dedicated mental health foundation to support fighters grappling with psychological challenges. The Northern Irish boxing legend, who recently made a highly publicised comeback to the sport, said that as long as fighters are considered “gladiators” without adequate support, the culture of the sport must change. McGuigan's call has come after a recent wave of media attention on mental health in boxing, prompted by the tragic deaths of former world champions Ante Milic and Derry Maths, both of whom struggled with mental health prior to their deaths. It has also followed reports of fighters who have publicly spoken about depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and the emotional toll that the sport can take, particularly after years of concussive hits and life spent in the spotlight. McGuigan, now a Member of the European Parliament for Northern Ireland, described the lack of proper mental health provision as a “shame” and urged the sport’s governing bodies to act. “We tell fighters they can handle anything in the ring, but once they walk away, we leave them to it,” he said in a recent interview. “We need a structure, as with other high-contact sports, to look after these people properly.” The idea of a mental health foundation, he added, should be funded – at least in part – by the sport’s top promoters and sanctioning bodies. McGuigan argued that organisations such as the World Boxing Council (WBC), the World Boxing Association (WBA), and the European Boxing Union (EBU) must not only acknowledge the problem but also take financial responsibility. “They make the money, they control the titles and they send out the message about what it takes to be a champion,” he said. “That includes the mind as much as the body.” There have been previous attempts to provide mental health support for fighters, but these have often been piecemeal and limited. McGuigan’s proposal would create a centralised body that can provide free access to therapy, psychological assessments, and education on emotional well-being for current and retired fighters. He also suggested that such a foundation could partner with sports charities that have proved successful in football, rugby and athletics. McGuigan’s intervention has been backed by some in the boxing community, although others have questioned how such a proposal would be funded and enforced.

In a country where freedom of expression is a vibrant and often chaotic reflection of its democracy, India has increasingly found itself at the crossroads of legal and political debate over what constitutes sedition. Recent cases have highlighted how the colonial-era law, first enacted in 1870, is being interpreted in modern times. Under India’s Sedition Law (Section 124A of the Indian Penal Code), any act that brings "or attempts to bring into hatred or contempt or disaffection toward the Government established by law" is punishable by life imprisonment or up to seven years in jail. What makes this particularly striking in 2025 is not just the content of sedition cases, but also how flexible, and at times, arbitrary, their application has become. Last week, a controversial ruling sent shockwaves through India’s legal and rights communities when a man was charged with sedition for liking a Facebook post that questioned the ruling party’s economic policies. Though details of the case remain unclear, experts have voiced concerns over a growing trend in criminal cases being filed over opinions and expressions, however minor, shared on social media. The accused, whose name has not been disclosed, is a university lecturer and says he was simply engaging in online discourse. Even more alarming, human rights groups have noted that people have been charged for seemingly innocuous acts such as supporting a rival national cricket team at a live match, drawing a cartoon with a satirical message about political leaders, or failing to stand in a cinema when the national anthem is played. In one case, a young student was investigated for failing to arrive at school in time for the national anthem, which a teacher believed was an act of disrespect—though the matter is now under legal review. The sedition law has also been weaponised against critics of prominent spiritual and public figures. Last year, a journalist was accused of sedition after publishing an article questioning a wealthy yoga guru’s political influence. Though the charges were eventually dropped, the case revealed how powerful individuals and institutions can use the law to quiet dissent. Such incidents are not new. Section 124A was famously used to prosecute scientists and writers during British colonial rule, including Mahatma Gandhi. Since independence, numerous legal scholars have called for its repeal or reform. In 2016, the Supreme Court of India reinstated the law after a nearly 50-year hiatus, ruling that sedition charges could be used in cases of incitement to violence, but not for expression alone.

Rangers secured a vital 2-1 victory over Aberdeen at Ibrox Stadium on Saturday, climbing to second place in the Scottish Premiership in a tightly contested match that saw both sides reduced to ten men. The Scottish champions, chasing a first league title since 2011, extended their lead over their rivals in a clash that was as dramatic as it was decisive. The Light Blues took control of the game in the 23rd minute when Alfredo Morelos converted a penalty after being brought down in the box by Aberdeen defender Daryll Meggat. It was the striker’s 13th league goal of the season and gave Rangers a crucial lead. However, the respite was short-lived as Aberdeen equalised just before half-time when Joe Lewis nodded in a cross from captain James Maddison to restore parity. The second half was a far more physical affair, and the referee’s red card turned out to be an inevitability. In the 58th minute, Rangers midfielder Barrie McKay was shown a second yellow card for a reckless challenge, leaving Mark Warburton’s side a man down. The decision sent shockwaves through Ibrox, but it proved to be a turning point as Rangers showed greater intensity. With their backs against the wall, Aberdeen responded with increased aggression, and in the 74th minute, substitute Declan Gallagher was sent off for a dangerous challenge on Lewis, leaving both teams with ten men. The final 20 minutes were a spectacle of urgency and high stakes, with Rangers stepping up their attacking efforts. In the 86th minute, substitute Martyn Waghorn capped a chaotic evening with a late winner, finishing a swift counter-attack with a composed left-footed strike. The goal sent the home fans into raptures and halted Aberdeen’s hopes of a first league win of the season. Speaking after the match, Rangers manager Mark Warburton praised his team’s resilience. “In difficult circumstances, the players showed the character, determination and composure to win a very important game,” he said. “We knew Aberdeen would be tough opponents, but the quality of our performance in the second half was excellent.” For Aberdeen, manager Ian McKellar acknowledged the missed opportunities but also praised his side’s effort. “I’m proud of the players, but we need to be delivering the results this season if we want to push up the table,” he said. With this victory, Rangers tightened their grip on second place in the league, closing the gap on the leaders by two points.

Local councils across England have sounded the alarm, warning that care services for the elderly and disabled are “at breaking point” as soaring costs and rising demand outstrip funding from planned council tax increases. The warnings come as social care providers reveal a “perfect storm” of challenges, including the rising cost of living, staff shortages, and an increasingly elderly population, which together are straining the system to the point of collapse. In a rare public intervention, a coalition of local authorities, led by the National Council for Voluntary Organisations (NCVO) and the Local Government Association (LGA), has called for urgent government action. They argue that even under the most optimistic assessments, the proposed council tax rises—designed to plug shortfalls in care budgets—will fall far short of what is needed. One council leader described the situation as a “care crisis unfolding in real time.” Care sector leaders say the pressure is already manifesting in delays in assembling packages of support and, in some cases, the refusal of new referrals while agencies scramble to find enough carers. Home care agencies report an exodus of staff, many of whom have left for better-paid roles in hospitality or retail, where pay and conditions have improved faster than in care. “The reality is that as council tax increases are only temporary, and as we gear up for an ageing population, we’re looking at services buckling under the weight of unmet need,” said one senior local authority official, who wished to remain anonymous. The Department of Health and Social Care has previously announced a commitment to a shake-up of the social care system, including a proposed cap on the amount a person can be expected to pay for their own care. However, with no concrete timeline for reform and a lack of additional central government funding, councils say they are left to navigate the crisis with stretched resources. In north-west England, a local authority has already had to furlough a number of care staff due to insufficient funding. In the south-east, a provider revealed that to maintain basic levels of service, it has had to merge multiple care packages, often at the expense of individualised support. “There is a danger that the very fabric of social care is beginning to unravel,” said the LGA’s chief executive. “We are calling once again for a long-term solution to this funding mismatch—one that goes beyond the immediate tweaks and delivering something sustainable for the future.”

When a new fitness coach joined England’s Women's World Cup preparations in 2015, he was left stunned by the limited emphasis on strength and conditioning within the program, according to recently revealed insights into the national team’s physical preparation. The unnamed coach, who has since spoken out in an exclusive interview, described the situation as “shocking” and highlighted concerns that the team was being left at a disadvantage compared to their international rivals. At a time when elite women’s football was undergoing rapid transformation and growing in both financial and sporting prestige, the coach's concerns raised urgent questions about the investment—and lack thereof—in physical development, injury prevention, and long-term athletic performance. The appointment of the strength and conditioning expert followed a string of high-profile injuries during warm-up matches and a general perception among players that they were not being prepared for the physical demands of World Cup play. England manager Mark Sampson, who took charge of the women’s team in 2013, had incorporated significant changes in training and tactics since his arrival, but in his early days, the fitness side of squad readiness was reportedly not up to the standard expected in top-tier football. The new coach noted that, at the time of his appointment, many of the players were not accustomed to the high-intensity strength and conditioning work that is now considered integral for female footballers competing on the global stage. “There was a clear gap,” the coach explained. “We were barely touching on strength training. The focus was on short-term fitness, not the kind of program that builds long-term resilience and performance. It’s fair to say that at the time, the girls weren’t being given the tools to compete at that level on a consistent basis.” His arrival brought a major overhaul of training protocols. Workouts were redesigned to include more resistance training, sport-specific conditioning, and recovery strategies. Players such as Lucy Bronze and Steph Houghton—key figures in the 2015 campaign—benefited from the changes, with both athletes later crediting the new approach for playing a part in their improved form. However, the revelations have raised broader questions about where the responsibility for athletic development lies in national programmes. With the men's team increasingly being held up as a model for player welfare and sustained performance, the situation surrounding the women’s team in the lead-up to 2015 stands as a stark reminder of the sometimes uneven progress in elite women’s sport.

The UK Parliament has announced a formal inquiry into the widespread issue of sexual harassment and sexual violence in England's schools, as public concern over the matter continues to grow. The inquiry, to be conducted by a Commons committee, will examine the scale of the problem, how serious it is, and the effectiveness of the current measures in place to protect students and support victims. The announcement has come amid mounting calls from education experts, teachers’ unions, and advocacy groups for a more thorough and transparent review of how schools and local authorities are addressing these issues. In recent years, a number of high-profile cases have brought the issue into the spotlight, with reports of teenage girls being targeted by groups of older boys in some secondary schools, as well as cases of staff failing to intervene or report misconduct. A 2019 report by the Department for Education found that, on average, each school in England had reported two cases of sexual violence or harassment per year, but the true figure is believed to be much higher due to underreporting. The inquiry comes at a time when the government is also reviewing child sexual abuse policies and the role of Ofsted, the schools watchdog, in enforcing safeguarding standards. Education Secretary Lucy Frazer said in a recent statement: “No child should feel unsafe in their own school. We must ensure that schools are places of learning and protection, not places where children are subject to abuse or intimidation.” The committee, made up of cross-party MPs, will have the scope to gather evidence from school staff, students, parents, and organisations working with vulnerable children. Questions will be asked about the extent to which schools are implementing government guidance, the training teachers receive to deal with such incidents, and how well reporting mechanisms are working. Teachers’ unions have welcomed the move, calling it a crucial step towards ensuring that schools are fulfilling their statutory duties to safeguard children. Jo Gummer, deputy general secretary of the National Union of Teachers, said: “This inquiry is long overdue. We need to be clear-eyed about the scale of the problem and ensure that schools have the resources and clarity they need to take meaningful action.” The inquiry is expected to take several months, with preliminary findings due to be published early next year. As the committee prepares to begin its work, the announcement serves as a reminder that sexual harassment and violence in schools remain a pressing issue that demands urgent and sustained attention.

Iraqi Forces Launch Offensive to Retake Last IS Stronghold in Mosul   Iraqi security forces have begun a major offensive to retake Mosul's Old City, the final district under the control of so-called Islamic State (IS), sparking intense fighting on the first day of the operation. Tanks and warplanes were deployed in a coordinated ground and air assault aimed at dislodging the militants from the ancient heart of the city. The assault marks a pivotal moment in the year-long campaign to reclaim Mosul from IS, which has been a focal point of international efforts to defeat the group. The Old City, once a thriving medieval quarter, has become a labyrinth of makeshift defences, booby-trapped buildings and snipers, as IS fighters cling to their dwindling hold in Iraq’s second-largest city. Despite numerous setbacks and heavy casualties, Iraqi forces — backed by the US-led multinational coalition — have pressed ahead with the offensive. Coalition airstrikes targeted IS positions overnight, creating a smokescreen of destruction as troops advanced through narrow streets.
