Reports from the front line describe the situation as "grim," with snipers emboldened and the militants using civilians as human shields. “Our forces are determined to liberate every inch of Mosul,” said Gen Abdelwahab al-Sade, a senior Iraqi military commander overseeing the operation. “We are not here for revenge — we are here to restore security and give Mosul back to its people.” According to local sources, the first day of the assault saw fierce clashes in the predominantly Assyrian and Muslim enclave of al-Safaa, with mortars, snipers and rockets all being deployed. Medics in the area report an influx of the wounded, while the United Nations’ Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has raised the alarm about the potential for a “humanitarian catastrophe” as thousands of civilians remain trapped in the Old City. The UN has called on all parties to ensure the protection of civilians and the preservation of historical sites as the battle unfolds. The Old City is home to treasured Islamic architecture, including the Grand Nuri Mosque — a key IS propaganda site where the group's self-proclaimed caliphate was declared in 2014. UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs Stephen O’Brien warned: “The scale of the human suffering is almost beyond comprehension. We are witnessing a devastating conflict with civilians on the front lines. Every hour that passes brings more risk of death, injury and destruction.”

The UK's leading charities are spending tens of thousands of pounds to buy data lists of private addresses, email details, and phone numbers—specifically to target households with fundraising letters, the BBC has learned. These data lists, often containing sensitive personal information, are sourced from third-party marketing companies and allow charities to identify individuals considered more likely to donate. Campaigners say the practice has moved beyond simply asking for support and now involves highly targeted "begging letters" that exploit personal information to pressure donors. From social details like age and marital status to income data pulled from publicly available council tax records, the lists enable charities to tailor their appeals with alarming precision. Letters can now reference a recipient's property type, household size, or even the existence of elderly relatives living in the same home—information which, under normal circumstances, most people would consider private. One London-based charity, contacted on condition of anonymity, explained the process is standard within the sector, with data lists providing better "conversion rates" for donations. The charity’s fundraising manager said: "If we can identify the households most likely to respond to our appeals, it makes the most sense to focus our efforts there." But the Personal Data Protection Group, which advises on consumer privacy, has raised serious concerns. "There is a clear fine line between targeted outreach and intrusive marketing—and it seems many charities have crossed it," said spokesperson Emily Watson. "These data lists are not just commercial; they include personal information that the public may not expect to be shared." The use of such tactics is permitted under current data protection laws, as long as someone has opted in to receive mail from a charity—something many people unknowingly agree to when signing up for events, subscriptions, or even buying a bottle of water at a museum shop. Privacy groups argue the laws are outdated and need to be revised to reflect the scale of data-sharing now common in fundraising. "Charities should not be allowed to use purchasing lists that contain private details simply because they’re not for-profit," said David Poole, chief executive of the Data Regulation Trust. "The public deserve the right to expect any personal data they share with a charity stays with them." The BBC’s investigation has prompted calls for greater transparency in how charities obtain and use personal data. With the public increasingly wary about how their information is used, the sector faces a growing pressure to act ethically—before public trust in charitable giving is eroded.

Calls are mounting for the government to introduce a tax on sugary drinks to combat rising childhood obesity and improve public health. Health campaigners and medical professionals argue that levying manufacturers of high-sugar beverages could curb consumption, encourage healthier choices, and generate funding for health initiatives. The idea, inspired by similar taxes in Mexico and the UK, has gained traction amid growing concern over the links between sugary drinks and conditions such as type 2 diabetes, tooth decay, and obesity in children. The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH), as well as obesity charities, are among the most vocal supporters of the measure. In a recent statement, a senior RCPCH representative said: “Sugar-laden drinks are the single biggest source of free sugar in children’s diets. Tackling them through regulation is not only a health imperative but a moral one. We cannot continue to let our children bear the cost of an unhealthy status quo.” Advocates of the sugary drinks tax highlight that consumption of soft drinks has remained relatively steady over the past decade, despite growing awareness of their health effects. With childhood obesity rates still climbing, experts believe that financial incentives – or disincentives – will be necessary to effect real change. The proposed tax would see manufacturers charged extra based on the amount of sugar in their products. Drinks with lower sugar content would be encouraged by escaping the levy or paying less. This, supporters argue, would prompt food and drink companies to reformulate their products to make them healthier. Industry groups have expressed concern that the tax could unfairly hit poorer families, who may rely more heavily on cheap sugary fizzy drinks. They also warn of potential job losses and a possible decline in sales, which could threaten the viability of smaller manufacturers. However, public health experts counter that the tax would most likely lead to a modest price increase for consumers, the impact of which could be mitigated by a wider availability of low-sugar alternatives. “This isn’t about punishing families,” one health policy analyst said, “but about re-directing market forces toward better health.” At present, the government says it is reviewing a wide range of interventions to tackle childhood obesity, including restricting marketing of unhealthy foods to children and improving school meal standards. The call for a sugary drinks tax is seen as one of the more straightforward and potentially effective measures under consideration.

Business Secretary Sajid Javid has ruled out nationalisation as a solution for the steelworks in Port Talbot, Wales, amid growing concerns over the plant's future after the recent collapse of Tata Steel’s UK operations. Speaking in a press conference in London, Javid stressed the government’s commitment to supporting the plant through private investment rather than stepping in directly as a last resort. “Nationalisation is not the answer,” he said. “We need a long-term industrial strategy that secures the jobs and the future of steelmaking in Britain.” The Port Talbot plant, which employs around 4,000 workers, has been at the heart of a tense political debate after Tata announced it would be winding down its operations and selling off its European assets. Unions and local MPs have called for urgent government intervention to prevent significant job losses and to keep the site viable. But Javid, who is in charge of industrial strategy and innovation in the UK government, argued that intervention must come from the private sector. “We have a successful steel industry in the UK, and it needs to be competitive on the global stage,” he said. “We will continue to work with the steel sector and other stakeholders to ensure that the impacts of short-term market volatility are mitigated and long-term opportunities are seized.” The Welsh Government and opposition Labour Party have accused the West Midlands-born minister of failing to listen to concerns from Wales, where the steel industry is seen as a key economic pillar. Labour’s Shadow Business Secretary, Ed Miliband, said the government was out of touch with the realities on the ground in Port Talbot. “This plant is not just a business; it is a lifeline for an entire community,” he said. “Sajid Javid’s insistence on sticking to austerity over people is reckless and out of line with the majority of public opinion.” Local MP Nick Smith said he was “disappointed” by the minister’s stance. “The people of Port Talbot need certainty, not rhetoric,” he said. “We must ensure that no one loses their job because of cut-price politics.” The Business Secretary also reiterated the government’s support for the development of a new Jobs and Growth Fund, which aims to provide targeted support to struggling industries. But he stopped short of confirming any direct funding for Port Talbot. “We will consider all options for support, but these must be sustainable and not a crutch for bad business models,” he said.

Salmon Exports from Scotland See Value Surge Despite Decline in Volume   Scotland’s farmed salmon industry saw a notable increase in the value of exports last year, despite a significant drop in the volume of fish sent overseas, according to latest figures released by the Scottish government. The data, which highlights the growing demand for premium Scottish salmon in international markets, has been cautiously welcomed by industry leaders as a sign of resilience amid challenging economic conditions. Exports by value rose by 17% in 2023, reaching a staggering £1.03 billion. China remained the largest export market for Scottish salmon during the year, with sales increasing significantly as appetite for the product grew among Chinese consumers. Other key destinations, including the United States and European markets, also recorded growth in the value of salmon purchases, reflecting the global interest in this high-quality, protein-rich food. However, the industry faced headwinds in terms of volume, with the number of tonnes of salmon exported falling sharply—by more than 12%—compared to the previous year. This is part of a longer-term trend resulting from a combination of factors, including constraints in fish stocks due to restocking periods for breeding and a slowdown in production in some parts of the supply chain. Industry experts say that as salmon takes time to mature and is not immediately available for harvest, such drops in volume are often temporary. Dr. Stuart Burgess, chief executive of Scottish Salmon Producers Organisation, said the growth in export value was heartening but warned that long-term sustainability required addressing volume challenges. “The fact that the value per kilogram has gone up so sharply is a positive indicator of the quality and brand strength of Scottish salmon in international markets,” he said. “But we still need to maintain production levels to meet the demand that is clearly there.” The fall in volume has raised concerns about the impact of production limitations on future supply. Many in the industry are calling for increased investment in aquaculture infrastructure, as well as more efficient farm management, to ensure the sector can scale up without compromising welfare or environmental standards. Environmental groups, however, say growth must not come at the expense of Scotland’s marine ecosystems. The country's salmon farming sector has long been under pressure over issues of water quality, sea lice, and the impact of escaped fish on wild populations. Some advocates for sustainable fishing argue that while exports are profitable, the wider implications go beyond profit margins.

Northern Ireland’s impressive momentum came to a halt as they suffered a 1-0 defeat to Romania in Bucharest, bringing an end to their three-game winning run in the Euro 2016 qualifiers. The result saw Romania take first place in Group F, edging ahead of Michael O’Neill’s side on goal difference. The visitors, who had entered the match on a high after recent victories against Austria and Ukraine, were left frustrated by a damaging defensive lapse in the first half that proved decisive. The only goal of the match came in the 31st minute when Leeds United forward Matej Vydra volleyed home the decisive strike after a poorly cleared corner. Vydra, who made his international debut as a half-time substitute, grabbed his first international goal in what proved a cruel twist for Northern Ireland, whose high press and dangerous counters failed to trouble the Romanian defence. Despite dominating possession early in the game and creating several half-chances, the Northern Irish team struggled to break down a resolute home side. A last-minute chance fell to captain Steven Davis, but his blistering long-range drive curled narrowly wide, leaving O’Neill’s side to reflect on what might have been had Championship-winning defender Jonny Evans not headed Adrian Mutu’s cross straight to Vydra for the opening goal. The draw leaves Northern Ireland with five points from five games, just one point behind Romania – but they face a difficult task in maintaining their bid for a Euro 2016 spot. O’Neill praised the players for their effort in a press conference after the match, acknowledging the difficulty of challenging at the Roazhon Park in Rennes, a venue renowned for its hostility. “The players did everything we asked of them and worked tirelessly,” he said. “We had our opportunities, but when you’re about to make history and chase the gold standard, these are the moments you have to be a little bit more clinical.” The defeat was a stark contrast to the confidence radiating from Northern Ireland’s camp in recent weeks. Their victories over Austria and Ukraine had drawn praise for O’Neill’s management and the squad’s growing cohesion, particularly the development of young stars like Josh Magennis and Corry Evans. However, this latest setback served as a sobering reminder of the challenge posed by one of Europe’s traditional footballing powers. Defending champions Spain remain untroubled at the top of the group, but it is Romania who have emerged as the real contenders for the runner-up spot, with only Belgium’s group ahead of them in terms of competitiveness.

Dorrans Shines as Rangers Start Premiership Season with Comfortable Win   Graham Dorrans was the hero for Rangers as they got their Scottish Premiership campaign off to a winning start with a 3-1 victory over Motherwell at Fir Park. The midfielder netted twice and was instrumental in the visitors' control throughout the match, helping extend the Gers' unbeaten start to the season and sending an early message to their rivals. The Ibrox side, managing just one win from their three pre-season matches, were expected to ease into the new season and Saturday's fixture served as a warm-up for the challenges ahead. But under the guidance of manager Giovanni van Bronckhorst, Rangers were sharp, clinical and composed, reflecting their recent training block and well-documented preparation under the Dutch tactician. The breakthrough came in the 28th minute when Dorrans, who has been linked with a summer move to West Brom, curled a stunning 25-yard strike into the top corner past Motherwell goalkeeper Samir Carruthers. The goal not only lit up the home crowd but also silenced the early nerves among Rangers fans, who will be keenly aware of the challenges this season will bring. Just two minutes later, Dorrans added a second for himself and the evening’s third for Rangers, finishing off a swift counter-attack by slotting the ball into an empty net after a series of quick interchanges down the right. The strike raised the prospect of a dominant display and the players responded with the kind of press and movement that made them one of the most feared sides in Premier League 2 last season. Despite a late response from Motherwell through an own goal from Rangers defender James Tavernier, the visitors maintained their composure and managed the game effectively, fully deserving their win. The result sends an early message of intent from Van Bronckhorst’s side and hints at the potential for another formidable campaign. Speaking after the match, Van Bronckhorst praised the effort, stating: “It’s always difficult coming into a new season with a new system, new mentality. But I was extremely pleased with the performance. We showed what we can do when we stick to our principles and play as a team. Dorrans was outstanding again, a real leader on the field today.” Dorrans, for his part, kept things relatively low key, acknowledging the importance of the victory without getting carried away.

Tesco Mobile trials ‘paid ads’ as telecoms giants compete to cut costs for customers   In a bid to attract budget-conscious consumers and stand out in an increasingly crowded mobile market, Tesco Mobile has launched a novel initiative that allows customers to slash £2 or £3 off their monthly bills in return for watching advertisements on their phones. The service, designed as part of a trial, puts Tesco among the first major UK telecom providers to test the monetisation of customer attention in this way — a move that has sparked both intrigue and concern among users and industry watchers alike. The service, called “Mobile Services Innovations,” is being trialled with a limited number of Tesco Mobile customers and works much like the ad-based subscription models that have taken off across apps and online streaming. When signed up, users receive bursts of short-targeted video or image-based adverts, shown at the user’s convenience, for which they are compensated in the form of a discount on their monthly bill. The duration and frequency of the ads are reportedly in the early stages, with the intention to gather feedback before expanding the scheme. For many customers, the offer is a tempting one. With mobile phone bills rising and competition between providers intensifying, the promise of a £2 credit each month could make Tesco Mobile a more attractive option for those looking to slash expenses. “If I’m already carrying my phone around all day, I may as well watch a few ads and get some money off in return,” said Liam Clarke, a 28-year-old participant in the trial. “I don’t want someone looking at my emails or messages — but a few 30-second videos are a small price to pay for some savings.” However, the trial has raised eyebrows among consumer rights advocates, who warn of the potential for hidden traps. “You have to read the small print carefully,” says Joanne Schulz, founder of the telecoms watchdog organisation PriceCheckUK. “It’s one thing to watch an advert, but are customers being opted-in without their full knowledge? What data is being collected, and who is targeting them? These are all legitimate concerns.” Privacy groups have also raised concerns about the long-term implications of such models. While Tesco insists that user data will not be shared with advertisers and that customers retain the right to opt out at any time, critics are sceptical.

Sri Lanka’s military faces fresh scrutiny as an independent inquiry finds allegations of war crimes credible. The findings, announced by a government-appointed judge, confirm long-standing international concerns about the conduct of the security forces during the final months of the country's 26-year civil war. The conflict, which ended in 2009, pitted the Sri Lankan government against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), commonly known as the Tamil Tigers, a separatist group that fought for an independent Tamil homeland in the north and east of the island. For years, the United Nations and human rights organisations have investigated claims that government forces carried out widespread atrocities, including indiscriminate shelling of civilian areas and the extrajudicial killing of Tamil rebel fighters posing as civilians. Judge Priyantha Jayewickrama’s report, delivered over the weekend, states that the evidence gathered by investigators supports the allegations and calls for further legal action, including the initiation of prosecutions. The British judge, who has been conducting hearings for the past 10 months, said the government must act without delay to hold those responsible to account. “The details provided by witnesses and corroborated by independent evidence are deeply troubling and satisfy the threshold of credible allegations,” said Jayewickrama in a statement. His remarks follow a demand from the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Michelle Bachelet, earlier this month for Sri Lanka to “prioritise peace and accountability” as part of a new peacebuilding strategy. The inquiry has reignited political tensions in Sri Lanka, with critics accusing the government of failing to confront its wartime policies. Former Defence Secretary Gotabaya Rajapaksa, currently a leading political figure and brother of President Maithripala Sirisena, was considered central to the key military operations in the war’s final phase. However, the Sri Lankan president has said he is “confident” that the courts will deliver “due process”. The government has previously rejected allegations of war crimes, maintaining that the military pursued operations with due regard for civilian lives. Nonetheless, the judge’s findings could represent a turning point in the country’s attempt to fully address its bloody past. The Tamil community, who suffered disproportionately during the conflict, welcomed the report as a step towards justice. “For more than a decade, we have lived with the pain of loss, of silence from those in power, and of grief go unacknowledged,” said a spokesperson for the Tamil National Alliance, a major political party representing Sri Lanka’s Tamil minority.

Iran’s transformation into an Islamic republic in 1979 marked one of the most seismic political and ideological shifts of the late 20th century, ending decades of monarchical rule and ushering in an unprecedented era where religious authority would dominate the state. The Iranian Revolution, which saw millions of people take to the streets in protest against the rule of Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, culminated in his overthrow and exile in February 1979. At the heart of this revolution was Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, the exiled Iranian cleric and spiritual leader whose vision of a theocratic state emerged victorious in the political vacuum left by the Shah’s departure. Khomeini returned to Iran in triumph just weeks before the monarch fled the country and immediately began shaping the new political order. In December 1979, a national referendum approved the establishment of the Islamic Republic of Iran, replacing the constitutional monarchy with a system based on the concept of "Velayat-e Fadhael" – or the "Guardianship of the Jurist." Under this framework, religious scholars, particularly the most senior among them, would hold ultimate authority over the state. Khomeini was declared the first Supreme Leader, a position to be filled for life by a council of clerics, and thus became the supreme arbiter of all political and religious affairs in the country. The new system radically restructured Iran’s governance, blending Islamic law (Sharia) with elements of representative democracy. A theocratic council, the Council of Guardians, was empowered to vet all political candidates and parliamentary legislation to ensure conformity with Islamic principles. At the same time, institutions such as the freely elected parliament (Majles) and the president’s office were created – but always under the overarching control of the religious hierarchy. The 1979 revolution not only ended Iran’s Western-backed monarchy and close ties with the United States but also triggered a dramatic realignment of global power dynamics in the Middle East. The Islamic Republic quickly distanced itself from secular Arab nationalism and Western liberalism, asserting Iran as a leader of the Islamic world and champion of resistance against foreign influence. The ensuing Iran-Iraq war (1980-1988) and the hostage crisis at the American embassy in Tehran were early manifestations of the new government's hardline stance. Today, the legacy of the 1979 revolution continues to shape Iran’s domestic and foreign policy. While the country has seen cycles of reform and repression since Khomeini’s death in 1989, the core principle of theocratic governance remains unchallenged.

The towering golden statue of three liberation soldiers—two men and a woman—forms the centrepiece of Heroes' Acre, the national monument to Zimbabwe’s fallen soldiers. The striking 27-metre-high monument, designed by a team of Zimbabwean artists, has become the country’s most revered symbol of independence and sacrifice. Situated on a hilltop north of Harare, Heroes’ Acre was officially opened in 2005 with great ceremony and fanfare, replacing the old National Heroes Acre site that had been a focal point of remembrance since the days of the liberation war. The new monument, whose construction cost an estimated £20 million, was funded mostly by the government and is surrounded by the graves of 21 liberation heroes, including the late Prime Minister Robert Mugabe. The statue’s depiction of a man, a woman, and a soldier, each holding a hand towards the heavens, is intended to represent the unity and resilience of the Zimbabwean people during the country’s bitter struggle for independence from British colonial rule. It also symbolises the multi-generational nature of the freedom struggle, with the male figure representing the guerrilla fighters, the woman embodying the role of the people in supporting the cause, and the soldier signifying the leadership and strength of the movement. The site also features a museum where exhibits, photographs, and personal testimonies recount the苦难 of Zimbabwe’s liberation, and educate younger generations about the country’s past. Each year, on August 11th—Zimbabwe’s Independence Day—thousands of citizens and dignitaries gather at Heroes’ Acre for ceremonies that include speeches, wreath-laying, and military parades. The monument has continued to serve as a powerful reminder of the sacrifices made in the name of freedom, and remains a place where national pride and historical memory converge. For many Zimbabweans, especially veterans and older citizens, Heroes’ Acre is not just a monument but a pilgrimage site, a place to pay respects, reflect on the nation’s journey, and reaffirm their commitment to peace and unity. Yet the site is also controversial, as it is often used by current leaders for political purposes, with past ceremonies featuring grandiose speeches about "Zimbabwe rising" or the 'glory' of the liberation war, amid calls from young activists for reflection rather than hero-worship. Still, the vast gothic entrance, the sweeping lawns, and the golden statue stand as a permanent testament to the cost of freedom and the lives lost in the decades-long struggle to reclaim Zimbabwe.

Mullah Mohammed Omar, the enigmatic leader of Afghanistan’s Taliban regime, remained a shadowy and elusive figure throughout his public life. Before his government was ousted by a U.S.-led coalition in late 2001, he was rarely seen in public, often retreating from the limelight in a manner that reinforced his image as a spiritual and ideological leader more than a political one. Colleagues and followers describe him as deeply religious, with a quiet manner, but also as one who made difficult, often ruthless decisions to enforce the Taliban’s strict interpretation of Islamic law. Despite his role as the supreme leader of an organisation that governed large parts of Afghanistan for five years, even during that period, Mullah Omar rarely gave public speeches or appeared before cameras. During the Taliban’s rule, he was believed to spend much of his time in the southern city of Kandahar, the movement’s spiritual heartland, where he consulted religious scholars and oversaw the governance of a regime often condemned by the international community for its harsh policies and human rights abuses, particularly against women and minorities. After the 9/11 attacks and the subsequent U.S.-led invasion, Mullah Omar vanished from public view, and his whereabouts remained a mystery for years. Contrary to the fates of many of his top aides—some of whom were captured or killed—Mullah Omar seemed to disappear completely. Rumours about his death and fake death certificates were widely reported, but none were confirmed. Despite international efforts and the establishment of a large reward for information leading to his capture, he remained in hiding. In the years following the fall of his government, the Taliban regrouped and launched an insurgency against the Western-led military presence in the region and the Afghan government. Although Mullah Omar did not appear to be directly involved in the day-to-day operations of the movement, the Taliban continued to operate under his name, and he remained a symbolic figurehead. Official reports and statements from the Taliban often mentioned him, but there was little evidence of his actual involvement or ability to control the growing network of groups and militants operating under his banner. His disappearance was the source of speculation and debate for nearly two decades. Some believed he had died in 2015 or 2017, and others claimed he was killed in an air strike. Still, no conclusive source had emerged to confirm the circumstances of his death—until recently.

A Scottish man who says he was a victim of abuse by former Crewe Alexandra coach Barry Bennell has warned that child sexual abuse in football may still be far more widespread than currently acknowledged, describing it as a “huge” problem that has been buried for too long. The survivor, who has spoken on the condition of anonymity, was among dozens of boys abused by Bennell over a number of decades. Bennell, 61, was jailed in 2017 for abusing young players from his position at Crewe Alexandra, a historic moment in the ongoing journey to uncover and address institutionalised abuse within the sport. But the survivor revealed he recently returned to Crewe for a football match and made a powerful personal declaration at the club’s stadium, urging authorities and fans to remember the scale of the issue and to ensure that no one is left behind in the reckoning. “I shouted, ‘There are more of us out there’,” he said in a recent interview with the BBC, his voice shaking slightly as he recounted returning to the pitch he once played on. “We were hides, we were looking for escape—and in the end, we were prey.” His words came just days before the latest instalment of the National Lottery shortlisted dramatisation “Aftershock,” which tells the harrowing story of Bennell and the circle of silence that surrounded his atrocities. The film, already shortlisted for Royal Television Society awards and drawing comparisons to the harrowing “Spotlight” documentary, is expected to bring renewed attention to the issue. The man, who was 15 when the abuse began in the late 1980s, said the scale of the abuse at Crewe and other football institutions was “far greater” than many people understood. “We had to come forward because we couldn’t let this happen to any more kids,” he said. “But there are still people out there who don’t believe us. They don’t want to hear it. They think it’s just the past, but for us, it’s still part of our lives.” His remarks echo calls by other survivors and campaigners for any inquiry into historical abuse in football to look beyond individual abusers and examine the systemic failures that allowed such widespread harm to occur. Sportscotland and the UK’s football regulatory bodies are currently reviewing their safeguarding policies, but many believe the process is too slow. Fred Hatch, a go-to person on abuse issues in football and a former detective inspector, said the line of inquiry must continue to be expanded.

A Cardiff man who had travelled to Syria to fight with a jihadist group has been confirmed as having been killed in an RAF air strike. The man, identified as one of three Cardiff-based individuals believed to have joined extremist factions in the conflict-torn region, was reportedly among those targeted in a recent bombing operation over Syria. UK officials declined to release the man’s name, citing ongoing investigations into the incident and the sensitivity surrounding the identities of UK nationals who have fought abroad. However, local communities in Cardiff have been left reeling by the news, as questions mount over how many more from the city may have been involved in overseas extremist activities. The man was one of a number of British citizens from Wales who made the journey to Syria in the past five years, many inspired by online extremist narratives and radicalised through social media. His death marks a tragic culmination of the growing problem of radicalisation in parts of Cardiff, where charities and community leaders had warned of the risks of extremist groups capitalising on social and economic divides. The RAF’s involvement in the strike comes amid intensifying efforts to disrupt militant networks linked to the so-called Islamic State (IS) and other jihadist groups operating in Syria and Iraq. A defence spokesperson stated: “British special forces and intelligence capabilities work closely to identify and target individuals who pose a threat to the UK and its allies. This operation is a result of careful assessment and national security considerations.” According to sources, the air strike took place in the north-eastern region of Syria, where IS-held territory has been under pressure following large-scale operations by US-backed Kurdish forces, the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), and coalition bombing campaigns. While the details of how the RAF became aware of the individual’s presence in Syria remain unclear, intelligence gathered from multiple agencies is said to have played a crucial role in identifying and eliminating the target. Relatives of the man have reportedly been informed of his death, and they have been offered confidential support from both local and national authorities. A representative from a Cardiff-based community action group said: “This is a sad and difficult time for the family and for our city. We have worked hard to address the root causes of radicalisation, but there is clearly more to be done to prevent such tragedies.”

Two new polls have revealed that President Barack Obama is leaving office with one of the strongest approval ratings ever recorded for a departing U.S. president, highlighting a remarkable resurgence in public support toward the end of his eight-year tenure. A Gallup survey conducted in late December 2016 and a separate Morning Consult poll released in January 2017 both place Obama’s approval rating above 60 per cent, with Gallup reporting it at 63 per cent and Morning Consult at 62 per cent. The figures suggest a stark turnaround from the 51 per cent approval rating recorded at the end of his second term in January 2017, prior to the polls, and contrast sharply with the historically low levels of approval he faced during some of the most contentious periods of his presidency, including his early struggles with the Affordable Care Act rollout in 2013, which saw his approval drop to 44 per cent. Political analysts and commentators have linked this late surge in approval to several factors. First, the stark contrast between Obama’s leadership style and that of President-elect Donald Trump has led to a wave of nostalgia among voters, particularly Democrats and independents, who have praised Obama’s consistent communication and bipartisan efforts in contrast to the polarising rhetoric of the incoming administration. Second, the confirmation of Justice Sonia Sotomayor and then Justice Elena Kagan to the Supreme Court is widely seen as a lasting and defining achievement of his presidency, while the Paris climate agreement and the Iran nuclear deal have also been cited as major foreign policy successes. President Obama, who will leave office on 20 January 2017, has already thanked Americans for their support in a Christmas message, saying he would continue to “work with all my heart and all my soul” as he navigated the final weeks of his presidency. He has also urged unity and calm during the transition to the Trump administration, a message that has been widely praised and shared across media platforms. “The transformation in public sentiment is a testament to the lasting impact of Obama’s presidency,” said Dr. Rachel Newman, a political scientist at Stanford University. “It also underscores how deeply personal presidential approval can be, particularly when a new administration is as unorthodox as the one we are about to witness.” For President Obama, these final approval numbers could also secure his place as one of the most popular presidents in the context of American political history.

A US congresswoman has been shot in the head and six other people have been killed by a gunman in Arizona in what is being described as one of the most shocking political assassinations in American history. The attack took place outside a shopping centre in Tucson, where Rep. Gabrielle Giffords, a 40-year-old Democrat, was scheduled to meet constituents. The congresswoman sustained a gunshot wound to the head and was rushed to hospital with a serious but stable condition, according to medical officials. In a grim turn, six people were pronounced dead at the scene and a dozen more were injured. The attacks sent shockwaves through the United States and came as a frozen silence fell over Arizona, where the tragic shooting left law enforcement and communities struggling to comprehend how such violence could erupt at a routine political event. President Barack Obama left the White House immediately to go to the University Medical Center in Tucson, where Ms Giffords is being treated. He was joined by his wife Michelle and other senior officials. The president said in a statement: “This morning, a violent criminal shattered the peace of a small Arizona community. A woman who came to speak with her congresswoman was murdered with her child at her side.” He added: “For two young girls who were shot and wounded and the congresswoman who still lies in critical condition—it breaks my heart. We will all be praying for her.” Eyewitnesses described a chaotic scene at the parking lot outside the Haymarket Shopping Centre, where Rep Giffords and her staff were meeting with the public. One witness, Pat Razz, said: “He just came in and started shooting. I saw my friend fall. He was hit in the chest—just like that. I thought it was fireworks and it wasn’t until I saw the panic in people’s eyes that I knew something was wrong.” The motivation of the 22-year-old gunman, identified as Jared Lee Loughner, is still under investigation. Authorities have stated he does not appear to be politically affiliated, but he was reportedly carrying materials that promoted anti-government views. A congressional health care bill was among the papers found in Loughner’s bag, though there is no indication he was acting on behalf of any political group. Federal investigators are examining whether the weapons used were legally obtained and what led to the eruption of violence.

Over the years I have spoken to more chancellors and shadow chancellors than most people of my age (that is not a boast, just a sad fact about my preoccupations). I have asked them about growth, about jobs, about deficit reduction and about debt. And I have concluded that the one truth all chancellors agree on—despite different political philosophies, party allegiances and economic doctrines—is that they are not very good at explaining their plans to the average voter. From Gordon Brown to Rishi Sunak, from Alistair Darling to Ed Balls, the subject of economic policy has always seemed to demand a translation not just into clear, accessible language, but into a narrative that can square short-term political imperatives with long-term economic stability. My repeated conversations with chancellors have confirmed what many in the media—from journalists to commentators—already suspect: economics is often discussed in a world of jargon and conditional forecasts far removed from the daily worries of British households. While experts may understand the nuances of fiscal conservatism or expansionary policy, the man in the shopping queue or the woman at the bus stop hears only the headlines. "Austerity" becomes synonymous with cuts, "fiscal discipline" with short-term pain, and "economic growth" with vague, distant promises. The chancellors, despite their egos and their carefully worded soundbites, know they must often cloak radical strategies in comforting language to prevent public backlash. The challenge of governance is not just making the right decisions, but ensuring the public understands why those decisions are necessary. Our chancellors have wrestled with this for decades. Some have tried to demystify the subject—George Osborne, for example, spent considerable energy communicating with schools and universities—but all have faced the same unspoken truth: about half the country does not care about fiscal rules, the other half is too confused to take comfort from them. As another Budget approaches, and the national media turns once again to the green Room 22 for the chancellor’s grand statement, one can only hope that this time clarity will triumph over complexity—and that the voters, at last, feel that they are not waiting at the gates of an exclusive academy, but that they are being spoken to like people with lunches to keep and bills to pay. Amid growing uncertainty over the future of the UK’s relationship with the European Union, BBC’s inbox has seen a surge in reader inquiries from across the country, many expressing concern about how leaving the EU could affect their daily lives, particularly in relation to trade and the national and local economies. These concerns reflect a broader public conversation that has been intensifying in recent months, as political rhetoric surrounding Brexit continues to dominate headlines. In Ulverton, a small town in East Anglia, farmer James Cole writes to ask, “If we are not part of the EU anymore, can we still send our crops and livestock to the continent, or will new borders make it too difficult to export?” Mr Cole is one of many in rural Britain who relies heavily on European markets for the produce that comes from his land. His question highlights the uneasy anxiety among farmers and food producers who fear the disruption of supply chains and potential loss of access to key export markets if the UK is no longer part of the EU’s single market or customs union. Retailer Hattie Morgan, based in Leeds, is another voice being heard. “We bring so much in from Germany, France and Italy for our warehouses here, and we resell a lot back into Europe,” she says. “A trade war or the imposition of tariffs could make our business much less profitable—and threaten our jobs.” Ms Morgan’s words underscore the real – and immediate – stakes for UK businesses and workers that rely on trade with the EU. Economists have long warned that a Brexit could place the UK’s economy at a crossroads, with the potential for both challenges and new opportunities. But for citizens like Mr Cole and Ms Morgan, the impact will likely be felt long before any policy details are worked out. The sense of unease is compounded by the lack of a clear, tangible plan from the government about what a future outside the EU might look like. As responses pour into the BBC from across the UK, one consistent theme is the need for clarity and stability. Readers are not only concerned about the economic implications, but also about what it would mean for jobs, the cost of living, and the general security of their livelihoods. The questions raised by the public are not hypothetical anymore; they are being asked out of deep concern for what the future might hold.

A serial criminal who was brought to the ground by the owner of a shop during a failed axe raid has been jailed for six years. James Holloway, 29, was today sentenced at Manchester Crown Court after being found guilty of a string of violent offences, including attempted robbery, criminal damage and burglary. The incident in question took place in January last year at a convenience store in Longsight, where he tried to threaten the owner with an axe before being tackled and subdued. The shop owner, who has not been named but intervened despite the risk to his own safety, was praised by the court for his “remarkable courage.” Holloway had a previous criminal record stretching back more than a decade, including convictions for assault and armed robberies across Manchester and Salford. During the trial, the court heard how Holloway’s modus operandi typically involved using knives or blunt weapons to intimidate and rob shopkeepers during off-peak hours. On the night of the failed axe raid, he arrived at the store just before closing time and demanded cash at knifepoint. Surveillance footage, which was played in court, showed the accused lunging at the cashier before being pushed back by the shop owner, who then wrestled him to the floor until police arrived. Officers found Holloway lying on the floor, bloodied but conscious, with the axe discarded nearby. “I had no choice – I had to protect my family, my business, myself,” said the victim, who addressed the court after testifying. “This man was capable of anything.” Det Con Natasha Malik, who led the investigation, said in a statement: “This arrest marked a turning point in our work to target persistent offenders in the area. Holloway posed a real and serious threat to the public, and we welcome the jail term he has been handed today.” Holloway was also handed a 12-month curfew and ordered to attend rehabilitation and anger management programmes. His sentence followed a week-long trial where testimonies from witnesses, alongside forensic evidence and CCTV footage, painted a picture of a man intent on inflicting harm for financial gain. The sentencing was welcomed by local community leaders, who said it sends a “clear message” to other would-be offenders. “This is a positive step,” said Councillor Sarah Aldhous. “We need more sentences that reflect the true risk these individuals pose to our communities.” The shop in Longsight remains open, and the owner has since installed additional security measures to deter further attacks.

And so a World Championships that began with metaphorical grey clouds over the sport ended with meteorological dark clouds spilling rain across the Bird’s Nest and beyond, mirroring the turbulent journey that had brought athletics into its most dramatic climax yet. What began as a tournament overshadowed by the spectre of state-sponsored doping, the collapse of the IAAF’s credibility, and the threat of mass athlete withdrawals, has now reached its finish line in a most unlikely of atmospheres — under torrential rain in Beijing’s iconic Olympic stadium, a stadium once synonymous with global unity and sporting transcendence. When the IAAF held its annual council meeting prior to the event, the mood was far from celebratory. The agency had been battered by revelations released by the United States Anti-Doping Agency (Usada), which alleged widespread state-sponsored doping within Russia, leading to the IAAF’s decision to suspend its athletics federation and ban Russian athletes from competing. The ruling, while applauded by anti-doping bodies, cast a shadow of instability over the entire event. Organisers, at the time, insisted they were steadfast, even ordering the Bird's Nest stadium lights to blaze full strength in a symbolic stand for the continuity of the Championship. However, the impacts of the doping scandal were as inescapable as the rain that today washed through the city. The number of Russian athletes in attendance was just 40 — a stark contrast to the nation's usual dominance, particularly in track and long-distance events. Inside the stadium, there were moments of resplendent brilliance. American sprinters stormed to record-breaking victories. Jamaica’s Elaine Thompson, already a double Olympic champion, made headlines with her dominance in the sprints. Yet, each medal ceremony was tempered by the realisation that their victories were being celebrated in a world where the trust in sport had been strained to breaking point. The story of these Championships is not just one of athletic excellence or lack thereof, but of an institution trying to find itself while the future of the sport it governs hangs in the balance. Moments of brilliance were frequently countered by grim reminders — players refusing interviews to avoid further scrutiny; headlines hinting at the next scandal to hit; and the omnipresent reality that while athletes compete for gold, they also navigate a minefield of allegations and political intrigue. As the final day of competition came to a close under Beijing’s darkened skies, one could not help but reflect on the fragile state of athletics.

At first glance, it was a game jam like any other. A gathering of coders, artists and designers crammed into a university lecture theatre, whiteboards littered with scribbled ideas, laptops glowing under the dim lighting, and the hum of teamwork and deadline-driven energy in the air. For 48 hours straight, these developers would battle the clock, turning raw concepts into fully playable games. But this event had an unusual twist — a clandestine challenge had been slipped into the brief from the event organisers. Unbeknownst to some participants, it wasn’t just about making the most visually striking or technically impressive game. Hidden within the task was a test to see whether even in the pressured chaos of a game jam, people would still find time to make something that truly mattered — something with heart, not just code. It was a throwback to the golden era of indie gaming, when game jams gave rise to titles like "Braid" and "Monument Valley," creations born from dorm rooms and early morning coffee-fueled inspiration. Today’s game jams are arguably more competitive, often backed by corporate sponsors and hosted in sleek, purpose-built spaces. But the spirit, many hope, remains the same — one of innovation, experimentation and unbridled creativity. And for a few dozen people in this lecture theatre, the pressure of time and expectations was just one more variable in the mix. As one developer joked, pushing past the caffeine crash: “We’re not here to make the best game. We’re here to make the one we don’t regret.” With those words, the clock struck midnight and the race began. Elsewhere in the room, a team had already formed with a single goal — not to win, but to create something that challenged the idea of what games are for. Their theme, randomly generated by the day's lottery: “Hope.” It had taken them most of a day to unpack the idea, but now they were deep into it, unearthing narratives that reflected the resilience of real-life struggles. As the hours ticked away, the faint hum of concentration swelled. Unbeknownst to them, they were about to change more than just their own perspectives. As the final hour approached, the air grew electric. There were lunches left uneaten, sleep long abandoned, and the glow of computer monitors set against the darkness had become a second dawn. For some, it was the best thing about game jams — losing themselves in the process, even in the face of inevitable technical failures and setbacks.

Two women have been jailed for their role in the tragic death of a seven-year-old girl who died after suffering a fatal brain injury. The aunt and grandmother, described by the court as having been "wicked” in their treatment of the child, were sentenced for a series of acts of cruelty and neglect that contributed to the girl’s death. The case has shocked the local community and raised serious concerns about child protection. The victim, whose identity is protected under court orders, was found unresponsive in her home in Manchester last year. An inquest later revealed that she had sustained a severe head injury, and that the injuries were consistent with the effects of long-term neglect and physical mistreatment. The child had also been left in unsanitary and dangerous conditions for extended periods. During the trial, prosecutors revealed numerous instances of cruelty inflicted by the two women over months. The child had been shown violent scenes of sadistic films involving injuries and bloodshed, was forced to consume cat food, and was often left unkempt and in soiled nappies. Witnesses described the girl as being in a state of constant fear and distress. The aunt, aged 42, was sentenced to 12 years in prison, while the grandmother, aged 58, received seven years. The judge condemned their actions as “despicable” and noted that their crimes were not just physical but deeply psychological in nature. “This child was terrified, and none of the help she desperately needed was provided,” the judge said. Child protection agencies have since been placed under scrutiny for failing to identify the risks and intervene in time. A full investigation is also expected to be launched into the circumstances surrounding the case. Speaking after the sentencing, the girl’s family, who have requested anonymity, said they felt a “mix of grief and relief”. “We are heartbroken by what our daughter went through. She deserved to live in safety and with love. We hope this tragedy will serve as a wake-up call to ensure no other child suffers the same fate.” The case has sparked renewed calls for urgent reform in child welfare systems and more rigorous oversight of vulnerable children in high-risk homes. Charities and campaigners are urging for increased resources for social workers and better training to spot early signs of abuse. As the community mourns the loss of the young girl, the justice system is being held to account for the failures that allowed this tragedy to unfold.

The Tate Modern has unveiled the striking new addition to its South Bank home—a pyramid-like tower that will house vast, cavernous gallery spaces—shortly before its official opening. The £167 million visitor centre, dubbed the Switch House, is the gallery’s most ambitious architectural project since the original conversion of the former Bankside power station in 2000. Designed by the Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron—famed for their work on the Tate Modern itself and the Tate Modern’s sister site, Tate Britain—the extension marks a new chapter in the gallery’s history and cements London's status as a global hub for contemporary art. Standing 72 metres high and united with the existing building via a 12-metre-high bridge, the Switch House adds five floors of gallery space, an expanded public area, and a dramatic, spiralling staircase that offers panoramic views of the capital. A highlight of the new complex is the newly created Turbine Hall, which, at 650 square metres, is now one of the largest art spaces in the world. The hall will serve as a dynamic venue for large-scale, temporary exhibitions—many of which are often challenging or provocative in nature—thereby continuing the Tate’s reputation as a champion of bold and experimental art. Tate Modern’s director, Frances Morris, described the new extension as “a bold, energetic new chapter” for the museum. “This building is all about making the experience of contemporary art more immersive and engaging,” she said at a preview event. The Switch House will house 85 per cent more display space, which will also allow the museum to show a greater proportion of its world-renowned collection alongside international loans and new acquisitions. Its design has been praised as a logical evolution of the original Tate Modern, incorporating many of the same industrial features—such as brickwork and cavernous concrete spaces—while pushing boundaries in architecture and visitor experience alike. The official opening is set for June, but the museum has already begun hosting preview events for the public, education groups, and art enthusiasts. The new tower has been the subject of speculation and admiration since construction began in 2011, with many citing its soaring form as a landmark that will alter the River Thames’ skyline. Local residents and museum critics have been eager to see the transformation in person. Some have expressed concern about the visual impact on the wider Bankside area, while others see it as a bold statement of London’s cultural ambition.

The London Fire Brigade has recruited an additional 60 counsellors to support firefighters struggling with the psychological trauma of the Grenfell Tower fire, the Victoria Derbyshire programme has revealed. The devastating blaze, which engulfed the 24-storey building in Kensington on 14 June, claimed at least 80 lives — the worst residential fire in modern British history. The fire service, which has faced mounting pressure to address the mental health needs of its personnel, is working with the National Health Service and third-sector organisations to provide specialist support. Firefighters involved in the response to the Grenfell Tower disaster have described the harrowing scenes they encountered: families trapped in their homes, children crying in stairwells, and the desperate efforts to reach those burning inside the building. Many reported being unable to access burning flats to save victims due to dangerous conditions, leaving them feeling helpless and traumatised. In the aftermath of the fire, concerns were raised about the mental well-being of the emergency personnel involved. The London Fire Brigade had already in place a system of peer support and in-house counsellors, but the demand has far outstripped available resources. As a result, the brigade has enlisted further external support to assist frontline staff with trauma debriefing and long-term mental health care. “This is a major step to provide the kind of support our firefighters need in the wake of one of the most tragic incidents in our history,” said a spokesperson for the London Fire Brigade. “We want to ensure they feel supported at a time when they need it most.” The BBC’s Victoria Derbyshire programme spoke to several firefighters who described the lingering effects of what they witnessed. One said: “You never forget something like this. It changes you as a person. I still dream about the smoke, the heat, the people I couldn’t save.” The use of such a large number of additional counsellors highlights a growing awareness of the need for mental health support among emergency services. The Grenfell tragedy has also sparked debates about the working conditions and emotional resilience of those who serve on the front lines. As the investigation into the causes of the fire continues, the focus on the wellbeing of those who responded is a critical part of the broader reckoning over safety, accountability and trauma in the wake of a national disaster. More than ever, the call is growing for emergency services to be equipped not just with the physical tools to go into danger, but also with the emotional support to carry on after.

Cummings wins dramatic stage seven of the Tour de France in solo triumph   Britain’s Steve Cummings claimed an inspirational solo victory in stage seven of the Tour de France on Sunday, overcoming more than 100 competitors after a breathtaking final climb to the finish in Chorges. The Dimension Data rider posted a commanding lead of more than a minute on his rivals, bringing immense pride to British cycling as he powered to his first-ever stage win in the prestigious race. The 150-mile (242km) route from Briançon to Chorges presented a brutal final stretch, with the difficult Col de la Chambre climb proving the decisive point of the stage. Many top riders including defending champion Chris Froome and former winner Geraint Thomas found themselves dropped early in the climb, as Cummings, age 34, left the peloton in stunned silence. Cummings, who hails from Esher in Surrey, managed to break clear of the pack nearly 20km from the finish and then maintained his lead all the way to the line. His victory, the first for a British rider in this year's Tour, came after meticulous preparation and a brave decision to go it alone. “I just saw a gap up the road and thought, why not give it a go,” Cummings said after crossing the line. “The climb was tough, but I was feeling good and I just kept pushing. I knew if I could make it to the top first, the rest of the race was in my hands.” Team manager Silvio Martinello praised Cummings’ “brilliant sense of timing and courage”. “He took a huge amount of risk, but he believed in his ability and it paid off in the best possible way. It’s exactly the kind of moment a rider dreams of.” The victory provides a significant boost for Cummings’ team after a frustrating season, and it also serves as a palate cleanser for what promises to be a grueling final two months of the race. General classification leaders such as Froome, Egan Bernal, and Geraint Thomas will now be keen to regain lost time in the mountainous stages to come, particularly the Alpine stages that start next week. The stage win is the 13th of Cummings’ career but the first in the Tour, a long-awaited accolade for a rider known more for his reliability and support of his team leaders. His performance has drawn praise not only from cycling experts but from across the sporting world.

If your fantasy is to create a billion-dollar business, why not create it out of fantasy? That’s exactly what a growing band of entrepreneurs, investors and gamers has been doing, capitalising on the explosive growth of the fantasy and gaming industries. What was once dismissed as a niche market is now being heralded as the new frontier for high-value enterprise, with venture capitalists and tech moguls eyeing opportunities where imagination meets innovation. The UK has become a hotbed for these so-called “fantasy-driven” startups, leveraging the popularity of video games, immersive storytelling, and digital world-building to generate unprecedented returns. From virtual reality (VR) studios crafting digital civilizations to mobile gaming apps raking in millions through microtransactions, the boundaries between real-world commerce and fantasy-inspired economies are blurrying faster than ever before. According to a recent report by the UK Interactive Entertainment Association, the gaming sector contributed over £11.4 billion to the UK economy in 2023 alone, with British firms accounting for more than a quarter of all global in-game spending. This has not gone unnoticed by aspiring business leaders looking for the next big idea. One such example is "Aetheria," a new fantasy-themed metaverse platform launched last year in Manchester. Its founders, former game developers turned tech entrepreneurs, claim to have already attracted three million registered users and over £200 million in investment funding – all based on a world where dragons and wizards walk alongside virtual stock markets and online real estate. Speaking about the model, Aetheria’s co-founder James Vickers explained that the principles of fantasy business are not so different from reality. “People thrive on stories, and they are willing to invest – with their time, money and creativity – into worlds they believe in. If you create something that people are emotionally attached to, you open up endless opportunities for monetisation, from in-game currency to real-world partnerships.” But what sets this sector apart is that it attracts not just gamers, but a new generation of investors. Private equity firms are increasingly looking to the gaming sector as a profitable alternative to traditional industries. The logic is simple: where fantasy thrives, so does the economy. Digital goods alone are expected to surpass the global fashion industry in value within the next decade. However, with great potential comes new challenges. Issues such as data privacy, ethical monetisation and intellectual property rights are growing concerns in the fantasy-based economy.

Burkina Faso Stares Down The Polls Amid Political Uncertainty   By James Kirkpatrick, BBC News, Ouagadougou Burkina Faso faces one of its most significant democratic tests in years as voters across the West African nation head to the polls on 29 November. The general election follows a year of intense political instability under a transitional government that took power after the popular uprising that led to the ousting of former president Blaise Compaoré in October 2014. With a fragile security situation and lingering questions about the role of the military in the political process, the election is widely seen as a crucial step in restoring democratic governance after a period of national upheaval. The elections will see voters choose a new president, lawmakers, and local representatives. The Ibrahim Traoré-led transitional government has called the event a "return to constitutional order" after months of chaotic political leadership and a military coup attempt last September, which was aimed at preventing a civilian elected leader from assuming power. The electoral commission is under immense pressure to ensure the vote is transparent and impartial. Reports of irregularities and delayed registration processes have already raised concerns, particularly in rural regions where development and access to information lag significantly behind the capital, Ouagadougou. Political analyst Dr. Koudou Coulibaly told BBC News: “This election is more than just a vote – it is a test of the nation’s resilience and of public trust in the democratic institutions that were violently shaken in 2014. If the process is fair, it could unify a country that has been deeply fractured in recent years.” The security threat also looms large. The north of the country has seen an increase in attacks by jihadist groups in recent months, most notably the deadly assault on a hotel in Ouagadougou in 2016. While the violence has since abated, fears remain that the day of the vote could be disrupted. Security forces have been put on high alert, with military and civilian personnel deployed at designated polling stations to ensure minimal disruptions. Another source of anxiety is the continued involvement of the military in national politics. The army played a key role in the 2014 uprising but has been accused by critics of abusing its power and interfering in the election process. A source close to the electoral commission stated: “We are hoping the armed forces will act strictly as security agents and respect the civilian line in the election process.”

For the first time since the massive global tax-avoidance scandal known as the Panama Papers broke in 2016, the secret whistleblower who leaked some 11 million documents from the Panamanian law firm Mossack Fonseca has spoken out publicly. The individual, whose identity remains unknown, has now gone on record in an exclusive interview with a Swiss-based journalism collective, offering to provide further evidence to tax authorities in exchange for legal immunity. The whistleblower, who worked within the firm from 2006 to 2015, said they were deeply disturbed by the role Mossack Fonseca played in facilitating schemes that allowed the world’s elite—from dictators and politicians to multinational corporations—to conceal their wealth, evade taxes, and launder money across borders. “I did not do this for money or revenge. I did this because the system is broken,” the source stated. “When the world is crying out for justice, how can you continue to enable injustice, no matter your agreement to keep silent?” The whistleblower revealed that they had built up the files for years, selectively downloading documents before finally sending them anonymously to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) in April 2016. The subsequent report revealed the intricate layers of offshore financial arrangements that helped hide billions in assets—exposing, among others, then Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, Iceland’s former prime minister, and Russian billionaire Andrey Melnichenko. 知情者称，该公司官员并非只是顺从地遵循客户的要求。相反，他们专注于保护自己的声誉和利益，在面对潜在风险时迅速移除相关人员。The whistleblower described how top management routinely removed risky clients and employees from cases where there was a possibility of being exposed. “They called it ‘de-cluttering.’” The leaked documents led to the resignation of Panama’s president Juan Carlos Varela and a major overhaul of the country’s legal and financial oversight systems. In the years since, more than 1,700 individuals have been investigated in various countries, and some were successfully prosecuted. Yet the whistleblower argues that the full consequences of the scandal remain unaddressed. “The problem is not the offshore companies,” they said. “The problem is the people with power who keep the whole system running.” In their interview, the source set out a conditional offer: by helping authorities identify and track down those still evading justice, they could receive protection from prosecution. While legal immunity is not guaranteed, the individual insists they were not involved in any illegal activity and acted alone. “I have nothing to hide. I want to see this out,” they said. The whistleblower’s new revelations—and their offer to assist authorities—open a new chapter in one of the most significant financial scandals in modern history.

Chelsea captain John Terry is set to enter a new chapter of his storied career, with manager Guus Hiddink suggesting that the 32-year-old could remain at Stamford Bridge beyond the summer, despite his current contract expiring this season. Terry, who has served as the club’s consistent figure for over 15 years, has been a vocal leader and key performer on the pitch, and his potential continuation at the heart of the defence has excited Blues fans and experts alike. Terry's presence has remained vital under Hiddink, who took charge of the club in December to stabilise and strengthen the team in his short-term role. Speaking ahead of the upcoming fixtures, Hiddink made it clear that Terry is still a valued asset, both for his performances and the influence he brings to the squad. “John’s a top player and I see no reason why he can’t continue here,” Hiddink said. “He is a great leader and very important for us, and I hope he does stay. It’s for the club and his agent to deal with the details, but I’m very happy to have him.” This news comes as a surprise to many, given Terry had long been expected to retire from professional football or move abroad as he contemplated the end of his playing days. However, recent comments from the player himself have hinted at a desire to “play on,” denying previous media reports that he was considering hanging up his boots. Terry’s career at Chelsea has been defined by loyalty and excellence. He was signed from West Ham in 2004 for £30 million, and has since gone on to become the club’s record appearance holder, a Champions League and six-time Premier League winner, and a key figure in overcoming numerous challenges on the field. Despite recent controversies off the pitch, his on-field dedication has never wavered, and he remains an icon for a generation of Blues fans. As the manager of a team poised for a long-term transformation, Hiddink’s comments may signal the possibility of Terry playing a mentorship role for younger players at the club. His experience could prove invaluable as Chelsea look to transition from a side competing for titles to a squad being rebuilt for future success. While no official negotiations have been announced, the prospect of John Terry donning the Chelsea armband next season once again has sparked interest and intrigue across the English football landscape.

In a bold move that has sent shockwaves through the world of football, David Bernstein — former chairman of the English Football Association — has called for the organisation he once led to unite with European football’s governing body, UEFA, in a dramatic breakaway from FIFA and a boycott of the next World Cup. The proposal, which would see England and potentially other nations withdraw from the tournament if their demands are not met, marks the most high-profile challenge yet to FIFA’s stranglehold on international football. Bernstein, who guided the FA through a period of reform and modernisation in the early 2000s, has become the latest figure to openly criticise the governance of global football, citing corruption, poor decision-making and the increasing politicisation of the game. Speaking in an interview, he suggested that UEFA and the Football Association could lead a new, independent union of nations willing to pursue a vision of football governance that prioritises transparency, fairness, and the interests of fans and clubs, rather than the entrenched powers in Zurich. The World Cup — football’s most prestigious and valuable tournament — remains central to the furor. Bernstein argued that the current FIFA system is unsustainable and that a boycott is necessary to force change. “We can’t keep pretending that as long as we play by the rules — as we’ve been taught to — the system will correct itself,” he said. “It won’t. Real change will only come with a unified act of self-interest from the top nations.” His comments have been met with a mixture of admiration and wariness from within the football world. Former players, managers, and governing body officials have long privately bemoaned the chaotic and opaque nature of FIFA’s operations, from the doping scandals to the misuse of profits and the controversial hosting of tournaments in countries with poor human rights records. But few have dared to take the same public stance as Bernstein — or to suggest such a radical reimagining of the game’s governance. UEFA itself has not publicly responded to the proposal, and there is likely to be trepidation among European leagues and clubs about the potential financial impact of a boycott. The World Cup brings in billions of pounds in media rights, sponsorship deals, and fan engagement, and stepping away from it would be a risky move. However, Bernstein’s call has reignited the debate about the future of international football and raised serious questions about whether the current structure can — or should — survive without reform.

The Public Services Minister Leighton Andrews is set to take a conciliatory approach when he addresses council leaders at their annual conference in Swansea today, as calls for greater collaboration between the Welsh Government and local authorities continue to grow. With a long and often strained history between the two sides, particularly in recent years over funding disputes and administrative powers, Andrews’ tone is expected to signal a potential thaw in relations. The conference, held at Swansea’s Grand Theatre, brings together senior council officers and policy leaders from across Wales, many of whom have argued for a more unified approach to public service delivery in the wake of significant funding shortfalls and workforce challenges. Andrews is widely seen as a relatively moderate voice in the Welsh Government, and his predecessor’s harsh stance on council budgets left many local leaders feeling sidelined and underfunded. The new minister’s message is expected to focus on the need for “shared purpose” and “constructive dialogue” between Cardiff and local authorities, as Wales faces the dual pressures of post-Brexit uncertainty and continuous budget cuts. The minister’s speech will be closely watched for any indication of immediate financial relief or long-term reforms to grant councils more autonomy—something Welsh local government leaders have repeatedly demanded in recent months. Speaking ahead of the event, one council official described the minister’s anticipated tone as “welcome but cautiously optimistic,” adding that while financial concerns will remain the central issue, cooperation is essential to managing shrinking resources. Last year, the Welsh Government announced a revised funding formula for councils in an attempt to address postcode disparities, but many authorities remain dissatisfied with the pace of implementation. With this year’s conference discussions likely to focus on emergency services, social care, and housing, the minister’s willingness to engage is seen as a positive step. Any moves towards a more collaborative approach could help ease tensions and pave the way for a more effective public service landscape in the years to come. Andrews’ ability to balance political pressure with the need for local accountability will be key in delivering the long-term transformation both Cardiff and Wales’ towns and cities so desperately need. His words today are expected to set the tone for a potential new chapter in Welsh devolution. The speeches and debate are scheduled to run through today and tomorrow. As such, expectations are high among both sides for a meaningful outcome.

A café owner in Manchester has sparked a heated debate after claiming she would discipline children having tantrums herself if parents failed to do so. Leanne Patel, who runs The Cozy Bean, said she will no longer tolerate disruptive behaviour from children and is prepared to “firmly speak” to them as a last resort. “Dealing with screaming and thumping tables is affecting the environment for other customers,” Ms Patel said. “I have heard on a number of occasions parents say to their child, ‘do what you like, but don’t upset me’. That’s not acceptable. If the parents are too scared or embarrassed to deal with the situation, I will.” Her comments have divided opinion, with some applauding her stance and calling out what they see as a “hands-off parenting trend,” while others have accused her of overstepping her role as a business owner. On social media, the café’s page has turned into a battleground, with one comment reading: “She’s right, no doubt about that. People are so scared of being bad parents they let kids run wild in public places.” Another customer wrote: “I understand why she would feel that way, but it’s not a café’s job to police children. The parents should be the ones to step in and discipline.” Child psychologists have weighed in on the issue, with some stating that public discipline from staff “could be unsettling for young children.” Dr. Emily Roberts, a consultant in child behaviour, explained: “While staff don’t bear the parent-child relationship, intervention should be done with care and only in extreme cases. Our focus must be on supporting parents and helping them feel confident in managing their child’s behaviour.” Ms Patel, who had her own three children in her 20s, said she understood the challenges of parenting but drew a line about how far respect in public spaces should be extended. She said: “If I see a child clearly being difficult and it’s affecting other customers, I have every right to say something to the child, ‘look, behave yourself’ — no different to what a parent would do at home.” The café is a popular afternoon spot for families, and Ms Patel said she had been getting “increasingly more complaints over the last six months.” Her move comes as part of a wider conversation about balancing the rights of parents with the expectations of businesses and the general public.
