Cuba has taken a small but significant step into the digital age as Etecsa, the state-owned telecommunications agency, has officially granted approval for the installation of the country’s first public wireless hub at a Havana-based cultural centre run by internationally renowned artist Carlos “Kcho” Garaudy. The announcement follows years of cautious progress in expanding internet access in a nation where connectivity remains both limited and closely regulated. The wireless hub will be located at a cultural space known as “El Almacén,” a multidisciplinary arts venue developed by Kcho, where local and international visitors have gathered for exhibitions and performances. The new service will allow internet access not only for the centre’s regular visitors but also for neighboring communities, offering a rare opportunity for Cubans to access the web in public without the cost and constraints of mobile data. Kcho, whose art has addressed themes of surveillance, isolation, and architectural alienation, has long been an outspoken voice for cultural and civic freedoms. His approval, somewhat unexpected given the state’s usual oversight of digital infrastructure, may reflect a broader, if still cautious, shift toward allowing intellectual and artistic spaces to serve as forums for open dialogue. Etecsa did not immediately comment on the scope of the project or how it would be funded. However, officials have indicated that the hub will adhere to national regulations, including time limits and restrictions on certain content. Despite these limitations, many view the move as a symbol of modest yet important progress in the government’s approach to controlling and opening up the internet. For many Cubans, internet access remains a luxury. According to recent figures, less than 50% of the population regularly uses the internet, and mobile data—Cuba’s primary means of connectivity—remains prohibitively expensive for all but the wealthiest citizens. Public Wi-Fi centres, known as “términales de internet,” have been established in recent years, but they lack the scale or accessibility that the new hub in Havana could represent. “The approval of this public wireless hub is not just about technology—it’s about expressing trust,” said María Curbelo, a local arts advocate. “It shows that the government is slowly beginning to see the cultural sector as a partner, not as an adversary.” While the installation is not expected to lead to a flood of unrestricted access, it marks an evolution in how Cubans are learning to navigate the online world.

Six people have lost their lives after a whale-watching boat capsized off the coast of British Columbia, as it struggled to evade a sudden and powerful wave. The incident, which has sparked concern over sea safety, left rescue teams scrambling to retrieve bodies from the water and recover those who survived the ordeal. The tour, which was taking place near the northern tip of Vancouver Island, was one of many popular excursions in the region where visitors come to witness grey whales up close during their annual migration. The vessel, carrying 12 people, was caught in treacherous conditions when a massive wave – likely the result of erratic tides and strong undercurrents – struck the boat with such force that it flipped it onto its side and sent it sinking into the cold Pacific waters. Eyewitness accounts suggest the crew did everything they could to avert disaster. One survivor, who was rescued from the water and is in stable condition, described how the wave approached seemingly out of nowhere. "It came up fast, much faster than we expected," the survivor said. "There wasn’t time to react, and the next thing I knew, the boat was upside down and I was in the sea." Both the Canadian Coast Guard and local volunteers mobilised quickly in a large-scale search and rescue operation. Four individuals were pulled from the water alive, while six – including both crew members and passengers – have so far been confirmed dead. Authorities are still working to locate the remaining two people reported missing. Initial investigations suggest the wave was not caused by unusually rough weather or a storm, but by the confluence of currents and geographical factors in the area. A meteorological report from earlier that day had listed conditions as "moderate" with no predicted danger. However, researchers say abnormal wave patterns – sometimes termed "rogue waves" – can appear without warning in certain coastal regions, particularly where deeper ocean currents meet shallower coastal waters. The tragedy has reignited calls for stricter safety guidelines for whale-watching operators, many of whom have faced criticism in recent years over the rapid expansion of the tourism industry in sensitive marine areas. While such tours are heavily regulated, this incident has prompted questions about whether current safety measures are sufficient, especially in the event of unexpected and extreme conditions. A spokesperson for the affected tour company said a full review of the incident would be conducted, and that additional measures would be taken to ensure the safety of passengers and crew in the future.

In a culture where long working hours and a relentless workload are often celebrated as signs of dedication and ambition, prioritising sleep is seen by many in the corporate world as almost a weakness. For years, boardrooms and offices across the UK have been shaped by the notion that success is measured not just by results but by the number of night shifts worked and early mornings survived. The idea that one must sacrifice sleep to outperform colleagues has become deeply ingrained in the ladder-climbing ethos of the so-called “macho corporate world”. In many industries, pulling all-nighters and surviving on coffee has become part of the unspoken yet powerful code of professionalism. But now, experts are questioning whether these outdated values are doing more harm than good, both to individuals and to the organisations that perpetuate them. Sleep deprivation, studies show, can severely impair cognitive function, reduce decision-making ability, and increase the risk of chronic health issues such as heart disease and depression. And yet, the glorification of sleeplessness remains alarmingly common. "There's a misguided belief that needing rest means lacking ambition," said Dr. Ruth Franklin, a cognitive psychologist at the University of Manchester. "We're beginning to see the consequences of this worldview — impacts that stretch from personal health to productivity and workplace culture." Many young professionals today — often in their prime earning years — have internalised the idea that “sleep is for the weak” as a rite of passage. At firms in London’s financial district and beyond, telling colleagues that you’ve been at work all night or got only a few hours’ sleep is often met with nods of approval and grins. But not everyone is a fan of this macho bragging. A growing number of companies, including Google and Unilever, have started promoting “sleep-friendly policies” and incorporating wellness into their company culture. They’re beginning to embrace the idea that rest is not a shortfall — it's a fundamental part of performance. “I barely slept for three months after starting my first job," said 29-year-old development manager Samuel Greene, who now works for a health-conscious firm in the north-east. "It was normal. People would laugh about how long they’d been up all night or how they were surviving on caffeine. It took me two years to finally ask myself: what are we doing? Was it really helping?”

A prominent student leader charged with sedition in India has been released from prison following a court’s decision to grant him bail — a development that has drawn widespread relief from legal activists, student groups and opposition parties across the country. The individual, Kavin Senapathy, 21, had been incarcerated for over three weeks after being booked under Section 124A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), which criminalises speech that “excites or attempts to excite disaffection against the government established by law.” The bail was granted by a session’s court in Tamil Nadu’s Chennai district late on Monday night, just hours after he was arrested by central anti-terror police. Senapathy is a former president of the Tamil Nadu chapter of the Students' Federation of India (SFI) — a left-wing student group accused by critics of having ties to the Communist Party of India (Maoist). He gained national attention last year for his role in organising a campaign against the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), a controversial law that granted amnesty to undocumented migrants from Muslim-majority countries, but not to those from Pakistan, Afghanistan and Bangladesh. He was arrested following a video that surfaced of him allegedly inciting violence at one of the protests. In a statement read out early Tuesday, his legal team said they would file an appeal if the case is not withdrawn. “Bail is a basic human right, and the law, in its purest form, should not be weaponised to curb dissent,” said his lawyer, Meena Somasundaram. The ruling came as a blow to the Ministry of Home Affairs, which has increasingly used sedition laws to target dissidents, journalists and students in recent years. Criticised as colonial-era tools, sedition charges have been deployed against over 100 people since 2019, according to the People’s Union for Civil Liberties. Many legal experts and human rights advocates condemned the use of the law to suppress peaceful assembly and expression. “This arrest was emblematic of the troubling trend under Section 124A. It sends a chilling message to students and activists that peaceful protest is not tolerated,” said Sudha Aravindan, a senior lawyer and human rights activist. Even within the Indian government, there have been murmurs of concern. Some lawmakers from the opposition Congress party have called for reforms to the sedition law, arguing that it is incompatible with democratic values. Despite his release, Senapathy is not in the clear.

The television industry is mourning the loss of a broadcasting legend as Gareth Gwenlan, the former producer of the beloved British comedy  Only Fools and Horses , has passed away at the age of 79. Gwenlan, best known for reviving the long-running and much-loved series during its final revival in the early 2000s, leaves behind a legacy that has indelibly shaped British comedy. The actor-turned-producer took on the challenge of reviving  Only Fools and Horses  after a 12-year hiatus, a decision initially met with considerable skepticism from fans who feared the spirit of the show would not hold up. However, under Gwenlan’s stewardship, the programme returned to screens in 2003 and received an enthusiastic reception, with numerous episodes still considered among the best in the show’s storied history. Gwenlan, who had previously forged a successful career in acting in the 1960s and 1970s, stepped behind the camera in his later years, using his deep understanding of comedy, character, and the mechanics of the medium to help bring  Only Fools and Horses  roaring back to life. His work in keeping the Trotter family’s antics alive and well for a new generation has been widely praised, and the revival run is often cited as one of the most successful – and ironically touching – returns to air in television history. Born in Merthyr Tydfil in 1944, Gwenlan spent much of his early career on the stage and screen in roles that showcased his sharp wit and natural charm. He was a familiar face in television dramas and comedies, before the call of producing lured him into a new chapter of his career. Throughout his career, he demonstrated a keen ability to respect source material while still pushing the envelope creatively. His vision for the  Only Fools and Horses  revival was to ensure the show remained true to its roots while still feeling fresh, and for many fans, he succeeded. The news of his passing has been met with heartfelt tributes from colleagues and fans alike. Terry Gilliam of Monty Python recently described Gwenlan as a “true force of creativity and a constant behind the scenes,” with many agreeing that his contributions to British comedy have left an enduring mark. As tributes pour in from across the entertainment industry, the focus has rightly turned on the life and legacy of a man whose talents helped define a television classic, and continue to entertain decades after his work first hit our screens.

The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) has confirmed that Test openers Alastair Cook and Haseeb Hameed are available to play all of their county matches before England’s first Test against South Africa in July, easing concerns over scheduling conflicts that have often troubled the national team during the domestic season. The timing marks a significant breakthrough for the ECB, which has long struggled to align international fixtures with county cricket's packed schedule. Cook, England’s most capped player and one of the most experienced openers in the modern era, and Hameed, the 20-year-old Mancunian called up to the Test squad under ICC Emerging Player rules, will now be free to participate fully for their counties — the ECB said no restrictions will be placed on their availability before the four-Test series begins in Durban on 10 July. The move comes as a relief to both players and their respective counties. Hameed, who made his England Test debut earlier this year following an agreement to pool his cricketing responsibilities in his early career, has frequently been caught between playing for England’s Test team and fulfilling his duties for Lancashire. Cook, over the course of his 13-year international career, has similarly expressed frustrations about being unavailable for high-profile county fixtures, particularly during pivotal moments in local domestic contests. Timings of international appointments are often left to national selectors – but recent tensions with the county game and its stakeholders prompted the ECB to review the issue carefully. It was widely understood that the players were awaiting confirmation before committing to county commitments. “We are committed to ensuring that all players have the best environment in which to develop and perform, and this arrangement gives both Alastair and Haseeb continued opportunity to play and be successful at county level,” ECB head of men’s cricket Ashley Giles said in a statement. The confirmation has been welcomed by the professional game’s governing body and county representatives, who have long argued that better coordination between the national and domestic calendars could help sustain interest and competition at every level of the sport. It also generates much-needed clarity for fans and players eager to follow the progress of both men as they adjust to their roles within England’s formidable Test setup. With the 2023 Ashes looming as a key target next summer, the ECB’s message appears clear: retain the best talent, support player development, and foster a sustainable cricketing ecosystem that benefits the entire nation.

Conservative Leader William Hague pledges to freeze key taxes   Former Conservative leader William Hague has presented a bold new pledge designed to restore public confidence and reinforce his party’s reputation as the standard-bearer of fiscal responsibility. Speaking at a policy event in Westminster, Hague announced that “putting finances back on track" had enabled the Conservative Party to propose a new Parliamentary Act that would legally bind the government from increasing income tax, Value Added Tax (VAT) and national insurance contributions. The move is intended to reassure households and businesses that tax levels will remain stable under Conservative rule and to strengthen the party’s appeal ahead of the next general election. Hague, who served as Foreign Secretary under David Cameron and as Conservative leader from 2001 to 2005, framed the proposal as a continuation of his party’s legacy of prioritising economic discipline. “This is not a political stunt—it is a recognition that after years of restraint in managing public finances, the British people must see long-term commitment to stability in taxation,” he said in his address. The legislation, if enacted, would bind future Conservative governments and require a supermajority to override, thereby ensuring enduring protection against tax hikes. The announcement came as the UK economy faces renewed uncertainty amid rising inflation and high public borrowing. Recent forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility have warned that while the government has managed to reduce the national deficit – a key Conservative achievement since 2010 – further fiscal consolidation is needed to prevent future public service funding shortfalls. However, critics argue that such a tax freeze could limit the government’s ability to respond to unforeseen economic shocks or invest in key public services like the National Health Service or education. Labour’s shadow chancellor, John McDonnell, was among the first to respond, questioning whether the freeze would come at the expense of necessary public investment. “The Conservatives are talking the language of stability, but they must be clear: if you are not going to raise taxes, where is the money coming from to pay for our hospitals, schools and flood defences?” he told reporters. For his part, Hague insists the initiative is a positive step forward. “The Conservatives have made difficult decisions when it comes to public finances, and as a result we are now in a strong enough position to give people the long-term security they deserve.”

The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370, which vanished in March 2014 with 239 people on board, has entered what Australia has officially described as a "new phase", following the conclusion of a years-long underwater search that came up empty. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) announced on Monday that the original search area, where the aircraft was believed to have crashed into the Indian Ocean, has been thoroughly scoured but yielded no trace of the Boeing 777. The search, led by the Australian government in coordination with China and Malaysia, has spanned nearly four years and covered 120,000 square kilometres of ocean floor. Satellite data had initially pinpointed the area, and despite the vast and remote nature of the search zone, numerous high-tech sonar surveys and ultra-deep sea drones had been deployed in a bid to locate the aircraft’s wreckage. Despite the official conclusion, officials have confirmed that the search will not cease entirely. Instead, a re-evaluation of data — including the initial satellite connections and flight path calculations — will be undertaken. This could lead to the designation of a new search area. Dr. Tim Gall, a principal aviation investigator at the ATSB, said in a press conference: “We have followed the data as best we can, using the latest available science, but we have come to the conclusion that we have exhausted the most plausible and calculable search areas. It is now time to reassess assumptions and technologies and consider whether new tools or understandings might help us identify where MH370 is located.” The news has been met with a mixture of frustration and hope among the families of the passengers and crew, who have continued to campaign for answers and further investigation. A spokesperson for the Chinese families’ association said in a statement: “We are deeply disappointed that the area we were told was the most likely rest site for the plane has been declared devoid of wreckage. But we also understand the scientific challenges involved. We are determined to continue the search, no matter how long it takes.” China and Malaysia have both announced that they will join Australia in reconsidering the search parameters, with a focus on alternative data sources. There have been numerous theories over the years, including the possibility of a cabin breach en route from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing, a potential diversion route beyond the original search area, or even the notion that the plane may have landed elsewhere.

The Dutch team who have grown the world's first burger in a lab say they hope to have a product on sale in five years. In a scientific breakthrough hailed as a milestone for food technology and environmental sustainability, a consortium of scientists, led by Dr. Mark Post of Maastricht University, unveiled the cultured beef patty — a product made from animal muscle cells — to the public in London earlier this month. The project, which cost around £250,000 and took two years to develop, has captured the imagination of chefs, environmentalists and food technologists around the globe. Speaking at a press conference prior to the event, Dr Post said the miniature burger represents more than just a scientific novelty: “This is a small first step towards an animal-free meat supply,” he said, stressing the urgent need for alternatives to traditional livestock farming. The cultured beef, grown from a single cow in a laboratory environment, was grilled in front of a live audience by chef Richard McGinnis of the Soho Garden restaurant in London. Though the product’s texture and taste were reportedly not perfect — the patty was described as “soft, spongy” and somewhat bland, and lacked the natural juices of a conventional burger — the symbolism of the event is powerful and profound. As global population continues to rise and meat consumption increases, the environmental impact of cattle farming has come under intense scrutiny. According to the United Nations, livestock production is responsible for more greenhouse gases than all forms of transport combined. In response, the Dutch initiative is part of a growing movement to develop sustainable food sources that do not rely on animal slaughter or the extensive use of land and water. The team, which includes virologists, cell biologists and food technologists, is currently working to make the process more cost-effective and scalable. They are experimenting with new methods of cell cultivation and improved tissue structuring to enhance the taste and texture of the meat. Their ultimate goal is to produce a market-ready product that can be bought alongside, or instead of, conventionally farmed meat. Earlier this year, the Dutch government provided a further £1.5 million in funding to support continued development, acknowledging the potential economic and environmental benefits of such a product. Investors and food companies have also shown keen interest, with some speaking of cultured meat as the "next revolution in food technology."

The secret love affair of John Burgoyne, the aristocratic founder of the Fitzwilliam Museum, has finally emerged into the light 200 years after his death, offering a vivid glimpse into a bygone era where passion and propriety often collided with dramatic consequences. Burgoyne, a prominent Cambridge landowner and collector in the 18th century, is best known for his bequest of his remarkable art collection to the University of Cambridge—a legacy now housed in one of the UK’s most celebrated art museums. But records unearthed in recent years have revealed a more romantic, and arguably scandalous, side to the man behind the glass cabinets and marble statues. At the heart of this surprising revelation is a Parisian dancer, Marguerite Lecœur, whose name had been virtually erased from historical records until now. According to newly discovered correspondence and letters exchanged between Burgoyne and Marguerite during his visits to France in the 1780s, the couple shared an intense and enduring affection—one which defied the rigid social expectations of the time. Burgoyne, a man of the English gentry, became captivated by Marguerite, who performed under the stage name "Lecœur de Fleur," as he described in a letter sent from Paris. "She is not only gifted with beauty and rhythm," he wrote, “but possessed of a soul as refined as the finest porcelain and as spirited as Haydn’s best symphonic dance.” Burgoyne and Marguerite exchanged several letters over the course of his visits to the French capital. While the language is often filled with poetic metaphors and romantic idealism, it also exposes the deep connection the two shared. Burgoyne even attempted to invite Marguerite to live in England, writing to a mutual acquaintance: “She is not of our world—but the soul of mine. I would not be denied.” The idea was met with swift and firm resistance from Burgoyne’s family and the prevailing social order of the time. Engrained class consciousness and a growing fascination with British nationalist sentiment made it unthinkable for any aristocrat to publicly acknowledge a relationship with someone from the performance arts—especially a foreign one. Despite the obstacles, the relationship sustained itself in the shadows of 18th-century Europe, with Burgoyne continuing to send gifts of fine fabrics and books to the woman he affectionately referred to as his “fine muse of Paris.” The letters reveal a side to Burgoyne that stands in stark contrast to the austere image of a man known for his vast contributions to art and academia.

The illegal use of Global Positioning System (GPS) jammers in the UK is far more widespread than previously believed, according to a new study that has raised significant concerns about the safety implications of these devices. Published by the UK’s Satellite Applications Catapult, the report sheds light on the growing use of GPS jammers — handheld devices capable of blocking satellite signals — and warns of the potential harm they pose to critical infrastructure and transport systems. The most startling finding is that these devices are not confined to a handful of rogue individuals; instead, they are being used increasingly by a range of transport and haulage companies. GPS jammers are marketed globally as tools to prevent tracking of lorries, cars, and even planes. However, their use is illegal under UK law, and they are strictly prohibited by the Department for Transport. The study’s findings suggest that enforcement of the law has lagged behind the rise in demand for the devices, with haulage operatives using them to circumvent company surveillance. The researchers estimate that up to 10% of lorries across the UK currently use GPS jamming, with the highest prevalence in the east and south-east of England. By blocking GPS signals, drivers and company managers can mask speeding, idling, or even falsify their locations to appear productive when, in fact, they are not on the road. According to the study, the implications extend far beyond the transport industry. GPS is not only used for navigation but is also critical to the operation of the UK’s electricity grid, air traffic control systems, emergency services, and financial networks. Researchers noted that in just one month in 2021, GPS signals across the UK were disrupted by jammers on over 100 separate occasions, some lasting as long as 12 hours. The interference affects not only private vehicles and company fleets but also the reliable functioning of public services that rely on precise satellite data. Ron Givens, research lead at the Satellite Applications Catapult, said the study highlighted a “potentially fatal overreliance on GPS.” He added that while the technology is indispensable, its effectiveness is being undermined by the reckless use of jammers. The Department for Transport has acknowledged the findings and said it is working closely with police and industry bodies to crack down on the illegal sale and use of the devices. A recent crackdown saw road pricing units fitted to thousands of trucks in the Network Rail project go offline due to GPS jamming interference.

Pig heads have been dumped outside a disused ambulance station in London, raising concerns over far-right activity and religious tensions, following claims that the building was being used illegally as a Muslim prayer space. The grotesque display, which appeared overnight and is believed to have occurred in Southall, a historically diverse area of West London, was discovered early on Tuesday morning by a local business owner. Police confirmed that an investigation was underway. The incident has sparked a wave of condemnation from local politicians and community leaders, who have decried the act as a form of hate crime. Cllr Sandip Patel, a borough council member, called the decision to use the site for Muslim worship “deplorable,” adding that regardless of the building’s status, such treatment of fellow citizens is “unacceptable.” Despite Patel’s condemnation, Muslim community leaders have questioned the credibility of the claims against the building, which was said to be turned into a temporary prayer room for worshippers attending a nearby event. Asma Ahmad of the London Muslim Action Group said: “The criminal act of planting pig heads is a despicable tactic to incite unrest and fear. It is not the solution to disputes over spaces, and it is not consistent with the values of London or the rule of law.” The site of the dumped pig heads has a long and contentious history. Once used by West London Ambulance Service, the building – long derelict and abandoned – became the focus of local controversy after a local newspaper published an article alleging that Muslim groups were using it as a makeshift prayer room during a Ramadan event. There has been no official confirmation of an illegal use of the premises, though a spokesperson for the local council said an investigation into the matter is ongoing. The dumping of pig heads is a disturbing but not uncommon act in Britain, often associated with anti-Islamic sentiment. Such incidents date back to the 1970s and 80s, typically linked to far-right or neo-Nazi groups. However, in recent years, similar acts have also been carried out by lone individuals expressing anti-Muslim hostility. The Metropolitan Police has raised the alarm over a rise in anti-religious threats, particularly against Muslim communities. Prime Minister Theresa May has reiterated the government’s commitment to tackling hate crimes and extremism. “This incident is not representative of the values of this country,” she said in a statement.

For decades, the Finnish education system has baffled observers across the globe with its unorthodox yet highly effective approach. How does a country where students spend fewer hours in the classroom, complete less homework, and face minimal standardized testing consistently rank among the world leaders in reading, science, and mathematics? According to data from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), administered by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Finnish 15-year-olds have regularly appeared at the top of the rankings, often outperforming students from countries that place far greater emphasis on grinding academic hours. In recent assessments, Finland, though no longer at the absolute summit, still remains among the top performers—despite a schooling model that seemingly defies conventional wisdom. At the heart of this success is a culture of trust and autonomy. From the earliest stages, Finnish children are treated as individuals, with schools designed to nurture curiosity and a love of learning, rather than to churn out top scorers. Compulsory education in Finland begins at the age of seven, later than the typical age in many Western countries, giving young minds time to develop emotionally and socially before formal learning takes off. The school day is relatively short—typically around six and a half hours—compared to the eight- to nine-hour days in many other developed nations. Class sizes are small, and the emphasis is on high-quality teaching rather than high quantities of curriculum. Teachers in Finland are among the most respected and highest-paid in the world, and all have completed a master’s degree in education. This sets a benchmark for professional status that contributes to an exceptionally low teacher turnover rate. Homework is minimal—often no more than 30 to 90 minutes a week in primary schools—and schools rarely use standardized testing beyond the final year of high school. Instead of drilling for exams, students are assessed through continuous evaluation by their teachers. The focus is not on competition among pupils, but on collaboration and personal growth. “The key to Finland’s system is that it is not about pushing education down young throats, but pulling them into learning by building it into a positive, meaningful part of their lives,” says educator and researcher Arto Saari. “It’s not that Finnish students are inherently smarter, it’s that the system is designed to maximise human potential.” As pressure mounts on education systems worldwide to replicate Finland’s success, the question remains: can other countries adopt these principles—or will they get lost in the push for more hours, more tests, and ever higher scores?

The start of the Easter holiday weekend is set to trigger one of the busiest car journeys on British roads this year, with an estimated 11 million vehicles expected to be on the road from Thursday. Families across the UK are preparing for long-awaited breaks, whether heading to sun-drenched coastal resorts, traditional countryside getaways or popular holiday parks. The beginning of the Easter weekend has long been one of the most traffic-heavy times of the year, with a recent spike in caravan holidays and stays in rural destinations adding to congestion. Transport officials are bracing for a chaotic road journey and have issued warnings to drivers to be prepared for considerably heavier traffic and extended delays. The National Highways Agency said it expects major highways and motorways to experience the worst congestion, particularly between early morning and late evening rush hours. "We urge drivers to plan their journeys carefully and allow extra time," the agency stated. "Slower speeds in areas of heavy congestion can reduce journey times by avoiding unnecessary frustration and refuelling stops in prime flow areas." Brian Bell, Chief Operating Officer at the RAC, echoed these concerns, saying: “We’re expecting a tough period over the next few days with over 11 million people on the move. Our advice is to consider your route as carefully as your destination. For instance, avoid motorways if local country roads can take you where you want to go more directly.” Highways England is managing diversion planning around key incidents, but delays are inevitable. Some of the worst-affected roads are expected to be the M25, M6, M1, M5 and M62 — with the London-Thames Valley route also likely to experience significant congestion. Enforcement agencies are also reminding drivers to be mindful of the rules of the road, as more police patrols are deployed in tandem with Highways England about offenders who place themselves and others at risk. Meanwhile, rail and ferry services are also expected to see a surge in passengers. London's Euston and Waterloo stations, for example, have recommended advance booking for the four busiest days of the Easter period — Friday, Saturday and Monday (6th to 9th April) and again Easter Monday (16th April). As the Easter getaway gets underway, the nation is being asked to stay safe, take lunches to keep fuel costs low and plan for longer travel times than usual. With a mixture of sun and showers forecast, the early days of the holiday are promising pleasant if occasionally unpredictable weather for road and rail journeys alike.

John Robertson could barely believe his own feet as he stood on the touchline at Caledonian Stadium this week, guiding Inverness Caledonian Thistle through pre-season training. For the Ibrox legend, who spent 19 years at Rangers and earned 40 Scotland caps as a player, returning to coaching was never on the agenda. Yet, after more than a decade away from the dugout, the 61-year-old has found himself back in the game, this time as assistant to Tim Sherwood, former Tottenham manager and current boss of the Scottish Premiership side. "I’m still surprised it worked out," Robertson admitted during a Press interview prior to a friendly match. "I was retired, enjoying the fishing, the golf, being around my family. I wasn’t looking for a job, not at all. But Tim came to me, and I suppose, given my background in the game and what Inverness is about, I couldn’t say no." Robertson was part of the famous Anglo-Scottish Cup-winning team at Ibrox in 1994, before retiring from playing in 1998. He worked briefly as technical director for Championship outfit Hibernian, but in recent years had distanced himself from football entirely. "There were times I was like, ‘What am I doing here?’” he said. "I remember the first training session I was in and thinking, ‘This is huge. This is proper football.’ But that’s what gets you back in the game, the buzz, the energy, the players. They’re not full of themselves, they’re not like some of the ones you see on the telly. They’re genuine, hard-working lads and it’s refreshing." Robertson’s return to the game has come at a crucial time for Inverness Caledonian Thistle, who narrowly avoided relegation from the top tier last season. The club is undergoing a transition under Sherwood, who moved quickly to the Highlands after leaving his post as England Under-21 coach. His recruitment of players such as Nicklas Bendtner and Billy Sharp has caused controversy, but his enthusiasm for the job is clear. Joining such a project has meant Robertson is learning once again, with modern coaching methods and management styles differing vastly from the ones he knew at Rangers. "There's so much more data, so much more go-to-it on your own if you don’t get it right," he admitted. "In my day, it was different. You barked orders, your team listened, and that was it.

The number of requests from government bodies for personal information of Twitter users in the UK more than doubled in 2015 compared to the previous year, according to the latest transparency report from the social media giant. The report, published by Twitter, offers a rare glimpse into the scale and nature of such queries, raising questions about privacy concerns and the balance between state surveillance and user rights. According to the document, Twitter received 1,165 valid requests from UK authorities in 2015, a significant jump from 468 in 2014. The firm complied with 37% of these requests, underlining the extent to which personal data can be accessed when warranted. These figures exclude the undisclosed number of national security requests, which are handled separately by Twitter under protocols that are not made public. The most common types of data requested included account records, such as the names, email addresses, and phone numbers of users, and sometimes details of when and where a user logged in. These requests are typically made under criminal investigations, with the majority coming from law enforcement agencies looking to track down drug-related crimes, cybercriminals, or terrorism suspects. Caitlin Vogus, Twitter’s senior director of global public policy, stressed the company’s commitment to user privacy while acknowledging the need to support legitimate investigations. "We will continue to comply with law enforcement requests for information where required by law, while pushing for policies that protect user rights," she said. The UK Transparency Report comes amid growing public scrutiny of digital privacy and the role of tech firms in safeguarding personal data. The revelations are likely to reignite debates surrounding the Investigatory Powers Act, passed by the UK parliament in November 2016, and its provisions for bulk data collection and user surveillance. Civil liberties groups have expressed concern over the increasing frequency of such requests, arguing that they represent a dangerous normalisation of state access to private information. “While we support the fight against serious crime, the sharp rise in requests must be tempered by proper oversight and transparency,” said Shona M. Lindsay, spokesperson for Big Brother Watch. Government spokespersons insisted that the increase in requests reflects improved enforcement activity and a commitment to crack down on online criminality. "These requests are always necessary and proportionate, and Twitter works closely with law enforcement to keep the public safe," a Home Office spokesperson said. As the number of social media users continues to rise, so too does the demand for information access by authorities.

Drinking Overindulgence May Spark Skin Cancer Risk, Scientists Warn   A new study has revealed that excessive alcohol consumption may not only damage the liver or impair judgment, but could also increase the risk of skin cancer by triggering a chain reaction in the body that leaves the skin more vulnerable to DNA damage. The findings, published in the journal  Carcinogenesis , have raised fresh concerns about the long-term health effects of heavy drinking. Scientists from the University of Edinburgh, working in conjunction with researchers at King’s College London, used laboratory models to investigate the effects of alcohol at the cellular level. They discovered that alcohol metabolism can lead to the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) — unstable molecules that can damage DNA, proteins and lipids in human cells. This oxidative stress is a known precursor to numerous diseases, including cancer. In the study, researchers exposed human skin cells to metabolites of alcohol and observed increased levels of DNA damage and cell death. Lead author Dr Emily Hartley, a senior research fellow at the MRC Protein Phosphorylation and Ubiquitylation Unit, explained, “The body is not designed to process large quantities of alcohol efficiently. When it breaks down alcohol into harmful byproducts, the impacts can be felt well beyond the liver and into the skin.” The study also suggests that this process is exacerbated by exposure to ultraviolet light from the sun. Alcohol appears to compromise the body’s ability to repair DNA, making the skin more susceptible to the damaging effects of UV rays. “If you have high levels of alcohol in your system at the same time as being in the sun, the cells are more likely to sustain irreversible DNA mutations — and that is a classic pathway to skin cancer,” Dr Hartley added. Although the study is in its early stages and has not yet been tested in human trials, the findings align with existing evidence that alcohol consumption is linked to several cancers, including oral, breast and bowel cancer. The World Health Organization classified alcohol as a Group 1 carcinogen in 2017, placing it in the same category as tobacco and asbestos. Health experts are now calling for public awareness campaigns focusing on the connection between alcohol and skin cancer. “There is a general misconception that as long as you use sunscreen, you’re protected,” said Dr Sarah Granger from the British Skin Foundation. “But our study suggests that something as simple and everyday as the number of alcoholic drinks you consume on a sunny day could affect your cellular defences in ways we hadn’t previously considered.”

The British and Irish Lions will skip the traditional midweek Test traditionally played against a provincial team and instead rest for the clash with the All Blacks after emphatically defeating the Maori All Blacks 32-10 in Whangarei on Saturday. Head coach Warren Gatland confirmed on Sunday that the side that started the match against the Maori would also be unchanged for the first Test against New Zealand on June 12 in Auckland. The decision came despite the Lions securing a resounding victory with tries from Stuart Hogg, Ali Price and Dan Biggar among others. Gatland was delighted with his side’s performance in the match, which saw them dominate both in attack and defence. “The lads were excellent,” he said. “We trained hard during the week and the players came out with bags of intensity and left nothing in the tank. I’m confident the match will provide us with good game footage and help us make the most of the time remaining before the first Test.” Gatland added that he had been reluctant to make any changes to his side’s approach ahead of the blockbuster, which will see the Lions take on the world champion All Blacks in front of over 80,000 fans at Eden Park. “We’re not going to be messing around with the team that won in Whangarei,” he said. “Everyone feels like we’re in a good place at the moment, and I want to build that momentum into next week.” The Lions have not faced the All Blacks in a Test since 2005, when they lost 16-36 at Eden Park. This summer's tour is seen as a key opportunity for British rugby to close the gap with the All Blacks, and Gatland is hopeful his side can deliver the performance expected by fans and players alike. The confirmation of the unchanged team has been welcomed by the players, who have spoken positively about their form and preparation. “We’re ready and focused,” said captain Alun Wyn Jones. “This is what we’ve been playing for since the squad was announced, and we want to make sure the fans get a great show when it matters most.” With the build-up to the Test now in full swing, supporters and pundits are eager to see whether the Lions can finally end a long run of indifferent results against their fiercest rivals. New Zealand, who come into the match with the number one ranking in the world, are expected to make several changes of their own, led by coach Steve Hansen.

Hillary Clinton’s retreat in the face of the persistent controversy over her use of an off-site email server while US secretary of state is now complete. The former secretary of state and Democratic presidential candidate has abandoned all efforts to defend the use of a personal email account during her tenure in Barack Obama’s administration, acknowledging for the first time that it was an “extremely poor judgment call.” The admission, made in a recent interview with the BBC, marks a significant shift in tone from Mrs. Clinton, who had previously insisted that protecting classified information was her “top priority” and that no sensitive material was compromised. The reversal follows years of mounting pressure from within her own party, congressional investigators, and even some members of the public, who questioned the security and propriety of her handling of government communications. At the heart of the scandal was the revelation in 2015 that Mrs. Clinton had used a private email server housed in her upstate New York home to conduct official State Department business. More than 60,000 emails were later repatriated, some of which were released publicly, revealing not only the casual blending of personal and professional correspondence but also the presence of highly sensitive and classified information. The FBI concluded in October 2016 that while she and her team were careless, there was no malicious intent or intent to evade security protocols. Nonetheless, the controversy loomed large over her presidential campaign and contributed, in part, to Donald Trump’s victory the following November. It also led to a sharp division within the Democratic Party, with some prominent figures calling for legal action, although no criminal charges were ultimately filed. In the aftermath of the election, Mrs. Clinton largely avoided addressing the issue, but now, in the wake of a new biography and a wave of post-election accountability scrutiny, she has finally expressed regret. “I accept full responsibility,” she said in the interview. “Looking back, I see that I should have done more and I should have done things differently.” The admission has been welcomed by some as long overdue, but critics argue that it comes too late and offers no new information. “Damage was done, and the truth is that there is no way to undo the consequences of that decision,” said one senior Democrat who did not want to be named. The new phase of the email scandal also coincides with fresh questions emerging about the source of the server setup, with reports suggesting that her husband, former President Bill Clinton, had direct involvement in its creation.

Young Voices: ‘Life Isn’t Sunshine and Rainbows’ — Teen’s Open Letter Sparks Uplifting Conversation   In a heartfelt and surprisingly moving open letter published online, a 16-year-old girl from Edinburgh has shared a courageous and deeply personal reflection on living with parents who struggled with drug addiction — and how their challenges ultimately taught her “the truth about life.” The letter, written under the pseudonym “Jess,” has gone viral on a popular Scottish parenting forum, with thousands of comments from readers moved to tears, but also inspired by its message of strength and understanding. In it, the teenager explains how growing up in a home affected by addiction was not the ideal life she had once imagined, but how it has shaped the resilient, empathetic person she is now. “I don’t wish for my parents to be perfect,” she writes. “They made bad choices, but they made me understand that life is not sunshine and rainbows — it’s harder and sometimes unfair. I see people expecting everything to go their way, and I’m just grateful that I know the truth.” Jess recounts difficult moments: missed school events, the fear of returning home, and the confusion of not understanding why her parents prioritised drugs over her. But, she adds, their struggles were not only real, but also deeply human. “They didn't hide their pain," she wrote. “They showed me – even though they often mistreated me – that it's okay to break. And that sometimes people don’t know how to fix their own lives, let alone others’.” The teenager, who said in a statement that she no longer lives with her parents but still wants to maintain a relationship with them, also made a point to clarify that the letter was not a “cry for help,” but a celebration of how her parents have, in their own broken way, brought her to where she is today. “I’m standing here now thanks to them — because they showed me what I didn’t want to become,” she concluded. “And they also showed me compassion, not for them, but for others. I have no regrets. I have a strength I never would have believed I could have.” The letter has prompted thousands of responses from parents, former addicts, and young people alike, many of whom said they were “humbled” by the teenager’s maturity and empathy. Some even described it as a rare and powerful reminder that the impact of addiction is far-reaching and often transforms not just the users, but the generations after them.

Catalans Dragons delivered a stunning performance as they surged to the top of the Super League table with a commanding 42-6 victory over the struggling Hull KR at the Broughton Road. The French exponents of rugby league ran in seven tries, displaying a seamless blend of technical precision and physicality that left the Robins reeling and outsiders to the Super 8s with four games remaining in the regular season. The visitors from Perpignan were in imperious form, capitalising on a jittery Hull KR side who had lost their last three matches and now sit in the bottom half of the table. Catalans, who made the switch to Super League from the NRL in 2006, have long been regarded as one of the most unpredictable sides in the league, but on Saturday, they left no room for doubt as they made their intentions clear from the first whistle. Timote Maquin, playing in his first Super League game since moving from Toulouse, opened the scoring with a well-timed break through the middle in the fifth minute. The lead was extended shortly after when James Roby, the heart of the Catalans’ midfield, touched down, before being immediately converted by Remi Casty. Hull KR did their best to respond when Liam Watts crossed the line in the 17th minute, but it was all undone by further tries from Jordan Baptiste and David Mead, who both made the most of huge defensive errors by the hosts. By half-time, the scoreline was 24-6 in favour of the visitors, and the Robins appeared to be on the brink of a disastrous second half. The second period was an unrelenting procession for the Dragons, as they extended their dominance with two more tries through Joe Wakely and Wade Yiadom. Each try was a combination of powerful running and sharp passing, showcasing the clinical efficiency of Ronan Le Claerc’s side. “I told the lads at half-time that we’re not just here for the show, we need to play like we mean it,” said Catalans head coach Le Claerc after the match. “I thought we matched it with them in every department. We’re still early in the season, but this performance gives us a big boost heading into the Super 8s.” Meanwhile, Hull KR boss Willie Poching was left fuming after the defeat. “We were really flat today, no doubt about it. We just didn’t match their pace, their energy, or their ambition.

The French government is set to shut down a UK border post in Calais following Brexit, according to a senior ally of Alain Juppé, the leading candidate in the upcoming French presidential election. This comes as tensions continue over cross-border trade and administration between France and the UK, particularly in the aftermath of the UK’s decision to leave the European Union. Jérôme Chartier, an adviser to Mr Juppé's campaign, told the BBC that the closure was "definitely" in the offing, citing the changing nature of trade patterns and the desire to streamline border infrastructure in the post-Brexit era. While the exact border post in question has not yet been officially identified, it is likely to be one of the outposts associated with the Channel Tunnel or the port of Calais, both of which are major transport hubs for freight destined for the UK. The move would mark a significant shift in the relationship between the two nations in the region, and would leave only a single border inspection station at the main Anglo-French crossing in Calais. This change is not being viewed without controversy, however. Industry representatives have warned that reducing the number of border facilities could lead to delays and disruptions for goods in transit, impacts that could ripple through the supply chains of businesses supplying the UK and beyond. The Calais area is also considered a key economic and logistical nerve centre between France and the UK. According to local trade experts, any reduction in the number of border facilities could exacerbate staff shortages already being felt in the sector. Officials are reportedly already stepping up collaboration with the UK’s Department for Transport to ensure businesses are given time to adapt to the potential closure. While the UK government has not yet made any public response to these reports, Whitehall sources have previously indicated that preparations for post-Brexit border management are about to enter a critical phase. Decisions on customs procedures and the operation of key transport links across the Channel are expected to be finalised in the coming months, as both governments seek to establish clarity for business and hauliers. For now, the prospect of a French border post closure underlines the complex interdependencies between the UK and France, which continue to shape policy decisions on both sides of the Channel even as political realities shift in the wake of Brexit.

The father of a teenager whose life was cut short in the 1989 Hillsborough disaster was told in harrowing detail on Thursday how his hopes and aspirations for his son were dashed by a series of human failures, as a long-running inquiry into the tragedy continued in South Yorkshire. John Smith, 68, who was giving evidence during the inquest, recounted how his son, Michael, a 15-year-old Liverpool fan, had once dreamed of becoming a teacher or a social worker. His ambitions, he said, were as vivid and bright as the red of his beloved club’s shirt. “He was full of life, always helping others, always asking about what I did at work,” Mr Smith said through the glaze of wet eyes. “I had dreams of him growing up, of his first pay cheque, of him marrying, of watching him walk down the aisle. Now I’ll never see any of that.” Michael was one of 96 fans who lost their lives when an overcrowded terrace at Hillsborough football stadium collapsed during the FA Cup semi-final between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest. The inquest, which is determined to uncover the truth behind the disaster, heard how inappropriate crowd control measures and dangerous policing decisions had led to fatal conditions. Mr Smith described how, in the immediate aftermath of the match, the family were informed of their son’s death in a small, bleak room at Royal Liverpool Hospital, and how he had been forced to identify the body of the boy who, just hours earlier, had been happily making his way to the game. “When the officer came out and told us, I collapsed. That moment… it changed everything. I had a life with my son, and it ended abruptly,” he said. The inquest has already heard from several witnesses, including police officers and stadium officials, who admitted the chaotic scenes were the consequence of poor communication, flawed procedures and a lack of failsafe measures that might have saved lives. The Ministry of Justice, which is overseeing the inquest, said the hearing is expected to last at least another six weeks and will consider new evidence that has emerged since the 2012 Hillsborough inquests ruled the disaster was a manslaughter by gross negligence. As Mr Smith gave his testimony, many in the public gallery and jurors wiped away tears. Some among the Liverpool supporters in attendance raised their hands in solidarity, a gesture that has become a hallmark of the campaign for justice that has kept the memory of the disaster very much alive, even 35 years on.

On 25 April 2016, the British retail name BHS went into administration, sending shockwaves through the retail sector and leaving thousands of employees in limbo. For 83 years, British Home Stores had been a staple of UK retail, with its iconic yellow and blue colour scheme and its cheerful "Household Happiness" motto. But behind the friendly façade was a company nearing collapse, its finances in tatters after a disastrous investment by its then-owner, Dominic Chappell. The administration marked not only the end of an era for a beloved high street institution, but also raised deeper questions about the governance and decision-making of private equity in the UK. The story of BHS’s demise is one of misplaced trust, soaring debts, and a system that, critics argue, failed to protect its staff and pensioners. Chappell had acquired BHS for £1 and paid himself a salary of up to £8m a year while running it into the ground. He then secured a £400m loan against the value of the company, despite forecasts that showed the retail group would not survive the year. When the administrator, FRP Advisory, stepped in, it became clear that the pension deficit stood at around £571m and only ten viable stores remained. The chain, once boasting 350 outlets, was now left with no obvious buyer. The collapse triggered a political firestorm, with the Labour Party calling for the activation of the failed banks and companies Bill, which would place the state in control of viable businesses in administrations and ensure jobs are protected. The then-Conservative government rejected the idea, saying it was inappropriate to impose an employer in such circumstances. The debate over the treatment of employee pensions and jobs in corporate insolvency took on renewed urgency. BHS’s employees were suddenly faced with redundancy, the promise of TUPE protection seemingly evaporated as no buyer was willing to accept the financial burden. Meanwhile, the 20,000 workers in the company’s pension scheme found themselves in danger of losing their promised retirement benefits. The Pensions Regulator later issued a fine of £3.7m to Chappell, citing a lack of good faith and gross misconduct in how he funded the business and mismanaged its pension scheme. But the £3.7m fine was seen by many as symbolic and insufficient in the context of the scale of the crisis. The BHS saga stands as a cautionary tale of the perils of private equity's short-term profits over long-term stability.

A prominent Muslim cleric is currently under investigation in connection with the murder of Qandeel Baloch, one of Pakistan’s most high-profile social media influencers and celebrities, according to police. The cleric, whose identity has not yet been officially disclosed, is believed to have played a key role in the events leading to Ms Baloch’s death in July 2016, raising fresh questions about the circumstances of the case that had previously been widely perceived as a domestic dispute. Qandeel Baloch, a social media sensation with a large following on platforms such as Facebook and Instagram, was known for her provocative posts and unapologetic stance on gender rights in a country where conservative values are deeply entrenched. Her public persona often sparked controversy, and she frequently faced criticism and backlash from religious and traditional sectors of society. In July 2016, her estranged brother Waseem Akram was convicted of her murder and sentenced to death in a trial that drew international attention. However, details of his motivations remained unclear, with Ms Baloch’s criminal complaints against him over alleged financial disputes being central to the case. Now, nearly three years after her death, new developments have emerged, challenging the narrative that Akram acted alone. Police sources have said that their renewed investigation into the murder, prompted by fresh evidence, has led them to circle in on a leading religious figure known for his public sermons and staunch opposition to what he and other clerics describe as the “corruption” of Western influence and individualism. The cleric is reported to have interacted with Akram around the time of the murder and allegedly provided justification for the killing based on religious grounds. Investigations suggest that he may have encouraged or supported the act. The possible involvement of a prominent cleric in Ms Baloch’s murder has stirred political and social debate about the influence of religious authority in Pakistani society and the broader challenges of free expression and women’s autonomy. Human rights organisations are calling for a transparent and thorough investigation, warning that any attempt to downplay or whitewash the role of religious figures in such cases could deter victims and activists from speaking out. Provincial police spokesperson Rana Ijaz said yesterday: “Our inquiry has revealed new leads. We are looking into the cleric’s role and whether there was any complicity or incitement related to the crime.” Ms Baloch’s death remains a source of national and international controversy, symbolising the tension between progressive ideals and deep-rooted social conservatism in Pakistan.

A Thai court has issued an arrest warrant for a senior Thai army officer over alleged involvement in human trafficking operations involving Rohingya migrants from Myanmar and Bangladesh, according to court documents released on Monday. The officer, whose identity has not yet been officially disclosed by authorities, is accused of playing a pivotal role in what has become one of the most controversial and sensitive issues in the region: the clandestine trade in Myanmar’s persecuted Rohingya minority. The warrant has been met with a wave of public concern and international condemnation, as human rights organisations have long warned of the systemic exploitation faced by Rohingya refugees. Thailand shares a long coastline and porous borders with southern regions of Myanmar and has frequently been used as a transit point for these forced journeys. Many activists fear that the involvement of Thai military personnel suggests an institutionalised complicity in the trade, despite repeated government assurances that Thailand is not a party to the trafficking. The suspect, a respected figure in the armed forces, is said to have orchestrated the transportation of Rohingya migrants through clandestine sea routes and land corridors. Prosecutors allege that he abused his official position to facilitate these operations, which often see victims subjected to forced labour, sexual exploitation, and brutal crackdowns. The case is being handled in a closed-door special court in Bangkok, a procedural choice that has drawn criticism for lacking transparency. A court spokesperson said the bail hearing would be held in secret due to “national security concerns,” adding further fuel to the controversy surrounding the investigation. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have both expressed dismay at the Thai military’s alleged conduct. In a joint statement, the organisations said, “It is deeply troubling that members of Thailand’s armed forces would be complicit in gross human rights violations. The international community must watch this case closely.” The United Nations has also raised concerns over the trafficking routes in the Andaman Sea and about the treatment of Rohingya refugees in the region. This development is the latest chapter in a troubling saga that has seen successive Thai governments struggle to balance maritime security with refugee policy. Thailand has argued that pushing back boats filled with Rohingya migrants is necessary to prevent further tragedy at sea, while activists accuse the country of turning a blind eye to the suffering of those fleeing persecution. The waiting warrants will now see the army officer either handed over voluntarily to the judiciary or taken into custody by internal security agencies.

A Celebration Like No Other: The Edinburgh Commonwealth Festival Steps Into the Spotlight   Under a sky promising rain but delivering only a string of sparkling moments, the heart of Edinburgh pulsed with music, colour, and an undeniable sense of community as thousands gathered in Princes Street Gardens for the annual Commonwealth Festival. The event, now a much-anticipated highlight of the Scottish calendar, brought together performers, families, and dignitaries in a jubilant expression of national pride and global solidarity—raising more than £250,000 to support children's charities across the Commonwealth. But beyond the numbers, the festival was, as always, a testimony to Scotland’s ability to blend pageantry with humour, tradition with modernity. The night kicked off with a rousing bagpipe rendition by the city’s finest pipers, their melodies piercing the early evening London calling the audience to attention, while tartan-clad crowds swayed to the rhythm, hand collisions and selfies inevitable. The traditional Scottish attire was not just a fashion statement; for many, it was a symbol of heritage and identity, reimagined for the 21st century. Among the performances was one of the most lighthearted—perhaps one of the most iconic—acts to steal the show: the Scotty dogs. These shaggy-haired pups, trotting in little tartan kilts, were the stars of a new skit, and, it must be said, considerably more composed than some of the human performers. The audience’s laughter was punctuated only by the occasional bark, and the dogs’ spontaneous dance to an upbeat rendition of “Skyscraper” brought the house down. Not to outshine them, but a troupe of dancing teacakes—yes, teacakes—daggered their way through a medley of folk tunes, standing on their tiptoes and twirling with a grace that belied their ceramic charm. Whether or not the handle helped their balance, it was the whimsy of the performance that left the crowd in stitches. The human performers were no less daring. Two local schoolboys, fresh from their rugby training, took to the stage in a lip-synced duet that ended with them planting a passionate kiss—much to the delight of a section of the crowd waving rainbow flags and the bewilderment of a couple of senior citizens. The moment became an instant go-to meme on social media, suffused with self-deprecating Scotland humour: “Well, that’s us in a box, then.” Interwoven throughout the evening was a rich historical narrative, cleverly stitched into song and spoken word.

The justice committee wants the government to create a new independent policing funding formula to ensure resources are distributed fairly. The current system, which has not been updated in over a decade, is described as "increasingly outdated" and lacking transparency. In a new report, the Commons committee said the lack of a published spending formula "impedes accountability and scrutiny". Home Secretary Sajid Javid was urged to explain why his department had rejected "formal formal consideration" of a new formula policy before the next spending review, which is expected to be announced in the autumn. Shoreditch and Finsbury Labour MP Caroline Pomeroy, the committee's chair, said the Home Office had failed to act quickly enough. She added: "Without a clear, transparent funding formula that is regularly updated, we risk leaving our communities exposed to bursts in crime and underfunded forces who are already stretched too thin. "The Home Office has to take responsibility for assembling a cross-party and independent panel of experts, including those from the police and devolved areas, in order to establish a formula that is robust, fair, and fit for the challenges of the 21st century." The committee noted that, while crime is at a 40-year low, police forces continue to face high demand and real-terms budget cuts. The current funding model, known as the West Midlands formula, dates back to 1998 and has not been recalibrated to reflect changes in population, the nature of crime, or new technologies. Previously, attempts to create a new model collapsed after objections from the Association of Police and Crime Commissioners. The report also highlighted concerns regarding the Home Secretary's "considerable discretion" over police budgets and the need for a more statutory basis for central funding. A Home Office spokesperson said it understood the importance of a "fair and proportionate policing funding model" but declined to comment further on the report. The department said it had allocated record funding to policing and was continuing to support forces as they handled complex public safety challenges. Luis Enrique accepts blame after Barcelona’s Champions League humiliation by Paris St-Germain   Barcelona manager Luis Enrique has taken full responsibility for his side’s catastrophic 4-0 defeat at Paris Saint-Germain in their Champions League last-16 first-leg clash, acknowledging that the Spanish giants were well below their best — and that the heavy loss leaves them with a mountain to climb in the return match. In an emotional post-match press conference at the Parc des Princes, the Barcelona boss insisted that the result was due to a combination of poor individual performances and collective implosion, rather than any failure by his players to give their all. "I can’t expect fans to be united if I’m not," Enrique said. "This result is my fault. The organisation of our team, the mentality — there were too many gaps. We were exposed, and PSG punished us for it." The Catalan club, the defending La Liga champions and one of the most successful sides in European football history, arrived at this stage of the competition with only four points from six group matches and were viewed by many as underdogs. Yet even the most hardened Barcelona critics were stunned by the scale of the defeat — highlighted by a goalscorer in each of PSG’s first four defenders and a thoroughly deserved margin that has left the draw at 4-0 in Paris. Enrique, known for his typically calm and measured approach, could not hide his disappointment. “I have huge respect for PSG and their manager, Unai Emery, but I am not looking for excuses,” he said. “We should have been at our peak for this competition. That didn’t happen.” The defeat came against a PSG side flattered by plenty of pre-match confidence but arguably still searching for their own consistency after a mid-season coaching change and a host of high-profile signings. Yet they picked the right time to deliver a ruthless performance — a statement of intent that leaves Barcelona with the daunting task of overturning the deficit in the Nou Camp next month. Some within the Barcelona camp have already questioned whether Enrique’s approach was correct. He chose to rest several key players — including Lionel Messi and Luis Suárez — for the game, citing a desire to “look after them for the season ahead.” He also opted for a 4-4-2 formation, an unusual choice for a team that prides itself on tiki-taka fluidity.

Ryan Day believes a strong showing at the World Snooker Championship could prove to be a decisive turning point in his career after earning a return to the world’s top 16 for the first time since 2015. The 38-year-old, who claimed the title in Sheffield in 2001, has enjoyed a resurgence in form over the past 12 months and is now set for his return to the most prestigious stage in snooker. Speaking before the Crucible event, Day said a deep run in the tournament would offer more than just personal validation. "A good run in the World Championship would be a big plus," he told BBC Sport. "It’s not just about winning — it’s about getting back up there and proving that what I’ve been doing on the tour over the last couple of years has been real." Day missed the top 16 for the past four years, which ruled him out of the World Championship. His return, secured by finishing 15th in the rankings in 2023, is a major boost, given the Crucible’s unique status in the sport. The Northern Irishman has long maintained a passionate fan following, known for his smooth style and clutch abilities in pressure moments. Day qualified for the World Championship by defeating Ryan Meikle 10–7 in the final round of qualifiers at the York Dome last week. He will face Mitchell Mann in the first round — the defending champion Judd Trump did not contest the draw for the tournament. Last year, Day reached the semi-finals of the Masters, signalling improvements in his game. He has also enjoyed a steady run of good results on the World Snooker Tour, including a victory over three-time world champion John Higgins in the China Open. "Consistency has been key," Day explained. "I’m playing better than I have in a long time — not only in the big events but across the season. It’s helped me regain the level I know I’m capable of." His return to the top 16 is seen as a testament to a mentality shift after a difficult stretch in recent years. Day has spoken about restricting his schedule to focus on the key events and managing his energy more effectively. World Snooker chairman Barry Hearn has also been keen to retain the best players at the top of the sport. Day’s inclusion at the Crucible goads a rival snooker tour — the rival World Grand Prix event, run in separate quarters, will see only the top 16 players compete due to UK government restrictions at the time.

In a rapidly evolving media landscape where traditional news outlets face increasing competition from digital platforms, one question has sparked intense debate among journalists, scholars, and influencers alike: what is the most important source of news, and by extension, the most powerful media organisation in the world today? The answer may not lie in the well-established pillars of journalism — The New York Times, The Guardian, or BBC — but rather within the digital ecosystem that shapes public discourse on a daily basis. Platforms such as Google and Facebook have become the de facto gatekeepers of news consumption, pulling in billions of users each month and determining which content rises to the top through complex algorithms. Recent data shows that more people now discover news via social media and search engines than through the websites of traditional news organisations. If power is measured by influence, reach, and the ability to shape what the public sees, hears, and believes, then these tech giants arguably hold the world’s most powerful media platform. They do not produce the news themselves, but they control the distribution channels. A story can be buried or promoted, amplified or suppressed, often without editorial oversight, based on the unseen rules of an algorithm. This shift has raised significant concerns about the consequences for democracy, transparency, and the free flow of information. Unlike legacy news organisations, which generally adhere to professional journalistic standards and are often held accountable by editors and ombudsmen, platforms like Facebook and Google are not traditionally bound by such constraints. Instead, they are governed by corporate interests and driven by engagement metrics — likes, shares, and clicks — which can prioritise sensationalism over substance. “In many ways, we are in an age where the algorithm is the editor,” said Professor Mary-Anne Bobbett, a leading media and communications scholar at RMIT University in Australia. “The power to shape public opinion has shifted from journalists to engineers — people who are not bound by the ethical frameworks that underpin journalistic standards.” What becomes evident is that the new era of media is less about who produces the news and more about who controls the platforms on which news is delivered. As traditional media organisations grapple with declining ad revenues and the dominance of digital giants, the question remains: can journalism survive unless it reclaims control of its own distribution? While the debate continues, one thing is increasingly clear — the most influential media organisation today is not the one telling the story, but the one deciding who gets to be heard.

Glen Campbell — the golden-voiced country music icon whose smooth melodies and grinning charm made him a household name — passed away in 2017, leaving behind a legacy that would shape the genre for decades. Now, as tributes pour in to mark the passing of one of the most successful country singers of his generation, his influence is being reaffirmed once more. With a career spanning more than five decades, Campbell not only entertained millions but also redefined the boundaries of country music, helping to bring it into the mainstream and winning over audiences far beyond the American heartland. Born in 1936 in the small town of Arkansas, Campbell’s journey to stardom was as unlikely as it was extraordinary. After drifting through a variety of jobs and working as a session musician in Los Angeles, he bursts onto the national scene in the early 1960s with a string of smash hits. His most iconic,  Rhinestone Cowboy , released in 1975, became not just a chart-topper but an anthem of American pop culture, capturing the spirit of the nation in the heartland. With more than 100 top 40 singles, 22 No. 1 country hits, and a long list of awards — including Grammy, CMA, and ACM awards — Campbell’s credentials are among the most impressive in the genre’s history. His signature, warm, and smooth voice, often accompanied by his tight band The Allman Brothers (now regarded as one of the best backings in country music history), gave him a distinct sound that resonated with listeners young and old. But it was his versatility that truly set him apart. From heartfelt ballads to rock-tinged hillbilly boogie, Campbell displayed a talent for interpreting a wide range of material.
