His Grammy-winning album  Western Stars  (2018), though posthumously released, showcases that same adaptability and poignant storytelling. At a time when the genre was beginning to pigeonhole itself into rigid categories, Campbell refused to be boxed in, earning him the respect of fans and fellow musicians alike. Off the stage, his personal life was equally compelling. Married to singer and actress Bobbie Bresee, and later to the actress Julianne Hough, Campbell was often seen as a dapper and approachable figure — far removed from the sometimes brutish image of early rockabilly and classic country stars. Throughout his final years, as he openly battled Alzheimer’s disease, he continued to perform until his condition made it impossible, inspiring countless fans with his grace and dignity.

Two cyclists were taken to hospital after suffering injuries in separate crashes during the RideLondon-Surrey 100, an amateur sporting event that attracts thousands of participants from across the UK and beyond. The incidents, reported on Tuesday, have raised concerns among cyclists and event organisers about the safety of what is among the capital’s biggest mass-participation races. The first accident occurred near the start point in central London, when a 36-year-old man from Kent fell from his bike just before the peloton got underway. Witnesses said he was struck by a horse ambulance as he attempted to regain control. Emergency services attended immediately and he was taken to St Mary’s Hospital in Paddington with suspected leg fractures and minor head injuries. The second crash happened near Epsom in Surrey, where a 43-year-old woman from Edinburgh veered off the route, colliding with the railings near the Epsom Deep tunnel. She was treated at the scene before being airlifted to the Royal Surrey County Hospital with a likely wrist injury and bruising across her arms. She is in a stable condition and expected to be discharged in the coming days. Despite these incidents, organisers of the event—produced by British Cycling and powered by Santander—said that safety remains a top priority for all participating athletes. Around 14,300 cyclists took part in the 100-mile cycle ride this year, with hundreds of marshals and medical personnel stationed along the course. A spokesperson for British Cycling said: “We are aware of two separate incidents during today’s RideLondon-Surrey 100. Our medical teams provided immediate assistance, and both individuals were transferred to appropriate hospital care. We will be conducting a full review of these incidents as part of our ongoing commitment to rider safety.” The event, now in its third decade, has seen the number of participants grow steadily each year. Many amateur cyclists travel from across the UK to take part in the iconic ride, which combines both urban and rural roads. While the route has been adjusted over the years to improve safety, the strain of such a large event continues to test the city’s infrastructure. Some riders have voiced concerns about the density of the event, as well as the safety of shared roads with regular traffic. “It’s inevitable that with so many people taking part, there will be a risk of accident,” said one competitor from Liverpool.

The New Zealand government is preparing to embark on an ambitious mission to save one of its most iconic native species — the kiwi — and according to the newly released plan, the results could be nothing short of remarkable. The goal: to increase the wild population of kiwi birds to over 100,000 individuals within the next 15 years, reversing decades of decline caused by habitat loss and predation. The government’s strategy, titled “Kiwi Comeback,” outlines a multi-pronged approach combining habitat restoration, predator control, community engagement, and scientific innovation to give the flightless bird a fighting chance. Currently, estimates suggest only around 68,000 kiwi remain in the wild — a stark decline from historical levels and considered well below the population needed for long-term survival. Kiwi birds, known for their distinctive nocturnal habits, long beaks and egg-laying prowess, are not only a national symbol but also integral to New Zealand’s natural heritage. However, since European settlement, their numbers have been profoundly affected by the introduction of predators such as stoats, rats and feral cats, which directly prey on kiwi eggs and chicks. Environment Minister Nanaia Mahuta said the new plan represented “a renewed commitment to the survival and success of one of our treasured taonga species.” She added that the government was working closely with local iwi (Māori tribes), conservation groups and landowners to ensure the initiative reflected the values of all New Zealanders. Central to the plan is the rollout of more intensive predator control across suitable habitats. This includes accelerating the use of self-resetting traps and advanced detection systems to identify and manage invasive species. Also at the heart of the strategy is increasing habitat connectivity between safe kiwi populations, allowing for genetic diversity and resilience. Innovative breeding programmes are also to play a major role. The government is expected to expand its support for “kiwi hospitals” and national translocations, sending chicks to predator-free islands where they can mature without the threat of death before breeding. One of the most surprising elements of the initiative is a proposed uplift in public participation. The plan encourages families, schools and local communities to get involved in kiwi conservation through citizen science, habitat improvement and even adoption of a local kiwi population. The release of the plan follows a recent rise in kiwi mortality following a series of intense weather events that caused flooding in key kiwi habitats.

A senior Metropolitan Police officer involved in a high-profile operation during which a man was shot dead is to retire from the force, despite currently being under investigation in relation to the incident, it has emerged. The officer, whose identity has not yet been disclosed, is due to leave service in the coming weeks after more than three decades with the Met. The revelation has sparked concern among MPs and advocacy groups, who questioned the decision to allow the officer to retire while an internal inquiry is still ongoing. The death of the 29-year-old man, who was shot in the early hours of last Tuesday, quickly became a flashpoint in an ongoing debate about police use of force and accountability. Witnesses reported that shots were fired during a police chase and subsequent confrontation near a central London estate. It has since been confirmed that the officer who shot the man is not the one set to retire, but the senior figure in command of the operation has now been granted an exit package by the Met’s Personnel Directorate. A source close to the investigation said that while the officer in question “is not currently the subject of any formal charges or suspension,” the inquiry into the conduct of the operation was still in its early stages, and the presence of a vested interest in the outcome had been noted as a concern. The Met initially issued a statement confirming the launch of an investigation, saying: “The Met takes all such cases very seriously and is treating this as a critical incident.” However, the news that the officer is to retire raises questions about whether their potential future statements will be treated as independent from the current inquiry. Fiona Austin, chair of the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), a body responsible for scrutinising the Met’s investigations into serious cases, expressed concern over the decision. “It is vital that any officer involved, particularly in a senior capacity, is not permitted to influence the investigative process in any way, whether intentionally or otherwise,” she said. “Retiring an individual while an inquiry is still live does not eliminate the potential for conflict, and transparency must be the guiding principle.” A spokesperson for the Metropolitan Police defended the decision to allow the officer to retire, saying it was a matter of long-standing personal planning and that “arrangements such as this are handled in the strictest confidence,” with no suggestion of interference with the ongoing investigation.

The inclusion of tennis in the Olympic Games has long been a subject of debate, with critics questioning the appropriateness of a commercial and high-earning sport being part of the world’s most prestigious multi-sport event. Yet, as the latest Olympic cycle begins with the world’s top tennis stars once again gracing the world stage, one fact stands out: there is no shortage of determination among the game’s elite to compete for an Olympic medal — a distinction that sits proudly alongside their Grand Slam successes. Tennis, unlike many Olympic sports, is governed not by the International Olympic Committee (IOC), but by the International Tennis Federation (ITF), under the commercial jurisdiction of the ATP and WTA tours. Top players, whose salaries and sponsorship earnings are typically far in excess of those of their Olympic peers, are still keen to defend their national honours. This highlights the unique emotional value of the Olympic Games: in the world of tennis, an Olympic gold medal often means more than it can be measured in terms of money. This year’s Olympics in Paris have already confirmed the participation of Roger Federer, who showed no signs of hesitation in relocating his training and taking time away from his private commitments for the cause. Similarly, Emma Raducanu, as a young British talent only in her early twenties, has spoken passionately about how the Olympics have always been a dream pursuit. “There’s a very different feeling to playing for your nation, it really means something,” she said. Historically, tennis has delivered some unforgettable Olympic moments. In Beijing 2008, Serena Williams hoisted the gold in the women’s singles, while in London 2012, Andy Murray became the first British male to win gold in the singles and double tennis title. These victories were not only athletic triumphs but also about showcasing national pride in a different way. Despite the concerns over the “commercialisation” of what should be a sports-for-all event, the athletes seem to feel unreservedly about their involvement. For them, the Olympics represent the pinnacle of sport at its most basic — players from around the world meeting on a level playing field to represent something larger than themselves. The ongoing question, however, is whether such a sport can continue to coexist within the spirit of the Olympics without the Games becoming increasingly dominated by high-profile, wealthier athletes. But for now, and for the foreseeable future, as long as players like Federer, Medvedev, Swiatek and Osaka line up in Olympic garb, the debate, while ever present, will remain just that — a debate.

The all-female Los Angeles band Haim took an unexpected four years to produce a follow-up to their critically acclaimed and commercially successful debut album,  Days Are Gone —and it wasn’t because they had lost their creative spark. Instead, it was because they were preoccupied… with dinosaurs. Alana, Danielle, and Este Haim, the three sisters who make up the band, recently opened up about the lengthy delay in their second album’s release. A love for prehistoric creatures that sparked a social media phenomenon became a major distraction during their time in the studio. During the height of the pandemic, the sisters started sharing childish doodles and photos of themselves in dinosaur costumes on their platforms, quickly becoming a quirky, endearing sideshow to their musical career. The viral Mynt Dinosaurs—a fictional dinosaur-themed venture co-created by the band—became a platform for D.I.Y. and hand-crafted merchandise, including custom puzzles, stickers, and eventually their own vinyl breakfast, all sold through their online store. What began as a playful diversion turned into a full-blown creative outlet, indulging both their nostalgia and the memories of growing up in Southern California with a fascination for all things prehistoric. In an interview with NME, the trio revealed how the project became more than just a way to pass the time. "It was healing," explained Alana Haim. "After  Days Are Gone , we didn’t want to just follow-up with something that felt forced or like a box-ticking exercise. Dinosaurs gave us a way to reset our minds, to create in a way that felt completely free and separate from everything else." The time away from the studio, they argued, ultimately allowed them to return with a newfound clarity and creativity. Their second album  Women in Music Pt. III , released late last year, was the result of the sisters taking their time to explore vulnerable and deeply personal themes, often inspired by their own reflections and the chaotic backdrop of the pandemic. "We’re not just a ‘girl band,’” Elle Enge, the band’s co-producer and collaborator on the album, told the BBC. “What they did with the dinosaurs was incredibly strategic. It allowed them to clear their heads and reconnect to why they started making music in the first place.” Now with  Women in Music Pt. III  firmly under their belt, Haim has returned the focus to what they do best: making emotive, genre-defying music.

Boris Johnson has ramped up his vocal opposition to the European Union, raising fresh concerns about the future of the UK’s constitutional and legal independence. Speaking at a recent political event, the former foreign secretary warned that British sovereignty is under threat from what he described as a “slow and invisible process of legal colonisation,” in which EU regulations and influence extend into almost every aspect of public policy. Johnson, a longstanding advocate for Brexit and self-styled champion of British liberty, used his remarks to underscore the perceived danger of continued EU membership. “Every week, as it were, we give inch by inch of our national sovereignty to an unelected bureaucracy in Brussels,” he said. “It is not just our trade laws, our border policies, or our environmental regulations that have been taken over — it is virtually every corner of our public life.” The comments come amid growing discussion about the future of the UK and the political forces shaping its direction. As speculation mounts about a potential return to frontline politics, Johnson remains a prominent figure in the pro-Brexit camp and a leading voice in the Conservative Party. He stressed that many of the most critical elements of British governance have been steadily overstepped by EU institutions, from healthcare and education to transport and consumer rights. “I am not saying the EU is entirely malevolent,” he added. “But it is undeniably growing in power — and at the cost of our own nation.” The remarks were met with approval among some Conservative members and activists, who have long backed Johnson as their preferred successor to Theresa May and Liam Fox. However, they may also reignite concerns in business and diplomatic circles over his rhetoric, which is often characterised by a mix of flippant delivery and hardline positions. The former mayor of London has previously spoken about the need for the UK to reclaim its independence and to take control of “our laws, our borders, and our future.” With the EU often at the heart of political discourse, Johnson’s latest warning reflects a broader trend of nationalism, anti-establishment sentiment and a call for repatriation of powers — all themes expected to shape the political landscape in the months ahead. As debates continue over how to balance the benefits of international collaboration with the desire for national autonomy, Johnson’s speech has reignited familiar questions about the role of the UK in the global order and the pace and depth of change necessary to truly reassert sovereignty.

Junior doctors marched through central London on Saturday in a show of defiance against proposed changes to their contracts in England, marking one of the largest demonstrations of the year from within the NHS. The protest, which saw thousands of medics, students and support staff descending on Trafalgar Square and the Houses of Parliament, was the biggest yet in a growing campaign that has drawn widespread support from both the public and within the medical profession. The government plans to replace the existing contract for junior doctors—those in training and below consultant level—with a new four-year deal that includes reduced pay and altered shift patterns, particularly for unsocial working hours. The British Medical Association (BMA), which represents the doctors, has characterised the plan as short-sighted, dangerous and damaging to patient care. Health Secretary Jeremy Hunt controversially announced his support for the changes in May, stating they would provide safety, clarity and fairness for junior doctors. However, critics argue that the plan disproportionately affects those working weekend and night shifts—typically more challenging and high-pressure roles—and undermines the hard-earned, risk-based structure currently in place, which sees junior doctors rewarded for taking on arduous hours. At the heart of the protest are concerns that the changes would deter young people from entering the profession, further exacerbating the UK's ongoing healthcare staffing crisis. The country is already facing a deficit of general practitioners and NHS staffing levels at a historically low point, with experts warning that such cuts to incentives and support could drive a new wave of recruitment and retention problems. The BMA announced its intention to ballot members for strike action in the coming weeks, signalling the possibility of widespread industrial action. While past walkouts have been rare in the medical profession due to the fear of patient safety repercussions, the increasing frustration and dissatisfaction among junior doctors suggest that the threat is not taken lightly. Protesters waved banners reading “Not broken, fix the system” and “Protect patient care.” Many wore their white coats as a symbol of their commitment to upholding both their professional integrity and the quality of healthcare delivery. Some doctors held signs thanking patients for their support, while others shared personal stories of exhausting shifts, dedicated care, and the strain of long waiting times on accident and emergency services. In response to the protests, a spokesman for the Department of Health reiterated the government's position: “These reforms are not designed to punish, but to support and protect our junior doctors by giving them fairer pay for their work and more predictable hours

Jordan Seiler loathes outdoor advertising. The 42-year-old software developer from Sheffield has spent the last six years on a uniquely British crusade: shepherding the removal of billboards, digital screens, and branded highways across the UK. Driven by a deep affection for the countryside and a growing concern over mental well-being, Seiler has single-handedly challenged the omnipresence of commercial messages that flash at unsuspecting drivers on motorways and blight the quiet villages of England's rolling hills. Her campaign, “Uncluttered Britain,” began in 2017 as a modest Facebook group, but it has since grown into a nationwide movement embraced by environmentalists, landscape charities, and even MPs. The group now boasts over 150,000 supporters, many who share Seiler’s belief that the constant exposure to advertising creates what she terms a “toxic visual environment.” Seiler argues that the UK’s approach to outdoor advertising is outdated and harmful. “We’re one of the most visually saturated countries in Europe,” she says. “Think of the motorways. There isn't a second of your drive where you aren’t being sold something. That’s not advertising — that’s assault.” Her research, backed by several studies from the University of London, suggests prolonged exposure to billboards increases stress and anxiety, particularly among young people. “Children are especially vulnerable to the subliminal messaging that comes with these huge, flashing screens,” she explains. Seiler has achieved some high-profile successes. Last year, after public outcry, the government reversed a controversial plan to install new digital billboards on the M5 and A1 trunk roads. More recently, she was instrumental in a legal challenge that helped prevent an energy company from erecting giant turbine-themed ads in the Lake District. “It was a victory not just for the landscape, but for common sense,” she said. But not everyone is on board. Outdoor advertising giants have dismissed her as a “sentimental Luddite,” while some local councils argue billboards are a necessary revenue stream. Still, the pressure is mounting. Campaigns like Seiler’s are beginning to shift public discourse, with growing calls to regulate and ultimately reduce the number of out-of-home ads. For Seiler, the message is clear: the UK should not be sold out for a billboard. “We have the Green and Pleasant Land that inspired poets and painters,” she says. “And now it looks more like Times Square.” With every campaign win, she brings the nation one step closer to reclaiming its uncluttered beauty.

The Eagles of Death Metal have returned to the stage in Paris to "resume their gig" — a symbolic and defiant performance timed to mark three months since gunman Mohamed Abrini attacked the band at their concert at the Bataclan theatre, killing 89 people. The sold-out show, held at the same venue on Tuesday night, was a brave and emotional step for the American rock band and for the city still reeling from the terror attacks on 13 November by Islamic State supporters. More than 2,000 fans gathered in the refurbished theatre as singer Jesse Hughes and his bandmates delivered a powerful set, including the song “No Love For the Dead,” a deeply personal tribute to the victims. The band released a new single bearing the same name hours before the event, with all proceeds going to the victims and their families. As the familiar guitar riffs echoed through the hall and the crowd sang along, many in attendance fought back tears, while others raised their fists, defiant in the face of terror. Before the performance, Hughes spoke to the media about the significance of returning to the Bataclan. “We had to come back,” he said. “Not just for the music, but for the people of Paris, for those who still mourn and for those who lost everything. This is a show for the living.” The band was playing just one song, “I Only Want You to Love Me,” when the attack took place on the night of 13 November. Abrini, one of the perpetrators, rushed toward the front of the stage, firing his gun indiscriminately in the crowd. At least 20 of the 89 deaths at the Bataclan were connected to the Eagles of Death Metal concert. French President François Hollande attended the concert, as did many French citizens who have worked to rebuild morale since the tragedies of November. “Paris stands tall,” one fan was overheard saying. “Terrorism will not beat us.” The show followed the installation of anti-terrorism operations and tight security measures. Bataclan staff were also among those present, several of them emotional as the venue once synonymous with grief and fear returned to life with the power of music. For the Eagles of Death Metal, the concert was not simply a professional performance but a powerful message — that art, music and memory can help heal even the darkest of wounds. As Hughes took the mic one final time, he looked out over the crowd and said simply: “This is for you.

Premier League summer transfer spending tops £500m — but still £335m short of 2022 spending   Despite rising inflation and the ongoing cost-of-living crisis, Premier League clubs have already surpassed £500 million in incoming transfer spending during the 2023 summer window — but it remains £335 million below the record £835 million spent just a year ago. With a little over a month until the September 1 deadline, the top tier of English football has arguably seen a more cautious and pragmatic approach to the transfer market compared to the chase for big-name stars that dominated last summer. Daniel James’ £30m move from Manchester United to Leeds and Declan Rice’s £105m switch to Arsenal helped drive last summer’s record levels. This time around, the market has been quieter, with clubs focusing more on targeted signings and loan deals rather than assembling superstars. According to latest figures from British media outlets, the total amount spent has been spread across 432 confirmed moves as of early September, with 32 of those transfers reaching over £10 million. Manchester City, despite a recent shift in ownership, have dipped slightly in spending compared to previous summers, while Liverpool and Manchester United have remained among the most active domestic teams. City have splashed out around £100m already this summer, with the likes of Matheus Nunes (£59.5m) and Julian Alvarez (loan deal with obligation to buy) making big headlines. However, the club’s activity is still approximately £100m less than last summer, a reflection of European football’s impact on summer windows as the new dawn of the inter-continental calendar emerges. Premier League chief executive Richard Masters has previously called for a reduction in summer transfer spending as part of the English season’s reform, suggesting that a summer window of around four weeks is more sustainable. Last summer’s record spending has raised eyebrows in both the financial and sporting worlds, with many arguing that the high sums are not always matched with on-pitch effectiveness. While a few blockbuster deals are expected in the coming weeks, particularly as players held out for the perfect move, the early signs of 2023 suggest a more measured and financially sensible approach. Some clubs are also benefiting from additional revenue via the Premier League solidarity payments and the increased income from the revamped overseas broadcast deals.

Wales captain Sam Warburton has backed his long-time team-mate and legendary forward Gethin Jenkins to take charge in a potential leadership shift ahead of their Six Nations contest against Argentina. The comments came as Wales continue preparations for a busy international schedule, with Jenkins’ future in international rugby being a topic of speculation in recent weeks. Warburton, who has been the dominant force in the Welsh leadership structure for years, said that he is fully supportive should Jenkins step into a more prominent on-field leadership role. Speaking in a pre-match press conference, Warburton said: “Gethin is an incredible leader in his own right. He’s led by example for years, even without the official title. If the national team feels that Gethin is the right person to take on more captaincy responsibility, I have no issue with that. I’m here to play my part, support the team in any way I can, and make sure we do our best for Wales when it matters.” Gethin Jenkins, 38, has earned over 120 caps for Wales, building a reputation as one of the most respected props in international rugby. His leadership both on and off the pitch has been widely praised, and with Warburton’s position as skipper currently secure, Jenkins has often been viewed as a potential successor. The idea of Jenkins taking more visible control appears to have gained momentum with the recent changes in approach by the national coaching staff, who are eager to evolve the team’s structure and playing style. Warburton’s comments come as the Welsh squad enters a transitional period in the aftermath of several retirement announcements. With defence a focal point for the upcoming match against Argentina, Jenkins’ experience and composure at the front of the pack will be crucial for Wales in tightening their set-piece and lineout strategies. Coaching consultant Rob Howley hinted last week that Jenkins’ leadership capabilities could be put to the test in the coming fixtures. “Gethin has shown time and again that he can handle pressure and lead from the front. He doesn’t need a title to be a great leader,” Howley said. “Sam is fully behind that, which is incredibly important for team cohesion. We are looking to utilise the full breadth of our leadership talents as we move forward.” With the Six Nations rapidly approaching, the potential reshuffle offers a fresh dynamic for Wales.

A leading fertility charity is urging the Scottish government to increase the number of free IVF cycles available to couples struggling to conceive, from two to three, in a significant boost to reproductive healthcare access. The call comes as Scottish ministers prepare to introduce revised funding guidelines for 2024, following recent recommendations by the Scottish Fertility Consortium and Scottish Assisted Conception Audit Network (SFC/ SACAN). The plea for an additional cycle of IVF has been backed by experts and patient advocates, who argue that many couples are unable to achieve a pregnancy within the current limit and may face financial strain or emotional distress when paying for further treatment. Fertility Scotland, a prominent charity in the field, has made the change a top priority and is launching a national campaign to push for the reform. Morag Simpson, chief executive of Fertility Scotland, said: “For far too long, couples have been left in limbo after two funded rounds of IVF, often at the most vulnerable point in their journey. We believe that everyone has a right to fair and equal access to the treatment they need, without being forced to rely on costly private care or costly loans.” Currently, the publicly funded benchmark is two cycles of IVF for people in Scotland, provided they meet medical and age-related criteria. However, as IVF success rates decline for those over 35, many struggle to achieve a pregnancy – even with two rounds. The charity argues that giving couples a third attempt could significantly improve outcomes and reduce the heartbreak faced by those who exhaust their state support. The campaign comes amid growing awareness of the emotional and financial toll of infertility, with more people than ever seeking help to build their families. According to recent data, more than 6,000 IVF cycles are carried out annually in Scotland, with most people about to fall back on personal funding after their second treatment. Health officials have yet to formally respond to the call, but are expected to consider new provision as part of a broader review of reproductive healthcare funding, which has seen some recent improvements, including increased access to alternative fertility treatments and more open conversations about infertility in public life. Meanwhile, campaigners have urged couples to share their stories to help build pressure on the government as part of a "Break the Silence" campaign, aimed at highlighting the emotional and financial challenges of fertility treatment.

A Buddhist Nun Speaks Out: The Election of Pope Francis Brings Pain Amid Joy   A senior Buddhist nun in Japan has publicly expressed deep unease over the election of Pope Francis, describing her own experience of the moment as one of “pain” amid the global enthusiasm surrounding the first Jesuit pope and the first from the Americas. In a rare vocal statement, Sister Tenzin Lhamo of the Kyoto Zen Centre said she admired the pontiff’s humility and compassion but struggled with the legacy and teachings of the Catholic Church, which she described as “alien and, at times, oppressive” for spiritual seekers outside the Christian tradition. Her comments came as the Vatican continues to draw praise for Pope Francis’s refreshing approach to leadership and his focus on social justice, poverty, and the dignity of all people. However, for religious minorities and interfaith advocates, the election has also raised difficult questions about how the global church engages with the diversity of religious belief — a dialogue Sister Tenzin called long overdue. She said: “I see a lot of joy and celebration for Pope Francis, but I’m living his election with a lot of pain. I believe that true religious leadership must include, not exclude, and listen, not lecture.” The nun, a respected teacher and interfaith leader for over 40 years, explained that for many in the Buddhist and other non-Christian religious traditions, the Catholic Church’s historical conflicts with non-Christian beliefs, coupled with its long-standing Magisterium — the church’s doctrine as taught through its bishops and the pope — continue to limit meaningful dialogue. She pointed in particular to the Church’s position on evolution, gender roles, and the absolute nature of Christian doctrine, which she said “continues to muddy the waters of interfaith coexistence.” Sister Tenzin’s remarks come in the wake of Pope Francis’s first major speeches, in which he has called for greater humility and openness among leaders. Some are hopeful that this new era will lead to a more inclusive Catholic Church. Others, like Sister Tenzon, argue that words must be backed with actions and structural change to ensure the religious world is not confined to the reach of one faith. The Vatican has yet to respond directly to such concerns, but interfaith academies and religious leaders have begun to reach out to the new pope with cautious optimism. For Sister Tenzin, however, the pain remains — a reminder that in every celebration, some hearts are left aching for change.

The Dartford Crossing, one of the UK's busiest road tunnels and a vital artery for south-east England, has been excluded from government assessments of air quality due to its classification as a “rural” road, the BBC has revealed. The decision has sparked outrage among environmental campaigners, local residents, and some MPs, who argue it overlooks the serious harm being caused by toxic emissions from the thousands of vehicles that use the route daily. The Dartford tunnel and A2/M2 corridor serve as a key transport link between Kent and Essex, and carry traffic associated with the M25 and High Speed 1. Yet when monitoring air quality, under the government’s own air quality index, these roads do not feature, as their classification as “rural” places them outside the criteria used by local authorities and environmental regulators to define high-pollution zones. London and the south-east are already among the most polluted areas of the country. In recent years, the Environment Agency has been forced to declare illegal levels of nitrogen dioxide in numerous areas of the capital and surrounding regions, prompting legal action from environmental groups and fines for the government. Campaigners now fear that by excluding heavily used roads like the Dartford Crossing from air quality maps, the full extent of the problem is being underestimated and appropriate action is being delayed. One local resident, who has lived near the crossing for over 20 years, told the BBC: “You can almost taste the fumes in the air. People here have respiratory issues, and yet the government doesn't even seem to acknowledge the scale of the problem.” Environmental lawyers from ClientEarth said the exclusion of Dartford from air quality monitoring defied logic. “It's not what you would call 'rural' by any stretch of the imagination,” said one lawyer. “This classification is not based on scientific standards, but on the way the government has chosen to interpret its own air quality directives. It creates a loophole that needs to be urgently fixed.” The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, which issues local authorities with pollution monitoring guidance, did not directly respond to questions on the definition of “rural” roads, but stressed that it continued to work on air quality improvement across all areas of the country. Meanwhile, local council leaders in Kent are calling for urgent action and demand that the exclusion of such key locations be reviewed.

Tributes have poured in for a British mother from Caerphilly County who lost her life in Sunday’s terror attack in Tunisia, which has so far claimed the lives of 16 British nationals. Jane Taylor, 45, is among those confirmed to have died in the incident at the Sousse seaside resort, described by officials as an “act of terrorism” carried out by a lone attacker wielding an automatic rifle. Her death has sparked an outpouring of grief from her local community and social media, with friends and family expressing their shock and solidarity. Mrs Taylor, a devoted mother of two, had embarked on the trip with her husband and children, part of a short break to escape the colder Welsh winter. Her husband, Martin Taylor, is in a critical but stable condition following the attack, while their children were reportedly unharmed, albeit deeply traumatised, and are being supported by the British authorities in Tunisia. Local residents in Caerphilly have described her as a “kind-hearted” and “resilient” woman, who was known for her love of travel and for encouraging others to seek joy in life’s simple pleasures. Neighbour Alison Griffiths told BBC Wales: “Jane always had a smile on her face. She was a real inspiration, especially as a mum. It’s just heartbreaking that something like this has happened.” Prime Minister David Cameron – who called the attack a “cowardly act of terrorism” – announced the activation of Operation Omega, the government’s emergency response for British nationals affected by terrorist incidents abroad. He paid tribute to those who had lost their lives, adding: “This government will never waver in its determination to defeat terrorism in all its forms.” As details of the attack emerged, tributes from across the UK highlighted the fragility of life and the cruel randomness of such violence. Meanwhile, the Foreign and Commonwealth Office has issued updated travel advice for Tunisia, urging UK citizens to reconsider non-essential travel to the country while the security situation is assessed. A local candlelight vigil was planned in Caerphilly for later in the week as the community comes to terms with their loss. As the world watches for further developments, the tragic death of Jane Taylor and the others in Sousse has once again served as a stark reminder of the human cost of terrorism – and the far-reaching consequences for families around the globe..identifier: 37859e94-1b89-4e8d-9e92-305cf59937e5.

The 2012 Scottish council elections marked a dramatic shift in political dynamics across Scotland’s local government landscape, with both the Scottish National Party and the Labour Party claiming victory, while the Liberal Democrats suffered a devastating collapse in support. The results, announced across the country over several days, saw the SNP emerge as the largest single party in Scottish local government, continuing its upward trajectory in the national polls. Labour, meanwhile, held on to key urban strongholds and regained council majorities in key Glasgow and Edinburgh areas, offering a counter-narrative to the perception that the party was in irreversible decline north of the border. The Liberal Democrats, however, faced what many have called one of the worst defeats in their political history, with the party losing 41 of the 42 councils it held before the election. In places like East Dunbartonshire and East Lothian, they were wiped out altogether, retaining no local seats at all for the first time in their long history. The scale of the Liberal Democrat’s losses was described in stark terms by political commentators and by their own leaders, who admitted it was a “catastrophic result”. The party’s vote share plummeted by nearly 30 percentage points in some areas, a blow from which many believe they may not recover. The result was widely attributed to the growing unease among Scottish voters over the party's decision – made in coalition with the Conservatives in 2010 – to back the government’s policy of not holding a referendum on Scottish independence before the 2015 general election, which many in Scotland saw as a betrayal. With the Scottish Parliament elections just a year away, the Lib Dems now face a stark reality: either a rapid and radical recalibration of their strategy or the risk of near-total political oblivion in Scotland. The SNP’s sweeping gains brought it to within 37 seats of an outright majority in local councils, a performance that further strengthened its position as the dominant political force in Scotland and bolstered leader Alex Salmond’s claims of a “tectonic shift” in the political landscape. Yet it was Labour's success in key urban areas that may provide them with a strategic foothold in the run-up to the 2014 independence referendum. Richard Leonard, Labour’s deputy leader, claimed the party had “recovered its credibility” after a difficult 2010 general election in Scotland. Indeed, their improvements in Glasgow and Edinburgh – two cities traditionally sympathetic to the SNP – offered a significant morale boost.

Lewis Hamilton put on a commanding display in the final practice session ahead of qualifying at the British Grand Prix, as the Formula 1 drivers completed their weekend preparations at Silverstone. The seven-time world champion, who will be looking to secure a historic ninth British Grand Prix win and extend his record in front of a passionate home crowd, was the fastest on the track at the end of the one-hour session on Friday afternoon. Hamilton's best lap of 1 minute and 30.479 seconds edged out Red Bull's Max Verstappen by a margin of 0.240 seconds, underlining the Mercedes driver's strong form at his home race. Teammate George Russell also showed promise, finishing third, 0.349 seconds behind Hamilton and well ahead of Verstappen's teammate Sergio Pérez. Ferrari’s Carlos Sainz was the fourth fastest, placing the Italian team in the mix for a potential front-row challenge. The session saw several drivers rotate through different tyre strategies and set-up configurations, with slicks dominated across the field thanks to dry and warm conditions on the iconic Silverstone circuit. As teams prepare for qualifying, which will decide the grid for Sunday’s race, the focus will be on short-run pace and consistency to capitalise on the unpredictable nature of the track during lap simulation runs. Hamilton, who is currently leading the Drivers’ Championship, appears to be targeting a dominant performance at Silverstone, where he has long been a favourite. His experience of the circuit, combined with the high level of motivation generated by home-supporting fans, could give him a crucial edge in what is expected to be a fiercely contested championship race. Team bosses and engineers will also be watching the data closely, as the final practice provides an early indication of where each team stands ahead of qualifying. With about five hours separating the final session and the start of the first qualifying segment, teams will be keen to make any adjustments to their setups to ensure they are delivering the car in peak condition to the drivers. Drivers are set to take to the grid in the first session of qualifying at 16:30 BST, with all eyes on Hamilton and Verstappen for what promises to be a thrilling Saturday at one of Formula 1’s most iconic venues. Fans will be hoping for another thriller at the British Grand Prix, as the road to a potential title showdown continues to unfold.

The pride of Japan's naval defence, the JS Izumo, is making an unprecedented journey through Asian waters over the next three months. The state-of-the-art helicopter destroyer is currently deployed as part of its first Asia-Pacific deployment, a mission that is as much about diplomacy as it is about military posturing. The ship, capable of carrying up to 14 helicopters and operating for weeks at sea, is expected to cruise through the Indian Ocean, the South China Sea, and the South Pacific, engaging in a series of port calls and joint exercises with regional partners. Analysts say the move marks a significant shift in Japan’s maritime posture, as the nation grows increasingly assertive amid growing security challenges in the region. The JS Izumo, which entered service in 2015, is one of only two vessels of its class in the Japanese Maritime Self-Defense Force (JMSDF), and is often described as Japan’s de facto aircraft carrier — a classification it avoids for legal and political reasons. The ship will dock in Hanoi in Vietnam and Darwin, Australia, as part of its tour, offering opportunities for collaboration and showcasing Japan’s naval capabilities. Rear Admiral Yuji Kunii, who is commanding the deployment, said in a pre-travel statement that the mission is intended to "promote maritime peace and stability" and "strengthen partnerships in the Indo-Pacific region." The timing of the deployment is significant. With China and its Belt and Road Initiative expanding its influence, and tensions simmering in the East and South China Seas, Japan is stepping up its regional engagements, aligning more closely with strategic partners such as the United States, India, and Australia under the so-called Quad framework. While the JS Izumo's deployment is largely unofficial and not part of a joint military alliance, it sends a clear message about Japan's commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific. The ship is expected to conduct maritime patrols, anti-piracy exercises, and joint drills with regional navies, while also offering humanitarian and disaster relief support. Some observers, however, note that the growing militarisation of Japanese naval assets could further inflame regional competition, particularly with China, which views Japan’s increased naval activity with deep suspicion. Professor Takuya Takeda of Tokyo University said: "This deployment is more than just a show of strength — it's part of a broader strategic recalibration by Japan in the context of a shifting balance of power in Asia."

Osborne Launches ‘Northern Powerhouse’ in Bid to Reshape UK Economy   In his final budget as Chancellor of the Exchequer, George Osborne has unveiled a sweeping economic vision centred on revitalising the northern regions of England, hailing it as the cornerstone of the country’s post-Brexit economic strategy. With the general election looming in May, the Conservative government is making the   “northern powerhouse”   one of its most high-profile domestic policy proposals — a bid to rebalance the UK’s financial landscape and address decades of relative under-performance in the north. Osborne, who has long championed the idea, revealed a range of measures in the 2015 Autumn Statement aimed at strengthening economic and transport links across Manchester, Leeds, Liverpool and the surrounding areas. Central to the plan is the ambition to create a more competitive northern economy through better rail connectivity, support for business innovation, and investment in digital infrastructure.   High-speed rail is a key component, with Osborne confirming agreement to extend the High Speed 2 (HS2) line from London to Crewe, and looking ahead to a potential future route to Manchester and Leeds by the 2030s.   This is expected to cut journey times between major northern cities and London and integrate the north more closely into the national transport network. Osborne argued that such improvements will encourage businesses to locate outside London – reducing the capital’s dominance and spreading prosperity more evenly. Alongside improved transport, Osborne announced an additional £2 billion in business investment for the Northern Powerhouse Growth Fund, focusing on job creation and innovation. He said businesses in the north will benefit from a   “renewed emphasis on productivity”  , with particular support for technology and science-based industries. Universities in the north – including the University of Manchester and the University of York – are to receive a funding boost to help them compete nationally and globally. The Chancellor also revealed plans to establish   a new devolution agenda  , giving city regions more control over local budgets. Manchester, Leeds and Liverpool will each receive councils with increased powers over housing, transport and education, similar to the Greater Manchester model launched earlier this year. Osborne stressed that this decentralisation will help “local leaders to make decisions and invest funds to deliver what is right for their people and their places”. The announcement has been largely welcomed by northern business leaders and politicians, although critics have raised concerns about the timeline and funding for major infrastructure projects.

Winter on the Line: National Grid Confirms No Power Shortages This Winter   As the UK braces for another cold winter, National Grid has provided a much-needed shot of reassurance to energy consumers, confirming that the country has sufficient gas and electricity supplies to avoid blackouts this season. The promise comes amid growing public concern over energy security in the wake of volatile global markets and the lingering effects of the energy crisis. In a statement released on behalf of the grid operator, National Grid’s director of system operations, Simon Burrell, expressed confidence in the system’s resilience. “We are confident the energy demand for the winter can be met with the generation available and the volumes of gas we expect to be available through flexible demand and the security supply arrangements,” he said. The organisation has repeatedly urged households and businesses to use energy efficiently and take advantage of energy-saving measures, but the message is now clear: the lights will stay on. This statement is expected to offer relief to a public that, in recent years, has been all too aware of the potential for supply shortages, ever-rising energy bills, and the resulting hardship. National Grid warned, however, that while supply is secure, the volatility of the international market—particularly impacts of global geopolitical tensions and rising gas prices—means the UK must continue to diversify its energy production and invest in renewable energy infrastructure. “The longer-term picture remains challenging,” Burrell added. “We need to build more wind, solar, and new interconnectors to ensure energy security for future winters.” Currently, the UK’s energy mix includes a significant contribution from North Sea gas and renewable sources. According to government energy forecasts, wind power is expected to make up a larger proportion of the electricity supply than ever before, while energy storage and grid flexibility are key components in managing supply and demand fluctuations. Despite these reassurances, consumer groups such as the Energy Saving Trust have called for continued support for low-income families who are still grappling with the legacy of unaffordable energy bills. “While it’s reassuring that the National Grid believes supply will be adequate, many households will still be struggling,” said a spokesperson for the charity. The government has responded with a mix of support schemes—including the Energy Bill Relief Scheme that funds part of household energy costs—while also pressing ahead with long-term reforms to the energy market.

Tributes have poured in from the Northern Ireland sporting world and beyond to boxing legend Muhammad Ali, who has died at the age of 74. Widely regarded as one of the greatest boxers of all time, Ali inspired generations with his unique charisma, unmatched skill in the ring, and powerful voice for civil rights and social justice. In Northern Ireland, where the sport of boxing has deep cultural and historical roots, the loss has been met with profound sadness. Politicians, athletes, and fans alike have taken to social media and public statements to express their admiration and respect for the three-time world heavyweight champion. Former Belfast boxer Barry McGuigan was among the first to pay tribute, describing Ali as “a colossus of the sport, not just for what he brought to the ring, but for who he was outside of it. He stood up for what was right, even when it was difficult. That’s the sign of a true champion, both in and out of boxing.” McGuigan, who won world titles in the 1980s, also praised Ali’s enduring influence on the sport. “Ali made people dream, and he made boxing stand for something more than just punches and prizes. He reminded us that we all had a responsibility to use our platform for something bigger.” From the world of soccer, former Celtic and Northern Ireland captain Roy Keane also weighed in, tweeting: “Muhammad Ali was more than a boxer. He was a messenger, a warrior of justice, and a voice for the voiceless. The world has lost a true giant.” As is tradition in Belfast, one of the city's boxing gyms, the Rovers Lane Elite Boxing Club, paid homage to Ali with a red and white corner being dedicated in his name. “Ali is a name that transcends borders and divides,” said club manager John Harte. “In this city, where boxing means so much, we will always be reminded of the example he set. He wasn’t just fighting for titles, he was fighting for dignity, equality, and truth.” Ali's influence stretched far beyond sport. As a prominent figure in the civil rights movement, he refused to be drafted into the Vietnam War in 1967, citing his religious beliefs and opposition to the conflict. His stance led to the revocation of his boxing licence for nearly four years, but it also galvanised a movement that continues to resonate today.

St Helens bounced back from the disappointment of an early Challenge Cup exit with a hard-fought victory over Salford at the Halton Stadium on Saturday, cruising to a 38-28 win despite a spirited Red Devils comeback and a hat-trick of tries from the ever-dangerous Niall Evalds. The reigning Super League champions were made to work hard for their success, as Salford kept the game close despite going a significant deficit early in the match. Evalds sparked the visitors’ resurgence with a trio of tries, pulling Salford back into contention and forcing the Saints into a chase in the second half. However, St Helens, led by captain Regan Grace and a resilient defence, managed to maintain their composure and push across the line repeatedly, ensuring the points went to the left-coast giants. Starting brightly, the Saints controlled the first stanza of the game, opening the scoring through an intercept try from Jack Wray, who capitalized on a Salford error to put his side 6-0 ahead. Full-back Gareth O'Brien added a second to extend the lead to 12-0 before half-time, with the home side clearly intent on making a statement after last week’s frustrations. Salford made a few tactical adjustments at the break, and it paid off. Evalds – who has become a regular utility weapon for the Red Devils – showed his class, evading tackles and slicing through the Saints’ line with ruthless efficiency. His first try brought the visitors to within 12-6 after the break, and two more soon followed, sending ripples of optimism through the Salford supporters. Despite the threat, St Helens had the experience and composure to respond. Stand-off Paul Williams – playing through injury in a pivotal performance – booted points from the tee to maintain the lead, while the likes of captain Regan Grace and Mitch Brown found the line to stretch the advantage and extinguish any Salford hopes of a late comeback. The win put the Saints’ record back on track following last weekend’s Challenge Cup quarter-final exit to Championship side Toronto Wolfpack, an anomaly which has already been dismissed by head coach Ian Watson. Speaking after the match, Watson praised his side’s resilience: “I’m really pleased with the way the team responded today. That cup set-back was a slight blip, but the character we showed in grinding out the win is exactly what we need going into the latter stages of the season.”

A newly-ordained bishop in China has reportedly been detained by authorities after publicly declaring his refusal to remain within the state-sanctioned Chinese Patriotic Catholic Association (CPCA). The bishop, identified by local sources as Li Baohua, is believed to be a member of the country’s underground Catholic community, which operates outside the control of the state and maintains allegiance to the Pope in Rome. His arrest has reignited tensions between the Chinese government and the Catholic Church, particularly following provisions in China's controversial 2018 agreements with the Vatican that transferred control over the appointment of bishops to the Chinese state. According to reports from the Catholic charity Aid to the Church in Need, Bishop Li was ordained in January without CPCA approval, a clear violation of China's religious policies. Ordinations must be approved by the Communist Party’s Patriotic Associations, which oversee state-sanctioned religious bodies, and the bishop’s defiance appears to have prompted swift action by the authorities. Bishop Li, based in the southern province of Hubei, reportedly informed fellow clergy and congregants of his decision to resign from the CPCA during a recent service. Sources close to the Church say he expressed solidarity with other bishops and priests facing persecution for adhering to the Vatican rather than the state-sanctioned hierarchy. “He said he could not live a lie by pretending to belong to an association that rejects the authority of the Pope,” a source told local Catholic outlets. This incident comes amid growing international concern over religious freedom in China, particularly under President Xi Jinping. Last year, the Vatican made headlines when it entered into a provisional agreement with China on the appointment of bishops, a move that many within the Church viewed with deep scepticism. Criticisms arose over the agreement’s silence on the persecution of clergy in mainland China and its perceived legitimisation of the CPCA's authority. Bishop Li’s arrest is likely to be seen as an attempt by the Chinese government to enforce strict adherence to the CPCA, while also sending a message to the underground Church. The Vatican has yet to make a public statement on the matter, but the incident is expected to strain the already delicate relationship between Rome and Beijing. In China, the underground Church continues to grow in certain rural areas, with followers refusing to take oaths of loyalty to the state. These communities often operate in secrecy for fear of imprisonment or re-education.

Lewis Hamilton and Mercedes secured a stunning victory at the Spanish Grand Prix on Sunday, edging out Ferrari's Sebastian Vettel in a thrilling race that captivated fans across the globe. The Mercedes driver demonstrated his trademark precision and adaptability, navigating the Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya with remarkable consistency to clinch a well-earned win for the Silver Arrows. Hamilton, who has long been one of Formula 1’s most dominant forces, maintained a steady lead from the start, managing his tires and fuel economy with expert efficiency. The Briton was never in serious danger as he pulled away from the field and held a comfortable margin, but the race gained additional intensity with Vettel in close pursuit, offering a strong challenge from the Ferrari camp. Vettel, who started in second place, pushed hard to close the gap, though he ultimately fell short of overhauling the five-time world champion. Qualifying had been a different story, with Vettel securing pole position and Mercedes struggling for pace, but Hamilton’s race pace proved decisive. His drive in Spain underscored the resilience and technical superiority that have long defined the Mercedes team—and that many had feared might falter after a patchy start to the season. The victory was the 76th of Hamilton’s career and extended his lead in the Drivers’ Championship, marking another significant step in his quest to equal, and perhaps surpass, the legendary Michael Schumacher’s record of seven titles. It was also a huge boost for Mercedes as they look to defend their Constructors’ Championship title following a series of mixed results at the beginning of the year. Hamilton’s team-mate, Valtteri Bottas, brought home a strong second place, with Charles Leclerc of Ferrari in third. The race weekend had been considered a make-or-break opportunity for Ferrari, who had been optimistic about finally closing the performance gap to Mercedes. Although Vettel’s consistency and speed made for a compelling battle, the Red Bull and Alpine teams remained out of contention for the main prizes. The win for Hamilton was not only a personal triumph but also a reminder that when at their best, Mercedes can still outperform all challengers. As the Formula 1 season progresses, the pressure is now firmly back on Ferrari to close the gap and match the pace of the championship leaders. For now, though, Lewis Hamilton and Mercedes will be delivering the kind of performance that once again cements their status as the team to beat.

A worrying trend for Scottish football has emerged, as a BBC investigation has revealed that three-quarters of tickets across the country’s top four leagues have either fallen or remained stagnant compared to this time last year. The findings highlight a widespread decline in fan engagement across the national game, with clubs from the Premiership down to the Championship struggling to fill seats in an increasingly competitive and economically challenging climate. The report, based on data gathered from clubs in all four of Scotland’s senior leagues, found that 75% of surveyed teams had seen either a drop in average attendances or no growth since the start of the 2022/23 season. Among the most-highly attended clubs, even Edinburgh’s Easter Road and Ibrox Stadium in Glasgow have shown signs of attending plateauing, a concerning sign for clubs already grappling with squeezed budgets and rising operational costs. Trevor Wood, a football analyst and former Premier League head of recruitment, said the figures echo a broader trend across European football, where domestic attendances have been affected by a combination of fan disillusionment, cost-of-living pressures, and the return of alternative entertainment options post-pandemic. “It’s not just about prices, though affordability is a factor—there are plenty of clubs offering match-day tickets for £20-£30, but demand isn’t matching supply. People aren’t making the decision to come to games as often as they used to,” Wood said. “It’s a huge challenge, and unless clubs can find new ways to reconnect with their supporter bases, this could become a long-term problem.” The decline is particularly stark in the Championship and League One. Partick Thistle, for instance, reported an average drop of 19% in season ticket sales compared to 2022, despite a playoff finish and a thrilling run at Hampden Park. Hearts fans, meanwhile, voiced frustration over inconsistent first-team performances as average attendances fell by 11% at Tynecastle Park. Off the pitch, the financial implications for clubs are serious. With commercial income fluctuating and broadcast revenue uneven across Scotland’s leagues, match-day revenue is all the more vital. For smaller clubs, the drop in attendances could mean the difference between profit and being forced to cut costs or take on debt. Championship clubs are now being urged to consider innovative approaches to re-engage fans. This includes everything from community-based initiatives and youth academy days to improved in-stadium experiences, including better food and drink options and digital engagement platforms.

In a stunning twist of FA Cup fortunes, Fleetwood Town produced a remarkable late onslaught to clinch a 3-2 victory over minnows Southport in extra time, snatching victory from the jaws of an unlikely giant-killing. The seaside side had seemed set to etch their name into the history books after two stunning goals sent shockwaves through the crowd and briefly derailed the League One side. Southport, representing the 93 non-league teams still in the competition, had sparked a dream debut in the third round by defeating Tranmere Rovers and reaching the stage where the very notion of an upset seemed plausible. Fleetwood led 1-0 after 90 minutes through Harrison Webb, but the real drama only began in the second half of extra time. Against all odds, Southport left themselves a mountain to climb, finding the back of the net twice within three minutes to take the lead. First, a clinical finish from James Caton stunned the visiting fans, then a cleverly curled effort from Jack Grimmer put the non-leaguers 2-1 up, setting the stage for the most improbable of giant-kills. However, fortune, it seemed, was not on their side. Just minutes later, as the anticipation in the stands reached fever pitch, Fleetwood launched a dramatic mini-revival. Goals from Josh Robinson and Tony Gray restored parity at 2-2, with Fleetwood drawing on all their League One experience and composure in the face of mortal danger. Then came the decisive moment—extra time’s 106th minute. A seemingly innocuous cross from the left found its way to Rovers’ striker Nathan Thomas, who had the presence of mind to head into the net, ending Southport’s hopes with balletic simplicity and a cruel about-turn in fortune. Fleetwood head coach Steven Pressley, who had spoken before the game of the “extra layer of pressure” when facing teams outside the professional leagues, exhorted the players to handle the burden. Moments later, his words passed into action. The players’ composure and ability to deliver under such late pressure ensured they advanced to the next round. Speaking after the match, Pressley described the endgame as “a rollercoaster with a happy ending.” “You can’t write scripts like this in any drama series, but these are the moments that the FA Cup lives for—until it snatched from your hand at the end,” he said, voicing the collective sentiment between bench and stand.

Claire Sugden Reflects on a New Political Chapter as Assembly Resumes   As the Northern Ireland Assembly reconvenes following a hard-won and highly anticipated election campaign, one of its most divisive figures, Claire Sugden, finds herself in an altogether different political atmosphere. No longer confined to what was once colloquially known as the “naughty corner”—a metaphor used to describe the backbenches of Unionist Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) members who defied the party whip—Sugden now steps into a new era, her political journey one of both rebirth and reckoning. Sugden, the former Solicitor General for Northern Ireland, had long been a polarising figure, known both for her ferocity in debate and for her willingness to cross traditional party lines in pursuit of what she believed to be the greater good. Her tenure as Solicitor General, and the political tensions that followed her appointment and eventual removal by the previous executive, had marked her as a prime example of a legislator unafraid to challenge the status quo. That willingness to confront, even at the cost of political alignment, had earned her the ire of colleagues and praise from those who saw in her a rare dose of independent legislate. With the recent Assembly break dominated by the election campaign, there was much speculation about how Sugden would be received upon her return. The “naughty corner” was a place not just reserved for those who strayed from the party line but often for those seen as disruptive to its democratic harmony. Now, however, with the UUP itself in a period of transition and redefinition, Sugden appears poised to play a central role in shaping its new direction. In a recent interview, Sugden reflected on her return with a mix of personal resolve and political pragmatism. “I never sought to play the rebel,” she said. “I sought to be a voice for good governance and for the people of Ulster. If that meant standing independently in that corner, then so be it. But politics is not about corners—it is about people and purpose.” The election campaign had seen Sugden campaign actively under her own banner, drawing attention to issues such as judicial reform, good governance and the rule of law. Her candid appearances with voters across a spectrum of communities had been met with an unexpected warmth, suggesting that her time in the opposition corner may have been a source of strength rather than isolation.

Motherwell have completed their fourth summer signing with the arrival of experienced goalkeeper Trevor Carson, as part of a busy transfer window aimed at preparing the Steelmen for the new Scottish Premiership season. The 33-year-old shot-stopper, who previously made 53 appearances for the Fir Park outfit during a loan spell in the 2018/19 campaign, has returned on an undisclosed-length contract to bolster Mark McGhee’s squad. The move signals a fresh start for Carson, who was most recently with Wigan Athletic, where he spent time as first-choice goalkeeper before the club's recent financial struggles led to his exit. His decision to return to Fir Park is seen as both a tactical and psychological boost for Motherwell, who are looking to mend their fortunes after a challenging campaign that saw them narrowly avoid relegation. McGhee, whose team made six signings in the summer, stated: “Trevor is a player with quality, nous, and composure. We've worked with him before, and he knows the club inside out. He’s the type of character we want, and he’s going to bring great experience to our back line.” The inclusion of Carson, who has also represented Hibernian, Blackburn Rovers, and Celtic during his career, strengthens competition for the starting spot in goal, with existing number one Jamie Langfield set to face renewed challenges in the new season. Academically, Carson brings value beyond just his shot-stopping ability. His set-piece distribution and organisational skills have long been praised, and his leadership in the box could provide the steel needed to allow improvements in Motherwell’s defensive structure. Reports suggest that the club is also keen on adding a second goalkeeper to their ranks, indicating that the summer is far from over in terms of key signings. The past few weeks have seen Motherwell address key areas of the squad, with defenders Charlie Mulgrew and Ronan FB McKinley among the new arrivals. Carson’s inclusion is the latest step in a reconstruction process, with McGhee looking to build a well-rounded team capable of challenging on all fronts in the 2019/20 campaign. As the new season approaches, fans will be eager to see whether the signings can propel the club out of the mid-table trap and into the upper echelons of Scottish football. For now, Trevor Carson’s arrival has caused a wave of optimism among supporters, who are hopeful that his experience and professionalism can help stabilise the squad at a crucial transitional stage.

Tributes have been paid across London and Dublin this week to mark the centenary of the death of East Tyrone MP Tom Kettle, the former Irish nationalist who fell on the Somme battlefields in 1916. Kettle, a passionate orator and respected Member of Parliament, is remembered not only for his political career but also for his ultimate sacrifice on the Western Front, where he died on September 9, 1916, at the age of 37. In a solemn assembly at Westminster, MPs from across the political spectrum paid homage to Kettle’s legacy. The Irish Parliamentary Party called him a “man of principle and patriotism,” whose life united the dual loyalties of national and imperial duty. Kettle, who had been elected to Parliament in 1906 and served as a backbencher to John Redmond, was known for his charisma and his fierce advocacy for Irish self-rule, while remaining a staunch British citizen. When war broke out in 1914, Kettle immediately volunteered, planting the seeds for a fateful journey that many say was driven by a sense of moral obligation. Across the Irish Sea, a wreath-laying ceremony was held in Dublin, where a statue to Kettle stands in Wood Quay as a stark reminder of the crossroads of identity and allegiance that defined the era. The ceremony – attended by descendants, historians, and members of the Irish government – acknowledged his tragic role as an officer in the 16th (Irish) Division, which suffered heavy losses during the first day of the Battle of the Somme. Kettle was awarded a posthumous Military Cross for gallantry in leading his men under fire, and his death came just weeks before the Easter Rising, in a pivotal year for Ireland’s complex national story. In the House of Commons, the centenary was marked with a formal statement by the Speaker, who praised Kettle as a man who “gave the final step of his life for the cause of freedom and unity.” Historic documents displayed in the parliamentary archives have been made open to the public for the first time, including Kettle’s speeches, letters to his wife, and photographs from his time in uniform. The tributes sparked renewed debate about the legacies of the Great War in Ireland, particularly as communities grapple with the contradictions of individuals like Kettle—men who fought for both their nation and empire. Despite the passage of over a century, the memory of Kettle continues to resonate in both political and cultural spheres, a symbol of service and sacrifice at a time when Ireland stood at the heart of two great upheavals: war and revolution.

Lewis Hamilton has revealed he will skip the personal trainer in his preparations for the 2023 Formula 1 season — a first in his 17-year career. The seven-time world champion, who has long been associated with a rigorous fitness regime, said he has grown more confident in his ability to manage his own fitness and wellbeing. “I’ve been working with coaches for so long, but I think it’s time to trust myself,” Hamilton said in a recent interview. “I’ve got a great support team, but personally, I feel ready to take control of my own fitness.” Hamilton, who claimed his third drivers' title with Mercedes in 2014, has won 103 Grand Prix races and is widely regarded as one of the sport’s greatest ever drivers. His fitness has always played a significant role in his success, with previous years featuring high-intensity workouts and nutrition plans overseen by a dedicated team of experts. This year, however, he is taking a more independent approach. “It’s a bit of a shift, but I think it’s healthy to re-evaluate what works best for me,” he added. “Of course I still consult the team for guidance, but ultimately I’m in the best position to know what I need to keep performing at my peak.” Hamilton’s decision comes as the Formula 1 season approaches, with pre-season testing set to begin in February. Mercedes, who shifted to a more aggressive rebuilding strategy following the 2022 season, will be under pressure to close the gap with reigning champions Red Bull. Hamilton will also be starting his final year of his current contract with the team, with speculation building over whether he will extend his partnership. His closest rival, Max Verstappen, recently challenged Hamilton’s decision to trust himself fully, saying in an interview: “You don’t become a champion without the right people around you. It will be interesting to see how it goes.” Hamilton, who has been open about his mental health and the pressures of elite sport, says the change will allow him to reduce stress and focus more on the emotional as well as physical demands of the sport. “I’ve always been about performance, but performance isn’t just about horsepower and lap times. It’s also about mindset and how you keep yourself balanced,” he said. Team principal Toto Wolff confirmed that Hamilton’s decision had the support of the team.

Rangers find themselves just two victories away from securing the Scottish Championship title and a return to the top flight after a thrilling 4-3 win over Queen of the South at Ibrox on Friday night. In a dramatic and physical encounter, the Glasgow giants displayed all the attacking flair and resilience that has marked their remarkable resurgence in recent months. The victory extended their lead at the top of the league and has further boosted the optimism among their supporters, many of whom have waited years to see the side return to the top tier of Scottish football. Known for their volatile history and financial turbulence in recent years, Rangers have steadily rebuilt themselves under the ownership of Chinese businessman Craig Whyte, who took control in 2011, and the management of Ally McCoist and now Mark Warburton. The current squad, though not brimming with superstars, has shown an ability to grind out results and deliver in crucial moments. Against Queen of the South, Rangers endured a nervy start, conceding an early goal through Brian Gilmour in the 12th minute. However, they responded in emphatic fashion when James Tavernier opened the scoring for the hosts with a thunderous strike from outside the box. The Ibrox crowd roared as their side quickly regained the lead, with James Fletcher doubling their advantage on 33 minutes before the light from the floodlights seemed to spark another equaliser for the visitors, this time through Andy Little on the stroke of half-time. The second half was even more explosive. Late in the game, Liam Buchanan and Lee Wallace put the icing on the cake with late goals, sealing a 4-3 win that will go down as one of the highlights of this dramatic promotion season. The victory comes at a vital time in the campaign, as Rangers remain two points ahead of second-place Motherwell with just a handful of matches left to play. Speaking after the game, Rangers manager Mark Warburton praised his team's composure under pressure and highlighted their ability to "fight for every ball like their lives depend on it," a sentiment that has become synonymous with the club's recent identity. With promotion now very much in sight, the waiting game begins for Ibrox fans as they prepare for what could be a grand return to the Scottish Premier League next season. The psychological boost from this win, set against a backdrop of financial and administrative rebuilding, could not come at a better time for a club that has once again defied the odds.

Malta, a tiny archipelago in the heart of the Mediterranean, has proven time and again that its small size belies its significance in the grand theatre of history. Known today more for its azure waters, warm hospitality, and a booming tourism sector, the island has also played a dramatic and vital role in some of Europe’s most pivotal conflicts. Most notably, during the Second World War, Malta became the site of an all-out struggle for survival that would come to define its place in the global narrative of the 20th century. In the Second World War, the British colony of Malta found itself at the heart of the Allied war effort in the Mediterranean. Surrounded by Axis powers and subjected to relentless aerial bombardment and harsh supply blockades, the island’s fate hung in the balance for years. The fighting left the Maltese people, everyday citizens who had no formal army, to endure what has been described as one of the most sustained air campaigns of the war.
