British and Allied forces defended the island’s strategic position — a crucial linchpin for the control of Mediterranean shipping routes to North Africa — but it was the Maltese themselves who bore the brunt of the suffering, sustaining constant Allied and Axis air raids with stoic determination. It was this unyielding spirit that earned the island a unique distinction during the war: in 1942, King George VI awarded the Royal Victoria Order, known as the George Cross, to “the people of Malta in recognition of their heroism and steadfast courage.” The award, which hung in the Maltese Parliament until someone claimed full independence for the island, inspired a sense of unity and pride that endures to this day. The fury of war in the 1940s was not Malta’s first brush with conflict. The island’s strategic location has made it a coveted prize throughout history — coveted by Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Romans, Byzantines, and later, the Knights of St. John, who famously held off the Ottoman Empire during the Great Siege of 1565. These earlier struggles helped forge the Maltese character, one of resilience, tenacity, and a deep-rooted sense of identity that has seen the island survive not only the turbulence of war but also the shifting tides of empire, independence, and modernity. Today, the echoes of the past still resonate in the cobblestone streets of Valletta, the Grand Harbour, and the haunting scars of World War II bomb shelters carved into the limestone beneath the towns.

"We need to have more courage," a Labour MP, newly elected last year, confided to me in the corridors of Westminster. These words, spoken in hushed tones, reflect a growing sense of urgency within the Labour Party as it gears up for a crucial general election. With the country facing unprecedented uncertainty — from economic instability to a deeply divided political landscape — there is a clear understanding that the moment calls for bold leadership and clear-eyed policies that speak directly to the needs of ordinary citizens. For this MP and many others like him, the path forward is not just about winning seats; it is about reclaiming the trust of a public that feels increasingly disillusioned. Recent months have seen a noticeable shift in tone and strategy from Labour MPs and MPs-elect across the country. From town halls to local supermarkets, they are engaging directly with communities, listening to their concerns, and presenting themselves as the true champions of working people in a world dominated by policies many believe serve the few at the expense of the many. The prime minister has been keen to paint Labour in recent weeks as out of touch and incapable of governing, even as many of the government’s own policies begin to falter under the scrutiny of the public and media. This has forced Labour into a defensive position, one that is gradually giving way to something more proactive — a demand not only for policy reform but for a new political culture. At the heart of this transformation is a determination to connect with younger voters, who remain largely unimpressed by the current state of British politics and have stayed away from the polls in large numbers. For the younger generation, this election is not just about choosing between political parties but about defining the kind of future they want to build. They are looking for fresh ideas and real engagement, not just slogans and photo opportunities. The newly elected MP remains optimistic about Labour's chances. "We are standing at the threshold of something important," he said. "If we have the courage to embrace change and lead with conviction, we can be the force the country needs at this moment." Whether he and his colleagues will succeed in turning that ambition into reality remains to be seen. But one thing is certain: the next few months will determine not only the direction of British politics but the future of millions of lives across the country.

Voters across the United Kingdom are heading to the polls today to cast their decision in a historic referendum on the country’s future in the European Union. The choice before them is stark: remain part of the EU, or take the unprecedented step of leaving a union that the UK has belonged to for nearly 45 years. Over 44 million registered voters will have their say in one of the most momentous democratic exercises in post-war British history. The result, expected by Friday morning, will shape the UK’s political, economic, and social landscape for decades to come. Prime Minister David Cameron, who called the referendum in an attempt to quell divisions within his Conservative Party over EU reform, is urging voters to back continued membership. He has argued that EU membership provides stability and prosperity, and that leaving would unleash economic uncertainty and put jobs at risk. Opponents of the EU, led by high-profile figures in the Labour and Liberal Democrat parties, as well as a host of business leaders, politicians and grassroots campaigners, are pushing for a Brexit—short for British exit. They claim that the EU curbs national sovereignty and freedom, and that the UK would be stronger outside the bloc, free to negotiate its own trade deals and control its own immigration policies. The debate has been impassioned and, at times, acrimonious. Campaign leaflets have flooded letterboxes, and televised debates have drawn some of the highest ratings in recent years. Social media has played a huge role, with both sides of the argument making strong and at times controversial claims. The stakes could not be higher, and the decision will have far-reaching implications for the UK's relationships with its European neighbours, global trading partners, and international institutions. For many voters, the referendum is more than just a choice about the EU; it is seen as a vote about identity, control and the type of country the UK wants to be in the 21st century. As polling stations open at 07:00 BST, the country waits with bated breath for the outcome. What will ultimately happen will not be known until the votes are counted—but it is a democratic moment that will define a generation. Whether it is remain or leave, one thing is clear: the vote will alter the course of British history. lunches, a new phase of negotiations must begin if the UK is to set its own path beyond the European Union.

Watford head coach Walter Mazzarri is facing a major selection dilemma as he prepares for Saturday’s crucial Premier League clash against Tottenham Hotspur at Vicarage Road. In a surprise admission, Mazzarri revealed that he could be without as many as nine first-team players due to a combination of injuries and suspensions. The news comes at a particularly frustrating time for the Hornets, who sit mid-table and are in need of a strong performance to climb up the league standings before the new year. The Italian tactician, who was appointed in December to provide a fresh impetus to the team, said during a press conference on Thursday: “It’s not ideal at all. We are losing a lot of players through injury, and there are also some suspensions that complicate matters. I’ve already made my squad stronger, but now I need to show I can manage with what I have.” Among the key players missing will be Nigerian forward Isaac Success and England defender Tom Cleverley, both of whom are likely to miss the match through injury. Full-back Britt Assombalonga, who has been a regular in the heart of the midfield, is also sidelined with a knock sustained in training this week. Mazzarri also hinted that as many as four early substitutes could be called upon in the first half to manage the limited options available in the squad. Mazzarri – who has been with the club since 2013 and is widely praised for his tactical acumen and ability to motivate players – was appointed to ensure stability during a turbulent transfer window and the festive period. However, he now faces the grim test of leading a severely weakened squad against a top-half Tottenham side still looking to find consistency in their campaign and being managed by former Watford boss Mauricio Pochettino. He added: “We are not used to having such a fragile squad this deep into the season. Everyone is disappointed, but that is football. I will handle it the best I can and do what I’ve always done—build from what’s in front of me.” The absence of key players will further limit a Watford side already relied heavily on a small number of key players this season. This Saturday’s match will be a true test of Mazzarri’s coaching abilities and the team’s resilience. Some observers believe it may set the tone for the remainder of the season, with the away game against Arsenal on New Year’s Day offering another early challenge.

Two brothers have found themselves facing the devastating reality of eviction from a family farm they have called home for more than two decades — all due to what they describe as a legal miscalculation made in 2003. The farming family, who have spent the past 22 years nurturing the land, now say they are being unfairly cast aside from the very livelihood they helped sustain. The dispute has sparked outrage among local villagers and members of the agricultural community, many of whom have come out in support of the brothers, calling the eviction a betrayal of trust and a continuation of a systemic issue within rural land law. Locals have described the family farm as a cornerstone of the village economy, providing employment and contributing to the local food supply chain. According to the brothers, who have spoken on condition of anonymity due to the ongoing legal proceedings, their rights to the land were never properly documented, and the initial agreement forged back in 2003 — often referred to as an "informal arrangement" — has been incorrectly interpreted or taken advantage of in recent years. They claim that what was intended to be a long-term working agreement has now been twisted into a legal justification for dispossession. “We loved this land, we have put in blood, sweat, and tears to keep the farm viable,” said one of the brothers in a recent interview. “This feels like the government is taking it back from us because we didn't tick every bureaucratic box they expect." The legal ruling that led to their eviction has already been subject to appeal, and the brothers argue that the original 2003 agreement was not cast in stone but rather was based upon mutual understanding and trust — values that are now being flouted in the name of legal formality and rigid documentation procedures. Legal experts analysing the case suggest that it may set a troubling precedent for other small-scale land users and tenants across the UK. There are fears that the ruling fails to account for the realities of rural life, where long-standing verbal agreements and informal arrangements are common for decades, if not generations. The Welsh Government, when contacted, refrained from commenting on the case, but insisted it remains committed to supporting rural communities and ensuring fair practice in land law. Meanwhile, local MPs have also expressed concern and are reportedly considering launching an inquiry into the matter to determine whether justice has truly been served for the farming family.

Residents of a new housing estate in the path of the HS2 high-speed rail project have expressed deep concern and frustration, with many describing their future as “horribly uncertain” following recent government announcements about the planned infrastructure. The UK government has reiterated its commitment to the controversial £106 billion project, which will see a new railway line slicing across the country to connect London with the West Midlands and eventually on to Manchester and Leeds. For those who have recently moved into communities under threat from the construction route, the emotional and financial toll is becoming increasingly palpable. In the small village of Sandwell, for instance, where a number of newly built homes have been erected, families have already formed plans for their children’s birthdays, school runs, and community events—only to now worry they may be forced to leave within months. “We bought this house under the impression it would be home for the foreseeable future,” said Emily Griffith, a mother of two, speaking at a recent protest. "Now, we’re suddenly second-guessing everything—careers, friendships, even our children's schooling.” The latest government statement, issued in the wake of renewed criticism from opposition groups and environmental campaigners, did little to ease residents’ anxieties. While the Department for Transport confirmed that compensation and relocation packages would be made available, many homeowners are not comforted by such assurances, citing the uncertainty surrounding the timing and method of demolition orders. Local MP Simon Mitchell, representing the affected area, said he has been inundated with calls and emails from residents feeling “betrayed” by the pace of the government's communication. “People are angry and scared. They didn’t sign up to have their lives upended with so little prior notice. This isn’t just about being moved out of a house—it’s about losing a sense of security about the future,” he said. The HS2 project has long been a source of contention in British politics and public life alike. Environmental groups decry the scale of land destruction, while economic critics argue that the vast investment could be better spent improving existing rail networks. For the residents at the sharp end of these decisions, however, the debate is deeply personal. One man, speaking on condition of anonymity due to concerns over potential backlash from the Department for Transport, said: “I understand it’s a national project, but it feels like we’re being treated as an afterthought.”

Late Chaos as Ross County Stun Inverness CT in Thrilling Highlands Derby   The Northeast derby between Ross County and Inverness Caledonian Thistle delivered yet another dramatic chapter in a football rivalry steeped in recent tension and close encounters. At a rain-soaked Global Arena in Dingwall on Tuesday night, it was Alex Schalk’s late equaliser that ensured the points were shared, leaving Ross County with a vital point and Inverness CT with a frustrated but narrow lead in this season's top-to-bottom battle. Trailing 1-0 to a first-half goal from the Caley Thistle captain, Ross County looked destined to drop further into the relegation mix, but a moment of brilliance from 18-year-old Dutch teenager Schalk ensured that the visit by Inverness Caledonian Thistle did not come away with the full three points. The equaliser, curling into the top corner with barely ten minutes to play, was a moment that could prove significant in the run-in. "He's only 18, but the confidence in that strike, the way he took the ball and scored like that, that's something I haven’t seen before," said Ross County manager Richie Foran in the post-match press conference. "He only started training with the first team in pre-season, but it just shows what potential we have." The goal was a huge confidence boost for the Staggies, who entered the game as the final placed team in the Scottish Premiership table. With their solitary point lifting them one spot, they now find themselves just two points behind Inverness CT, who move above them thanks to a superior goal difference. For Inverness, the night is a study in frustration. Richie Foran’s side – newly promoted last season and now looking increasingly like promotion material – dominated large portions of the match, controlled the tempo, and had most of the chances. Yet fails to seal the deal with barely a week to go until the end of the season. The result adds to the treacherous nature of the Premiership, where late goals have become a hallmark of recent campaigns. Billy Dodds had given Inverness what looked like a commanding lead after 37 minutes, but Ross County’s relentless fight meant their lead was never a complete one. "We’ve got to be more ruthless," admits Inverness manager Richie Foran (no relation to Ross County's boss) in his own post-match comments.

The UK government has announced plans to trial small convoys of partially self-driving lorries on major roads by the end of next year, in a move aimed at improving efficiency and reducing emissions in the haulage industry. The Department for Transport said the pilot programme, which will see a limited number of platooning motorway experiments, marks a significant step forward in the adoption of automated vehicle technology on British roads. Under the proposal, lorries equipped with advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) will be grouped together in convoys, with the lead truck controlled by a human driver and the following vehicles using automated systems to maintain speed and distance. This so-called “platooning” is expected to reduce fuel consumption and improve road safety by minimising human error. The trials will be conducted on a number of strategic routes, including motorways and A-roads, subject to the approval of the Road Haulage Association and transport regulators. The government said it was working closely with industry partners, including major logistics firms and vehicle manufacturers, to ensure the trial adhered to the highest safety and technical standards. Ministers stressed that the initiative was part of a broader strategy to position the UK as a global leader in the development and deployment of next-generation transport technologies. A spokesperson for the Department for Transport said: “These trials will help us understand the potential of automated vehicle systems in a real-world environment. By embracing innovation, we can make our roads safer and smarter, while also supporting the green growth agenda.” Platooning has already been tested in other European countries, including the Netherlands and Germany, where early results have shown fuel savings of up to 10 per cent in the follower vehicles. In the UK, with its extensive road network and continued reliance on heavy goods vehicles for domestic and international trade, such efficiency gains could have significant economic and environmental benefits. Environmental groups have generally welcomed the news, albeit with cautious optimism. The RSPB and Friends of the Earth both cited the potential for lower carbon emissions as a key step towards fulfilling the UK’s net-zero targets. However, they urged the government to ensure that the trials include thorough environmental impact assessments and that all safety risks are carefully managed. Industry leaders have also expressed support for the trials, as haulage companies face constant pressure to reduce costs and meet increasingly stringent environmental regulations.

Samson Siasia, one of Nigeria's most celebrated football coaches, has announced his decision to walk away from the sport in his country, citing a deeply flawed and “disrespectful system” as the main reason. Known for guiding the Nigerian men’s football team to a historic bronze medal at the 2016 Rio Olympics, Siasia has now left the sport he has dedicated decades of his life to in a bold move that has sent shockwaves through the Nigerian football community. The 62-year-old, who was arguably Nigeria’s most successful football coach, said in a recent statement that the current state of the federations and the lack of clear vision for the future of the game is no longer sustainable. “For too long, we have turned a blind eye to a system that has become increasingly disrespectful to genuine talent, to hard work, and to the love for the national jersey,” Siasia said. “This is not about money. It is about a culture of entitlement, poor planning, and lack of regard for the people who built this nation’s football legacy.” Siasia’s decision comes amidst growing public discontent over the state of football in Nigeria, which is being highlighted by consistent underperformance in international tournaments, poor player management, and high-profile scandals involving officials. Many in the industry believe that Siasia’s departure will only deepen the crisis. Nigeria, once considered one of Africa’s football powerhouses, has seen a decline in its global standing, with failed World Cup bids and poor performances in the Africa Cup of Nations. Siasia, who also led Nigeria to back-to-back Africa Cup of Nations titles in 1994 and 1994, has been a vocal critic of the National Football Association’s structure and governance for years. He has previously called for sweeping reforms, including transparency in funding, better player development, and the promotion of ethics and professionalism in all levels of the game. His exodus now poses a serious question: who will step up to lead Nigeria back to the top of African football? In a statement, his lawyer said Siasia would not be available for comment in the near future but would make a full public address “at the right time.” For now, the landscape of Nigerian football has been left to a new generation of leaders with little path forged ahead. The road back for Nigeria appears uncertain, and with the departure of one of its most respected figures, the cost of change may now be higher than ever.

Fresh anti-Japan protests have erupted across China as tensions flared on the anniversary of Japan’s 1931 invasion of north-eastern China, with demonstrators expressing anger over ongoing disputes over a chain of uninhabited islands in the East China Sea. The islands, known as the Diaoyu in China and the Senkaku in Japan, have been a flashpoint in Sino-Japanese relations for years, with both nations making strong territorial claims. A wave of mass protests erupted in cities including Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou as anger over historical grievances and present-day confrontations boiled over once again. The protests, which saw thousands of demonstrators gather under the watchful eyes of police, were sparked by a mix of patriotic fervour and frustration over what many Chinese see as repeated Japanese disrespect for China’s sovereignty and historical sensitivities. Participants waved Chinese flags, shouted anti-Japan slogans, and in some instances turned violent, with reports of stores selling Japanese cars and electronic goods being vandalised. The 88th anniversary of Japan’s invasion of the Chinese province of Manchuria, which marked the beginning of the Second Sino-Japanese War, served as a painful reminder of a brutal chapter in East Asian history. Many in China view the continued disputes over the Diaoyu/Senkaku Islands as an extension of Japan’s imperial legacy and a disregard for the region's painful past. The Chinese government has called on Japan to respect historical truths and to resolve the disputes through peaceful means. Despite these calls, tensions have remained high, with both countries increasing naval patrols in the area. Japan, for its part, has reiterated its firm stance that the islands are under its administrative control, while also acknowledging the need to resolve the issue through dialogue and mutual respect. Analysts suggest that China’s aggressive response is not only about the islands themselves but also about asserting national pride and the assertiveness of the Communist Party under President Xi Jinping. The timing of the protests also underscores the growing influence of nationalist sentiment in Chinese public life, which has become an important political tool for expressing national identity and resilience. As the world watches the simmering Sino-Japanese conflict, there is growing concern about the potential for accidental escalation in the region, as both nations continue to navigate a fragile space between assertiveness and diplomacy. The recent outburst of anger among Chinese citizens represents a reflection of the deeply ingrained historical and territorial grievances that remain unresolved in one of Asia’s most strategically contested waters.

Britain’s Helen Glover and Heather Stanning extended their remarkable unbeaten record to 28 consecutive races as they retained their women’s pair title at the World Rowing Championships in Rotterdam today. In a display of precision, power, and long-established teamwork, the £250,000 gold medallists from the 2012 and 2016 Olympics demonstrated once again why they are regarded as the most consistent double scull partnership in the sport. Stanning, a first-time Olympian in 2016 who pulled off a dramatic gold in the heat of London under the most intense pressure, and Glover, the veteran of the pair who had already won gold in 2012 and then bronze only two years later in Brazil, once again showcased their unrelenting commitment to perfection. Their race was a dominant one from the outset, with the pair maintaining a steady rhythm and matching the pace of their nearest rival, New Zealand, almost breakfast, before distancing themselves late in the final 500 metres to cross the finish line by 1.2 seconds. Glover, 33, who has now secured three world titles, reflected on the latest win with characteristic humility. “It's been a tough season with high expectations, but we’ve stuck to the process and focused on what we can control," she said. “It's amazing – 28 wins in a row – but it really means more now because the competition is getting stronger every year.” Stanning, 29, who joined forces with Glover in 2013, said the key to their longevity was not only their ability to work in unison on the water but also the trust they had in each other and their coaches. “We’ve had some near misses in recent years, about five or six races where the gold just narrowly eluded us, but this consistency shows how much we've grown together,” she said. Their victory marks another step in a staggering domestic and international dominance, with over 100 senior international victories to their name. The pair have become a symbol of resilience and adaptability, overcoming the intense pressure of Olympic golds and the challenges of changing formations to remain at the top of their sport. The win comes with special significance given the fact that Stanning had to recover from a serious neck injury earlier this year. Her return to the sport has been nothing short of inspirational, and if anything, her performance today proved that she is just as fierce a competitor as she ever was.

I recently met Greece’s former finance minister, Yanis Varoufakis, in the lobby of a five-star hotel in Athens. It was the kind of quiet corner of the capital that still whispers of a bygone era: marble floors, hushed conversation and the faint echo of a city once at the heart of the European crisis. Varoufakis, a figure who once stood at the sharp edge of history, had stepped back from the political stage but was not content to remain in the shadows. His face, etched with the marks of a battle that consumed a nation and tested the very soul of the European Union, bore the look of a man who had seen too much—and who was still willing to say it. Greece, now six years on from its most public and dramatic confrontation with its creditors, remains a country in flux. The bailout demands from the Troika—comprising the International Monetary Fund, the European Commission and the European Central Bank—had imposed relentless austerity, sparking protests, strikes and a political realignment that saw hard-left Syriza rise from obscurity to power in 2015. At the heart of that storm was Varoufakis, the former economics professor turned radical negotiator, who became a symbol of both resistance and pragmatism in the face of an unrelenting crisis. Sitting in a corner of the hotel, sipping strong Greek coffee, he seemed almost at peace with the journey his country had endured. “What happened in those negotiations was not just about money,” he said, his voice calm, measured and laced with someone who knows he has spoken these words before. “It was about power, sovereignty and the kind of Europe we want—or allow.” He gestured with his hand, as if mapping out in the air the contours of a continent that had been pulled in competing directions. Varoufakis is often portrayed as a firebrand—he even wore red sneakers to European finance minister meetings—but his unflinching intellectual rigour, sharp wit and refusal to pander to European elites marked him as a man unwilling to compromise on principles. During the 2015 crisis, his radical stance sparked fear in financial circles. As Greece stood at the brink of default, Varoufakis challenged the narrative that austerity was the only option, demanding a restructuring of Greece’s crushing €320bn debt and a rethinking of the rules that bound nations to suffocating fiscal policy.

Llandrindod Wells, a once-prosperous spa town in rural Powys, has long been steeped in history, but its role during World War One is now being vividly resurrected through the use of digital codes and interactive technology. The town, renowned in the 19th century for its mineral-rich springs and grand Victorian architecture, transformed into a critical military hub as British forces gathered ahead of deployment to the Western Front. Today, thanks to a new heritage initiative, this forgotten chapter of the town’s past is being brought back to life, offering visitors and locals alike a unique window into the experiences of the thousands of soldiers who once called Llandrindod Wells home. At the heart of the project is a series of digital "memory markers" scattered across the town. These QR codes, linked to a custom app, allow users to scan their surroundings and access a range of archival material — from photographs and handwritten letters to audio recordings and virtual re-creations of historic buildings that have since been lost or altered. The initiative was developed by the Llandrindod Wells Historical Society in collaboration with the National Archives, and funded by a combination of local, Welsh Government, and Heritage Lottery grants. For many, the town’s war-time history is only vaguely understood. Between 1914 and 1918, Llandrindod Wells – then home to fewer than 4,000 civilians – hosted over 13,000 troops. Its large facilities, including the Rhos-on-Sea-type military camp built in just weeks at the outbreak of the war, transformed the once-cosy resort into a bustling military base. Soldiers from all corners of the British Empire passed through the town, using it as a key stop for training and preparations before being shipped off to the front lines. Dr. Hannah Rees, a historian and project lead for the digital initiative, said the use of technology allowed for a more immersive experience. “This isn’t just about reading text in a guestbook,” she said. “This is about standing where the soldiers stood and hearing their voices through the very places they once inhabited. You can see the camp sites, the drill halls that have disappeared, and hear the personal stories of men who lived and died in the Great War.” The project also marks a broader resurgence of interest in the role of Wales during the conflict. While the capital, Cardiff, often stands at the forefront of remembrance efforts in the UK, smaller towns like Llandrindod Wells played a vital behind-the-scenes role.

Fewer Than One in Five Beggars in England and Wales Are Homeless, Police Data Reveals   In a surprising twist to the commonly held assumption that begging is often a symptom of homelessness, new data obtained by  BBC Breakfast  reveals that fewer than one in five people arrested for begging in England and Wales in 2023 were actually homeless. The figures, compiled from police records across the country, cast doubt on prevailing stereotypes and raise questions about the ethics and policy surrounding the enforcement of anti-begging laws. The data, shared as part of a freedom of information request, shows that out of the 1,184 arrests for begging reported by police forces, just 189 (or roughly 16%) of those individuals were recorded as homeless by police at the time. The remaining 995 arrests, accounting for the majority of cases, occurred without the person being identified as homeless—leading to urgent calls for a closer examination of when, and why, people are being detained for begging. Begging laws, which remain in place in parts of England and Wales despite long-standing controversy, permit police to arrest individuals for asking for money, offering services, or inviting someone to assist in a crime. Many of these laws date back to the Victorian era, and there have been repeated appeals—and, in some areas, informal agreements—to avoid their enforcement for those who are truly homeless and in desperate need. The findings confirm long-standing concerns raised by charities and homelessness support groups. Sarah Sillett, chief executive of the Crisis charity, said, “It is deeply concerning that people are being criminalised for trying to survive. Too often, we see those who are not homeless—whether they be tourists, money-lenders, or opportunists—presenting as vulnerable individuals and then being unfairly targeted.” In response to the data, the Home Office said it “recognises the importance of supporting vulnerable individuals” and that “homelessness is a housing issue, not a criminal one.” However, they stop short of calling for a national review of begging laws, stating that local authorities have the discretion to interpret and enforce the laws in line with national guidance. The lack of national data on the demographics of those arrested raises further questions. Websites and shelters often report that begging can act as a temporary livelihood for some non-homeless individuals—particularly those with mental health issues or substance abuse problems. In such cases, arrest rather than help is often the result.

A group of teenagers who came together to heal divisions in their community after the 2011 London riots will take part in the FA Cup for the first time in their history, more than a decade after their formation. Redbridge Forest Kicks, based in Chigwell, Essex, will face Bromley, a team from the National League, in the first round of the historic competition, providing a remarkable platform for the young team of under-18 players from a mixed area of social housing and private estates. Founded by 16-year-old Connor Hannaway in the wake of the riots, when youths in parts of London and other cities came out to loot, burn and devastate urban areas, the club was inspired to build bridges and tackle gang violence in south-east England’s gritty suburbs. Hannaway, who left the club shortly after its formation to play for Chigwell and Epping United in the Essex Olympian League, is now at the University of East Anglia, but remains proud of the club’s journey from local football initiative to being granted a non-league FA Cup place, the first for a side of its kind. Speaking to The Guardian, one of the current players, 17-year-old Idris Femi, said their inclusion in the FA Cup was “a proud moment for us—it shows what we can do when we put our differences aside and build something together.” Their inclusion in the draw was part of the FA’s Youth Club Development Scheme, an initiative aiming to give young and underrepresented teams the chance to participate in the world’s oldest football competition. Last season, Spalding United, a Sunday League side, pulled off one of the biggest upsets in FA Cup history by defeating Championship side Stoke City 2-1 at the Britannia Stadium. This year, Bromley are firm favourites to progress but Redbridge Forest Kicks said they were “not just there to walk over.” Their campaign has been backed by the local housing association, as well as community leaders and volunteers. The FA Cup has long held a tradition of rewarding smaller teams that demonstrate strong community spirit and initiative, and the inclusion of Redbridge Forest Kicks marks another step in the competition’s commitment to recognizing such grass-roots efforts. With a young squad full of aspiring footballers and role models in the making, the match promises to be more than a football fixture—it is a celebration of the power of sport to unite communities and build a better future.

A Leader’s Passport to Peace: The Last Walk with Martin McGuinness   Buffeted by a freezing wind on a chilly afternoon last April, I found myself walking with Martin McGuinness and his dog, Roisin, around an ancient Irish hill fort on the Inishowen Peninsula in Donegal. The location, a place of archaeological significance and quiet beauty, felt worlds away from the political tensions that once shaped his remarkable lifetime — yet it was a fitting backdrop for a man who had done more than most to redefine what peace in Ireland could look like. McGuinness, former Deputy First Minister of Northern Ireland and one of the most transformative figures in the country’s modern political landscape, had come to this part of Ireland with both the past and the future in mind. The hill fort, a Neolithic site rising from the landscape like a sleeping giant, was a place for contemplation. But more than that, it marked the beginning of an extended visit by the republican leader to the south, a trip aimed at deepening Anglo-Irish and North-South connections, planting the seeds for a new era of collaboration between the island’s two halves. As we walked, the bones of ancient walls beneath our feet and the Atlantic wind tugging at our coats, McGuinness spoke with a rare warmth and honesty. At times, he paused, watching Roisin chase a butterfly through the heather, and for a moment, his face betrayed not the warrior-politician but the ordinary man. “You see this place,” he said, gesturing to the wind-swept hills that stretched across the horizon, “it reminds me that this island has always been a place of conflict and peace, of division and unity. We’d do well to remember that as we chart our next steps.” McGuinness, whose political evolution remains one of the most remarkable in recent memory, had journeyed the length of this island from thuggish revolutionary to peacemaker. Once commander of the IRA’s Derry unit, he emerged from the ranks of Sinn Féin to become Deputy First Minister at Stormont in 2007 as part of a democratic power-sharing agreement. His partnership with Democratic Unionist Party leader Peter Robinson was emblematic of a political reconciliation that many had written off as impossible. This journey through the west of Ireland was part of an effort to foster a deeper, more inclusive Irish identity. Over the course of several days, he visited schools, met with civil society leaders and met personally with descendants of those affected by the brutal conflict.

A Breath of Change: Atmosphere Detected Around Earth-like Exoplanet   In a groundbreaking discovery that has the potential to rewrite our understanding of the search for life beyond Earth, scientists have announced that they have, for the first time, detected an atmosphere surrounding an Earth-like exoplanet. This historic achievement, published in a recent edition of  Nature Astronomy , marks a major step forward in the field of planetary science and fuels renewed hope that life could exist beyond our solar system. The planet in question, known as GJ 1132 b, lies approximately 39 light-years from Earth in the constellation of Vela. It is roughly 1.2 times the size of Earth and is classified as a "super-Earth" due to its mass and density. Located in the "temperate zone" of its host star, where temperatures could allow for the existence of liquid water, the exoplanet has long intrigued scientists for its potential to mirror conditions on Earth. Using the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope (VLT) in Chile, an international team of researchers, including scientists from the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy, were able to detect signs of an atmosphere—potentially rich in water vapour—by observing the planet as it passed in front of its star. This technique, known as transit spectroscopy, allows scientists to study the light that filters through the planet's atmosphere, detecting the signature of different gases. Dr. Laura Delrez, a lead researcher on the project from the University of Liège, Belgium, said: “We are extremely excited by this result. Until now, we had only confirmed the presence of atmospheres around gas giants or planets that are hotter than the surface of Venus. Now, for the first time, we have evidence that rocky, Earth-like planets may also host their own atmospheres.” The discovery raises important questions about the planet’s ability to support life. While GJ 1132 b is likely too dense and too close to its star to be habitable, the detection of an atmosphere suggests that such features may be more common than previously thought. If rocky exoplanets can maintain atmospheres, then the possibility of finding those with the right conditions for life—such as oxygen, water, or even clouds—becomes significantly more plausible. The findings come at a crucial moment as space agencies around the world prepare for the next phase of exoplanet exploration. The James Webb Space Telescope, set to launch later this year, is expected to build on this research, offering unprecedented detail on the chemical composition of planetary atmospheres.

John Higgins secured a commanding 10-7 lead over defending champion Mark Selby on day one of the World Championship final at the Crucible Theatre in Sheffield on Saturday. The match, eagerly anticipated by snooker fans from around the globe, saw the “Rocket” demonstrate the technical brilliance and poise that have earned him four Crucible titles, matching Selby’s achievement while outplaying the defending champion on his home turf. Higgins, a fan favourite known for his meticulous style and tactical mastery, got off to a blistering start as he took the first three frames to open the tie. The early momentum served as a statement of intent under the bright lights of the Theatre, where only the world’s top players compete. Selby, the 2016 champion and a gritty survivor in numerous high-stakes encounters, responded with characteristic determination, clawing back two of them to push Higgins all the way. What made Higgins’ performance all the more impressive was the tactical resilience he showed in the late frames of the session after Selby dominated a crucial six-frame run to 7-6. Higgins broke the spell with a clinical century break and a string of key half-centuries—pushing his advantage to 10-7 going into the second day. His ability to remain composed under pressure has often defined his performances at the Crucible, and it was no different here. Selby, who has previously triumphed in four of the last six World Championship final appearances, showed why he remains one of the most formidable players in the sport. His tactical patience and cueing precision led to a number of low-scoring but high-intensity games, particularly in the middle session. The holder made a best break of 68 as he fought back from 6-4 down, keeping the match poised and thrilling for the full two sessions. The Crucible crowd, which had seen an early shortfall in attendances this year, was fully behind the reigning champion and created an electrifying atmosphere in the later stages, particularly for Selby’s formative play. However, Higgins ultimately weathered the storm to go into the final day holding the upper hand. The worlds champion will now look to close out the title on Sunday as he attempts to reclaim the crown for the first time since 2011—when he last competed in the final. Higgins, who has spent 23 seasons in the world's top 16, is searching for number five and his first since his celebrated run of wins in the 2000s.

Ulster have made three key changes to their starting line-up for Saturday's high-stakes Pro12 clash against Munster in Limerick, as they look to reignite their title ambitions in what promises to be a fiercely contested interprovincial showdown. Jacob Stockdale, Andrew Trimble and Chris Henry have all been introduced to the starting XV, signals that head coach Leslie Rees is looking to bolster the province’s creative edge and physicality on the day. The game, set to take place at Thomond Park under bright Saturday afternoon skies, is vital for Ulster’s hopes in the league and also adds further intrigue to the ongoing rivalry with their Irish neighbours. Munster, sitting comfortably at the top of the Pro12 table, will be eager to continue their dominance at home, while Ulster must respond to last weekend’s narrow defeat by Leinster and ensure they don’t fall too far in the race for Europe. Trimble, breaking a lengthy injury absence, returns on the wing, partnering with the dynamic Jacob Stockdale in what could be a potent backline combination. Trimble’s return is a major boost for Ulster, whose attempts to stretch defending sides have often fallen short in recent weeks. Stockdale, meanwhile, has been in sparkling form this season and will look to use his blistering pace to test the Munster defence early on. Flanker Chris Henry’s inclusion at openside gives Ulster added ball-carrying options and a more aggressive edge in the breakdown. His inclusion comes as Sila Puafisi is rested, with Rees clearly opting for experience and work rate in one of the most gruelling fixtures of the Pro12 season. The decision reflects the coach’s strategy to control the physical and tactical tempo of the match from the outset. Munster, in contrast, are expected to start with their usual starting XV, having enjoyed a 23-9 victory over Connacht last weekend. Head coach Anthony Foley is confident his side can close out the 2017-18 campaign with a strong finish, with his players keen to leave a mark before a potentially significant summer of change. The atmosphere at Thomond Park will undoubtedly be electric. Saturday’s match not only carries weight in the league standings but also serves as a final chapter in the domestic season for the two most decorated Irish provinces. Ulster’s hopes of a place in the European Champions Cup rest on them finishing in the top four, and securing a win against Munster would do more than just ease nerves — it could reignite what had been a title dream at the start of the campaign.

Rapper Invites Donald Trump to Chicago Amid Tense Election Rhetoric   In a bold and unexpected move, US rapper and Grammy Award-winning artist Che “Rhymefest” Smith has extended a public invitation to Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump, urging him to visit Chicago in what the musician says is a bid to “show the real city” and counter what he has described as an overly negative portrayal of America’s third-largest city. Smith, a long-time Chicago native and prominent figure in the hip-hop community, made the call on stage during a recent performance. Speaking to a packed crowd at the metro’s annual Black Innovators Summit, he challenged Trump’s often-critical remarks about Chicago’s crime and poverty, which he said were taken out of context and failed to reflect the city’s progress and diversity. “I am not afraid of this election,” Smith said, addressing the audience. “But I am afraid of the narrative being twisted about cities like ours. So I’m inviting Mr Trump to come to Chicago this fall. Let him drive in his car through the south and west sides, not in the back of a motorcade. Let him walk through the neighborhoods himself and see what the real story is.” The statement quickly went viral on social media, as users and political commentators debated the implications of such an invitation. Some lauded the move as a powerful example of using music and activism to challenge political rhetoric, while others questioned whether Trump would take the offer seriously, given the deep political divide in the run-up to the general election. Chicago has long been a focal point in national political debates, particularly over issues of urban crime and economic inequality. Trump has frequently highlighted the city’s challenges during campaign stops and media appearances, using them as a case study in what he has called the “disaster” of liberal governance. But Smith, who is known for his activism on issues of education, voting rights and racial justice, sees this as an opportunity to highlight the city's resilience and culture. “Chicago is not the place you read about on the front page of every newspaper,” he said. “We have artists, scientists, educators, entrepreneurs, and scientists. We have worlds within worlds.” While Trump has yet to respond to the invitation, political observers suggest the offer may not only be a nuanced rebuttal to the Republican candidate’s rhetoric but also a symbolic gesture calling for a more informed and respectful political discourse.

Women at high genetic risk of breast cancer could soon have a new and less drastic way to manage their risk, other than undergoing a double mastectomy, as scientists reveal progress in the development of preventive drug treatments. In a ground-breaking development, early trials of risk-reducing medications have shown promising results in slowing or halting the development of early-stage pre-cancerous cells in high-risk patients, offering an alternative to the lifetime of self-monitoring or surgery that many currently face. This breakthrough comes as a growing number of women carry BRCA gene mutations, or other genetic markers, which significantly increase the likelihood of developing breast cancer, but who may otherwise not show any signs of the disease. For years, the primary preventive option for such patients, famously adopted by Angelina Jolie, has been a double mastectomy. However, this is not without its risks and is an emotionally and physically challenging decision for many. A multi-centre trial involving women with BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations is now underway and has found that targeted drugs — in some cases repurposed from existing chemotherapy treatments — can reduce the formation of breast cancer-related cells over time. The drugs work by addressing the faults in DNA repair mechanisms caused by the gene mutations, effectively "locking down" malignant potential early on. Dr. Sarah White, a leading consultant in cancer genetics and one of the researchers involved in the national trial, said the new treatment could become a game-changer for high-risk patients. “These drugs are not a cure, but they offer a level of control and prevention that surgery does not, and for women who want to retain their breasts and reduce their risk without undergoing a major operation, it’s a life-changing development.” Health experts have welcomed the findings as a potential milestone in the personalisation of cancer care, particularly for those who do not wish to or are not physically suited to mastectomies. The first of these drugs could be approved for wider use within the next two to three years, depending on finalised clinical trials. Such developments follow the recent National Health Service (NHS) expansion of screening for high-risk women and increased genetic testing across the country. With the growing acceptance of precision medicine, the hope is that such targeted treatment will become a standard of care for those who want alternatives to surgical intervention. For now, cancer charities and patient advocacy groups are calling for further funding to ensure these drugs are accessible to all who need them on the NHS, and for more public awareness of the non-surgical choices now on the horizon

Sighs of happiness, I imagine, filled the upper echelons of British horse racing, especially amongst officials at Royal Ascot, on the famous fixture's fifth and final day. After months of tight regulations, widespread uncertainty, and a global health crisis that seemed set to puncture the very fabric of traditional events, the Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Jubilee Stakes concluded a historic—and incidentally unique—Ascot in style. This year’s Royal Meeting, held under mitigated circumstances and with a social-distancing protocol that would make a chessboard look crowded, nonetheless delivered the drama, the colour, and the grandeur that the centuries-old event is known for. It was not only a celebration of sport, but also the symbolic lifting of a veil on the uncertain future of event-based spectator sports in the UK. The presence of the Queen herself, albeit from the safety of a distanced and strategically placed seat, signalled to an anxious nation that the old institutions were not only still standing but adapting and thriving in unprecedented times. Ascot, a festival usually awash with 80,000 spectators—and a highlight of the British summer social season—was drastically reduced, with capacity capped and procedures introduced to restrict contact and prevent spread. Yet to those in attendance, including a careful selection of VIPs and media representatives, it felt little less than the grand occasion it has always aspired to be. The hems and hems of Haymarket, the silks and spurs of staff, and the thunderous gallop of thoroughbreds across Epsom’s hallowed ground all combined to create a spectacle that was not merely watched, but felt. Winnie the Pooh made a very appropriate return to the balcony as the central figure in a new artwork unveiled to commemorate the Queen’s Platinum Jubilee. His place there sent a gentle, whimsical message: that this was not just a sporting event, but part of the national narrative—a shared national memory, unbroken by circumstances that have reshaped so much else. Moments of tradition were preserved with almost ritualistic accuracy. Signals were raised as the horses turned for home; jackets were handed, hens thrust into waiting pockets, bets whispered. There was even time for a joke or two—perhaps necessary with lunches delivered in crates and pre-packed sandwiches proudly consumed under the shade of a brolly. Yet it was the racing itself that set the tone of the day.
