This Christmas will be like no other thanks to an unforgettable proposal that turned a difficult year into a promising new chapter, write  Reader Helen James , 32, from Glasgow. Just weeks after I lost my job, found out my long-term flatmate was moving out and finally allowed myself to believe things were settling down again, my boyfriend Radek threw caution to the wind – both literally and figuratively. We had enjoyed a quiet evening at home with a bottle of wine and some Christmas cards when he insisted on taking me out for a midnight walk, as it was one of the first warm December nights this year. I was too exhausted to argue – too exhausted, perhaps, to even notice the plan unfolding before me. But the real plan only revealed itself when we reached the Mycești Park near our flat. There’s a specific bench there, one I’d sat on on several occasions and I jokingly asked why he had brought me there again. That’s when Radek dropped to one knee – in front of a dozen friends he’d arranged to be hiding in the hides, with fairy lights strung along the bare branches over our heads and a sign that read, 'Helen, will you be my wife? Yes, no, maybe?' It was unexpected, moving, and as we’ve since found out, also quite photographable – our friends got some beautiful images of the moment. I said yes, of course, because really, what else could you say? It was the perfect end to a year that was full of peaks and valleys. Radek and I met five years ago in Glasgow, and over the last two years, we’ve built a life together – with all the ups and downs that entails. We've shared through tough jobs, difficult house moves, and even a few ugly Christmas jumpers (his). But this moment, right here, right now, is one I’ll never forget. As we prepare to open the first of our Christmas cards together, I can’t help but feel that this year will always be remembered as the year everything changed – and for the better. As Radek said as he slipped the ring onto my finger: 'We’re just getting started.' Now, I can’t help but wonder what comes next – and I’m looking forward to finding out, together.  Have you got a story you’d like to share with the  Glasgow Echo ?

British Cycling has announced a comprehensive overhaul of its medical services for athletes in response to an independent review commissioned to assess the club’s support structures in the wake of rising concerns about athlete welfare. The governing body, which has enjoyed widespread success in disciplines ranging from track cycling to road racing, described the review as a "timely" opportunity to ensure that medical support is meeting the evolving needs of both elite and developing athletes. The announcement comes as British Cycling continues to dominate the international cycling scene, with riders such as Sir Bradley Wiggins, Chris Froome and Laura Kenny winning Olympic and World Championship medals in recent years. However, behind the success stories, questions have been raised about the pressures on athletes and the nature of the support they receive from the organisation, particularly in terms of physical and mental health. The review, conducted by an external panel of sports medicine and well-being experts, highlighted several areas for improvement, including the integration of mental health support within the club’s medical framework and the better monitoring of athletes’ overall well-being throughout their careers. Current protocols in place at the club have also been subject to scrutiny, particularly concerning the transparency of drug testing procedures and the handling of injuries. In a statement, a spokesperson for British Cycling said: "We are committed to ensuring that all our athletes receive the highest possible standard of care, both on and off the track. The recommendations from the review have highlighted key areas for development, and we are proud to be taking these steps to strengthen our support systems and protect the long-term health of our riders." Among the initiatives to be introduced are enhanced access to sports psychologists, improved communication between team doctors and riders, and a new athlete feedback system to assess medical care. British Cycling also confirmed that all medical staff would undergo additional training in trauma management and athlete-specific dietary support. The move has been welcomed by both athletes and athletes’ unions, who have long called for greater accountability and transparency in the management of rider health. One professional cyclist, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said: "Many of us feel like numbers rather than people. To know that the club is taking active steps to address these concerns is a relief. It's about time." The changes are set to be phased in over the next 12 months, with the first round of updated protocols expected to be in place by the time of the UCI Track Cycling World Championships in Australia later this year.

Welsh Conservative leader Andrew RT Davies has called on UK ministers to do more to involve people in Wales in the Brexit process, stressing that Welsh citizens must have a “bigger stake” in the complex negotiations shaping their country’s future outside the European Union. Speaking at a party event in Cardiff, Davies said that while the UK government was responsible for leading Brexit negotiations, there was a “clear need” for greater transparency and engagement with Welsh communities. Davies argued that Wales, which voted to leave the EU by a margin of 52.5 per cent to 47.5 per cent in the 2016 referendum, has not received the same level of attention as Scotland and Northern Ireland. “The national interest is vital, but we must also remember that the interests of Welsh communities must not be overlooked,” he said. “This is not just about Whitehall; it is about the people of Wales and how they will be affected by the decisions made in London.” His comments come as concerns grow in Wales over areas such as agricultural subsidies, devolution powers, and the impact of new trade barriers. Wales is the most agricultural of the UK nations, and many farmers, fishermen, and small business owners have expressed fears that the UK’s withdrawal from the EU could disrupt supply chains and reduce access to European markets. The Welsh Labour government, led by First Minister Mark Drakeford, has repeatedly called for a shared approach between the UK and Welsh parliaments to manage the impact of Brexit. Welsh Labour has also pushed for a Welsh Brexit minister and greater control over the principles guiding the UK’s withdrawal negotiations. However, the UK government has so far resisted calls to expand the role of the devolved administrations. Davies, while committing the Welsh Conservatives to a pro-Brexit stance, said there must be “clarity” from Westminster about how Wales will benefit from leaving the EU. “We must be clear that the doors are open to Welsh voices,” he added. “Brexit is not just for England; it is for the whole of the United Kingdom.” His remarks were welcomed by some pro-Brexit groups in Wales, though critics have accused the Welsh Conservatives of waiting too long to speak out on such an issue. Meanwhile, unions and business leaders have called for urgent action to mitigate the economic impact of Brexit on Wales, particularly in sectors such as manufacturing and agriculture.

A new government study has revealed the devastatingly high toll of gun-related injuries on American children, with approximately 1,300 children under the age of 17 dying each year from gunshot wounds. Published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the report underscores the urgent need for targeted legislative measures and community-based interventions aimed at reducing the frequency and impact of gun violence on the nation’s youngest citizens. The findings have been met with a wave of concern by public health advocates, who argue that gun violence remains a preventable public health crisis requiring immediate action. According to the study, children under the age of 10 account for a small but alarming share of these fatalities, with the majority occurring in teenagers. The study found that suicides and homicides make up the bulk of gun-related deaths, with an increasing number linked to school and home environments. Linda Wood, a pediatric epidemiologist at the CDC and lead author of the report, described the statistics as a "wake-up call for policymakers and community leaders." "These are not isolated incidents. This is a national pattern that reflects the deep structural issues surrounding gun access and safety," she said in a press briefing. Gun violence is not evenly distributed across the country. The report pointed out a marked difference in mortality rates between urban and rural areas, with children in densely populated regions facing a significantly higher risk. However, it also noted a concerning rise in fatal incidents in suburban and rural communities, areas traditionally considered to be safer. The findings come as Congress deliberates over new federal legislation to tighten firearm regulations, particularly those affecting younger individuals. Proposals currently under consideration include universal background checks, a ban on high-capacity magazines, and the expansion of red-flag laws, which allow the temporary removal of firearms from individuals considered a risk to themselves or others. Public vigils and calls for action have already started to spread across the country, with prominent child advocacy groups pushing for stronger gun control measures. "Every death is one too many," said Sarah Mason, spokesperson for the Children for Peace Foundation. "We need action at every level—to protect our children, to ensure that gun violence is removed as a threat to their safety and their future." The study adds to an already growing body of evidence highlighting the need for sustained focus on the issue of youth and gun violence.

The heartbreak of families bereaved by the devastating effects of drug abuse is sharply in focus in Tuesday's newspapers, with real-life tragedies serving as a painful reminder of the ongoing crisis tearing through communities across the UK. The emotional toll on loved ones is laid bare in harrowing personal accounts and investigative reports that highlight the rise in drug-related deaths and the urgent need for a more robust response from government and healthcare bodies. In the wake of yet another record year for drug-related fatalities, newspapers have turned their attention to the personal stories behind the staggering statistics. One article details the journey of Sarah Johnson, from Swansea, whose son, aged just 21, died from a fentanyl overdose last year. In an open letter published in the  Daily Wales , she writes: “The grief is a constant companion. I never get used to it. I just keep hoping someone – anyone – will do something to stop this from happening to other mothers and fathers.” Such stories are becoming alarmingly common. Health officials have reported that drug-related deaths have surged by 30% over the past decade, with Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland among the worst affected regions. The lack of effective treatment services, combined with the rampant availability of potent synthetic drugs like fentanyl and xylazine, is raising fears among public health experts that the crisis is spiralling further out of control. In response, papers call for a compassionate yet firm approach to tackling the issue, one that goes beyond the current system of punitive measures. Community support groups and addiction specialists are urging the government to invest in education, prevention, and expanded access to treatment services. "We need to treat this like the public health emergency it is," said Dr James Porter, a consultant at Cardiff Addiction Services. "This is not just about locking people up or waiting for another death to hit the headlines." The human cost of drug addiction is beyond measure, but for vulnerable families like Sarah's, the pain is all too real. As the nation is reminded of the faces and names behind each stat, the need for action has never been more urgent. Parents, siblings, and friends are demanding answers – and desperately hoping for change. The heartache is waiting to happen again – unless something is done. As one editorial in  The Welsh Gazette  poignantly states: “Every story like Sarah's is a plea for reflection, for action, and for a future where no family has to live with this kind of loss.”

Morrisons layoffs to hit 720 jobs at Bradford headquarters   A significant blow has been dealt to the retail sector in West Yorkshire as supermarket chain Morrisons announced plans to cut 720 jobs at its headquarters in Bradford. The move, part of a broader strategy to streamline operations and reduce costs, has sent shockwaves through the local community and sparked concerns over the future of the company’s presence in the city. The affected employees work in a range of departments, including finance, marketing, logistics, and customer services. Morrisons, which is headquartered in Bradford and is the UK’s fourth-largest supermarket chain, said the job losses were not a result of financial instability, but part of a "reorganisation" involving the adoption of new technology and the automation of key processes. In a statement, Morrisons confirmed that voluntary redundancy packages would be offered to employees who are eligible. Those who choose to stay will see their roles evolve with increased reliance on digital tools and systems. However, details of further support for those likely to lose their jobs remain scarce, with workers and local unions calling for more clarity on retraining and support packages. Unite the union, which represents many of the employees at the headquarters, expressed its disappointment at the decision. Steve Davis, regional officer for Unite, said: "It is devastating to see such a major employer in Bradford announce these cuts. These are skilled jobs, held often by long-serving staff, and the loss of these roles will be felt not just by those affected, but their families and the local economy as a whole." The job losses form part of a wider trend in the supermarket industry, where automation, increased online shopping, and cost-cutting measures are leading to widespread restructuring. Morrisons has faced increasing pressure in recent years from more agile online competition and the encroachment of discount retailers such as Lidl and Aldi into major supermarket markets. Reacting to the news, local MPs are urging the company and the government to step in to mitigate the social and economic impact. Burgess of Steornagh MP Eddie Hughes called for an explanation and clarity on whether the cuts will affect any planned regeneration projects in Bradford, including the Morrisons-owned Arndale Centre. “We need to understand what this means for sustained investment in the city and how the company plans to support the affected workers,” he said. The announcement comes as Morrisons continues to report slowing sales in its high-street stores, although it has seen some growth in online and click-and-collect services.

Calls have been growing for stronger legal measures to safeguard ambulance control room staff who face regular verbal abuse from members of the public when they attempt to assist in emergency situations. The plea follows recent reports of callers using offensive language, swearing, and even making death threats during 999 calls, putting added strain on already overstretched emergency services. Campaigners, support groups, and unions representing ambulance staff are urging the government to introduce harsher penalties for those who deliberately abuse workers in these critical roles, arguing that the current threat of penalty fines is not a sufficient deterrent. According to the National Union of Public Employees (NUPE), abuse from the public is now one of the top three causes of stress-related illness among emergency call-handlers. The union’s latest report highlights a 40% increase in recorded incidents of abuse over the last two years, with verbal attacks on control room staff rising from 120 in 2021 to over 200 in 2022. The report adds that some calls are taken in silence by police, leaving the perpetrators unchecked and, in some cases, returning to make more abusive calls. Among the most high-profile incidents was the case of a call-handler from the West Midlands Ambulance Service who received a series of abusive calls including death threats while responding to an elderly couple who had called for help after a fall. “It's not just about the language—it’s about the menace, the threats, and the constant dehumanisation of our workers,” said Sarah Thompson, a spokesperson for the Ambulance Staff Association. MPs from across the political spectrum have now added their voices to the call for reform. Labour leader Keir Starmer said, “These are public servants risking their lives to protect and save others. The idea that some people are free to hurl abuse about without consequence is an outrage.” Conservative MP John Bickford, who chairs the Health and Emergency Services Committee, also backed the move, suggesting the government should consider introducing up to two years’ imprisonment for repeat offenders of the most serious incidents. Such abuse not only affects the health and morale of the workers but also has the potential to delay life-saving responses, as distracted or distressed call-takers may struggle to accurately and efficiently manage incoming emergencies. The Department of Health recently acknowledged the growing concern and said it would “consider all reasonable options for protecting those who serve us in these vital roles.”

A Breath Test That Could Detect Parkinson’s: Breaking Through Long-Lasting Diagnostic Delays   A team of scientists has identified a potential game-changer in the fight against Parkinson’s disease: a simple, non-invasive breath test that could allow doctors to detect and even predict the condition before traditional symptoms appear. If proven successful in further trials, the test could radically transform the way one of the most debilitating neurological disorders is diagnosed—and offer hope to the millions of people worldwide who live with the disease. Currently, Parkinson’s is diagnosed largely through observation of symptoms such as tremors, rigidity, and slowness of movement. But these often appear only after the disease has already caused significant damage to the brain. There is no single blood test or scan to confirm a diagnosis, and the process can be lengthy, frustrating for patients and their families. Now, researchers at the University of Edinburgh and the University of Kaiserslautern in Germany claim to have discovered a distinctive chemical signature in the breath of people with Parkinson’s. The compound in question, eicosane, is found in higher concentrations in the breath of those suffering from the disease, even in its early stages, and serves as a consistent biomarker. This discovery puts the idea of mass-screening and early intervention firmly within reach. Professor Perdita Barran, a key figure in the research and a professor of chemical physics at the University of Manchester, said, “This is a huge step forward. Until now, diagnosing Parkinson’s has been a process of waiting for symptoms to appear and ruling out other conditions. A breath test could change everything—enabling earlier treatment, better management of symptoms, and potentially even the development of drugs that slow or halt the progression of the disease.” The method works through a device that analyses volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in the breath using a machine learning algorithm. In trials, the test correctly identified Parkinson’s disease in patients with an accuracy rate of around 80 per cent—rates that, with further refinement, could rise significantly. The team believes it can soon improve the test to the point where it is both widely available and accessible. The implications are staggering. Parkinson’s affects an estimated seven to 10 million people globally, and the number is expected to reach more than 12 million by 2040. In the UK alone, nearly 150,000 people are living with the condition, with around one in 35 people likely to develop it in their lifetime.

Accrington Stanley secured a crucial victory over promotion-chasing Colchester United at the Wham Stadium on Saturday, easing brief relegation fears in the process, despite being reduced to 10 men for a large portion of the game. The Reds, who have spent most of the League Two season at the foot of the table, showed real grit and determination to overcome the U's with an impressive display of resilience. A narrow 1-0 win came against the odds, with Accrington's defensive organisation and clinical finishing proving decisive. The winning goal came in the 38th minute when substitute Omar Bogle, stepping into the lineup with aplomb, latched onto a loose back pass and tucked the ball past Colchester goalkeeper Sam Walker. It was a moment that summed up the afternoon for Accrington — left with a mountain to climb, they found the breakthrough at a pivotal moment and never looked back. What made the victory even more impressive was the fact that Accrington were a man down following an early injury to Jack Mulhall, who went off five minutes in with a suspected hamstring strain. Manager John Coleman was forced to reshuffle his side, and it looked as though Colchester would exploit the numerical advantage in the early going. However, Accrington’s tenacious defending stood firm, with captain John O’Shea towering in the heart of the backline and goalkeeper Baptiste Guillaume producing a series of smart saves to deny his former teammates. The hosts defended as a unit, and their collective willpower kept them in the game as they waited for the crucial moment. Colchester, in contrast, struggled to break down a disciplined and focused Accrington side. Manager Adam Murray, who had been in the stands and was later appointed under new ownership after the game, made a string of changes late on in an attempt to find a breakthrough, but found the going tough. The win marks only the third time this season that Accrington have picked up a victory against side above them in the league table. It lifts them four points above the drop zone with seven games remaining, offering a glimmer of hope in their fight to maintain their EFL status. Speaking after the match, Coleman said: “I’m extremely proud of the lads. To do it with 10 men against a strong Colchester side who are chasing promotion shows the character in this group. That’s the spirit that we need right now if we’re going to fight our way out of trouble.”

Letters from the 1980s unearthed this week reveal a sharply worded plea from Labour MP Geoffrey Dickens urging then-Home Secretary Leon Brittan to ban a group described as "pro-paedophilia" nearly four decades ago. The documents, now made public as part of a wider release of parliamentary correspondence, expose a previously undisclosed chapter in the UK’s political history on issues surrounding child protection and civil liberties. In a series of letters exchanged in 1985, Dickens, a backbencher at the time, expressed grave concerns about the activities of a private organisation advocating for the decriminalisation of certain relationships involving minors. He argued that the group, which had not yet been made illegal, represented a moral and legal threat to society. "If this organisation is allowed to operate under the guise of victim advocacy or free speech, we risk sending the wrong message to the public," Dickens wrote in one letter to Brittan, who was then a prominent Conservative Cabinet minister. Dickens pushed for action to outlaw the group under the proposed Children and Young Persons Act 1985, which was due to receive royal assent later that year. "This is not just about ideology," he wrote. "It impacts the most vulnerable members of society. The government must not be seen as indifferent to the welfare of children." British politics in the 1980s was characterised by deep ideological divides, and the letter adds another layer to the era’s contentious debates over crime, morality and individual rights. At the time, Brittan was known as a staunch opponent of what he described as "lax" sex laws, proposing tough measures against indecency and advocating a tightening of the age of consent. The previously secret communications come at a time when the government is under renewed scrutiny over how it has dealt with historical cases of child abuse. Experts from the Child Exploitation and Online Protection Centre (CEOP) note that such disclosures are increasingly important in understanding how policy was shaped in response to evolving social attitudes over the decades. Geoffrey Dickens passed away in 2007, but his papers remain a significant source for historians and those revisiting how political institutions tackled issues of protection and ethics in the 1980s. Leon Brittan, who served as Home Secretary until 1986, died in 2013. A spokesperson for the National Archives, which released the letters, stated that the material offers a "vital record of how MPs and ministers debated some of the most difficult issues of their time."

The lack of contract documentation for two-thirds of Cameroon’s local footballers is raising serious concerns about the protection of players and transparency in the sport, according to the head of the Cameroon Footballers’ Association (COFAC). Roger Milla Jr., the union’s president and son of the legendary striker Roger Milla, has called for urgent action to address the issue, warning that the practice leaves many players exposed to exploitation and legal uncertainty. Speaking at a recent media briefing in Yaoundé, Milla Jr. highlighted that the absence of records creates fertile ground for disputes over wages, transfers, and termination clauses. “How can a player assert their rights if they can’t even present a copy of their contract? This is a national problem, and it has to change,” he said. Cameroon, a nation with a proud footballing legacy, qualified for the 2023 Africa Cup of Nations and is currently ranked 43rd in the world by FIFA. Yet behind the successes, concerns are growing about the lack of professionalism in some corners of the domestic game. Numerous players have reportedly been unable to produce written proof of their employment, forcing them to rely on verbal assurances or incomplete, unofficial records. This situation is particularly alarming given the frustrations over player earnings in the country and the apparent reluctance of some clubs to properly adhere to national regulations. According to data from COFAC, most affected players are based in lower-tier clubs, although Milla Jr. stressed that “no one is immune.” He urged professional leagues and their governing bodies to increase oversight and enforce stricter financial and administrative checks. “If someone signs a contract, it must be in writing, and they must have a copy. That’s basic. Until this is addressed, we can’t be surprised when underpayments, disputes over registration, or even identity fraud about contract binding occur,” he added. Experts from the Cameroonian football administration and legal observers have echoed Milla Jr.’s concerns. One informed source explained that unregistered contracts can also have implications for international transfers, as many European clubs require verifiable documentation to facilitate moves. “If a player can’t show any proof, it becomes very difficult to secure them a spot abroad or even sell them to a club in Africa beyond the CAF regional space,” the source said. In response to the growing outcry, the Cameroon Football Federation (FECAFOC) has announced it will hold an emergency audit of player contracts in the coming weeks.

Reducing Migration ‘Major Policy Imperative’ Says Brexit Secretary   The Conservative Party’s long-standing pledge to bring net migration in the UK down to the tens of thousands remains a "major policy imperative", Brexit Secretary David Davis has said, as the government sets out to detail its post-Brexit immigration strategy. Speaking in a recent speech at a policy event in Westminster, Mr Davis reiterated the government’s commitment to reducing the number of people entering the country from non-EU countries. He stressed that this goal, which was central to the Leave campaign in the 2016 referendum, has not diminished in importance during the ongoing Brexit negotiations. “During the referendum, people were promised change, and one of the most vital changes the people of this nation asked for was about having control of our borders and our immigration levels,” Mr Davis said. “Bringing net migration down to the tens of thousands and ensuring every single job is given to an eligible UK resident is a major policy imperative for this government.” Prime Minister Theresa May previously reiterated this pledge in her Conservative Party conference speech in 2016, saying it remains one of the most important promises the government will deliver over the next few years. However, progress has been slow, with immigration levels remaining stubbornly high despite early optimism. The UK has already moved away from free movement with the European Union and will now control immigration from the EU – but it faces new challenges in setting and enforcing strict immigration rules in a global economy. Mr Davis acknowledged the complexity of the issue, but was clear that the government intends to act decisively. “Controlling our borders is one of the most powerful demonstrations of our sovereignty. That is why it remains one of our central priorities,” he continued. “We want a system that is safe, secure, and selective.” The government has been consulting on proposals to introduce a "points-based" system that would prioritise skilled workers and reduce low-skilled migration. Under the current plans, applicants would need to meet strict criteria to work in key sectors such as healthcare, construction, hospitality and agriculture. Critics, including some within the government itself, have argued that focusing too heavily on reducing migration could have a negative impact on the economy. The hospitality and healthcare sectors have already issued warnings that without access to overseas workers, the demand for certain roles may not be able to be met.

The right of UK Members of Parliament to a degree of protection from communications surveillance remains in place—but it does not prevent intelligence agencies from targeting MPs in all circumstances, Home Secretary Theresa May has confirmed. This clarification comes amid growing concerns over the breadth and secrecy of the security services’ powers, particularly in light of the recent revelations about mass surveillance practices in the United States and ongoing scrutiny of the Intelligence and Security Committee (ISC). In a written statement to the House of Commons, Mrs. May explained that the protection MPs enjoy under Schedule 2 of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act (RIPA) has not been overturned. The schedule, which was revealed under the Freedom of Information Act in 2010, states that law enforcement and security agencies are generally barred from intercepting communications of MPs, unless under exceptional circumstances. However, the home secretary stressed that this protection is not absolute, and special permission from the Prime Minister and the inspector of intercept is required to conduct targeted surveillance. The confirmation has raised eyebrows among MPs and civil liberties campaigners, some of whom argue that the loophole remains too wide and not sufficiently safeguarded. Labour Shadow Home Secretary Emily Thornberry said that the lack of a "clear and absolute" protection for MPs showed the weakness of the current legal framework. “MPs are entrusted with scrutinising government action on behalf of the public, and it is deeply troubling that they can still be subject to surveillance without any transparency or accountability,” she said. The revelation follows a growing number of claims by former staff members and whistleblowers about the extent to which the intelligence community might monitor political figures. Despite reassurances from the government, questions remain over how often this exemption is used and whether it has been exploited in recent years to monitor internal political debates or unofficial discussions. Ms. May said the government is committed to maintaining a “balance” between national security and the rights of the public and their elected representatives. She denied any suggestion that the PM or her office had been improperly informed of surveillance activities unconnected to genuine security concerns. The response has however failed to quiet critics, who will now be pressing for greater clarity, transparency, and legal protection for those elected to represent the public in Parliament. A full review of RIPA is due in early 2015, which may yet provide an opportunity for the rules to be clarified—or changed.

Jonny Hayes believes that Niall McGinn could still play a big part in Aberdeen’s future, despite speculation pointing towards a summer exit for the midfielder. The Dons captain has yet to sign a pre-contract agreement with a potential new club, and with only a few months left in what would be his final season at Pittodrie on current terms, there is plenty of time for the 33-year-old's next destination to become clear. Speaking ahead of Sunday’s Scottish Premiership clash with Hibs, Hayes, who signed a new long-term contract with the club earlier in the season, hinted that the chase for McGinn might still be far from over. “I think it's too early to write Nials off and say he's definitely gone,” Hayes said. “He still has a year left on his contract and he’s shown over the past few years what he can do for this club. A lot of clubs are making interest known, but eventually it will come down to what's best for Nials and for the club in the long term.” Since joining Aberdeen in 2014 from Hibernian, McGinn has become a fan favourite and a key figure in the team’s consistent mid-table finishes in the league. Known as much for his long-range goals as for his captaincy on and off the pitch, McGinn has helped inspire the Dons to European qualification twice in recent years. He has also amassed 93 goals in all competitions, earning him a place in the hearts of players and supporters alike. A number of clubs have been linked with McGinn this season, with Premier League and Scottish Championship sides both reportedly interested in securing his services. However, with the Dons facing a crucial period as they look to solidify their position in the top six, there is a feeling about the club that they would prefer to keep the reliable midfield general around for the remainder of the campaign. “There's no point wasting energy trying to predict where he is going to end up,” Hayes added. “What we need to focus on is making sure we keep giving our players the confidence to believe in this team. Nials has been a huge part of what we’ve done over the past few years, and he’ll continue to do that whether he’s with us for a little longer or not.”

Bryan Yan, a 32-year-old real estate agent in Vancouver, is riding high on one of the most extraordinary property booms in the city’s modern history. With home prices soaring and demand outpacing supply, Yan has found himself at the heart of a market that is both lucrative and fiercely competitive. In a city long associated with high costs of living, the current surge in property values has turned his career into something of a gold rush. Vancouver’s real estate scene has been a topic of national debate for years, with critics accusing foreign investment—especially from China and the Middle East—of inflating the market beyond the reach of local buyers. However, for agents like Yan, these challenges translate into opportunity. “It’s an agent’s dream scenario,” Yan said, speaking from his downtown office. “Everyone’s in a hurry. Offers are coming in fast, and they’re often way above the asking price. It feels like the housing market doesn’t slow down when it comes to prime properties.” According to the British Columbia Real Estate Association (BCREA), home prices in Vancouver rose by nearly 20% in the past year alone, with some high-end properties seeing double-digit increases in a matter of months. Yan puts much of this down to Vancouver’s status as a global financial hub and its reputation as a prime location for second home ownership. “Buyers from overseas see Vancouver as stable, safe, and a gateway to the rest of North America,” he explained. “And with interest rates still at record lows, it’s the perfect storm for the market.” As for what lies ahead, Yan is cautiously optimistic. While government measures like the foreign buyer tax and a speculation and vacancy tax have been introduced to cool the market, he believes their impact has been more psychological than practical. “Price growth has slowed a bit in the lower-end market, but the upper tiers keep rising. It’s like two different markets in one city,” he said. For now, Yan is focused on closing the next big deal. With four offers on a single high-rise condo last week alone and more open houses planned for the weekend, he shows no signs of slowing down. For him and countless others in Vancouver’s real estate scene, the boom isn’t just sustained—it’s accelerating. Whether it can continue is another question, but for the moment, Bryan Yan is thriving in the heady days of the market cycle.-president of Harvard University, Claudine Gay, has stepped down following days of intense scrutiny, internal dissent, and criticism of her academic

Froome Remains in Yellow as Kittel Dominates Stage Six   Britain’s Chris Froome retained the leader’s yellow jersey at the Tour de France after a thrilling sixth stage, won by Marcel Kittel in a blistering sprint finish across 216km of the French countryside. The stage, which ran from Arras to Lens, saw the peloton battle through windswept roads and fast-paced finishes, as expected of a traditional flat day in the famed race’s early stages. Kittel, the German sprinter representing Team Etixx–Quick-Step, was unstoppable at the line, further cementing his position as one of the tour’s most dominant sprinters. In a closely contested sprint, he edged out world champion Peter Sagan and André Greipel of Lotto-Soudal, who had narrowly missed the previous day’s win. The result was a fitting reward for Kittel after he rode aggressively from the start of the stage, positioning himself perfectly for a repeat success following his earlier victory in Nice. While the sprint dominated the narrative, the stage also featured a dramatic early breakaway attempt. Riders from the Groupama-FDJ and IAM Cycling took an early lead, hoping to shake up the general classification in the pre-race chaos. However, the gap remained marginal as the peloton quickly regrouped, and by the final 20km, the breakaway was absorbed with seemingly no chance of hanging on. This allowed Froome, the defending champion and Team Sky’s star rider, to conserve his energy. The Briton remained within the main field for much of the stage, and his race against the clock to maintain a time advantage over nearest threat Nairo Quintana continued to look promising. Quintana, the Colombian climber currently in second place, finished safely in the bunch, about five seconds behind Froome but still standing strong in the overall standings. The stage did not feature significant climbing, but it did include two short but technical sectors of gravel, which created brief chaos within the peloton. Some riders struggled with their lines and others took the opportunity to test their rivals’ initiative. However, no meaningful general classification threats were made, and the yellow jersey remained unchanged on the shoulders of Froome. The route of the day provided a challenging but scenic route through northern France, with spectators filling the roadside in droves, delivering the usual roar and support that the Tour is known for. The final run-in to Lens was characterised by two sharp left turns just before the sprint, which complicated team tactics but added an extra tactical edge to the finish.

The eagerly anticipated light-heavyweight title showdown between Nathan Cleverly and WBO champion Juergen Braehmer has been called off after Braehmer sustained an eye injury during training, casting a shadow over what was expected to be a major event in the British boxing calendar. Organisations had been preparing for the clash in April, but Braehmer is now expected to require surgery on the damage, which he suffered while in camp in Germany, a source close to the champion revealed. Cleverly, 29, had promised a fiery, explosive performance to claim one of boxing’s most sought-after titles. The Welshman has been building momentum over recent years, but this opportunity represents a pivotal moment in his career as he looks to follow compatriots Carl Froch and Enzo Maccarinelli in capturing a world title on home soil. However, the cancellation leaves the former European champion and IBO title-holder in uncertainty as he must now wait for an alternative contender or a rescheduled fight date. Juergen Braehmer, 33, has defended his WBO title on multiple occasions since winning it in 2010 and is renowned for his disciplined, technical style. The champion is expected to take two or three months to recover and will not be fit to defend the title in the immediate future. With Braehmer out, the WBO is now expected to open negotiations with other high-profile names in the division to confirm a new challenge. Speaking after the news broke, Cleverly expressed his disappointment but showed understanding for the situation. “It’s never great when someone gets injured, especially so close to a big fight. It just shows how unpredictable boxing can be. I’d hoped for a red-letter day and a chance to make history in front of my fans, but it’s about waiting for the next opportunity. I’m ready when the WBO is.” British boxing fans had been looking forward to another sell-out at Wembley Stadium, where Cleverly previously defended his European title to a raucous crowd. Now, discussions about alternate opponents and revised timelines are already under way among event organisers, though no new date or rival for Cleverly has yet been confirmed. Promoter Eddie Hearn said: “It’s frustrating for everyone involved, but Nathan is patient and professional. We’ll work with the WBO to find the best course of action. No one wants to see a man suffer, and our number one concern is Juergen’s recovery.

Seventeen-year-old Agnes (not her real name) was forced into marriage just three months ago to a man she had never met, in a practice she describes as both terrifying and degrading. Her story, shared in confidence with  The Times , paints a stark picture of the persistence of child marriage in parts of the UK, particularly within certain communities where tradition often trumps consent and equality. Agnes, who now lives in isolation with her new husband, spoke under anonymity for fear of being sent back to him or punished by her family. “I didn’t want to marry him,” she said softly. “He was older, someone I’d never even met before. My parents told me it was what was best for me and the family. That was it. No choice. No say.” Despite numerous laws and policies aimed at protecting young people, cases like Agnes’s continue to surface, often hidden in the shadows of cultural practices and religious customs. The minimum age for marriage in England and Wales is 16, with parental consent required until the age of 18. However, child marriage advocates have long warned that the current legal framework is not enough to prevent girls like Agnes being forced into lifelong partnerships they have no say in. In recent years, high-profile investigations and reports by charities such as Traidcraft and GIRL have exposed a dark underbelly to British society – one where underage marriages are sometimes legitimised by families and even religious leaders. These unions often see girls taken to other countries for their weddings before being returned, effectively bypassing local social services and authorities. The Ministry of Justice has said it is “fully committed to tackling the issue of child marriage” and has made efforts to better monitor and prevent intercountry and domestic marriages under 18. Yet, as Agnes’s story shows, the barriers to fulfilling this promise remain high. “I’m scared I can't get out,” she admitted. “I don’t know what I’m going to do next, but I know I didn’t choose this. I wish someone had asked me.” Her case is expected to contribute to the ongoing debate on whether the UK needs to fully outlaw child marriage, restricting the existing exceptions. As parliament continues to consider tighter measures, the lives of young girls like Agnes will keep the issue at the forefront of the public conscience. Whether legal changes are enough, however, remains a question that leaves many in the dark.

Security will be increased at polling stations across the UK as voters cast their ballots in Thursday’s general election, in response to heightened terror concerns following last weekend’s attack in London. The Met Police and security services have issued specific guidance to electoral staff and local authorities, with extra resources being deployed to ensure the safety of both voters and polling officers. The unprecedented measures come as the UK remains on high alert, with the security threat level at “severe,” a step below the highest level. The Election Commission confirmed that additional police personnel and protective equipment will be present at polling stations, particularly in major cities like London and Manchester. The steps reflect the government's commitment to safeguarding the democratic process, even in the face of potential threats. In the wake of the deadly attack on Saturday night that left five people dead and numerous others injured, Prime Minister Theresa May pledged that the election – the first in over 120 years to take place while the country is under a state of terror alert – would go ahead as planned. The election, originally delayed for a month at the request of the Queen in light of the attack, has seen the political campaigning continue under the shadow of national security considerations. Home Secretary Amber Rudd highlighted that the police would be working in close cooperation with counter-terrorism units to monitor any suspicious activity leading up to and on polling day. "It is vital," she said, “that people can – and do – exercise their democratic right in safety and without fear." Local councils across the country are also receiving support from counter-terrorism specialists to ensure that all necessary precautions are taken. In London, the largest concentration of polling stations in the country, extra emergency services teams are already being positioned to respond swiftly should any incident occur. The Electoral Commission has urged voters to be vigilant and report any suspicious package or individual, while also reassuring people about the security of the process. "We are committed to ensuring this is an election that demonstrates what is good about our democracy," the commission said in a statement. The attack, in which two men, later killed by police, drove a van into pedestrians near Parliament, has raised urgent questions about the vulnerability of public spaces to terrorism. Security measures introduced for the election are expected to include increased surveillance, security clearances for polling staff, and reinforced protection for high-profile polling stations.

British planetary scientist Colin Pillinger, who became an iconic figure through his ambitious 2003 attempt to land a spacecraft on Mars, has died at the age of 70, his family announced on Monday. Mr Pillinger was the driving force behind the Beagle 2 mission, a daring project developed in relative obscurity and on a shoestring budget compared to the US space programmes. The lander was designed to search for signs of life on the Red Planet but failed to return a signal after it was deployed from the European Space Agency’s Mars Express orbiter in December 2003. For years, the mission's fate remained a mystery, but in 2015, images from Nasa's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter confirmed that Beagle 2 had indeed reached the Martian surface though it remained partially folded and presumably non-functional. Despite the mission's failure, Mr Pillinger’s work and the public support he was able to rally highlighted a growing interest in space exploration in the UK and inspired a generation of scientists. His relentless optimism, creativity and media-savvy helped to make the project a national cause, with £20 million raised from both the government and public donations. Born in 1948 in London, Mr Pillinger initially studied mathematics and geology before turning to planetary science. He was a professor of planetary sciences at the Open University and worked at the Natural History Museum and Imperial College London. His colleagues remember him as a passionate and visionary scientist, unafraid to pursue what others deemed impossible. In the years following the Beagle 2 launch, Mr Pillinger continued his work in planetary science, serving as a consultant on international space missions and advocating for continued exploration of the solar system. He was knighted in 2007 for his services to science and public understanding. Tributes have poured in from across the scientific community. Tim Peake, the UK’s first astronaut, wrote on Twitter: “RIP to the great Colin Pillinger. Your ambition and passion for space will live on. A true British pioneer.” Professor Ian Wright, dean of the Open University’s Faculty of Science, described Mr Pillinger as an “incredible figure of inspiration to both scientists and space enthusiasts alike,” adding that the “Open University has lost one of our most outstanding alumni and friends.” Mr Pillinger is survived by his wife, gothic novelist Melanie Mart为重点, and their two children. A full inquest into his death is expected to be held in the coming weeks.

New Dinosaur Species Discovered in the Deserts of Utah   Researchers have announced the discovery of a remarkable new species of dinosaur unearthed in the sun-scorched deserts of Utah, offering fresh insight into the diverse ecosystems that once thrived in North America during the Late Cretaceous period. The find, which includes a partially intact skeleton, is being hailed as one of the most compelling additions to the known dinosaur record in years. The species has been named  Nanuza , a name derived from the native Ute language and meaning "eagle journey," in reference to the soaring feathers that adorned the creature, as suggested by fossilised impressions found alongside the remains. Preliminary analysis indicates that  Nanuza  was a small, carnivorous theropod, roughly the size of a large modern-day dog, and appears to be a close relative of Dromaeosauridae — the group that includes the famous Velociraptor. The skeleton was discovered by amateur fossil hunter and museum volunteer Brian Johnson during an excavation near the town of Price, in eastern Utah, which is part of the environmentally rich and historically significant Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument. This area has long been a hotbed for paleontological discoveries, with several new species having been identified over the past decade. Dr. Emily Stewart, a lead researcher from the University of Utah's Department of Geology, said the discovery was particularly significant due to its completeness and the unique features of the specimen. “Nanuza reveals a previously unknown lineage of small raptors, possibly indicating that this group was more diverse and widespread than previously thought,” she said. “What we’re seeing here could challenge some long-held assumptions about the inter- and intra-dinosaur relationships during this period.” The desert location of the find adds another layer of mystery to the specimen. While many raptor fossils have been uncovered in forest or marsh-like environments,  Nanuza  appears to have lived in a more arid ecosystem, raising questions about the adaptability of these agile predators. Carbon dating places the fossil at approximately 75 million years old, during the Maastrichtian stage when the last non-avian dinosaurs roamed the Earth. The landscape at the time was vastly different to today — lush with ferns, cycads, and coniferous forests, with large rivers and floodplains crisscrossing the terrain. Local authorities and academic institutions are now working together to preserve the site, with hopes of developing a dedicated exhibition in the coming years. Police in Italy have arrested a 36-year-old unemployed man after uncovering a brazen impersonation fraud in which he passed himself off as a licensed airline pilot. He reportedly gained access to restricted areas of the airport and, on at least one occasion, was found in the pilot's seat of a short-haul flight while breakfasting with the real crew. An unnamed aviation source told  The Guardian  that the man appeared “fully at ease” in the cockpit and was treated as a full member of the crew by the flight attendants and ground staff. “He laughed, joked, even dressed as a pilot. The UK's leading broadcasters have been accused of making a "complete and utter mess" of their plans to host televised general election debates, according to the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP). The criticism comes as the Scottish separatist group, the Scottish Greens, and the Liberal Democrats have refused to participate in the agreed-upon format put forward by the broadcasters and the Electoral Commission. The DUP, which holds just one seat in the House of Commons, has said that the planned debates — involving the main parties — are "unrepresentative and unfair". DUP leader Sir Jeffrey Donaldson called the scheduling of the debates “deeply flawed”, arguing that it underrepresents the number of parties with parliamentary seats and diminishes the voices of smaller but significant political groups. The BBC and ITV had announced a deal earlier this year to stage a total of seven live election debates, to be held between April 2 and May 3. They followed the format used in the 2015 and 2017 general elections, in which Conservative Prime Minister Theresa May and Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn took centre stage, to the near exclusion of other parties. That format has long been condemned as partisan, and this time, it has raised even more questions about fairness and inclusivity. Under the latest proposals, two prime minister’s questions-style debates are scheduled, as well as a general debate on “the national economy”; another on health, education, and social care; and a final unnamed “national issue” debate. All four would be restricted to the Conservatives, Labour, and the Liberal Democrats — the only parties in Parliament that currently hold leadership positions in the debates. The remaining three debates will focus on devolved issues — Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland — and will be split between the respective parties in those regions, excluding the national parties unless they are relevant to a specific issue. The Scottish Greens and the Liberal Democrats have expressed frustration at the limited access to the debates, with Scottish Green co-convener Patrick Harvie stating the process "was not inclusive and left no room for alternative perspectives". Meanwhile, the Liberal Democrats, who finished third in terms of vote share in the last general election, have refused to agree unless the schedule is reworked to include them beyond the economy debate. The Electoral Commission recently stepped in and urged the broadcasters to “act fairly” in granting additional debate slots where justified. This has left the proposal in limbo, with the final details about who will be included still unclear.

The Grenfell Tower fire has sparked a new wave of fury and public outcry, with many accusing the government of failing to learn from a series of deadly tower block fires in the UK over the years. As the death toll rises and searches continue in the smouldering wreckage of the 24-storey residential block in north Kensington, concerns are being raised that poor fire safety regulations and inadequate building materials have once again led to a preventable disaster. Grenfell Tower caught fire on the early evening of June 14, after a faulty fridge in a fourth-floor flat caused a fire to spread quickly and uncontrollably through the building. The blaze was exacerbated by the spread of fire up the exterior cladding, much of which the fire department said was non-fireproof. It has since been revealed that numerous fire safety recommendations left unheeded in the wake of previous incidents bear a worrying resemblance to the failures in Grenfell. One of the most poignant examples is the 1990 fire at Lakanal House in Camberwell, South London, which killed five residents. An inquiry found that the property's cladding and flammable insulation directly contributed to the rapid spread of the fire. Recommendations following the tragedy included ensuring that buildings with flammable materials had sprinkler systems and other adequate fire precautions in place. These measures were never fully implemented, and similar failings have now cost at least 30 lives in Grenfell. Labour's shadow housing secretary, John Healey, described the situation as “a damning indictment of a government that has ignored the lessons of the past and put people at risk.” Spokespersons for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government have so far failed to respond specifically to questions about why fire regulations have not been updated in light of historical tragedies. Campaigners and bereaved families are now calling for an urgent independent inquiry into the fire, as well as an immediate review of fire safety standards across all high-rise residential buildings. Firefighters have also spoken up, with one senior officer, speaking on condition of anonymity, stating that “this tragedy was foreseeable. The government knew the risks. They turned a blind eye.” As communities come together to mourn the victims and support those who lost their homes, the fire has also ignited a broader debate about the state of social housing in the UK. Many point to recent government policies that have prioritised cost-cutting over resident wellbeing, including the go-ahead of the controversial leasehold reforms and the use of inferior materials in high-rise developments, often in the pursuit of energy efficiency targets.

The new US-based Haas Formula One team is likely to be competitive in the near future, according to American former NASCAR driver Danica Patrick. Speaking ahead of this weekend’s season-opening Grand Prix in Australia, Patrick, who is widely viewed as one of the most high-profile female drivers in motorsport history, expressed her confidence in the new entrant, which made its debut on the Formula One grid at the end of last year. While the team struggled in its inaugural season, finishing well down the grid, Patrick believes that with time, experience and investment, it will soon start to challenge its European and Asian rivals. “The car’s still pretty green, and Formula One is so technical and constantly evolving, but I think their future is bright,” Patrick said in an interview with CNN. “Gene Haas is a very smart and capable businessman, and if he puts in the resources and drive in Formula One the way he has in NASCAR and other ventures, I have no doubt they’ll be up there.” Patrick, who made history by becoming the first female driver to win the Indianapolis 500 in 2008, commended Haas for taking on the challenge of Formula One. The team also fields an experienced lineup of drivers, with Romain Grosjean and Kevin Magnussen set for the 2016 season. Patrick, who retired from full-time racing in 2015, said the rise of Haas is a positive sign for motorsport fans in the United States. “It brings a different perspective and excitement,” she explained. “It’s about more than Formula One—it's about inspiring a new generation of American drivers and engineers.”

Obama Vows ‘Very Specific’ Plan to Revitalise US Economy   US President Barack Obama has pledged to unveil a “very specific” economic plan in the coming weeks as he seeks to address growing concerns over the slowing US economy and rising unemployment in key sectors. Speaking at the White House during a press briefing on Friday, the President called on Congress to act swiftly to support American workers and foster long-term economic growth. This is a real, actionable plan,” the President said. “We must move decisively to put people back to work, to invest in the future of American industry, and to make sure that the middle class – the backbone of our economy – is no longer being left behind.” The move is expected to be a key component of the administration’s efforts to set the agenda for Congress in the final months of the Obama presidency and to counter Republican proposals, which have focused on tax cuts and reduced regulations. While supporters welcomed the development, critics, including some within the Democratic Party, warned that such late-stage proposals might come too late to make a significant impact on a struggling economy.

Young voters in the UK are significantly more concerned about the availability of affordable housing and issues around immigration than they are about crime, a recent survey commissioned by BBC Radio 1’s Newsbeat programme has revealed. The poll, which surveyed thousands of 18- to 24-year-olds, suggests a marked shift in the priorities of the so-called "Gen Z" electorate ahead of both local and national elections. The findings reflect a growing disillusionment among younger voters with traditional political topics such as crime and policing, which have long dominated campaign rhetoric. Instead, respondents highlighted the struggle to rent or buy a home as the most pressing issue of the day. More than 70 per cent of those questioned said that affordable housing was their top concern, with many expressing frustration over the rising costs of living and the difficulty of entering the property market in much of the country. Immigration followed closely behind, with nearly two-thirds of the surveyed group citing it as a major worry. Many respondents linked immigration with pressure on public services, housing shortages, and wage competition — a narrative that has become increasingly common in political discourse in recent years. However, the survey also suggested that views on immigration among young people are not black and white, with many calling for a controlled and fair system that still allows for the welcome of skilled workers. Perhaps most notably, crime — a key issue in general elections for decades — ranked lowest in the survey of concerns. Only 20 per cent of young respondents placed the issue within their top three worries, suggesting that their political focus is shifting toward the challenges of living in modern Britain. The Radio 1 Newsbeat report also highlighted a general sense of political disengagement among young people. Some 40 per cent of young voters polled admitted being unsure about which party to support, with many feeling that their concerns about housing, jobs and immigration are not being adequately addressed by major political parties. Political analysts said the survey results could signal a turning point in British election politics. “Young voters are reshaping the agenda, and for parties looking to win their votes, housing and immigration are now areas they can’t afford to ignore,” said one senior commentator. The findings come as several political parties prepare their campaigns ahead of key elections, and could influence the direction of future policy statements and manifestos.

In a sterile intensive care unit at a government hospital in Srinagar, 14-year-old Insha Mushtaq lies on a bed, wracked by pain and semi-conscious, her body trembling with seizures. Raziya Begum, whose only education was a brief schooling in an informal madrassa, weeps silently at her child’s bedside, clutching a small photograph of Insha holding her infant sister.

Bale Fires Real Madrid Past Getafe in Quest to Dethrone Barcelona   Gareth Bale made history on Saturday night as Real Madrid emphatically dismantled Getafe 5-1 at the Santiago Bernabéu, closing the gap to just one point behind league leaders Barcelona as the Spanish giants continue their relentless pursuit in La Liga. Djokovic, meanwhile, celebrated a return to form in Melbourne, justifying his reputation as one of the most adaptable and enduring champions in the history of the sport.

The qualifications regulator Ofqual has come to the defence of a new mathematics exam following an unexpected failure rate that has left both students and teachers concerned. The advanced-level AQA exam, taken by students in their final year of pre-university education, saw 53 per cent of candidates receive a failing mark — well above the historical average. The results have sparked criticism from educators who say the exam was unnecessarily hard and poorly aligned with the teaching of the subject. In a written statement, Ofqual defended the exam, asserting that the high failure rate was a direct result of the new specifications introduced to the subject and that the standards of difficulty were consistent with those of previous exams. It also noted that exam grades remain "comparable with previous years" and that students will have the opportunity to re-sit the paper later in the year. The exam, which replaced the old specification for mathematics in A-level Qualifications, features increased emphasis on problem-solving and extended, application-based questions — a change incorporated as part of a broader effort to align with education systems in other high-performing countries. However, critics, including teachers' unions and head teachers, argue that the transition was rushed and that many teachers were not given enough time or support to adapt their teaching methods accordingly. One teacher from a state secondary school in Birmingham, who requested anonymity due to fears of repercussions, said: “This wasn't just a one-off paper. This new curriculum doesn't seem to fit the way students today are taught. We're seeing a lot of frustration and disappointment from families who weren't prepared for results like this.” Despite the backlash, Ofqual maintains that adjusting the difficulty of the exam to a lower standard would undermine its purpose. “The exams are designed to be fair and to uphold the integrity of the qualifications,” the agency said. “Students and centres are encouraged to use the retake option to achieve the results they deserve.” The debate over the new standards has reignited wider concerns about the rollout of reformed A-levels across the UK. Similar issues have emerged in other subjects, with physics and history also seeing increased failure rates among students. With the education sector under increasing pressure to produce high grades for university admissions and performance metrics, the controversy is unlikely to fade soon. As of now, Ofqual has not indicated whether the exam paper will be reviewed or modified ahead of next year's sitting.

Goal-line Technology Makes World Cup Debut as GoalControl Preps for 2014 Tournament in Brazil   German-based manufacturer GoalControl has been confirmed as the provider of goal-line technology (GLT) for the 2014 FIFA World Cup in Brazil, marking the first time such technology will be used at a World Cup on a global stage. The announcement has been met with widespread support from football officials and fans alike, who hope the system will eliminate one of the most contentious elements of the beautiful game — disputed goals. Previously, matches have been marred by controversial decisions, most notably when England’s Frank Lampard was denied a clear goal during the 2010 World Cup clash against Germany, a moment that many still consider a turning point in the push for technological intervention. Now, after years of testing and consultation, FIFA has made the decisive step towards modernisation by incorporating GLT into the 2014 tournament. GoalControl’s GLT system, developed in collaboration with Sony, uses a combination of high-speed cameras and magnetic field sensors to determine whether the ball has fully crossed the goal line. The system is designed to provide instant feedback to the match officials within one second of the ball crossing the line — a crucial detail to maintain the flow of the game. Dr. Klaus Brand, managing director of GoalControl, said the technology would “ensure that every goal is seen and every decision made with precision, giving fairness a new dimension in the world of football.” According to Brand, the technology will be capable of distinguishing the ball’s position to within 5 millimetres — a level of accuracy expected to surpass even the most eagle-eyed spectators. The GLT system will be installed at all ten host stadiums across Brazil and will be operational during all matches of the competition, including the group, knockout, and final stages. Referees will be equipped with a specially designed watch that alerts them immediately if the ball has crossed the line, eliminating any need for video replay in such instances. FIFA President Sepp Blatter has praised the move as a significant milestone in the union of tradition and innovation. “足球 is a game of moments,” Blatter said in a statement. “By introducing goal-line technology, we are doing what is right by the game — upholding its integrity and ensuring justice is done, no matter where you are in the world.” Fan reaction has been broadly positive, with many on social media celebrating the decision.

NASA has delayed the first crewed flight of its long-awaited Orion Multi-Purpose Crew Vehicle until at least 2023, according to the US space agency. The announcement has sparked concern among lawmakers and aerospace experts who had hoped the spacecraft would be operational sooner to reassert the US as a leader in human spaceflight after the retirement of the space shuttle programme in 2011. The Orion capsule, developed in partnership with aerospace giant Lockheed Martin, is intended to carry astronauts beyond low Earth orbit, including to the Moon and, eventually, Mars. It is a key component of NASA’s Artemis programme, which aims to land the first woman and the next man on the Moon by 2024. But the White House deadline is widely considered overly ambitious given the repeated delays in launching the uncrewed Artemis I mission, which was originally scheduled for as early as 2017. A recent inspector general’s report highlighted risks of further setbacks if technical issues, such as software development and engine testing, are not resolved promptly. In a statement, NASA administrator Jim Bridenstine said the delay was necessary to ensure the spacecraft was "safe and capable." He added that while progress had been made, development of the associated Space Launch System (SLS) rocket, which will carry Orion on its first test flight, remained a major bottleneck. “We’re building the rocket that will take us back to the Moon, but we have to do it right,” he said. Orion’s first crewed mission was meant to coincide with the completion of the International Space Station's life expectancy — expected in the 2020s — and to pave the way for deep space exploration. Until now, NASA has been reliant on Russia’s Soyuz spacecraft to transport astronauts to the ISS, a situation about to change with the upcoming debut of private US companies SpaceX and Boeing under the agency’s Commercial Crew Programme. But Orion is expected to plug the gap in the future, sending humans to destinations beyond low Earth orbit for the first time since the Apollo era. The spacecraft can hold up to six astronauts and is designed for missions lasting up to three weeks, though it is also being considered for longer deep-space missions with support from the agency’s Gateway lunar outpost. Lawmakers from both parties have called on NASA to clarify the schedule and secure additional funding to meet the 2023 deadline.

Ukraine's win at this year’s Eurovision Song Contest has sent shockwaves through the bookmakers and stunned the commentary teams, who had heavily favoured Russia or Australia to take the coveted title. The Eastern European nation, which last won the contest in 2016, defied expectations as singer Kalush Orchestra claimed victory with their ballad  Stefania , earning a record-breaking total of 631 points — the highest ever in the contest's history. The unexpected triumph has sparked a social media frenzy, with fans hailing it as a "remarkable comeback" and a "light in the darkest of times" — a sentiment many have associated with the Russian-Ukrainian conflict. Among bookmakers, the result marked one of the biggest upsets in the contest’s 67-year history. Russia’s entry, delivered by frontman Sergey Lazarev with  Scares Me , had been installed as the pre-contest favourite and would have been a significant win for the Russian state broadcaster. Australia, meanwhile, dominated betting markets in the UK and Australia, with fans indulging in nationalistic goodwill and memories of Tones and I’s monumental third-place finish in 2020. Commentators were also left scrambling as their predictions were dashed. One leading Eurovision analyst had called Ukraine's entry "charming but unlikely to win," while others mistakenly suggested the contest had been reduced to a duel between Russia and Australia. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky later sent a message to Kalush Orchestra, calling their win “proof that even in war, someone can still sing for peace.” Kalush Orchestra, a hip-hop band hailing from the city of Khmelnytskyi, quickly became a symbol of hope for many in Ukraine. The band’s lead singer, about whom the song is written — "Stefania" — is his mother, and a deeply emotional and patriotic message of family love permeated the performance. The chorus, performed in both Ukrainian and English, moved audiences and judges alike, with several contestants applauding after the performance. The win will mark a bittersweet moment for the Eurovision host, which is currently being held in Malmö, Sweden, and raises renewed questions about the role of political tensions in the largely lighthearted show. Since 2016, the contest has increasingly become a proxy for wider geopolitical divides, with Russian and Ukrainian delegations often standing in silent protest during each other's performances. As Ukraine prepares to host the contest in 2024, speculation is already mounting as to whether the 2023 triumph could spark a homegrown repeat in the coming years.

For the first time in 43 years, England have defeated France to seal a place in the semi-finals of Euro 2017, in a dramatic and emotionally charged match at the IJsselsteil Stadion in Deventer. The historic win ended the Lionesses’ long wait for victory over their continental rivals and sent shockwaves through the footballing world as they displayed resilience and composure in what many expected to be a difficult battle. The game, played before a passionate and vocal crowd, lived up to its billing as a battle of the titans. France, the reigning European champions, had dominated the tournament with a blend of ruthless efficiency and individual brilliance. England, however, arrived with a sense of rediscovered purpose, buoyed by a well-structured team coached by Marco Silva and a squad hungry for glory on home soil. The decisive moment came in the 73rd minute when captain Steph Houghton, breaking a tie at 1-1, struck a late winner that sent the English fans in Deventer’s stands into wild celebration. Spectators wearing red and white waved flags and sang anthems, overwhelmed by the monumental achievement. France had initially held the advantage, with striker Louisa Necib putting them ahead early in the second half, capitalising on a defensive lapse. But England, undeterred, fought back with grit and character – Baptiste showed her evolving maturity with a finely worked equaliser shortly after. The match ebbed and flowed, with moments of high intensity and nail-biting tension, as both sets of players gave their all. In the final moments, Houghton made headlines with her dramatic intervention, a moment that will be replayed and celebrated across the nation. It was not just a goal, but a statement of intent by a team about to make history. England's triumph marks the furthest they have advanced in any major tournament in 15 years. Their manager Marco Silva spoke of the team’s unbreakable spirit. “This team has heart, unity, and fight,” he said after the match. “They believed in themselves, and tonight was all about belief.” As the Lionesses prepare for the semi-finals, the nation is holding its breath for what could be a fairy-tale run to a first-ever major tournament final. Their remarkable victory over France has set a new high point in the history of English women's football and sparked renewed hope and excitement across the country. And for fans watching from the comfort of their homes and in the lively pubs across England, what had started as a dream seven decades in the making feels ever more like a reality.

For decades, Virtual Reality (VR) has captured the imagination of scientists, filmmakers, and technologists alike. Once the stuff of science fiction, the dream of slipping into a fully immersive digital world has, at last, become a tangible reality. With recent advances in computing power, graphics, and wearable technology, VR is no longer a novelty but a transformative force reshaping industries from entertainment to healthcare, education to real estate. The concept of VR is not new. A century ago, inventors experimented with immersive visual experiences, and in the 1960s, Morton Heilig’s “Sensorama” machine offered a rudimentary form of multisensory simulation. By the 1990s, early VR headsets were showcased at tech expos, though they were clunky, expensive, and underwhelming. Fast forward to today, and the technology has matured, with sleek, affordable headsets like the Meta Quest 3, PlayStation VR2 and the HTC Vive capable of tracking movement, rendering high-resolution environments, and offering haptic feedback that blurs the line between the real and the virtual. At the forefront of this revolution is the gaming industry. High-profile titles such as “Half-Life: Alyx” have demonstrated the power of VR to transport users into richly detailed worlds, creating a level of interactivity never before possible. But games are just one part of the story. In healthcare, VR is being used to help treat PTSD, manage chronic pain, and train surgeons in complex procedures without the risk to patients. In education, universities are using VR to offer immersive virtual field trips and complex simulations for students learning everything from anatomy to astrophysics. The architecture and construction industries are also benefiting, with firms using VR to give clients “walkthroughs” of future buildings, helping visualise designs and make changes before any walls are built. Employers are even starting to use VR for remote onboarding and employee training, reducing the need for physical travel while improving engagement and retention.
