One of its managing partners, a former investment banker with a background in competitive chess, has said in the past that human capital in business is as much a game of strategy and timing as any financial instrument. “If you want to build a position, you often need to create a bit of noise,” he told Fortune in a recent interview. “Sometimes, the message you want to send is just as important as the numbers on the screen.” This statement has led to speculation that the firm’s high-profile approach is not just a PR strategy, but a calculated method to weigh in on the companies and politicians they invest against — or for. Some industry insiders argue that Chasing Alpha Capital’s tactic is not entirely out of touch with typical Wall Street practice. Others see it as a dangerous game, that risks alienating key partners and regulators who may not appreciate being the subject of public jabs and aggressive market bets. The hedge fund’s CEO, speaking at a private luncheon last week, was asked directly about the firm’s recent provocations. “We don't shy away from a fight if we feel we’re right,” he said. “In the long run, the truth and the market usually agree.”

With a record-breaking number of Northern Ireland supporters making the journey to France for Euro 2016, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has been working behind the scenes to ensure fans are properly looked after on the ground. An estimated 8,500 supporters are expected to attend matches at seven different venues across the country, and Ireland’s embassy in Paris has been activated as an 'away office' to provide consular assistance in case of emergencies. A team of five embassy staff have also been seconded to the Consulate General in Marseille, where three Northern Ireland matches are to be played and where the majority of fans are based. Recent political tensions have not dampened enthusiasm among supporters, and unlike previous tournaments, no official policing plan has been drawn up by the PSNI to deal with potential hooliganism. The Football Association of Ireland, meanwhile, has co-ordinated special pick-up points in the UK for fans to meet in, prior to charter flights to France. As well as logistical support, the diplomatic service will be on standby in the unlikely event of fan-related incidents, such as arrests or sudden ill health. One issue that has arisen is the confusion over travel documents—many supporters applied too close to the tournament and did not anticipate that their passports would expire during the competition. While Northern Ireland fans have generally been praised for their organisation and decorum, protesters from national organisations – such as Fianna Fail, Sinn Féin and the Labour Party – are expected to attend matches in Marseille to mark what they have described as the “political significance” of Irish nationalism on the world stage. However, with no official protests expected to disrupt the tournament, the main concern remains fan safety. Some fans had previously expressed concern over the lack of a central ‘fan zone’ in Marseille, in contrast to other European Championship host cities. But after a meeting between the FAI and local officials this week, a 400-person cap was introduced to each of the city's four unauthorised fan parks. Northern Ireland’s first match of the tournament will take place at 5pm on June 12 against Ukraine in Marseille. The supporters’ experience, it is hoped, will be remembered for the passion and unity they displayed, rather than any diplomatic or organisational hurdles. 'We have the best of intentions,' said Ireland's embassy in Paris in a statement earlier this week.

EDF Casts Shadow Over Hinkley Point Nuclear Plant Amid Rising Doubts   Fresh uncertainty has emerged over the ambitious £18 billion plan by French energy giant EDF to build a new nuclear power plant at Hinkley Point in Somerset, as warnings grow over soaring costs, technical uncertainties, and the shifting landscape of energy demand in the UK. The proposed nuclear facility, one of the most significant energy infrastructure projects in the UK in decades, has long been positioned by successive governments as a cornerstone of the nation’s clean energy strategy. Yet, according to insiders and industry observers, the project is once again being called into question following revelations within EDF about escalating financial pressures and delays in finalising contracts. A report seen by the  Financial Times  suggests that EDF is re-evaluating the long-term viability of the Hinkley Point C project, with concerns mounting over its ability to secure the necessary long-term electricity price guarantees with the UK government. Under the original agreement, British consumers would subsidise the project’s energy output for 35 years, with the so-called "strike price" fixed at £92.50 per megawatt-hour—more than double the current market rate. Energy experts have warned that with the wholesale price of power falling and the UK increasingly investing in cheaper renewable sources like wind and solar, the financial model for Hinkley is no longer as attractive as once assumed. According to a source close to the project, “EDF is undoubtedly feeling the squeeze as energy markets evolve much faster than anticipated. The company is now in a difficult position, balancing its commitments in the UK with the need to invest in a more diverse European energy strategy.” The turmoil at EDF is not confined to Hinkley. The energy company has also struggled with its other major European project in Finland, where the Olkiluoto-3 reactor has been significantly over-budget and years behind schedule. These fails have done little to inspire confidence in the French firm’s ability to deliver complex nuclear projects on time and on budget. For residents in Somerset, the delays are deeply concerning. The Hinkley Point project was expected to create thousands of construction jobs and provide long-term employment once the power station is operational—planned for as early as 2025. Local business leaders and politicians have warned that the recent doubts could set back the region's economic development and strain the fragile negotiations between the UK government and EDF about cost overruns.

The British and Irish Lions kept their World Cup-winning momentum on track with a dominant display against a hard-pressed but outmatched Melbourne Rebels side in the Victorian city on Saturday. The match, played at AAMI Park, provided a timely opportunity for Warren Gatland’s squad to fine-tune their tactics ahead of the second Test against Australia in Perth on Saturday. With a rabid home crowd expecting a spirited challenge, the Rebels were all but overpowered by the Lions’ physicality and tactical discipline in a 42-12 victory. With a place in the World Cup final still fresh in their collective memory, the Lions showcased the same intensity and composure that brought them success in New Zealand last year. Captain Alun Wyn Jones, still basking in the glory of the World Cup triumph, was instrumental in the early bursts of play, anchoring the pack at the breakdown while young forwards and open-side flankers displayed a hunger for success in a vibrant and competitive environment. Johnny Sexton, the seasoned Ireland fly-half, was in his element under the Melbourne lights, orchestrating attacks with clinical precision. His first-half try, a well-timed strike following a clever continuation off a rolling maul, typified the smooth interplay between the forwards and backs. The Lions took a commanding 24-0 lead into the break, with both sets of scrum-half, Ali Price and Harry Lloyd, playing vital roles in maintaining possession and tempo. The Rebels, coached by Tony McGahan, offered brief respite in the second half with a well-worked try from young winger Jordan Chatfield, but for much of the game they struggled to match the tempo and physicality of the Lions. Their forwards, despite a valiant effort, were outmuscle in the contact areas, particularly in the set pieces where the Lions’ dominant front-row trio of Tadhg Furlong, Wyn Jones and Rory Sutherland gained valuable minutes and scorched the Rebels’ scrum up the track to the dismay of the home supporters. For the Lions, the match was more than just preparation for the Australia Test – it was a celebration of unity and momentum. Gatland, whose strategic acumen guided the Lions to their first World Cup win in nearly 40 years, acknowledged the importance of the result in team morale and cohesion. “The boys are buzzing,” he said. “They showed the same spirit and hunger on the field as they did in New Zealand.

Ed Miliband has hailed Labour’s performance in the European elections as a sign of "progress," promising that the party would continue to build momentum in the run-up to the general election next year. Speaking at a press briefing after results were declared, the Labour leader said the party’s second-place finish—despite a challenging political climate—showed “the clear sense that people want change.” However, Mr Miliband was careful not to overstate Labour’s position, acknowledging that while the party made gains from the 2014 elections, there is still “further to go” to close the gap on the Conservatives. Labour emerged as the second-largest party in the UK's European Parliament, securing 30 seats, compared to the Conservatives’ 27 and the Brexit Party’s 29. The results were broadly seen as a repudiation of the Brexit Party, which, while gaining the most seats, fell short of an outright majority, and indicative of a tactical shift, with many voters turning to pro-Remain or centrist parties. Mr Miliband praised his candidates, calling them “strong and united,” and warned that the real test would come in December when the nation votes in the local elections and next year in the general election. He said: “We sent a message today that there is a country behind us that wants to be part of building a better future at home and standing up for the UK in Europe.” The European election results come as the Labour Party continues efforts to rebuild following years of low polling and internal divisions. The party’s defeat in the 2019 general election and the departure of Jeremy Corbyn from leadership have brought a more moderate tone under Mr Miliband’s leadership, with a focus on commanding the central ground in UK politics. Some analysts have suggested that the European results, while not a victory, reflect growing dissatisfaction with the Government’s handling of Brexit and its economic priorities. Shadow Chancellor Anneliese Dodds told the BBC: “We believe people are fed up with a poisonous culture of division and are looking for a more positive alternative. The results today show that the country is ready for fresh leadership and unity." The Conservatives, led by Chancellor Rishi Sunak, said the result was “a vindication of our strong campaign and people’s trust in our message.” They pointed to the 54 additional members of the European Parliament who support Brexit, including the vast majority of Brexit Party MPs, as evidence of a majority for leaving the EU.

This week promises a politically charged atmosphere as the UK’s longest-running constitutional drama moves into a decisive phase with the announcement of the Brexit referendum date. The government will reveal its chosen day for the momentous vote on Monday, after months of speculation and parliamentary wrangling over the timing. The EU referendum, likely to take place in June, marks a pivotal milestone in the UK’s relationship with the bloc and will shape the country’s political and economic future for a generation. A consultation by the Cabinet Office had sparked questions about whether turnout could be enforced, as some supporters of the Leave campaign called for the vote to be held on a working day to exclude commuters. However, the government ruled out a working-day referendum, and it is now expected the date will fall on a Saturday in June. The prime minister will also outline new legal powers for the intelligence services MI5, MI6, and GCHQ, which were promised in the government’s 2015 manifesto. These powers would allow British spooks to obtain much greater authority to monitor and respond to criminal and terror threats, as part of a wide-ranging counter-terrorism and surveillance bill. The announcement is expected to reignite the fierce national debate over the balance between security and civil liberties that has emerged since the 2013 Investigatory Powers Act, which critics called the “Snooper’s Charter.” Speaking from the House of Commons, a senior minister warned that the UK must be “prepared for the evolving threats we face,” and that the new framework would ensure the intelligence agencies are “fit for purpose in the 21st century.” Meanwhile, parliamentary businesses are set to debate the emergency services bill, which will expand the responsibilities of the police and other public services in times of major incidents and national emergencies. The legislation has drawn concerns from privacy groups and human rights campaigners, who fear it could lead to increased state control and undermine individual rights during periods of crisis. In other developments, the House of Lords will examine the housing crisis, calling for urgent action to address the UK’s shortage of affordable homes. With tensions mounting across a range of domestic and foreign affairs, it is a week that will test the government’s determination to deliver on its promises while managing deep divisions within the electorate and Parliament. The coming days may well set the tone for a year of political upheaval, as the country braces for one of the most significant democratic decisions in its modern history.

Leigh Halfpenny, one of Wales’ most celebrated rugby full-backs, has confirmed his move to French club Toulon, marking the latest chapter in his glittering professional career. The forward-thinking decision by the 33-year-old star sets him up for a new challenge in one of the most competitive leagues in Europe, as he prepares to partner with some of the game’s most high-profile talents. Halfpenny, who has represented Wales on over 100 occasions and was a key figure in the 2019 Rugby World Cup squad, has spent the majority of his playing career in the UK, with stints at Ospreys, Toulon, and more recently Cardiff Rugby, before the undisclosed financial terms of his transfer to the French Top 14 giants were finalised. The announcement, made official by both the player and the club on Monday, was met with a wave of reaction from fans, pundits, and fellow players alike. Toulon, currently captained by Brian Jackman and in the early stages of rebuilding under new coach Fabien Galthié, is eager to restore its former glory after fluctuating performances over the past few seasons. The club, which proudly boasts a short but storied history of attracting rugby legends such as Jonny Wilkinson, George North, and Stuart Hogg, is hopeful that Halfpenny's exceptional kicking ability and experience will prove a vital addition in both the Champions Cup and the domestic league. Speaking of his decision to re-join Toulon, Halfpenny commented: “It's a proud moment for me to be returning to a club with such a vibrant rugby culture and global appeal. I’m looking forward to the challenge of working in France again and being part of a team that’s aiming to compete at the very top.” The timing of the move has sparked speculation about Halfpenny’s future with the Welsh national team, though the player has been careful to leave the door open. “As long as I have the opportunity to play for Wales, I will always do everything I can to be ready,” he said. “Representing your country is an honour, and I hope I can continue to do so while being part of a strong club team as well.” Head coach Warren Gatland, who recently led Wales to the 2023 Six Nations title, did not immediately comment on Halfpenny's departure, leaving room for speculation over his place in the national side.

A giant sixgill shark, suspected to be the largest of its kind ever caught on a fishing line in Europe, has been reeled in off the coast of County Clare, Ireland, sparking both excitement and superstition among anglers and marine biologists. The enormous creature, described as a "monster" by those present, was reportedly estimated to weigh in excess of 1,000 pounds and measure approximately 11 feet in length. The shark was caught by a local angler this week, details of which have begun to circulate rapidly through local and online media. Sixgill sharks, also known as "sixgillers," are rarely encountered by recreational fishermen due to their deep-water habitat, typically found at depths of 300 to 6,500 feet (91 to 1,981 meters), far below the reach of most fishing gear. The species is considered a type of "megamouth," part of an ancient lineage of sharks that include the cowshark family (Hexanchidae). Their five oversized gill slits — not six — and stocky, bear-like appearance have given rise to the nickname, and their presence in shallower waters is considered a rare event. Ireland is no stranger to unusual marine encounters. In recent years, locals have reported sightings of giant squid, sea lions, and even penguins washed up along coastal stretches. But a sixgill shark being caught on the end of a rod is unprecedented in European waters. Experts consulted by the BBC and Science Ireland say the creature is the largest of its kind ever recorded to have been caught in this way, surpassing previous records by a significant margin. The fisherman, who has not been named at this stage, used heavy-duty tackle in a deep-sea fishing expedition off the Atlantic coast. After what can only be described as a battle of epic proportions — with the shark reportedly thrashing for over two hours — the angler managed to bring in the colossal sixgiller for identification and processing. To preserve the welfare of the creature, and at the behest of marine protection groups, the scientists involved have confirmed that accurate measurements will be taken, but the fish will then be released back into the ocean. Local marine biologist Dr. Seán Grimes told Radio Ireland: "This is a very rare and possibly historic find. Sixgill sharks are believed to go back 150 million years or more. They're prehistoric in line and encountering one, let alone catching it, is an extraordinary event. To find one on the Irish coast — in such size — is impressive."

Serena Williams has vowed to focus solely on her own game rather than the possibility of surpassing Steffi Graf’s long-standing Grand Slam record as she prepares for this year’s Australian Open. The American tennis legend, currently tied with Graf on 22 Grand Slam singles titles, has refused to allow the milestone to become a distraction, insisting that her priorities remain on delivering her best performance on the court. The 38-year-old, who has already etched her name into history with an Open Era record for most titles won on each major surface, has approached the tournament with trademark determination. "I’m never going in thinking about the past or what else could be added to my name," Williams said in a recent interview. "My focus is always on the present and doing what I love. I respect Steffi and her achievements, but I can't live someone else's dream. I live mine." Williams has turned to a new team in recent months, including working with Patrick Mouratoglou, and has been reinvigorated in her pursuit of another Grand Slam title. Her return to the Grand Slam scene was marked by a title win at the US Open in 2023, her first since the 2017 tournament. The victory demonstrated that the ten-time Wimbledon champion is still in formidable form, despite her age and the physical challenges that come with motherhood – Williams is currently raising two young daughters and has spoken openly about the difficulty of balancing family life with professional tennis. Graf’s record, set in 1998 with 22 Grand Slam championships, has stood unchallenged for over two decades. It counts among the most elusive achievements in sport and has been a benchmark for generations of female tennis players. Margit Farra, Graf’s longtime coach and former national team director in Germany, has hinted that the former world No.1 had no expectation of being surpassed and even doubted it would ever happen. "Serena is a once-in-a-lifetime talent, but for her to go beyond what Steffi did…” Farra trailed off, declining to speculate further. For Williams, the attention surrounding her achievements has long been a double-edged sword. While she is widely celebrated for her skill, resilience and impact on the sport, she has also faced intense media scrutiny and public debate over her legacy and achievements. This latest milestone, if reached, will add another layer of commentary to her already storied career.

The Labour Party is facing a moment of existential crisis, with its very survival hanging in the balance unless the deepening leadership crisis is urgently resolved, according to senior Labour MP Wayne David. Speaking in a rare and forthright warning, the Caerphilly representative said the party is at a “crucial point” in its history and that “without unity and coherent purpose, it could very well cease to exist.” David's comments come amid a widening divide within the parliamentary Labour Party over the government's handling of key issues, including Brexit, the economy, and domestic policy. The row was further exacerbated by recent resignations of prominent Labour figures, including suspended MP Tom Watson, who accused senior leaders of allowing a “poisoned” internal culture to fester. The unrest has led to a growing faction of MPs expressing frustration with the direction of the party, with some calling for Oliver Dowden, chair of the 1922 Committee of backbench Tory MPs, to intervene. However, David suggested that this would be a last-resort step and that the party needs to initiate its own reformation from within. “We need to speak with one voice again,” he said. “This is not about one side or another winning short-term arguments; it’s about saving the party for the long term.” Labour leader Ed Miliband has called for dialogue and unity, but many within the party – particularly younger members – are concerned that his approach does not go far enough. They argue that the lack of clarity over policy and the absence of internal discipline is alienating both members and voters. According to internal Labour sources, discussions are also underway over a potential leadership review, although no formal motion has yet been tabled. Shadow Home Secretary Emily Thornberry and Energy Secretary Ed Davey have both been speculated as possible candidates for a reshuffle or leadership bid if the situation continues to spiral. David, who has served as a Labour MP for over 20 years, urged the leadership to listen to the concerns of members. “We cannot afford to look like a party in disarray,” he said. “The message to the leadership is clear – this is our last chance to get it right.” The question now is whether the Labour Party can find common ground in time to prevent a political collapse that could redefine the British political landscape. Labour’s next election could well be its most important one yet – or it may not even come.

Police forces across the United Kingdom have paid a total of at least £22 million to informants over the past five years, according to new figures obtained by BBC Radio 5 Live through a freedom of information request. The data reveal a broad and often controversial £20 million spent during the 2021-22 financial year alone, sparking renewed debate about the role, cost, and regulation of informants in UK policing. The payments include money given to so-called “Cleverpersons,” a term used by police to refer to individuals who assist in the surveillance of suspected criminals, often for months or years at a time. Figures obtained from 37 of the 43 UK police forces show a vast range of spending, with some forces paying informants well into five figures. South Wales Police revealed it spent £781,388 on payments in 2021-22, while Greater Manchester Police spent £2.8 million during the same period. While the use of informants is not in itself unusual in law enforcement, the sheer scale of the spending has prompted questions about transparency and accountability. Critics argue that the lack of publicly accessible, detailed records on how informants are selected, managed, and compensated undermines public trust in the system. The issue has been exacerbated by high-profile cases, including the Hillsborough inquest into the 1989 disaster, where the testimony of a paid informant was later found to be instrumental in misleading the public and the police inquiry. Earlier this year, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) also admitted that someone acting in an official capacity had given a false account of the Hillsborough events to a senior officer in 1990, and that this was not disclosed at the inquest. In response to the recent figures, the Home Office confirmed that the statutory limit on payments to informants is currently set at £400,000 per year. However, it is believed that many of the most expensive payments are for operations that require long-term surveillance and intelligence-gathering roles that justify higher sums. “Paying for intelligence is part of the operational cost of policing,” a Home Office spokesperson told the BBC. “In some cases, police need to pay to access the information required to protect the public.” Nevertheless, the scale of the spending has raised questions about whether police are following strict procedural guidelines when vetting and managing their informant networks. Concerns have also been voiced about the potential line between payment and inducement—particularly when individuals are rewarded for what can sometimes be dangerous or morally ambiguous work.

Volvo's chief executive, Håkan Samuelsson, finds himself at the helm of a carmaker undergoing a dramatic transformation — and when asked to describe exactly what makes Volvo the company it is today, he gives an answer as deft and enigmatic as the man himself. “Who are we?” he replies with a smile, turning the question back on to his interviewer. It is an answer that is neither an evasion nor an outright refusal, but a subtle challenge — one that echoes the brand's evolving identity. Volvo, long associated with Swedish reliability, safety and a certain no-nonsense attitude, has never been a name synonymous with bold reinvention — until now. Since its acquisition by Chinese automotive giant Geely in 2010, the company has made a series of high-profile strategic moves that have sparked both interest and uncertainty. Most recently, the brand announced its commitment to a fully electric future by the 2030s — a bold step into an era when internal combustion engines look increasingly anachronistic. Samuelsson, who has been steering Volvo through this transition for nearly a decade, is keenly aware of the questions surrounding the company’s role in a rapidly shifting industry. Yet he remains confident in the direction it is taking. “We are moving from being a traditional carmaker to a modern, global company focused on electrification, autonomous driving, and – above all – innovation,” he said in a recent interview at Volvo’s head office in Gothenburg. This repositioning has already begun to bear fruit. The XC40, launched in 2017, marked a dramatic departure from Volvo’s earlier, more conservative designs. It was fresh, compact, and connected — a car for the here and now. The success of the XC40 and its successors, such as the XC90 and the Polestar 2 (Volvo’s electric performance brand), signals Volvo is no longer simply trying to keep up with the market — it is setting the pace. Such confidence is hard to build when your brand has spent decades as a supplier of practicality over performance. But as the automobile industry enters a new phase — one defined by sustainability, technology and the reimagining of what a car should be — Samuelsson and his team have the wherewithal to do just that. Whether you ask “Who are we?” or simply watch their accelerating progress, the answer appears to be shaping up — one electric revolution at a time. What remains, perhaps, is to define the question nobody yet dares to ask.

Chris Wood Scores Late Decider as Leeds Edge Past Blackburn in Hard-fought EFL Cup Clash   A late goal from substitute Chris Wood secured a narrow 1-0 victory for Leeds United over Blackburn Rovers in a tense and physical EFL Cup third-round encounter at Elland Road on Wednesday night. The scrappy match, which failed to ignite the sort of fireworks many had hoped for, saw the Whites grind out a crucial win that keeps their cup defence on track. With just minutes remaining, Wood latched onto a loose ball in the box and expertly bundled it over the line to break the deadlock and send the Elland Road crowd into raptures. It was a moment of clinical finishes that proved decisive, despite the harsh, often frustrating nature of the game that preceded it. Both sides struggled to impose themselves early on, with the conditions, albeit dry, contributing to a gritty, stop-start tempo. Leeds, playing with an extended squad due to the competitive nature of manager Daniel Farke’s midweek fixtures, frequently rotated their line-up. Blackburn, currently five divisions below their hosts, were expected to be underdogs but came to the match with confidence following recent improvements under interim manager Paul Lambert. Leeds showed occasional glimpses of quality, as expected, but were unable to convert early chances. Forward Honor Muragijimana – on a first start for the club – was a bright spark in the first-half, but found it difficult to break down a resolute Blackburn backline. Blackburn offered their own threats on the counter, with Liam Feeney, the young forward making his first full Premier League 2 start at a senior level, coming close with a low strike that forced a smart save from Leeds’ former Blackburn and Bolton ‘keeper, Illan Meslier. As the game developed, both managers made a series of substitutions, seemingly to test the different areas of their squads. The breakthrough finally came in the closing stages when Wood pounced on a misplaced Blackburn pass, quickly advancing the ball, and squaring it to the feet of Marcus Antonsson, who was pushed off the ball as it fell kindly for the New Zealand international to steer it into the net. Speaking after the match, Farke praised Wood's composure in a vital moment: “It’s a difficult game with so many moving parts, but Chris showed experience and a ruthless streak. We needed that moment today.”

The developer behind a heavy-load drone capable of lifting up to 500kg has revealed ambitious plans to test its ability to navigate autonomously between trees and other obstacles by the end of the year. The drone, produced by a London-based tech startup, represents a significant leap in unmanned aircraft technology and is being hailed as a potential game-changer for industries including logistics, farming, and construction. The company, which has not yet disclosed its name ahead of a planned media launch this summer, has sparked interest in both the tech and transport sectors by adapting drone capabilities to match the demands of heavy cargo. While smaller drones are already used for tasks such as surveying land and delivering packages, this new model is unlike any seen before in the UK, with a payload capacity that rivals that of a small van. During a recent closed demonstration for a panel of industry experts, the drone successfully lifted a 500kg load and maintained stable flight in open conditions. Now, engineers are focusing on the next challenge: refining the drone’s navigation system for complex environments. The team is exploring the use of advanced machine learning algorithms and high-resolution LIDAR mapping to enable the drone to identify and evade obstacles—such as tree canopies or building structures—without human intervention. A spokesperson for the company explained: “We want this drone to be able to move independently through terrain that would normally require a manned flight path. That means flying between trees, navigating narrow construction sites, and even avoiding unexpected obstacles in real time.” Such capabilities could have profound implications for the UK’s green infrastructure projects and disaster response capabilities. For example, the drones could deliver essential supplies to remote communities affected by floods or wildfires, bypassing damaged roads and other ground obstacles. The project has also attracted interest from the Department for Transport, which is reportedly in discussions with the company regarding potential applications in rural logistics and transportation of cargo to remote areas unserved by roads. Environmental campaigners have praised the potential of the technology to reduce the carbon footprint of transportation, particularly in the delivery chain. A spokesperson for the National Farmers' Union said: “If this works at scale, the ability to transport heavy goods using electricity-powered drones could significantly cut road traffic and emissions in rural areas.” As the company moves into its intensive testing phase, it plans to begin trials in the countryside of Southern England, with the goal of achieving full autonomous capability by year’s end.

A passenger jet flying into Heathrow Airport today avoided a potentially catastrophic mid-air collision after it is believed to have flown into a drone. The incident, which occurred at approximately 5pm as the Airbus A320 descended over Hounslow, has prompted an urgent investigation by the Metropolitan Police and the Airprox Board. According to initial reports, the pilot made an emergency report to air traffic control, saying he had struck an object "mid-airspeed," though no immediate damage to the engines was apparent. The crew carried out a routine inspection while still in flight and continued to land the aircraft safely. Passengers told reporters that the aircraft had made a sudden jolt but there were no visible signs of damage. Heathrow Airport released a brief statement, confirming "an object strike" and saying all other flights at the airport were operating normally. However, the incident has reignited calls for stricter enforcement of drone regulations, particularly in the densely populated airspace surrounding London’s major airports. The UK’s strict no-fly zone for drones within five miles of airports is already being enforced using geofencing technology, which prevents drones from operating in restricted areas. Yet experts warn that malicious or poorly maintained drones, or those with disabled geofencing, can still pose a significant risk to commercial aviation. Transport for London said today that there was “no evidence at this point” of a deliberate attempt to interfere with flight operations but added: “This is under active investigation.” The drone involved is suspected to be no larger than a standard model used for recreational purposes, yet the potential consequences were alarming. In 2018, a commercial flight bound for Glasgow was forced to divert after a drone strike caused massive damage to the fuselage, and similar incidents in France and the US have raised global concerns about the growing threat. Prime Minister Rishi Sharma expressed his concern after being briefed on the incident. “This is a clear reminder of how seriously we must take the issue of rogue drones and the need to ensure unauthorised devices are not flying in sensitive areas,” he said. “We will work closely with the police and aviation authorities to ensure those responsible are brought to justice and to prevent further incidents.” The Airprox Board, which handles air security threats, has already deployed investigators to monitor the area around Heathrow and surrounding airfields for any clues. Drone operator Johnny Malone, a campaigner for safer drone use, said the incident was “a wake of the day” for both drone users and regulators.

The justice system in England and Wales is taking a major step towards streamlining and improving family-related legal processes as new combined Family Courts officially came into operation on Monday. The reform is part of a long-awaited overhaul of the family justice system, aimed at ensuring faster, more efficient and child-focused outcomes for families going through legal disputes. The new courts will consolidate the work of the existing County Courts and the existing Family Division of the High Court into a single jurisdiction. This means all family-related cases, including child custody, domestic abuse, adoption, divorce and financial settlements, will now be dealt with in the same set of courts by specialist judges and magistrates. The move is expected to reduce delays, make the system more transparent and, most importantly, focus on resolution rather than adversarial proceedings. The reform follows years of criticism about the slowness and complexity of the current system, which often leaves families in limbo for months or even years. In recent years, there have been several high-profile cases where children suffered needlessly while parents were delayed in getting legal resolutions. Home Secretary Suella Braverman, who announced the reforms in a statement, said the new system would “put the child at the heart” of family justice and make it “simpler, clearer and fairer”. Judges and magistrates undergoing training specifically on family law will now oversee these combined courts. The Legal Aid Agency – which provides funding for legal help in family cases – will also be adapting its services to support the new system. Campaigners and legal experts have welcomed the change, albeit with cautious optimism. Dr. Rachel Hearn, a solicitor and legal commentator, said: “This is a long overdue reform. For years, the family justice system has been creaking under the weight of its own complexity. Combining the courts is about more than just efficiency – it’s about the impact on real people’s lives. If a child can get the right care arrangement faster, or a parent can secure a divorce without unnecessary delays, that’s a step in the right direction.” However, concerns remain about the capacity and resources available to the new courts. With a backlog of thousands of cases already in the system, critics question whether the reform will be as swift as expected. Also, there is apprehension about the potential for confusion among the public and legal professionals during the transition.

Another senseless tragedy marks the tragic rhythm of America   Once again, American television screens are filled with the grim images of first responders, the audible wail of ambulances, and the muted voices of community leaders struggling to make sense of yet another mass shooting. This time, it happened in a quiet town in Ohio — but it might just as easily have been Las Vegas, Orlando, Parkland, or countless other towns that have become synonymous with national grief and political paralysis. President Barack Obama, now in the final months of his presidency, issued yet another heartfelt and sombre statement. "Losing lives in yet another act of gun violence reminds us that we cannot afford to stand by when we know we can do something," he said in a televised address from the White House on Tuesday. "These tragedies are not isolated incidents — they are symptoms of a broken system, and they demand a real solution." It is an all-too-familiar script. Each shooting brings a spike in public debate and media coverage. Survivors and grieving families speak out, demanding action. Politicians, including the president, echo the call for tighter gun laws and stronger background checks. Then, as weeks pass, the headlines fade — and the cycle continues. Even as Obama's grief is real, so is the frustration of many watching. Over the years, he has pushed for comprehensive gun control measures – most notably after the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting in 2012. His administration championed the reinstatement of the federal assault weapons ban, and he has frequently condemned the influence of the National Rifle Association (NRA) on American politics. Yet, the legislative landscape has resisted meaningful change. The latest shooting is a grim reminder of the stark divide in American society: where the majority of Americans support common-sense measures like universal background checks, the political machinery of the gun lobby remains deeply entrenched. The NRA, with its vast financial and political resources, continues to block even the most modest attempts at reform. The president has made it clear he will not leave office without making one last push for gun control. White House officials confirmed he is planning an executive action to close what is known as the “boyfriend loophole” – which currently allows individuals with a history of domestic violence but no criminal conviction to legally purchase firearms. Some lawmakers, both Democrats and Republicans, have come forward in support of the proposal, though many others remain on the sidelines, wary of backlash.

All Your Favourites in One Place: The Ultimate Sports Hub Launches   For fans of all teams and sports, a new era in digital sports coverage has arrived. In a bid to revolutionise how sports content is accessed, a groundbreaking online platform has launched, offering fans a one-stop shop for all the sports they love — from football and rugby to cricket, tennis, and even niche competitions. Whether you’re an ardent supporter of Arsenal, a fan of Aneurin Benford in the Welsh Premier League, or a follower of international darts or snooker, this new service aims to bring everything to your screen in one place. Developed by a consortium of digital publishing experts and backed by some of the UK's leading sports broadcasters, the platform is being hailed as the most comprehensive sports portal in the UK to date. It promises real-time scores, live commentary, in-depth news, and exclusive features — all tailored to the individual user’s preferences. By leveraging cutting-edge algorithms, the site personalises content delivery, highlighting match highlights, breaking news, and player updates from the sports, leagues, and teams each user supports. One of the key features of the platform is its 'All Access Championship' section, which allows subscribers to keep up with both domestic and international fixtures across all sports. From Premier League action to domestic Cup finals, and from international rugby series to local cup tournaments, the site ensures fans don’t miss a moment, regardless of location or time zone. The Welsh Football Trust voiced support for the initiative, commenting that the portal could help boost the profile of Welsh teams in both football and rugby in an increasingly competitive global media landscape. “This is exactly what we need at a time when Welsh clubs and athletes crave more visibility,” said a spokesperson. Similarly, cricket lovers will welcome the fully integrated live scores and video highlights from key matches in the County Championship and the T20 Blast. The portal is also designed with casual fans and data enthusiasts alike in mind, offering a ‘smart stats’ section with breakdowns on player performances, form trends, and much more. Parents of young players, too, can benefit from sections dedicated to youth sports development, including guidance on talent spotting, training schedules, and event calendars for emerging sports bodies in academies across Wales. Mark Thomas, a football fan from Cardiff and early adopter of the service, said: “It’s brilliant.

Tottenham Hotspur kept up the pressure on Premier League leaders Chelsea with a dramatic 3-2 victory over Everton at Goodison Park, moving to within seven points of the summit as their rivals were denied by a midweek FA Cup tie. The win, earned in bruising and often chaotic fashion, saw Spurs move up to second in the table and underline their credentials as genuine title challengers. While the Blues played West Ham on Monday, a fixture that conveniently allowed Antonio Conte’s side to avoid losing ground, Spurs delighted in attacking Premier League form that has seen them go 14 matches unbeaten. The chase for the title is well under way, with the difference between top and second now made up of points, not the seemingly insurmountable gulf of form that loomed earlier in the season. After a frustrating week for Harry Kane, the English striker was finally on the scoresheet as Spurs took the lead in the 29th minute. Dele Alli, often the prime supplier this season, curled a beautifully weighted cross across the six-yard box, and Kane, pressing forward from near the byeline, converted with a clinical finish past Jordan Pickford. Yet it was Everton who came close to capitalising on a nervous defensive showing from the hosts early in the second half. Richarlison, on for the first time this month, pounced on a loose Spurs backline to equalise just after the hour, drawing roars of support from the Goodison crowd. But Tottenham, buoyed by their manager Mauricio Pochettino’s ability to galvanise his players at critical moments, responded with a counter-attacking flourish just minutes later. Heung-Min Son, who had continued his blistering goal-scoring form this term, found space in the box and curled a stunning shot into the top corner. Everton, to their credit, did not lie down and immediately countered again, with Gylfi Sigurdsson scoring an equaliser after a mazy run from the halfway line that left the Spurs’ backline in disarray. With the score at 2-2 deep into stoppage time, it seemed Goodison would escape with a draw – but Kyle Walker, unfairly treated over the course of the game by the referee, delivered a right-wing cross that Jan Vertonghen met with a powerful header beyond Pickford. The goal sent the travelling Tottenham contingent into delirium and emphatically sealed the points. Pochettino made no secret of the significance of the result.

At least 27 migrants have died off the Turkish coast while attempting to reach the Greek island of Lesbos, according to reports from Turkish state media. The tragedy unfolded after the rubber dinghy carrying the migrants capsized in rough seas, leaving dozens thrown into the water and unable to swim to safety. Coast guard teams were quick to respond but rescue efforts were hampered by the difficult conditions, with only a handful of survivors pulled from the water before a deadly wave of cold and fatigue set in. The incident has once again brought into sharp focus the perilous journey that many asylum-seekers undertake in search of a better life in Europe. Migrants from conflict-torn Syria, as well as countries like Afghanistan and Pakistan, often rely on smugglers to arrange transport across the Aegean Sea, despite numerous high-profile deaths in the region this year. Lesbos has become one of the frontline locations for the migrant crisis, with local authorities and humanitarian agencies struggling to cope with the relentless inflow of arrivals. Reports suggest that the victims of this latest tragedy included women and children, as is often the case in such incidents. Survivors, many of them still in shock, were taken to the port of Lesbos, where they are now being assessed by health officials. The Turkish coast guard has opened an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the capsizing, while Greek and European officials have called for renewed cooperation to address the growing humanitarian challenge along the eastern Mediterranean route. This latest disaster occurred just days after the International Organization for Migration (IOM) reported that more than 1,000 people have died this year alone in Mediterranean crossings—placing 2017 already on course to match or exceed the death toll of the previous year. The IOM and other agencies have urged governments to do more to save lives at sea, with calls for increased funding for safe transportation, better border coordination, and an acceleration of asylum procedures. In the wake of the Lesbos tragedy, the European Union has reiterated its plea to Turkey and other countries for cooperation in processing and managing the flow of refugees. With borders stretched thin and distrust among local communities rising, the situation remains volatile—and the question of how to balance security with humanitarian obligations persists as one of the most pressing challenges of our time. Officials in both Turkey and the EU have been contacted for further statements.

A brutal attack on a vulnerable pensioner has led to a conviction after a man was found guilty of her murder in a harrowing case that has shocked the local community. The defendant, 37-year-old Nathan Price, entered the home of 82-year-old Doris Shaw in the quiet village of Halesworth, Suffolk, in January, and subjected her to a terrifying ordeal before fatally attacking her with a rolling pin. Police were called to the property following reports of a serious assault. Inside, officers found Miss Shaw critically injured, with signs of violent abuse. She died days later in hospital from her injuries. An investigation revealed the horror of what had taken place prior to her death: Price had apparently demanded Miss Shaw's bank PIN, and when she refused to give it up, subjected her to prolonged torture. During the trial, the court heard how Price had bound the elderly woman, pressed pins into her skin and screamed at her while she was forced to wait for several hours before the attack was carried out. The prosecution painted a chilling picture of criminal intent, highlighting the calculated and sadistic nature of the crime. Miss Shaw, a retired schoolteacher, had lived alone for many years and had no known enemies. She had been described by neighbors as “quiet and polite,” raising further questions as to why such an atrocity occurred. During his trial, Price showed no visible signs of emotion as the graphic details of the case were laid bare. The jury, after just over two days of deliberation, returned a unanimous verdict of guilty to murder. Speaking outside court, Miss Shaw’s family described her as a "much-loved member of the community" and thanked the police and the emergency services for their swift response. “She deserved to live her later years in peace,” they said in a statement. “This crime is a stain on us all.” The sentencing is expected to take place in the coming weeks. Given the severity of the crime, Price is likely to face a long prison term, if not life. Such brutal violence against the elderly has sparked renewed debate about the safety of vulnerable groups in society. Local councillors have called for increased security measures in residential areas, while charity groups have urged the public to be more vigilant and report any suspicious behavior. Miss Shaw’s tragic death is a sobering reminder of the dangers that can lurk even in the most peaceful of places.

Leach Hails ‘Finishing the Job’ as Key to Worcestershire’s Strong Start   Worcestershire captain Joe Leach has credited his side’s ability to "finish teams off" as the key reason behind their impressive start to the cricketing season. The county, riding high on a series of crucial victories, has shown improved form and resilience, with Leach insisting that the team has finally found the consistency they have been striving for. Speaking ahead of Worcestershire's next fixture, Leach reflected on a campaign so far marked not just by early dominance, but by the ability to close out games when it matters most. “We’ve had a good run of form, but more importantly, we've learned the knack of finishing teams off,” he said. “In the past, we’ve been in games and let chances slip – this time around, we're making sure that doesn’t happen again.” Worcestershire’s performances this season have highlighted better tactical discipline, improved batting structure and a revitalised bowling attack. The standout early season victory came against a county squad, where the team’s ability to execute under pressure sealed a vital win. Leach, who has played a pivotal role with both ball and leadership, pointed out the importance of mental toughness and unity. “It’s not just about starting well—it’s how we finish games," he added. “When you build a position of strength, you have to take the moment and see it through. That’s what we've learned to do this year.” Leach, who has captained the county for several seasons, also praised his team for adapting to the challenges of a tough early-season schedule. With fixtures against top county sides and a need to maintain a strong push in both the County Championship and the T20 Blast, there is a feeling about the squad that they are finally beginning to harness their full potential. Former skipper and coach Steve Rhodes has often spoken of the importance of ‘momentum’ in cricket, and it seems the 2025 campaign has provided that for Worcestershire. With a blend of experienced players and emerging talent, the county appears to have struck the right balance. The performance has also been a reward for hard work and planning over the off-season. Technical improvements with the coaching staff and a better integration between various formats of the game have set the foundations for a successful season.

Plans to restructure the entire state school system in England by making all schools academies will be presented by the government in Wednesday’s Budget, in what would mark one of the most sweeping education reforms since the 1944 Butler Act. The move, long anticipated by ministers, is set to end the traditional local authority-maintained school system, transferring control entirely to headteachers and governing bodies under the academy model. Chancellor Jeremy Hunt is expected to include education reforms within a broader policy aimed at reducing bureaucracy, increasing school autonomy, and accelerating targets for school building and staff recruitment. The Department for Education confirmed that the timeline for the transition would be phased over several years, but insisted that all school budgets would be processed through academy trusts and not local councils by the early 2030s. The announcement has sparked immediate controversy among teachers’ unions and local authority leaders who argue the shift will remove vital oversight and support for schools serving disadvantaged communities. Amanda Spielman, chief inspector of Ofsted, warned that the plan risks creating "gaps in accountability and accountability’s absence can become a breeding ground for poor practice." Labour’s education spokesperson, Sarah Owen, called the proposal "a political stunt dressed up as educational reform," adding that it would "undermine local democracy and fail to address real issues like teacher shortages and crumbling school buildings." Under the current system, academies have operated alongside local authority – or “maintained” – schools since 2010, but the majority of state-funded secondary schools have already converted under pressure or incentives. Last year, education secretary Gillian Keegan stated her vision was to "move the system entirely toward a self-improving one where schools are not dependent on central government or local authorities.” However, critics say the government is using crude financial levers—including tying grant funding to academy status—to coerce conversions. Parents’ groups have also raised concerns, saying the change could "spark chaos and confusion." The Academy Trusts Forum, which represents hundreds of existing academy trusts, has backed the plan, saying it will "allow for greater innovation and autonomy for headteachers to shape their schools according to their communities’ needs." The Budget is expected to include a commitment to increase funding for the rollout, as well as funds to academize 700 schools a year by 2027–28. Still, delivering the plan will require overcoming fierce resistance from councils, many of which have played a central role in providing special educational needs support, extracurricular activities, and safeguarding in local schools.

ORACLE TEAM USA ELECTRIFIES THE WORLD WITH RECORD-SMASHING SAILING COMEBACK   In a display of astonishing resilience and heart-stopping intensity, Oracle Team USA has launched into the history books by defying impossible odds in the final race of the America's Cup against Team New Zealand. After trailing 8-1 in the best-of-17 series, the defending champions pulled off the most dramatic turnaround in sailing history with a breathtaking 44-second victory in a winner-takes-all finale that left spectators and analysts alike spellbound. What had seemed an inevitable title for New Zealand turned into an epic script rewritten under the hot California sun. The finale, held in San Francisco Bay, became the culmination of a thriller that had gripped sailors and sports fans alike. On numerous occasions, Team New Zealand had appeared poised to claim the Cup, their high-tech, high-speed catamarans cutting through the water with precision and panache. Yet Oracle, helmed by the legendary skipper James Spithill and backed by tech mogul Larry Ellison, showed an uncanny ability to claw back each time they were on the ropes. Monday’s final race, the 17th and deciding one, began with nerves frayed and determination sky-high. Oracle started off on the back foot but quickly found their rhythm, executing flawless strategy and execution from the very first mark. The crew’s seamless coordination and radical tactical decisions, often seen as high-risk but astonishingly effective, turned the tides in their favour. For the fans watching from the deck of the fan zone barge, the tension was almost unbearable—each tack and gybe a rush of hope and dread. At the finish line, the crowd erupted in cheers as the Oracle boat crossed 44 seconds ahead of its New Zealand rival in about five minutes of sailing time. The win was not just symbolic but mathematically impossible a week ago. No team in the 162-year history of the America’s Cup had ever come back from an 8-1 deficit. Oracle passed that marker with exceptional style, earning them the right to retain the Cup as well as a place in maritime history. Speaking after the win, Oracle’s communications director, Dr. Ivan Phillips, described the victory as 'a testament to the team’s belief, their technology, and their willpower'. He added: 'This isn’t just about sailing. It’s about never giving up, about believing in the impossible—and making it happen in front of the world's eyes.'

Oldham Athletic director ‘has no regrets’ over Ched Evans request   A year after the controversy rocked the club, a senior figure at Oldham Athletic has insisted there is no shame in the football club's attempt to sign Ched Evans, the former Wales striker who was convicted of rape in 2012. Barry Owen, a former player and current director at the club, has publicly stated he has “no regrets” over the move, despite the backlash from fans and the wider football community at the time. The saga came to light in December 2018, when the club's then-owner, John Bowler, made public his efforts to sign Evans, even offering to raise his personal funds to support the player, then registered with Salford City. Bowler, who later placed his shareholding up for sale amid growing pressure, was eventually forced to step down from the club in January this year. However, it was Owen’s remarks at a recent breakfast event—relayed earlier this week by local media—that reignited the debate around the ethics of employing a high-profile sexual offender in football. Addressing a gathering of Oldham AFC supporters and local dignitaries, Owen claimed the request was made in good faith and said he did not believe Evans’ off-the-field conviction should negate his on-field talent. “It was a difficult situation, but we looked at the player’s record, the opportunities, and what it could mean for the club. I have no regrets about that,” he stated, according to the  Oldham Evening Chronicle . The comments have led to renewed calls for an inquiry into the club’s handling of the matter, with local councillor Janette Jackson prompting a formal response from Oldham Council over the involvement of public officials in the decision. Jackson, who represents the Failsworth ward, said: “How many council officers were involved in this? It needs to be made public.” The local authority has since been asked to clarify whether any staff were approached in relation to the signing attempt. Meanwhile, the National League has also passed on a request for details to the club’s football board. A spokesperson for the league said it was reviewing how the matter was handled “to ensure due diligence was undertaken in accordance with the league’s safeguarding and employment policies.” Ched Evans, now playing for FC Salford in the North West Counties Football League, has not publicly commented on the renewed coverage.

A new £60 million GPS tagging system designed to monitor offenders in England and Wales is five years behind schedule and has failed to deliver any measurable benefits, according to a damning report published by the National Audit Office (NAO) last week. The system, initially planned for full nationwide deployment by 2018, is now not expected to extend beyond a limited pilot until at least 2023. The report highlights years of mismanagement and ambitious overpromises by policy-makers in the Ministry of Justice (MoJ), which was unable to provide accurate cost projections at the time of the project's launch in 2015. Instead of a clear financial roadmap, MoJ officials made "high-level assumptions" and allowed supply companies to set their own budgets and timelines, a process the NAO described as "lacking transparency and oversight." The GPS tagging scheme, intended to support and extend the use of electronic monitoring for offenders in the community, was supposed to enable more effective tracking of high-risk individuals while reducing prison overcrowding. Tagged offenders, typically non-violent but flight risks or reoffenders, could be monitored through real-time GPS data, with the aim of allowing for swift intervention in case of curfew breaches or attempts to flee to other areas. Instead, the project has been plagued by delays, software problems, and financial concerns. As of last month, only a small pilot of fewer than 400 offenders had been enrolled in the system, and no tangible outcomes—such as reduced reoffending or cost savings—had been achieved. Justice Secretary Robert Buckland said in a statement that the system was still a "key part of our long-term strategy to modernise the justice sector," but the NAO noted that neither the MoJ nor the pilot contractors had fully evaluated the technology’s effectiveness or cost-benefit ratio. One of the most significant criticisms in the report is the lack of involvement from local probation services and police, who are expected to be key users of the system. The delivery model put the development of the GPS software and hardware in the hands of third-party contractors, without sufficient collaboration with一线 (frontline) officials tasked with incorporating the technology into daily operations. This has led to numerous compatibility issues and delays in rolling out necessary updates. Civil liberties groups have also expressed concern about the scale of surveillance involved in the system, warning that it could feed into a wider trend of over-policing and disproportionately impact vulnerable or marginalised communities.

Rory McIlroy has confirmed that he has taken a step back from social media following a highly publicised row with former PGA champion Steve Elkington. The Northern Irish golfer has been at the centre of recent controversy after a heated exchange on Twitter led to increased scrutiny of his comments and conduct as a sportsman. In a recent interview, McIlroy revealed that he has decided to quit the platforms altogether to allow him to focus on his game and personal life away from the spotlight’s glare. The dispute began when Elkington, a former major winner who is now a TV commentator, was caught on camera making critical remarks about McIlroy's approach to the game and his role as a leader among the younger generation of players. The video, which circulated widely on social media, led to a flurry of online criticism directed at Elkington, much of it from McIlroy’s followers. Rather than remain silent, the world number two took to Twitter, where he eventually replied to Elkington, sparking a debate that quickly escalated into a broader discussion on sportsmanship and social media etiquette. McIlroy, who has always been a prominent figure in the media, said he was not surprised by the way the public reacted. “Social media can be a double-edged sword,” he said. “It gives fans a voice, which is great, but it also amplifies every word said—even if it’s taken out of context. I’ve had enough of the noise and the negativity. I need to be able to play without the phone in my head.” The decision marks a significant shift for McIlroy, who was once one of the most active golfers on social media, regularly interacting with fans and sharing insights about the Tour and his personal life. While many will see this as a move to distance himself from the increasingly polarised online world, others believe it reflects a growing trend among professional athletes to limit their exposure in what can be a highly toxic digital environment. McIlroy is currently preparing for the US Open, where he will be hoping to put controversy aside and concentrate on contending for his first major title on American soil. With the focus returning to the fairways and greens, the 26-year-old is banking on a strong end to the season to silence any detractors and move forward on his own terms. “I just want to play for the love of the game,” he said.

Black Monday Again: NFL Shakeup as Three Coaches Lose Jobs    London:  History repeated itself in the National Football League (NFL) on Monday, with the day infamously dubbed “Black Monday” living up to its name once more. Three head coaches found themselves out of jobs after a day of sweeping personnel changes across the league, a tradition that often sees the start of the off-season marked by high-profile sackings. The move came amid a wave of disappointment for fans and players alike, as teams look to turn around their fortunes ahead of next season. While no official statements were immediately released from all the teams involved, reports suggest the decisions were driven by poor on-field performance and a lack of progress over the last season, with franchises eager to reset and invest in new direction. Among those affected was John Harbaugh, head coach of the Baltimore Ravens, who had led the team for over a decade. The Ravens had an uninspiring season this year, failing to qualify for the playoffs for the second time in three years. Harbaugh’s departure marks the end of an era, with the team now set to begin the search for a new leader. Joe Philbin, the head coach of the Miami Dolphins, also left the building after a season that saw the franchise struggling for consistency. Philbin’s contract was not renewed, with the Dolphins looking to bring in “new energy” – a phrase often used by teams undergoing coaching changes. The third name added to the growing list of Black Monday casualties was Bill O’Brien, previously head coach of the Houston Texans. O’Brien’s tenure in Texas came to an end after a season filled with unmet expectations and internal dissension. His exit was reported to be at mutual agreement, though exact details remain scarce. The term “Black Monday” is believed to have originated about a decade ago after a single day in the 2011 season when 14 NFL coaches were fired. Since then, it has become synonymous with the dramatic transformation period that the league undergoes at the beginning of the NFL calendar. Fans are now turning their attention to the upcoming coaching carousel, where any combination of current assistants, external candidates, or former players could take the helm. As one observer put it: "Black Monday is always tough, but it’s the brutal beauty of the NFL — the pursuit of excellence never stops, even for those who once led the charge."

Composer and multi-instrumentalist Anna Meredith has made history by winning the prestigious Scottish Album of the Year (SAY) Award with her third studio album,  Varmints . The music prize, known for its support of Scottish artists across all genres, marks a new chapter in the rising star’s career — one that sees her becoming the first composer to ever clinch the accolade. Released in September 2021 on NMC Recordings,  Varmints  received widespread acclaim for its bold, orchestral soundscapes, which blend classical instrumentation with pulsating electronic beats. The album was called “a majestic and gloriously chaotic collision of symphonic ambition and dance-floor energy” by  The Guardian , and it has now officially been crowned the best Scottish album of the year by a panel of 40 renowned critics and music industry professionals. The award, which is accompanied by a £20,000 prize, is expected to open new doors for Meredith, who has long been celebrated for her versatility in both classical and contemporary music. Known for her work with the National Orchestra of Scotland and the BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra, as well as for penning orchestral arrangements for bands such as Wolf Alice and FKA twigs, her breakthrough into the live performance scene as a solo artist has been nothing short of meteoric. Live shows for  Varmints  have seen Meredith at the helm of a 29-piece ensemble, featuring violins, cellos, trumpets, and electronic elements, captivating audiences with its grandeur and energy. The album's title,  Varmints , translates to a colloquial Scottish term for mischievous children — a fitting moniker for a record that defies genre boundaries and revels in musical mischief. Meredith, who studied music at the University of Glasgow before completing a doctorate at King’s College London, said in an interview that the win was both “a surprise and a huge compliment” to her efforts. “This award gives such recognition to the realm of contemporary classical and cross-genre work — it’s a huge deal for any composer,” she said. She joins an illustrious list of previous SAY Award winners, such as Young Fathers, RM Hubbert and Yellow House, but her inclusion as the first composer in the award's 14-year history cements her as a pioneer in the Scottish music landscape. As  Varmints  continues to echo through concert halls and airwaves alike, the future looks bright for Anna Meredith — and Scotland’s music scene can only benefit from her visionary sound.

In the middle of a narrow alley in Cairo's Ain Shams district, one shop stands out from the rest. Tucked away between a greengrocer and a local sweets stall, it offers no grand display or flashy lighting — just a plain wooden sign with the words “Sabah El-Kasr" (King of Dawn). But within, the air is thick with the scent of aromatic coffee and the hiss of drowsy cats. The shop is not just a place to buy a cup of coffee — it is a cornerstone of the community, a place where time seems to stand still and generations of Cairenes have gathered to speak, scribe, share jokes, and make memories. Managed by Muhammad, 52, and run for decades by his father before him, Sabah El-Kasr is a relic of Egypt’s traditional coffee culture, now under threat from the rapid gentrification transforming Ain Shams and Cairo’s other densely populated working-class districts. As new developments rise and urbanisation redefines the city's character, small, family-run shops like this one are being priced out or bulldozed to make way for modern apartments and fast-food chains. Muhammad, who oversees the shop’s smooth-running with the precision of a man who has only ever had one job — and he did it exceptionally well — recalls how it was once packed with local schoolteachers, doctors, and university students who lingered over rich, slow-brewed coffees and deep conversations about politics, football and the future of the country. “You used to find three or four people just here at the same table for two hours or more,” he says, his hands gently grinding freshly arrived coffee beans from the nearby market in Nasr City. “They didn’t need to speak much, but the feeling was about being together.” That feeling is now fading. The nearby tramway is under construction and a new housing complex looms over the block. The government has promised jobs and improved infrastructure, but the residents, like Muhammad, are left questioning what will happen to spaces like this — and to them. “Some people say it’s progress,” he shrugs. “But where will our stories go? This place is as much a part of Ain Shams as the people who live here.” The decline of small businesses such as Muhammad’s represents more than a loss of economic diversity. It is the slow erosion of the soul of Cairo, where tradition and modernity have long coexisted in a delicate balance that now risks being permanently upended by the city’s breakneck pace of development.

A Sweet Success: Chocolate Factory Captures Hearts in the Golan Heights   Once a symbol of conflict and contested borders, the Golan Heights has found a new flavour of diplomacy—dark chocolate. Nestled among the rolling vineyards and verdant hills of this strategic region, the De Karina chocolate factory has become an unexpected beacon for tourists and confectionery lovers from around the world. Run by a family known for their artisanal approach, De Karina has positioned itself as one of the Golan Heights’ most treasured attractions. Since its founding in the early 2000s, the factory has drawn thousands of visitors annually, many of whom add it to their itineraries as part of a broader journey through the region's wine trails, archaeological sites and majestic landscapes. In recent years, the factory has experienced a surge in popularity, particularly from Israeli and Druze communities and international tourists. Visitors are invited to take guided tours that offer an insight into the chocolate-making process—roasting cacao beans, tempering melt, and hand-rolling truffles in a blend of indulgence and artistry. The factory also prides itself on using locally sourced ingredients, including olive oil and honey from the Golan’s own land. Located in Katzrin, the Golan Heights’ largest town, De Karina has become a symbol of resilience and collaboration. The area, which was captured by Israel during the 1967 Six-Day War and later annexed in 1981—a move not internationally recognised—has long reflected the tensions of the wider Middle East. However, businesses like De Karina seem to blur the lines of political reality, fostering a shared space where Israelis, Jordanians, Syrians and others can gather through the universal language of chocolate. The owners, the Karina family, are keen to highlight the cultural story behind their product. “This place is more than just chocolate,” said Yossi Karina, the factory’s marketing director. “It’s a chance for people to connect, to learn about our traditions and to celebrate the beauty of the Golan. We want visitors to leave with more than a box of truffles—we want them to take a piece of our story with them.” While the factory may not rival the grandeur of the chocolate houses of Europe, it offers a unique, intimate experience that aligns with growing global trends for ethically sourced, handcrafted goods. The growing tourism numbers have also brought economic benefits to the local community, creating jobs and supporting nearby suppliers.

Chinese President Xi Jinping has called on global leaders to respect the concept of "cyber sovereignty" and to embrace the diversity of internet governance models, in a speech underlining Beijing’s vision for the future of digital diplomacy. Addressing a high-profile international forum, Xi emphasized that no single country or system holds a monopoly on the internet’s future and warned against the imposition of foreign models on sovereign nations. His comments reflect China’s longstanding stance on digital autonomy and serve as a subtle rebuke to the West, particularly the United States, which has traditionally promoted open, decentralized internet governance and criticized Beijing’s censored and state-regulated online environment. Xi's remarks came as governments worldwide continue to grapple with the challenges and responsibilities of managing the digital age, from cybersecurity threats to the rise of state surveillance and misinformation. "The internet is not a lawless zone," Xi said, stressing the importance of multilateralism and "harmonious coexistence" in the digital sphere. He added: "We must adhere to the concept of cyber sovereignty... and promote the building of a community with a shared future in cyberspace." The concept of cyber sovereignty, widely promoted by China’s state-backed institutions, asserts that countries have the right to govern their own online spaces as sovereign entities and to tailor policies according to their cultural, legal, and political frameworks. This view is in stark contrast to the principles of net neutrality and digital freedom often championed by Western democracies, who argue that global online cooperation should not be dictated by geopolitical rivalry. Earlier this year, Beijing announced plans to further expand the principles of its 'Great Firewall' in an effort to control the flow of information and ensure "internet stability and security." Some experts suggest that Xi's continued advocacy for cyber sovereignty comes amid growing tensions over data privacy, AI development, and the regulation of multinational tech firms. The U.S. and its allies have increasingly pushed back against Beijing’s digital ambitions, imposing export restrictions on advanced chips and pressuring tech companies to remove Chinese platforms like TikTok, citing national security concerns. Xi's message will resonate strongly in countries that have expressed discomfort with the dominance of Western tech firms and values. In recent years, nations from Russia to Ethiopia have explored regional or state-controlled internet models, suggesting a global shift in online governance priorities. The President’s speech also appeared to signal an intent to position China as a leader in shaping the next phase of the internet's evolution, rather than merely following global trends.

A digital games programmer from Angus has claimed a unique place in sporting and gaming history by completing the iconic Land's End to John o'Groats cycling challenge entirely within a virtual reality (VR) environment, making him the first person to achieve this feat in the virtual world. Scott Murray, 28, a software developer from Forfar, spent two weeks training in the virtual environment before embarking on his 532-mile digital journey on a stationary indoor cycling trainer, which was synced to a VR headset to replicate the terrain and weather conditions along the traditional road journey. Murray's journey, which mirrors the physical challenge of the well-known pilgrimage across the UK, was documented as part of a personal challenge and as a trial run for future immersive fitness experiences in gaming and beyond. Speaking to the BBC, Murray said the experience pushed him just as hard as if he had been on the road physically: "You still have to fight the hill gradients, the wind resistance – it doesn’t feel like you’re just pedalling in a room in Forfar."
