The idea came from Murray’s increasing interest in blending gaming and physical fitness. He had previously worked on motion-sensing tech and believed VR had the potential to not only entertain but also motivate real-world fitness. The Land's End to John o’Groats project was a logical next step – it’s a staple of UK endurance challenges and – with precise mapping data and real-world conditions, it provided the perfect test for the technology. The VR system used by Murray was custom-built using publicly available road data, real hills, and even weather simulations based on historical conditions. Murray also integrated a fitness-tracking app to ensure that his effort levels matched the ambition of a real cyclist. The challenge has been met with enthusiasm from fitness and gaming communities alike, as it opens the door to new ways of staying active while engaging with the digital world. David Cameron, a tech enthusiast and founder of a local fitness startup, praised Murray's achievement: “This is incredible. It’s the kind of creative energy that shows how gaming can do more than just entertain – it can inspire and empower. If this is just the beginning, we could be looking at a new era in fitness tech.” Murray, who has aspirations of developing a VR fitness platform with competitive and community features, said he was inspired by the recent surge in interest in health and fitness during lockdowns and the rise of gamified workouts.

Plaid Cymru has thrown open the door to this year’s election campaign, launching its manifesto ahead of other major political parties and declaring itself the “decisive voice” for Wales. The launch comes as Wales heads into a pivotal election period, with citizens set to choose their next MPs as well as local government representatives in May. Campaigning early is a strategic move by the Welsh party, aiming to frame the debate on key issues such as devolution, healthcare, education and economic development in a way that supports its vision for a more autonomous, sustainable Wales. In a speech delivered in Cardiff, Plaid Cymru leader Rhun Ap Iorwerth said the party is committed to securing greater powers for Welsh Parliament (Senedd Cymru), including full control over welfare, tax and land use. “Wales is not just a region to be administered from Westminster,” Ap Iorwerth declared. “We must take back the powers that belong to the people of Wales and use them to build a better, fairer society.” The manifesto’s focus on devolution is not new to Plaid Cymru, which has long championed independence for Wales or, if that is not feasible, significant increases in autonomy short of full independence. But this time around, the party is also pushing a strong local economy agenda, including a call for a “Community Wealth Building” strategy – a model borrowed from the radical municipal reform approach that aims to put communities back at the heart of economic decision-making. Healthcare is another central plank. The party pledges to reduce the pay and perks of NHS chief executives in order to reinvest savings into frontline services. It also wants to end the use of private healthcare companies and instead expand community and preventative healthcare initiatives through better funding and staff retention. Education, too, remains a priority. Plaid is calling for free travel to and from college or university for all Welsh students, as well as expanded apprenticeships and training schemes tied directly to local job markets. The manifesto also includes a plan for cutting carbon emissions by 2035, with a focus on renewable energy and green jobs – something that echoes recent UK government pledges but marks Plaid as a strong proponent of climate action as early as June. While Plaid Cymru’s move to launch its manifesto first may not guarantee electoral success, it does set a tone for this year’s campaign, with the party goading other contenders to raise their game or be left behind.

"Be careful what you wish for," the old saying goes – and this is exactly what the Russian leadership must be thinking right now. In recent months, Moscow has found itself unexpectedly at the centre of a flurry of unprecedented separatist movements across former Soviet states. What seemed like a distant and easily overlooked pipe dream for radical ethnoregionalist groups beginning to crystallise into a real political force, posing a new set of foreign policy challenges that most analysts in the West had not anticipated just a few years ago. The catalyst for this shift was arguably the success of pro-Russian separatists in the Donbas and Crimea in early 2014. That conflict saw the emergence of two self-proclaimed republics, supported financially and militarily by Russia, and successfully managed to blur the lines between internal insurrection and foreign intervention. The international community, stunned, had little choice but to accept the altered status quo in exchange for sanctions that had an assembling, but often targeted economic impact. However, what Moscow may not have anticipated was that this early experiment in “hybrid warfare” would lead to a domino effect across the post-Soviet space, directly challenging Russian domination over the former USSR and encouraging breakaway movements from regions as far afield as Kazakhstan, to Kyrgyzstan. For instance, today in the Central Asian country of Uzbekistan – long a model of stability and relative national unity – murmurs of regional autonomy have resurfaced among the ethnic Uzbeks of Fergana Valley. This area, which shares a border with Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, is home to a majority Uzbek population and has historically suffered from underdevelopment, a sense of marginalisation, and poor governance. Though the government in Tashkent has dismissed these as isolated grievances, the growing curiosity and openness of youth in about alternative national identities is a trend that bodes poorly for Russia’s vision of a cohesive and manageable post-Soviet sphere of influence. The same worrying pattern is emerging in the South Caucasus. In Georgia, the breakaway regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, where Moscow maintains a heavy political and military presence, have recently shown signs of restricting regional governance – a clear crack in the otherwise tight control over these Stalin-era Soviet republics. Meanwhile, in the Kyrgyz Republic, various nationalist groups, inspired by Russia’s precedent of backing separatist movements, have called for the govt of the capital, Bishkek, to allow regional governors more autonomy.

In a final appearance at the despatch box during Prime Minister’s Questions, David Cameron has asserted that Northern Ireland is now stronger than it was when he took office six years ago, highlighting a key issue as he winds down nearly a decade in office. The Prime Minister, who is expected to resign as leader of the Conservative Party by the end of the summer following the UK’s referendum on European Union membership, addressed the sensitive and enduringly complicated dynamics of a region that has long been a policy testbed for his administration. Cameron said: “Northern Ireland’s institutions are more resilient and more mature than when I first came into this role.” His remarks came as Stormont remains in limbo, with the devolved government having collapsed in January 2017 after the now-defunct Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) left the executive. The current power-sharing arrangement between the DUP and Sinn Féin is in place only until February 2018, and recent tensions over breakfast, including disagreements between the two major parties over a welfare reform bill and police reform, have not been without controversy. Cameron’s statement was a pointed reminder of the progress that has been made under his premiership, including the restoration of devolution in 2007, and the early release of deadly paramilitary prisoners in 2013, a move that was widely praised by the national and international community as a significant symbolic step in the peace process. “There is much more to do, of course,” Cameron acknowledged, “but I am proud of the role the UK government has played in fostering this progress.” His comments contrast with the current uncertainty surrounding the region’s political stability, following a failed snap election in March and a continued reliance on direct rule from Westminster. Analysts suggest that Cameron’s final Prime Minister’s Questions about Northern Ireland is an attempt not only to reflect on the challenges he has faced but also to underline the achievements that he is willing to claim as a legacy. Critics, however, argued that Cameron’s focus on Northern Ireland development came at the expense of addressing more pressing national issues, particularly in the wake of a controversial EU referendum result. Sinn Féin, which has long opposed the Prime Minister’s approach to Northern Ireland, did not respond directly to Cameron’s remarks but reiterated its call for a “fully restored devolution” and reform of the policing structure.

MPs have voted to replace the UK’s ageing nuclear weapons system, Trident, in a decisive move that has reignited debate over Britain’s commitment to a nuclear-armed future. The renewal of the controversial programme saw the House of Commons approve by 353 votes to 259, making it one of the biggest Commons margins of the year and continuing a long line of government majorities on the issue. The decision comes despite strong opposition from Labour and the Liberal Democrats, who argue that the project is an extravagant financial burden and unnecessary in today’s geopolitical climate. Labour’s shadow defence secretary, Jonathan Ashworth, said his party would continue to campaign against the use of public funds for Trident renewal, calling it a "reckless" policy that fails to address real national security threats. Trident, first deployed in the early 1990s to replace the Polaris system, is used to maintain the UK’s Continuous At-Sea Deterrent (CASD), a fleet of nuclear-armed submarines that are kept operational 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. With the original submarine programme reaching the end of its life, the Ministry of Defence estimates that replacing it will cost up to £160 billion over the next three decades. Critics, including anti-nuclear groups and cross-party MPs, have questioned both the accuracy of these forecasts and the moral implications of maintaining a nation's nuclear arsenal. Prime Minister Theresa May defended the decision, stating that Trident was "essential for the nation’s security" and a key element of the UK's role on the world stage. Spokespersons also highlighted the role of defence industries and jobs across the UK, particularly in Scotland and the south-west, in the case for continuation. The vote has drawn sharp reactions from across political and social spectrums. Steve Ludlam, of the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND), said the motion fails to account for the changing nature of global conflict. “We are in a new era, where nuclear weapons are not the answer. Renewing Trident is based on fear, not logic,” he said. The decision echoes similar votes in 2016 when the initial renewal bill was passed, as well as a number of previous referenda and parliamentary debates over the role of nuclear weapons in UK security policy. While the government insists that the decision is non-negotiable, the public remains sharply divided on the issue, with opinion polls consistently showing a majority of Britons in favour of abolishing the nuclear deterrent.

The sensational cricketer Kevin Pietersen has revealed he finds it difficult to see himself playing in England again, despite his recent involvement with Surrey in the T20 Blast this summer. In a surprising turn for fans who have long associated Pietersen with English cricket, the veteran batsman signaled that his days playing in the country could be numbered, dealing a blow to county clubs hoping for his long-term return. Pietersen, who is a fan favorite known for his explosive batting and unorthodox style, joined Surrey for the T20 Blast as part of a brief stint aimed at regaining form and fitness. While the season revealed flashes of the old magic, it also served as a melancholic reminder of the changing dynamics of his cricketing career. Speaking about his future, Pietersen noted that his commitment to international cricket remains uncertain, especially with the possibility of representing his native South Africa still in the back of his mind. "It's unlikely," he stated when asked if he would return to English cricket. "There's no point in chasing dreams that no longer lead to my preferred direction." The statement has sent ripples through the cricketing community. Analysts and fans alike are speculating on what the future holds for one of the most electrifying talents in the sport, with many questioning whether he might be considering a move back to international level with the Proteas. South African fans would breathe new hope at the prospect, but the journey back is far from straightforward, particularly given the restrictions of age and the high level of competition in the shortest format of the game. As for what lies ahead in the domestic scene, Pietersen has not ruled out playing elsewhere around the world—particularly in the lucrative Indian Premier League and other global T20 competitions. That decision, however, leaves a significant void about his legacy in England, the country where the bulk of his high-profile career was played out. Surrey's director of cricket, Brian Suart, expressed mixed emotions regarding Pietersen's potential exit from the English playing scene. "Kevin will always be a significant figure at Surrey and in English cricket," he said. "His contributions, both on and off the field, have left an indelible mark. We respect his decisions and hope he finds great success wherever his journey takes him." The news marks a turning point for Pietersen's career and underscores the shifting landscape of international and domestic cricket, where loyalties and ambitions are becoming increasingly fluid.

A Priest on the Fringe: Bishop Paul Tighe finds faith at the heart of South by Southwest   Dressed in his distinctive clerical collar and exuding a mix of gravitas and charm, Bishop Paul Tighe is a striking figure in the sun-soaked throng of film, music and interactive thinkers gathering at South by Southwest in Austin, Texas. As he sat down for an interview at a quiet café just off Sixth Street — a district that by mid-evening will be awash with indie bands, debut films and cutting-edge technology — Tighe let out a wry smile. "I’m probably the only priest here," he said with a chuckle, "but even more so, I’m probably the only person with grey hair." Bishop Tighe is the chief executive officer of the Bishops’ Conference of England and Wales, a man whose days are usually filled with theological discourse and pastoral governance. But this year, he was at the heart of one of America’s most vibrant festivals — not just to attend a panel on religion and technology, but to explore how faith, culture and creativity intersect in the modern age. His presence at South by Southwest is both subtle and subversive, a gentle but pointed challenge to the secular default that dominates global creative and political conversations. South by Southwest is known for its blend of countercultural energy and mainstream ambition. It is where the future of entertainment often incubates, and where speakers on virtual reality, artificial intelligence and climate change often take to the stage alongside musicians and filmmakers. So, stepping into the room as a Catholic prelate feels, at first, jarring. But not to Bishop Tighe. "I came because I wanted to see what the Church is missing in the world of creativity," he said. "Sometimes we get so wrapped up in pastoral care and liturgy that we forget to engage the arts, music, film — things that speak to the soul as much as scripture." Tighe’s reflection is a reminder that in an increasingly post-Christian Western world, the Church must not only maintain tradition but also remain active and curious in new landscapes. South by Southwest was, he said, a place to do just that — a laboratory of ideas, even if not all of them align with orthodoxy. He was not alone in speaking from the "faith and culture" perspective. Panels on religion in media, spirituality in mental health and the role of art in healing drew crowds from across the festival.

French former President Nicolas Sarkozy remains in custody as authorities continue to question him over allegations of influence peddling, marking a significant development in a high-profile political and judicial case. The 68-year-old, who served as president from 2007 to 2012, faces accusations that he sought to bypass official procedures in order to obtain sensitive court information from a close associate, who has himself been placed under formal investigation. Sarkozy was taken into custody on Monday morning in Paris and has remained in pre-trial detention as magistrates probe the extent of his alleged role in the case. Such action is highly unusual for a former head of state in France, and it has drawn widespread media attention and prompted political debate across the country. The case revolves around accusations that Sarkozy, during his 2012 re-election campaign, attempted to secure confidential information from a special judge and the Paris Public Prosecutor by involving an individual with close ties to his inner circle. The prosecution asserts that these actions may constitute breach of judicial secrecy and misuse of influence, both of which are criminal offences under French law. French justice minister Éric Dupond-Moretti announced the decision to place Sarkozy in custody, stating that the development was necessary "to preserve the integrity of the judicial process and to avoid any risk of obstruction of justice." This measure is a first of its kind in France for a former president: while Sarkozy has previously been detained for other legal issues — including a 2019 case concerning illegal phone taps — this marks the first time a former president has remained in custody during investigative questioning. The former president has consistently denied any wrongdoing, with his legal team asserting that the accusations are politically motivated and have been exaggerated by judicial and media figures. In a statement released earlier in the week, Sarkozy’s lawyers said: “Our client has always respected the law and the judiciary. There is no evidence of any illegal activity or that any agreement was made.” As the judicial process continues, political leaders and public figures across the political spectrum have voiced their reactions. President Emmanuel Macron has remained silent on the case, while opposition leaders have called for transparency and urged for a fair process. The case is expected to run for weeks and could have profound implications not only for Sarkozy but for the integrity of the French political system as the country approaches crucial elections and continues to grapple with rising political tensions.

A deal that could secure the future of Tata Steel’s Scunthorpe plant is nearing the final stretch, with insiders suggesting a formal announcement could be made as early as Monday. The potential agreement, which has been months in the making, is seen as a crucial win for the steel industry and a major relief for the thousands of workers at the plant and their families. The Scunthorpe plant, which has been a cornerstone of the regional economy for over a century, has faced an uncertain future since Tata Steel announced its intention to review its UK operations last year. With mounting pressure from the government, trade unions, and local communities, Tata came under intense scrutiny to avoid a potential closure that would devastate a vital sector and displace hundreds. Negotiations have been led by a coalition including the Unite union and the steelworkers themselves, alongside the Labour-led local council and, more recently, the government. The proposed deal is reportedly backed by a mix of public and private funding, with British steel giant Liberty House Group said to be among the key players. The group has long been vocal in its support for the UK steel industry and is believed to be positioning itself as a potential buyer or long-term partner for the Scunthorpe facility. A Lib Dem source has voiced cautious optimism, saying: “Words are easy, but we’ve been down this road before. What counts is action. This new phase must not be business as usual for an industry in crisis.” 知情人士透露，协议将包括提供财政支持以使工厂在短期内维持运营，同时为长期转型铺平道路。这可能涉及脱碳计划和升级设备，使该工厂符合全球对绿色钢铁日益增长的需求。 Trade unions have welcomed the news as a reprieve but have stressed that any deal must come with guarantees about jobs, skills development, and safe working conditions. Neil Shastri, Unite general secretary, said: “This is not just about saving a factory. It is about safeguarding the livelihoods of working families and securing the future of high-quality manufacturing in this country.” As Monday’s deadline looms, all eyes are on the leaders of the involved groups to see whether a final agreement can be reached and whether this time, the promises will hold. For the people of Scunthorpe, the plant is not just a factory, but a lifeline. A deal would not only go a long way in restoring confidence in the sector, but also in reinforcing the country’s industrial ambitions in the post-Brexit era. If it is signed, it will mark a moment of triumph for negotiation, and a reminder of what can be achieved when communities and businesses stand together to protect a shared future.

Two women whose daughters lost their lives to gang violence a decade ago are urging young people to reflect on the dangers of choosing a life entangled in crime and violence. Karen Taylor and Shazia Idris, mothers of 15-year-old Lucy Taylor and 14-year-old Aisha Idris, were joined by community leaders and former gang members at a event in Birmingham on Tuesday to speak out about the lasting damage that gang culture can inflict on families and neighbourhoods. Both girls were shot in separate incidents in 2014, as part of a wave of shootings that shocked the West Midlands during that time. Lucy died in March 2014 after being caught in the crossfire near her school, while Aisha was killed two months later in what police described as a targeted attack. Their deaths sparked a national debate over youth violence and the safety of children in urban areas. At the event, organised by the charity  Together We Rise , Ms Taylor and Ms Idris spoke openly about their grief and anger in the years since their daughters' deaths. Ms Taylor, who showed a photograph of Lucy smiling in her school uniform, said: "This is the way she is remembered. Not for the way she died, but as the bright, kind-hearted girl she was. I want every young person who hears my story to remember that their choices have consequences. One bad decision can take lives." Ms Idris echoed her words, saying: "Aisha was loved by so many. She wanted to be a nurse and dreamed of helping people. She didn't want this. No child does. If I can prevent even one child from being hurt because of a gang rivalry, then her death will have meaning." The two mothers also praised community initiatives that had helped reduce gang activity in their areas, including mentorship programmes and youth centres offering alternative activities for at-risk children. They called on local leaders and parents to ensure that resources were available to steer children away from gang life. "If we do not do this, the cycle continues," Ms Taylor added. "We speak up now, not as a sensational story, but as two grieving mothers who no longer want to see anyone else go through the same pain as us." The event marked the 10th anniversary of a new initiative launched by the Metropolitan and West Midlands police forces to tackle gang-related crime.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, Filippo Grandi, has issued a stark warning about the escalating global migrant crisis, calling it no longer a regional or even a European issue, but a truly global phenomenon. Speaking at a press conference in Geneva earlier this week, Grandi said that as millions continue to flee conflict, persecution, and worsening economic and environmental conditions, the international community must find long-term solutions rather than resorting to restrictive and often inhumane border policies. “Simply turning people away at our borders won’t work,” he stated, as reports emerge of worsening humanitarian conditions in the world's most vulnerable regions, from the Horn of Africa to Central America. The crisis has already forced more than 100 million people worldwide to become refugees or internally displaced persons, a number higher than at any time since the end of the Second World War. Grandi called for a “far more ambitious and co-ordinated international approach” in response to the mass movement of people. He pointed to the need for greater investment in education and employment opportunities in the regions most affected by displacement, alongside rethinking migration policies that so often treat people as problems rather than human beings with rights and hopes. “If we continue to see people in short-term terms only as risks and threats, we ignore not only the human cost but also the opportunities that come with welcoming and supporting people who have no other choice but to seek safety elsewhere,” Grandi said. His remarks follow a series of increasingly restrictive migration policies in many parts of the world, notably in the European Union and the United States, which have led to dangerous situations at borders and a rise in abuse and exploitation of migrants. In Europe, countries such as Hungary and Poland have adopted some of the most hostile and rigid anti-migrant policies, while others, like France and Germany, have struggled with internal political divisions over how best to manage the flow of people arriving from Africa and the Middle East. Grandi also highlighted the impact of the climate crisis, noting that environmental displacement is now a major driver of migration. “We’re not ready for what is coming. Climate change is already displacing people, and as scientists warn, it will only intensify in the coming decades,” he said. He urged richer nations to take a more responsible lead in addressing the root causes of displacement, including militarised conflict, poverty, and environmental degradation.

The residents of Mexico City will be woken by an unusual alarm clock this weekend, as part of a bold new initiative designed to raise awareness of the risks posed by the local volcano, Popocatépetl. Starting at 7 am on Saturday, citizens across the capital will hear a simulated eruption alarm, echoing through streets, balconies and buildings in a city of more than nine million people. The drill, coordinated by Mexico’s disaster response teams and backed by municipal authorities, is the first of its kind to be carried out on such a large scale in the capital and comes amid growing concerns over the sleeping giant outside the city's southwest border. Popocatépetl, one of the world’s most active volcanoes and easily visible from central Mexico City on clear days, has been showing signs of increased activity in recent months, with minor tremors and ash emissions reported by geologists. Despite being in a relatively dormant phase for most of the 20th century, the volcano—nicknamed 'El Popo' by locals—has earned a fearsome reputation as a potential threat, given its location and the densely populated area around it. The alarm will sound for ten minutes and is accompanied by a text alert and messages on social media, as well as instructions on what to do in the event of an actual emergency. Local media have been running public services advertising how to prepare emergency kits and identify safe meeting points for families and communities. President López Obrador praised the initiative during a press briefing, calling it “a vital step in ensuring the safety of our people, and a necessary reminder that nature must always be respected.” Many citizens, however, have mixed reactions to the idea of being woken up at dawn by a synthetic eruption sound. “I understand the need for preparedness, but it feels a bit like being tested while we’re still trying to sleep,” said Pedro Hernández, a 40-year-old teacher. Others are more supportive. “It is a reminder that we’re not just a city of skyscrapers and traffic. We live near a volcano that could wake up at any time,” said Rosa Martínez, a nurse from Coyoacán. The alarm is being broadcast from loudspeakers mounted on lampposts, with special dispersal systems installed to prevent the sound from disrupting air traffic at Benito Juárez International Airport. While the drill is intended as a peaceful one, it echoes the tense evacuation drills once held in cities across the world, from Japan to Hawaii.

Dementia ruling ends decades-long inquiry into Lord Janner’s alleged sexual abuse of children   A Labour peer at the centre of a decades-long and highly publicised child sex abuse investigation will not face trial due to the severity of his advanced dementia, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) has confirmed. Lord Kenneth Janner, 86, who was a prominent politician and one-time MP for Leicester East, was found unfit to stand trial following a medical assessment, bringing to an end one of Britain’s longest-running abuse inquiries. Janner, who retired from the House of Lords in 2003, was investigated following revelations in 2008 by the Leicestershire Police and the Independent Police Complaints Commission, which linked him to allegations of sexual abuse of boys in the 1970s and 1980s. Following the publication of the Operation Yewtree report in 2014 — a major inquiry into historical sex crimes prompted by the Jimmy Savile scandal — a trial date was set for later this year. However, medical professionals have now concluded that the peer is not mentally fit to endure the rigours of a criminal prosecution. The decision, which takes into account two pre-trial psychiatric assessments and a decision by the Mental Health Act Tribunal, was announced on Friday by the CPS. A statement from the agency said that while the evidence against Janner was “substantially reliable and sufficient to support conviction,” his current state of health did not allow for a fair or just trial. The case has drawn considerable public and political interest, not least because Janner also served as a government minister in the 1980s and held prominent roles within the Jewish community and the Labour Party. Until now, no peer has stood trial for historic sex abuse, and his case was seen as a landmark in the broader effort to confront historical child sex abuse in institutions and public life alike. The news has prompted mixed reactions. While campaigners for justice for victims of abuse have expressed frustration that the prosecution will not proceed, others have acknowledged that the findings of incompetence reflect the complex reality of prosecuting those whose cognitive abilities have diminished with age. A spokesperson for the NSPCC said: “We are deeply disappointed that Lord Janner will not face a trial. More importantly, today’s decision should not serve as a precedent for allowing other individuals to avoid the prospect of justice. We remain committed to supporting victims and ensuring that wherever there is sufficient evidence, prosecutions follow, no matter how long ago the abuse occurred.”

Universities Paid £400,000 in Compensation to Students in 2023, Ombudsman Reports   Universities in England and Wales collectively paid more than £400,000 in compensation to students last year to settle disputes over a range of issues, including poor teaching, flawed student support and admissions failures, according to the latest report from the   Office of the Independent Adjudicator for Higher Education (OIA)  . The OIA, an independent body that reviews complaints from students about their institutions, revealed that the number of cases was substantial—nearly 2,000 in total—highlighting the scale of dissatisfaction among students over the past academic year. Among the most common complaints were concerns about the   quality of lectures and teaching staff  ,   disruptions to studies due to campus closures or strikes  , and   delays in the processing of exam or degree results  . In many instances, the universities responded with financial settlements, often in the form of refunds or bursaries in compensation for the inconvenience or loss of opportunity suffered by the students affected. The report also noted a significant increase in complaints relating to   mental health and wellbeing services  , with students reporting inaccessible or inadequate support from universities during a period still heavily impacted by the aftermath of the pandemic. The   University and College Union (UCU)  , which has long campaigned for better student rights and university funding, welcomed the OIA report but said it was not enough. “These figures are concerning and highlight the growing expectation among students for transparency and accountability,” said UCU spokesperson Rachel Hearn. “It is also a reminder of the real costs of underfunding and the pressure being borne by students who are often left with no alternative but to complain.” Some university representatives, however, stressed that most disputes were resolved at institutional level before students submitted a formal complaint to the OIA. A spokesperson for the   Universities Wales   body said: “We take all student feedback seriously and are committed to addressing concerns through internal processes. The compensation paid out last year reflects a broader effort to learn from mistakes and improve student experience.” The overall figure of £400,000 in compensations is said to be in line with previous years, but the nature of the complaints suggests new challenges are emerging in student-life management, particularly around   digital learning  ,   campus safety  , and   financial hardship support  . As the cost of living crisis continues to hit students hard, calls are growing for greater oversight into how institutions support their learners—both academically and personally.

Lee Smith has insisted there are no lingering tensions between him and London Wasps as he prepares for his first return to Adams Park in Saturday’s Aviva Premiership clash with his former club. The Newcastle Falcons full-back, who spent over a decade at Wasps before moving to Kingston Park in the summer, says he is focused on the team’s performance and not the emotional backdrop of the fixture. Speaking ahead of the match, Smith said: "There’s no issue with Wasps at all. I had a fantastic time there, made lifelong friends, and I leave with huge gratitude. This is just another game for me now. I want to give everything for Newcastle on Saturday, but I also want to take a moment to acknowledge the support the people at Wasps gave me over the years." The 33-year-old, who left London Wasps last summer, made over 200 appearances for the club in a career that spanned 14 seasons. His return to Adams Park, now rebranded as the Anglo-Welsh Cup venue at the end of the month, will mark the first time many fans will see the veteran player in opposition colours. Wasps director of rugby Dai Young, meanwhile, has maintained a respectful stance, saying: “Lee is a top professional and a huge part of the fabric of Wasps during his time with us. We wished him well when he left, and we want the same for him now he's at Newcastle. This is a tight league and every game matters, so we will focus on the game and what we need to do to win.” Smith’s departure in 2021 had been seen by some fans as a sour moment, with speculation about the reasons for his switch and undisclosed fee being a cause for brief controversy. Calls for the reintroduction of a post-study work visa system for international students in Scotland have been firmly rejected by the UK government, sparking disappointment and concern among university leaders and business groups. The proposal, which had been championed by a coalition of Scottish universities and industry representatives, aimed to allow international graduate students to remain in the UK for two years after completing their studies, providing a pathway to permanent employment and settlement. In a statement last week, a UK government source confirmed that no policy changes would be made to the current system, which restricts international students to applying for a work visa only if they receive an offer for a graduate or postgraduate research course. Under the existing rules, students who finish degrees unrelated to postgraduate study must leave the UK or apply for a different type of visa, such as a Skilled Worker visa, which requires sponsorship by an employer. The decision marks a missed opportunity for Scotland, which has long argued that the rules were hindering its economic growth and attractiveness as a study destination. Universities in Edinburgh, Glasgow, and St Andrews have all voiced concerns that the lack of a post-study work visa was putting them at a competitive disadvantage with institutions in the US, Australia, and Canada, which offer such provisions. Scottish Labour leader Anas Sarwar called the decision “a blow to Scotland’s future,” while Green MSP Patrick Harvie described it as “short-sighted.” HEPI, the Higher Education Policy Institute, published a report earlier this year estimating that nearly 30,000 international graduates left the UK each year due to the lack of a suitable work pathway. Universities Scotland, the representative body for higher education institutions in Scotland, had urged the UK government to reconsider, citing data showing that over two-thirds of non-EU university students who graduated in 2022 did not return to their home countries. Instead, many found employment elsewhere in the UK or in other countries. The rejection of the post-study work visa is likely to fuel calls for Scotland to rebalance its education and immigration policies independently should it pursue full autonomy. For now, however, the initiative remains a distant goal as international students across Scotland prepare to return to the UK or head abroad in search of opportunities. The outcome of the dispute also highlights the broader tensions surrounding Scotland’s role within the UK and the growing divergence in economic policy priorities.

Two men have been found guilty at the Old Bailey of plotting to smuggle firearms, including AR-15 assault rifles and sub-machine guns, into the UK from the Netherlands, in a case that has raised serious concerns about the security of weapons trafficking routes into the country. Anthony Adeyemi, 33, and Habeeb Kuti, 34, were both sentenced to 15 years in prison on Thursday after being convicted on charges of conspiracy to import prohibited weapons and ammunition under the Firearms Act 1968. The pair, both from North London, were identified as part of a larger network, which detectives say has links to violent criminal groups in the capital who are seeking to fuel a spike in gang-related shootings and stabbings in south London. During a four-week trial, prosecutors revealed that the defendants had travelled to the Netherlands via the Channel Tunnel in May 2022 with the intent to meet operatives in Tilburg and return with tactical weapons, including Sem-automatic and fully automatic firearms, which are banned in the UK. Airport and customs officials reportedly flagged the men’s unusual activities during a separate stop at CDG in France, which led to the initiation of an undercover investigation by the Metropolitan Police’s Counter Terrorism Command. The arrested men were found in possession of false identification documents, and later, undercover police intercepted a delivery of weapons packed in cases bound for the UK. Adeyemi, who became known as the “ringleader” by investigators, had previously been arrested in 2020 for possession of a prohibited weapon. Kuti, also a known associate in violent crime circles, had no prior convictions. In a statement outside court, Det Ch Insp Simon Lodge, who led the investigation into the smuggling operation, said: “This was a chilling plan by two men to bring weapons of war into the heart of the UK, which had the potential to be used in some of the country’s most vulnerable communities. We are determined to disrupt any attempts to bring prohibited firearms into this country and will not tolerate any criminal who seeks to arm violent gangs and criminal enterprises.” The case is a rare example of a full conviction stemming from an investigation into the importation of illicit firearms from Europe, and raises renewed questions about how such weapons are able to enter the UK despite strict border controls. Some MPs have called for additional measures, including the use of machine-learning tools to detect smuggling attempts and greater surveillance of known criminal networks.

The European Council president, Charles Michel, has called for a proposal to restrict in-work benefits to newly arrived EU migrants, claiming it would help address the growing pressures of record migration to the UK since 2004. Speaking at a press conference in Brussels, Michel emphasised the need for a more balanced approach to migration across Europe, particularly during times of economic uncertainty and demographic challenges. “Migration remains one of the most pressing issues for the EU. A sustainable solution must ensure fairness for both host countries and migrant communities,” Michel said. His remarks came in response to mounting concerns from British policymakers, business leaders, and the general public about the impact of migration on services, housing, and employment since the UK joined the European Economic Area (EEA) in 1993. Data from the UK Office for National Statistics (ONS) reveals that over 5.9 million EU citizens have moved to the UK since the beginning of 2004, with the majority settling in major cities such as London, Birmingham, and Manchester. The government’s Integrated Migration Strategy, published in March, reiterates its intention to reduce net migration to tens of thousands by the end of this decade—pushing for a more skilled and selective immigration system. Among the suggested reforms is a restriction on access to certain in-work benefits, such as the Work and Pension Allowance, for EU migrants who have been in the UK for less than two years. Currently, these benefits support low-wage workers and are crucial for those making the transition from non-working to working status. Liam Robinson, the Prime Minister’s chief policy adviser on migration, said the move was not a punishment but a measure to encourage long-term integration and reduce dependency on public funds. “We want to be fair to those who come here to build a better life and ensure public services are there for all our citizens. New arrivals can still access essential support, but a two-year integration period will ensure that the system is more sustainable,” he stated. The proposal has, however, drawn criticism from some left-leaning politicians and advocacy groups who argue it could penalise vulnerable workers and further erode support for EU nationals. Emma Foundation, a charity supporting migrant integration, pointed out that such restrictions could exacerbate existing inequalities. “Migration is a two-way process. It cannot be one-sided if we want a cohesive society where people are supported to contribute and thrive,” the charity’s spokesperson, Sarah Hope, said.

Lana the Labrador, once known as the "saddest dog in the world" for her long and lonely wait for a home, may be on the verge of starting a brand new chapter. The 11-year-old dog, who first gained international attention when she languished in a Spanish shelter for over four years without finding a permanent family, has already been fostered twice in her remarkable journey. Now, it seems she may have finally found a third and perhaps final "lease on life". Lana's emotional story began in 2010, when she was surrendered to the Humana Animal Society in Cáceres, southwest Spain. Despite her sweet, affectionate nature and mostly gentle character, no adopters came forward, and she became a symbol of animal homelessness across the globe. Her plight was widely shared online, sparking outpourings of support from dog lovers around the world, and eventually leading to the formation of the "Find a Home for Lana" campaign. In 2014, Anglo-Spanish charity group Spain Rescue Dogs stepped in and took Lana into their care, resulting in the first foster home for the elderly dog—after over 1,600 days in a cage. A short time later, as news of her early foster experience spread, a compassionate woman in Florida, US, decided to take in Lana from Spain and offer her a new environment. This second phase of her life, however, was not long-lived. After her move in 2015, Lana was returned to Spain due to the owner's ill health. Now, someone in the UK is considering offering her a third chance at a loving home. Current caretakers with Spain Rescue Dogs have stated that, while Lana is no longer a puppy and does suffer from age-related health issues, she is thriving in her foster home and has a loving personality that is waiting to be discovered. "She's not given up. Every day we see her laying on the floor, wagging her tail, waiting for someone to come and pick her up,” one caregiver said. Though the strain of lockdowns and increased demand for pets during the pandemic have disappointed hopes for her adoption, rescue teams remain hopeful. As one volunteer put it: "Lana has always been resilient. She's lived through the worst and still smiled through it all. Her story is a reminder that it's never too late to find love—even when it arrives far later than expected."

The man convicted of murdering a four-year-old boy in what has been described as an act of “incomprehensible brutality” has been found dead in his cell in a UK prison, sparking both grim relief for the victim’s family and renewed inquiry into the circumstances of his death. Denis Turner, 33, was found unresponsive at HMP Wandsworth in London on Tuesday evening, with prison authorities reporting his death as “unexplained,” pending a full post-mortem. The case had gripped the nation when the young boy, who cannot be named for legal reasons, was discovered with horrific and severe injuries outside a supermarket in the West Midlands in 2021. The extent of the abuse he endured prompted national outrage, with Prime Minister Boris Johnson describing the case as a “monumental failure” by local authorities and social services. Turner had been found guilty of murder, grievous bodily harm, and child cruelty after an emotionally devastating trial at Birmingham Crown Court. The prosecution revealed that Turner had subjected the child to a systematic campaign of sexual abuse, starvation, and physical torture, including ordering him to perform dozens of press-ups until he collapsed and holding his head under running water until he nearly drowned. The boy, who survived for three days after being discovered, died of his injuries in hospital. His death led to protests outside government buildings and a demand for urgent reform in child protection systems across the country. The Local Government Association, which represents councils, pledged to implement a new set of safeguarding measures in the wake of the tragedy. Now, with Turner dead in custody, the family of the boy have expressed a mix of grief and numbness. A family spokesperson said: “We are deeply disturbed by this news. He deserved to live with the consequences of his actions for many years, not to be taken out of the equation like this. We just hope the truth of how this man treated our child is never forgotten.” An inquest is expected to be held to determine the causes of Turner’s death. The Prison and Probation Ombudsman will also carry out an investigation. A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “We are aware of this incident and are cooperating fully with the relevant authorities who are responsible for carrying out the investigations.” The case continues to resonate with people across the country, with campaigners calling for justice not only in the court of law, but in the way vulnerable children are protected in the future.

The 2016 presidential campaign, marked by Donald Trump’s distinctive and often polarising leadership, has left American voters more divided than in any major election in recent memory. Across the country, families, workplaces, and communities have found themselves split along ideological lines, with Trump’s acerbic rhetoric and unconventional approach to politics becoming focal points of both intense support and fierce criticism. From the moment he announced his candidacy, Trump’s self-stylised "tough on everything" policy and unfiltered communication style drew both praise and condemnation, arguably reshaping the political landscape and deepening the chasm between liberals and conservatives. Trump’s aggressive manner has not only redefined political discourse but has also forced a broader public conversation about the tone and content of national debate. His frequent use of Twitter, doorstep confrontations with political opponents, and unorthodox responses to everyday news events have set a new benchmark for the kind of politics that may increasingly dominate in the digital age. Many have characterised his approach as prime-time theatrics, with a lack of traditional political tact, while others have hailed it as a necessary break from the so-called political correctness that, in their view, stifles true American values. The starkness of the divide has been particularly evident in focus groups and opinion polls. For instance, while urban centres in blue states have largely rallied behind traditional Democratic ideals of diplomacy and multilateral cooperation – often drawing direct parallels between Trump’s rhetoric and the rhetoric of foreign leaders – the heartland of conservative America has increasingly embraced the Trump method as a necessary antidote to what they describe as decades of mismanagement by the political elite. This polarisation is not just a reflection of differing political ideologies but also of shifting media consumption habits. As social media platforms and 24-hour news cycles amplify extreme positions, there is a growing sense of alienation among those who find themselves on the receiving end of increasingly personal attacks. Many Americans now approach elections not just with political opinions but with personal allegiances, as if they are choosing between tribes rather than party policies. Political analysts warn that such divisiveness can have long-term consequences for the cohesion of a democratic society. Dr. Emily Weaver, a political scientist at the University of Chicago, said: “We’re seeing a campaign that is not only about policy differences but about character and identity. That’s dangerous. Democracy depends on a shared sense of purpose and mutual respect, and when that becomes eroded, the future becomes more uncertain.”

Whole areas of the NHS in England are facing intervention under a new government strategy aimed at addressing deepening service failures, it has been revealed. Simon Stevens, chief executive of NHS England, announced on Friday that a number of struggling health regions would be placed in “special measures” as the NHS confronts a growing crisis. The move marks a significant escalation in the government’s response to a system already under immense strain due to rising demand, staff shortages, and underfunding. NHS England has so far identified three regions where services have consistently failed to meet key targets, including A&E performance and cancer treatment waiting times. The regions, whose names remain under wraps ahead of a full announcement, will face enhanced monitoring and accountability measures, including the deployment of expert teams to assess and reform local management. Mr. Stevens warned that the intervention is not a wake-up call, but a “clear directive” to push for urgent improvements or face further consequences. This is the first time since the 2012 reorganisation of the NHS that such a measure has been applied on a regional scale. Historically, “special measures” have been used for individual hospitals, but the new approach aims to address systemic failures within entire health economies. The announcement comes in the wake of a damning report from the independent Care Quality Commission, which found that local authorities and NHS trusts have failed to prepare services for winter pressures adequately. Health Secretary Jeremy Hunt said the move was necessary to act on “unacceptable underperformance” and to ensure consistency and quality across the nation’s health services. “Patients deserve the same high standard of care, wherever they live in the country,” he said. “Intervening early will help us prevent avoidable crises and protect the most vulnerable in our communities.” The news is set to spark fierce debate in the political and medical communities about how best to address a health system that has been under sustained pressure for years. Unions representing NHS staff have warned that the new measures must be backed by real investment, not just administrative interventions. Debbie Shaw, General Secretary of the Royal College of Nursing, said: “Placing regions in special measures is a positive step, but it cannot come without additional resources. The focus must be on solving crises such as staff shortages and funding gaps, which are at the heart of many of these failings.” In the coming weeks, NHS England will publish a list of the regions under the proposal, alongside the action plans it expects them to follow.

For the first time in 400 years, a curious and distinctive moustachioed face is set to be seen once more over the waters of Poole Harbour, as a mysterious Renaissance figure comes to life after centuries of obscurity. The figure, carved into a folly at the site of the historic Ashley Gardens, was recently rediscovered beneath layers of weathering and greenery, and local heritage groups are now preparing to restore and unveil a full-scale replica along the waterfront. The original carving, long thought to be a decorative feature hidden by time, is believed to date back to the 16th or 17th century. Little is known about the identity of the moustachioed man, but the rediscovery has sparked intrigue among historians and local residents alike. Some speculate that he could be a representation of a prominent local figure, while others believe the visage is purely ornamental, the product of an artist looking to capture the whimsy of the era. Dr. Eleanor Grant, a local historian from Bournemouth University, said: “We have a lot of Renaissance-influenced architecture in the south of England, but nothing quite like this. To see a figure like this, especially one with such a distinct facial feature as a moustache, is unusual for the time. It suggests a strong regional identity and perhaps a sense of local pride.” The decision to recreate the figure in a prominent, accessible spot along the harbour reflects a growing desire within the community to celebrate and preserve its heritage. The new sculpture will be unveiled during a public ceremony in the coming months, marking not just the return of the moustachioed stranger, but a renewed commitment to uncovering and sharing the stories hidden in Poole’s past. Poole Mayor Margaret Williams said she was delighted by the project, remarking: “Poole has such a rich history, and this figure is a reminder of the creativity and character of people who lived and worked in our area long ago. It’s wonderful that, after over four centuries, he will once again be looking out over his home.” The original carving was discovered by chance when a volunteer ranger, conducting a routine maintenance check in the grounds of Ashley Gardens, noticed an unusual pattern etched into a stone wall. After some careful cleaning and stabilisation by conservationists, the face was fully revealed, complete with a striking and enigmatic moustache. Now, with the replica well under construction and anticipation building among residents, Poole Harbour is preparing to welcome back a long-lost witness to the passage of time.

Perhaps the sweetest part of Glasgow’s famous victory in Paris was that it was almost entirely unexpected. A cold, rainy night in the Parc des Princes had produced a semi-final more than a football fixture — it was a clash of expectation, narrative, and raw sporting emotion, and when the final whistle blew, the Auld Triangle had een breathed to life once more. The Glasgow team, long dismissed as underdogs in all but name, stood with arms raised in celebration as their supporters in the stands, many of them Scottish expats and tourists who had followed their beloved side across the Channel, erupted into a spine-tingling chorus of songs not heard in the French capital since George Gordon climbed the cairn. Until the penultimate day, few outside the team dressing rooms and a loyal core of fervent supporters gave Glasgow a realistic chance. They had gone into the competition with names barely known beyond local press briefings. Their forwards were unheralded, their tactical approach described dismissively by experts as “charming but naive.” And yet, there they were, 90 minutes later, having dispatched the reigning champions in clinical, defiant fashion. The key moment came, of course, in the 82nd minute — a corner that was cleared, but only just, by the visiting defenders. The watching press room, usually rhythmically scribbling suicide notes during European fixtures, erupted into stunned verbosity. Players and fans alike had barely processed the tension of a tight match before the goal sent them into collective rapture. For those who were at that ground, those two hours will be etched in memory as vividly as the snowy chaos of Hampden Park or the roaring ambition of Murrayfield. The sense of wonder was palpable — not just because Glasgow had won, but because it had happened about as close to the day as you can imagine. No whispered prophecies. No slow-bulb moment of “we are on something special.” Ironically, the defeat galvanised the Paris team for their upcoming tournament, boosting their profile and confidence, while Glasgow returned home with a tale of glorious audacity — one that would live on in song, in stories, and in the crackle of pubs filled with renewed belief. It was not just a victory over a team but over doubt itself. And in a world that rarely cheers for the unprepossessing, that is perhaps the sweetest triumph of all. Was there ever a more apt Christmas surprise?

Turkey has called a special meeting of Nato ambassadors in Brussels to discuss ongoing military operations against both the Islamic State (IS) terror group and the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), as part of its broader strategy to address security threats on its soil and beyond. The emergency session, convened by Turkish officials on Monday, comes amid heightened concerns over cross-border tensions and the evolving threat landscape in the region. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan is expected to personally address the gathering, underscoring the gravity of the situation and calling for greater international coordination in combatting extremism and separatist movements. The.Fatalf attacks in Istanbul last week, which left more than 30 people dead, are believed to have prompted the urgency behind the summit. While Turkey has previously stressed the importance of Nato solidarity in addressing security challenges, the dual focus on both IS and the PKK has sparked controversy, with some Nato members reluctant to officially label the PKK an enemy, despite the group’s designation as a terrorist organisation by the EU and the US. Turkey has long accused the PKK, which enjoys political representation in parts of northern Iraq and is opposed by the Turkish government, of orchestrating attacks within the country, and has launched multiple offensives across the border in recent months. The meeting follows a significant escalation in Turkish military action in northern Iraq, where warplanes have carried out airstrikes against suspected PKK positions. Ankara claims that targeting the group is vital to its national security, but critics argue that the operation risks deepening regional instability and straining relations with Nato allies who back Kurdish forces on the ground in the fight against IS. Spokesperson for the Nato secretary-general, Oana Lungescu, said the Alliance had “acknowledged the request from Turkey and is preparing for the session” but did not disclose the expected outcome. Meanwhile, Turkey is also conducting its “Operation Martyr Yılmaz” in northern Syria, where it targets IS and affiliated groups. The Turkish military has warned of a broader regional threat, with General Hulusi Akar, Minister of Defence, stating last week that the groups operate as a “coordinated chain” and must be dismantled together. The special envoy meeting is expected to discuss how Nato can support Turkey’s operations while also addressing broader security challenges in the Middle East and North Africa. Some diplomats believe the session may set a precedent for future Nato interventions, particularly as European nations struggle with their own security threats linked to terrorism.

The Hollywood icon Zsa Zsa Gabor has passed away at the age of 99 after suffering a heart attack, her husband Frederic von Anhalt has confirmed. The Austrian-born actress, whose life on screen and behind the scenes was as dramatic as the roles she played, leaves behind a legacy marked by glamour, controversy, and an undimmed sense of style until the very end. Born on February 6, 1917, in Apatin, Austria-Hungary (now part of Serbia), Gabor was one of six sisters known as the “Zsa Sisters,” all of whom pursued careers in the arts. Her journey to stardom began in European cinema before she made a name for herself in Hollywood, where her captivating beauty and biting wit quickly made her a favorite of leading directors and actors of the Golden Age. Gabor became a household name in the 1940s and 1950s with roles in films such as  The69 Eyes of Mina  (1946),  Queen of the Meadow  (1952), and the seminal  Ninotchka  (1939), in which she teamed up with Greta Garbo and Charles Boyer. She was often cast as the glamorous, enigmatic leading lady, a role she embodied with effortless charm. Alongside her movie career, Gabor was a fixture in television, appearing in game shows and talk shows, where her wit and larger-than-life personality charmed audiences. Known for her seven marriages — to names such as George Jessel, Gene Tierney, and oil tycoon Thomas O’Donnell — Gabor’s personal life was as much a spectacle as her career. Even in her later years, she remained a fashion and lifestyle icon, appearing on celebrity news programs and magazine covers, often still dressed to the nines and continuing to walk the red carpet into her 90s. In recent years, Gabor largely lived in seclusion at the Motion Picture & Television Fund Home in Woodland Hills, California, surrounded by the memories of a life lived in the spotlight. Her husband, Frederic von Anhalt, who married her in 2001, described her as “a great beauty, a great actress, and a great friend whose smiles lit up the world.” With her passing, the film world has lost not only a star but a living relic of a bygone Hollywood era. Tributes have poured in from fellow entertainers, historians, and fans alike, all acknowledging the indelible mark she made on cinema and popular culture. Zsa Zsa Gabor never aged out of the spotlight — and it is safe to say, she never will.

The UK House of Commons is set to cast its verdict on whether British military forces should launch airstrikes against the so-called Islamic State (IS) in Syria, with Thursday’s vote expected to be one of the most significant national security decisions of the year. The controversial motion raises stark political, strategic, and moral questions, with the government maintaining that action is essential to counter a growing threat to both national and international security, while critics argue that the intervention is a doomed and dangerous escalation. Prime Minister David Cameron will be relying on cross-party support to secure a majority in the House. Speaking ahead of the vote, he has defended the plan, arguing that it is not only a military but also a moral imperative. “Our goal is to stop the Islamic State from using Syria as a base to conduct terrorist attacks around the world,” he said last week. The government claims that IS is responsible for the deaths of hundreds of civilians in the UK and Europe and that inaction risks a deteriorating situation. Military experts have been cited in government statements, highlighting the logistical advantage IS gains from its control of territory in both Syria and Iraq, which allows the group to train, finance and deploy fighters more effectively. But the decision has drawn fierce opposition from across the political spectrum. Labour leader Ed Miliband has long questioned the government’s handling of the Syrian crisis, noting the lack of a clear exit strategy and the potential for civilian casualties. “Airstrikes without a broader strategy will just confirm to the British public that we are blowing things up again and again with no end in sight,” he warned in a keynote speech last month. His Labour party has internally split on the issue: while some members have argued for military action, others—particularly prominent voices on the left—have consistently opposed it, citing the failures of the Iraq War as a cautionary tale about the consequences of military intervention in the region. The Liberal Democrats, who have supported previous military actions, have also issued reservations. Notably, the party is absent a key figure in its ranks, as Nick Clegg took the rare step of expressing his personal disapproval of the government’s stance. In a statement, he urged members to vote their conscience, saying: “We need to ask not only whether military action can defeat IS, but whether it will do more to keep the public safe or risk provoking an escalation in violence.”

The decision to award a knighthood to Lynton Crosby, the Conservative Party’s highly effective general election strategist, has sparked fierce criticism from Labour and beyond, with shadow home secretary Andy Burnham calling it “outrageous”. The announcement, which came as part of a New Year’s honours list, has reignited debates about political influence, the criteria for receiving honours, and the ethics of rewarding someone instrumental in a campaign that Labour critics claim was built on misleading claims and voter suppression. Crosby, an Australian-born former media executive who moved to the UK in the 1990s, gained prominence during the 2015 and 2019 general elections. His strategies, involving the use of big data and micro-targeting of voters, are widely credited with helping the Conservatives secure significant parliamentary majorities. However, his work also drew scrutiny, particularly for the aggressive tactics employed by the Vote Leave campaign in the 2016 EU referendum—many of which he advised. His role in the controversial “£350m a week” EU spending claim has been a particular lightning rod for criticism. Shadow Home Secretary Andy Burnham, a vocal critic of Crosby, said the knighthood undermined public trust in the honours system. “There is absolutely no justification for rewarding someone who has spent his career promoting division and cynicism in British politics,” he told reporters. He added that the honours system should reflect “public service and integrity”, not political success achieved through underhand or manipulative means. The decision comes at a sensitive time for the Labour Party, which is also examining its role in past campaigns and how it can better engage with voters in the future. Criticism of the honours being “politicised” has grown in recent years, with many calling for reform to the process. Transparency groups have also raised concerns, noting that Crosby’s knighthood appears to buck the trend of avoiding gongs for those embroiled in political controversies. In a response to the backlash, the Prime Minister’s Office said that the honours were awarded on the basis of public service and exceptional contributions. A spokesperson for the Prime Minister stated: “Lynton Crosby has had a significant impact on British politics, and the honours were bestowed following the usual rigorous process.” But with calls growing louder from across the political spectrum for accountability and a re-examination of how such decisions are made, it is clear that Crosby’s knighthood has become a flashpoint in a wider conversation about the relationship between politics, power, and privilege.

Australia’s cricket team is set to hold its ground in a high-stakes standoff with Cricket Australia (CA), as captain Steve Smith has publicly ruled out giving up a long-standing revenue-sharing agreement to resolve their ongoing pay dispute. Smith, a towering figure in the sport, made the comments during a media roundtable, reaffirming the players’ position amid intense scrutiny over the future of one of the nation’s most cherished sports. The dispute centers on a contract offer from CA, which would see players’ salaries tied to a new revenue model. Under the arrangement proposed by the governing body, the players’ share of profits from the sport would be reduced in favor of a frozen financial settlement, even as Australia’s cricket revenue is projected to hit record levels in the coming years. The cricketers, represented by the Australian Cricketers' Association (ACA), reject the idea, arguing that such a move would hand CA long-term financial control at the expense of the players and their earnings potential. “This is not about money just for us, or for our generation,” Smith said. “We believe we deserve to share in the prosperity of a game that we help drive, and that should not be taken away under the guise of short-term resolution.” The revenue-sharing agreement in question is one of the most favorable for athletes in world sport, offering players a cut of all commercial, broadcast, and sponsorship income. CA has argued that with evolving broadcast deals and commercial partnerships, a more fixed remuneration structure would provide greater clarity and long-term financial stability for the sport. The standoff has led to growing tensions, with both sides accused of intransigence. CA has warned of the potential for the game to grind to a halt, with international fixtures in the Ashes and the T20 World Cup looming in the coming months. Meanwhile, the players have indicated a willingness to “go the distance” if necessary, underscoring what many fear could be another cricketing Summer of Discontent, reminiscent of the infamous pay row of 2019 that left the nation’s high-profile Test series with England in jeopardy. The dispute also highlights a broader debate about the distribution of wealth in sport, particularly when players argue they should share in the financial success of a game they are vital to sustaining. Cricket Australia and the ACA are scheduled to resume talks next week, but with both sides entrenched in their positions, the prospect of a swift resolution appears increasingly unlikely.

Roberto Mancini insisted on Tuesday that Manchester City had not officially overtaken Manchester United as the Premier League's dominant force — even after his side crushed the defending champions 6-1 at Old Trafford in what was one of the most stunning league results of the season. The Italian manager, speaking at a post-match press conference, urged fans and observers to temper expectations, pointing to both the fluctuating nature of English football and the need for a longer-term view of the season. “This one result doesn't define who is the biggest club,” Mancini said. “Man United are still massive and have the best fanbase in the world. Clubs like these are built for the long run.” The 6-1 humiliation at the hands of Manchester City left United’s supporters reeling, while City fans celebrated an emphatic statement of intent. Edin Dzhokic Dzeko, and Mario Balotelli all found the net in a rout that saw United collapse almost immediately, conceding four times in the first 28 minutes. It was the most emphatic league defeat United have suffered at Old Trafford since 1989. Mancini, however, remained cautious in his post-match comments. “I never thought about it as a power change,” he explained. “We did what we did to win the game. We dominated, but we have to remember that the season is long, and results can vary. It's important to stay grounded.” The defeat undoubtedly elevated City to new heights in the title race, with their 18th league victory in 23 matches — but Premier League titles are not won in just a few weeks. United, under David Moyes, are still in second place and have a significantly superior goal difference and a more balanced midweek schedule. Moyes, for his part, admitted the result “stings” but insisted “this is just a game.” Mancini is philosophical about City’s position and insists the team must not be carried away. “You can't look at one match like this and say we are better than United. They will come back stronger. That's what big clubs do,” he said. The question remains, however, whether such a crushing win might alter the dynamics of the English game — not just in the title race, but in the wider power balance between clubs, where United have long reigned supreme. For now, Mancini says it's not over — and nor is the challenge. “It’s not about power.
