Leak Not to Blame for Seepages, Gulf Official Says   A significant development has emerged in the ongoing crisis surrounding the BP oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico, as officials downplay fears that recent seepages on the ocean floor may be linked to the ruptured wellhead. Eugene Redmond, the federal incident commander overseeing the response to the disaster, has stated that the new seepages discovered near the Deepwater Horizon site are "not necessarily connected" to the leaking well. His comments come amid mounting concern over the stability of the sea floor and the spread of the oil leak from the Macondo well, which has continued to spill thousands of barrels of crude oil into the Gulf every day since the 22 April explosion that killed 11 workers. Satellite imagery and undersea footage revealed new plumes of oil and methane escaping from the seabed in the vicinity of the Deepwater Horizon drill site. These seepages, often natural occurrences in the Gulf, have raised fears that the well’s explosive blowout in late April might have triggered instability in the surrounding geology. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) confirmed that such seepages are not uncommon in the Gulf and are typically the result of natural geological activity. However, the apparent increase in such activity near the well site has led to speculation that the drilling operations may have somehow disturbed the area. Redmond, however, has warned against drawing direct links between the well failure and the new seepages. “We have to be careful not to blame the well for everything we see in the area,” Redmond said in a press conference on Sunday. “Our foremost concern is containing the flow from the Macondo well and preventing further damage to the environment.” BP, which has been under intense scrutiny since the disaster, did not immediately comment on the incident commander’s remarks. The company has been scrambling to implement a top kill and containment cap to stop the oil from leaking into the ocean. Despite these efforts, the well continues to spew oil into the waters, with much of it drifting toward the fragile ecosystems of the Gulf Coast. Scientists have raised concerns about how the combined effects of the well leak and the natural seepages could impact marine life and coastal communities. Some experts have suggested that the new seepages could lead to the formation of undersea oil plumes, with unknown long-term consequences for the region'senvironment.

The UK energy regulator Ofgem has issued a stark reminder to energy suppliers that they have no justification for further increases in standard variable tariffs, as soaring costs threaten to burden households already stretched by the cost of living crisis. In a strong intervention, Ofgem emphasized that energy firms must review and potentially freeze prices for customers who remain on default tariffs, which are generally more expensive than fixed deals. This comes as millions of households continue to face record energy bills amid ongoing volatility in global gas and electricity markets. The regulator, which is responsible for ensuring a fair deal for consumers and a competitive energy market, has called for a “reset” in the way energy companies interact with vulnerable customers. Maria Miller, Chair of Ofgem, stated, “Now is not the time for more turkey tariffs. Suppliers must do more to support families who are unable to switch to better deals.” The warning follows mounting pressure on Ofgem from consumer groups and politicians, who have highlighted the growing number of households slipping into fuel poverty. With inflation at decade highs and wages lagging, many consumers have found themselves unable to move to fixed-rate tariffs, which have generally offered lower rates in recent months. Ofgem is expected to place new conditions in its next market review, to be published early next month, that will compel energy suppliers to offer customers guidance on switching and improve their services. “We will not hesitate to take enforcement action against companies failing in their responsibilities to customers,” added Miller. The move by Ofgem comes as the government also faces calls to reconsider emergency energy support for households and small businesses. However, with discussions ongoing about the sustainability of government subsidies, the energy regulator’s push on the industry puts the spotlight back on energy companies and their profits. Energy UK, the industry body representing energy suppliers, responded by stating its members are “working hard to offer the best possible deals to consumers during these difficult times.” It added that many firms have already frozen standard tariffs and have helped connect thousands of customers to fixed-rate, cheaper options. Ofgem’s intervention signals a renewed determination to hold energy suppliers to account as it seeks to prevent further hardship for UK households amid continued uncertainty in the global energy markets. However, whether such regulatory pressure will be enough to curb rising costs remains to be seen.

Wales prop Samson Lee has made a surprising personal sacrifice to stay fit and in peak condition ahead of the 2023 Rugby World Cup in France – giving up his hobby of ferreting for rabbits. The Ospreys and Wales international, who earned his 50th cap in the recent Six Nations win over England, has turned to more passive weekend pursuits to avoid the physical risks associated with his former sport. Ferreting, a traditional activity in rural Wales involving the use of terriers to flush rabbits from their burrows, requires extended periods of crouching and physical exertion. For a front-row player competing at the highest level, even low-impact hobbies can pose injury risks. Lee, 28, has become a vital component of Wales’ pack, renowned for his scrummaging power and work rate at the breakdown. “I love the countryside and spending time in the hills,” Lee said. “But with the World Cup coming up, I need to be 100 per cent injury-free for training and matches. I’ve had to step back from some of the things I used to do to make sure I’m ready for France.” Lee, who initially played as a tighthead prop before switching to the loose-head position, is expected to start for Wales in the tournament after forming a formidable scrummage in domestic and international fixtures. His decision to stop ferreting has been backed by Wales’ coaching staff, who are monitoring his conditioning closely ahead of their opening match against Tonga on September 9. “Samson is a big part of what we’re building in this squad. Making the tough decisions for yourself counts for a lot at this level,” said Wales forwards coach Neil Jenkins. “He’s shown his commitment – not just on the field but in his lifestyle choices. That’s what a World Cup player needs.” Lee’s move follows a string of other Wales players modifying their off-field habits to stay fit ahead of the global showpiece. Props like Tomas Francis, Ken Owens and Aaron Jarvis have all had high-profile seasons, with injury prevention at the forefront of their preparations. The Wales squad will begin intense training sessions later this summer as they aim to recapture their 2019 form, when they reached the quarter-finals of the last World Cup. With Lee now devoted to rugby full-time, his focus will be on helping Wales make their mark in the expanded 20-team tournament.

MPs have called for a “realistic timetable” for the High Speed 2 (HS2) rail project, warning that the current schedule is “overly ambitious” and at risk of falling further behind due to a combination of financial and logistical challenges. A recent parliamentary report, published by the House of Commons Transport Committee, highlighted concerns that the £106 billion line – one of the most expensive transport projects in British history – is on a collision course with delays, cost overruns and a lack of political direction. The committee, chaired by Sir William Cash, said while the project has the potential to “transform the UK’s transport network”, the government’s current plans lack a credible timeline. “Our review shows that the current timetable for Phase One of HS2 is overly optimistic and not rooted in the ground reality of the challenges facing this huge and complex project,” the committee stated in its report. The document raises particular concern about the £43 billion first phase of the line, which is intended to run from London’s Euston to Crewe and was initially scheduled to open in 2026. However, the current target is now 2031, and the committee warned that missing this would be “highly likely” as supply chain constraints and inflation continue to bite. Shadow Transport Secretary Louise Haigh welcomed the committee’s findings, adding that “the national cost of living crisis means that the government must be smarter with the billions being spent on HS2 and set realistic goals.” Meanwhile, the government’s Transport Secretary, Mark Harper, defended the project, claiming the current schedule is “robust” and insisting that HS2 is a “national priority that will deliver transformational change for the UK’s transport system and economy.” However, some Conservative MPs have echoed concerns from across the political spectrum, suggesting that ministers are “out of date” on the evolving challenges of the project. The committee also pointed to the need for greater accountability and transparency in the management of the £106 billion railway, which has already exceeded its projected costs by billions. Environmental groups remain divided, with some acknowledging the need for a high-capacity rail network but questioning whether HS2 is the most sustainable solution given the current state of planning. As the debate over HS2 continues, the committee’s report has added to the growing pressure on the government to set a deliverable timeline for the controversial project. Ministers are now expected to respond in the coming weeks as the country grapples with how best to spend billions on vital transport infrastructure.

The UK is home to more than 600,000 people of Italian origin – one of the largest migrant communities in Europe. Many are British-born with Italian roots, yet others were born in their homeland and have spent years, sometimes decades, building new lives in the UK. But as Italy grapples with a future shaped by political uncertainty, economic stagnation and a growing anti-immigration sentiment, some are wondering whether these expatriates might help determine the country’s direction in a way never anticipated. In recent months, as Italy’s governing parties have clashed over policies and corruption scandals have continued to erupt, the Italian diaspora has grown increasingly restless. Many believe it is time to re-engage with the country of their birth and help reshape its political and social narratives. With an estimated 3.5 million Italians living abroad, the UK represents one of their largest strongholds, and the community has turned to local cultural events, petitions, and even informal lobbying to get their voices heard. “We’re not returning en masse in the near future, but our opinions and influence can still carry weight,” says Marco Belli, founder of the Italian Cultural Association in London, which recently hosted a panel on Italy’s future in the era of a rising right-wing movement and the legacy of old-school leftist parties. The country’s political class – long dominated by Silvio Berlusconi-style populism and more recently by Matteo Salvini’s anti-immigrant League – is under growing pressure to appeal to younger voters and those who feel alienated by the current direction of the nation’s affairs. Some Italian expats in London suggest that they could serve as a bridge to European values, a point reinforced by recent events at the Italian general election in September 2022, when over 200,000 expatriates cast their votes. With such numbers, the diaspora is being seen as more than just peripheral spectators to Italy’s unfolding drama. Some have even proposed the formation of a “Diaspora Council” to represent expatriate opinions on matters of national and international significance. Yet it is a delicate balance. Many Italians living abroad are wary of political entanglements, while others are too far removed from daily life in Italy to feel truly connected. Still, the fact that Italian flags proudly unfurl at London's Piazza Italia on match day and that expat communities hold vast go-to-meetings over matters like education, identity and trade, suggests that the UK’s Italian expat community could yet surprise Italy by offering a powerful new voice in its future.

The prospect of a radical overhaul of the UK prison system was warmly received by politicians, charities and legal experts as the government unveiled new powers to allow some prison governors to set their own rules, budgets and rehabilitation strategies. The proposals, outlined in this year’s Queen’s Speech, mark the latest in a long line of attempts to address a system that has long struggled with high rates of reoffending, chronic overcrowding, and persistent reports of poor conditions. Under the reforms, a number of prisons will be given devolved powers under a new “prison academy” model. These establishments will be free to set their own operational standards, develop innovative rehabilitation programmes and manage their budgets to prioritise education, employment training and mental health support. The government described the changes as a “step towards more localised, flexible and effective management of our prison estate,” and a crucial move towards reducing reoffending, which currently stands at more than 60% in some categories of offenders. The reforms are expected to be trialled in a small number of sites in the early stages, with the intention of scaling up if the results are positive. Prisons minister Morgan Jones told the House of Commons that the plan would “restore dignity and purpose to prisons that have too often become as much about punishment as they are about reform.” The announcement was welcomed by a number of key stakeholders in the criminal justice system. The Howard League, one of Britain’s oldest penal reform charities, praised the government for “finally recognising the importance of tailoring rehabilitation to the needs of individual prisoners and the communities they will eventually re-enter.” Similarly, Labour leader Keir Starmer acknowledged the need to break the “cycle of reoffending” and said his party would support continued funding and oversight of these initiatives. Criticism has not been entirely absent, however. The National Union of Probation Officers (NUPO) warned that devolving too much decision-making could risk standards being eroded without proper accountability. “We welcome any move towards innovation, but we must be cautious that these localised models do not undermine the essential minimum standards required for effective rehabilitation,” said a union spokesperson. Meanwhile, the Prison Governors' Association has voiced enthusiasm for the new responsibilities. Association chair Mark Brook, who oversees a number of major regional prisons, said: “For too long, we’ve been constrained by rigid national policies that don’t account for the complex realities on the ground.

New rules introduced by the government have sparked a wave of concern among environmental campaigners, legal experts and conservation groups, as they claim the changes could significantly hamper the ability of individuals and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) to challenge environmentally damaging decisions in court. Critics argue that the reforms represent a major shift in the UK’s commitment to environmental justice and transparency. Under the revised regulations, which took effect earlier this month, individuals and NGOs will face stricter requirements before they can initiate judicial reviews or legal actions against government or corporate decisions that may harm the environment. For example, claimants will now be expected to show a “sufficient interest” in the issue at hand, potentially requiring personal financial harm or direct impact. Campaigners fear this could act as a barrier for community groups or well-meaning individuals who identify environmental threats but may not themselves be directly affected by them. Lena Wood, a solicitor and director of the law firm EarthRights UK, said the move could be a tactical means of limiting public scrutiny. “This feels like a drive to limit accountability. Environmental issues often impact people indirectly, or even future generations. Should a community not have the right to challenge a project that could pollute their river or destroy local habitats simply because they don’t live in the immediate vicinity?” she explained. Environmental groups, including Friends of the Earth and Greenpeace, have condemned the changes as politically motivated and a departure from international environmental legal standards, such as those upheld by the European Convention on Human Rights. The organisations claim they have already started to consider legal action themselves to challenge the validity of the new rules. The Ministry of Justice has defended the move, stating that it is part of a broader push to make the courts more “targeted and fair” by preventing “frivolous” or “malicious” legal claims. A government spokesperson said: “Our legal system should not be abused by those who have no standing in a matter. These changes are about ensuring that those who take legal action have a legitimate interest to do so, thereby upholding the dignity of the judiciary.” However, many remain unconvinced. Dr. Emily Porter, lecturer in environmental law at King’s College London, argues that the rules could drastically reduce the number of successful legal actions to protect green spaces, challenge extraction projects, or allow environmental damage to go unchecked.

The United States remains the largest single donor of overseas aid in the world, despite ongoing debates over the purpose and efficiency of foreign assistance. According to the most recent figures from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which tracks development aid from developed nations, the US disbursed more than $33 billion in overseas development assistance in 2022, far ahead of the second-largest donor, Germany, which contributed nearly $15 billion. A further $50 billion in military and economic aid was also extended to allies and partner nations as part of broader foreign policy and national security strategies. The US has long positioned itself as a global leader in humanitarian aid, pledging support to countries affected by conflict, natural disasters, and economic crises. Recent years have seen the US increase funding for humanitarian efforts in Ukraine following Russia’s invasion, as well as aiding nations in the Global South impacted by the climate crisis and food insecurity. However, the size of the US aid budget is often overshadowed by criticism from both political sides of the aisle. Critics argue that the aid is sometimes used to advance American geopolitical interests rather than address the most pressing needs of recipient countries. Others question the transparency and effectiveness of how aid is distributed, particularly in regions where corruption undermines local governance. President Joe Biden, who has repeatedly defended aid to Ukraine and Afghanistan, recently reiterated his commitment to “foreign assistance as a tool of diplomacy and humanitarian relief” in a speech at the State Department. “It is not an act of charity,” he said. “It is an investment in our own security and principles.” Yet, Congress has at times been reluctant to approve such funding, with a number of amendments proposed to curtail what some lawmakers call “wasteful” spending. Meanwhile, non-governmental organizations and development experts continue to argue for a more coordinated and locally driven approach to aid. Dr. Hannah Reimer, an aid policy analyst at the Overseas Development Institute, told the  Guardian : “The US has immense resources, but there’s a lot of work to be done in making sure that aid is not only large in volume but also effective and equitable in practice.” As the debate over how to balance strategic interests with humanitarian goals continues, one thing remains clear: the US plays a pivotal role in shaping the landscape of international development.

Falkirk maintained their position in third place in the Scottish Championship despite a frustrating 0-0 draw with Queen of the South at the Falkirk Stadium on Thursday evening. The result, although leaving their league standing unchanged, saw the Bairns fall further behind title challengers Hibernian, as their rivals edged closer to sealing another convincing victory on their return to the top flight of Scottish football. The match at the Falkirk Stadium was a tightly contested affair that failed to produce a goal, as both sides displayed a mixture of cautious attacking play and disciplined defending. Falkirk, fresh off the back of a slim win over Raith Rovers, made a determined bid to push forward early in the game, but were met with a staunch Queen of the South side, managed by well-known figure Mark McGhee, who remains determined to ensure his team finish the season on a positive note. Falkirk manager Peter Houston, who has guided the team back into promotion contention since taking charge last summer, admitted that his side had been creating enough opportunities to be victorious. “We had the better of the chances, and I felt we deserved a little more than a point, but I give credit to Queen of the South for standing up to the pressure and making it a very difficult night for us,” Houston said in his post-match interview. The third-placed position is a significant achievement for Falkirk, given the historically tough nature of the Championship, and one that marks a return to consistent form after an inconsistent start to the season. With their title ambitions seemingly slipping out of reach due to the pace set by Hibs, attention now turns to securing a top-four finish, a result that would guarantee a place in the play-offs. Meanwhile, Queen of the South remain in mid-table, safe from the relegation scrap but aware of the challenge of finishing higher up the league ladder. McGhee, speaking after the draw, expressed a mix of pride and disappointment. “I thought we were excellent defensively, but we didn’t create the chances we needed to put the game to bed. A point here is never a bad result, but the fans deserved a better return,” he said. As the race for the Championship title heats up, Falkirk fans will be hoping for a late surge in form from their side to keep the play-off dream alive.

A Land of Forests and Finnish Ties: Estonia’s Unique Identity   Nestled between the Baltic Sea and the Russian expanse of the east, Estonia is the most northerly of the three Baltic states, standing as a verdant gateway between Western Europe and the East. With its long coastline, dense forests, and a rich cultural heritage, Estonia offers more than just natural beauty—it also has an intriguing linguistic link to one of its European neighbours that sets it apart from Latvia and Lithuania. Estonia shares more than just a shoreline with Finland. The linguistic connection between the two nations lies at the heart of a deep-rooted cultural bond. Both Estonian and Finnish belong to the Uralic language family, a classification that starkly differentiates them from the Indo-European languages spoken by neighbouring countries. The shared vocabulary and grammatical structure between the two languages reveal their common origins, a linguistic bond that has turned into a cultural bridge in numerous ways. This connection dates back centuries, long before Estonia and Finland found themselves entangled in the web of Russian, Swedish, and later Soviet rule. During the 19th and early 20th centuries, the Finno-Ugric unity became a powerful idea, particularly in the face of rising nationalism and the push for independence from foreign powers. The shared language and folklore became a point of solidarity, lending Estonia and Finland a unique – and shared – sense of identity in a region often marked by political upheaval. The historical relationship was not just cultural but also practical. During the interwar period, when both nations were independent, Finland was a key ally and trading partner. Many Estonian officials and intellectuals found refuge in Finland during the Soviet occupation, and the Finns, in turn, provided diplomatic and humanitarian support. This alliance remains a cornerstone of mutual respect and cooperation today. Estonia’s embrace of the Finnish language is not limited to historical or academic settings. While Finnish is not widely spoken among the general Estonian public, it has a strong presence in business, education, and tourism. The high level of literacy in both countries, combined with the minimal linguistic differences, means that many Estonians can understand Finnish with some exposure, a fact that has contributed to a strong travel and professional link between the two nations. This nuanced relationship between Estonia and Finland continues to evolve, with both countries working together in the European Union and NATO spheres, their shared history and language serving as a quiet but powerful undercurrent to modern collaboration.

Old man found with crucifix shot dead by California police after reports of firearms, sparking outrage   By our correspondent A 73-year-old man with dementia was shot and killed by police in California after officers responded to a call suggesting he may have had a gun, the sheriff’s office confirmed on Tuesday. However, it was later revealed that the man, identified as David Lopez, was carrying a crucifix at the time of the incident. The tragic event has sparked fierce criticism and raised questions about use-of-force policies involving vulnerable individuals and mental health training among law enforcement. According to the Riverside County Sheriff’s Department, deputies were dispatched to a residence in Perris, near the city of Inland Empire, after receiving a report of a man "brandishing a weapon". Myron Morata, the father of the victim’s niece, said he called 911 in a panic, believing the man—his 73-year-old uncle—had a gun. "He called me saying he saw this man holding something shiny," Mr Morata told the  Riverside Press . "He didn’t say it was a gun. I told the operator I was concerned, and maybe it was a firearm." Upon arrival, two deputies immediately shot Mr Lopez dead in the front yard, where he was reportedly standing holding the cross. Surveillance footage obtained by local media showed him dressed in a red shirt holding a silver object, with no visible weapons on his person. The sheriff’s office confirmed that after the shooting, the object was identified as a crucifix—an object Mr Lopez, who had dementia, often carried with him for comfort. Steve Lopez, Mr Lopez’s son, said his father—who was described as “docile”, “friendly” and “always non-confrontational” — had been out for a walk about half a mile from home when he encountered the officers. “He was not going to hurt anyone. He had no idea what was happening. He didn’t know who the officers were,” the family said in a statement. “This was a tragic misunderstanding.” Eyewitnesses and activists have raised concerns about the quickness of the deputies’ response, particularly given Mr Lopez’s age, apparent vulnerability and non-threatening demeanour. “This is a perfect example of why de-escalation and better mental health training are needed,” said Riana Dessauer of the Center for Justice Research. “This man didn’t pose a threat, but he was killed anyway.”

U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin held a previously undisclosed conversation at a private dinner of world leaders in Germany earlier this month, according to multiple U.S. and European officials. The talks, which took place over a long meal hosted by German Chancellor Angela Merkel during the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Hamburg, were not disclosed publicly at the time and have now emerged as part of an ongoing inquiry into Trump’s dealings with Russian officials. White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders confirmed that the two leaders “had some time to speak briefly” at the meal, but refused to provide further details, including the subject of their discussion or its duration. The revelation comes at a sensitive moment, as Trump faces increasing scrutiny over allegations of Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. election and the subsequent investigation into whether Trump or his aides coordinated with Moscow. The dinner itself was attended by 20 world leaders, but the U.S. and Russian heads of state reportedly spent much of the meal conversing in a semi-private corner, setting them apart from the rest of the group. According to sources present at the dinner, the pair engaged in a conversation lasting around 45 minutes, during which they did not make any public statements or appear to be recorded by media. It is unclear whether other officials or aides were present during the exchange. The national security advisor at the time, General H.R. McMaster, was reportedly among those in the dinner party but did not accompany Trump and Putin at all times, according to press reports. The undisclosed conversation has raised concerns among lawmakers and members of Trump’s own administration regarding the potential for unmonitored discussions between the U.S. president and the Russian leader, particularly as the U.S. seeks to counter Russian influence in international affairs and European security. The G20 summit in Germany had previously been the stage for chaotic encounters, including a dramatic row between Trump and French President Emmanuel Macron and a heated argument between Trump and Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull. This revelation adds to the controversy that has surrounded Trump’s approach to his dealings with authoritarian regimes. White House officials have repeatedly insisted that Trump does not meet with foreign leaders in private unless doing so is in the interest of national security. However, the apparent lack of transparency surrounding this new conversation with Putin has left many observers frustrated and anxious for further clarity.

You have to feel the Office for Budget Responsibility's (OBR) pain — especially if you’re trying to get any real clarity on Britain’s economic future. The independent body, tasked with assessing public finances and acting as the UK’s fiscal watchdog, finds itself in a quagmire of uncertainty as the government’s spending plans clash with economic reality, and as Brexit looms ever closer. On Tuesday, the OBR released an update of its Economic and Fiscal Outlook (EFO) document in response to the government’s Autumn Statement. It was meant to be a routine exercise — evaluating the Treasury’s assumptions on public finances through the lens of independent macroeconomic analysis. Instead, it became yet another platform for harsh truths and difficult questions the government would rather avoid. The OBR’s reaction to the Autumn Statement was met with immediate criticism. It revised its growth forecasts downward, warning that the risk of a no-deal Brexit has increased. It also flagged the risks of the government’s long-term borrowing strategy and suggested that public debt could rise to 100% of GDP within five years — a level not seen since the end of the Second World War. OBR officials, who are often seen as the sturdy, unflappable economists keeping the Treasury honest, now find themselves caught in the political crossfire. Their projections, accurate and data-driven, are being conveniently ignored or reinterpreted by ministers who are preparing for a general election, and who may prefer headlines to hard figures. The OBR’s difficulty is compounded by the government’s refusal to rule out a no-deal Brexit, which the Bank of England has warned would trigger a deep recession. Yet, the OBR must model its forecasts on what it describes as “the continued operation of UK and EU law as currently written,” rather than on hypothetical political outcomes. Essentially, it is asking the OBR to make the impossible possible: to predict an unpredictable future. And so, the OBR does what it has always done: it does its job. It produces detailed, thorough assessments of the government’s fiscal plans against the backdrop of an increasingly uncertain economy. Yet the further these exercises go, the more evident it becomes that accurate analysis alone cannot override political reality. In this sense, the OBR’s pain is also the public’s. Whether or not one agrees with the government’s policies, no one should be surprised when informed economic analysis is sidelined for short-term political convenience.

The Shard, western Europe’s tallest building, marked a new chapter in its illustrious history on Monday as its observation deck officially opened to the public, offering panoramic views of London’s skyline from 85 floors above the ground. The long-awaited unveiling of the £20 million visitor attraction has already drawn crowds, with the first guests capturing photographs and beginning the new tradition of experiencing the city from the heights of this 306-metre glass and steel marvel. Located at 72 storeys and 320 metres up, the observation deck is among the highest in the world, rivaling views from New York’s Empire State Building and Chicago’s Willis Tower. Visitors now have the chance to step into a glass-enclosed space where they can see in all directions—over the River Thames, across the bustling City of London, and into the London suburbs on a clear day. The architectural icon, which has dominated the skyline since its completion in 2012, is now firmly transitioning into a major tourist destination. The opening comes at a time when the Shard is striving to re-invent itself after initial struggles. Formerly known for its luxury retail and fine dining, the building has seen a significant upturn in visitor interest since the launch of its Sky Deck last year, offering more exclusive access. The new standard observation deck is expected to attract millions of visitors annually, adding a fresh impetus to the city's tourism sector. “We are thrilled to welcome the public to experience the Shard,” said Nick Robinson, chief executive of the building’s owner, Sellar Property Group. “This is not just an observation deck—it's a vantage point from which to see the city in all its glory, and it's a testament to the architectural ambition that defines London.” Tickets for the observation deck have already sold out for the weekend, with the public queuing in the thousands to secure a spot. The Shard plans to expand its visitor experience further with new audio guides, interactive displays, and themed packages. The opening has also reignited discussions about the role of skyscrapers in London’s urban fabric. As the city continues to grow vertically, with new high-profile projects on the horizon, the Shard remains a symbol of modernity and ambition. And now, thanks to this latest addition, it also stands as a gateway to the views that make London a city of infinite perspectives.

Northern Ireland's health system is facing a growing crisis in mental health care, with none of its five health trusts currently meeting waiting time targets for non-emergency mental health treatments. The revelation comes amid heightened awareness of mental health issues and increasing demand for services in the wake of the pandemic, and raises concerns about the well-being of those dealing with anxiety, depression and other common mental health disorders. According to recent data obtained by the Ulster Unionist MLA Graham Stevenson through a Freedom of Information request, every trust has reported delays in delivering services. In some cases, patients are waiting far longer than the six-week target set for initial assessment, which the government has long highlighted as a key benchmark in improving accessibility to mental health support. The problems are not confined to one area; the Belfast Health and Social Care Trust, for example, is left with a backlog of over 5,000 patients, while the Southern Health Trust faces delays of up to ten weeks in some services. The waiting times, often considerably longer than acceptable thresholds, have led to growing frustration among those needing care and their families, many of whom fear that the delay could exacerbate conditions or result in worse outcomes. The lack of progress has drawn condemnation from health professionals and patient groups, who argue that mental health services are being chronically underfunded and neglected in comparison to physical health treatments. "When services struggle to meet national waiting time targets for operations or scans, there’s usually an outcry," said Anna Maguire, director of Mind in Northern Ireland. "But for mental health, it's as if it's normal to wait for months. This is an affront to anyone trying to seek help and contributes to the cycle of stigma and shame." Health Minister Simon Hamilton has been pressed to address the shortcomings, but no comprehensive plan has been announced to resolve the crisis. Ministers have repeatedly cited the "rising demand and the severity of cases" as a contributing factor, but fails to account for the necessary investment in resources and staffing. At the same time, funding for mental health services has not kept pace with the needs of a growing population. Mental health charities are calling for urgent action, including the hiring of more therapists, clinical psychologists and support staff, while also pushing for better integration between primary and specialist services.

In a brazen act of wildlife theft, 101 Chinese box turtles were stolen from a temporary shelter in Kenting National Park in southern Taiwan during the dark hours of the night, sparking alarm among conservationists and local authorities. The incident, first reported over the weekend, has raised questions about the security of wildlife sanctuaries in an area renowned for its biodiversity and natural beauty. The turtles, an endangered species native to China, were housed in the park as part of a recovery and breeding programme aimed at protecting their dwindling numbers. Kenting, a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve and one of the most visited national parks in Taiwan, is well known not only for its stunning coastlines and coral reefs but also for its efforts in the conservation of wildlife, both native and imported for endangered species programmes. The theft of such a large number of animals from a monitored facility is an unusual and worrying event, and investigators are now urgently reviewing security footage and assembling a list of suspects. Park officials revealed that the stolen turtles were to be rehomed in a repurposed facility soon, as part of a long-term collaboration between national parks and conservation NGOs. Their sudden disappearance has thrown the programme into disarray, with conservation workers facing the daunting task of tracking the missing creatures to prevent them from entering the illegal pet trade. Chinese box turtles are highly sought after by collectors in Asian countries, known for their ornate shells and longevity, and can sell for thousands of dollars on the black market. Experts fear the thieves may have already moved the animals to a distant location, making recovery efforts even more challenging. According to police spokesperson Ming Chen, who addressed the media on Monday, a reward of NT$1m (roughly £25,000) has been offered for information leading to the arrest of those responsible. "This was not a random act—it was well-organised and deliberate," Chen said. "We believe the involvement of a professional network cannot be ruled out." The Ministry of the Interior has also announced an urgent review of security protocols at wildlife facilities across the country, while environmental NGOs have called for increased anti-poaching measures and international cooperation to combat wildlife trafficking. The theft has sparked widespread condemnation on social media, with many netizens expressing outrage over what they describe as a 'shameful act of greed.' Some users have also questioned whether additional measures, such as GPS tracking or biometric tagging of high-value animals, should be introduced to prevent future incidents.

The pound has retreated to near 31-year lows against the US dollar, reversing earlier gains that had briefly lifted it amid a broader recovery in global markets. Sterling touched $1.1670 in early trading after recent economic data and positive investor sentiment had seemed to offer a glimmer of optimism for the UK currency. However, that improved momentum has since waned, with the pound struggling to hold above the critical $1.17 level. Analysts point to mixed policy signals from the Bank of England and uncertainty over the path of inflation and interest rates as key factors behind the renewed weakness. The pound had gained ground following the decision by the central bank not to cut rates at its latest meeting, fueling speculation that the Bank may still hold rates steady in the near term. Nevertheless, concerns over weak UK economic growth and the lingering impact of Brexit continue to overshadow the short-lived gains. The pound’s fall has been further exacerbated by surging US Treasury yields, which make dollar assets more attractive to investors. Rising inflation expectations in the US, coupled with optimism about the American economy, have strengthened the dollar’s position in global markets. Against the euro, the pound was also seen weaker, trading at €1.07 in early afternoon, a level not seen in several months. The UK has been in prolonged economic difficulty, with GDP growth remaining stubbornly low and inflation still above the Bank of England's 2% target. The Office for National Statistics recently revised growth figures for the second quarter, showing only a marginal expansion of 0.1%, reinforcing concerns about a sluggish recovery in the world’s sixth-largest economy. 金融市场分析师 Kevin Thompson said the pound's performance is a reflection of broader uncertainty about the UK's economic outlook and the effectiveness of current policy measures. “Sterling remains vulnerable until there is clearer evidence of sustainable growth and a path to reducing inflation without crashing the economy,” he said. The Bank of England has kept interest rates at 5.25%, the highest level in 16 years, for the past four meetings as it attempts to curb inflation. However, some analysts believe the Bank is holding fire on rate cuts due to fears that cutting too soon could reignite price pressures. There are also concerns that a rate cut at this stage could be misinterpreted by the markets as a signal of weakness in the Bank's anti-inflation stance.

British businessman and former BBC chairman Sir Christopher Bland has died at the age of 78. A towering figure in public life and a fervent advocate for broadcasting excellence, Bland will be remembered for his distinctive voice, his unflinching integrity, and his commitment to the highest standards of journalism and public service. Deputies in-house and outsiders alike praised his formidable intellect and his ability to command a room with both eloquence and wit. Lord Hall, the current BBC director-general, described Bland as “a man of extraordinary wisdom and vision who brought gravitas and clarity to the role of chairman at the BBC when it was most needed.” During his time at the BBC, Bland oversaw a crucial period of reform and modernisation, navigating the Corporation through an era of increasing scepticism and political scrutiny. His tenure from 1992 to 1996, and then as a non-executive director until 2002, saw the organisation through significant changes in structure and public expectations. His emphasis on editorial independence and accountability was seen as instrumental in maintaining public trust in the BBC's impartiality. Born in 1943, Christopher Bland—KCB (Knight Companion of the Order of the Bath)—was the son of Sir Anthony Bland, a renowned journalist in his own right. From an early age, Bland was immersed in the world of media and public affairs, attending Eton College and later reading modern history at Magdalen College, Oxford. Following a brief spell in the army, he entered the world of journalism and publishing, eventually founding The Spitting Image Group in the 1980s, which became a leading advertising and media agency known for its bold and original approach. Bland’s career was marked by his fearless political commentary and his ability to challenge authority while maintaining the respect of the establishment. His resignation as leader of the 1992 general election debate was widely regarded as one of the most dramatic moments in BBC history. The row over whether the polls should be published before the debate was cut short and Bland’s decision to halt proceedings was seen as a principled stand for accurate and responsible journalism. Beyond the BBC, Bland was also a respected figure in British business, contributing to the development of the advertising and media sectors. He served on the boards of numerous companies and charities, and was a man known for his generosity and his capacity to rally others around a cause.

Call Centre Staffing ‘Crisis’ Emerges as Major Flaw in M9 Crash Response   A damning revelation has surfaced in the wake of the tragic M9 crash that claimed the lives of two teenage girls, highlighting a significant problem with the performance of the emergency call centre handling the initial 999 call. It has emerged that Fircroft Ltd, the private company responsible for answering emergency calls for Police Scotland in the central belt of the country, faced a serious staffing crisis just a month before the incident. The records indicate that the control centre had a 10% absence rate at the time when staff should have been at optimal levels to handle emergency calls, including the one made on January 13 last year. The absence rate, which appeared well beyond acceptable levels, raises troubling questions about the readiness and capacity of the call centre to respond swiftly and effectively in life-threatening situations. The crash occurred between Junction 18 and 19 of the M9, near Bucksburn, when a car veered off the road and collided with a tree. Both Muireann O’Connor and Georgia McCloy, aged 16 and 17 respectively, died at the scene. Their driver, Sean Williams, 18, survived and is recovering. The call centre, based in Aviemore, is part of a regional services contract known as the South East Regional Operating Centre (SEROC), and is one of the key support facilities for Police Scotland. It is staffed by trained operators who are meant to ensure that emergency calls are prioritised and passed to the appropriate services in an efficient and timely manner. Yet, a report obtained by the Daily Record shows that in the weeks leading up to the tragic crash, the staff at Aviemore had to contend with unacceptably high rates of illness and absentees. One operator, who wished to remain anonymous, said: “We were often short-staffed. At times, it felt unmanageable. The pressure on each officer to multi-task and respond to multiple high-priority calls was enormous. I feared we were one call away from being overwhelmed.” The revelation has sparked anger among bereaved families, politicians, and policing watchdogs. Dr. Niall Kennedy, co-chair of the Police and Fire Public Audit Committee, condemned the 10% absence rate as “unacceptable and unacceptable for a service as critical as 999 operations.” He added: “Every second matters in an emergency, and that gap in staffing could have cost lives.” Police Scotland said it was aware of the staffing issues and has since been working with Fircroft to improve response times and operational efficiency across its third-party call centres.

Power cuts and flooding linked to a series of severe winter storms have continued to disrupt lives across parts of England, with some households still without electricity more than a week after the chaos began. Utility companies confirmed on Tuesday that up to 1,000 homes had been affected by the storms, which battered southern England with high winds, torrential rain, and hail over the weekend. Many of the worst-hit homes were located in rural areas of Devon, Cornwall, and Somerset, where emergency crews have struggled to restore power amid difficult winter conditions. Southern Power, one of the primary electricity providers in the region, said that while the number of homes still under the dark had fallen to 800, some could remain without power until the end of the week. "Repair teams are working round the clock to restore electricity, but the damage is extensive and weather conditions are making the situation even more complicated," a company spokesperson said. The Environment Agency reported that 22 homes had been inundated, with rivers spilling over in some areas after days of intense rainfall. In Exeter, a culvert near the city’s train station was reported to have collapsed under the weight of floodwater, leading to the temporary closure of nearby roads. The Met Office has said that although the worst of the rain and gales has moved on, there are still concerns over secondary flooding from saturated ground. Residents in affected areas have shared their frustrations on social media and with local newspapers, with some saying the scale of the outages and flooding has caused significant disruption to their lives, particularly during the Christmas period. "It's just someone needing to phone up and say they're sorry," one resident from West Cornwall told the  Cornish Times . "We've spent three days without central heating and no way to make a hot drink." The National Grid, which monitors energy supply nationwide, has urged the public to avoid non-essential use of electrical appliances where possible to reduce load on the system and assist crews with repairs. Meanwhile, local councils have begun assessing the long-term damage caused by the storms, warning that some infrastructure may require more than a month to fully repair. The prime minister, reacting to the crisis, said the government was “closely monitoring the situation” and would provide support to affected areas as needed. The events have reignited the debate over the country’s preparedness for extreme winter weather, with some environmental groups calling for more investment in flood defences and improvements to the electricity grid.

Two men accused of playing a key role in the illegal hunt and killing of Zimbabwe’s most famous lion, Cecil the ‘iconic’ lion, have been released on bail after appearing before a local court in Hwange, where the incident took place in July 2015. The men, identified as James Allen and Steele Allen – who are also cousins – were released on bail of Z$50,000 (£2,535) pending further legal proceedings. The case has sparked international outrage and reignited the debate on trophy hunting and the protection of wildlife in Africa. The Alans are brothers to Walter James Palmer, the American dentist accused of shooting and killing Cecil. Mr. Palmer, who is the primary focus of another legal case in the United States, faces criminal trespassing and wildlife violations charges. However, due to the difficulty of extraditing foreigners for alleged animal cruelty under U.S. law, he has not faced prosecution there. The court hearing in Zimbabwe comes after months of investigation into the roles played by the two local guides, who allegedly facilitated the illegal hunt, even though they had promised conservation authorities not to permit such an act. Cecil, a 13-year-old male lion, was a beloved figure among conservationists and tourists alike and had lived in Hwange National Park for over a decade. According to reports, he was lured out of the park by one of the Alans and then shot by Palmer using a bow and arrow. The hunt took place without the appropriate permits and was carried out in a manner that breached the principles of fair chase, a key tenet of ethical hunting. Conservationists have condemned the action, noting that Cecil was not only a tourist draw but also a keystone species within his ecosystem. The incident has had a devastating impact on Zimbabwe’s tourism industry, with several travel companies and airlines vowing to review their operations in the country. Zimbabwe’s Environment Minister, Saviour Kasukuwere, responded to the killing by promising to step up wildlife protection efforts and to ensure that those responsible for facilitating the hunt would face the full weight of the law. Provincial Environment Minister Nyasha Makusha, who presided over the Hwange hearing, said the release of the Alans was a procedural move necessary to allow for a full judicial process to unfold. Some local Zimbabweans, however, have expressed concern that the legal system is slowing down proceedings in the case, given the global attention it has attracted.

Parents face hurdles in accessing nurseries as eligibility gaps widen, report reveals   A significant number of parents across the UK are finding it difficult to access the childcare they are legally entitled to, according to a new report by the campaign group Families and Work Institute. The findings highlight a growing divide between what is promised by government policy and what is experienced on the ground by working families struggling to balance child-rearing and employment. Published on Thursday, the report exposes a range of barriers, including long waiting lists, a shortage of quality nurseries, and a lack of clarity among parents about how to claim the government-funded early education entitlement. It also suggests that some local authorities are not fulfilling their legal obligations under the Childcare Act, leaving parents to navigate a complex and often opaque system. The report’s authors, who consulted with over 1,000 working parents across the UK, argue that these gaps are disproportionately affecting low-income families. In many cases, parents are forced to subsidise breakfast clubs and after-school care to cope, despite being legally entitled to at least 15 hours of free early education per week for children aged between three and four. Among the most striking examples shared in the report is the case of a single mother in Manchester, who said she was still waiting for a nursery place for her two-year-old son three months after requesting one. “I was told there is no available space,” she said, adding that the nearest alternative was located 10 miles away and offered no support for funding. Nurseries across the country have also voiced concerns about the ability to meet the demand, with many reporting an increase in the number of children waiting for places, combined with a lack of government investment in the sector. The Department for Education has acknowledged “ongoing challenges” but insists it is fully committed to expanding access to high-quality early years education. “We are working closely with local authorities and providers to improve availability and make sure families can access the support they need,” a spokesperson said. Campaigners, however, say that current policies are failing to keep pace with the growing need. “Parents are entitled to it, but it’s as if the system doesn’t exist for them when they need it,” said Daisy Brook, chief executive of the campaign group. “Childcare isn’t a luxury—it’s a fundamental part of the working family's experience and a vital support for children’s development.”

The search for ripples in the fabric of spacetime is making rapid progress, with scientists heralding the remarkable development of the Advanced Ligo instrument, a cutting-edge laser system designed to detect gravitational waves. These elusive ripples, predicted a century ago by Einstein’s theory of general relativity, are caused by some of the universe’s most violent and energetic events—black hole mergers, neutron star collisions and even the reverberations of the Big Bang. Advanced Ligo, which stands for Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, is a colossal scientific experiment operating in the United States. It consists of two observatories, one in Hanford, Washington, and the other in Livingston, Louisiana. Each is equipped with an L-shaped interferometer with arms four kilometres long. By firing ultra-stable laser beams down each arm and measuring minuscule changes in the time the light takes to return, the instrument can detect gravitational waves with unprecedented precision. In a recent development, scientists have confirmed that upgrades and improvements to the system are accelerating faster than anticipated. This means the instrument is set to re-commence its search for gravitational waves with enhanced sensitivity and dramatically increased chances of success. “We are witnessing a transformation in our ability to look at the universe not as it is, but as it was when some violent cosmic events shook reality itself,” said Dr. Rana Adhikari, a leading researcher at the California Institute of Technology and part of the Advanced Ligo collaboration. “The progress of the upgraded system has exceeded our most optimistic forecasts.” The significance of detecting gravitational waves cannot be overstated. These ripples in spacetime offer a new way to observe the universe, complementing traditional methods such as optical, radio and X-ray astronomy. Already, their detection has led to ground-breaking discoveries—including the first direct observation of two colliding black holes in 2015. With this latest acceleration in development, the scientific community is eagerly anticipating the next phase of Advanced Ligo’s mission. The renewed capabilities of the instrument are expected to open new frontiers in astrophysics, potentially revealing more about neutron stars, testing Einstein's theories under extreme conditions, and even providing insights into the very early universe. Meanwhile, international collaborations such as Virgo in Italy and future Indian and Japanese detectors add to the growing global network of gravitational wave observatories, set to deliver even more profound discoveries in the coming years.

Teenage girl raped on Glasgow open-top bus in chilling attack as police urge anyone with information to come forward   A teenage girl has bravely come forward with details of a harrowing sexual assault that took place on an open-top double-decker bus in Glasgow over the weekend, as police continue to investigate the attack. India is in the middle of an extraordinary economic experiment — one that has sent shockwaves through its financial system, reshaped public life and forced millions to adapt to a new normal overnight. On November 8, 2016, in an abrupt and unprecedented move, the Indian government declared that the country’s 500 and 1,000-rupee notes — which accounted for 86 per cent of all cash in circulation — would cease to be legal tender. The stated aim of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s decision, which he described as a "surgical strike" against corruption and black money, was to eliminate illicit cash hoards, curb counterfeit currency and make the tax system fairer. But the real-world impact has been far more complex and controversial. With overnight sunset on high-value notes left India’s cash-dependent economy grinding to a halt. Small businesses, daily wage workers and schoolchildren screamed for rupees in ATMs that often dispensed nothing. Farmers couldn’t sell their crops; hospitals couldn’t pay staff; and millions were forced to queue for hours, day after day, in the hope that freshly printed 500 and 2,000-rupee notes would be distributed in time. In one of the most visible signs of the turmoil, crowds gathered outside banks countrywide, sometimes waiting for 12 hours only to be turned away with empty hands. In rural districts and small towns, the lack of digital infrastructure and internet connectivity exacerbated the problem, making the transition to a digital economy almost impossible for the poorer classes, who form the backbone of India’s economy. Even two months into the demonetisation phase, many had yet to open bank accounts, and some continued to rely on unofficial currency exchanges — a development that has done little to curb the underground economy about which Modi’s government has been so concerned. The experiment has had mixed results. On one hand, there has been a surge in digital transactions and an uptick in new bank account openings. On the other, the abrupt withdrawal of 99 per cent of the country’s currency has raised concerns about deepening inequality and the disruption of livelihoods. The Indian government has defended the move, claiming that 98.7 per cent of old banknotes were returned to the system by the end of the formal exchange period in December 2016. But economists and critics remain divided. Some hail it as a bold step toward a more transparent and cashless economy, while others warn of the human cost behind the headlines, particularly on the poor and vulnerable.

A Florida officer shot and injured an unarmed black therapist while responding to a request for help from a man with autism, local media reported on Monday, sparking an investigation into the use of force and raising concerns over policing practices. Facebook timeline reveals ‘killer’ engaged in inflammatory online chats five months before Lee Rigby’s murder   Facebook, the world’s largest social media platform, has been revealed as the site of troubling conversations by one of the killers of Fusilier Lee Rigby, five months before the British soldier was brutally murdered in Woolwich in May 2013. For once, that overused word “turmoil” is justified. That is how many business leaders and ordinary citizens would sum up recent weeks in the wake of mounting political instability, economic uncertainty and public unrest across the globe. From revolutions reverberating in the Middle East to bruising leadership battles in traditional Western democracies, it is clear that 2014 will be remembered as one of the most volatile periods in living memory. Few regions have felt the aftershocks as keenly as this one, where a once-stable government now finds itself clinging to power in the face of coordinated civil and military challenges. Just last week, Prime Minister Thomas Thabane of Lesotho, a small kingdom enclaved within the borders of South Africa, fled the country after what he described as a coup by his own armed forces. Arriving by helicopter to the safety of a South African base, Mr Thabane claimed his life was in danger and that his government had been unlawfully overthrown. “I will return as soon as I know I am not going to get killed,” he said in a chilling statement to the BBC. His assertion has plunged the nation – and its powerful South African neighbour – into acute diplomatic tension. Lesotho, one of Africa's few constitutional monarchies, has been no stranger to upheaval since it gained independence in 1966. A history of army interventions, power struggles, and fluctuating coalitions means that while the current crisis captures public attention, it is far from unprecedented. Yet the speed and sophistication with which the military is said to have moved has cast an even greater shadow over the legitimacy of the ongoing political process. Current reports suggest soldiers occupied key government and military buildings in the capital, Maseru, and that the nation is now under a de facto military administration. Officials from the army have roundly denied the coup allegations, with army spokesperson Major Ntlele Ntoi insisting that “the situation has returned to normalcy” and that there has been no attempt to depose the democratically elected leader. Such claims remain at odds with on-the-ground accounts, where editor Basildon Peta of the Lesotho Times described a “media blackout” and warned that “this is clearly a military coup aimed at removing the prime minister.” At the heart of the dispute is a growing hostility between Mr Thabane and the armed forces, believed to go back to his recent attempts to dismiss the head of the army, Lieutenant General Kennedy Tlai Kamoli.

Three years ago, Andy Murray arrived at the Roland Garros tournament in Paris with more doubt than confidence. Australia is on the brink of a major environmental and reputational crisis as conservationists and environmental groups raise the alarm over the potential listing of the Great Barrier Reef as “in danger” by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO). The classification, to be considered this week in Paris at a UNESCO World Heritage Committee meeting, would mark a devastating blow to the country's tourism industry and international standing as a steward of natural wonders. The Great Barrier Reef, a sprawling marine area off the coast of Queensland, is not only one of the seven natural wonders of the world but also the largest coral reef system on the planet, stretching over 2,300 kilometres. It is home to thousands of species and has long been a symbol of Australia’s rich and diverse natural heritage. Every year, it attracts millions of tourists from around the globe, directly contributing around five billion Australian dollars to the national economy. However, in recent years, the reef has suffered unprecedented damage from mass coral bleaching events linked to rising ocean temperatures, a consequence of climate change. In 2016, scientists declared the worst coral bleaching the reef had ever seen, with nearly one third of corals perishing in a single season. A second, consecutive bleaching event followed in 2017, further decimating large sections of the reef. Environmental groups, including the World Wildlife Fund and the Australian Marine Conservation Society, have cited these incidents as clear evidence of the reef's deteriorating health and the failure of the Australian government to take sufficient action toward its protection. The UN, which has previously warned that the reef was at risk of being placed on its “List of World Heritage in Danger,” has made it clear that it will now move forward with consideration unless Australia provides a convincing package of new measures to restore and protect the reef. Such a listing would not only bring international scrutiny but could also have far-reaching implications for Australia’s tourism industry, which supports around 64,000 jobs in the region. The Australian government has defended its record, claiming that more than four billion dollars has been invested in the reef over the past decade through the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority and other initiatives. Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull has described the reef as "nationally significant" and pledged to do everything in the government’s power to prevent the listing.

Sudan’s youth are turning to poetry as a form of expression and protest in a nation still reeling from decades of political upheaval, economic hardship, and authoritarian rule. In a vibrant resurgence of lyrical resistance, young poets are using their words to challenge the status quo, demanding change and reclaiming a proud literary heritage. Journalist and former BBC presenter Yousra Elbagir, who has covered the region extensively, highlights this movement in a compelling piece from Khartoum, where poetry isn’t just art—it’s survival. In a country once known as the “Land of the Two Niles,” where ancient civilisations gave rise to poetic traditions that spread across the continent, the modern poets of Sudan are breathing new life into an age-old craft. Under the remnants of a collapsing dictatorship and amid an ongoing transition to democracy, their verses serve as both mirrors and maps—reflecting the pain of the present and charting a path for the future. Elbagir reports that in universities, bars, and open-air gatherings, Sudanese youth are gathering to share their words, often performed to the rhythms of qasida, the traditional poetic form that has long been a cornerstone of Arab-African cultural identity. Far from being a relic of the past, this form of poetry is being reimagined in local dialects, spoken over rhythm and beat, and amplified on social media – platforms where many young Sudanese, like their peers around the world, are growing up. “We don’t just write for the page,” says Ahmed Salem, a 22-year-old poet from White Nile. “We write for the people. Our words are a call to justice, to unity, to action. We don’t want to just be heard—we want to be felt.” The themes in their poetry range from the personal to the political—poignant meditations on broken dreams, lost homes, and the longing for peace and dignity. They write of scorched harvests, absent fathers, and the weight of inherited war. But they also write of hope. Of resilience. Of the belief that language can be a catalyst for transformation. Elbagir underscores how, in a context where traditional media is still tightly regulated, poetry provides unfiltered space to critique power and celebrate people. It is a democratic platform where voices that have long been silenced in state arenas can rise. With this growing movement, the notion of Sudan as a nation on the edge of suffocation becomes one of quiet defiance—defiance in language, in rhythm, in the everyday act of speaking truth to power.

The national board of the Boy Scouts of America (BSA) has postponed a long-anticipated vote on ending its controversial ban on openly gay scouts and leaders, according to a statement released by the organisation on Tuesday. The decision, which had been expected to mark a new chapter in the century-old institution’s approach to inclusion, has instead sparked further concern and disappointment among advocacy groups and the wider public. The postponed vote was originally scheduled as part of a broader effort by the BSA to modernise its policies and align itself with contemporary social attitudes. It had been seen as a moral and strategic necessity, given the increasing public criticism of the group’s stance on LGBTQ+ issues. Many had hoped that the change would come ahead of the 2017 centenary of the organisation’s founding, a milestone that has already been overshadowed by internal divisions and shifting cultural tides. A BSA spokesperson stated that the delay was necessary to allow for "additional review and consultation," but provided no specific timeline for when the vote may now take place. Reports in recent weeks had suggested disagreements within the leadership, with some members urging caution and others arguing that the time for change was long overdue. The controversy surrounding the BSA’s position on LGBTQ+ members has been a growing flashpoint for several years. In 2013, the organisation allowed openly gay youth to join, but leaders remained barred from being openly gay. Critics argued that this compromise still left the group’s stance in conflict with the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which bans discrimination based on sex, religion, national origin, and, in many interpretations, sexual orientation. Legal challenges from advocacy groups have therefore continued to mount. James Ward, executive director of the Freedom to Breathe campaign, expressed dismay at the decision to delay. "This is a setback for inclusivity and a frustrating move for the many young people and families who trust the Boy Scouts to reflect the diverse world they live in," Mr Ward said. "We urge the BSA to act with courage and ensure that no child or young adult faces discrimination based on who they are." Public opinion has long supported the inclusion of LGBTQ+ individuals in scouting groups, with polls consistently showing majority backing from parents and young people. The delay has also sparked questions about the BSA’s long-term viability in a society increasingly intolerant of discrimination and exclusion.

Dr. Haya al-Khatib, a senior advisor to the Palestinian leadership, said the formation of the national unity government was a “milestone” in the pursuit of peace and political cohesion. “The people of Palestine deserve to have a government that represents all their voices, not just one faction,” she said. “This is not the end of the road, but a crucial beginning.” The European Union and the United States have cautiously welcomed the development, though both have urged Hamas to renounce violence and accept previous agreements, particularly the Oslo Accords. Meanwhile, Egypt and the United Arab Emirates, who supported the negotiations, have expressed optimism that the new government will stabilise the region and open the door to future negotiations with Israel. However, Israeli officials have made it clear that they will not engage directly with the new administration until Hamas disarms and fully embraces democratic principles. Speaking to a press conference, Israeli Foreign Minister Israel Katz said, “We are watching closely. Political reconciliation is a positive move, but Palestinian security coordination and renunciation of terrorism must also be part of any progress.” For the average Palestinian, the desire for peace is vast.

The UK government recently published the findings of an independent review into tidal lagoon energy, a technology promising a sustainable and predictable source of renewable power. The review, commissioned by the Department for Business, Energy, and Industrial Strategy, has sparked renewed debate over the role of tidal energy in the country’s transition toward net-zero carbon emissions. While advocates argue tidal lagoons offer immense potential, environmental groups and scientists have raised concerns over the potential ecological consequences of large-scale installations. Tidal lagoons work by harnessing the movement of seawater into and out of man-made enclosures, using turbines to generate electricity. The Crown Estate, which manages the seabed around England, Wales, and Scotland, has granted licences for several proposed lagoon projects, including one in Swansea Bay that never materialised due to cost and environmental objections. The latest report focuses on lessons learned from previous projects and evaluates whether the technology can be deployed responsibly in the future. Environmental concerns centre around the impact on marine ecosystems. Experts have warned that the construction and operation of tidal lagoons could disrupt sediment movement and water flow, affecting migratory patterns of fish and other marine species. Shellfish beds, in particular, are believed to be vulnerable to changes in tidal regimes that could deplete oxygen levels or alter water quality. For instance, the proposed Swansea lagoon was found during regulatory scrutiny to potentially harm sea trout and herring fisheries – concerns cited as one of the key reasons for its eventual cancellation. Another issue is the impact on coastal habitats and bird populations. Tidal lagoons could reduce the area of intertidal zones, which serve as critical feeding grounds for wading birds. Reports have highlighted how such changes can impact the delicate balance of estuaries and inshore areas, potentially leading to a decline in biodiversity. Supporters of tidal energy argue, however, that these challenges can be mitigated through improved design and careful site selection. The review acknowledges this possibility, noting that advances in technology and environmental screening processes could significantly reduce ecological harm. It also underscores the potential of tidal energy to play a vital role in diversifying the UK’s renewable portfolio, providing a stable and predictable power source compared to wind and solar. As the UK moves forward with its net-zero target for 2050, the findings of the review are expected to inform policy decisions and potentially pave the way for future tidal lagoon projects.

The release of the Marikana massacre report by South African President Jacob Zuma has reignited a national debate over the rule of law and state accountability in the country. The 600-page document, compiled by former judge Ian Farlam, details the events of 16 August 2012, when 34 striking miners were shot dead by South African Police Service officers near the Lonmin platinum mine in the town of Marikana. The report, which was released in May 2015 but only made public in full last week, has been described by many as a long-awaited step toward justice but also as a deeply unsatisfying attempt to avoid political blame. The tragic shooting, which marked the worst instance of deadly violence on South African soil since the end of apartheid, sent shockwaves around the world. The report, Farlam says, concludes that the police used excessive force, but he did not recommend criminal charges against the officers involved. Nor did it hold the then-president Jacob Zuma directly accountable for failing to live up to the expectations of leadership in the aftermath of the violence. Instead, the report offered a broad account of the events and outlined faults on both sides — workers and the police — while also calling for reforms to mining and human rights protections. Zuma defended the decision to withhold the full report until now, arguing that the government had to prioritise efforts to stabilise the platinum sector and prevent further unrest. But critics argue the delay has undermined public trust and exposed what they see as a systemic reluctance among the leadership of the African National Congress (ANC) to allow full transparency. “This is not a defence of the police actions, it's an indictment of a government that chose to shield itself from scrutiny,” said renowned legal scholar Faranaaz Veriava of the University of Cape Town. “The rule of law can only exist when those in power are held to account.” The report also raises fresh concerns about the ongoing role of private security in South Africa’s mining industry, where over 100 deaths have been recorded since 2008. It details how security forces hired by Lonmin relied heavily on coercive tactics rather than persuading or protecting the workers. At the time of the massacre, Zuma praised the mining company for its “honest mediation” and the police for bringing “peace” after a violent week of protests. That stance drew heavy criticism from the public and from within the ANC itself, with some calling into question the president’s understanding of law and human rights.

In a spellbinding display of T20 batting, Alex Hales smashed a staggering 95 runs off just 30 balls to lead Nottinghamshire Outlaws to a record-breaking Powerplay score in a thrilling win over Durham Jets. The monumental knock not only earned Hales the accolade of the fastest to 95 in professional cricket but also helped Notts post the highest Powerplay total in the history of Twenty20 cricket. The game, held at Trent Bridge, was a showcase of explosive batting, with Hales single-handedly dismantling the Durham bowling attack in the opening six overs. His innings included a breathtaking 11 sixes and saw the Outlaws posting 94 runs in the Powerplay, the highest such score in the format and a remarkable new benchmark for T20 batting. Hales’s monumental effort left stunned fans on their feet and sent a ripple through the cricketing world. Hales reached his half-century off just 14 balls, the fastest in English T20 history, and continued in his destructive style, planting the ball into the stands with clinical precision.
