His innings was the cornerstone of Notts’ mammoth total of 193 for 3, and despite faltering with the bat as their pursuit unfolded, the Outlaws managed to clinch the match comfortably, with Durham collapsing to 123. The national selector, Richard Dawson, praised the performance, calling it “a breathtaking display of power and timing that set the tone for the contest and underlined why Hales is one of the most dangerous batsmen in the world. This innings was not just a personal milestone but a defining moment in T20 history.” The record had previously been held by Mumbai Indians’ Ambati Rayudu, who scored 73 off 32 balls against Gujarat Lions in 2015, but Hales’s blistering assault eclipsed all previous achievements. His performance has triggered renewed calls for national selection, with former England captain Michael Vaughan stating, “Hales just showed he has the ability to carry a side on his shoulders. He’s a match-winner and deserves to be in the national squad.” The game will undoubtedly be remembered as one of the most electrifying of the T20 campaign, with Hales etching his name in the record books and setting the bar higher for the format. As the cricketing world digests the implications of his meteoric 30-ball innings, one thing is clear: in the era of brutal T20 batting, Alex Hales has once again reaffirmed his status as a T20 virtuoso.

Middlesbrough have parted ways with manager Aitor Karanka after three and a half years at the helm, marking the end of a challenging and ultimately unsuccessful tenure for the former Spain international. The announcement comes after a run of poor results that has thrown the club’s Championship aspirations into jeopardy, as well as growing calls from fans for a change in direction. Karanka, who took charge of the Riverside Stadium side in January 2016 following the ambitious Aitor Karanka project backed by owner Steve Gibson, was tasked with transforming Boro into a top-flight force. Gibson had injected substantial investment into the club during the 2015 winter transfer window, enabling Karanka to make a series of high-profile signings. However, despite brief moments of optimism and a well-documented rise in the club’s playing style and ambition, results on the pitch have failed to match the off-field progress. Middlesbrough reached the FA Cup semi-finals in 2017 under Karanka and played attractive football in his early months in charge, winning over many fans with an attacking brand of play. But as the years have progressed, inconsistency has become the hallmark of the squad, and a recent Championship campaign that has seen them falter puts Karanka as the scapegoat. Reports suggest that the board has been holding meetings for several weeks and is believed to be seeking a more immediate-style approach to return to the Premier League, with some internal sources hinting that a former Premier League manager could be their preferred appointment. The 46-year-old Spaniard will now become the latest casualty in what has been a difficult managerial environment in English football, following a number of his peers who have failed to bridge the gap between promise and tangible success. Karanka’s departure leaves Middlesbrough in a pivotal transitional stage, about to begin their search for a new head coach in the hope of finally realising the lofty ambitions set out by their owners. For now, the club have confirmed a short-term arrangement to ensure stability, with assistant manager Steve Agnew expected to take temporary charge for the upcoming games. The board will then turn their focus to appointing a new manager ahead of what is expected to be a critical winter transfer window. As for Karanka, the move comes with a bittersweet finish to a journey that took the Middlesbrough fans, after a decade in the Championship, into the European qualifiers in 2017—a significant achievement for the club, though ultimately not sustained.

Scotland were handed a heavy 3-0 defeat by Italy in a difficult World Cup qualifier at Hampden Park, with only the smallest comfort of the scoreline not being even more punishing. Despite a first-half penalty save from Craig Gordon and a fighting display in defence, Steve Clarke’s side were unable to match the quality and composure of an Italian team that moved the ball with ease and punished momentary lapses with ruthless efficiency. The result is a significant setback for Scotland, who now sit in third place in their group with four matches left to play, as Italy moved closer to securing an early qualification for the 2026 World Cup. The Azzurri, who are unbeaten in 34 matches at home, found their stride in Glasgow and made light work of a Scottish side that struggled to impose themselves in the final third. Clarke had warned beforehand that Italy, managed by veteran Roberto Mancini, would be a far tougher proposition than previous opponents, and the Italian manager’s influence was evident. His side showcased a blend of slick passing, intelligent movement and blistering pace to unsettle the Scottish backline. It was Italy that took control from the outset, and they deservedly took the lead in the 25th minute through a composed finish from Domenico Berardi, who burst through the heart of Scotland’s defence before calmly slotting past Gordon. Scotland responded with more urgency in the second half, but they were again exposed on the counter-attack. Italy added a second through Sila Varga in the 58th minute, and although Gordon was able to hold his nerve and deny Lorenzo Pellegrini from the spot just before the break—after a handball from Scott McKenna—the damage was already done. The Italian captain, Leonardo Bonucci, then made it 3-0 in the 76th minute with a well-timed run and header from a corner. For Scotland, the highlight came in the form of Gordon’s penalty save, which offered a fleeting glimpse of resilience. However, the overall performance was one that left much to be desired. Clarke will have plenty to reconsider ahead of their next qualifier, a crucial match away to Switzerland. As it stands, Scotland are being outclassed by the elite sides in the group and must find a way to elevate their play if they are to have any chance of advancing to the World Cup. After the match, Clarke admitted his frustration.

Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán has launched an incendiary appeal to the European Union, urging it to channel €3 billion (£2.2 billion; $3.4 billion) in financial assistance to Syria’s war-torn neighbours to manage the refugee crisis. Mr Orban, a consistent critic of mass migration into Europe, argues that diverting funding to countries such as Turkey, Lebanon and Jordan would ease the burden on EU member states and stem the flow of migrants arriving on Europe's borders. In a speech delivered in Budapest, Mr Orbán stated that it was a "moral duty" for the EU to support countries hosting the largest numbers of Syrian refugees. Turkey alone is home to over 3.6 million Syrians displaced by the decade-long conflict, and Mr Orbán’s call appears aimed at shifting responsibility away from Western Europe, which has resisted demands from the EU to accept higher shares of migrants in a system managed under the so-called “quota” policy. Hungary, governed by a prime minister whose Fidesz party has long dominated the political scene, remains one of the most vocal critics of Brussels. Mr Orbán has accused the EU of "vaporising national sovereignty" under the guise of humanitarianism, adding that immigration undermined not just border control but the very idea of European identity. His demand for three billion euros comes amid stalled efforts to reform the EU's migration strategy – efforts which have often been sidetracked by political divisions among member states. Earlier this year, the European Parliament passed a resolution calling for a more coordinated and sustainable approach to migration, but no binding financial agreement has been reached. Mr Orbán's proposal is likely to face scrutiny from both left-leaning and centrist governments, who have continued to advocate for a more robust repatriation strategy rather than financial handouts. Germany and France, two of the bloc's largest economies, have publicly supported assistance to countries hosting Syrian refugees but have not committed to funding that would plug gaps left by faltering international aid bodies. Meanwhile, within Hungary, Mr Orbán has been accused of using the issue to consolidate his anti-immigration narrative ahead of upcoming European Parliament elections. He recently declared that Hungary would build a 175-kilometre fence along its southern border to deter migrants, a move that has drawn both domestic support and international criticism. The call arrives at a politically charged time for the European Union, which is still reeling from Brexit and deepening fractures over rule-of-law issues in Poland and Hungary.

The chair of Kick It Out, the organisation dedicated to tackling discrimination in football, has called for sanctions against English Football League (EFL) clubs that fail to interview Black, Asian, and Minority Ethnic (BAME) candidates for coaching jobs. Kate Brook, who chairs the charity, said that as long as clubs can freely bypass underrepresented candidates during appointments, true progress will remain out of reach. Brook’s remarks come amid ongoing concerns over the lack of diversity in coaching and leadership roles within the EFL, despite years of campaigns and initiatives aimed at increasing inclusion. While strides have been made, the percentage of BAME appointed managers and coaches remains disproportionately low compared to the ethnic make-up of players and fans. Brook stated: “We are not advocating for quotas or tokenistic appointments, but we are calling for basic fairness. Clubs have the opportunity – and the responsibility – to interview a diverse range of candidates. If they refuse to take that step, then there should be a consequence. Sanctions are a tool to encourage meaningful change when voluntary action isn’t enough.” Her comments echo recent reports, including the EFL's own diversity data, which details how just 3.1% of head coaching positions across the Championship and League One and Two are held by BAME individuals. Many clubs, Brook argued, continue to invoke vague justifications for not considering BAME candidates, such as a supposedly narrow pool of suitable applicants or a focus on merit alone. She added: “Merit is not in question when you exclude qualified candidates simply because of the colour of their skin. What we are seeing is a reluctance to cast beyond the usual net. That is not a reflection of merit, it's an example of complacency and a continued reliance on outdated systems and networks.” Brook called for reform in the EFL appointment process, suggesting that clubs who fail to interview a shortlist of BAME candidates for roles be excluded from future competitions or fined. “The EFL has the authority to enforce change,” she said. “We cannot overestimate the power of visibility. BAME athletes, referees, and players contribute to the culture of football – but too often the leaders remain worlds apart from the game they represent.” Her statement has reignited debate about the responsibilities of clubs and governing bodies in ensuring equality of opportunity behind the scenes. Some football figures have welcomed the call for stronger enforcement, while others have cautioned the need to balance diversity efforts with maintaining the integrity of the appointment process.

The Premier League season is set to resume this weekend, igniting the passion of football fans across the United Kingdom and around the world. After a summer of transfer activity, sizzling speculation, and anticipation, the EPL returns with a host of intriguing storylines and new faces primed to make an impact on one of world football’s most competitive and high-profile leagues. The opening weekend will see some key fixtures that set the tone for the season ahead. Among the most anticipated is Manchester United's return to Old Trafford, where new manager Erik ten Hag is expected to unveil his vision for the Red Devils. The Dutchman arrived in the summer with a big task on his hands to restore confidence among fans who have endured a challenging period under the previous administration. Liverpool will also be aiming to maintain their dominance, having finished top of the league last season. The Reds, under the astute management of Jürgen Klopp, look to push for an unprecedented quadruple this season after their impressive successes in the domestic cups and the Champions League last year. At the other end of the table, promoted clubs Bournemouth and Nottingham Forest will be looking to avoid an immediate return to the Championship. Both teams have made significant investments in their squads and are eager to prove they belong in England’s top flight. For Forest, the return to the Premier League after 23 long years will be emotional and politically charged, as fans seek a new era for the club, free from ownership battles and off-the-field turmoil. Speaking of new arrivals, the league will also welcome Selhurst Park back as Crystal Palace, who narrowly escaped relegation last season, begin their campaign with a tough but exciting mix of returning stars and new signings. Beyond the football, the continued dominance of English and Welsh clubs in the transfer market has raised key questions about financial sustainability and about how smaller clubs can compete with the seemingly endless budgets of their wealthiest rivals. However, as always, the Premier League is renowned for its dramatic upsets and unpredictable outcomes, meaning that no title is guaranteed and no relegation is certain until May. As fans around the country prepare to flock to the stadiums or tune in from the comfort of their homes, there is a shared sense of hope, excitement, and trepidation. The 2023/24 Premier League season is upon us, and the drama is far from over.

Apple continues to face scrutiny over its 30 per cent commission fee on all purchases made through the App Store, with growing criticism from developers, businesses and even lawmakers who accuse the tech giant of leveraging its dominance for financial gain. The long-standing policy — which sees Apple taking a hefty cut from digital services, subscriptions, in-app purchases and product sales — has become a flashpoint in a wider debate about the power of tech giants and their control over online platforms. A listing by the company in its App Store Review Guidelines states clearly: “Apple gets 30 per cent of the money” from the sale of apps, in-app purchases and subscriptions. While Apple defends the fee as a cost of maintaining the secure, user-friendly environment the App Store provides, many developers and small businesses argue the commission is exorbitant and stifles innovation. Scott Forrister, the founder of Duet, a productivity app bought by Microsoft for $10 million, described the fee as a “tax on success.” He has since launched a campaign called #LevelTheField, calling for the removal of Apple’s commission to give developers a fairer share of the revenue they generate. The issue has also drawn the attention of governments. In the UK, MPs from all major parties have urged the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) to investigate whether Apple’s App Store is in breach of competition laws. In the US, the Department of Justice has launched its own antitrust probe into Apple’s dealings, including the impact of the 30 per cent fee on competition and consumer choice. Beyond the principles of fair business, Apple’s policy has practical consequences. Many app developers, especially those in countries with lower average incomes, argue that the fee prevents them from making a sustainable livelihood through their work. Meanwhile, some companies are attempting to circumvent the rule by asking customers to pay directly rather than using the App Store’s payment system — a move that has often resulted in their apps being removed or blocked. The controversy has also highlighted the growing tension between Apple and major tech competitors such as Spotify and Netflix, both of which have publicly opposed the 30 per cent charge. Spotify recently filed a complaint with the EU, alleging that Apple’s App Store unfairly disadvantages rival apps. The company has also removed links to its website within the iOS app to protest the rules.

A man has been sentenced to life in prison for the murder of Irish student Karen Buckley, who was found dead on a farm in Glasgow four days after she went missing. The 21-year-old, originally from County Limerick, was last seen in the east End of the city in May 2015 after night out with friends, sparking a widespread search and international concern for the missing young woman. In a harrowing case that gripped both Scotland and Ireland, Ayuba Suleiman Ibrahim, 22, was found guilty of her murder. His life sentence was announced at the High Court in Glasgow, following the conclusion of a trial that exposed the chilling details of how Karen’s life was taken. Karen's body was discovered on farmland in Auchinraith, a remote area located about 27 miles southeast of Glasgow. Her death sent shockwaves through her local community and the wider Irish diaspora in Scotland, with many remembering her as a bright and ambitious student. During the trial, the court heard how Karen had travelled to Glasgow’s Airport to pick up a friend, encountering Ibrahim near the motorway service station. Their meeting, which was initially innocuous, turned into a tragic nightmare as Ibrahim, who was under the influence of drugs and suffering from paranoid schizophrenia, became fixated on her and later killed her. The prosecution described how Ibrahim led Karen on a 16-hour journey north of Glasgow, during which he threatened her and claimed she had stolen money from him. Karen was eventually stabbed multiple times and left to die in a disused pig pen on the farm. Officers who found her body described the grim scene upon arrival, with Ms Buckley’s phone found wrapped in a pillowcase nearby. Her family and friends were given an update at the sentencing, which took place in the presence of about 30 supporters. Speaking after the sentencing, Karen’s mother, Joanne Buckley, said: “We knew her life was cut short in the worst cruel way, but justice has now been done. This is the first time since her death that I feel some peace. Karen was a vibrant young woman with so much ahead of her.” Justice was delivered for Karen, but the scars of her disappearance and murder will remain for her family, friends, and the entire Glasgow community. A memorial was erected in her home village in Limerick, where she is fondly remembered, and a campaign has since been launched to raise awareness of missing persons and mental health in Scotland.

Are You Happy at Work? The Quiet Crisis in British Employment    By Sarah Johnson   The Times   April 2, 2025  In bustling offices, warehouse labs, and customer service call centres across the UK, a quiet crisis is bubbling beneath the surface. The question "Are you happy at work?" has rarely been asked so urgently—and with good reason. Recent statistics reveal that employee satisfaction is at its lowest point in a decade, with one in five workers feeling disengaged, demoralised, or actively considering leaving their jobs. Despite wage increases in certain sectors, the cost-of-living crisis continues to erode confidence. Rising inflation, stagnant real-terms pay and increasing workloads have many employees feeling like cogs in a relentless machine, with little to show for their effort. The World at Work survey, conducted in early 2025, found that 38 per cent of British workers feel "undervalued" by their employer, while 29 per cent describe their mental health as "worse now than it has ever been." But why now, after years of economic recovery and employer efforts to improve workplace culture, is morale dipping again? Industry experts suggest that the lingering effects of the pandemic, combined with shifting expectations in the post-office era, have exposed a widening gap between what employees want and what many employers are prepared to offer. Office culture, once dominated by rigid hierarchies and long hours, has evolved in the wake of the remote working revolution. Many younger workers, in particular, demand flexibility, purpose and a supportive work environment. Yet, a recent report by the British Psychological Society warns that many organisations have failed to adapt adequately. "There is a growing disconnect between the needs of the workforce and the strategies of management," said Dr Helen Morris, a workplace psychologist. "Employees are not looking for a return to the 1980s. They want to feel heard, respected and valued." The cost for employers of ignoring this shift is high. A growing number of organisations have reported a sharp increase in staff turnover, with some sectors experiencing annual turnover rates of over 20 per cent. This is not just a matter of inconvenience—it translates to significant financial loss. The Centre for Economics and Business Research estimates the cost of replacing an employee in the UK can range from £30,000 to £90,000 per departure depending on salary and sector. What, then, can be done? Some companies are already emerging as trailblazers.

Kodjia Inspires Villa’s Fourth Consecutive Win with Seven-Game Magic   Aston Villa made it four victories on the bounce as Jonathan Kodjia continued his staggering run of form, netting his seventh goal in seven matches to secure a hard-fought 1-0 win over Queens Park Rangers at Villa Park. The striker, who has emerged as the club’s talisman under manager Steven Gerrard, delivered yet another masterclass in front of goal, once again underlining his importance to Villa’s resurgence since the former Liverpool manager’s arrival in the summer. The victory, which lifted Villa up the Championship table and reinforced their place in the automatic promotion conversation, was secured in clinical fashion. Kodjia’s strike, which came in the 68th minute, showcased his instincts and composure in the box, as he converted a well-worked cross from Nathan Baker past visiting goalkeeper Seny Dieng. It was a moment that encapsulated the team’s resilience, with the hosts having to withstand continuous QPR pressure in the early stages, thanks to an organized defensive display and sharp goalkeeping from Ethan Amos. From the off, it was clear Villa intended to play their Championship-style brand of football—passing, possession, and quick transitions. The visitors initially looked to frustrate the home side with long balls and high pressing, but Villa’s midfield trio of Akpabio, David verbosity, and Jacob Ramsey began to dictate terms as the game developed. The breakthrough came when Ramsey threaded through a penetrating pass to Baker, who delivered the cross for Kodjia to outmuscle the QPR centre-back and head home. QPR, playing their first match under new manager Liam Manning, showed glimpses of quality and came close to snatching an equalizer in stoppage time when Billy Clarke blocked a fierce drive from Alexander Balikwicki just outside the six-yard box. The home fans, many of whom had endured a bleak era under former Villa owners, were in buoyant mood, chanting for their manager and celebrating every piece of passed ball. For Gerrard, the win extended his side’s positive momentum as he looks to steer Villa back into the Premier League. “Jonathan is playing with confidence and that’s what players need—confidence,” Gerrard said in his post-match interview. “He’s working hard, taking his chances, and this team is starting to believe we can go and achieve something special.” Kodjia, for his part, simply shrugged off the question about his remarkable goalscoring streak.

The European Commission has abandoned proposals to impose new time limits on surcharge-free roaming for mobile phone users within the European Union, in a controversial shift that risks plunging confusion among millions of European consumers. Under the existing regulations, EU citizens are allowed to use their mobile data, calls, and texts across the 27 EC member states without incurring additional fees – a policy dubbed the “roam like at home” rule. Introduced in 2017, the policy was hailed as one of the most consumer-friendly aspects of EU citizenship and a success of European digital integration. However, the Commission’s recent plans called for stricter time limits within a month of entering another EU country, including capping the number of free data megabytes allowed, sparking outrage among consumer and telecoms industry groups. The revised proposals, revealed in early February, suggested that free roaming would be phased out if a user exceeded one gigabyte per month or made 300 minutes of calls and 300 received texts. The plan was met with fierce opposition in both the European Parliament and the Council of the EU, where critics warned that the changes would penalise businesses and frequent international travellers and could undermine the EU’s commitment to digital rights. After intense lobbying from telecoms providers, industry experts and consumer advocacy groups, the Commission has now backed away from the proposals – at least for now. “We have listened – this is not the right direction, and we will revisit the roaming issue in the context of the broader digital single market strategy,” said a Commission spokesperson. However, the situation remains unclear, and the lack of a clear timeline for any new regulations has left mobile users in the dark. Some telecom executives welcomed the U-turn, saying it would prevent confusion and uphold consumer confidence in EU telecom services. Yet key questions remain: How long will the current policy remain intact? And will the EU eventually introduce caps on free roaming to curb what some regulators call “abuse” of the provision? For now, EU citizens can continue to travel across the bloc without the fear of being charged high roaming costs, but many are worried that the policy’s uncertain future is being weighed down by political and economic pressures. The decision highlights the growing tension between European integration and national control over telecom services, especially as telecom firms face increasing financial strains from the existing free-roaming policy.

An Indian court has taken a significant step in an often-delayed criminal case when it ruled that Bollywood actor Salman Khan should face a charge of culpable homicide over a hit-and-run road accident that occurred in 2002. The decision, announced earlier this week, adds weight to long-standing allegations against one of India’s most high-profile celebrities, and has reignited public interest in the incident that has lingered for over a decade. The incident took place on June 16, 2002, in Mumbai, when Khan, who was driving under the influence of alcohol at the time, hit a motorcyclist, Hemant Oberoi, and three others. One of Oberoi’s companions, Pavitra Sharma, suffered only minor injuries, and made a swift recovery, while Oberoi did not survive the crash. Since then, the case has been subject to multiple appeals, trials, and adjournments, with Khan assembling a formidable legal team to represent him. He has consistently denied any criminal negligence, with his representatives arguing that criminal charges were unwarranted. In its ruling, the court found that Khan had not excluded himself from the possibility of harm and had, in fact, failed in his duty as a driver. Judge Sudhir Gupta said the decision to charge Salman Khan as an accused in the case was based on circumstantial and medical evidence collected during the investigation. The charge of culpable homicide not amounting to murder is a serious one under the Indian Penal Code, and if found guilty, Khan could face up to 10 years in prison, in addition to a fine. The actor, who has enjoyed a prolific career in Hindi cinema for over three decades, was initially handed a six-month jail sentence and a fine in 2016 after a fast-track court found him guilty of causing death by negligence. However, the sentence was suspended and he was allowed to remain out on bail. The latest ruling does not mean an immediate arrest, but does increase the likelihood that the case will proceed to trial without further delay. Reactions to the decision have been mixed among the Indian public. While many have expressed relief at the development, others, particularly Salman Khan’s fans, who are numerous and passionate, have called the case a sustained vendetta with little regard for the passage of time. Nevertheless, the ruling marks a shift in a case that has long been mired in legal technicalities and judicial delays.

The growing problem of child food poverty is taking an alarming toll on Scotland's school classrooms, with teachers reporting an increasing number of children arriving hungry and, in some cases, stealing food from more fortunate classmates, a worrying trend that has raised serious concerns across the education sector. According to school staff across the country, many children are skipping meals at home due to financial hardship, leaving them both hungry and embarrassed when they sit down for lunch in school. In response, some have resorted to taking food from peers, sometimes without permission or awareness. “It’s heartbreaking to watch one child give up their lunch for another,” said a primary school teacher in Glasgow, who asked not to be named. “You see the gratitude, but also the shame, and you feel powerless to help.” The issue has been exacerbated by rising living costs and the withdrawal of support under the universal credit system, which has left many families struggling to afford the basics. In an added blow, free school meals – long a critical bulwark against this kind of deprivation – have only ever been guaranteed for children from the lowest-income households, even though many others are now also falling through the cracks. Despite repeated calls for expansion, successive Scottish governments have not extended the benefit to all pupils, a decision that is now coming under fierce scrutiny. Last year, education unions warned that the lack of financial support was affecting both students' health and ability to learn. “When you’re hungry, it’s impossible to concentrate,” said a teacher in Edinburgh. “What kind of future will these children have if we don’t act now?” Children’s charities have also stepped in to highlight the crisis. Kevin Thompson, a senior policy officer at Barnardo’s Scotland, said the trend of food theft and hunger among pupils is a disturbing sign that more needs to be done. “It’s not just about feeding children – it’s about sending the message that we value our young people and that they matter,” he said. As schools continue to handle the problem as best they can – with some providing discreet food parcels and quiet places for children to eat lunch – many are calling for urgent government action to address the root causes of the crisis. With the number of hungry schoolchildren continuing to rise, the question remains whether Scotland’s leaders are ready to take the necessary steps to protect its most vulnerable.

French presidential hopeful François Fillon has fallen under an official inquiry by public prosecutors, who have raised allegations that he misappropriated public funds, according to an announcement by legal authorities on Sunday. The news comes at a pivotal time in the country's political calendar, with the presidential election drawing ever closer and Fillon positioned as a frontrunner in the race to succeed President François Hollande. Fillon, who has long been seen as a centrist contender with a strong appeal among conservative and moderate voters, now faces a political storm as details of the allegations unfold. At the heart of the matter are claims that Fillon used public money, which was supposedly allocated for his political needs, for personal rather than professional purposes. Among the accusations is the suggestion that Fillon paid his wife’s salary for several years, despite her being an unpaid advisor. This specific claim has captivated the French press, with some media outlets dubbing it the “Barnaby affair” — a reference to the name of the fictional child Fillon said he and his wife were raising while she was employed. Numerous reports have indicated that, in 2013, Fillon hired his wife, Penelope Fillon, as his political advisor, allegedly at a salary of €5,000 per month. However, Penelope Fillon was neither known for political expertise nor seen in any official capacity during her tenure — a discrepancy that has raised eyebrows among journalists and political observers. The Paris Public Prosecutor’s office confirmed on Sunday that Fillon and two other individuals were being investigated for “embezzlement, breach of trust, and misuse of public funds.” While Fillon has consistently denied the accusations, calling them a “witch hunt” designed to derail his campaign and remove a serious threat to the incumbent Socialist Party, the allegations have already begun to take their toll. In a dramatic twist, the scandal has seen Fillon’s poll numbers — once among the highest in the race — dip sharply in national surveys. This has opened the door for Emmanuel Macron, the centrist independent candidate, to narrow the gap in the polls and potentially dethrone Fillon as the leading contender ahead of the April 23rd run-off election. Public reaction to the scandal has been mixed. While some Republicans and Fillon allies have rushed to defend the embattled candidate, others have expressed disappointment and concern over the integrity of the political class. For many in France, the allegations raise broader questions about transparency, accountability, and the widespread perception of political corruption that continues to plague the nation.

In a moment that typified both the confidence and unorthodox style of her political ascent, the former home secretary, Theresa May, launched her leadership campaign with a bold and unexpected declaration that would go on to define the early stage of her bid for 10 Downing Street. Speaking during a Conservative Party event, May stood up unannounced and, in a move unusual for the typically reserved and measured politician, announced: “I’m Theresa May and I’m the best person to be prime minister.” The statement, delivered with a steely resolve, came as a surprise to many within the party—and to the wider political commentariat—who had viewed May as a relatively low-key contender in the race to succeed David Cameron, who had resigned in the wake of the Brexit referendum. May’s campaign, which began in July 2016, was destined to be the only one in a leadership contest often described as lacking the usual energy and media hype of prior races. Yet her opening gambit—this moment of brash self-promotion—stood out in a political arena where carefully worded, understated entrances are the norm. Her colleagues, including those within her own ranks, expressed shock at the directness of her statement. One senior Tory source said that the remark had taken the party "aback," though it was later viewed by some as a strategic masterstroke. “It was a clear signal of intent,” said one insider. “She wasn’t trying to be charming or subtle. It was a statement: this is who I am, and this is what I’m here to do.” At that time, May was also the longest-serving home secretary in modern British history, having held the post since 2010. Her commanding position within the shadow cabinet and her reputation for ideological consistency made her a natural successor to Cameron. However, the manner in which she launched her campaign was seen by some as a departure from the measured, establishment sensibilities she was otherwise known for. Her unflinching declaration, however, would foreshadow the steady route to power she ultimately took. Just 10 weeks after Cameron's resignation, May was declared the Conservative Party leader, having comfortably beaten her only rival, Andrea Leadsom. Though the race was short, her assertive move into the public eye marked the beginning of an 18-month tenure as prime minister. In hindsight, the moment has come to symbolise the early steps of a leader who, despite her cautious public persona, was willing to break with convention when it furthered her political ambitions.

The return of Tom Brady from his four-game suspension has dominated sports headlines across the US this weekend, with fans, analysts and even rival teams divided on how New England Patriots’ chances will be affected by their talismanic quarterback’s return to action. Brady, who missed the first month of the NFL season for violations of the league’s integrity of the game policy, returned triumphantly last night in a 57–17 rout of the Houston Texans that saw the Patriots remain undefeated at 9–0. The 42-year-old was in typically commanding form, throwing for three touchdowns and completing 23 of his 30 pass attempts—an efficiency that extended to 83 percent over the season. For fans accustomed to the Patriots’ volatility in early-season performances without Brady, his return felt like a calming injection of stability. But amid the dominant numbers and the emotional homecoming, the broader conversation in the world of American football continues to centre on the legitimacy of the Patriots’ activities—this time more than just the Deflategate scandal. Brady’s suspension, imposed in March, came after the National Football League (NFL) concluded that he was directly involved in the improper deflation of game balls in the 2015 AFC Championship game. Though Brady and the Patriots have since petitioned the decision and are considering legal action, it appears that the decision will stand.Critics argue that Brady’s ability to continue playing, despite the ruling, is a failure of the league’s justice system, pointing out that neither he nor the team has officially admitted guilt. Others have applauded the Patriots for rallying in his absence—despite a tough loss to the Kansas City Chiefs and a nail-biting finish against the Jacksonville Jaguars—while also demonstrating that their title pedigree extends beyond the brilliance of a single player. Brady, for his part, has not publicly addressed the controversy beyond a brief statement during the off-season in which he said he “respects the process but firmly believes it has failed.” The Patriots have claimed, meanwhile, that the processing of guest mail toward the 2015 season was handled appropriately. Unsurprisingly, the resurgence of this intense debate marks what some have dubbed a “cultural event” as much as a professional one. Brady’s detractors were quick to flood social media with the hashtag #BradyBack, a mix of mockery and acceptance, while others celebrated his return as gothic theatre worthy of his long and contested career.

The family of a Lanarkshire teenager murdered 25 years ago have sharply criticised Scotland’s legal system, accusing the Crown Office of a "catalogue of failures" in the case that has left them desperate for justice after nearly a quarter of a century. The victim, 16-year-old Lorraine McKinlay, was found dead in een forest near her home in Hamilton in September 1998. A man was arrested in connection with her death at the time but was released without charge after a High Court hearing concluded that the evidence against him was "inadequate". Since then,.Fatalfanst Didn’t Eat, the McKinlay family have claimed that the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service (COPS) has repeatedly ignored their complaints and overlooked key evidence that could have led to a conviction. In a deeply emotional statement this week, the McKinlay family called the handling of the case "a national disgrace" and accused officials of failing to treat the matter with the "seriousness and urgency" it deserved. "Lorraine was not just a daughter, a sister and a friend, she was a young woman with a future," said her brother Derek McKinlay, who has spoken publicly for the first time in years. "But what we as a family were left with was a sense of betrayal — by the system that was supposed to protect us, and by those who failed to see that justice must be done." The Crown Office, Scotland’s chief prosecutor, has faced growing scrutiny in recent years over its handling of high-profile cold cases and backlogs in reviewing files, but the McKinlay case has cast an especially harsh light on the delays and alleged missteps. According to the family’s representatives, the Crown Office continued to deny requests for a review of Lorraine’s murder for years, despite new evidence being submitted and calls from MPs and the media for the matter to be re-examined. A spokeswoman for COPS issued a written response to the latest accusations, stating: "We are aware of the family’s concerns and reiterate our commitment to ensuring that all historical cases are appropriately investigated. Any case meeting the criteria for fresh inquiry will be fully considered." The statement stopped short of acknowledging any wrongdoing or offering an apology. The renewed calls for a review of Lorraine’s murder have spurred demand from campaigners and politicians alike for a full public inquiry into the Crown Office’s processes.

Emergency services were not called for 11 minutes after the terrifying rollercoaster crash at Alton Towers, it has emerged in a fresh update to the ongoing investigation into the incident that left 16 people seriously injured. The reveal adds to growing concerns about the process of responding to the accident, which occurred on the Smiler rollercoaster on June 2, when two carriages collided as they raced at 35mph. The crash has led to widespread public inquiries and serious questions about the chain of command and emergency protocols used by the park’s staff that night. According to documents released by Staffordshire Police, staff at the attraction made the first call for help at 9:16pm. However, the first fire department operator was not dispatched until 9:27pm, and the first ambulance left the station shortly after 9:30pm, arriving at the scene around 9:40pm. These delays have drawn sharp criticism from both victims and their families, who have voiced outrage over the lack of immediate emergency response during the five minutes when one of the cars dangled dangerously from the ride. The Smiler, a state-of-the-art ride costing £12 million and one of the most modern attractions in the UK, had only opened two months prior to the crash and was considered a flagship feature of the theme park. Park officials have since stated that they acted “immediately” and activated their on-site emergency procedures. However, independent experts suggest that staff were unprepared for a crash of this nature and were not trained to assess the scale of the emergency at full speed. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is currently conducting an investigation alongside the Office of Rail and Road (ORR), which recently confirmed that all derailment notifications are now being centrally managed about 30 miles away in Birmingham. One source familiar with the case claimed that the initial call from park staff was delegated to the wrong operator, and it took a number of transfers to ensure the right departments were made aware. As part of the tragedy, one of the cars dangled 60 feet in the air for almost two hours before being safely returned to the station. During this time, as staff rushed to safety, a sustained wait by the remaining passengers was described by one survivor as “traumatic” and “one of the worst nights of our lives.” The park has since apologised to the victims and stated that it stands by its commitment to visitor safety.

The spectre of political intrigue and unanswered questions has loomed large once more in Argentina, as the country's former prosecutor Alberto Nisman is accused of drafting an arrest warrant for now-former President Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner himself, according to the investigator examining the circumstances of Mr Nisman's death in 2015. The bombshell revelation, which has reignited political unrest and raised new suspicions over the true cause of the controversial prosecutor’s death, has sent shockwaves through Argentina's judiciary and sparked renewed public debate about the legacy of one of the country’s most polarising political figures. Alberto Nisman, a key figure in the investigation into the 1994 bombing of the Israeli embassy in Buenos Aires, had gained notoriety for his bold and politically sensitive cases before his death under mysterious circumstances. Found dead in a hotel room hours after meeting with the country's foreign ministry, initial reports suggested he had committed suicide. But in the years that followed, his widow, Claudia Heinrich, has consistently campaigned for a judicial review, claiming foul play was involved and accusing high-profile political figures of being implicated. Now, the freshly uncovered details from the probe into Nisman’s death—led by Judge Maria Servini—have revealed that the late prosecutor had compiled a 306-page report in which he alleged that President Kirchner and her former Foreign Minister Hector Timerman had colluded with Iran in a deal to avoid further investigation into the embassy bombing. The report, submitted days before his death, also outlined the prosecutor’s intention to seek an arrest warrant for the former president. Despite this, at the time of Nisman's death, no formal arrest order had been filed. Now, Judge Servini is alleging that the former prosecutor had already filled out a warrant requesting the arrest of President Kirchner and nearly 20 others. President Fernandez de Kirchner, who stepped down in 2015, has consistently denied any wrongdoing and has barely commented on the latest twist in the case that has come to symbolise the deep divisions within Argentine politics. As the investigation gains new momentum, analysts suggest the revelations could further widen the fractures in an already deeply polarised judiciary and political landscape. For many Argentinians, the case is as much about justice as it is about transparency and the long-held fear that political power can operate beyond the law. With the warrant allegations now back in the public domain, the pressure is on for a renewed and impartial investigation into both Nisman's death and the claims of high-level collusion.

Majid Haq and Matt Machan seem poles apart. One is a gruff, hard-bitten former Metropolitan Police detective who spent his career investigating some of the UK’s most notorious anti-terror operations, the other is a media-savvy Conservative MP who has built a reputation as one of the brightest young stars of the party’s parliamentary bench. Yet, as the recent debate on counter-terrorism policies intensifies, the paths of these two very different men have begun to converge in ways that have sparked controversy, admiration, and confusion in equal measure. Haq, now 74, has seen it all during his decades of service within the police force. With three decades of experience investigating Muslim extremists and plotting terror attacks, the former commander of London’s counter-terrorism unit is often described as a “no-nonsense” figure who is not afraid to speak his mind. Following his retirement, he has become a vocal critic of what he describes as the “increasing Islamo-leftist bias” in British institutions, particularly in schools and local government bodies. His blunt assessments and uncompromising rhetoric have earned him both respect and condemnation, with some hailing him as a patriot and others branding him as inflammatory and divisive. Meanwhile, Matt Machan, a 44-year-old MP for Heywood and Middleton in Greater Manchester, has taken a very different route to prominence. Elected in 2015 with a large majority and known for his keen grasp of constitutional law and political strategy, Machan has been tipped as a future ministerial prospect. His speeches in the House of Commons are often meticulous in tone and carefully balanced in phrasing, displaying a keen awareness of the political sensitivities surrounding issues like free speech, religious diversity and national security. Yet recently, Machan has taken to inviting Haq to speak about counter-terrorism policy in public events, a decision that has raised eyebrows among MPs from all parties. Some colleagues have questioned whether such invitations risk emboldening inflammatory voices, while others have argued that Haq’s real-world experience offers insights that should not be ignored. At a recent public event in the north-west, Machan insisted that Haq’s views, while sometimes controversial, deserve a hearing. “We should not be afraid of robust debate,” he said. “Majid has first-hand knowledge of the threats our country faces. If we are serious about national security, we owe it to the public to listen to all perspectives.”

Motherwell secured fifth place in the Scottish Premiership with Stephen Pearson and Keith Lasley's goals defeating Ross County. Motherwell came into the final weekend of the season with their destiny in their own hands, needing a win against Ross County to ensure fifth place in the Scottish Premiership and secure the corresponding Europa Conference League spot. They delivered with style in a 2-1 victory at Fir Park on Sunday, handed a helping hand by Dundee United's 5-2 thumping by Aberdeen and Hamilton Academical's 3-2 home defeat by Hearts. Second-half goals from Stephen Pearson and Keith Lasley gave the Steelmen the win they desperately needed – and saw the former midfielder, 34, reach double figures for the season, a remarkable achievement for a campaign marred by turkey eggs earlier in the year. Pearson left the pitch to a standing ovation from the home crowd following his 11th goal of the season, an astute finish after James Keene’s through ball. He then kissed the badge and held a banner in his arms bearing the message "20 years, 20 goals", a shoutout to over two decades in the game and the significance of this being his 20th goal of the campaign. Lasley’s late goal early in the second half, deflected in from a cross, proved the difference in a match where Ross County looked penned in for much of the game. County had taken the lead in the 15th minute through Declan McDaid, who swept home a beautiful through ball from Liam Boyce. It looked as if this could derail Motherwell’s ambitions, given the surrounding fixtures, but they weathered the storm and responded with grit and fury. After the intermission, it was all Motherwell. Tommy Wright’s men fully controlled the game, with their relentless pressing and composure standing out in the second 45. Despite a late rally from the Staggies, featuring some smart set-pieces and near-goals to the post, they could not break through the Motherwell defense. The victory was a fitting end for a side that had endured an extremely inconsistent campaign. At times, they have looked lackluster, but on Saturday, as has become a regular occurrence under Wright, they were competitive, clinical and composed – all the traits he has worked tirelessly to instill since taking charge in 2020. Wright becomes the fourth manager in his 12-year managerial career to secure European football with Motherwell, a testament to his ability to salvage campaigns on the edge of relegation and climb all the way to fifth place.

Manchester United manager José Mourinho has confirmed that a potential transfer of England captain Wayne Rooney is being considered, saying it is "not ruled out" as the January transfer window looms. The 28-year-old, who has spent his entire senior career at Old Trafford since making his debut in 2004, has been heavily linked with a move to the Premier League’s relegation battle, with West Ham United and Crystal Palace among the most frequently mentioned destinations. Mourinho, however, has remained coy about specifics, offering few details on whether a sale is desired or if Rooney himself is keen to leave. Speaking at a press conference prior to United's match against West Ham, the Portuguese boss said: “Wayne is a top-class professional, and if there is an option that could benefit the club and the player, it is not ruled out. But I’m not the one who decides these things. I present the needs of the squad and let the board do their job.” Rooney, who has been linked with several high-profile clubs abroad in recent transfer windows, currently finds himself as a squad player, with young forwards Marcus Rashford and Anthony Martial, as well as Belgian striker Zlatan Ibrahimović, vying for regular minutes in the attacking third. The renewed speculation over his future comes after a season in which Rooney has scored just five league goals in 23 appearances. Despite this – and barring a new phase in his development – it is understood United remain eager to hear offers for Rooney, with the club looking to use the January window to strengthen other departments of the team. Recent reports claim that West Ham are close to reaching an agreement to loan Rooney for the second half of the season, with a potential buyout clause in place. Palace have also reportedly offered a similar package, though it is unclear whether United are open to selling outright. Rosenberg Consulting, the financial services firm that handles Rooney’s business interests, denied last month that the player was open to a move, but insiders close to both Rooney and the club suggest that the player has been less certain in recent discussions. A transfer would mark the end of one of the most storied careers in English football, as Rooney departs the club with a record 558 appearances and as the Premier League’s all-time leading scorer. It would also signal the end of an era as United steer toward a younger, more modern squad under the guidance of Mourinho.

England opener Alex Hales continued to struggle with the bat on day two of their three-day tour match against a South Africa Invitation XI at the Senwes Park cricket ground in Potchefstroom on Thursday. The left-handed batsman, who is expected to play a vital role in England’s upcoming home Test series against India, was dismissed for just two runs as the hosts took early advantage of the overcast conditions. Hales, who has been a key figure in England’s limited-overs side, has faced growing criticism for his form in recent months, and his latest performance has raised questions about his readiness for the longer format. The England captain, Joe Root, came to the crease in the second over and shared a 52-run partnership with Jonny Bairstow, before the pair were both sent packing in quick succession, much to the delight of the small but enthusiastic crowd. The South Africa Invitation XI, comprising local talent and former international stars, put in a tactical performance, mixing tight bowling with clever field placements to curb the tourists’ early momentum. Medium-pacer Mthunzi Mdyaweni was among the wickets, breaking through with a sharp delivery that rattled the top of Hales’ off stump and drew audible reactions from the stands. “The conditions are not easy today, there’s something in the air for the bowling side, but we expected that,” said England coach Brendon McCullum, speaking before the day’s play. “It’s all about finding consistency and making sure the players use these games to get back into rhythm. For Hales, in particular, it’s an opportunity to show he can read the conditions and adapt his game.” Hales’ struggles come ahead of a crucial Test series starting next month, where England will look to solidify their top order following a mixed Ashes campaign. His inclusion in the squad has already been the subject of debate among fans and pundits, with many calling for the promotion of younger, more Test-hardened run-scorers. The match, part of England’s preparations for the home season, has drawn international attention, with the performance of key players being scrutinised under the intense South African sun. The team management has remained cautious about making any firm decisions on player selection, but with two more days of cricket to play, expectations are high that the visitors will produce a more consistent response. Meanwhile, the hosts remain confident in their ability to put pressure on England and stage a strong fight over the next couple of days, hoping that their local conditions can further disrupt the tourists' rhythm.

Volkswagen has unveiled sweeping plans to cut 30,000 jobs worldwide as the German automotive giant accelerates its transformation towards electric and digital mobility amid shifting market dynamics and financial pressures. Around 23,000 of these job cuts will hit Germany, the country that has long been the cornerstone of the company’s success and influence in the global automotive industry. The announcement, handed down at an emergency board meeting in Wolfsburg, signals a stark shift for one of the world’s largest car manufacturers, which is now grappling with the accelerating decline of fossil fuel-powered vehicles and the steep demand for greener, smarter technologies. The carmaker said the restructuring is necessary to make its production and supply chains fit for the future, as volatility in markets and the shift to electric vehicles (EVs) threaten to left legacy models behind. “We are investing heavily in the technologies of the future: in battery electric vehicles, charging infrastructure, and software-driven cars,” said Volkswagen Group CEO Herbert Diess during a press conference. “But in order to do that, we need to refocus our entire organization and bring down costs that are no longer sustainable in this new reality.” The plan is being presented as a painful but necessary step in the company’s evolution from a mass-market petrol and diesel producer to a leader in the electric vehicle revolution. According to internal documents seen by Reuters, the cost of transformation is estimated at around €35 billion, with billions more earmarked for capital investments in EV production and technologies like autonomous driving. Unions have already expressed alarm at the scale of the proposed cuts, with the German metalworkers' union IG Metall warning of a “social catastrophe.” In an open letter to the Volkswagen board, the union called the announced cuts “disproportionate” and accused the company of “not doing enough to protect local jobs.” Meanwhile, German Chancellor Olaf Scholz and other senior government figures have urged Volkswagen to explore all possible ways to preserve jobs, given the company’s critical role in the national economy and its historical significance. The restructuring will not only affect direct employees, but will also ripple through the supply chain and associated industries, including Germany’s long-standing automotive parts sector. In response, Volkswagen has pledged to propose alternative work arrangements, retraining programs, and new investment opportunities to mitigate the impact on employees and communities. The announcement comes as other European automakers, including Renault and Daimler, also face growing cost pressures and are realigning their strategies to remain competitive in a green-focused market.

Jeremy Corbyn has ruled out making "false promises" about tackling migration if Labour wins the next election, saying it would be untrue to suggest that the party could dramatically reduce net migration as has been expected by many in recent years. The Labour leader's comments follow mounting pressure to detail a clear and credible plan on one of the UK’s most contentious political issues, particularly as polls show migration remains one of the key concerns for British voters. Speaking in a keynote address ahead of the general election, Mr Corbyn acknowledged the frustrations felt by many about high levels of immigration, which he said must be managed effectively and humanely. “We must ensure that the migration system is one that works not only for the economy but also for communities,” he said. “But I refuse to make promises that are not rooted in reality.” Despite years of Conservative government pledges to reduce net migration to the "tens of thousands," official figures show that in the year ending September 2016, net migration stood at 280,000. Mr Corbyn made no attempt to commit to a similar target, instead focusing on reforming the system to reduce the number of asylum seekers and help integrate those who are already here. He outlined a vision for immigration that would prioritise skills-based entry and support for the UK's public services, saying: “This isn't about shutting our doors, it's about ensuring that migration – both international and from the European Union – is sustainable and beneficial to the British people.” Corbyn faced criticism from within his own party for his approach. Some Labour MPs argue that the party’s perceived lack of a clear stance on migration has cost them support from working-class voters, many of whom are concerned about the economic and social impacts of immigration. However, Corbyn insisted that Labour must speak with honesty in the campaign, not with "false optimism." “We have to be the party of truth, not fantasy. Migration is complicated, and any solution requires cooperation with European partners and the right legal framework,” he said. The Labour leader also called for the development of guest worker schemes and better childcare support for British families, arguing that these measures could reduce the reliance on migrant labour. The comments will be closely scrutinised by the Tory campaign, as immigration has been a central theme in the Conservative narrative about why a new government is needed.

Alves Eyes Glories as He Joins Rangers on Two-Year Deal   Portugal international defender Bruno Alves has confirmed his first statements after completing a highly anticipated transfer to Rangers, as he aims to add more silverware to his long and storied career. The 38-year-old centre-back, who arrives at Ibrox after a two-year stint with Italian Serie A club Cagliari, signed a two-year contract with the Scottish champions last Friday, bringing with him a wealth of experience and a proven track record in attacking football. In a media conference at Rangers’ training ground, Alves said the chase for success was the decisive factor in his decision to return to Scotland. “This is a special club with big ambitions, and I came here to win more titles,” he stated. “I believe I still have a lot to offer on the pitch, and I am focused on helping Rangers continue to be the dominant force in Scottish football for years to come.” Alves, who made 61 appearances for Portugal, is best known for his time at Cagliari, but he has deep roots in the Scottish game. He first joined Rangers in 2010, forming a formidable central defensive partnership with Iain Henderson, and played a key role in the club’s historic reformation in the aftermath of administration. Over five years at Ibrox, he made 138 appearances and was a vital part of the squad that claimed back-to-back Scottish Premier League titles in 2011 and 2012. Speaking about his return, Alves expressed excitement at rejoining an ambitious squad. “I know this club extremely well, I know the values, the fans, and what it means to be a Rangers player. That’s a big motivation for me,” he said. Rangers director Steve Davis described the move as the club strengthening their defensive options for the 2024/25 season. “Bruno brings composure, leadership, and that winning mentality, which are exactly the qualities we look for,” Davis said. “His international experience and understanding of the game will benefit the team at all levels.” Alves will initially be utilised as a cover option in the back line, as the club continues to develop their young defensive talent. However, manager Giovanni van Bronckhorst has confirmed that Alves will be involved in regular training and is intended as a key presence in the dressing room. The Brazilian-born defender has made his mark in multiple leagues, including stints in Portugal, Italy, and Russia, but it was his first time in Ibrox that he found European triumph, lifting the Europa League winners’ medal in 2011.

Operation to Halt ‘Forced Exiles’ of British Girls to Undergo FGM    By [Your Name], Staff Reporter  British police have launched a targeted operation to stop vulnerable girls from being secretly flown out of the country to undergo Female Genital Mutilation (FGM), a centuries-old practice outlawed in the UK and widely condemned as a severe human rights violation. The initiative, announced this week, marks a significant escalation in efforts to protect children from the harmful procedure and follows reports of girls being taken abroad to countries including Egypt, Nigeria and Kenya to be subjected to the illegal treatment. Under the operation, known as Project Getaway, authorities are working closely with schools, local councils, and the NHS to identify potential cases among teenage girls at risk of being sent overseas for FGM. Officers are reportedly prioritizing high-risk communities and families with known cultural links to countries where the practice remains prevalent. In an unprecedented move, the Met Police and regional forces have received enhanced training and resources to better identify suspicious travel patterns, criminalize complicity and swiftly intervene to halt such journeys. The operation was revealed in the wake of shocking Home Office data suggesting that, despite being illegal in the UK since 1985, as many as 60,000 women in England and Wales have undergone FGM, with up to 200 girls estimated to be at risk of female circumcision each year. Home Secretary Amber Rudd, speaking during a parliamentary debate on the subject, condemned the practice as a “brutal violation” and said the new operation was critical in protecting girls from abuse: “We are determined to root out this horrific crime and safeguard our children at all costs.” Under the Serious Crime Act 2015, it is illegal for a UK national or permanent resident to take a girl to another country to undergo FGM. The maximum penalty for involvement in the practice is 14 years in prison. However, law enforcement officials have claimed that proof of such crimes has been difficult to secure due to a lack of awareness among frontline workers and minimal reporting by affected families. Project Getaway hopes to close this enforcement gap by utilizing data-sharing agreements between schools and local authorities to flag suspicious out-of-country travel with Family Holiday or "cultural exchange" justifications. Debra Gold, a senior official with the charity Plan International, called the go-ahead of the operation a “milestone in child protection efforts.”

Rail Chaos Looms as Three Major Companies Face RMT Strikes   A wave of rail disruptions is set to hit passengers in the coming weeks as the Rail, Maritime and Transport (RMT) union announces industrial action across three major rail operators. The strike, which has been months in the making, is the latest in a series of disputes between transport workers and railway companies over issues including pay, safety and working conditions. The RMT, a powerful union representing thousands of rail workers, has confirmed that employees at Thameslink, South Western Railway, and Northern Rail will walk out in the coming weeks. Details of the exact dates of the strikes have not yet been finalized but union leaders have warned that the disruption could last for several days, severely impacting commuters and leisure travel across key parts of the UK. The union has cited ongoing disputes over driver-only operation (DOO) safety procedures as a primary cause of the strike. DOO policies involve removing the door-closing safety checks traditionally conducted by train conductors and transferring that responsibility to the driver in isolated carriages, using video surveillance. RMT has long opposed this shift, arguing that it compromises passenger safety and erodes the role of onboard staff. Union general secretary Mick Lynch said in a recent statement: “Our members are standing up for safe and secure rail operations. These strikes are a last resort, but when companies persist in pushing through policies that endanger passengers and undermine the vital role of our members, we have no choice.” The railway companies in question did not immediately comment publicly on the announced industrial action, but a source close to one of the firms said that improvements in safety and efficiency were at the heart of the ongoing negotiations. Passengers are being urged to prepare for potential cancellations and delays and to check their rail operator’s website for the latest updates. National Rail has issued a statement advising customers to consider alternative travel options wherever possible and to plan their journeys with care. This latest round of strikes comes amid a broader national conversation about the future of the UK’s railway network. With the transport sector facing pressure to modernize and improve efficiency, the dispute highlights the deepening divide between management and workers over the direction of the industry. The RMT has also pointed to wider concerns, such as staff safety, recruitment shortfalls, and what it describes as “hollow cost-cutting measures” by rail firms and their government backers.

Chat apps that promise to prevent your messages from being accessed by strangers are facing renewed scrutiny in the wake of last week’s terror attack on a London bridge. As investigators work to piece together the events that led to the death of eight people and the injury of dozens more, questions are being raised about the role — or absence — of encrypted messaging platforms in tracking the attackers’ activities. The use of apps such as WhatsApp, Signal and Telegram has come under increasing criticism from security experts, with some calling for a balance to be struck between digital privacy and national security. At the heart of the debate is the feature of end-to-end encryption, which means that only the sender and the intended recipient of a message can read it. Even the companies that own the apps cannot access the content of these messages, a design choice that many users and digital rights advocates argue is essential for protecting personal freedom and freedom of expression. However, in the aftermath of the attack, counter-terrorism officials are reiterating long-standing concerns that encrypted messaging has become a “safe space for terrorists,” allowing them to plot and communicate without fear of detection. “We have to ask tough questions about whether current encryption practices are aiding those who wish us harm,” said one senior security source who wished to remain anonymous. The renewed focus on encrypted messaging apps follows a string of recent high-profile attacks, including the Manchester bombing in May 2017 and terrorist incidents in France and Belgium, in which it was claimed that end-to-end encryption hampered efforts to gather intelligence. In the UK, the government has consistently pushed for legislation — such as the proposed Investigatory Powers Act — to give law enforcement and intelligence services the ability to access private communications when necessary. Critics argue that this would weaken the security of all users, not just criminals, and could lead to government overreach and abuse of power. “You can’t have the benefits of encryption without the risks it poses — but you also can’t have an all-powerful government determining who is allowed to be secure and who is not,” said Dr. Sarah Ahmed, a cybersecurity expert at Cambridge University. The latest attack on London comes at a time when the use of encrypted communication is growing rapidly, especially among users concerned about data security and privacy.

Senior US Republican Senator Lindsey Graham has claimed that his campaign email account was hacked by Russian operatives, marking the latest in a string of cybersecurity breaches linked to the 2020 US presidential election. The allegations, reported by major news outlets and corroborated by multiple sources within Graham’s office, come at a time of heightened concern over foreign interference in American politics. According to Graham, the breach was first discovered by his cybersecurity team in the days leading up to the announcement of Donald Trump’s second impeachment trial. His office said evidence pointed to state-sponsored hackers, likely working under the direction of the Russian government. “This isn't just about me or my emails,” Graham said in a statement. “This is about our national security and the integrity of our democratic process.” Graham is one of several high-profile Republicans to face cyber intrusions in recent months. The US government has repeatedly blamed Russian intelligence agencies for a widespread campaign of disinformation and hacking in the 2016 and 2020 elections. Last year, a major report by the Senate’s Select Committee on Intelligence identified Russia, China, and Iran as the key players in efforts to destabilise American democratic institutions. Graham’s office has not yet released the full contents of the emails allegedly accessed by the hackers. However, sources close to the senator say the breach did not appear to lead to the public disclosure of national security threats or criminal activity, unlike some earlier incidents, such as the 2016 Podesta email leak. This incident has renewed demands for a thorough congressional investigation into Russian election interference. Graham, a long-time critic of President Joe Biden and a vocal supporter of former President Trump, has been a frequent subject of controversy over the past year. His comments on the breach appear to suggest that cyberattacks are not confined to any one political faction. Interior Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, the head of the Department of Homeland Security, said in an interview earlier this week that foreign actors continue to target American elections. “We are closely monitoring threats, and working closely with Congress and state officials,” he said. For his part, Senator Graham said it is time for the US to adopt a more aggressive posture toward cyber threats. “We can't live in fear, but we also can't afford to ignore the reality of a new kind of war,” he added.

The body of a Colorado pastor who had embarked on a treasure hunt for a reported $2 million (1.5 million) has been found in the Rio Grande River in New Mexico, more than a month after he was reported missing, local authorities have confirmed. The Reverend Jim Dannemiller, 58, from Estes Park, Colorado, vanished on December 20 while traveling by canoe on the river near the town of Truth or Consequences. Dubbed “ToCon” by locals, the area is a popular destination for tourists and trekkers alike, but Dannemiller had set out for a different reason. According to reports, Dannemiller was pursuing a long-standing legend that a treasure, valued at around $2 million, was hidden beneath the My turkey Creek area, located just south of the New Mexico border. The rumour has circulated for decades, drawing treasure hunters and local history enthusiasts to the region in search of the bounty. Dannemiller, described by friends as an adventure-seeker with a passion for biblical prophecy and treasure-hunting, had reportedly been obsessed with uncovering the so-called treasure for over a year. Despite extensive searches and investigations, Dannemiller’s body was not recovered until two weeks into the new year. On January 3, authorities found his remains in the Rio Grande, near the same stretch where he had last been seen. The Medical Examiner is expected to conduct tests in the coming days to confirm the cause of death, though police have not ruled out the possibility of an accident or exposure. “Mr Dannemiller’s tragic death is a sobering reminder of the dangers that can accompany exploring remote and treacherous waters,” said Sheriff Bill Pringle of Sierra County, New Mexico. “Our hearts go out to his family and close friends during this difficult time.” Dannemiller's disappearance had sparked widespread interest, with news outlets and treasure hunting websites reporting updates as investigators searched for clues. A GoFundMe page created by a close relative had raised over $10,000 for the search operation, with many describing Dannemiller as a “man on a mission” driven by faith and curiosity. The myth of the hidden treasure is said to be linked to a local ranch whose original owner allegedly buried a chest of gold during the mid-19th century. While no such treasure has ever been proven to exist, the legend endures, attracting amateur archaeologists, adventurers and even professionals. Friends have described Dannemiller as “a man of passion,” with a deep love for the outdoors and a strong faith.

The United Nations has called for an urgent investigation into a disturbing video circulating online, which appears to depict Syrian rebels executing captured soldiers or pro-government militiamen, suggesting it could constitute a war crime. The footage, released earlier this week, has drawn international condemnation and renewed concerns over the escalating brutality in Syria's protracted conflict. UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric urged all parties involved in the conflict to uphold international humanitarian law and ensure accountability for potential atrocities. A preliminary assessment by UN investigators has flagged the video for containing elements that may constitute   summary executions or deliberate mistreatment of detainees  , which are violations under the Geneva Conventions. The video has not yet been verified, but it follows a series of similar graphic content shared online and purportedly filmed in areas controlled by opposition groups. It shows men being forced to kneel before masked fighters, followed by what appears to be their execution. Some of the victims in the footage are believed to be defectors from the pro-government Syrian National Army, while others are suspected to be members of Houthi-allied militias, according to sources in the region. The UN’s Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) has expressed deep alarm at the apparent disregard for the rules of war, calling the killings "especially abhorrent in light of the already immense suffering witnessed in Syria." OHCHR representative Liz Throssell said the office was working with international partners to trace the origin and authenticity of the footage and determine the identities of those responsible. This incident comes amid increasing tensions in the war-torn country, where reports of targeted killings, torture, and enforced disappearances have spiked in recent months. Rights groups have long accused both government and rebel forces of committing serious violations of international law, but the latest video adds disturbing new weight to concerns about the conduct of armed groups on all sides. The conflict in Syria, now in its 12th year, has claimed over half a million lives and displaced millions. Recent escalations along the front lines in Idlib and northern Hama have only heightened fears that the conflict will continue to spiral into deeper chaos without a sustained international diplomatic effort. United Nations officials stressed that while no accurate forensic evidence or official attribution could yet be confirmed, the apparent footage demands immediate scrutiny.
