The International Criminal Court (ICC) and other judicial bodies have been cited as potential avenues for holding perpetrators to account, though the political complexity of the Syrian conflict has long complicated such efforts.

Ciaran Clark scored a stunning late header as Newcastle United produced a remarkable turnaround to draw 2-2 against Bristol City in a dramatic Championship clash at St James’ Park on Sunday. The result, a huge boost for the Magpies following recent rocky form, saw them come from two goals down in a thrilling encounter that left fans on the edge of their seats until the final whistle. Trailing 2-0 with just minutes remaining of normal time, Newcastle were seemingly heading for another frustrating result under manager Eddie Howe. But a last-ditch effort from Clark, the accomplished central defender, changed the course of the match when he powered home a header from a corner in the 89th minute to send the home fans into raptures. The draw lifts Newcastle to 11th in the Championship table, though they remain seven points adrift of the play-off places, while Bristol City remain rock bottom, having managed just one win in 20 league games this season. The Robins started the brighter side, with a slick counter-attack routine causing problems for the Magpies, who have struggled for consistency under Howe in recent weeks. Bristol took the lead in the 23rd minute when goalscorer Sean Maguire curled a beautiful shot into the top corner after a smart through ball from on-loan Everton winger Josh Onomah. The visitors doubled their advantage 12 minutes later with a well-worked move that ended with a composed finish from substitute Yaser Patel after a clever cross into the box was not dealt with effectively by the Newcastle defenders. Despite the deficit, Newcastle refused to lie down and gradually grew into the match. Their hopes of a miracle revival gained momentum in the 79th minute when substitutes Jonjo Shelvey and Ayoze Perez were introduced, and it was about five minutes later that a frustrating afternoon suddenly turned into one of high drama. Paul Dummett curled in a measured cross that Clark rose highest to meet with a clinical header, finding the bottom corner to make it 2-1. The equaliser sparked a frenzied finale, with the visitors defending nervously but ultimately holding firm to preserve a rare point for the Magpies. Speaking after the match, Newcastle boss Eddie Howe praised his side’s spirit: "I’m incredibly proud of the lads today. Coming back from two down in a run-of-the-mill game is not something you write home about usually, but the way we showed fight and belief was very important."

When Sheikh Tamam bin Hamad Al Thaqi succeeded his father as emir of energy-rich Qatar in June, few observers knew very much about him. The change of leadership has already seen a sea of sweeping reforms, as Qatar's new leader tackles the £200bn-a-year oil and gas revenues. But who is this new emir and what does he want? A graduate of Britain's Sandhurst military academy and fluent in English, Sheikh Tamam is considered to be the best-educated and most liberal of the royal family. During his time as heir apparent and head of the Qatar Foundation for Education, Science and Community Development, he gained a reputation for pushing to modernise education and encourage women's rights, as well as investing in arts and culture. Early reports suggest the new emir is also keen to modernise the economy and expand Qatar's influence beyond the Gulf, with special emphasis on the Middle East and Asia. In an exclusive interview with the TIMES, several diplomats and business leaders in Qatar said they believe he has a visionary outlook, and his long-term goal is to position Qatar as a regional intellectual and economic powerhouse. In recent months, he has announced over 80 new initiatives, spanning everything from digital infrastructure development to greater investment in renewable energy and water security. One of the more visible changes is the country's gradual move towards liberalizing domestic services and utility regulation, which – if it continues – could help make Qatar one of the most attractive places in the Gulf for international business. Qatar has also pursued a controversial foreign policy toward countries such as Saudi Arabia, which has led to regional tensions. Some observers suggest that Sheikh Tamam may use this energy wealth to push a more assertive regional strategy, possibly with a softer approach and more diplomatic openness than his father had pursued in the past. As he settles into his new role, all eyes are on the 33-year-old emir as he sets about reshaping the future of this tiny but increasingly ambitious nation. Whether he can balance the pressures of domestic reform with the treacherous geopolitical terrain will be a true test of leadership. For now, his early moves have raised hopes among some, but also deep concerns among others – both within the country and abroad. As one of the youngest emirs in the modern Arab world, Sheikh Tamim must navigate the complexities of power, diplomacy and a rapidly changing global landscape.

Sergeant Martin Courtney, a 45-year-old reservist with the Royal Air Force, has spoken for the first time about the dramatic and life-saving operation in which he helped rescue 23 sailors from the stranded container ship  Blue Horizon , off the coast of South Wales in March 2024. Over 24 hours, the crew faced freezing conditions and rising tensions as their vessel ran aground on jagged rocks after a collision with a smaller fishing boat. Speaking in a heartfelt interview to the BBC, Courtney described the ordeal as “absolutely one of the most harrowing and rewarding experiences of my life.” The  Blue Horizon , carrying three Russian, seven Ukrainian, and 13 British crew members, suffered severe engine failure during a storm that lasted several days. When the ship eventually found itself wedged between dangerous rocks, the crew were left in a limbo of sorts — unable to move forward or backward, and with dwindling food and fresh water. Rescue efforts had begun to pool in with the Coastguard, but Courtney’s involvement came as part of a re-inforced Search and Rescue (SAR) team based in Pembroke Dock. “Climbing aboard that ship was the most intense two minutes of my life,” said Courtney. “Visibility was poor, we were in treacherous waters, and time was against us. You just don’t see that kind of human determination until you're actually there, witnessing it up close.” Courtney led efforts to transfer the crew through a hazardous cargo hold to a lowering point at the stern, from where RAF helicopters could extract them one by one. Many of the men had already been adrift for over seven days and were suffering from hypothermia and exhaustion. For their part, the crew had taken it upon themselves to try and steer the ship off the rocks — using winches and the limited propeller power they had — in an attempt to avoid another life-threatening emergency. The rescued sailors, who have not spoken to the press, have since thanked the RAF for their “unwavering commitment and exceptional skill.” A spokesperson for the RAF told the Wales Today programme that Sergeant Courtney was among several airmen who “demonstrated fearless and resilient actions in one of the most trying conditions recently faced by the force.” For Courtney, the experience is not something he will ever forget. “It’s burnt into my memory,” he said. “You see faces you won’t see again.

The High Court recently hosted a landmark legal inquiry lasting three days, uniting some of Britain’s most distinguished legal figures in a case described by one participant as an issue of “fundamental constitutional importance” to the government, Parliament, and the future of the United Kingdom. The hearings, marked by intense scrutiny and sharp legal reasoning, brought to the fore longstanding tensions over the balance of power between the executive branch and Parliament. The case centred on a recent executive decision by the government to bypass formal parliamentary approval for a major policy initiative, a move some critics argued undermined the sovereignty of the legislature. The judge at the heart of the proceedings, Sir Michael Jeffcott, presided over a courtroom packed with legal scholars, civil servants, and MPs, reflecting the gravity of the issue at stake. One of the key moments came during the second day, when counsel for the government argued that the decision, while contentious, was necessary for national security and the swift implementation of a policy aimed at addressing a growing domestic crisis. The government’s legal team pointed to historical precedents where ministers had taken similar actions in times of emergency, asserting that the constitutional framework allowed for flexibility under such conditions. However, the opposition counsel presented a compelling rebuttal, citing the Rule of Law and the constitutional principle that no government should act beyond the law or above parliamentary authority. They argued that such a precedent could open the door to further executive overreach, with potentially long-term and dangerous consequences for democratic governance in the UK. Inside the court, there was a palpable sense of what one senior lawyer described as “constitutional principles colliding in public view.” The discussions extended beyond legal technicalities to questions of governance, trust, and the democratic process in a modern, constitutional monarchy. What started as a technical legal dispute soon became something far larger, with the potential to set a binding precedent for future executive powers. As the litigants and justices mulled over what was said, outside the courthouse, Parliament Square became the venue for a series of protests and counter-protests. Demonstrators gathered to voice their support for greater parliamentary autonomy, while others backed the government’s initiative, holding posters proclaiming “Policy not politics” and “Get things done.” The case is now in abeyance pending the court’s decision, expected within the coming weeks. Whatever the ruling, it is clear that the outcome will be a significant milestone in British constitutional law, with wider implications for the evolving relationship between government, Parliament and the governed.

A Philosophy on Mortality: The Bold Advice of W. Somerset Maugham   The great British writer W. Somerset Maugham, famed for his shrewd observations on human nature and biting wit, once delivered a particularly striking commentary on death. “Dying is a very dull, dreary affair,” he wrote, before offering a sharp prescription: “Have nothing whatever to do with it.” The words, now as bold as when Maugham uttered them, reflect his typically unflinching approach to life’s big questions and his preference for steering clear of anything that might dampen the joy of being alive. Maugham, whose literary career spanned decades and whose works such as  Of Human Bondage  and  The Razor’s Edge  made him one of the most respected and controversial writers of the 20th century, had little patience for what he saw as the sad theatrics of mortality. Living most of his life in the early to mid-1900s, a period still marked by relatively high mortality rates, Maugham's attitude appears, to some, both pragmatic and harsh. Yet, for others, it is a refreshingly honest take on a subject that too often gets buried under sentiment. In an era where grief is often glamorised in literature, cinema, and philosophy, Maugham’s stance remains startling. He was – above all – a man who preferred looking forwards rather than reflecting on the inevitable. His remark captures the essence of his mortal philosophy: live intensely, engage fully, and leave room for nothing that will distract from that pursuit. It is also a reminder of the man himself – a writer who left a legacy rich in narrative, character, and meaning, but who was rarely sentimental when it came to personal sentiment, especially when it came to his own demise. Though the quote may sound flippant, it is part of a larger worldview that Maugham expressed throughout his life and works. He believed in the primacy of experience, in the power of the individual will, and in the human capacity for self-determination. To concern oneself with death was, in his eyes, to rob oneself of the vibrancy of the present. Maugham's bold words continue to provoke thought nearly a century after he first wrote them. They challenge us to consider not only how we deal with the end but how we approach the beginning and go about everything in between. His philosophy may not be for everyone, nor is it immune to criticism, but it remains a compelling and provocative reflection on what it means to be alive.

Thousands of Malaysian opposition supporters have poured onto the streets of several major cities to protest allegations of election fraud, in a bold public challenge to authorities who have declared the demonstration illegal. The mass gathering, one of the largest such events in years, took place in defiance of a police warning that the rally—organised by the centre-left opposition coalition Pakatan Harapan—was not officially sanctioned under the country’s strict public assembly laws. The demonstrators, who filled key thoroughfares in Kuala Lumpur, Penang and Johor Bahru, accuse the ruling Bersatu-led coalition of widespread vote rigging in the recent general election. Although the election result gave a narrow victory to the ruling party, opposition leaders have claimed that irregularities, including the misuse of postal ballots and coercive tactics in rural constituencies, have undermined the legitimacy of the outcome. The rally appears to mark the beginning of what could become a sustained campaign of civil resistance by the opposition, who now face a difficult balancing act between pushing for democratic accountability and avoiding criminalisation. Under the Peaceful Assembly Act, any public demonstration not registered with local authorities can result in arrest—and several key opposition figures have already been placed under house arrest. Cikgu Azmin, a prominent activist in the Malaysian capital, said the protest was a response to "the grave threat to our democracy". Azmin, who is also a former teacher known for his vocal support of reformist causes, told reporters: "If the election was free and fair, why are they so afraid of contesting the results? We will not back down—we are the people’s voice, not someone who can be silenced with legal tactics or threats." The police response has been met with international concern. Reports from the scene suggest a heavy deployment of officers, although no clashes have been reported thus far. Nonetheless, human rights groups are closely watching the situation, with the Malaysian Human Rights Commission issuing an urgent appeal for police to “exercise restraint and uphold the right to peaceful protest”. In a statement, Prime Minister Islam bin Hadri said the ruling coalition would not “dance to the tune of agitators trying to destabilise the state”. He insisted the election had been conducted within legal parameters and urged the opposition to pursue their grievances through the judiciary. "There are proper channels,” the Prime Minister said in a speech to the National Assembly.

Erroneous use of data led to 13 wrongful arrests, independent report finds   A recent investigation has revealed that 13 innocent individuals were wrongly arrested due to errors in the use of communications data by British police forces, according to an independent watchdog. The report, published by the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), highlights concerns over how law enforcement agencies access and interpret data from mobile providers and other digital platforms. The findings have been described as "alarming" by civil liberties campaigners, who warned that the growing reliance on digital records in criminal investigations must be underpinned by greater oversight and standards. The ICO report, which examined how data is used under the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act (RIPA) between 2014 and 2016, found a number of cases where insufficient checks left innocent people vulnerable to false accusations. In five of the instances, the report said police extracted the telecoms records of individuals, but the information was either misinterpreted, incorrectly stored, or wrongly linked to crime scenes. The result in each case was the wrongful arrest of individuals, often based on the mistaken belief that they had been directly involved in criminal activity. In one case, a man in Manchester was arrested in connection with a property burglary. Officers had obtained the mobile location data of people in the area at the time of the crime and, due to a technical error, the data incorrectly showed him near the property. The man was held in custody for 12 hours before tests revealed the error and led to his release. Another case involved a teenager who was wrongly flagged in a sexual assault investigation due to a suspicious match between a SIM card and call records. The ICO said it had referred the cases for criminal or disciplinary action and that further investigations were ongoing. “This is a serious issue,” said Elizabeth Denham, the Information Commissioner. “When such powerful tools are used to target and arrest individuals, they must be used with the utmost accuracy and care. The public must be able to have confidence that they are not being wrongly implicated by flawed data.” The Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act (RIPA) enables police and intelligence agencies to obtain communication data, which includes when calls or messages were sent, the location and the person being contacted, but not their content. According to the ICO, while the law is clear, the implementation has been inconsistent.

Two late goals proved decisive as Aberdeen sealed a dramatic European night at the ASIM Ferhatović-Hase Stadium, advancing in the Europa League qualifiers with a crucial 2-0 win over Bosnian side Siroki Brijeg. Goals from Greg Stewart and Gary Mackay-Steven in the second half ensured a night to remember for the Scottish Premiership side, who were chasing an improbable victory on the road. The atmosphere inside the 5,500-capacity stadium in Tuzla, Bosnia, was electric as stewards, supporters, and fans alike gathered to witness the clash between the UEFA-introduced teams of the North Sea and the Balkans. Siroki Brijeg, a modest outfit from the Herzegovina region, had managed to unsettle their more renowned opponents early on. Terry Gardestad, their diminutive forward, tested goalkeeper Oliver McBurnie with a curling effort in the 28th minute, and Siroki looked content to sit deep and frustrate the visiting side for much of the first half. But as clockwork, Aberdeen began to take control after the break. Stewart, who had spent time with Celtic and Hibernian, became a constant threat down the left, and it was from his flank that the breakthrough came in the 58th minute. A composed run into the box from the winger saw him curl a low shot into the bottom corner, sending the Dons’ travelling support – estimated at around 200 – into raptures. Mackay-Steven, the prolific winger known for his work rate and eye for goal, delivered the second just 13 minutes later. Cutting inside from the right, the 26-year-old fired a clinical shot past the outstretched hand of Siroki goalkeeper Mirnes Cavic to double the advantage. With the match well and truly beyond the hosts, Aberdeen switched into containment mode, ensuring manager Derek McInnes’ side managed the run-in to the final whistle without overexposing themselves. The victory will resonate deeply in Scottish football circles, where European qualification is always a matter of pride and progression. For Aberdeen, it is a continuation of a strong summer run, as they prepare for what promises to be a tough group stage featuring some of the continent’s giants. Speaking after the match, Stewart hailed his side's character and resilience. “Going to away games in Europe is never easy, but our lads showed great spirit and belief,” he said. “It's always a box-tick to get the goals, but the main thing is that we get to the next stage.”

Spanish scientists Dr. Bernabé Ruíz and Professor José Moya found themselves staring in disbelief at the results of their routine soil analysis in the remote Granada region of southern Spain. What they had unearthed was unlike anything documented in their decades of geological and mineralogical research. A rare mineral — previously only known to exist in meteorite samples and outer space — had been found deep within the Earth’s crust. The discovery has sent ripples through the scientific community, with experts questioning how this extraterrestrial-like material came to be hidden in a place so firmly rooted in the terrestrial world. The mineral, identified as "bushlanite," is a rare, oxidized form of copper and is known to form under the intense heat and pressure of asteroid impacts or in the vacuum of space. Until now, it had only ever been found in meteorites from the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. The Granada find challenges existing theories of how such minerals can form naturally on Earth, and scientists are working to understand whether this was the result of a long-forgotten meteor impact or, more controversially, a natural geological process yet to be discovered. Dr. Ruíz, a geologist at the University of Granada, expressed his astonishment to reporters. “We initially thought it was contamination from a meteorite sample we had used in a previous experiment. But after multiple tests – spectroscopy, electron microscopy, crystal lattice analysis – the evidence was overwhelming. This is real. It’s not just here; it’s embedded in the surrounding rock.” Professor Moya, a mineralogist with the Spanish National Research Council, added: “We are talking about a mineral that should not exist in this area under these conditions. Its presence suggests something extraordinary happened here – something powerful enough to create the right environment for such a mineral to form.” The site, located near the Sierra Nevada mountain range, is a known area for geological activity, but nothing like this has ever been recorded. Initial hypotheses suggest that the area may once have been the site of a meteor impact thousands of years ago. However, no evidence of a crater has been found, and the surrounding geological strata do not display the sort of ejecta layers typically associated with such events. With funding from the Spanish Ministry of Science and Innovation, a team of international experts is now being assembled to investigate further. Some have even suggested that the mineral may have formed in a deep subterranean chamber under extreme heat and pressure, mimicking the conditions of space.

Scientists have made a major breakthrough in the battle against influenza, with the development of a potential universal flu vaccine capable of protecting against all known strains of the virus, including those yet to emerge. In a study published today in the journal  Nature , an international team of researchers detail how the prototype vaccine targets a conserved region of the influenza virus that remains relatively unchanged across different strains. This contrasts with current influenza vaccines, which must be reformulated annually to match the predicted dominant strains, often leaving populations vulnerable to unexpected or mismatched mutations. The research was led by scientists at the University of Oxford in collaboration with teams at the J. Craig Venter Institute in the United States and several pharmaceutical companies. The vaccine, known as FluHead-20, has shown promising early results in laboratory trials and has begun initial human testing. “This represents a paradigm shift in how we approach flu prevention,” said Dr. Emma Bell, a virologist at the University of Oxford and one of the study’s lead authors. “By targeting a protein component of the virus that doesn’t change from year to year, we can move towards a one-time vaccine that offers long-term, broad-spectrum protection.” Influenza is a significant global health challenge, with seasonal outbreaks responsible for millions of cases of illness and hundreds of thousands of deaths each year. Pandemic strains, such as H1N1 in 2009, can cause even greater disruption, highlighting the urgency of a more effective and long-lasting solution. Current vaccines work by stimulating the body to produce antibodies against the outer surface protein of the influenza virus, known as haemagglutinin. However, this protein mutates frequently, necessitating the annual update of vaccine formulations. The new approach being tested in FluHead-20 focuses on a different part of the hemagglutinin molecule known as the “stem” or “stalk” region — a structural component that remains largely consistent across all known flu strains. The immune system often overlooks the stem, focusing instead on the more variable head of the protein. The breakthrough lies in the use of a modified version of the stem, designed to direct the immune system’s attention to this stable region. In trials with ferrets — a standard animal model for vaccine development — FluHead-20 provided protection against various influenza A subtypes, including H1N1, H3N2, and even bird flu strains such as H5N1 and H7N9. The team is now moving into Phase 1 human trials, which will assess the vaccine’s safety and ability to stimulate an immune response in healthy volunteers.

Scotland earned a hard-fought 1-1 draw against the Republic of Ireland in a tightly contested Euro 2016 qualifier at Hampden Park, ensuring they retained a two-point cushion at the top of Group D. The result was edged with controversy and missed chances, but ultimately allowed Scotland to maintain their position in the race for qualification to next summer’s European Championship tournament in France. Goals from Lee Camp and James McClean helped lift the teams from a frustrating-evening stalemate before the visitors found an equaliser in the 66th minute through McClean. The Republic, who were searching for their first point under newly appointed manager Martin O’Neill, came close to snatching victory in the final moments, but the well-organised Scottish backline ensured that the point was shared. The goal came after a cruel accident for Rangers goalkeeper, albeit via an own goal. In a desperate attempt to prevent the ball from entering the net, Camp’s clearance hit the back post, bounced off his own crossbar, and dropped into the net at his feet. The replay later revealed he had attempted to punch the ball, but his over-rotation and lack of timing resulted in the ball ricocheting inside the frame. For Scotland, the match marked their first home game of the campaign since November 2014, during which they had been unsuccessful in securing a win. Despite the defensive resilience displayed, the visitors, and indeed the home supporters, will feel the match was an opportunity missed to establish greater depth in their qualifying run. Manager Mark Clark will be encouraged, however, by the performance of full-back Kieran Tierney, who was a constant threat down the left wing. Tierney’s delivery into the box, and his compact central-drawing ability, caused problems for the Republic’s midfield and defenders about half-chance after half-chance. Republic of Ireland’s equaliser was clinical and a moment of individual brilliance from McClean, who pounced on a misplaced long ball from Scotland’s captain, Alan Hutton. Running onto the loose ball in the 59th minute, McClean finished it off with a composed, side-footed effort that left Camp rooted to the spot. With the two teams now level on 10 points ahead of their next matches, Scotland face a trip to the Faroe Islands next month, where they are expected to secure another win and extend their advantage even further.

Poland has experienced a remarkable turnaround in its educational performance, according to results from the Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) tests, which measure the academic skills of 15-year-olds in reading, mathematics, and science across countries. Since 2000, the country has moved from among the lowest-performing nations in Europe to a position that now exceeds the international average—and in some areas, even outpaces many developed countries. The latest Pisa assessments, carried out in 2012, marked a significant leap in achievement for Polish students. According to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which administers the test, Poland is one of only a handful of countries worldwide to improve its scores in all three core subjects over that period. This rise has drawn widespread attention from policymakers and education experts around the globe, who are now seeking to understand the factors behind the success. The improvements came after an overhaul of the country’s school system following Poland’s transition from a centrally planned economy. A 1999 education reform, designed to bring the country’s system into line with global standards, introduced sweeping changes, including increased funding for schools, the implementation of teacher salary raises, and the development of national curriculum standards. The reform also eliminated the middle school exam, which had traditionally allowed only the top 50% of students to proceed to gymnasium (secondary school). As a result, more students than before were given access to higher levels of education. Dr Bronisław Silicki, then-Minister of Science and Higher Education, described the reforms as a "revolution in the system of Polish education," and the Pisa results seem to vindicate that assessment. The continued improvements over the next decade solidified Poland’s transformation into a key success story in Eastern Europe about how national policy can reshape the educational landscape. This resurgence has had real-world implications. The OECD noted that Polish students are now better equipped with the skills needed to compete in a modern economy. Poland, once seen as lagging behind Western Europe in educational attainment, is now demonstrating that with targeted policy and investment, it is possible to close—and even overcome—the gap. Yet, while the past 12 years have seen positive developments, experts caution that maintaining this progress requires continued effort. More recent Pisa data, particularly from 2015 onwards, indicate some stagnation in the rate of improvement. With that in mind, education officials are now exploring new measures, including better digital resources and improved teacher training, to sustain the momentum.

Björk is once again defying convention as she launches her highly anticipated world tour, unveiling a set of custom-made instruments that promise to transform the live music experience into a multisensory spectacle. Among the most striking innovations are a “musical lightning generator” and four harp-playing pendulums—each designed to blur the boundary between nature and technology, and to echo her long-standing fascination with organic forms and experimental soundscapes. The Icelandic artist, known for her avant-garde approach to music and performance, has consistently challenged what it means to produce and present sound. Her latest installation for this tour, staged in a converted exhibition space in London before its global rollout, represents a new frontier in her creative process. The “lightning generator”—a collaborative project with Mycle Schneider, a noted technologist and co-founder of the Tenrhythmics music platform—uses lightning-like electrical sparks to generate percussive beats. Each flash, timed to the rhythm of her songs, is captured and converted into a sound, creating an eerie, thunderous pulse that moves in step with her music. The harp-playing pendulums, meanwhile, are a mesmerising fusion of art and engineering. Suspended from the ceiling in a controlled rhythmic swing, each one is equipped with its own harp and robotic arm, programmed to pluck strings in response to the tempo and key of the performance. Inspired by the pendulum-like motion of natural systems, these instruments evoke a sense of inevitability and balance, their swinging arcs visual metaphors for the flow of the music they help to compose. John Spacil, the American inventor who has designed several of Björk’s instruments over the years, described the creation of the machines as being “about bringing the energy of nature into the studio and stage” and helping the artist “translate the organic into the audible.” From the chaotic swing of a pendulum to the crackle of an electrical current, the instruments reflect Björk’s philosophy that sound is not merely to be heard but to be experienced in all its physicality. As the world tour begins, fans can expect a performance that is as intense and unpredictable as the elements themselves, marking what many are calling a landmark moment in the evolution of live music. With this latest tour, Björk continues to do what she has always done best: reinvent not just how we listen, but how we feel. Whether through a plucked string or a flash of synthetic lightning, Björk remains a force of nature in every sense of the word.

Tech Visionaries Unite Against Controversial Legislation   In a rare display of consensus among Silicon Valley's most influential figures, the founders of Google, Twitter, and eBay have come together to issue a strongly worded warning about a controversial piece of US legislation currently making its way through Congress. The proposed bill, which has drawn fierce criticism from civil liberties groups, seeks to expand government surveillance powers under the guise of national security. The letter, jointly authored by Larry Page and Sergey Brin (founders of Google), Biz Stone and Evan Williams (co-founders of Twitter), and Pierre Omidyar (founder of eBay), was made public ahead of a key congressional debate expected to take place imminently. In the letter, the tech magnates argue that the legislation poses a “direct threat to the fundamental rights of privacy and free expression, the bedrock of American democracy.” The bill in question has been backed by members of both major political parties but faces widespread opposition, particularly from digital rights activists and tech companies concerned about the precedent it would set. The legislation would reportedly allow federal agencies to bypass traditional legal barriers in accessing user data from large platforms, with minimal judicial oversight. This, critics say, would effectively undermine the Fourth Amendment protections against unreasonable searches and seizures. The founders’ open letter warns that such legislation would not only endanger individual rights but also “stifle innovation and erode trust in the digital economy.” They argue that the United States has the opportunity to set a global standard for responsible and ethical use of digital technology, and that the proposed bill risks damaging the country’s reputation at a time when democratic institutions are under pressure worldwide. In particular, the letter highlights what it describes as the bill’s “broad and vague language,” which could be weaponised against journalists, whistleblowers, and even ordinary citizens. “We are standing at a crossroads,” the letter states. “We can choose to regulate technology with accountability and respect for rights, or we can retreat into a model of unchecked power that risks the freedoms our nation was founded on.” While the US government has defended the bill as a necessary response to evolving security threats, including online radicalisation and cyberattacks, the reaction from the tech sector has been uniformly negative. The move by the tech entrepreneurs marks the latest in a long-standing tension between Silicon Valley and Washington, a relationship that has increasingly become a central point of political debate in recent years.

The UK experienced a blazing September day as the mercury soared to 34.4°C (93.9°F) in Gravesend, Kent, setting a new record for the hottest day of the year so far and the warmest September day since 1911. The sweltering temperature, recorded at Gravesend Rainham during the late morning, left weather experts stunned and many across the country breaking out sunhats and sunscreen in a bid to cope with the unexpected summer return. The event has brought renewed attention to the country's increasingly volatile weather patterns and raised questions about the role of climate change in such extreme heat waves well into the autumn months. The previous September record, also held by Gravesend, had stood for over a century at 34.3°C, recorded back in 1911. This year’s new high was confirmed by the Met Office, which said the temperature marked an unusual thermal peak in a traditionally more temperate month. Across the country, swathes of the south and east basked in high temperatures, with some places in London, Essex and Surrey reporting readings of 33°C or above. Schools in certain areas voluntarily closed early for the day, and rail operators issued warnings about landings as the heat threatens to distort tracks and cause travel disruptions. Meanwhile, emergency services reminded the public to stay hydrated and avoid excessive outdoor activity during the peak of the day’s heat, particularly for the elderly and children. Environmental groups and climate scientists seized upon the event as a stark reminder of the shifting climate and the need for greater action to mitigate its effects. “Weather records are increasingly being broken not just in the summer, but now into the autumn and even winter,” said Professor Martin Helmert, a climate expert at the University of East Anglia. “This highlights a disturbing trend that cannot be ignored.” The record-breaking day also sparked lively debate on social media, with many Britons taking to their phones to share selfies and photos of snow-dusted mountain ranges abroad alongside sunbathing on the beach closer to home. As the UK sundresses and flip-flops become the uniform of the afternoon, scientists and meteorologists continue to monitor the long-term implications of such soaring temperatures in an unseasonably warm September. For now, the heatwave offers little respite to the various path and air quality advisories set in place around the country.

Claims that a move is being made to remove Douglas Alexander from his role as Shadow Foreign Secretary have been hurled back as “ludicrous” by senior figures within the Labour Party. The comments were reportedly sparked by speculation that changes to constituency boundaries in Scotland could threaten the traditional Labour heartlands in places such as Falkirk and Motherwell, where Alexander has long been a key political figure. However, Labour has dismissed such assertions as baseless and a product of ambitious political myth-making. Alexander, one of the most senior names in Scottish Labour, was first elected as the MP for Falkirk in 1997 and has since emerged as one of the party’s most respected voices on foreign affairs. Last month, he was reappointed to his post by Labour leader Keir Starmer, a sign of confidence in his abilities within the shadow cabinet. The rumour emerged amid ongoing discussions over the proposed Boundary Commission review, which is expected to take place in the coming years to better reflect shifting population patterns and voter distribution across the UK. Conservative sources in Westminster have been quoted as suggesting that Labour is now rethinking its internal strategy to protect key parliamentary seats, including that of Alexander, who is believed to have held Falkirk for over 25 years. Labour insiders, however, refuted the idea that Alexander’s position was under threat. One senior member of the party said: “It is absurd – even preposterous – to suggest that Douglas Alexander is in any way under the radar of removal. His experience, his depth of knowledge on global affairs, and his consistency within the party cannot be in question. This is just another attempt to stir up trouble.” The controversy comes at a tricky time for Labour, as the party weighs its general election prospects and seeks to consolidate its grip on key marginals, particularly in Scotland and the north of England. Alexander has consistently been the face of Labour’s stance on foreign policy, often speaking out against government decisions on Brexit, trade agreements and international diplomatic efforts. His close association with past Labour leaders—including Gordon Brown and Ed Miliband—has only added to his stature within the party. As the political landscape continues to shift under new leadership, Labour is stressing that strategic changes, if any, will be undertaken transparently and internally, not through speculation or misdirection. For now, Douglas Alexander remains unfazed, with his parliamentary team delivering a terse response to the claims: “These insinuations are without foundation and are being made by those seeking to pre-emptively undermine the Labour Party’s momentum.

Plaid Cymru has called for a renewed and more ambitious focus on the teaching of the Welsh language in schools and public life if Wales is to meet its target of one million Welsh speakers by 2050. The Welsh nationalist party is urging the Welsh government and local authorities to take urgent action to reverse the decline in Welsh-speaking communities and invigorate language learning from early childhood through to higher education. The call comes as concerns over the stagnation of Welsh language growth have resurfaced following recent statistics, which show a marginal increase in the number of Welsh speakers—currently standing at around 19 per cent of the population. The 2050 target is a key part of the Welsh government’s broader national mission to promote and protect the language, but Plaid Cymru warns that current efforts are not sufficient to achieve the dramatic increase in speakers required. “We risk falling short of the 2050 goal if we continue at the current pace,” said a Plaid Cymru spokesperson. “More investment is needed in early language education, and Welsh must be given equal status in both the curriculum and the public sector.” The party is advocating for increased teacher training and recruitment, particularly in areas where Welsh is not yet well established as a community language. It also wants statutory requirements for Welsh language education to be enforced more rigorously in all schools, not just those in the most Welsh-speaking regions. Plaid Cymru is further pushing for more Welsh-medium options in higher education and professional fields to ensure long-term economic and cultural sustainability for the language. The Welsh government has previously committed to improvements in language policy, including a new Welsh language standards framework and expanded support for Welsh-medium education. Welsh Secretary for Education, Jeremy Miles, acknowledged the importance of the issue but stressed that progress is being made. “Education is central to fulfilling the statutory duties of the Welsh language,” he said. “We are already seeing more young people learning Welsh at school and increasingly choosing it as a subject in their later years, but there is no hiding from the fact that more needs to be done if we are to meet the 1 million target.” Critics of the current system argue that waiting for a top-down approach from the government will not be enough. Websites and community-led language initiatives, such as “Cymraeg 2050” and “Welsh in 1000,” have been gaining traction on social media, encouraging parents and professionals to adopt the language at home and in the workplace.
